title: Zelenskyy and Netanyahu brave the whims of Trump’s darkly confounding White House | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian and Israeli leaders converge on Washington with criss-crossing fortunes, but knowing they can count on little from US counterpart
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Ukrainian and Israeli leaders converge on Washington with criss-crossing fortunes, but knowing they can count on little from US counterpart
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu (left) and Volodymyr Zelenskyy (right) with Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha (centre) at the funeral service for the late US senator and ally Lindsey Graham  at the Washington National Cathedral.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu (left) and Volodymyr Zelenskyy (right) with Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha (centre) at the funeral service for the late US senator and ally Lindsey Graham  at the Washington National Cathedral.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesUS foreign policyAnalysisZelenskyy and Netanyahu brave the whims of Trump’s darkly confounding White HouseJulian BorgerUkrainian and Israeli leaders converge on Washington with criss-crossing fortunes, but knowing they can count on little from US counterpartTue 28 Jul 2026 14.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 16.02 EDTShareThe converging visits of Benjamin Netanyahu andVolodymyr Zelenskyyto Washington offer an unusually eloquent snapshot of a world in turmoil, unmoored from decades-old certainties.Some things remain the same. The US is still an almighty military and economic power and for both foreign visitors, a White House encounter withDonald Trumpis critical to their governments and the wars they are fighting.Trump hosts back-to-back meetings with Zelenskyy and NetanyahuRead moreThe imperial presidency Trump has tried to forge is in decline, however, in large part as a result of his own erratic leadership. He may see his visitors as client-potentates flying in from the edges of empire to kiss his ring. But they will be as aware of Trump’s weaknesses as they are of their own.Netanyahu and Zelenskyy arrive in Washington on opposite trajectories. The Israeli prime minister’s star hasdeclined dramatically since he persuaded Trump to join him in an ill-conceived war on Iranfive months ago, on the groundless promise that the Tehran regime would quickly collapse.Since then, a viscerally disappointed president has publicly scolded Netanyahu and insisted Netanyahu would ultimately do his bidding, while the White House has liberally leakedTrump’s foul-mouthed tiradesbelittling him.Israel has been left out of negotiations with Iran, and its views were ignored when it came to selling F-35 stealth fighter planes to Turkey, or making a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia. AnEconomist/YouGov surveyfound that nearly half of Americans polled thought that Netanyahu should be arrested on arrival for war crimes.By contrast, Zelenskyy arrived in Washington in the ascendant.Ukrainehas defied the US administration’s predictions of inevitable defeat to Russia’s might, his country is now a world leader in drone warfare, and parts of the Magaverse are now warming to the accidental war leader they once scorned as a loser.In traditional administrations, both men and the countries they represent would be natural allies and both could be sure of solid welcome in the Oval Office. It is telling that the occasion of their coinciding visits was thefuneral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican hawk of the old school who could be relied on for wholehearted promotion of the Israeli and Ukrainian war efforts. In that respect, he was one of a dying breed.But this is no normal administration, led by a president who rules on a whim, and neither visitor can predict how he will be received. Neither wanted cameras in the room. Trump began his presidency by throwing all-in support behind Netanyahu and his wars, dropping even the pretence of concern for the lives of Palestinians or the people of southern Lebanon that had tempered backing forIsraelfrom earlier presidents.Facing a hostile electorate, the president is trying to extricate himself from the region, but in doing so is finding Israel the most recalcitrant party on every front.In Ukraine, Trump threw out the American foreign policy handbook altogether, proposing peace deals that often echoed Moscow’s talking points, rewarding aggression with territory Russia had not even won on the battlefield.Rather than capitulate, Ukraine showed it could fight on despite drastic cuts in US military aid, relying more on Europe and its own hard-won improvised expertise.Now Zelenskyy finds himselfthe unlikely darling of far-right Maga influencers such as Lara Loomer, formerly an apologist for the Russian invasion, who interviewed the Ukrainian president in his garden last week, and called for “moral clarity” in Kyiv’s support.Zelenskyy’s recent ascent may mirror Netanyahu’s simultaneous decline, but that does not mean they came to Washington with comparable status. When it comes to the Trump administration, they arrive from very different starting positions.Just about anything would count as an upgrade for Zelenskyy compared with hisinfamous White House ambushin February 2025 by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, who tried to humiliate the Ukrainian visitor in front of the cameras, demanding gratitude and acceptance of defeat with “no cards” left to play.Zelenskyy does have cards this time but well short of a winning hand without US support. The Ukrainian’s immediate aim is modest: for Trump to honour Senator Graham by backing a Russia sanctions bill he was pushing at the time of his death. He knows that direct US military aid to Ukraine is not likely to return in meaningful quantities any time soon.The Patriot interceptors and other weapons Ukraine once counted on for its defence have been used up wholesale in the Middle East, many of them to protect Israel. It will take years for the US to rebuild its own stocks. Netanyahu may be out of favour in the current White House, but the US is committed to Israel’s defence in a manner and on a scale of which Ukraine can only dream.Netanyahu and Zelenskyy came to Washington on different paths and footings but they do at least share an awareness that their relationship with the administration can be upended with scant notice, without any clear reasons, in a matter of mere seconds in the court of the irascible, flagging would-be emperor.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyVolodymyr ZelenskyyBenjamin NetanyahuUkraineIsraelDonald TrumpanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Captain Chris ‘Hunter-Killer’ Philp single-handedly takes on French navy | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Shots fired in the Channel are all in a day’s work for the intrepid shadow home secretary
Author: John Crace
Headline: Shots fired in the Channel are all in a day’s work for the intrepid shadow home secretary
Content: Chris Philp claimed the shots could have been an attempt to stop his coverage of the small boats crisis.Photograph: Chris Philp MP/XView image in fullscreenChris Philp claimed the shots could have been an attempt to stop his coverage of the small boats crisis.Photograph: Chris Philp MP/XThe politics sketchConservativesCaptain Chris ‘Hunter-Killer’ Philp single-handedly takes on French navyJohn CraceShots fired in the Channel are all in a day’s work for the intrepid shadow home secretaryTue 28 Jul 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 16.07 EDTShareC’est magnifique, mais ce n’est pas la guerre.Captain Chris “Hunter-Killer” Philp had been on patrol since first light in the Channel. While the rest of the country was still asleep, the Philpster was scanning the horizon for rubber dinghies full of illegal immigrants. Something he had never done in his previous life as immigration minister. Back then he had sought to rehouse new arrivals in hotels. Now he wanted to send them to a watery grave.It had been a quiet morning. Too quiet. Just the one sighting of a child with a rubber ring paddling off the beach in Boulogne. But Hunter-Killer was taking no chances. All it takes is one child and before long there will be hundreds of thousands making the crossing with swimming aids bought from the local Carrefour. So the Philpster had called in the RAF. Minutes later, a Typhoon FGR4 had blasted the kid out of the water. Job done.Pour encourager les autres.Half an hour later, all hell broke loose. A French warship had appeared starboard. The next thing Hunter-Killer heard was the sound of 17 indistinct pops in the distance. “Get down,” he shouted to his crew. “We’re under attack.” Weirdly, no one on board the Philpster’s MTB disguised as a fishing vessel seemed remotely worried. How come they were so slow to sense danger? There again, few had the finely tuned antennae of the Philpster. Those years of training with the Special Boat Service had paid off.Hunter-Killer threw himself on the floor of the wheelhouse, waiting for the gunshots to stop. “I think it’s safe now,” a deckhand said. “It was just some French sailor firing some shots from a handgun away from us into the sea. It wasn’t as if he was aiming at us or anything. He was probably just test-firing. It’s no big deal.”“You don’t understand,” squeaked Captain Philpster. “This was a definite attempt by the French to intimidate me. Typical of Johnny Foreigner to send out a warship to track the shadow home secretary. They don’t like it up ’em. They’ve probably got special guns that fire round corners. So you think they’re shooting in a harmless direction but the bullets turn 90 degrees in flight. I came within a whisker of being hit. Not that anyone gets to intimidate Hunter-Killer. Help! Help!”The crew looked rather nonplussed. Most of them hadn’t even heard the shots – “he was probably using a silencer”, said the Philpster – let alone had any idea they had come under serious attack. But Hunter-Killer was adamant. The Frenchies had been out to eliminate him. He had got too close to stopping the small boat crossings and Macron would never stand for that. So he was prepared to stop at nothing. Even risk starting a global conflict. Well, it had ended badly for Napoleon and it would end badly for Macron. Nor should the French forget that it had been the English who saved them in the second world war. Well, we wouldn’t make that mistake again.“Sacrébleu!” said one member of Border Force. “There are often exercises at sea involving the Royal or the French navy, and shots are occasionally fired, usually using blanks. This may be nothing at all.”The Philpster ordered him to keep quiet. The last thing he wanted was any collaborators speaking in French. Careless talk costsvies. He pulled the burner phone out of his pocket and speed-dialled Kemi. “I’m under attack,” he gasped. “Even though the French aren’t shooting at me, they are definitely shooting at me. They don’t want me to stop any small boats crossing the Channel, even though I haven’t yet seen any small boats. We need to be on our guard. The smuggling gangs must now be using invisible dinghies.”Kemi’s eyes lit up. If only she was prime minister, she would be able to launch a tactical first nuclear strike on Calais. OK, there might be some collateral damage in Kent but it would still be worth it. Instead, she had to order the Philpster to disengage with the enemy.“I can’t do that,” said Hunter-Killer. “While most politicians run from danger, I am trained to run towards it. So what I will do is film a clip of me being extraordinarily brave by doing nothing and then phone the French embassy to complain. If only they put as much effort into intimidating the people smugglers as they put into intimidating me. Not that I was intimidated. But it would be good to see the French navy also firing shots in the opposite direction to the dinghies.”Explore more on these topicsConservativesThe politics sketchChris PhilpImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He liked to get people’s blood boiling’: metal masters Mastodon on the loss of bandmate Brent Hinds – and his shocking words before his death | Mastodon | The Guardian
description: The Grammy-winning band had an acrimonious rift with Hinds – then he died in a motorbike crash. They explain how they’re paying tribute on their new album, and why their love for each other never ended
Author: Matt Mills
Headline: The Grammy-winning band had an acrimonious rift with Hinds – then he died in a motorbike crash. They explain how they’re paying tribute on their new album, and why their love for each other never ended
Content: Mastodon in 2026, with Troy Sanders centre, and Brann Dailor second left.Photograph: William LacalmontieView image in fullscreenMastodon in 2026, with Troy Sanders centre, and Brann Dailor second left.Photograph: William LacalmontieMastodonInterview‘He liked to get people’s blood boiling’: metal masters Mastodon on the loss of bandmate Brent Hinds – and his shocking words before his deathMatt MillsThe Grammy-winning band had an acrimonious rift with Hinds – then he died in a motorbike crash. They explain how they’re paying tribute on their new album, and why their love for each other never endedTue 28 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMastodon are near the end of a tour where they’re playing 22 shows in 14 different European countries during a record-breaking heatwave, when they video-call me outside a Bordeaux venue. Bassist and co-lead singer Troy Sanders says the experience has been “31 days of musical bliss”. He’s not being sarcastic, either.“Things are super energetic, even at day 31,” he insists. “We’re contemplating even staying in Europe for a few days when this tour is over, because we’re enjoying ourselves so much.” It’s pleasantly surprising to see Sanders and drummer/co-vocalist Brann Dailor, sat to his left, in such high spirits, given the anguish and unrest they’ve endured over the last 18 months.In February 2025, Dailor’s mother, Michele Lawrence, died aged 69. The next month, the band announced they’d parted ways with co-founding guitarist/singer Brent Hinds, ending a25-year-long partnership. Hinds railed against his ex-bandmates on social media, calling them a “shit band with horrible humans … incapable of singing in key”, among plenty of other insults. He then died in a motorcycle accident, at the age of 51.Mastodon are one of US metal’s most imaginative and successful acts, with a Grammy win and three Top 10 albums, and Hinds, a hard-partying maverick, had been a big part of what made them so distinctive and respected. Where contemporaries such as Trivium and Killswitch Engage were thoroughbred metal acts, Hinds gave Mastodon a defiant country twang, reflecting his Alabama upbringing and early years playing the banjo. Combined with Dailor’s virtuoso style, inspired by vintage prog, and co-guitarist Bill Kelliher’s primal riffs, “what we had sounded original and different,” Dailor says. “We always saw ourselves rooted in metal, but we could shape shift if we wanted.” When Black Sabbath played their farewell gig last year – two weeks before the death of Ozzy Osbourne – it was Mastodon who were selected to open the show, a band capable of igniting a stadium as well as inspiring reverence from the genre’s greats.The deaths of Hinds and Dailor’s mother are the thematic core of the Atlantans’ upcoming ninth studio album, Marrow Deep. Its title references the fact that Dailor’s relationships with them were “the deepest you can get with a person. It’s hard to think of closer people that we could lose.”The lyric-writing was the members’ way of processing those losses. Lead single Your Ghost Again dissects their complex relationship with Hinds, whereas Out Like a Lamb is for Lawrence, who died in her sleep after suffering cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and other ailments during her life. Dailor likens both Hinds and Lawrence to Keith Richards: figures who lived far longer than people assumed they would.Hinds was arguably the most chaotic character in 21st-century metal. A former heroin addict, he lived in vans, boat sheds and abandoned apartments before joining Mastodon. He continued to party and drink long after his bandmates grew beyond such things – including co-guitarist Bill Kelliher, who almost died of alcohol-induced pancreatitis in 2009. “If any of us did half the stuff that Brent pulled off, we’d all have been dead years ago,” Dailor says. “We’ve always been a hard-partying band, but for the last 10, 15 years, the three of us really settled down and were focusing more on our live show and being productive in the studio. He was still rocking, which was, for a lot of people from the outside looking in, the most admirable thing about him. But from the inside it’s not always that much fun.”View image in fullscreenBrent Hinds performing in Oslo in 2016.Photograph: Gonzales Photo/Zuma Press/ShutterstockIn 2011, the drummer told Kerrang!: “People think [Hinds is] a fucking mental case, but there’s a beautiful person in there.” What was beautiful about him? Sanders answers: “He could find beauty in a lot of things: trees, mountains, caverns, oceans, music, people, handmade crafts. An appreciation for lots of originality and creativity.”Dailor says Hinds loved “the honest things. He was the real deal, you know? His emotions were right there all the time and he could easily access them through his instrument.”Following their breakthrough with 2004 single Blood and Thunder, the press touted Mastodon and their intellectual approach for “saving” metal. From 2007 to 2008, they supported Metallica on their stadium-filling World Magnetic tour. Their next album, 2009’s disorientatingly psychedelicCrack the Skye, was widely lauded; Hinds masterminded much of it, after being knocked out in a 2007 brawl outside an awards show and put into a three-day coma.“He had vertigo for months and couldn’t really get up, so he was just sitting at home with an acoustic guitar,” Dailor recalls. “There were no bars for him to go to. He was forced to stay at home, so I think that, as a result, you have Crack the Skye.”It started a string of successful records where the band wrestled with personal crises.The Hunter, a Top 10 hit in 2011, controversially stripped back Mastodon’s more brutal and progressive edges, was named after Hinds’s brother Brad, who died on a hunting trip in 2010. Dailor’s contributions to 2014’s Once More ’Round the Sun were inspired by his mother, who’d fallen off a chair in her kitchen and briefly been declared dead, and 2017’s Emperor of Sand was about cancer: Dailor’s mother and Sanders’ wife had been diagnosed with the disease, and Kelliher had recently lost his mother to a brain tumour. The album’s opener,Sultan’s Curse, won the 2018 Grammy for best metal performance.“It summarised the story of us four dudes,” Sanders reflects. “Starting because we all appreciated Iron Maiden, Thin Lizzy and Neurosis, and then, 18 years later, we’re on this stage winning this award that was the furthest thing from our minds ever.”View image in fullscreenMastodon’s Brent Hinds, Bill Kelliher, Brann Dailor and Troy Sanders in 2009.Photograph: Mick Hutson/RedfernsDespite the increased success, Hinds’s involvement dwindled. According to Dailor, the guitarist grieved for his brother through “alcohol, drug abuse and self-medication”. From The Hunter onwards, the drummer tried to make the rehearsal room “fun” to tempt Hinds to contribute, inadvertently leading to their change in sound: “Come down and we’ll have some fun! We’ll write Curl of the Burl and Stargasm and it’ll be fun! It doesn’t have to be heavy!”In 2015, Hinds madeheadlines when he told Guitar Player, “I fucking hate heavy metal, and I don’t want to be in a heavy metal band.”“Brent said a lot of things that he probably didn’t mean,” Dailor counters when I bring up the quote. “He liked to talk some shit and stir the pot and get people’s blood boiling, I guess. I feel like he felt he could control a situation if he threw a wrench.”The way that the band and Hinds parted ways remains a mystery. In their statement, Mastodon said it was a mutual decision; Hinds later claimed he was kicked out for “embarrassing them for being who I am”. Dailor and Sanders refuse to tell me what happened, but Dailor shoots down the rumour that Hinds punched him in the face, which stems from a public appearance he made just before the announcement where he had a black eye. “Brent texted me when that was all stirred up, and he was like, ‘Dude, I can’t believe people think I punched you in the face!’” he smiles.So you were still in contact after everything happened?“He reached out late at night sometimes, like, ‘Hey, I still love you, buddy.’ I was like, ‘Yeah, my mom just died, I don’t know. I love you too, but I need time in my life. I can’t even deal with Mastodon stuff right now.’ It was hard for me to get out of bed, to be honest with you.”At the same time, Hinds was bitter towards his former bandmates on Instagram, where he left the “shit band with horrible humans” comment. Sanders reacts sternly when I mention it: “He was trying to be funny. It was pretty cute.”Hinds later made more comments, in excruciating detail: “I’ve never seen anyone in my life look in the mirror more than Troy Sanders. He thinks he’s God’s gift to anything. I’ve never met three people that were so full of themselves. It’s disgusting.” But Dailor says that the drama became nothing but a “blip” after the guitarist’s death. The remaining members received the news over the phone from Hinds’s ex-wife while they were at Atlanta airport. “I was devastated,” Dailor remembers. “All the shit-talking that had happened – you reference the Instagram comment section shit – I didn’t think about any of that. We got 25 years of a deep relationship with this guy. I could tell who he was by the smell of his farts.”Marrow Deep is dedicated to Lawrence and Hinds, but it’s a celebration of the present and future, as well. It marks the debut of new guitarist Nick Johnston and the first album where former session keyboardist João Nogueira is a full-time member, and it contains their most technical and metallic music since the 2000s. There are also a host of guest spots from peers and influences, including Gojira’s Joe Duplantier, Lamb of God’s Randy Blythe, Queens of the Stone Age’s Josh Homme and Black Sabbath bassist Geezer Butler.“We listened to Geezer’s book and he name-checked us at the end, as far as being a band that he was into,” Dailor says. “Sabbath have been very kind to us over the years. The first time I ever met Tony Iommi, he came into the dressing room and he was like, ‘Oh, Mastodon! Me and Geez were listening to you guys on the bus last night.’”‘I nearly quit to become a fencing teacher’: Iron Maiden on 50 years of heavy metal, hard living – and hopeless communication skillsRead moreAt the start of second track Poisonous Weapons, there’s a sample from 1986 cult thriller film River’s Edge, where Dennis Hopper’s character Feck yells, “And I felt so fucking alive!” That’s because – for Dailor, who’s sporting a River’s Edge T-shirt – “the band Mastodon feels fucking alive”.“When one of the integral members, one of your brothers, dies, it’s obviously a very painful thing to go through, but it also makes you question where you’re at,” he explains. “Seeing Brent in his casket was so difficult to wrap our heads around, and it makes you want to feel fucking alive. We’re still here, so we better get to it.”Marrow Deep is released 28 August on Loma VistaExplore more on these topicsMastodonMetalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Topless modelling never aligned with me’: inside Everyone’s Seen My Tits, the play by a former page 3 model | Stage | The Guardian
description: As she brings her memoir to the Edinburgh festival, Keeley Hazell talks about trauma, exploitation, the hollowness of the high life – and her new career as a writer on Ted Lasso
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: As she brings her memoir to the Edinburgh festival, Keeley Hazell talks about trauma, exploitation, the hollowness of the high life – and her new career as a writer on Ted Lasso
Content: ‘I was just numb’ … Keeley Hazell.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I was just numb’ … Keeley Hazell.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianStageInterview‘Topless modelling never aligned with me’: inside Everyone’s Seen My Tits, the play by a former page 3 modelAnya RyanAs she brings her memoir to the Edinburgh festival, Keeley Hazell talks about trauma, exploitation, the hollowness of the high life – and her new career as a writer on Ted LassoTue 28 Jul 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a time in the mid-2000s when it felt as though “everyone” had seen her topless, says Keeley Hazell.Page 3 was a staple of the tabloid press, lads’ mags were booming and she was one of the country’s most recognisable glamour models. “There was excitement, but also a lot of shame and embarrassment,” the softly spoken Hazell reflects. “Topless modelling never really aligned with me as a person.”Hazell, who was born in Lewisham, London, left modelling in her early 20s and moved to LA to become an actor. But the emotional impact of her time in the industry has stayed with her, partly inspiring her 2025 bookEveryone’s Seen My Tits: Stories and Reflections from an Unlikely Feminist. She describes the writing process as a “release” when we meet in London, where she has been preparing for an Edinburgh fringe theatre/comedy show based on the book. “I was able to give myself a voice,” she says, for “a period where I felt voiceless”.double quotation markI’d drink a lot and tell myself to enjoy the partyThe show makes her think “of the image of Russian dolls – I’m performing as me, but then I’m also performing as a version of me”. This sense of having multiple identities is nothing new for her. She remembers “presenting differently” to the Keeley Hazell people saw on magazine covers, “in vintage clothes and very grungey”. So much so that she was rarely recognised in the street, even at the height of her fame. When asked if she was a Page 3 model, she would deny it. “I’d be like, ‘Are you saying I look like a Page 3 model?’ And it was a really interesting experiment because they’d often be like, ‘No, no, you’re way more classy than that.’ It was weird because they were talking about me but I also felt separate from it.”Hazell’s introduction to glamour modelling was fast and unexpected. At 16, she left school and started working in a hair salon, where a colleague encouraged her to apply to become a model. She had some photos taken and sent them off to “a bunch of addresses” given to her – one of which, unbeknown to Hazell, was the Daily Star’s “beach babe” competition. She won, and a few months later entered the Sun’s “Page 3 idol” competition. “I won that too, and that was the start of my career.”Modelling was very different to her life at home on a council estate. “I went from growing up there to owning a luxury apartment overlooking the Thames.” Hazell was a “canvas”, and she knew she could be made up to fit a photographer’s image. “I was so young, there was so much exploitation, I was not emotionally or mentally prepared for it.” Safeguarding, she says, was basically nonexistent. “There was so little protection for women entering that industry. I had no idea about the things I needed in place, and my family didn’t either.”View image in fullscreen‘Page 3 was a wild thing to grow up with’ … Hazell.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianLooking back, Hazell almost can’t believe Page 3 was real. “It was just a wild thing to grow up with … those images were so readily available in newspapers and in newsagents.” There are times when she thinks of those days fondly; she was earning more money than she thought possible and got to travel the world. But she regrets “not having more control” over things. “A lot of the time I was just numb. I’d drink a lot and tell myself to enjoy the party.”Today, she gives carefully considered answers, with the air of someone who has had the time and space to process it all. Therapy has helped enormously, she tells me, particularly when it came to dealing with the fallout from a sex tape sold to the Sunday Sport. It was “terrifying” to write about the experience and “in a way relive it” Hazell says. “So many women experience some aspect of sexual violation and abuse in any realm, the shame for me needed to be ridded.”The Edinburgh fringe show is the latest chapter in that process. It begins in 2019 with her auditioning to play Keeley Jones, a character inspired by her, in Ted Lasso. She didn’t get the part but she did land a recurring role in the series and serves as a staff writer. Hazell can’t tell me much more about her solo show’s structure – she’s still in the writing process. “Right now I’m just staring at a laptop, ordering food and thinking, this is difficult,” she says with a laugh. She is certain, though, that it will be funny. “Trauma and humour are intertwined … even within the spiralling and the PTSD of it all, it should be a humorous retelling.” And it feels freeing to have, at last, complete autonomy over the Keeley Hazell people see and hear from. “It is incredibly powerful to have a voice.”Keeley Hazell: Everyone’s Seen My Tits is atPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, 5 to 29 AugustExplore more on these topicsStageComedy (Stage)TheatreEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalMagazinesNewspapersinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day review – Zendaya saves Tom Holland’s semi-Cronenberg-style superhero | Movies | The Guardian
description: Now 30, Holland is back as the vexed webslinger in a sometimes shocking, occasionally sluggish new instalment opposite his Odyssey castmate
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Now 30, Holland is back as the vexed webslinger in a sometimes shocking, occasionally sluggish new instalment opposite his Odyssey castmate
Content: ‘Unprecedented new physical and mental health issues’ … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: CTMG/PAView image in fullscreen‘Unprecedented new physical and mental health issues’ … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: CTMG/PAMoviesReviewSpider-Man: Brand New Day review – Zendaya saves Tom Holland’s semi-Cronenberg-style superheroNow 30, Holland is back as the vexed webslinger in a sometimes shocking, occasionally sluggish new instalment opposite his Odyssey castmatePeter BradshawTue 28 Jul 2026 09.11 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust a few weeks ago,Tom Hollandwas telling us that his role as Telemachus in Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey was his “last chance to play a boy”. Well, Holland is back as the supposedly scrappy, gawky, arachnid young superhero Spider-Man. Not Spider-Boy admittedly, and these days Holland is actually a chunkier and more stacked Spidey than previously, flexing some pretty serious biceps. He is maturing in the role. But is the role maturing with him?View image in fullscreenPeter Parker (Tom Holland) peers through the web.Photograph: CTMG/PAThe point is that this film is a reset. At the end of the last movieSpider-Man: No Way Home, courtesy of Dr Strange’s colossal psychic powers – which might have come in handy in this episode incidentally, part of the narrative-universe inconsistency that you just have to overlook – Peter Parker was able to erase everyone’s knowledge that he is, in fact, Spider-Man, and that includes his goofy best friend Ned Leeds (Jacob Batalon) and more to the point, the love of his life MJ (Zendaya).So now Peter is simply back where he started, adored by New Yorkers for crime-fighting as Spider-Man, living in a scuzzy single room with all his screens and tech gear, his secret identity a secret once more, but pining for the people he loves. And he’s not getting any younger. How much of a “brand new day” is this?View image in fullscreenGiving proceedings a boost … Zendaya in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyNow Spidey has to tackle a sinister new entity that appears to be possessing the bodies of important people around town – starting with the villainous Scorpion (Michael Mando) – with a view to attacking and infiltrating a key government unit, the department of Damage Control, run by Bill Metzger, played by the excellent Tramell Tillman (from TV’s Severance). It is a disquieting new development that coincides with unprecedented new physical and mental health issues for Parker. He has headaches, and these appear to be taking our hero to what I can only describe as the David Cronenberg zone.To tackle these inner and outer crises, Parker/Spidey has to consult Black Widow (an amusing cameo from Florence Pugh) who talks to him while reclining in a plunge pool in which shy Spidey joins her while wearing his mask and also underpants. He also has to seek advice from ageing academic Dr Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo) AKA the Hulk, a revived acquaintance which ends in chaos. And Spider-Man finds himself in a fractious frenmity-bromance with the highly strung tough guy Frank “Punisher” Castle, whose life he once saved, played by Holland’s Odyssey castmate Jon Bernthal.But most importantly of all, Parker is obsessed with finding ways to cross paths with MJ, effectively stalking her and masochistically witnessing her making out with her new boyfriend. And he has some very big, even slightly shocking scenes withZendaya– the other Odyssey cast-member, in fact. These are encounters which hold out the painful hope that he can somehow rekindle the flame, somehow find happiness while pursuing his lonely vocation.Zendaya saves this film. She rescues it from silliness and the generic deja vu overfamiliarity that is always threatening to sink it. Something in MJ’s civilian status, her non-superhero identity, brings Zendaya’s grownup acting presence to the fore in ways denied to everyone else on screen, including Holland. Her naturally relaxed style and self-possession give the proceedings a boost, especially with the flash of transgressive sexuality that she shows us at one moment. Director Destin Daniel Cretton gets the best out of her.View image in fullscreenHolding a flame … Zendaya and Holland in the film.Photograph: CTMG/PAOtherwise, things are the same in Spideyworld in ways that we will recognise with affectionate exasperation. As ever, Spider-Man can swing through the air across Manhattan without the overhead horizontal plane that his web would surely need to attach to, even in non-built-up areas (although he might be using power lines). And Spider-Man: Brand New Day, like all MCU movies, always gravitates towards apocalyptic but weirdly temporary destruction in the digitally confected big city. It’s an entertaining spectacle, but really without the novelty of movie-iterations like the more experimental Spider-Verse animations. A more radical reboot is needed.Spider-Man: Brand New Day is out on 29 July in the UK, 31 July in the US, and 30 July in Australia.Explore more on these topicsFilmSuperhero moviesTom HollandZendayareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to seek cross-party consensus over urgent reforms to social care | Social care | The Guardian
description: Prime minister invites Badenoch and Davey – but not Farage – to discuss how to fix one of most intractable issues he faces
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Prime minister invites Badenoch and Davey – but not Farage – to discuss how to fix one of most intractable issues he faces
Content: Andy Burnham is expected to speed up publication of Louise Casey’s review of social care.Photograph: Jeff Overs/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham is expected to speed up publication of Louise Casey’s review of social care.Photograph: Jeff Overs/ReutersSocial careBurnham to seek cross-party consensus over urgent reforms to social carePrime minister invites Badenoch and Davey – but not Farage – to discuss how to fix decades-old funding crisisPippa CrerarandAletha AduTue 28 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has promised “problem-solving, not point-scoring” before a speech on social care in which he will set out his strategy for resolving one of the most intractable problems in British politics.The prime minister has invited Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, and Ed Davey, the Liberal Democrat leader, to discuss how to enact urgent reform on social care, as he attempts to find common ground across party lines. Davey confirmed he would attend via video call while the Conservatives said they would send the shadow health secretary, Stuart Andrew, in Badenoch’s place as she was having pre-planned minor surgery.However, the suggestion that the main Westminster parties could finally reach consensus to fix the crisis that has eluded a generation of political leaders in England already appeared optimistic after the Tories imposed their own red lines and amid negative headlines about inheritance tax.SeveralLabourMPs also expressed concern over how to manage the financial burden of a reformed care sector.Andy Burnham seeks cross-party agreement on future of social careRead moreBefore his speech on Wednesday, Burnham said: “We need a different kind of politics: problem-solving, not point-scoring. Nowhere is that more urgent than social care. For decades, governments have kicked this issue down the road because they’ve seen it as too risky, too difficult and too complicated.“Politicians might have different views but I’m serious about fixing this issue, and to do that we have to find common ground and listen to others to find a way forward. It’s time to draw a line under people playing politics when the human cost of that means carers struggling, families paying the price and our NHS buckling under the strain.”The prime minister is expected to stop short of presenting proposals for a new social care system in this speech, instead confirming plans,previously revealed by the Guardian, to speed up the independent review led by Louise Casey that has been considering possible options.Lady Casey, who will launch the Big Conversation on Care on Wednesday to give the public their chance to share their views on the future of adult social care in England via an online platform, has warned that money alone won’t fix the problem.However, Burnham’s push for a solution is set against a tightening economic backdrop. The economic thinktank NIESR has warned of “very difficult trade-offs” in the autumn budget if the Iran war keeps oil prices and inflation high.He is understood to be committed to exploring a new system that would be free at the point of use, the same principle as the NHS. He is understood to regard other options, such as a care costs cap, as less attractive, though they would be significantly cheaper for the taxpayer.A middle-ground option would be a model similar to Scotland’s, where personal care costs are paid by the state but other costs, such as accommodation and food in care homes, are borne by individuals and their families.My generation shouldn’t be scared of a care tax – we’re paying one already | Gaby HinsliffRead moreWhicheveroption the government pursuesis likely to involve significant extra investment over the long term, most likely through increases in taxation.When Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care as health secretary under Gordon Brown, he suggested replacing inheritance tax with a 10% levy on all estates. At the weekend he did not to rule out this option, which could raise as much as £18bn.Before visiting a care home on Wednesday, Burnham said:“This comes down to a choice. We can carry on passing the problem to the next generation, or we can face it head on and work together to build a care system that gives people dignity, security and the support they deserve.“This is about bringing back hope that we can finally fix the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long, and making Britain believe again. That’s why I’m making this choice and I’m prepared to put everything I’ve got behind it.”An average of 13,600 people a day were stuck in hospital beds last month despite being medically fit to leave, including some delayed because of the availability of adult social care, underlining the pressure on the NHS.While Labour MPs have broadly welcomed the prospect of reform, several cautioned that there would have to be serious consideration of how to protect people from losing their homes to care costs or penalising those who had already saved for retirement and care with new taxes.One minister said the prime minister “must exercise a lot of care” in managing the sensitive trade-offs between the quality of care versus the cost and who pays for it.“There are no easy answers, and I don’t think we can just dive straight into saying ‘This is the solution and this is what’s going to happen,’ because we have a prime minister and in many ways a government … with no specific mandate on a specific measure.”A centrist Labour MP said: “It’s vital that the UK at least tries to do something because we will never be able to contain the rising costs of the NHS. Our ability to genuinely improve the quality of health care will be stymied if we don’t have a quality social care service that relieves pressure.”The Guardian view on social care reform: Andy Burnham is right – this issue must be gripped | EditorialRead moreOthers on the party’s left urged the government to consider adopting a full NHS-style system that would rely on some taxation, but would also highlight that Burnham’s premiership is ready to not just “talk the talk but also walk the walk”.“If we’re talking big and bold we shouldn’t shy away from this option. It took from 1945 to 1948 to get the NHS up and running. We’ve still got years to start the process but we have to really try to shake this broken system,” one said.“Andy doesn’t have the goodwill from the electorate that Keir did in 2024 because we messed it up over the last two years so people feel betrayed and ignored,” another added. “This is a moment where we now have to prove ourselves.”A Tory source said: “If Burnham was serious about working cross-party he would have given us more than 18 hours’ notice for a 30-minute meeting during recess and the invitation wouldn’t have been immediately press released. It’s almost like it’s only being done for show.”Davey posted on X: “I’m with my family in France and as people know I have a disabled son who needs 24/7 care so I can’t be back in Westminster tomorrow but I look forward to meeting Andy Burnham over Zoom. I’m hopeful this call may prove to be the first step towards fixing our broken care service.Nigel Farage, who has not been invited to attend as he is not currently a sitting MP and Reform has just seven seats, accused Burnham of “conspiring behind closed doors with the failed political establishment”.Tell us: what has your experience of adult social care in England been like?Read moreThe Reform leader and candidate for Clacton added: “If Andy Burnham is serious about putting politics aside to solve Britain’s biggest problems, it’s remarkable that he’s chosen to ignore the party that led over 300 national opinion polls and represents thousands of councillors and millions of Britons across the country.”Explore more on these topicsSocial careAndy BurnhamLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: UK faces ‘very difficult trade-offs’ in budget because of Iran war, say analysts | Business | The Guardian
description: Leading thinktank says higher oil prices and inflation will give Andy Burnham a ‘challenging inheritance’
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Leading thinktank says higher oil prices and inflation will give Andy Burnham a ‘challenging inheritance’
Content: Ships anchored in the strait of Hormuz off Iran on Monday. The on-off closure of the waterway has pushed up oil prices, putting pressure on inflation.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/APView image in fullscreenShips anchored in the strait of Hormuz off Iran on Monday. The on-off closure of the waterway has pushed up oil prices, putting pressure on inflation.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/APBusinessUK faces ‘very difficult trade-offs’ in budget because of Iran war, say analystsLeading thinktank says higher oil prices and inflation will give Andy Burnham a ‘challenging inheritance’Phillip InmanTue 28 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has been warned by a leading thinktank of “very difficult trade-offs in the next autumn budget” if the Iran war keeps oil prices and inflation high.The National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) said the new prime minister faced a “challenging inheritance” and his plans to revamp public services would meet severe pressure from persistently higher prices.With oil prices having briefly gone back above $100 a barrel, and the strait of Hormuz all but closed since March, the thinktank said it expected inflation to rise to 3.8% over the next seven months, forcing the chancellor,John Healey, to find an extra £24bn by the end of the decade to maintain services and real-terms welfare payments.How the Bab al-Mandab blockade threat helped push oil back above $100Read moreThe thinktank said it had cut its forecast for the chancellor’s spending headroom in the budget from just over £7bn to nearer £3bn. TheOffice for Budget Responsibility, the government’s independent forecaster, estimated in March that the Treasury had about £22bn of spare capacity above existing spending commitments.Underscoring the cost of the Middle East conflict to the UK, the NIESR said the economy would grow at a slower pace this year and in 2027 as a result of higher energy prices and the spillover effects from uncertainty created by the on-off war.It said a downgrade of growth to 1.1% this year and the same slow pace next year meant the UK would suffer £28bn in lost growth over two years compared with forecasts in January.David Aikman, the institute’s director, said Burnham faced “a challenging inheritance” with spending “eroded by inflation”, coupled with the highest borrowing costs in the G7, new spending demands and cost-of-living pressures.He said there would be a temptation to ease the strain on the public finances and pay for new initiatives by raising the level of borrowing.Aikman said this would be a mistake and only cause further strife in later years, especially when another health or economic shock happened.He added: “New commitments on defence or household support should be funded through taxation or savings elsewhere, not through further borrowing. Rebuilding the capacity to absorb future shocks will require a determined attempt to bring debt down.”Burnham has made several announcements since becoming PM last week, including a pledge toimprove adult social care, with an estimated £18.5bn bill for providing an NHS-style system free at the point of use by 2035.He has also singled out for support the 1 million young people classified as not in education, employment or training (Neets), with more extensive mental health services and a revamp of the education system.The NIESR said the government’s total debt, which has reached almost £3tn, or 95% of annual national income, was likely to rise again if the chancellor used borrowing to boost public spending.The institute has proved to be one of the gloomier forecasters, predicting significant economic shocks that proved more muted.Rising oil prices could force up UK interest rates, say economistsRead moreStephen Millard, the head of the thinktank’s macroeconomic forecasting, said the UK economy had proved to be “surprisingly resilient” in the first half of this year “but a slowdown is still to come”.He added: “Even if peace is restored relatively quickly in the Middle East, inflation will still rise and the new chancellor will need to make some difficult decisions with respect to how to fund the latest policy announcements, from cuts to VAT on electricity and business rates for pubs, to the £2 bus fare cap.”Millard said tax changes should be given priority over increases in existing taxes.He said he supported the introduction of a land value tax to replace council tax and stamp duty on home sales. He said the government should also phase out the many exemptions and discounts that affect VAT, including those on energy and children’s clothes.There was further scope to tackle tax avoidance by wealthy individuals and companies, he added.Millard said the latest quarterly economic outlook showed the chancellor would need to cope with a 4% real spending squeeze by the end of the decade – equating to about £24bn in 2023 prices.He said higher and more persistent inflation would create “very difficult trade-offs in the next autumn budget”.The NIESR expects inflation to average 3.1% in 2026, peaking at 3.8% in February 2027 after energy price cap adjustments.It said it would take until early 2029 to fall back to the Bank of England’s 2% target, rather than 2028 as previously forecast.Bank of England officials meet on Thursday. Financial markets expect them to hold interest rates steady before raising them to 4% later in the year.Explore more on these topicsBusinessInflationOilEconomicsIranUS-Israel war on IranAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Adolescence or The Traitors? Netflix neck-and-neck with BBC as British viewers’ go-to | Netflix | The Guardian
description: Amid slowing streaming market, Netflix still produces hits that help make it default service for quarter of Britons
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Amid slowing streaming market, Netflix still produces hits that help make it default service for quarter of Britons
Content: The crime drama Adolescence, starring Owen Cooper, attracted a British audience of 16 million.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenThe crime drama Adolescence, starring Owen Cooper, attracted a British audience of 16 million.Photograph: APNetflixAdolescence or The Traitors? Netflix neck-and-neck with BBC as British viewers’ go-toAmid slowing streaming market, Netflix still produces hits that help make it default service for quarter of BritonsDan MilmoGlobal technology editorTue 28 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflix is neck-and-neck with the BBC as the default service Britons turn to when they switch on their TV, according to research.The home of Adolescence and KPop Demon Hunters is now the first port of call for 26% of viewers, Ofcom found. The national broadcaster is narrowly behind, as the go-to for 25% of audiences..Although growth in streaming platforms has slowed in the UK, Netflix in particular is still producing breakthrough hits with audiences.Ofcom’s annual Media Nations report showed the hit film Kpop Demon Hunters and the crime dramaAdolescencewere the most watched in the UK in 2025, with the former reaching an audience of more than 24 million; the latter 16 million. TheNetflixapp comes with many smart TVs or streaming devices but users still need to pay for a subscription to watch it.Graph shows popularity of the TV platforms Netflix, BBC, ITV and YouTube.However, Ofcom said viewing figures for the start of 2026 showed the BBC mounting a fightback, with the latest series ofThe Traitorsand Tom Hiddleston’s return to The Night Manager topping the ratings. That trend has continued into the summer thanks to theBBCand ITV’s coverage of the World Cup.Kate Davies, the group director for strategy and research at Ofcom, said traditional broadcasters were showing “resilience” through their live and event TV programming.Describing the competitive landscape between the likes of theBBC, Sky, Netflix and Google-owned YouTube as “fierce”, she added: “To thrive and survive in the current media landscape, it’s more important than ever for companies to continue to understand changing audience habits and adapt their strategies to meet people where they are.”View image in fullscreenClaudia Winkleman, hosting the BBC’s The Traitors.Photograph: BBC/PACiting another set of data from the audience measurement body Barb, Ofcom said the BBC remained ahead of other platforms in terms of share of total video viewing, accounting for 18% of the total in 2025, followed by YouTube on 15%, ITV on 11% and Netflix on 9%.BBC defeats ITV again in World Cup final viewing figuresRead moreYouTube is also becoming more of a fixture of TV viewing, with the amount it is viewed on people’s TV sets doubling over the past four years. There were also signs of a drop off among young audiences, with steep declines in live TV viewing among 16- to 24-year-olds and 4- to 15-year-olds of 17% each, although Ofcom said this was partly due to the absence of major sporting events in 2025, compared with the boost from the Paris Olympics and Euro 2024 the previous year.But alternative video viewing services were not necessarily the beneficiaries of the decline of young viewership numbers for broadcasters. Ofcom said young adults continue to watch TV and film less and less, watching 11 fewer minutes of broadcast, streaming and on-demand services at home last year, due to the allure of alternatives such as social media and gaming.Despite Netflix, Amazon, Disney+ and Apple shooting big series in the UK in recent years, from Sex Education to Masters of the Air to Rivals, public services broadcasters led by the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 delivered more than 30,000 hours of UK-originated content last year, not including repeats.Explore more on these topicsNetflixBBCTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple becomes second $5tn company as investors flee AI stocks | Apple | The Guardian
description: Share price rally driven by strong product demand as well as decision to sit out AI spending race, amid wider tech sell-off
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Share price rally driven by strong product demand as well as decision to sit out AI spending race, amid wider tech sell-off
Content: Apple’s shares hit a session high ⁠of $342.89 on Tuesday.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APView image in fullscreenApple’s shares hit a session high ⁠of $342.89 on Tuesday.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APAppleApple becomes second $5tn company as investors flee AI stocksShare price rally driven by strong product demand as well as decision to sit out AI spending race, amid wider tech sell-offGraeme Weardenand agencyTue 28 Jul 2026 16.33 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple has become only the second company to pass the $5tn valuation mark, as it benefited from investors fleeing AI and semiconductor stocks amid a wider tech sell-off.The iPhone maker’s shares hit a session high ⁠of $342.89 on Tuesday, giving it a market ⁠capitalisation of $5.04tn (£3.78tn), then eased back down to $340.08 – around the $5tn mark.Applebecame the world’s most valuable companyearlier this month, overtaking the chip giant Nvidia, which had been ⁠at the top since June 2025 and becamethe first company to breach the $5tn thresholdlast October.The US consumer electronics company’s rally has been driven ⁠as much by strong demand for its products as its decision to sit out the ​AI spending race that is sapping cash ‌flows at big tech ‌rivals.Its fresh high valuation came amid an intensifyingsell-off of AI stocks around the worlddriven by rising concerns about AI companies’ borrowing to fund datacentre expansion.US chip stocks extended their recent losses when Wall Street opened on Tuesday, with Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital and Seagate Technology all down by more than 4%.The Nasdaq 100 index of leading tech stocks fell by as much as 1.8% at one point, meaning since its early June record high it had fallen more than 10% – the technical definition of a market correction.Meanwhile South Korea’s stock market slid to its lowest level since mid-April, with semiconductor companies SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics falling by more than 10%.Analysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending, and competition from cheaper Chinese companies, aftera report by the Informationthat China had begun mass production of homegrown deep ultraviolet (DUV) chip-making tools.View image in fullscreenApple’s decision to hold iPhone prices steady, despite increases last month for MacBooks and iPads, has bolstered demand.Photograph: Lucas Jackson/ReutersInvestors may also be growing jittery aboutthe “circular funding” at the heart of the AI industry, through which artificial intelligence companies finance one another.They have also been spooked by the announcement from Google last week that it was further increasing capital spending this year to as much as $205bn to fund its AI plans, while reporting negative free cashflow for ​the first time in its history, burning through $5.9bn in the three months to the end of June.Apple has been shielded somewhat by being something of an AI laggard. Its difficulties in developing in-house models meant it has instead relied on Google’s ‌technology to power new services such as a revamped Siri. That has spared it the hefty infrastructure costs that have left big tech investors wary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionApple’s decision to hold iPhone prices steady last month when it announcedincreases for MacBooks and iPadshas also bolstered demand as buyers scooped up the company’s flagship device before expected ‌price hikes later this year, analysts have said.To aid demand, Apple on Tuesday also launched a device leasing programme in the US through the payments ​firm Klarna, under which monthly payments start at $17.99 for an iPhone, $11.99 for an Apple Watch or iPad, and $24.99 for a Mac.“Apple has resisted the AI spending race, betting that customer experience – not infrastructure investment – will ultimately determine the winners,” said Dipanjan Chatterjee, a vice-president and principal analyst at Forrester. “The ⁠new leasing programme is a clever response: it doesn’t reduce the price ​of an iPhone, but ​it changes how consumers perceive the cost ​by replacing sticker shock with a predictable monthly payment.”Including session gains, Apple ​stock has jumped ‌24% so far this year, ​widely outperforming the ​other six of the “Magnificent Seven” cohort of US technology stocks.Apple is to report its third-quarter earnings after the market close on Thursday, with analysts expecting a more than 15% jump in revenue for the period compared with a year earlier.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsAppleStock marketsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A control freak’: murderer James Desborough convicted of two further killings | UK news | The Guardian
description: Man already serving life for killing his cellmate while awaiting trial also murdered and dismembered his friends Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Man already serving life for killing his cellmate while awaiting trial also murdered and dismembered his friends Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman
Content: James Desborough. Police found notes suggesting he may kill again and planned to change his appearance before fleeing the UK.Photograph: FacebookView image in fullscreenJames Desborough. Police found notes suggesting he may kill again and planned to change his appearance before fleeing the UK.Photograph: FacebookUK news‘A control freak’: murderer James Desborough convicted of two further killingsMan already serving life for killing his cellmate while awaiting trial also murdered and dismembered his friends Claudio Aquilino and Daniel ColemanSteven MorrisTue 28 Jul 2026 12.58 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a spring day last year, James Desborough marched up to Cornwall’s county hall in Truro and began bombarding the offices with dozens of eggs stolen from a supermarket.It was a drug- and drink-addled protest at his plight – homeless, jobless and generally angry at the world. He expected to be arrested and messaged a friend: “If I’m going to get nicked, might as well round the charges up.”He certainly did that. In the weeks and months after the egg incident, Desborough committed three murders.He killed two vulnerable friends, Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, whose dismembered and burnt bodies were found in woodland close to a shack where he sometimes lived off-grid in south Cornwall.View image in fullscreenClaudio Aquilino, who was vulnerable and subjected to ‘cuckooing’ in the months before his death.Photograph: Devon and Cornwall police/PAThen while awaiting trial, he murdered Steven Kempster, his cellmate in Exeter prison, strangling him to death because he was annoyed with his snoring.Desborough, 40, is already serving a life sentence for the prison killing. After a jury at Winchester crown court convicted him of murdering his two friends, he may never be released. Mr Justice Saini will sentence Desborough on Wednesday, and made it clear he could face a whole-life term.The judge described the circumstances – a person being sentenced for two murders while already jailed for life for killing someone in prison – as “unique”.Acquaintances have said Desborough was a “control freak” with a terrible temper – he has an old conviction for grievous bodily harm – and was furious at what he saw as his bad luck in life. A civil engineer by profession and a father, he had fallen on hard times.Quite what tipped him over into an explosion of violence is unclear. He used Aquilino’s and Coleman’s bank cards after he killed them, but police do not believe it was a simple matter of theft.View image in fullscreenDaniel Coleman, who struggled with alcohol abuse and PTSD before Desborough murdered him.Photograph: Devon and Cornwall police/PAThe prosecutor in his trial, Ahmed Hossain KC, put it to Desborough that he might have killed them because he considered them worthless, deserving to die because of their troubled lifestyle and because they were “dinlos” – a local slang term for fools. Had he simply got annoyed with them and snapped? “I thought they were OK,” he replied in court. “They were good friends.”The trial has certainly put the focus on a different Cornwall to the one most holidaymakers to the county love. It highlighted not surfing beaches and historic landscapes, but the deep-rooted social issues that make life for many in the far south-west of England difficult. There are pockets of serious deprivation in Cornwall where people experience homelessness and addiction problems.Desborough, Aquilino and Coleman were among those who – in the words of the defence barrister, Sean Brunton KC – had slipped through the cracks in society. The three got to know each other when they lived in a hostel for homeless people in the seaside resort of Newquay.View image in fullscreenJames Desborough at the Falmouth Stable pub on 3 June 2025, the last day Daniel Coleman was seen alive.Photograph: Devon and Cornwall policeIn the months before he died, Aquilino, 57, was taking hard drugs, suffering from depression and subjected to “cuckooing”, in which dealers take over the home of a vulnerable person. Coleman, 43, abused alcohol and had cirrhosis. He had been kidnapped and stabbed at the age of 13, leaving him with post-traumatic stress disorder.The police were first called in after Coleman was reported missing. He had last been seen on 3 June 2025, drinking with Desborough. Police thought they had solved the case quickly when they found a body in woodland between Truro and the village of Probus.It turned out not be Coleman though, or Aquilino, but a third man, Lee Hockey, who had vanished from Truro. Police believe he too may have been murdered, but have not linked his death to Desborough.Attention began to focus on Paramoor Woods, near Sticker, once a mining settlement now popular with people who work in the town of St Austell.View image in fullscreenJames Desborough.Photograph: Devon and Cornwall Police/PADesborough had inherited land there from his grandfather and built a shack, though, to his frustration, he did not have the correct planning permission and had been told by the council that he was not allowed to live there permanently.He would let homeless friends camp there, grew cannabis and had a “stash tree” where he hid class A drugs in a hollow. Machetes, knives and saws were also scattered around the property.Police searched the woods for five months, eventually finding the remains of Coleman and Aquilino. The latter had last been seen alive on 18 April 2025, also drinking with Desborough.Codenamed Operation Honeyfall, the search was extraordinary. More than 700 officers and scientists were involved, with Devon and Cornwall police drawing on resources from five other forces. Dog teams, soil experts and anthropologists were brought in.The weather was very hot and the nature of the terrain jungle-like and boggy. Officers sometimes had to wade through water up to their chests as they searched.View image in fullscreenThe shack James Desborough built on the land he inherited.Photograph: Devon and Cornwall police/HandoutIn excess of 1,900 burnt bone fragments – Aquilino’s remains – were discovered in a stream, while Coleman’s charred body parts were found in a shallow grave. A hatchet hung on a nearby tree.Another unusual feature was that Desborough kept a beady eye on the search. Before there was enough evidence to remand him in custody, he hung around, at one point telling a forensic biologist that he liked the dismemberment scenes in the serial killer show Dexter.Sometimes officers smelled burning and at other times heard digging, perhaps as Desborough tried to destroy evidence.As well as discovering the victims’ remains, police came upon notes and plans Desborough had made that suggested he may have been planning to change his appearance through plastic surgery after the murders and flee the UK, perhaps to south-east Asia.View image in fullscreenA hatchet police found near the shallow grave containing Daniel Coleman’s remains.Photograph: Devon and Cornwall police/PADetectives also discovered he had used his victims’ bank cards to buy goods and services, including a roast beef dinner soon after cutting up Coleman’s body.He was eventually charged with the two murders and held in Exeter prison sharing a cell with Kempster, who had been jailed for drunkenly suffocating his 91-year-old father in north Devon.Desborough’s appearance in the witness box was remarkable. He was considered so dangerous that he was handcuffed to an officer when he was moved from the dock to the main area of the court.He was articulate when speaking about his time as a civil engineer and building regulations concerning his cabin, but he was less certain when he told the story of finding the bodies of Aquilino and Coleman.View image in fullscreenOne of the notes police found.Photograph: Devon and Cornwall policeHe claimed he had come upon one hanging in a tree, the other naked in a stream. It was, in his words, a “series of unfortunate circumstances”.Desborough repeatedly denying killing the pair, but accepted burning and hiding their bodies while high on ketamine and drinking tequila.During the trial there was a suggestion that Desborough might have carried on killing, murdering members of his circle who could have implicated him in the deaths of his friends or who simply annoyed him.In one note, he had written: “I’m a killer and ready to execute any predators.” In another, headed “bug out” – military slang for a retreat – he set out what appeared to be escape plans but added: “Take out the remaining muppets.”Det Supt Rachael Bentley, the head of Devon and Cornwall police’s major crime investigation team, said of the murders of Aquilino and Coleman: “Both men were vulnerable and trusted James Desborough as their friend. Desborough not only brutally murdered both men, but then savagely desecrated their bodies, seeking to hide the evidence of his crimes. In doing so, he denied both men of dignity and their families of the opportunity to say goodbye.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Director Mike Leigh likely to retire after his next film due to illness | Mike Leigh | The Guardian
description: Film-maker’s drama Tender Loving Care ‘likely’ his final one as he manages myositis, a disease affecting immune system
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Film-maker’s drama Tender Loving Care ‘likely’ his final one as he manages myositis, a disease affecting immune system
Content: Mike Leigh in Toronto, on 7 September 2024.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APView image in fullscreenMike Leigh in Toronto, on 7 September 2024.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APMike LeighDirector Mike Leigh likely to retire after his next film due to illnessFilm-maker’s drama Tender Loving Care ‘likely’ his final one as he manages myositis, a disease affecting immune systemBenjamin LeeTue 28 Jul 2026 16.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilm-makerMike Leighhas said his next film is likely to be his last.According toIndiewire, the Oscar-nominated writer-director was speaking at a recent Golden Globes-hosted roundtable in London about his next film Tender Loving Care, a drama set to premiere during this fall festival season.The 83-year-old, whose films include Secrets & Lies, Mr Turner and Another Year, said another film would be “very difficult” and is “not going to be possible” as a result of his health.Leigh has previously spoken about being diagnosed with myositis, a disease that affects the immune system and causes chronic muscle inflammation.When asked if Tender Loving Care will be his last film, he responded: “Absolutely. I think very likely, yes. I mean, I know the girls don’t like to hear me say that, but I think that is the case.”Marianne Jean-Baptiste: ‘I’d work for Mike Leigh again in a heartbeat – in fact, I’ll pay him!’Read moreThe film is a comedy drama starring Leigh’s longtime collaborator and partner Marion Bailey and recent Widow’s Bay breakout Kate O’Flynn. Specific plot details are unknown, but it has been described as “an insightful exploration of the contemporary world”.The film will have its Canadian premiere at the Toronto film festival with a world premiere at the Telluride film festival predicted just before it.“I was lucky in making this last film – people were very helpful,” he said. “You’ll see when I get up, that my two friends all helped me to stand up. So I probably can’t do much more. And doing a play is even more physically demanding, strangely enough, than making a film, because on a film you can be moved around.”Leigh’s last filmHard Truths, starring Marianne Jean-Baptiste, was a critical hit two years ago. The Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw called it “a deeply sober, sombre, compassionate drama” in a four-star review.Hard Truths marked the final time Leigh worked with his longtime cinematographer Dick Pope, whodied in October 2024.Explore more on these topicsMike LeighnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump pausing Iran attacks shows US military power is not enough on its own | Iran | The Guardian
description: Tehran has not been bombed into submission, leaving America unable to enforce its demands without a ground war that it does not want
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Tehran has not been bombed into submission, leaving America unable to enforce its demands without a ground war that it does not want
Content: A billboard in Tehran on Monday 27 July. Iran’s hold on the strait of Hormuz has given it an advantage over the US.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APView image in fullscreenA billboard in Tehran on Monday 27 July. Iran’s hold on the strait of Hormuz has given it an advantage over the US.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APIranAnalysisTrump pausing Iran attacks shows US military power is not enough on its ownDan SabbaghDefence and security editorTehran has not been bombed into submission, leaving America unable to enforce its demands without a ground war that it does not wantTue 28 Jul 2026 19.00 EDTShareHas Iran won a war it didn’t start against the United States? It is not a victory in any conventional military sense: about 3,500 Iranians have been reported killed and the US-led bombing has caused anywherebetween $150bnand$270bn of damage.YetDonald Trump’s decision to pause, rather than intensify,the 13-night summer bombing campaign in effect represents a degree of recognition that the US cannot achieve its stated goals by military power alone.“Iran’s initial standard for victory was simply to survive,” said HA Hellyer, a Middle East expert with the Royal United Services Institute. “If anything, that’s been raised. The regime has demonstrated it is not going anywhere, and Tehran has changed the calculus on the strait of Hormuz”.The past five months are a clear demonstration of how an asymmetric conflict can flip the tables. All Iran, helped by its extensive and mountainous geography, has needed to do is maintain enough of a missile and drone capability toscare merchant shipping from using the strait of Hormuz. It is a low bar Iran’s military is still clearing.Two tankers were attacked sailing north of Oman last week. One of them caught fire in the engine room and had to be evacuated, before being towed to Oman, one of a handful of serious attacks on merchant shipping that took place during the nearly two-week July escalation of fighting.The US, meanwhile, has spent at least $38bn and used more than 1,000 Tomahawk and 1,100 Jassm $2.6m cruise missiles,according to estimates by the CSIS thinktank, to bomb targets in Iran, a third and a quarter of total stockpiles. The Tomahawks, which cost up to $3.6m each, might not be replaced until 2031.It is surprising that the US has allowed key munitions to be run down at such speed. On Monday, Trump tried in part to blame Ukraine, arguing that “so much was given” to Kyiv in military aid – though the reality is that Ukraine was never given long-range cruise missiles, only Patriot air defence systems.Patriot missile interceptors were more heavily depleted, by 1,000 or so, or 50% of the total US stockpile, raising questions as to how well the US can continue todefend its bases in the Gulf. More were used during the 38 days of heavy fighting in the spring than the 600 or so that Ukraine has said it had received during four years of war.A fresh escalation in the Red Sea by the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen, complicates the picture further. The rebel group kept out of the first phase of the US-Iran war in the spring but, as Saudi Arabia seeks to redirect oil traffic through the Red Sea, they have stepped up attacks, targetinga refinery in the Saudi city of Jizanon Saturday.TheUS’s stated central war aim, meanwhile, may have repeatedlyshifted but it has always been maximalist – whether it was regime change (as demonstrated by the killing of Ali Khamenei), destroying Iran’s entire missile programme or, as most frequently stated, preventing the country from having a nuclear weapon.Yet the US has no means of enforcing this level of demand without committing ground forces in numbers to occupy Tehran – an unlikely move that the US has not shown signs of preparing for. Donald Trump’s previous threats to bomb Iranian power plants to try to force the regime’s capitulation have raised concerns they would amount to war crimes, and he dropped them in April and again last week.“I don’t think the Iranians can be bombed into accepting US terms,” said Peter Ricketts, a former UK national security adviser. “Until the US accepts it can’t get its way by bombing, Iran has effective leverage. Tehran can absorb the pain, and they know they can close the strait with the economic impact it has on the US.”The resulting situation is what Ricketts calls an “escalation dominance” that he says favours Iran. Tehran, faced with US pressure to abandon its nuclear programme, can string out peace negotiations, wait for the White House to get impatient and restart bombing, then close Hormuz until the US has to stop attacking because the oil price is tto high for too long.The question then becomes who gains as unstable equilibrium endures.Tehran may well believe it has leverage as the US heads towards midterm electionsin November, given how unpopular the war is. Just a third of all Americans support the war, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey out on Tuesday, though that rises to 71% of Republicans.Laurel Rapp, from the Chatham House thinktank, said that “a resumed ceasefire and promise of future talks is the least bad option for Washington” – though whether that is attractive to US ally Israel, whose prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu has his own election to fight in October, is another source of uncertainty.But if Tehran may have short or medium-term leverage, any idea that it has won the war is exaggerated. Hellyer argues that Iran, long struggling under western sanctions, cannot afford to rebuild without an agreement with the US: “Ultimately this isn’t sustainable for Iran, because its economy isn’t going to be able to survive”.Explore more on these topicsIranDonald TrumpUS militaryanalysisShareReuse this content
