title: This Booker longlist may have two previous winners, but it’s keen to experiment | Books | The Guardian
description: Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout may be names we know, but there’s a welcome element of absurdism and surrealist thought here
Author: Justine Jordan
Headline: Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout may be names we know, but there’s a welcome element of absurdism and surrealist thought here
Content: A trove of ideas … this year’s Booker prize longlist novels.Photograph: Booker Prize FoundationView image in fullscreenA trove of ideas … this year’s Booker prize longlist novels.Photograph: Booker Prize FoundationBooksThis Booker longlist may have two previous winners, but it’s keen to experimentJustine JordanMarlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout are names we know, but there’s a welcome element of surprise elsewherePrevious winners Douglas Stuart and Marlon James lead Booker prize longlistTue 28 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.59 EDTShareThis year’s Booker longlist is led by two previous winners. Twelve years on from A Brief History of Seven Killings, Marlon James returns to Jamaica inThe Disappearers, out in September: a polyphonic epic of a murderous mob attack on a gay theatre group in 1988 Kingston, and the two-decade aftermath of trauma and revenge that follows. A brutal expose of Jamaica’s homophobia, it’s also an energetic portrait of queer culture and the Caribbean diaspora. Douglas Stuart, whose debut Shuggie Bain won in 2020, is included forJohn of John, in which a young gay man returns to his childhood home on the Hebridean island of Harris, where his devout father is also hiding his sexuality. Both novels open up territory not often trod in literature, with Stuart illuminating faith, repression and the fading traditions of the Scottish Hebrides.It’s no surprise either to see a third nomination for Elizabeth Strout.The Things We Never Sayintroduces new characters to her fictional universe, in the story of a fiftysomething teacher with a secret in his marriage and a sadness in his heart. Strout has always been interested in class and deprivation in American society; the spectre of Trump brings a growing darkness, but as ever her spiky warmth and wisdom carry the reader through. The other big-name American author on the list is Emma Cline;Switzy, out in September, takes us inside the mind of a high flyer whose grip on the world is failing as dementia encroaches. David is taking his last journey, to a euthanasia clinic in Zurich, and on the way will hopefully make his final reckonings with friends and family while he can still recognise them. It’s a technical tour de force of the unreliable narrator, and a hugely moving account of life’s meaning as everything is stripped away.This year’s big omission is also American: Ben Lerner was widely seen as a shoo-in forTranscription, his compact but intricately allusive meditation on family inheritance, technology and the effect of smartphones on the way we see the world. But there will be rejoicing at a nomination at last for British author Gwendoline Riley, who has been writing devastatingly precise indictments of family relationships and emotional narcissism for a quarter of a century.The Palm Housefinds her in a more tender mood, investigating a long friendship against the precarity of London life.It’s fantastic too to see M John Harrison’sThe End of Everything, a fabulously destabilising vision of an England drifting through alien invasion into terminal decline. Harrison, who has been called “the missing evolutionary link between William Burroughs and Virginia Woolf”, began his career in the late 1960s as part of the science fiction New Wave, and has been subverting genre and perspective in steely modernist sentences ever since. This portrait of apocalypse-at-a-remove, with wars in the distance, reality bending, new forms of intelligence on the rise while humans dissociate and muddle confusedly through, perhaps speaks more to our times than realism ever could.Indeed judge Patricia Lockwood, known for her own dazzlingly idiosyncratic prose, claimed in aninterview with the Observer that“in the face of AI and the fractured attention span, I think we’re going to see a new avant garde that insists on the participation of the human … there is a new, weird literature emerging”. She jokingly threatened to choose “the craziest book on﻿ Earth!” And there’s certainly a weird and wild undercurrent in this year’s list, soaked through with absurdism and surrealism.If one theme is the journey from margins to mainstream, it’s been a rapid progression for Missouri Williams, only on her second novel after cult success The Doloriad. Set in a university town overrun by vegetation,The Vivisectorsis a deeply strange parable of culture wars, family dysfunction and civilisational decline, and an even stranger love story. “At the centre of my soul there was a big dead rock that wanted nothing to do with anything else,” says our young antiheroine, and while there are echoes of Ottessa Moshfegh here, Williams has a vision and energy all her own.Rebecca Perry’s debutMay We Feedthe Kingis similarly uncategorisable, contrasting a contemporary narrative about a curator who recreates furnishings and feasts in historic houses with the story of an unwilling medieval ruler. It’s a puzzle box of a novel that toys with the reader but keeps them rapt throughout. American Makenna Goodman’sHelen of Nowhereis more unusual still: organised as a series of dramatic scenes, it is a witty fable of male entitlement based around a university professor whose status is upended by the changing zeitgeist. Like The Vivisectors, it’s interested in nature v civilisation, culture wars and identity politics.“History repeats itself so fast in Turkey, faster than in any other country.” Kenan Orhan’sThe Renovationuses a Kafkaesque absurdity – a bathroom in an Italian flat that suddenly becomes a prison cell in Istanbul – to open up a story about migration, home and political repression, in which the trials of loss and memory extend to the narrator’s father’s dementia. Even Luke Kennard’s comic rompBlackBagis tinged with absurdism. Here a failing actor who has “measured out my life in coffees I cannot technically afford” takes part in a university experiment, hanging around campus dressed only in a black leather bag: his parents appear as stone menhirs, and his best conversations are with a dog. Full of zinging one-liners, this is a very funny take on work, friendship, masculinity and other modern confusions.Irish author Djamel White’s debutAll Them Dogs, a tale of drug deals, bad choices and queer desire in the ganglands of Dublin, has a similarly riotous energy, while the Mexican-British author Chloe Aridjis’sThe Shadow of the Objectis a quieter, almost dreamlike story of a woman drawn into a fascination with magic lanterns and the technology of illusion; the ruminative mood is reminiscent of WG Sebald. The shortlist, released on 22 September, may have a different emphasis, but for the moment this is a longlist that’s eager to experiment.Explore more on these topicsBooksBooker prizeAwards and prizesFictioncommentShareReuse this content

title: How close is the Trump administration to the toxic Tate brothers? Let’s ask the president’s son Barron … | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The 20-year-old crypto bro likes to keep a low profile. He could still be forced to testify before the House oversight committee, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The 20-year-old crypto bro likes to keep a low profile. He could still be forced to testify before the House oversight committee, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: ‘Barron is a full-blown adult and very influential in the Trump White House orbit.’Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Barron is a full-blown adult and very influential in the Trump White House orbit.’Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersOpinionAndrew TateHow close is the Trump administration to the toxic Tate brothers? Let’s ask the president’s son Barron …Arwa MahdawiThe 20-year-old crypto bro likes to keep a low profile. He could still be forced to testify before the House oversight committeeTue 28 Jul 2026 09.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTShareUnlike his garrulous father, Barron Trump seems to be a man of few words. The president’s youngest son has been busy floggingenergy drinksand making millions from cryptocurrency schemes, but he’s not big on public speaking. Indeed, the best-known clip of him talking is probably from when he was four years old and said “I like my suitcase” in aSlovenian accent.Still, while 20-year-old Barron Trump might prefer to stay behind the scenes, he may find himself hauled in front of Congress and forced to answer some difficult questions. Last week,Yassamin Ansari, a Democratic congresswoman and a member of the House oversight committee,called forBarron to testify about his alleged connections to the toxic influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate. The Tate brothers, who have become household names by monetising misogyny, wererecently arrestedin Miami, just before Andrew was due to co-host a bare-knuckle boxing event. They’re nowfighting extraditionto the UK, and face allegations of rape, assault, trafficking and offences relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography”. They deny these charges.What’s Barron got to do with all this? Over the years, the Trumps and the Tates seem to have forged a mutually beneficial alliance. Donald Trump Jr has been friendly with Andrewsince 2016and, while I wouldn’t go so far as to call Barron and Andrew besties, theNew York Times has reportedthat a teenage Barron admired the influencer and had a Zoom call with him. Accordingto the New Yorker, Barron also spent a lot of time with Justin Waller, who has called himself the Tates’ “third brother”, and gave Barrondating advice. Barron, in turn, gave his dad a political steer: he is widely credited, including by thepresident himself, for pushing Trump to tap into manosphere influencers such as Tate during the 2024 election in order to mobilise young male voters.In return for their help with the election, the Tates got friends in high places. “The Tates will be free, Trump is the president,”Andrew postedafter the inauguration. And that prediction was partly correct: it has beenwidelyreportedthat the Trump administration intervened in 2025 to get the Romanian governmentto lift travel restrictionson the Tates, who were under house arrest in the country for trafficking charges. (Romania’s foreign minister has said he did not face any pressure from the US regarding the Tates. The Trump administration has said it had no insight into the matter.)Will the Trump administration help the brothers when it comes to this new extradition request? Press secretary Karoline Leavitt has said the White Housewon’t get involved. Secretary of state Marco Rubio has alsodismissed the idea. Whether you should believe this is debatable, but it’s certainly possible the Tates have outlived their usefulness to the ever-transactional Trumps.Still, the Trump family can’t sever ties with the Tate brothers that easily. As congresswoman Ansari notes, there are plenty of questions that remain unanswered about the Tate-Trump relationship. Ina letterto the House oversight committee chair, Ansari said: “The committee must investigate whether back-channel communications between the Tate brothers, presidential advisors, and members of the First Family such as Barron Trump influenced official actions or administration policy regarding criminal prosecution and investigation of the brothers or international law enforcement cooperation.” The letter specifically recommends a subpoena for Barron to see if he had “any involvement” in relation to the Tate brothers’ allegedcrimes. Over the weekend,Ansari reiterated her callsfor an investigation on the MeidasTouchpodcast, noting that Barron “is a full-blown adult, and he is very influential in the Trump White House orbit”.Staff turnover is rampant under Trump 2.0 – with insidious results | Arwa MahdawiRead moreRepublicans have a slight majority in the House, so it’s highly unlikely that Ansari’s request will go anywhere. I don’t need to tell you that we still don’t have real answers about Trump’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein. Nor do I need to tell you that Trump is an adjudicated sexual abuser. This isn’t an administration that takes violence against women seriously. That said, if the Democrats win the House in the midterms, as they areexpected to do, the situation might shift and Barron might find himself with some explaining to do.And if the US government won’t demand answers from Barron, then the media should. As Ansari notes, Barron is very much an adult now. He may not have chosen to be born a Trump but he haschosen to profitfrom his name and connections. He’s not some little kid who needs protecting. But there are a lot ofvulnerable young kidsout there who do need protecting from the bigotry and hate that men like the Tates peddle.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsAndrew TateOpinionTrump administrationUS politicsViolence against women and girlsCrimeCryptocurrenciescommentShareReuse this content

title: GSK heads to Cambridge with long-awaited positive vibes  | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Pharmaceutical company’s move to new £400m research centre accompanied by encouraging news for shareholders
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Pharmaceutical company’s move to new £400m research centre accompanied by encouraging news for shareholders
Content: GSK is to move more than 1,000 of its scientists to its new Cambridge research and development centre.Illustration: GSKView image in fullscreenGSK is to move more than 1,000 of its scientists to its new Cambridge research and development centre.Illustration: GSKNils Pratley on financePharmaceuticals industryGSK heads to Cambridge with long-awaited positive vibesNils PratleyPharmaceutical company’s move to new £400m research centre accompanied by encouraging news for shareholdersTue 28 Jul 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.43 EDTShare“A vote of confidence in British business,” trumpeted Andy Burnham, seizing the political gift of GSK splashing out £400m on a shinynew research and development centre in Cambridge.For positive vibes, it definitely beats the early pharma news his predecessor as prime minister received. That was the painful tale of how AstraZeneca, frustrated by indecision in the Treasury,cancelled its intended £450m expansionof a vaccine plant in Speke in Liverpool.In reality, GSK’s investment in Britain is a specific one inCambridge. The group’s historic Stevenage facility will close and most of the scientists (or as many as want to go) will move to the Fens.One shouldn’t be surprised. Around the world, life sciences companies increasingly gather in clusters. Cambridge – thanks to its university, Addenbrooke’shospital, various science institutes and a healthy biotech and biopharma start-up scene – is a genuine world-class rival to Boston and Basel. The Cambridge biomedical campus is the natural place forGSKto be in the UK in the interests of “acceleration” of research and development. Only a cynic would suggest literal proximity to AstraZeneca’s facilities could come in handy for a future merger.The switch of UK research location is the most eye-catching big decision by Luke Miels, the chief executive since the start of the year, but Tuesday’s first-half numbers contained three sources of encouragement for shareholders.First, GSK thinks it can put at least 20 potential medicines into late-stage trials this year, an increase from 10 at the last count. Part of the boost flows fromthe near-£8bn acquisitionof the US-based cancer specialist Nuvalent last month. But the rest probably owes something to Miels’s focus on which drug programmes should be backed harder and which cut. If the 20-plus target indicates more ruthlessness in prioritisation, investors will applaud. It is easy to talk, as Miels has done, about displaying “scientific courage”, but you still need candidates to come through the drug pipeline to make it happen.Second, Miels surprised the market with a plan to cut £1.9bn of annual costs by 2029. Even for a company the size of GSK, that’s a big number to find from the general wash of procurement, frontline sales forces, AI efficiencies and a leaner manufacturing presence amid the shift from general medicines to specialist drugs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLuke Miels, the GSK chief executive since the start of the year, surprised the market with plan to cut £1.9bn annual costs by 2029.Photograph: GSK/ReutersThird, the dark cloud hanging over GSK – the expiry during 2028-30 of patents on the HIV medicine dolutegravir, which accounts for about a fifth of group sales – looks less threatening if the group’s latest forecasting proves correct.A critical line in the results was the prediction that operating profits margins will be “stable to improving” even during the patent crunch. Thanks to the intended cost savings, that is a notably clearer statement than the group has offered before now. Meanwhile, the grand target of hitting £40bn-plus of revenue in 2031 is “on track” with “accelerating growth” thereafter.Longstanding GSK shareholders know from experience never to underestimate the scope for disappointment. The past 20 years have witnessed many false dawns; improvements under Miels’s predecessor, Emma Walmsley, ran into bad luck in the form of US litigationover a heartburn drug from the 1990s.But the tone has definitely improved. It’s still too soon to speak about GSK replicating AstraZeneca’s remarkable 15-year blueprint for growth under Pascal Soriot (which also started with expansion in Cambridge). But the big-picture pieces are falling into place. The 2031 revenue target gets more credible with every telling; the pipeline is fuller; the patent cliff is less daunting; the share price is perkier. Put the merger talk on hold.Explore more on these topicsPharmaceuticals industryNils Pratley on financeGSKCambridgeCambridgeshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s time to prosecute climate crimes – with laws that already exist | Aaron Regunberg | The Guardian
description: Some have called for Nuremberg-style trials against big oil. But there are laws already on the books to describe companies’ conduct
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Some have called for Nuremberg-style trials against big oil. But there are laws already on the books to describe companies’ conduct
Content: ‘Next time you hear a climate disaster described as a crime, remember that this isn’t just rhetoric.’Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APView image in fullscreen‘Next time you hear a climate disaster described as a crime, remember that this isn’t just rhetoric.’Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APOpinionClimate crisisIt’s time to prosecute climate crimes – with laws that already existAaron RegunbergSome have called for Nuremberg-style trials against big oil. But there are laws already on the books to describe companies’ conductTue 28 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTShareThe sky outside is hazy orange, and my five-year-old son is screaming bloody murder. “Sorry, buddy, we have to stay inside,” I say. “It’s not safe to breathe out there.” I had told him we’d be going to the beach today. Something inside me tears a little as I wonder how many promises he’ll see similarly broken in the coming years.Far too many parents were forced to have some version of this conversation with their children this month, as smoke from record-breaking wildfires poured across the midwest and north-east. Some of them already had to tell their kids that theirFourth of July festivities were canceledbecause of the lethal heatwave that caused numerousmass casualtyevents earlier this month.According to scientists, these extreme weather events are not “natural” disasters. A team of researchers already published astudyfinding that the Fourth of July heat wave would have been “virtually impossible” but for the climate crisis. Other studies – using methods recentlyvalidatedby the National Academy of Sciences, the country’s top scientific advisory body – found that the pollution fromindividual big oil companiessuch as ExxonMobil, Chevron, Shell and BP made some past climate-exacerbated heatwaves at least 10,000 times more likely compared with preindustrial levels.The Guardian view on extreme heat: as risks escalate, adaptation plans are dangerously lagging | EditorialRead moreBig oil’s role in these disasters was no accident. Decades ago, these companies were predicting that their fossil fuels would cause, in their own words, “globally catastrophic” climate harms that would create “more violent weather” and cause “suffering and death due to thermal extremes”. Even as they used this knowledge toprotect their own infrastructure, they orchestrated fraudulent campaigns ofclimate denial and deceptionto lock us into the disasters we are currently experiencing.It’s no wonder, then, that climate harms are increasingly being interpreted not just as tragedies but as crimes. “We need Nuremberg trials for Big Oil,” wrote one climate advocacy group in arecent postthat received tens of thousands of likes – and the sentiment has been echoed by manyothers.The desire for an extraordinary tribunal is understandable given the scale of the harm. The Nazis were responsible for approximately 40m deaths; someanalysesestimate that climate change will cause more than1bnpreventable deaths this century.But we actually don’t need any special new legal innovations like the Nuremberg trials to begin to prosecute these climate crimes. In jurisdictions across the country, there are already criminal laws on the books that describe and proscribe big oil’s conduct in knowingly driving and deceptively covering up the climate crisis – offenses such as reckless endangerment, causing or risking catastrophe, and involuntary manslaughter.Most states have areckless endangermentoffense. These laws criminalize reckless conduct that creates a substantial risk of injuring another person. Recklessness means knowing something is dangerous – eg predicting your pollution would cause “more violent weather” – and engaging in that conduct anyway. That’s exactly what big oil did, and the resulting climate crisis is now creating a substantial risk of injuring people across the country.Some jurisdictions also criminalize conduct that creates a risk of catastrophe, meaning “widespread injury or damage”.PennsylvaniaandNew Jerseyboth have these laws on the books, and were two of the states hit hardest by the Fourth of July heatwave, with dozenskilledand thousands morehospitalized. Case law shows that these catastrophe laws in particular have been used to prosecute actors for exacerbating a danger by lying about it. In one such case, the operators of a pier in Philadelphia were warned by engineers that the structure was in danger of collapsing. Rather than addressing the problem, they covered it up. When the pier collapsed, the operators were charged with risking catastrophe, and the Pennsylvania supreme court agreed,writing: “After having been made specifically aware of the imminent danger that the pier posed to human life, [they] took affirmative measures to keep that knowledge to themselves and took affirmative steps that exposed others to the risk.” Swap out the word “pier” for “climate change” and that ruling applies perfectly to big oil.Will those responsible for global warming ever face the heat? | Fiona KatauskasRead moreFinally, there’s involuntary manslaughter – the crime of recklessly causing (or, in many states, substantially contributing to) the death of another person. Clearly, climate-caused deaths are accelerating – a recentanalysisfound that extreme heat from climate change may have caused more than 20,000 deaths in Europe last month alone. Already, there are victims and survivors who are connecting the dots to big oil. Earlier this month, a Washington state court ruled that a lawsuit against the fossil fuel industry for thewrongful deathof the plaintiff’s mother in a climate-induced heatwave will proceed toward discovery and trial. Prosecutors could follow suit and begin charging big oil companies in relation to the climate disasters that are, in some instances, taking the lives ofmoreof their constituents than are being lost to traditional homicides.Of course, the scale of big oil’s climate liability will only grow in the coming years – this is, after all, not just the hottest summer of our lives, but the coolest summer for the rest of our lives. Someday, we can hope that the corporate actors responsible for such breathtaking havoc will face a made-to-fit tribunal that can fully address the ways they have condemned my five-year-old and countless children like him to a dangerous future. But we don’t need to wait.Climate victims deserve justice now, and the officials responsible for pursuing that justice have all the laws they need to begin prosecuting big oil today. So next time you hear a climate disaster described as a crime, remember that this isn’t just rhetoric. These really are crimes. It’s time we treated them that way.Aaron Regunberg is director Public Citizen’s Climate Accountability Project and a contributing editor at the New RepublicExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionLaw (US)Greenhouse gas emissionsExtreme weatherOil and gas companiesOilcommentShareReuse this content

title: Britain promised to protect Hongkongers from China. Why does it now seem ready to sacrifice them? | Nathan Law | The Guardian
description: Activists under threat from Beijing are facing strange difficulties with UK immigration. Their safety must not be traded for warmer relations with China, says pro-democracy activist Nathan Law
Author: Nathan Law
Headline: Activists under threat from Beijing are facing strange difficulties with UK immigration. Their safety must not be traded for warmer relations with China, says pro-democracy activist Nathan Law
Content: Pro-democracy lawmaker Wu Chi-wai gives an interview at his Legislative Council office in Hong Kong, 19 November 2020.Photograph: Vincent Yu/APView image in fullscreenPro-democracy lawmaker Wu Chi-wai gives an interview at his Legislative Council office in Hong Kong, 19 November 2020.Photograph: Vincent Yu/APOpinionHong KongBritain promised to protect Hongkongers from China. Why does it now seem ready to sacrifice them?Nathan LawActivists under threat from Beijing are facing strange difficulties with UK immigration. Their safety must not be traded for warmer relations with ChinaNathan Law is a pro-democracy activist and former legislator from Hong Kong. He is currently a political refugee in the UKTue 28 Jul 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 07.24 EDTShareAs authoritarian countries such as Russia,Chinaand Iran are more active in engaging in long-arm strategies to silence their critics in the UK, transnational repression is garnering more attention. It is right that the Metropolitan police and other British law enforcement agencies have specific units and mechanisms to counter it. But it takes more than just confronting this long-distance repression to make political dissidents of these authoritarian countries feel safe in the UK, and the UK government is not living up to expectations.The threat is real. Members of the Hongkonger community have received threats from the Chinese regime – some have had threatening letters, some people were deepfaked into sexual content, some even had families questioned and arrested back home. With the level of this targeting linked to the deterioration ofHong Kongpolitics, many have utilised the humanitarian pathway enabled by the previous government to relocate.TheBritish national (overseas) visa route, opened on 31 January 2021, allows Hongkongers to come and stay in the UK. It has already granted more than 230,000 visas. It’s seen as a success: as proof that the British government honours its commitment to those facing political pressure in Hong Kong. But now, with more high-profile critics of the Chinese regime facing obstacles in the UK’s immigration system, more doubt is being cast on whether the current government still takes the commitment seriously.View image in fullscreenChloe Cheung protesting outside Morley town hall in West Yorkshire against China’s proposed mega-embassy in London, 28 June 2025.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianIn May,Chloe Cheung, for whom the Hong Kong authority has issued an arrest warrant with a HK$1m (£100,000) bounty, applied for indefinite leave to remainbut the approval was withheld(while her family’s applications were approved). The Home Office asked a victim of political persecution to explain her “criminality”, a term that echoes Beijing’s propensity to characterise political dissent as a crime. It has caused her an enormous amount of stress. Her leave to remain was granted after a public backlash and pressure from parliamentarians.Finn Lau, who also has a bounty on his head, applied for citizenship in June 2025 and ticked every box. By March this year, the Home Officehad spent more than eight monthsassessing his “good character”, despite a departmental target mandating a decision in 95% of applications within six months. The fear of his activism being counted against him loomed. He eventually had to make the incident public, and the Home Office finally approved his application after a series of public campaigns.View image in fullscreenFinn Lau: the Home Office spent more than eight months assessing his ‘character’.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianThe latest case breaks my heart. Wu Chi-wai, 63, was chair of Hong Kong’s Democratic party and an elected legislator for eight years. He was jailed for more than five years because of his bravery in safeguarding Hong Kong’s freedom and democracy. After serving the jail time, he flew to the UK, where his family has settled. The British consulate in Hong Kong had told him he could apply for the BN(O) visa once he was inside the UK.At Heathrow, he was refused entry. His passport was confiscated. He was told hewould be removed to Hong Kong within seven days. He is in the country now, but only on temporary admission. The Home Office has called it an administrative issue with his paperwork, andhas told the mediaof concerns that it was not a personal visit, but a bid to claim asylum. Only now, after his case became news here and abroad, has his length of stay been extended. He now has permission to remain in the UK with his family for six months.Where is the humanity here? After years unable to hug his family or hold their hands, Wu’s reunion was halted almost before it began. What would he have done with his family in seven days, after so long a separation? Even asking this question feels cruel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJimmy Lai’s sentencing tells me this: democracy is dead in Hong Kong, and I escaped just in time | Nathan LawRead moreMost importantly, Wu had done nothing wrong. He did not enter the country illegally. He did not lie about his intentions. His history of facing political persecution should be seen as a crucial factor in why he decided to come to the UK to visit with his family, rather than seen as evidence that he may not comply with immigration requirements. He is entitled to apply for a BN(O) visa, or travel back to Hong Kong in a few months, depending on his circumstances. In a sensible world, there was no reasonable ground for authorities to reject Wu’s request – they should consider his circumstances and help.Officials were right to think again, but they also need to reconsider their approach. A sense of security is not achieved only by countering transnational repression. It also comes from legitimately feeling that your host country is actively adopting measures that respect your choices and shield you from unjust political pressure. It is saddening that so many Hongkongers persecuted by the Chinese regime are facing hurdles and blockages from the UK government, exacerbating their already intense anxiety.Britain made us a promise of humanitarian assistance. This promise should not be compromised because the current government seeks a warmer bilateral relationship with China. Removing all unjustifiable hurdles posed to persecuted Hongkongers is the first step to steer back to the UK’s promise. Britain must take it.Nathan Law is a pro-democracy activist and former legislator from Hong Kong. He is currently a political refugee in the UKExplore more on these topicsHong KongOpinionImmigration and asylumChinaAsia PacificcommentShareReuse this content

title: Why has Christopher Nolan got rid of all the sex in The Odyssey? | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: It’s a bit of a mystery why it takes Odysseus so long to get home if he’s not shacking up with Calypso and others, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: It’s a bit of a mystery why it takes Odysseus so long to get home if he’s not shacking up with Calypso and others, writes Zoe Williams
Content: ‘A rumination on the double standards of godliness’ … Matt Damon in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreen‘A rumination on the double standards of godliness’ … Matt Damon in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesOpinionThe OdysseyWhy has Christopher Nolan got rid of all the sex in The Odyssey?Zoe WilliamsIt’s a bit of a mystery why it takes Odysseus so long to get home if he’s not shacking up with Calypso and others ...Tue 28 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 10.37 EDTShareIdid not walk intoChristopher Nolan’s The Odysseyintending to pick holes. If there was zero sexual chemistry between Odysseus and Circe, who was I to say that’s not how it went in the poem? I was most likely thinking of a feminist retelling (Madeline Miller’s novel Circe), rather than Homer, anyway.Nevertheless, even allowing for metaphor and whatnot, even factoring in that Circe’s passion for Odysseus is (almost?) definitely a rumination on the double standards of godliness, in which the guy gods are allowed to sleep with whichever mortals they please, but the lady ones are not supposed to (I don’t think?), I am sure something happened.Just on the balance of probabilities, I am also sure that something happened with Calypso on the beach; all that elaborate nymph-craft, all that gaslighting and coercive control and anguish-minimisation. Why would she do it if not to keep him for sex? It’s not as though she needed a warrior; she didn’t even need any DIY done.Christopher Nolan has made an Odyssey for our times – by sacrificing the delicious darkness of Homer's epic | Charlotte HigginsRead moreThe siren song, meanwhile, I had stored as a harmonic iteration of sexual longing. If it had instead, as in the film, been the plangent call of something unnamable that had been irrevocably lost (innocence? The past?), would you really have needed a siren? You’d have been better off with a male voice choir.Absent all these shagging adventures keeping Odysseus away from his missus, it’s a bit of a mystery why it takes him so long to get home. Enter his trauma. He explains carefully – in one of the best, most understated monologuesMatt Damonhas given – that all the bloodshed had made it impossible for him to return home, feeling that he is neither returning as himself, nor capable of inhabiting his home as the brutalised man he has become without sullying it.Totally understandable; I’d lose my sangfroid if I ever had to get inside a horse with no facilities. But this leaves us with a fresh conundrum: if he’s so damn traumatised, ending his journey with a mass suitor-killing event is a little counter-productive – one might even say rum.I understand why Odysseus has to be faithful to Penelope; these are the exigencies of modernity. But de-sexing the classics is harder than it looks.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on India’s gen Z revolt: the cockroaches are coming together | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A youth movement born from exam leaks and online mockery has pierced Narendra Modi’s aura of invincibility and may yet reshape Indian politics
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A youth movement born from exam leaks and online mockery has pierced Narendra Modi’s aura of invincibility and may yet reshape Indian politics
Content: CJP supporters take part in a demonstration at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on 25 July.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAView image in fullscreenCJP supporters take part in a demonstration at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on 25 July.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAOpinionIndiaThe Guardian view on India’s gen Z revolt: the cockroaches are coming togetherEditorialA youth movement born from exam leaks and online mockery has pierced Narendra Modi’s aura of invincibility and may yet reshape Indian politicsTue 28 Jul 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTShare“What if all cockroaches come together?” wasthe questionthat humbled India’s strongman prime minister, Narendra Modi. It wasposted on XbyAbhijeet Dipke, an Indian student in the US with a master’s in public relations. Enraged that India’s top judge likened unemployed youths to insects and “parasites”, and that millions saw medical exams compromised by leaks, Mr Dipke lit a fuse. For India’s nearly 400 million gen Z, public exams are often the only ladder to a secure future. When papers leak or tests are cancelled, that ladder is kicked away. By June, young people were protesting peacefully in Delhi as the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), a parody of Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). They demanded the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.Thisweekend, Mr Pradhan became the first senior minister in Mr Modi’s 12 years in power to be forced from office by a mass-protest movement. It came after credible reports suggestedpolice officersattacked protesters marching to parliament. Security sources say it was they who were attacked. This may be just the beginning. The concession has taught the Cockroach movement’s leadership that pressure works. They could have declared victory and gone home. Instead they haveaccusedthe government of breaching the terms of the settlement offered by Mr Modi’s government. The CJP claims at least 100 people have been arrested, many on non-bailable charges. Its leaders are now demanding the release of detainees and threatening to remobilise nationally.View image in fullscreenAbhijeet Dipke.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAMr Modi has built an authoritarian order which rested upon Hindu majoritarianism anddemonisingMuslims. Education in the country has been subordinated to ideology and political patronage. But corruption in public exams cannot be divided so easily along religious lines. A Hindu graduate in northern India and a Muslim graduate in its southern cone experience the same anger over leaked papers and worthless qualifications. The grievance, crucially, creates an economic identity that cuts across the BJP’s preferred religious cleavage.Until Mr Pradhan’s resignation, ministerial accountability to public protest had all but disappeared; loyalty to Mr Modi’s ideological project had mattered more. The CJP has also broken the spell of fear that hasdominatedthe public square. The movement’s leadership were not requesting generosity; they were asserting a claim to clean administration, fair exams and ministerial accountability. Writing in the Guardian, the historianMukul Kesavansays the CJP’s social-media dexterity is crucial. Like New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, they combine eloquence, message discipline and composure, making Mr Modi look leaden. Their victory may have produced not merely a protest movement, but a new generation of political leaders.A similar kind of unrest during ananti-corruption movementin 2011 paved the way for Mr Modi to wrest power from theruling Congress coalition 12 years ago. The next general election is in 2029 and predicting its outcome today is not a worthwhile exercise. But the political scientist Christophe Jaffrelotarguesthat the CJP represents a much deeper revolt than just anger over exam leaks. It has, he says, become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Many Indians are either cockroaches now or in the process of becoming them. If they were to come together in a meaningful political way then Mr Modi may be in much bigger trouble than he is in today.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on noise pollution: keep it down | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: New research linking the issue to Parkinson’s disease adds to the evidence of serious health repercussions from traffic volume and other sources
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: New research linking the issue to Parkinson’s disease adds to the evidence of serious health repercussions from traffic volume and other sources
Content: ‘Noise is not an uncontrollable part of city life.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Noise is not an uncontrollable part of city life.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOpinionEnvironmentThe Guardian view on noise pollution: keep it downEditorialNew research linking the issue to Parkinson’s disease adds to the evidence of serious health repercussions from traffic volume and other sourcesTue 28 Jul 2026 13.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTShareThe roar of late-night traffic is not just annoying for those trying to sleep. It can also have profound effects on their health. A pioneering new study, published this month, hasfound a clear linkbetween road noise and Parkinson’s disease. The research, which followed more than 3 million Danish participants, found a modest but consistent effect: for every 11.5dB rise in noise level, the risk of the degenerative disorder rose by 3% over the 18-year study.The study adds to the growing body of evidence that auditory nuisance is associated with serious physical consequences. The European Environment Agencyreported last yearthat more than 110 million people across the continent suffer high levels of health-damaging noise pollution, with physiological stress and sleep disturbance leading to 66,000 early deaths annually as well as heart disease, diabetes and depression. It found that the harm caused was greater than from secondhand tobacco smoke exposure.Yet a 2023 report from the UK parliamentary science and technology committeedescribednoise as a neglected pollutant, poorly understood and regulated. In the US, the 1972 Noise Control Act pledged to promote “an environment for all Americans free from noise that jeopardizes their health or welfare”, but exposure to harmful noise levelsremains widespread. That may be partly because it is unequally felt. Many neurodivergent people aremarkedly more sensitiveto unwanted noise, for example. But research in the US in 2017 found that neighbourhoods with higher proportions of poorer and of black or minority ethnic residentswere measurably louder. Wealthier people are also more able to soundproof their homes.View image in fullscreenSir Sadiq Khan.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PARoad traffic noise is not the only issue, though it is a big one. Automated hand dryers and leaf blowers proliferate. Sparser decor has made cafes and restaurants louder environments. The mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan,recently saidthat he is “particularly sensitive to the misery” that tube noise causes residents, following complaints that the screech of metal wheels on tracks is not being adequately dealt with. But hegave short shrift to campaignersseeking to challenge all new applications for pub and bar licences in central London,arguing: “Complaining about nightlife when you *checks notes* choose to live in Soho is like living in South Kensington and complaining about the museums”. What sounds objectionable to some is convivial to others.Noise is not an uncontrollable part of city life. China’s official statistics, as well as anecdotal reports,suggests significant improvementsthere in the last decade. That’s not just down to the rise of electric vehicles, declining construction and closures of loud venues. Authorities have also installed sound barriers andlaid tens of millions of square metres of quieter road surfacing.Improved engineering and even lower speed limits can pay dividends. Sound insulation for homes and reliance on noise-cancelling headphones should be a last resort. One of the subtler consequences of auditory pollution is not what it imposes on us, butwhat it takes away.Animalsand even aquatic plants are acutely sensitive to loud noises, and can be damaged by them. Traffic noise drowns out the rustling of trees. Those who learn to tune out what’s around them no longer heed the birdsong. Not all noise is unwelcome. But we should do more to address the sounds that bring misery, not least so that we can experience those that bring joy.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: In an era of hyperpolitics, the left needs to organise | Politics | The Guardian
description: Letters: Mark Bergfeld and Derrick Joad on Zoe Williams’ interview of the political theorist Anton Jäger
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Mark Bergfeld and Derrick Joad on Zoe Williams’ interview of the political theorist Anton Jäger
Content: ‘Intensity without organisation rarely produces power.’Photograph: Andrea Pittori/Alamy Stock VectorView image in fullscreen‘Intensity without organisation rarely produces power.’Photograph: Andrea Pittori/Alamy Stock VectorPoliticsLettersIn an era of hyperpolitics, the left needs to organiseMark BergfeldandDerrick Joadon Zoe Williams’ interview of the political theorist Anton JägerTue 28 Jul 2026 11.43 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.48 EDTShareZoe Williams’ article on Anton Jäger (Meet the man whose groundbreaking book is being devoured by the left, 23 July) reminded me of something that I encounter in trade union meetings: people no longer come to them. But neither do they go to church or the synagogue, nor do they volunteer as the youth football coach. They work intolerable hours or are logged in, like me, writing this from my beach vacation in Greece.In that sense, I agree with Jäger’s premise that we are in an era of hyperpolitics. Yet, as a trade unionist who dedicates his life to rebuilding the power of working people, I confront a problem that has led me to cave in to hyperpolitics. I co-produced a podcast on cleaners’ work and lives, and have been running an influencer campaign with hairdressers because that is how we get the union message out. People might not attend a meeting, but they will watch something on TikTok or Instagram, or listen to a podcast on Spotify.Jäger’s argument appears to have a nostalgia for Christian democracy and the system of “pillars”: a society divided between Christian and social-democratic institutions, in which a person could spend their life within one denomination.Living in Brussels, I met a trade union leader in his 60s whose father had been a miner. He joined the Christian union when he started in the printing trade, remained in the socialist health insurance system and joined the Christian Democrats because he thought it might help save his workplace. He attended one party meeting, hated the people there and never returned.Jäger is right that intensity without organisation rarely produces power. But the task is to build plural institutions to counter the monopolistic tendencies of corporate power. The weakness of today’s organisations cannot be resolved by harking back to a golden age; it needs to draw its inspiration from the future.Mark BergfeldBrussels, BelgiumHyperpolitics – politics practised now after the destruction of those institutions that gave the people a voice in politics – is a demonstration of the American political theorist Sheldon Wolin’s contention that democracy is a short-lived upsurge in people power that is soon nullified by the political actions of its powerful opponents. One example he quotes is the destruction of union power.It was claimed that Margaret Thatcher’s reforms introduced the democratic decision process to industrial relations. Successive Labour leaders have defenestrated trade unions from the decision-making process, claiming this would made the party more democratic. This institutional destruction was a popular “democratic” reform, claiming to return power to the people while intending the opposite.Anton Jäger is correct that the new hyperpolitics poses no threat to capital, as the real threat comes from the sustained struggle from organised interests. Some hope is to be found in the new trade unions such as the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain. Only they have put a check on the abuse of employer power in the retail trade. Ephemeral groups such as Occupy can be ignored as they lack the heft to force change.Perhaps this is the reason for the popularity of the Green party among young people – they believe it is the only organised political group that is openly opposed to the inequities that characterise Britain today.Derrick JoadLeedsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Chicken farms and the reality of food production in Britain | Farming | The Guardian
description: Letters: Richard Griffiths and Will Raw respond to an article by George Monbiot in which he argues that industrial poultry farming is killing our rivers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Richard Griffiths and Will Raw respond to an article by George Monbiot in which he argues that industrial poultry farming is killing our rivers
Content: ‘At some point, the reality of food production, and the fact that we do it well and responsibly, will have to supplant the social-media-friendly rhetoric.’Photograph: Michael Probst/APView image in fullscreen‘At some point, the reality of food production, and the fact that we do it well and responsibly, will have to supplant the social-media-friendly rhetoric.’Photograph: Michael Probst/APFarmingLettersChicken farms and the reality of food production in BritainRichard GriffithsandWill Rawrespond to an article by George Monbiot in which he argues that industrial poultry farming is killing our riversTue 28 Jul 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.17 EDTShareGeorge Monbiot is wrong in his belief that chicken farms harm rivers (Besieged by lobbyists, will UK ministers protect our ecosystems? No, they’ll chicken out, 23 July). Our farms have no direct contact with the soil and operate under permits issued and regulated by the Environment Agency, giving transparency on how manure is managed on site and where it goes when it leaves.The chicken manure produced in the UK is used either for energy generation or as a fertiliser by other farming sectors. Each destination has full traceability, and manure will often be transported across the country to be used where it is most needed.It may be convenient to blame a sector he does not like for a problem, but that diverts attention from addressing the issues that some of our rivers are facing. At some point, the reality of food production, and the fact that we do it well and responsibly, will have to supplant the social-media-friendly rhetoric.Richard GriffithsChief executive,British Poultry CouncilBy dismissing modern poultry farms as “factories”, George Monbiot does little to advance the serious discussion needed about the challenges of producing the nation’s food while also protecting and enhancing our environment.Policymakers have a responsibility to hear from all those affected by their decisions, not least farmers who have long balanced their custodianship of the land with producing our food. Constructive dialogue between the farming sector, government, regulators and the public over issues such as planning reform is essential if we are to meet environmental requirements and achieve our pressing need to secure domestic food security.British poultry farmers are continuing to support sustainability by investing millions of pounds into new technology and infrastructure, ensuring valuable nutrients that are crucial to producing food are utilised responsibly.The real challenge is not choosing between food and nature, but finding practical ways to deliver both. If Mr Monbiot wants to be part of the solution, he should come out with me and visit one of our farms, where he will see that British poultry farmers remain fully committed to playing their part.Will RawChair,NFU Poultry BoardHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Why migraines are often undiagnosed | Health | The Guardian
description: Letter: Dr Sally Cheseldine reflects on the experience of people who cannot articulate their pain and the significance of cravings
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Dr Sally Cheseldine reflects on the experience of people who cannot articulate their pain and the significance of cravings
Content: ‘There was a very high level of damaging head-banging, something that others say they feel tempted to do if they don’t have access to rapid pain relief.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘There was a very high level of damaging head-banging, something that others say they feel tempted to do if they don’t have access to rapid pain relief.’Photograph: AlamyHealthLettersWhy migraines are often undiagnosedDr Sally Cheseldinereflects on the experience ofpeoplewho cannot articulate their pain and the significance of cravingsTue 28 Jul 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.17 EDTShareDuring my clinical career, I noticed that migraine was rarely diagnosed in individuals with severe intellectual disabilities or autism who were non-verbal and therefore unable to say that they had a sore head (Letters, 24 July). Instead, there was a high level of damaging head-banging, something that others say they feel tempted to do if they don’t have access to rapid pain relief for their migraine.I was interested in the suggestion that cravings for cheese might be caused by migraine (The truth about migraines: what causes them – and how to find relief, 19 July). Cheese contains tryptophan, and it was shown in the 1990s (McDougle et al) that people with severe autism who had very low levels of tryptophan showed dramatic increases of several stereotypic behaviours, including banging.In addition to headaches being misdiagnosed, I would also suggest that there is a significant part of the population in which it is completely undiagnosed due to the “diagnostic overshadowing” effect of other labels, with harmful consequences.Dr Sally CheseldineRetired consultant clinical psychologistHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The mystery of the vanished beef joint | Dogs | The Guardian
description: Brief letters: Dog’s dinner | Short illnesses | Andy Burnham’s smart move | Missing brunch | Making a meal of it
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Dog’s dinner | Short illnesses | Andy Burnham’s smart move | Missing brunch | Making a meal of it
Content: Who ate all the meat?Photograph: imagebroker/AlamyView image in fullscreenWho ate all the meat?Photograph: imagebroker/AlamyBrief lettersDogsLettersThe mystery of the vanished beef jointDog’s dinner | Short illnesses | Andy Burnham’s smart move | Missing brunch | Making a meal of itTue 28 Jul 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.17 EDTShareThe humorous tale of Morris the staffie (The pet I’ll never forget, 27 July) reminded me of when I returned from work one evening wondering why my husband hadn’t roasted the joint of beef I’d taken out from the freezer that morning for the evening meal. There was no trace of it anywhere, nor the plate it was on. Next day, evidence of the butcher’s string tied round the meat appeared during our dog walk, but we never found the plate.Jeanette HamiltonBuxton, DerbyshireDr Terry Scragg (Letters, 27 July) would like to know what the “short illness” is that features so often in the obituaries so that he can avoid it. Death notices also frequently refer to people dying in “the excellent care” of a particular medical facility. I note the names of these institutions with a view to avoiding them, their reputation for excellence being somewhat belied by their mortality rates.Eoin DillonDublin, IrelandWhatever you think about Andy Burnham’s first few days in the job, you have to hand it to him. How many people start a new role and immediately move the office closer to their home? Respect.Mary FoleyWandsworth, LondonNigel Steel thinks he has an exhaustive list of meals (Letters, 26 July), but misses out brunch. No wonder he needs to ward off night starvation.Ian JenkinsStapleford, NottinghamshireIt’s quite simple: dinner is the main meal of the day, whether it’s eaten at lunchtime or teatime.Ruth DurrellCheadle Hulme, Greater ManchesterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
