title: ‘My fingers were underwater’: Amy Hunt settles for 100m silver in torrid conditions | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: New Zealand’s Zoe Hobbs won the women’s 100m in a personal best of 10.93sec, while Emmanuel Eseme surged to the men’s 100m title in 9.83
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: New Zealand’s Zoe Hobbs won the women’s 100m in a personal best of 10.93sec, while Emmanuel Eseme surged to the men’s 100m title in 9.83
Content: Zoe Hobbs (left) holds off England’s Amy Hunt to win Commonwealth Games gold in the women’s 100m.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenZoe Hobbs (left) holds off England’s Amy Hunt to win Commonwealth Games gold in the women’s 100m.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesCommonwealth Games 2026‘My fingers were underwater’: Amy Hunt settles for 100m silver in torrid conditionsNew Zealand’s Zoe Hobbs wins with 10.93secEmmanuel Eseme surges to men’s 100m victorySean Ingleat Scotstoun StadiumTue 28 Jul 2026 17.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a filthy summer’s night in Glasgow, Amy Hunt defied almost everything the elements dared to throw at her. The track was so wet that her fingernails were submerged underwater as she lined up. Her start was so horrendous it could have carried an X-certificate. And she spent most of the women’s 100m final sloshing through puddles. It was nearly enough.But while she hit top speed late in the race, it was too late to catch the New Zealander Zoe Hobbs, who ran the race of her life to takeCommonwealth Gamesgold in a personal best of 10.93sec.Commonwealth Games 2026: Hobbs and Eseme win 100m finals as Nowacki earns swimming gold for Jersey – liveRead moreFor Hunt there was at least a silver lining in coming second in 10.98, with Australia’s Torrie Lewis claiming bronze, after so much went wrong.“I had a really, really terrible first 60m,” Hunt explained. “I am a legitimate starter. But today I got it really badly wrong. I was able to dig myself out of the horrendous ditch that I dug in the first half of the race, but I think gold was definitely there for the taking.”Hunt made no excuses about the cold and the rain, but said: “It was pretty gross on the start line. My fingers were underwater, which is a bit novel. But you have to roll with the punches at champs, and bringing away a medal is the most important thing, no matter what happens.”Indeed it was so wet that several of her fake fingernails had come off – afterwards she pointed to them and her silver rings. “I need to start wearing some gold jewellery,” she joked, after adding another silver medal to the one she won over 200m at last year’sworld championships in Tokyo.And while nine Team England athletes have pulled out of these championships in the past week, Hunt also made an eloquent case for why it was important to show up.“I think it’s really important as a track athlete,” she said. “We don’t get much representation in terms of media. We’re not NBA players. We’re not on TV three times a week and everyone’s seeing our faces.“And it’s really important in terms of my journey and my legacy as an athlete,” she said. “I don’t want to go on my Wikipedia page in 30 years’ time and just see one or two medals. I want to see lists and lists of medals.”Earlier on a night where conditions could hardly have been more spiteful, Cameroon’s Emmanuel Eseme defied Australia’s Lachlan Kennedy in the final strides to take gold in the men’s 100m.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Eseme is all smiles after winning the men’s 100m final in a Commonwealth Games record.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersFor 95 metres, Kennedy ran a stormer. But moments before the line he stuttered slightly, as Eseme charged from third to first to come through in a Commonwealth Games record of 9.83sec. For Kennedy there was a compensation of a silver medal and an Australian record of 9.85.But this night will linger longest in memory for the rainageddon that settled over Glasgow and never stopped.As it hammered down, some high jumpers sported umbrellas in between jumps. Others winter coats. The Indian Pooja Singh, the 19-year-old Asian champion, took even fewer chances. She wore a thick coat, a woolly hat and gloves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionConditions had eased slightly by the time that the women’s high jump resumed at 9.08pm after a 90-minute delay. However conditions were far from ideal and England’s Morgan Lake went out early having failed three attempts at 1.82m, her opening height.Long after almost everyone had gone home it was finally won by Australia’s Eleanor Patterson, who jumped 1.96m, ahead of her compatriot Nicola Olyslagers.Other field events on the night were affected too. The first thrower in the hammer competition, Scotland’s Angela McAuslan-Kelly, found the protective net. So did Australia’s Stephanie Ratcliffe, who went second. No wonder there were ironic cheers when the third competitor to throw, England’s Charlotte Payne, found the field.But it turned out to be a great evening for Australia as Ky Robinson sprinted clear to win 10,000m gold in 27mins 48.93sec, ahead of India’s Gulveer Singh. Not far behind was the Isle of Man’s David Mullarkey, who won bronze – and his island’s first-ever track and field medal at a Commonwealth Games.Meanwhile, although Hunt left the track wanting more, she was eventually able to find perspective.“I might have a little glass of champagne,” she said. “Because I think you have to celebrate the moments. Otherwise, you kind of get 70 years old and think, have I even enjoyed my life?”And with that she broke into a broad smile.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026AthleticsCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jersey boy Filip Nowacki comes of age with showstopping gold | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jersey teenager Filip Nowacki led from start to finish to claim gold in the men’s 200m breaststroke, adding to the silver he got in the 100m version
Author: Yara El-Shaboury
Headline: Jersey teenager Filip Nowacki led from start to finish to claim gold in the men’s 200m breaststroke, adding to the silver he got in the 100m version
Content: Filip Nowacki enjoys the taste of success after winning the men's 200m breaststroke final at Tollcross Swimming Centre.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFilip Nowacki enjoys the taste of success after winning the men's 200m breaststroke final at Tollcross Swimming Centre.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Jersey boy Filip Nowacki comes of age with showstopping goldTeenager dominates men’s 200m breaststroke finalWin makes him island’s most successful Games athleteYara El-Shabouryat Tollcross Swimming CentreTue 28 Jul 2026 17.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilip Nowacki secured his status as Jersey’s most successfulCommonwealth Gamesathlete by storming to a historic gold medal in the men’s 200m breaststroke.The 18-year-old led from start to finish in a commanding display, touching the wall in 2min 07.87sec before erupting in celebration as he climbed on to the lane dividers and slapped the water in delight while soaking up the enthusiastic applause as Jersey flags waved. Canada’s Oliver Dawson won silver, with Australia’s Olympic champion, Zac Stubblety-Cook, taking bronze.It’s ‘Chico’ time: Glasgow curry restaurateur ready to face ‘creme de la creme’ of lawn bowlsRead more“It’s completely surreal,” said Nowacki. “Coming from an island like Jersey and competing against athletes from Australia, Canada, England and the other home nations is very special. To get my hand on the wall first in such a great time, and to back up the 59.7 I swam last year, is really special.”Having captured silver in the 100m breaststroke earlier in the Games, Nowacki arrived as the favourite and delivered under the weight of expectation. The teenager took control from the opening 50m, remained in front at halfway and produced a superb pull-out after the turn to extend his advantage.By the 150m mark, Nowacki had opened up a lead of more than seven-tenths of a second and never looked in danger of surrendering it, powering home to claim Jersey’s first Commonwealth swimming gold.It was Jersey’s first Commonwealth gold medal in any sport since Colin Mallett won the individual fullbore shooting title in Auckland in 1990 before teaming up with his father, Cliff, to take bronze in the pairs.Nowacki’s triumph marks another milestone in the remarkable rise of the world junior and British senior champion, who is widely viewed as the heir to the British breaststroke great Adam Ramsay-Peaty, having already finished ahead of the Olympic champion in the 100m breaststroke final in Glasgow. He has made it no secret that he is aiming for a place at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games with Team GB.“I’ve said before that the water doesn’t care who I am now, if I can’t do it again next year,” he said. “It’s all about continuing to track my progress over the next couple of weeks, then having a good summer break and consolidating everything I’ve been doing. After that, it’s about improving again next year and the year after.”View image in fullscreenAmalie Smith on her way to bronze in the 200m individual medley, adding to the silver she secured in the 400m individual medley.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianScotland produced a dramatic late comeback to claim bronze in the mixed 4x100m medley relay with Duncan Scott delivering a stunning anchor leg in front of a jubilant home crowd. Scott dived into the pool in sixth place but powered through the field with a blistering 48.03sec freestyle split to haul Scotland on to the podium, overtaking Canada in the closing stages.Australia claimed gold in a record time of 3min 40.46sec. The quartet of Iona Anderson, Sam Williamson, Matthew Temple and Meg Harris secured victory to match Australia’s Commonwealth Games record haul of 28 swimming gold medals.South Africa took silver after Pieter Coetze laid the foundations with a Games record backstroke leg to give his team an early advantage, although they were unable to hold off Australia over the remaining legs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland’s relay featured Katie Ward on backstroke, Kara Hanlon Evans on breaststroke, and Keanna Macinnes on butterfly before Scott’s remarkable freestyle anchor sealed bronze. England, featuring Ramsay-Peaty, finished sixth despite hopes of challenging for gold.England’s teenage sensation Amalie Smith claimed her second medal of the Games with bronze in the women’s 200m individual medley. The 16-year-old, who won silver in the 400m individual medley on her Games debut on Monday, again impressed against an experienced international field, finishing third behind Australia’s Jenna Forrester and South Africa’s Aimee Canny.“It’s quite hard to believe I’m here at 16,” Smith said. “If you’d said to me last year I’d come away from the Commonwealth Games with two medals around my neck, I wouldn’t have believed it. I still can’t quite believe it to be honest.”Smith qualified third fastest for the final, with Forrester the quickest and the favourite for gold. Scotland’s Katie Shanahan delighted the home crowd by leading at the halfway stage after 100m, while Smith remained firmly in contention throughout. The English teenager briefly hit the front during the closing stages before Forrester surged clear to win in 2:09.24, with Canny securing silver.Smith held on for bronze, adding another podium finish to an outstanding first Commonwealth Games campaign. Shanahan narrowly missed out on a medal in fourth after her fast start, while Wood was unable to challenge for the podium.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026SwimmingCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s ‘Chico’ time: Glasgow curry restaurateur ready to face ‘creme de la creme’ of lawn bowls | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Mohammed Ayub Qureshi has invited Pakistan’s opponents Australia for dinner at his local restaurant – whatever the result
Author: Yara El-Shaboury
Headline: Mohammed Ayub Qureshi has invited Pakistan’s opponents Australia for dinner at his local restaurant – whatever the result
Content: Pakistan’s Mohammed Ayub Qureshi in action during the Commonwealth Games.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenPakistan’s Mohammed Ayub Qureshi in action during the Commonwealth Games.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PACommonwealth Games 2026It’s ‘Chico’ time: Glasgow curry restaurateur ready to face ‘creme de la creme’ of lawn bowlsMohammed Ayub Qureshi has invited Pakistan’s opponents Australia for dinner at his restaurant – whatever the resultYara El-Shabouryin GlasgowTue 28 Jul 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe invitation has already been extended. Even if Australia beat Pakistan in their men’s pairs match at theCommonwealth Games, they are still welcome to dinner afterwards. There is just one small catch. “If we lose, they are still invited to the restaurant, but I will probably give them a spicy vindaloo as revenge,” Mohammed Ayub Qureshi says with a smile.Qureshi, better known around Glasgow’s bowls community as “Chico”, has spent decades serving food at Alishan Tandoori while also becoming Pakistan’s most recognisable lawn bowler. On Wednesday the restaurateur swaps the shirt and tie for Pakistan colours as he and his teammate, Maqsood Waseem Khan, face one of the toughest assignments in the sport.Standing across the rink will be Australia’s Corey Wedlock and Aaron Teys. Wedlock is a three-time world champion after starring at the 2023 World Outdoor Championships, while Australia have already stamped their authority on these Games, leading the medal table with over 60 medals overall.Jon McConnell chasing Commonwealth Games treasure after rejecting Love IslandRead more“I feel excited. I feel excited to be playing with the best,” Qureshi says. “Hopefully we’ll learn something and we’ll take something home. The experience, I mean, these guys, are the creme de la creme.”Beside him sits Khan, the secretary of the Pakistan Lawn Bowls Federation, who needs no reminding of the challenge awaiting them. “These guys are serious so we know we have to be as well.”Qureshi has lived in Glasgow for decades, while Khan remains based in Pakistan, training before flying in for international competition. “We make it work, it is not that difficult,” Khan says. “I play and train in Faisalabad or Lahore and he is here but it does not come to mind.”Their journeys into bowls could hardly have been more different. For Qureshi, it started almost accidentally nearly three decades ago through a relationship forged in business. “I started playing bowls nearly 30 years ago. And the reason I got into it was because our bank manager at the curry house helped. He was a bowler,” Qureshi says.“When we opened the business, we decided to do something for this club where I train, the Glasgow Indoor Bowling Club. We said to the manager: ‘We’d like to sponsor your club for the tournaments you hold every year.’ So for the last 30 years, we’ve been sponsoring them with three-course meals every year, trophies and prizes. Then I decided to join the club and play.”Khan’s introduction to the sport required a bit more improvisation. “I was impressed by the bowls but I couldn’t buy bowling balls in Pakistan,” he says. “They never even heard of the sport. I got the balls to be made out of wood.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMohammed Ayub Qureshi (left) with the chief executive of World Bowls, Neil Dalrymple, at his curry house in Glasgow.Photograph: FacebookCricket remains the country’s overwhelming sporting obsession. Bowls, by contrast, is still fighting for recognition, facilities and even equipment. But Khan has made it his mission to change that. “I train young people in Faisalabad and in Lahore. Mostly young people are interested in bowls in Pakistan now. Pakistan is known for their love of cricket. Bowls is a sport of luxury. But I try to help them financially and try to get them interested. I am trying to create an academy which can provide easy access. Pakistan is my home and I want to bring my love there.”Home, meanwhile, is a complicated concept for Qureshi. Born in Multan, he has spent more than 50 years living in Glasgow. He represents Pakistan but is cheered on by Scottish clubmates, loyal customers and friends. “My indoor club and the outdoor club and my customers, they all come and support me,” he says. “I see them in the crowd and sometimes I will give them a free poppadom in return.”Running a successful restaurant and competing internationally might sound exhausting but Qureshi insists they complement one another. “Running a restaurant for 30 years, you get adjusted to it, you find a good staff who would cover you. Being a restaurateur gives me an income. Being an athlete gets you away from the public in a sense. You go on the green, relaxed, and just play balls at your leisure.“Stressful days would be against the big teams. Like tomorrow. Your mind is always wondering what to do, what shot to play, all that sort of stuff. I mean, we’re kind of part-time club players becoming internationalists. It’s an amazing feeling. It’s a feeling you can’t describe.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesAustralia sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens next | World Cup | The Guardian
description: Gianni Infantino is under fire from Uefa over plans to sell off commercial rights for the tournament but he says they are ‘about the democratisation of football worldwide’
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Gianni Infantino is under fire from Uefa over plans to sell off commercial rights for the tournament but he says they are ‘about the democratisation of football worldwide’
Content: Gianni Infantino is poised to win an unprecedented fourth term as Fifa president next year.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino is poised to win an unprecedented fourth term as Fifa president next year.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAWorld CupExplainerIs the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens nextGianni Infantino is under fire from Uefa over plans to sell off commercial rights for the tournament but he says they are ‘about the democratisation of football worldwide’Paul MacInnesTue 28 Jul 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 16.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhatis Fifa up to now?A week after the World Cup finished, Fifa has yet to announce whether Argentina will be punished for the violence seen on the pitch at the end of the final. What it has been able to do, however, is devise an entirely new way of running international football, which – in the words of its president,Gianni Infantino– “is about the democratisation of football worldwide”. It is also an idea to allow private investors to take a stake in Fifa’s competitions and potentially make money from the World Cup.Fifa accused of ‘selling the soul of football’ over $20bn World Cup commercial rights sale planRead moreSo how will this idea work?After reporting in the Times and the Financial Times broke the news on Tuesday afternoon,Fifapublished a lengthy statement extolling the new venture. To be known as Fifa Forward Enterprise, or FFE, the new body would sell all of Fifa’s commercial rights – across broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing – and also take charge of “operational delivery” of Fifa tournaments. It would focus all Fifa’s money-making endeavours in one place and the governing body would “retain sole control of FFE”, but it would also “invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments”. These investors “would be selected against clear long-term, governance, and strategic criteria”.So Fifa is taking the people’s game and selling it off?Well, only a small “non‑controlling” bit of it. But whose game is it anyway? And yes, Fifa confirmed to the Times that the proposed lead investor to take a stake in FFE would be Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared, but why should that matter? As Infantino pointed out onhis 15-slide Instagram poston Monday, Fifa has been “on the front lines organising, working hard, and delivering the best show in the world”. Maybe give Fifa a break?View image in fullscreenFifa confirmed that the proposed lead investor to take a stake in FFE would be Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersWhat about Fifa’s member associations? Surely they won’t be happy to see money going out of the game?Sources have told the Guardian that the FFE plans would not allow investors to take dividends from the scheme (though the investors could later sell their stake). The governing body’s messaging, meanwhile, is very much focused on the financial benefits the scheme would bring to its member associations. Fifa has promised that any external investment would deliver an “optional” $20m in extra funding to any nation that wants it. It has also promised an increase in annual disbursements and predicted a total of $10bn in extra funding would eventually be shared around. Fifa has said that a majority of its 211 members must express an interest in taking the extra funding if the external investment is to be allowed. Many nations are already dependent on Fifa in order to run their operations, however, and this year Infantino said that without the governing body “there would be no football in 150 countries in the world”. So he would seem likely to receive the necessary expressions of interest.Who dares ridicule Gianni Infantino as the World Cup boss creates global peace? Not me: is it you? | Marina HydeRead moreInfantino has previous in this regard, does he not?Yes, he announced a deal with the Japanese investment management firm Softbank to fund the development of the Club World Cup in 2018 until a backlash brought it down. Reports in the Times suggested that that Infantino could become chief executive of the FFE once he leaves Fifa –he is poised to win an unprecedented fourth termnext year which would extend his stay until 2031. Fifa also insists that joint ventures are par for the course – Uefa has one such with the group known as European Football Clubs to sell the commercial rights to its competitions. Fifa said: “Many major sporting organisations have restructured their commercial operations in similar ways in recent years in pursuit of the same long‑term goal – sustainable growth that can be reinvested in the sport itself.”So what happens now?The Guardian reported on Tuesdaythat the launch of the FFE – which has been planned since well before the World Cup – has caught the rest of football by surprise. Members of the key decision‑making body, the Fifa council, were unaware of the scheme and not included in its development. Uefa, meanwhile, has released its second statement in a month warning of a Rubicon being crossed. There will probably be further expressions of discontent and questions will be asked as to the process that led to these events. But whether any football stakeholder will actually do anything to stop the plans is uncertain.Explore more on these topicsWorld CupGianni InfantinoFifaWorld Cup 2026Football politicsexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Retaining Rodri is key to Manchester City success under Enzo Maresca | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: New manager’s No 1 priority must be to persuade World Cup-winning captain to stay as Real Madrid circle
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: New manager’s No 1 priority must be to persuade World Cup-winning captain to stay as Real Madrid circle
Content: Rodri helped Manchester City win two trophies last season.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenRodri helped Manchester City win two trophies last season.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAManchester CityRetaining Rodri is key to Manchester City success under Enzo MarescaNew manager’s No 1 priority must be to persuade World Cup-winning captain to stay as Real Madrid circleJamie JacksonTue 28 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Welcome home,” was Khaldoon al-Mubarak’s warm greeting to Enzo Maresca onhis appointment last monthas Manchester City manager. Now, after two previous spells at the club, the Italian’s task is to keep the chair content, and ensure a three-year contract does not end early. To achieve that, Maresca’s tenure must continue Pep Guardiola’s glittering legacy of 20 trophies across a decade of excellence.The key to the 46-year-old, who was Guardiola’s assistant during the 2022-23 treble season and City’s elite development squad leader two years before that, being successful can be summed up in two words: “Keep Rodri”. Yet with Real Madrid almost certain to launch a bid for the peerless No 6, and him seemingly wanting to play for the Spanish giants, a move away from City may become inevitable.Manchester City hope Rodri will sign new deal as Real Madrid weigh up offerRead moreMaresca’s best hope of avoiding “doing a David Moyes” – who succeeded Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United in May 2013 and lasted a mere 34 Premier League games – and thriving as the man who followsthe manis to retain Rodri, whohas just captained Spain to World Cup glory, winning the Golden Ball as best player in the process. The 30-year-old is contracted until June. City’s stance is that they have no wish to sell and remain intent on persuading him to sign the new terms that have been on offer for a while.Saying City will definitely be contenders for the biggest prizes next season if they retain Rodri may sound simplistic until you examine his CV and are reminded of the pivotal role he has played for the club. Rodri was key to City’s treble glory, includingscoring the winner in the Champions League final against Inter. Then there was the 74-game unbeaten sequence with him in the colours that ran from February 2023 to May 2024. “He’s unbelievable, irreplaceable,” said Guardiola. “The best midfielder in the world by far.”The World Cup triumph also came after Rodri had been part of Spain’s Euro 2024 glory and City’s 2023 Club World Cup success, again winning the player of the tournament in each. In the two seasons before the World Cup, injury plagued him, however. The result: no Premier League titles in either year for City, halting a record four-in-a-row run for Guardiola’s garlanded team.Rodri’s ability to mould and control contests wasreiterated by his World Cup displays. Exhibit A: the chokehold imposed on France in the semi-finals. At domestic and international level, this is a priceless quality. So if Maresca can field Rodri, City will be feared in the league and on the continent. The back injury for which Rodri underwent surgery on Monday is minor, but the desire to broaden his club horizons – primarily in Spain – remains, meaning there is no certainty he will stay put. Particularly so given the initial resistance of Real Madrid’s president, Florentino Pérez, to acquiring Rodri has shifted, due, surely, to his resurgence at the World Cup and maybe José Mourinho, returning as head coach, expressing a need for the player’s calm and elan.View image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca worked under Pep Guardiola as Manchester City won the treble in 2023.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPACity haveinvested £116m on Elliot Andersonthis summer, an England first-choice midfielder who may be joined by another midfielder inLille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi, the 18-year-old who also impressed at the World Cup for Morocco, and would cost around £85m. However, neither of them or Tijjani Reijnders, Mateo Kovacic nor Nico González can claim to be in the class of Rodri, who may well be in line to claim a second Ballon d’Or following his World Cup exploits.Maresca won the Championship with Leicester in 2024 and the following season led Chelsea to fourth in the Premier League and to a Conference League triumph, following that up with glory at the expanded Club World Cup, which featured the3-0 demolition of Paris Saint-Germainin the final. All of this convinced al-Mubarak and his chief executive, Ferran Soriano, that Maresca is the one who can thrive after the era-defining Guardiola.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideGvardiol says 'great things' will happen under MarescaShowJoško Gvardiol has signed a new five-year contract with Manchester City, the defender stating that “great things” can be achieved with Enzo Maresca, the new manager.While the terms include an option of a further 12-months, the Croatian is confident that the Italian’s first season will be successful. “I remember when he was at Chelsea [2024-26] it was difficult to play against them – especially away. We struggled. He’s here and I think we can achieve some great things together,” Gvardiol said.The 24-year-old has made 122 appearances and claimed six trophies with City since joining from RB Leipzig in 2023 for £77m and was voted the club’s 2024-5 player of the season.Gvardiol said: “I remember my first season when I arrived – back then I was kind of still young. In these three years I’ve learned a lot of things from all my team-mates, my friends in the dressing room and on the pitch in the last three years."I still think there are a lot of things to improve and learn but I’m only 24, I have enough time.”Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.However, as Maresca made clear with his “after Sir Alex [Ferguson]” referencein his unveiling on Friday, directly following greatness can be treacherous. The comparison between him and Moyes is hardly precise, though. Moyes arrived at United trophyless and with no experience of the pressures of an elite club. Maresca’s résumé shows a season and a half in the Chelsea hothouse and, with his prior experience of City, he is versed in the organisation where he now plays a crucial role.City have five weeks of the market remaining to try to persuade Rodri his future is at the club. Guardiola’s stance was never to stop any player exiting who wished to do so. The logic is understandable: what is the point in retaining an unhappy employee? In this case it would also be one who wants to return to his native city. “Having played for Atlético [Madrid] before would not prevent me from playing for Real Madrid,” Rodri said in March. “There are other players who have done that before. Maybe not direct transfers, but eventually. You can’t turn down one of the world’s best clubs.”EvenReal Madrid boycotting Rodri’s Ballon d’Or-crowning ceremonyin November 2024 in protest at Vinícius Júnior’s failure to win the vote has clearly not dissuaded the midfielder that the Bernabéucan be the home al-Mubarak characterises City as for Maresca.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityEnzo MarescaPep GuardiolafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Wrexham face Liverpool with Premier League still in their sights despite setback | Wrexham | The Guardian
description: Ryan Reynolds says Wrexham playing Liverpool in a pre-season friendly at Yankee Stadium is a “punch me moment”
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Ryan Reynolds says Wrexham playing Liverpool in a pre-season friendly at Yankee Stadium is a “punch me moment”
Content: Ryan Reynolds has seen Wrexham climb from the National League to the Championship in five years since he and Rob McElhenney bought the club.Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PAView image in fullscreenRyan Reynolds has seen Wrexham climb from the National League to the Championship in five years since he and Rob McElhenney bought the club.Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PAWrexhamWrexham face Liverpool with Premier League still in their sights despite setbackClub have been promoted three times in four yearsPhil Parkinson’s side missed out on playoffs in 2026Andy Hunterin New YorkTue 28 Jul 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Wrexham co-owner Ryan Reynolds called it a “punch-me moment” – his club playingLiverpoolin a pre-season friendly at Yankee Stadium just five years after he and Rob McElhenney (now simply Rob Mac) completed their takeover of a club languishing in the National League. The knockout blow would be playing Liverpool at Anfield in the Premier League in 2027-28 and the manager, Phil Parkinson, accepts there is expectation on Wrexham to complete their remarkable rise through the divisions next season.Parkinson’s team face Liverpool with confidence in the Bronx on Wednesday having defeated Manchester United and Leeds in pre-season so far and moved on from the anguish of missing out on the Championship playoffs on the final day of last season. The near-miss was undoubtedly a setback to an ambitious club’s grand vision but finishing seventh in the Championship at the first time of asking, Parkinson insists, was an accomplishment that should not be dismissed lightly.Milos Kerkez: ‘I’m delighted – Andoni Iraola is the perfect fit for Liverpool’Read moreTheWrexhammanager said: “If we’re honest, to say five years down the line we’d have finished seventh in the Championship we would have said that was going to take some going. To get three promotions back-to-back-to-back is unheralded. Even though there’s always been ambition within the club and we’ve had resources, to take the club from the National League to seventh in the Championship is a lot of big steps and particularly the one last year. League One to the Championship is a huge step.“Of course we would have loved to have got in the playoffs but I think the staff and the players should be really very proud of their achievements because that was a tough ask, especially with making so many changes.”Wrexham are among the favourites for promotion next season but are the only Championship club not to make a signing – though a deal for Crystal Palace full-back Danny Imray is close – and will not be the only well-funded team with that aim, given the parachute payments availableto relegated West Ham, Burnley and Wolves.“I think the division is going to be stronger this season with the teams coming down,” Parkinson says. “We’ve got work to do within the squad to make us competitive again. We’re close to one signing but we need several more before the window closes. We have to be patient and we will be, but the squad’s not where we want it to be, to be competitive to meet the demands of a Championship season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It is going to be a tough second season, we know that, but we feel there is more to come from the existing group. It was difficult last season with a lot of players coming in later and having to relocate to the area and settle as the season started, but they were great for us and I feel there is more to come this season.”Explore more on these topicsWrexhamLiverpoolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Geraint Thomas and rebranded Ineos face hard truths after Tour de France misery | Team Ineos | The Guardian
description: Oscar Onley’s pre-race injury presaged a bleak three weeks and their new director of racing knows he has his work cut out
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Oscar Onley’s pre-race injury presaged a bleak three weeks and their new director of racing knows he has his work cut out
Content: The Ineos team take on the opening time trial in Barcelona, cycling past the Sagrada Família. They just failed to win, setting the tone.Photograph: Pete GodingView image in fullscreenThe Ineos team take on the opening time trial in Barcelona, cycling past the Sagrada Família. They just failed to win, setting the tone.Photograph: Pete GodingTeam IneosAnalysisGeraint Thomas and rebranded Ineos face hard truths after Tour de France miseryJeremy WhittleOscar Onley’s pre-race injury presaged three bleak weeks and new director of racing knows he has his work cut outTue 28 Jul 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.14 EDTShareCrashes, punctures and injuries ensured that the 2026 Tour de France campaign was one of the worst for the beleaguered Netcompany Ineos team. From the first stage, when Dave Brailsford’s team came close to winning the team time trial in Montjuic, the 2026 Tour was, in the words of their director of racing,Geraint Thomas, “tough going”.Thomas, who has taken Brailsford’s place as the team’s frontman, said: “I’m happy to not be racing any more, because I suffered way too much. But it’s good to still be involved in the nitty‑gritty of it.”It was a baptism of fire for Thomas in his first Tour managing his riders, as he had to hastily reimagine his lineup after Oscar Onley, the leader, was ruled out by injury. That led to a rapid realignment of the team’s goals.Motorbikes and mountains: photographing the 2026 Tour de France – photo essayRead moreThe optimism fuelled by Ineos’s acquisition of Onley, who finished fourth overall in 2025, and the arrival of a new co‑sponsor, Netcompany, has dissipated quickly. The Scot was injured in June and forced to miss the Tour, which scuppered Thomas’s best-laid plans.View image in fullscreenGeraint Thomas faced a lot of questions during the Tour de France but Ineos struggled for answers.Photograph: Stefano Sirotti/Alamy“We were there or thereabouts,” Thomas said of his riders. “The team time trial everyone wanted to win and believed we could win. We were close, and we’ve been there, but just not quite clicked.”More galling, perhaps, were the serial punctures and the sight of Remco Evenepoel, of the Red Bull‑Bora‑Hansgrohe team, riding to his best Tour finish in second place. The Olympic road race and time-trial champion, a friend of Thomas, had long been connected to a move to Brailsford’s team but the deal for him to join fell through. “With all the changes going on in that team, there were delays and I couldn’t really wait any more,” Evenepoel said last winter, but added: “It was close to being done.”Instead, Ineos opted to sign Onley, but his 2026 season has never really got started. With the Tour over, his next goal is likely to be the Vuelta a España.Without Onley as a podium contender, the emphasis shifted and Egan Bernal, the Tour winner in 2019, was brought in to boost the team’s climbing skills. The French signing Kévin Vauquelin failed to repeat the successes of the previous summer, leaving Thomas and his riders targeting stage wins. But the chances of achieving them were reduced by the domination of Tadej Pogacar and his UAE Emirates team, allied to a tougher course and higher average speeds.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron, France’s president, speaking to Ineos’s French cyclist Kevin Vauquelin after stage six, was a rare high point.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/ReutersThomas admitted that there had been “a lot of learning on the job” for him. “It’s easy to talk about [winning] stages but there are so few anyway that it is tough. But it’s the Tour, it’s not supposed to be easy.”By the time Thomas and his riders got to the foot of the double-header of finishes on Alpe d’Huez, their race was about survival. “Without being defeatist, you’re not exactly racing ‘Pog’ on days like that,” the 2018 Tour winner said. “Racing evolves and you need to adapt with it. Everyone’s been looking for opportunities because they’re few and far between.”A decade ago, as Team Sky, Chris Froome led the team to an emphatic overall win in Paris while British riders, spearheaded by Mark Cavendish, took seven stage wins. That success now seems a different era, with Froome retired, record climbing speeds being set on a regular basis, and Pogacar dominating almost every race he starts.Of the Slovene, Thomas agreed that challenging the five-time winner was a daunting task. “I think everyone, if they’re realistic, knew that he was on another level. It was only Jonas [Vingegaard] who really believed he could do it.“Racing is all mental, it’s all in the head. If you go off it, it’s so hard to switch it back on. As soon as you’re not doing everything right, you lose that couple of per cent. Everyone is so good now that you can’t afford to do that.”Explore more on these topicsTeam IneosTour de France 2026Tour de FranceCyclingGeraint ThomasanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not cricket’: cheating row as ‘Clicky Ponting’ appears to dupe umpire | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Viral video apparently shows a Saltburn 2nd XI fielder clicking his fingers to mimic a batter’s nick
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Viral video apparently shows a Saltburn 2nd XI fielder clicking his fingers to mimic a batter’s nick
Content: Cricket player seems to show fielder tricking umpire by clicking to imitate edgesCricket‘It’s not cricket’: cheating row as ‘Clicky Ponting’ appears to dupe umpireViral video apparently shows a Saltburn 2nd XI fielder clicking his fingers to mimic a batter’s nickMark BrownNorth of England correspondentTue 28 Jul 2026 09.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 17.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ball is bowled, the batter plays a shot and it’s caught by the wicketkeeper to cheers all round. The batter is clearly bemused. Did he hit it? Or … did a fielder click his fingers to mimic a nick?A row has erupted in the normally friendly, if ultra-competitive, world of English club cricket after footage went viral of alleged cheating. Australian cricket will always haveSandpapergate. The North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League now has clickgate – or, as it has been christened online, “Clicky Ponting” – a play on the name of the former Australian captain Ricky Ponting.The league has promised a full investigation in response to a complaint made after Saturday’s division two match between Saltburn 2nd XI and Norton 2nd XI.A videoposted on social mediashowing a fielder apparently clicking his fingers as the batter goes for the ball. He has been accused of trying to trick the umpire into thinking the ball clipped the edge of the bat before being caught.Thebemused batter can be seen protesting to the umpireas Saltburn players celebrate. Ben Mummery, who posted the video on social media, said it was “about the worst case of cheating I’ve ever seen in cricket”.“Apparently, their keeper has a huge amount of catches this season,” he said.Mummery said he was pleased to see the video had gone viral and was uniting the cricket world: “I’m genuinely really happy it’s being exposed. Harshest possible punishment please. It’s not cricket.”The One-Day Cup’s allure: familiar faces, cheap seats and relaxed placesRead moreThe footage has been shared more than 3m times and has prompted a lively debate as amateur internet sleuths pore over previous Saltburn scorecards.Rory Cotterill, who captained Middlesbrough CC’s 2nd XI in a 29-run defeat to Saltburn in June, said a similar situation had occurred in that match. He shared a video allegedly showing the same player clicking his fingers with commenters describing it as scandalous.Authorities said they were taking the matter seriously. NorthYorkshireand South Durham Cricket League said in a statement: “The league have received a formal complaint regarding alleged incidents in a division two game on Saturday 25 July 2026.“A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete no further comment will be made.”Saltburn won the game by 159 runs and are top of division two by 17 points. The club has been approached for comment.Clickgate is far from the first alleged cheating scandal to rock the world of cricket. One of the most infamous cases is Sandpapergate in a 2018 Test match between Australia and South Africa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTelevision cameras caught Australia’s Cameron Bancrofttrying to rough up a side of the ball with sandpaper.View image in fullscreenCameron Bancroft caught on camera taking a small piece of yellow material from his right hip pocket in 2018.Photograph: Sky SportsIn his autobiography, the England Test cricketer Marcus Trescothick said he hadeaten Murray Mints during games in 2005to make his saliva better at retaining the shine on balls. He wrote: “It had been common knowledge in county cricket for some time that certain sweets produced saliva which, when applied to the ball for cleaning purposes, enabled to keep its shine for longer and therefore its swing.”The sweets were extra strong mints but Trescothick “couldn’t get on with them”, he wrote. “Then I had a go at Murray Mints and found they worked a treat.“Trouble was, even allowing for trying to keep one going as long as possible I still used to get through 15 a day and the taste soon palled.”The story, was interpreted by some – especially in Australia – as an admission of ball-tampering. Having one side of the ball shinier and smoother than the other enables the ball to swing through the air more, making it trickier for the batting side.Explore more on these topicsCricketNorth of EnglandEnglandYorkshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Almost 4,000 people evacuated from tourist sites near Bordeaux as wildfires rage in France and Spain | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Return of winds and extreme heat threaten firefighters’ attempts to bring blazes under control
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Return of winds and extreme heat threaten firefighters’ attempts to bring blazes under control
Content: Firefighters work to put out a wildfire at Le Grand Crohot, near the Cap Ferret peninsula, in France’s Gironde department on Tuesday.Photograph: Florion Goga/ReutersView image in fullscreenFirefighters work to put out a wildfire at Le Grand Crohot, near the Cap Ferret peninsula, in France’s Gironde department on Tuesday.Photograph: Florion Goga/ReutersWildfiresAlmost 4,000 people evacuated from tourist sites near Bordeaux as wildfires rage in France and SpainReturn of winds and extreme heat threaten firefighters’ attempts to bring blazes under controlAngela GiuffridaandAjit NiranjanTue 28 Jul 2026 12.42 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly 4,000 people have been evacuated from tourist sites on France’s Atlantic coast as the return of winds and extreme heat jeopardises firefighters’ battles to contain wildfires raging inFranceand Spain.The precautionary evacuation order in France, which covers campsites, holiday villages and other tourist accommodation around the resort of Lacanau to the west of Bordeaux, exacerbated a wildfire emergency described by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, as the “toughest” situation the country had dealt with since the second world war.On a visit to a crisis centre in Bordeaux on Tuesday, Macron warned that “the coming weeks will be tough and we have to hold out”.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron with firefighters on a visit to the fire and rescue operational centre in Bordeaux on Monday.Photograph: Kenzo Tribouillard/EPAIn Spain, meanwhile, a woman who had been injured ina wildfirein the southern province of Almería this month died in hospital, bringing the death toll from that blaze to 14.The woman, who was not named, died at Seville’s Virgen del Rocío university hospital where she had been treated since suffering severe injuries in the wildfire, a hospital spokeswoman told AFP, without giving further details.In France,Rémi Lassoureille, a fire commander in the Gironde department, was quoted by Le Monde as saying that the blaze there, which has destroyed 42,000 hectares (104,000 acres) of forest, was “relatively under control”, although firefighters feared a “potential flare-up of the fire on its north-west flank towards Lacanau”.“That is why we decided to evacuate the campsites,” he said.Map showing burnt areas near French coast west of BordeauxOther large fires have been contained in the nearby Landes, where thousands of evacuees were allowed to return home, and the Écrins massif in the French Alps, although one in the Gros Bessillon massif in the Var area of south-east France has not yet been fully brought under control.Wildfires in France, Spain and Italy have forced the evacuation of about 330,000 people over the past week, with Spain entering Europe’s fourth intense heatwave of the summer attempting to contain some of the worst forest fires in the country’s history.‘Ash fell from the sky’: Tourists describe fleeing ‘apocalyptic’ wildfires in FranceRead moreThe Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said the country faced “difficult hours, complex hours” before the new heatwave, which is forecast to begin on Wednesday and warned about the urgency of responding to the climate emergency.He later said authorities were beginning to “see light at the end of the tunnel in the fight against wildfires”. Spain’s interior ministry announced the end of evacuation orders for 15 municipalities on Tuesday afternoon in rare good news.A fire in the hilly terrain of Ávila, west of Madrid, has become Spain’s largest on record, burning 50,000 hectares.Map showing burnt areas near Ávila, west of MadridA firefighter, Javier García, told Associated Press he had never faced anything like it in his two decades protecting woodlands and rural communities.“This doesn’t have a precedent,” he said, adding that the ferocity of the wildfire was forcing firefighters to fundamentally change their tactics by prioritising evacuations and property protection because of the danger from fast-moving walls of flames and blazes too powerful to attack directly.“The evolution is alarming,” García said.View image in fullscreenFirefighters use controlled burning to halt a wildfire near Cebreros in Spain’s Ávila province on Tuesday.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APAn EU spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said a number of firefighting planes and helicopters from member countries had been deployed to France and Spain.She said it was “important to clarify that no country can maintain alone all the resources that are needed to tackle every possible natural or other disaster and crisis”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year of burnt land area.Wildfire weather across the bloc has been more severe this year than ever before, according to data up to 22 July from the European Forest Fire Information System. In France, which had broken its full-year record for burnt area by then, and in Spain, the cumulative numbers of fires in 2026 have also set new records.Graph showing total burnt area in France so far in 2026, compared with the average and the minimum-maximum range for 2006-25Graph showing total burnt area in Spain so far in 2026, compared with the average and the minimum-maximum range for 2006-25European wildfires have struck at the same time as ferocious North American ones, with hundreds of blazes continuing to devastate the western US and swathes of Canada. Meanwhile,torrential rainshave flooded countries across Asia.“The climate alarm is blaring, from every direction,” Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of UN Climate Change, said on Tuesday. With Europe now facing another heatwave, he said the human and economic costs of the climate crisis were reaching “national emergency” levels.“These spiralling disasters are now the lived reality for billions in a world getting rapidly hotter, as humanity moves too slowly from fossil fuels to clean energy and to protect forests,” he said.Western Europe had a wet winter and also, in some parts, a wet spring, which encouraged heavy plant growth. It has been followed by a dangerously hot and dry summer, with back-to-back heatwaves forcing moisture from plants and leaving behind a surplus of fuel that has fed the flames.The climatic drivers have been made worse by the long-running abandonment of farmland that used to fragment the landscape, preventing small fires from growing into blazing infernos.“If the issue of fuel load isn’t addressed, I think we’re going to have to get used to [fires too strong to put out],” said Dr Jesús Notario del Pino, a soil scientist at the University of La Laguna in Tenerife. “As many forestry specialists and engineers often say: what we don’t manage, the fire will.”Dr Thomas Smith, a wildfire scientist at the London School of Economics, said: “If I was holidaying on the coast of Spain or the south of France, I would make sure I have any fire alerts or fire weather apps installed on my phone and familiarise myself with the evacuation plans for the hotel or residence. It’s very important to understand that timely evacuation saves lives.”Map showing fire danger levels across SpainThe June heatwave would have been “virtually impossible” without the added heat from more than a century of carbon pollution,a rapid analysis found last month, while the level of soil dryness in western Europe was made five times more likely by climate breakdown,according to a separate studyfrom the same international research network last week.Estimates of the death toll from the heatwaves, from national public health agencies and independent scientists, suggest they have claimed at least 10,000 lives.Stiell said: “The science on the cause is unequivocal: global heating, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making protracted heatwaves, severe floods and violent mega-storms more frequent, more intense and more costly.“What needs to be done is equally clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables, and protect people where the impacts are already hitting hardest.”Explore more on these topicsWildfiresFranceSpainClimate crisisExtreme weatherEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Abusive chanting against immigrants in English football on rise, new data reveals | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Kick It Out data said reported incidents of all discrimination had reached a new high, while abuse in grassroots football rose for a fifth consecutive year
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Kick It Out data said reported incidents of all discrimination had reached a new high, while abuse in grassroots football rose for a fifth consecutive year
Content: The growth in anti-immigrant rhetoric was consistent with a broader rise in reports of discrimination, both at matches and online.Photograph: Kick It OutView image in fullscreenThe growth in anti-immigrant rhetoric was consistent with a broader rise in reports of discrimination, both at matches and online.Photograph: Kick It OutSoccerAbusive chanting against immigrants in English football on rise, new data revealsReported incidents of all discrimination reach new highReports of abuse in grassroots football rose for fifth yearPaul MacInnesTue 28 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbusive chanting against immigrants has become a feature of football matches in England, according to new data fromKick It Out.Last season 39 reports of anti-immigrant chanting were made to the anti-discrimination charity, more than the previous two seasons combined. Phrases such as “stop the boats” and “send them back” were reported as being heard “at all levels of the game”, as part of a growing trend of discriminatory “mass chanting” at matches, Kick It Out said.Increase in racism during World Cup reflects ‘growing pattern of abuse’Read moreThe growth in anti-immigrant rhetoric was consistent with a broader rise in reports of discrimination, at matches and online. Kick It Out received 1,744 reports of discriminatory behaviour in total during the 2025-26 season, a record and a 25% increase on the previous campaign.The number of reported incidents increased across every type of discrimination to new highs. Reports of racism remained the most common, rising 19% year-on-year, the 792 reports making up 45% of the total. Complaints of sexist behaviour rose 12% to 216, homophobia rose 46% to 203, antisemitism rose 43% to 93, ableism rose 20% to 89, and Islamophobia rose 88% to 60. Kick it Out said all six areas had seen their biggest totals in five years.Reports of abuse in grassroots football rose for a fifth consecutive year, up by 33% in 2025-26 to a record 248 reports. Equally, the 98 reports of abuse against match officials was the same as the past three seasons combined.Samuel Okafor, chief executive at Kick It Out, said such behaviour at matches and in online spaces was matched by a rise in hateful rhetoric elsewhere in British society, but he praised the willingness of supporters – and players – to speak out.“These figures show that discrimination remains deeply embedded across the game at a time when we’re also seeing rises in hate crime and divisive political rhetoric in Britain,” he said. “But they also show that people are more willing to stand up to abuse when they see it, and it’s encouraging to see professional players set that example last season.”For example, in March, a 60-year-old man was given a suspended sentence forsending offensive messagesto the England Women defender Jess Carter, who went public over the attacks during the European Championship last year. In the men’s game, Antoine Semenyo drew attention to the racist abuse he had received over the course of the season, with a charge ofracially aggravated behaviouragainst one man scheduled to go to trial in September.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKick It Out’s findings concur with those reported by the UK Football Policing Unit last week. The police said that some of the increase could be explained by improved reporting mechanisms, with misogynist abuse only introduced as a separate category of discrimination at the start of last season. Both police and Kick It Out have called on online platforms to do more to stop abuse.Okafor said: “We will continue to work with football authorities, clubs, leagues, regulators and government to ensure we match the courage shown to report abuse with clear and consistent action so that football is welcoming to everyone.”Explore more on these topicsFootballKick It OutRacenewsShareReuse this content

title: US diplomats stage UN walkout after France criticizes human rights record under Trump | US news | The Guardian
description: France had also intervened after Trump administration had opposed the reappointment of UN human rights chief
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: France had also intervened after Trump administration had opposed the reappointment of UN human rights chief
Content: The US ambassador to the UN, Michael Waltz, speaking at the US Capitol in Washington DC.Photograph: Michael Brochstein/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe US ambassador to the UN, Michael Waltz, speaking at the US Capitol in Washington DC.Photograph: Michael Brochstein/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockUS newsUS diplomats stage UN walkout after France criticizes human rights record under TrumpFrance had also intervened after Trump administration had opposed the reappointment of UN human rights chiefMaya YangTue 28 Jul 2026 17.39 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS diplomats walked out of aUnited Nationsmeeting after France criticized the country’s human rights record under Donald Trump.The staged walkout, which occurred on Monday during a UN security council meeting on the Ukraine-Russia war, came days after the Trump administration cited “forced labor” allegations as it imposed sweeping tariffs on dozens of countries.Critics accused the US president of leaning on the claims as a“convenient”justification for the new duties, which were unveiled on Thursday.The following day, the Trump administration criticized the credibility of the UN human rights system and opposed the reappointment of Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, prompting an extraordinary intervention on social media from France’s UN mission in Geneva.Israeli attempt to annex West Bank would be ‘red line’ for US, says MacronRead more“The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore,” the French Geneva missionsaid in response. “Today, it stands alongside North Korea, Nicaragua, Mali & Russia, isolated. And the world no longer listens to it.“#AmericaAlone,” it added.Last March, Türksaidhe was “deeply worried by the fundamental shift in direction” in the US. In June, Türk took sharp aim at the Trump administration bycalling for“prompt, independent, impartial and effective investigations” into the deaths occurring in US government immigration custody.In addition to the US, nine other countries voted no to Türk’s re-appointment, including Russia, North Korea, Israel, Nicaragua and Mali. His re-appointment was ultimately approved, with 144 countries including France, China and the UK in favor, while 13 countries abstained.In response to the French mission’s post, the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, wrote on X on Sunday andsaid: “It is disappointing – though not surprising – that this is how France deflects on its shameful vote to coddle some of the worst human rights abusers.“France voted for someone who has been lecturing, free, sovereign democracies like the United States, the UK, and Israel, while cozying up to the world’s worst oppressors.”The US continued to criticize France during Monday’s meeting, with Dan Negrea, the US deputy ambassador,claimingthat the US “remains the beacon of liberty for the world”.“As such, we will not be affording them the benefit of listening to their politicized drivel until they renounce their condescending and disrespectful rhetoric and behave in a manner commensurate with their seat on this council,” said Negrea.France’s UN ambassador, Jérôme Bonnafont, did not mention the walkout, instead saying on Monday: “The United Nations was created with the goal of working towards international peace and security, human rights and development,” the Associated Pressreports.“All of that forms the spirit in which France works within the United Nations … to preserve this institution, its independence, its ability to act in service of the charter and act to serve human rights and peace.”The US walkout came after Trump faced bipartisan criticism over his use of “forced labor” as “a pretext” for imposing controversial new tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on imports from more than 80 countries. Those include longstanding allies such as the UK, Canada, Australia, and the European Union, alongside Mexico, India and China.Criticizing the tariffs, Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the House’s ways and means committee,said last week:“Forced labor is a real and pervasive problem in our supply chains and demands serious enforcement. It should never be cheapened into a pretext for a tariff policy built on dubious legal theories and personal grievances.’’Explore more on these topicsUS newsUnited NationsFranceTariffsTrump tariffsUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa accused of ‘selling the soul of football’ over $20bn World Cup commercial rights sale plan | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Fifa has announced plans to sell a share of its commercial operations to private investors, a deal that would include the media and sponsorship rights of the World Cup
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Fifa has announced plans to sell a share of its commercial operations to private investors, a deal that would include the media and sponsorship rights of the World Cup
Content: Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump clutch the World Cup at last month’s final between Spain and Argentina and at the end of a hugely lucractive tournament.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino and Donald Trump clutch the World Cup at last month’s final between Spain and Argentina and at the end of a hugely lucractive tournament.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoFifaFifa accused of ‘selling the soul of football’ over $20bn World Cup commercial rights sale planWorld governing body set to raise millions from ventureUefa hits out at proposal and could take legal actionExplainer: what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens nextMatt HughesandPaul MacInnesTue 28 Jul 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa has announced plans to sell the commercial rights to its tournaments, including theWorld Cup, to private investors in a controversial move that triggered an immediate backlash from Uefa, leading European clubs and politicians.Uefa released a strongly worded statement accusing Fifa of “attempting to sell the soul of football” and is believed to be considering its legal position, while sources at numerous elite clubs were highly critical of the proposal in private. Andy Burnham, the UK’s new prime minister, condemned the move.Is the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens next | Paul MacInnesRead moreFifa has confirmed it is working with the US bank JP Morgan on setting up a new entity – to be calledFifaForward Enterprise (FFE) – that would raise hundreds of millions of dollars by selling a significant stake in the commercial rights of the men’s and women’s World Cups, and the Club World Cup to investors, with promises of an increase in distribution of “over $10bn” (£7.5bn) then being redistributed back to Fifa’s 211 member associations.Thrive Capital, an investment company founded by Joshua Kushner – the brother of Donald Trump’s son‑in-law Jared Kushner – is leading the search for investors.Gianni Infantino, the Fifa president, said the plan would see “the commercial side of the game [operating] as a focused, dedicated business, with its value shared more and better all around the world”. The plans are subject to approval by a “majority” of member associations, but Fifa declined to comment when asked when a vote will take place.Numerous sources with knowledge of Fifa’s proposals said it is valuing the new commercial venture at about $20bn, with Infantino looking to cash in on football’s growing global popularity after this summer’s World Cup in the US, Canada and Mexico.The Guardian revealed this monththat Fifa’s revenues for the tournament would exceed $15bn, a significant increase onthe projected figure of $13bn, with such growth appearing to embolden Infantino to seek further riches.The revelation of the plans provoked an immediate backlash from Uefa, with the European governing body accusing Fifa of attempting to sell the soul of football. Relations between the two most powerful organisations in the sport are at an all-time low, with Uefa claiming Fifa undermined the integrity of the World Cup this month when it intervened to overturn the USA striker Falorin Balogun’s red card after Trumpcalled and asked Infantino to do so.“This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross,” Uefa said of the FFE plan.“Uefa takes it extremely seriously. So should every national football association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game. The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade – especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not Fifa’s to sell.”View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino is looking to cash in on football’s growing global popularity following this summer’s World Cup.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersBurnham, an Everton fan, posted on social media: “Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine. The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone’s to sell. Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInfantino had succeeded in keeping Fifa’s plans under wraps until reports of the proposal first emerged in the Times and Financial Times. Fifa council members are understood to have been surprised by the announcement, having been sidelined from the decision‑making process.It is the second occasion that Infantino has attempted to attract private capital to fund Fifa. In 2018, he agreed a deal in principle with the Japanese bank SoftBank to provide $25bn in funding for an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League, but failed to get sufficient support, largely due to opposition from Europe. Uefa and the clubs are again united against Fifa’s plans, but Infantino may have enough backing from elsewhere to be able to disregard them.In its statement, Fifa said the new enterprise would enable it to increase the funding provided to each of the associations from $8m to $20m each year, a huge sum for the majority of their 211 members.Fifa insisted it would retain responsibility for football’s governance and the international match calendar, but in reality inviting private investment in its commercial rights would subject the decision makers to significant external pressures. Investors could ultimately be given significant influence over decisions that affect the entire sport, leading to fears they would seek to stage the World Cup more regularly and permit it to be hosted in only the most lucrative markets, such as the US. Fifa said it would “carefully select long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests in FFE – all net benefits of FFE will be reinvested back into football worldwide”.Infantino is expected to be re‑elected unopposed as president next year despite the huge controversy he attracts, but under Fifa statutes must stand down in 2031 after serving three full terms. The Times reported, however, that Infantino has aspirations to serve as chair of the new commercial company, which could earn him tens of millions of dollars.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoUefaWorld Cup 2026World CupFootball politicsFinancesnewsShareReuse this content

title: World-class Jodrell Bank is under threat and UK risks a physics brain drain | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: Funding crisis could lead to an exodus that would be a blow for British science and national growth
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Funding crisis could lead to an exodus that would be a blow for British science and national growth
Content: The Lovell telescope at the Jodrell Bank observatory in Cheshire at sunrise.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenThe Lovell telescope at the Jodrell Bank observatory in Cheshire at sunrise.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAAstronomyAnalysisWorld-class Jodrell Bank is under threat and UK risks a physics brain drainIan SampleScience editorFunding crisis could lead to an exodus that would be a blow for British science and national growthTue 28 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTShareOn a chilly day in December 1945, Bernard Lovell, a physicist at the University of Manchester, struck out for the Cheshire countryside to study cosmic rays, the streams of high-energy particles that crisscross the universe. Peering at the signals from his army surplus radar, he made an unexpected discovery: radio reflections from the ionised trails of shooting stars.The work marked the birth of radio astronomy at Jodrell Bank. A year later, engineers at the site mounted a radar on the base of a searchlight, providing sweeping access to speeding meteors. When Sputnik launched in 1957, they had just completed the Lovell telescope, the largest radio telescope in the world, the only one capable of tracking the Soviet satellite.With decades of upgrades, Jodrell Bank has remained world-class, at the heart of a seven-telescope network called e-Merlin, the UK’s national radio astronomy capability. But as of Monday, the network, and Jodrell Bank itself, arethreatened with closure. The Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) plans to pull funding in March 2028. All observations will stop unless alternative support can be found.Radio astronomy is not an obscure endeavour producing esoteric data. It has changed our view of the universe. Armed with the technique, astronomers have spotted spinning neutron stars that emit powerful beams, illuminating space like a lighthouse. They have watched matter swirling around supermassive black holes, and glimpsed the faint afterglow of the big bang.Astronomers, of course, have other telescopes to peer down, at least metaphorically. But UK researchers working on many of these face hefty cuts too. Last month, the Rubin observatory in Chile embarked on a decade-long project to record the largest cosmic movie ever. The UK’s involvement will drop 20%. The same goes for an observatory on La Palma in the Canary Islands. Work on the Bison solar observation network will fall by 40%. And the country is withdrawing from the Event Horizon Telescope, whichcaptured the first image of a black hole. Astronomers converged on the same words to describe the news: devastating, shocking, disastrous.Throughout this year, the STFC has said it needs to make £162m in savings by 2030. The crisis follows cost overruns that arose from soaring electricity and staff costs and high foreign exchange rates for international collaborations such as Cern, home to the Large Hadron Collider, near Geneva. But figures obtained byResearch Professional Newssuggest the situation may be worse: a combined forecast cost overrun of £684m for the four years of the government’s latest spending review period.Other fields of physics have not been spared the axe. The Diamond synchrotron and the Isis muon and neutron source, both in Oxfordshire, face cuts but will remain operational. The Clara facility in Cheshire, which tests next-generation particle accelerator technologies, is being mothballed. The operating budget for Boulby mine, the only deep underground science facility in the UK, is being slashed by 40%. There is no funding for the LHCb experiment on the Large Hadron Collider, which could terminate it early, leaving 80% of data uncollected.With the money it does have, the STFC wants to prioritise specific areas of research. But the best scientists will go wherever the best science can be done. And on this the signs are ominous. Arecent surveyfound that nearly 80% of early-career physicists were considering leaving the UK after the funding crisis. The loss of even a fraction of that would be a blow for UK science and alsonational growth. The task now is to persuade them to stay.Explore more on these topicsAstronomyPhysicsScience funding crisisScience policyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘We have lost everything’: extreme rainfall across Asia brings flash floods and typhoons | Flooding | The Guardian
description: From Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdown
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: From Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdown
Content: Bangladesh is one of several countries in the region to experience heavy rains and flash floods. Photograph: Rayhan Ahmed/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockFrom Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdownByNatasha MayandJonathan WattsTue 28 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 00.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It rained for 10 days and 10 nights, non-stop – I’d never seen anything like it,” says Anar Gul, a construction worker who lives in the remote district of Dur Baba in easternAfghanistan.The houses in his village are built from stone and mud, which makes them extremely vulnerable to heavy rains. After days of rain, Gul’s kitchen collapsed and his neighbour, Sayed Afsar Sadat, saw a large part of his house completely destroyed. “Rains like this are coming heavier and earlier each year,” says Sadat. “They are destroying the roads and washing away our crops. It’s impacting us directly.”View image in fullscreenAnar Gul, who lives in a remote mountain village in the Dur Baba district of eastern Afghanistan, says he has never seen rain like it.Photograph: IFRC/Mark South.Last week, torrential rains and flash floods wiped out villages and towns in Afghanistan,leaving at least31 people dead and hundreds missing. It’s been a similar picture in neighbouring countries, with the monsoon rains sparking chaos across the region. India, Bangladesh and Pakistan have all seen erratic, sudden heavy dumps of water.Jesmin Akter lived in the city of Chattogram, on the south-eastern coast of Bangladesh, which received a record412.3mm of rainfall in 24 hoursin early July, leading to the flash flood that swept through the Banshkhali district where they live. She says her children “understand that we are in a very bad situation”.Overnight the rains took the little they had; their poultry died, their paddy field flooded, their house collapsed and all their belongings in it – children’s books, school bags, toys, clothes, kitchen items – ruined.Akter carried her six children through chest-deep water to her mother’s house. There they stayed in the crowded conditions for over a week until the water receded.View image in fullscreenResidents and rescue workers inspect buildings damaged by heavy flooding in the eastern province of Nuristan, Afghanistan.Photograph: Wahidullah Kakar/AP“We have lost everything,” Akter said. Their house beside the canal was not in a good condition, but a few months ago the family had repaired it. “Now the flood has destroyed it again. We have no money. We are surviving on the food assistance we receive from different organisations.” They have gone back to the ruins of their home, but her children sleep on plastic sheets laid on the wet floor and she worries for their safety, especially that the unsanitary conditions will lead to disease. Her daughter has developed a fever.Aswildfires rageacross Europe and North America, the unprecedented rains continue elsewhere.
