While South Korea swings between heatwave and downpour, inJapanand Vietnamtorrential rain has led to landslides. China, meanwhile, has seen bouts of extreme rainfall since the flood season began in April, according to thewater resources ministryin mid-July, marking the start of a month-long peak flood control window. More than 600 rivers have since risen above warning levels – a 35% jump from the average for the same period over the past five years.View image in fullscreenSayed Afsar Sadat in Dur Baba says rains are destroying the roads and washing away crops.Photograph: IFRC/Meer Abdullah Rasikh.In the south-western city of Chongqing, a huge landslide after torrential rain killed at least 11 people and left 50 missing, with rescue efforts still ongoing. Separately, a flash flood at a scenic camping spot in the north-central province of Gansu left 10 people dead and injured 23 others.The flood season across the region has been exacerbated by successive storms. Typhoon Noul, the strongest to make landfall in China so far this year, prompted the evacuation of more than890,000people in Guangdong as of Sunday evening, according to provincial authorities. In early July, Typhoon Maysak inundated parts of Guangxi and swept through commercialsnake farms, allowing hundreds of snakes to escape.Forecasters have warned that more wet weather is on the way. Much of northern China, including Beijing, is expected to receive 20% to 50% more rain than usual, while four to six typhoons are forecast to make landfall in or affect the country this summer, above the average of 4.2, according to theChina Meteorological Administration.Taiwan, an island that lies in the path of typhoons in the north-west Pacific, has also seen a rise in extreme rainfall. In June, repeated downpours caused more than NT$330m (about US$10.2m) in agricultural losses across Taiwan, according to theagriculture ministry, while the capital Taipeirecordedits highest monthly rainfall in more than a century.View image in fullscreenTorrential rain flooded the streets of Dhaka in Bangladesh.Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/ReutersThe extreme weather across the region can clearly be linked to climate change. Climate scientists have long predicted that large areas of Asia will disproportionately suffer from more intense heat, humidity and drought as a result of climate disruption caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal. Themost recent reportby the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change said rising temperatures raise the threat of “floods in monsoon regions in south, south-east and east Asia, and glacier melting in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd World Weather Attribution scientistshave warnedthat extreme rainfall from cyclones is being “supercharged” in south-east Asia, with a clear pattern of increasingly heavy rain over recent decades.View image in fullscreenIn early July, Typhoon Maysak inundated parts of Guangxi in south China.Photograph: Cao Yiming/Xinhua/APThe year 2025 saw devastating storms and rainfall across the region. It also sawocean temperaturesrise to record heights. So far, this year has broughtrecord-breaking heatwaves. Extreme rainfall is more common and more intense because of human-caused climate breakdown across most of the world,particularly in Europe, most of Asia, central and eastern North America, and parts of South America, Africa and Australia. This is because warmer air can hold more water vapour and flooding has most likely become more frequent and severe in these locations as a result.“More intense rainfall is an expected consequence of us heating the planet by burning fossil fuels and building up more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. A warmer atmosphere can carry more water, so when it rains, it rains harder. Also hotter conditions cause air to rise faster and drive more intense thunderstorms,” said Richard Betts, head of the climate impacts strategic area at the Met Office Hadley Centre.The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) in providing aid helped the Guardian obtain interviews with those affected.View image in fullscreenTyphoon Noul (pictured in Hong Kong) prompted the evacuation of more than 890,000 people in Guangdong.Photograph: Venron Yuen/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockDr Hosam Faysal, the head of IFRC’s country delegation in Afghanistan, said “these are the very real, humanitarian effects of a changing climate … becoming increasingly volatile”.Faysal urged governments to ensure there was more investment in locally-led preparedness and mitigation in order to reduce the loss of life and suffering before climate-related disasters happened.“The coming forecast El Niño is a clear example – waiting to respond to the extreme needs we can see coming only once they arrive will cost lives.”Research by Yu-chen LiExplore more on these topicsFloodingAsia PacificClimate crisisChinaAfghanistanSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Young people ‘expected’ to engage with new work support, says McFadden | Apprenticeships | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Work and pensions secretary echoes Andy Burnham as he announces funds to stop families in England losing benefits
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Work and pensions secretary echoes Andy Burnham as he announces funds to stop families in England losing benefits
Content: Andy Burnham (centre-right) and Pat McFadden (centre) meet some young people during a visit to Alstom Transport in Derby on Tuesday.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham (centre-right) and Pat McFadden (centre) meet some young people during a visit to Alstom Transport in Derby on Tuesday.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/PAApprenticeshipsYoung people ‘expected’ to engage with new work support, says McFaddenExclusive: Work and pensions secretary echoes Andy Burnham as he announces funds to stop families in England losing benefitsJessica ElgotDeputy political editorTue 28 Jul 2026 12.12 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYoung people will be expected to engage with new support to find work,Pat McFaddenhas said, as he announced parents receiving benefits could get £4,500 a year if their child starts an apprenticeship.Speaking to the Guardian, the work and pensions secretary echoed the comments ofAndy Burnhamwhen he suggested that access to support would be conditional on young people properly participating in the support that would be provided. To help with that, the new funds announced would stop families losing benefits when teenagers take up apprenticeships.“We have an obligation to put good support in place,” he said. “And then there is an expectation that people engage with the support.”McFadden – one of the few ministers to keep his job in the reshuffle when Burnham became prime minister – said the new bursary would compensate for a quirk in the system that could mean families lose some benefits if a teenager took up an apprenticeship.The penalty – where the family loses the child component of universal credit – is most likely to affect single parents or disabled teenagers under 18.McFadden said that welfare reform would mean both “opportunities and expectations”. He said: “We are trying to get the system to ask: ‘How do we help you live your fullest life? How do we maximise your opportunities?’“One of the things that struck me about the benefits system is how sticky it is, how when people get on to these long-term benefits they tend to stay in them for a long time.”The new bursaries of about £4,500 will be offered to families, particularly single parents with a disabled child, where they could otherwise lose approximately £80 a week because the apprenticeship salary – £258 a week – is lower than the lost benefits of £340 a week.Burnham is seeking to address the crisis of mounting unemployment among young people and said on Tuesday morning he would aim to implement fundamental changes in the education system to emphasise technical and vocational skills, especially those relevant to local businesses.Both Burnham and McFadden have said they are determined to reform the welfare system, especially by providing more opportunities for young people on long-term sickness benefits to return to the workforce.The prime minister also said on Monday he wanted to change the nature of the support and make some of it “conditional upon people taking opportunities that are presented in front of them … So you might increase the conditions required to receive benefits”.McFadden said the bursary was part of removing those unintended barriers on young people taking up work – £30m funded through the current departmental budget – but added it was crucial that young people responded to the support on offer.“The key to it is to remove this barrier to opportunity, really,” he said. “And to stop people being trapped in the benefit system when they would otherwise take up an opportunity which is in their interest, which would put them on to the next step of a career path.“These cliff edges are never created by design – they’re just in a big complex system, they are just there and I’m very grateful to the charities and campaigners who drew this to our attention.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham has said he wanted to avoid “crude cuts to benefits to get the welfare bill down … Often that just pushes people into even more crisis and then even more public spending in another part of the system.”McFadden said there would be a significant system redesign when the second stage of a report from the social security minister, Stephen Timms, and disability campaigners reports back in the autumn. An interim report has already found that the criteria for personal independence payments was not fit for purpose.“We’ll need a whole government response, not just a [Department for Work and Pensions] response, because the issues affecting young people go way beyond the boundaries of the DWP. If you take mental health issues among young people, that’s obviously going way beyond the DWP,” he said.The government is also expected to receive the second part of Alan Milburn’s review this autumn, looking at youth unemployment and lack of engagement with education and training.Charities have welcomed plans for the bursary but said young people needed to be directly made aware of its existence by potential employers.Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said: “If more young people are to take up apprenticeships it is vital their family isn’t worse off, so introducing a new bursary is a welcome step towards narrowing the income gap.“As the new scheme is rolled out, the government must ensure it is as easy as possible for young people to apply, and that nobody loses out because they were not directed towards support.“We know in families where wages should outweigh benefit payments there can still be real difficulty as payments shift from parents to young people who have to take on the responsibility of contributing to overall household income.”Explore more on these topicsApprenticeshipsWelfareEducation policyAndy BurnhamPat McFaddenEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour MP suing Elon Musk’s xAI says chatbot added own fake abusive content | Grok AI | The Guardian
description: Jess Asato’s particulars of claim states Grok added explicit sexual material users had not asked for
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Jess Asato’s particulars of claim states Grok added explicit sexual material users had not asked for
Content: Jess Asato, the MP for Lowestoft, said Grok’s design ‘recklessly allows sexualisation, even without being asked’.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJess Asato, the MP for Lowestoft, said Grok’s design ‘recklessly allows sexualisation, even without being asked’.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianGrok AILabour MP suing Elon Musk’s xAI says chatbot added own fake abusive contentJess Asato’s particulars of claim states Grok added explicit sexual material users had not asked forHaroon SiddiqueandDan MilmoTue 28 Jul 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Labour MPwho is taking legal actionagainst Elon Musk’s xAI company over fake sexualised images created by Grok says the AI tool was instructed to operate with “no restrictions on adult sexual content or offensive content”.Jess Asato’s lawyers published her particulars of claim in the case on Tuesday, which included details of publicly posted instructions that the claim says illustrate how Grok was trained to generate harmful sexualised content.Asato is suing xAI after she said its chatbot was used to create fake images of her, including in a bikini, and a video showing her as the victim of a sexual assault, causing her to feel “distressed and violated”.The claim says that as well as Grok being instructed to operate with“no restrictions on adult sexual content or offensive content”, the AI tool was told to offer“no restrictions on fictional adult sexual content with dark or violent themes”and to “assume good intent”.While not relevant to Asato’s claim, the instructions also state that “‘teenage’ or ‘girl’ does not necessarily imply underage”. However, they do prohibit “child sexual abuse material”.TheLabourMP for Lowestoft said: “No woman or child should have to live with the fear that their face or body can be taken, sexualised and shared around the world by an AI system without their consent.“For too long, this company has hidden behind the excuse that it’s the users who are responsible, when in fact the tool’s design recklessly allows sexualisation, even without being asked. What happened to me wasn’t an accident. Musk made a choice to profit from harm and trained Grok to abuse.“xAI must be held accountable for the harm they have caused and are causing, so that other women and children don’t have to go through what I did.”The particulars of claim say that Grok on occasion added explicit material users had not asked for. The claim alleges xAI breached data protection law and misused Asato’s private information.Ravi Naik, the legal director at AWO, the firm representing Asato, said: “The case shows that Grok did not malfunction. Grok’s training allowed it to generate harmful sexualised content. Grok behaved according to the choices its designers made. Those choices should carry legal consequences. The remedy our client seeks includes a court order requiring the systems be brought into compliance if xAI refuses to do so.”Clare McGlynn, a professor of law at Durham University, said some of the Grok-generated images cited in Asato’s claim included sexualised elements – such as a skirt being pulled up – that were not requested by users in the original prompt and that Grok had added.“I think one of the most significant aspects of the Grok phenomenon, and Jess’s case, is how it adds sexual, intimate and violative content that the user themselves did not request. We called this chatbot-driven abuse,” she said. “This is a new and distinctive form of abuse, where the chatbot themselves are driving the abusive content, drawing on the data on which they are trained.”Details like this, she said, raise concerns about controlling AI tools and their outputs, as technology companies push for autonomous AI products – known as AI agents – that can carry out sequences of tasks without human intervention or oversight.xAI has since said users would no longer be able to use the tool to generate sexualised images of real people, and it has now become illegal to create or request a non-consensual deepfake image of an adult in the UK. xAI has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsGrok AIAI (artificial intelligence)Internet safetyWomenSexual harassmentElon MuskXnewsShareReuse this content

title: Led By Donkeys wins compensation over seizure of Gaza protest banner | Led By Donkeys | The Guardian
description: Waste firm Veolia pays £27k after ‘Yes It’s A Genocide’ banner taken by Greater London Authority was destroyed
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Waste firm Veolia pays £27k after ‘Yes It’s A Genocide’ banner taken by Greater London Authority was destroyed
Content: The banner was unflurled in Parliament Square in London in December 2024.Photograph: Haroon Siddique/Jiri Rezac/Led by DonkeysView image in fullscreenThe banner was unflurled in Parliament Square in London in December 2024.Photograph: Haroon Siddique/Jiri Rezac/Led by DonkeysLed By DonkeysLed By Donkeys wins compensation over seizure of Gaza protest bannerWaste firm Veolia pays £27k after ‘Yes It’s A Genocide’ banner taken by Greater London Authority was destroyedHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentTue 28 Jul 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe campaign groupLed By Donkeyshas received £27,000 in compensation after a giant banner it displayed in Parliament Square saying “Yes It’s A Genocide” was seized by Greater London Authority officials and destroyed.Representatives of the GLA arrived on the scene in central London and confiscated the 40-metre by 40-metre banner after it was unfurled on 4 December 2024, just over a year afterIsraelbegan its assault on Gaza after the 7 October 2023 attacks by Hamas.Led By Donkeys said its 19-month campaign to get it returned was initially met with refusals before the GLA told the collective that it had been given to the environmental services company Veolia, which had destroyed it.After legal letters were sent on behalf of Led By Donkeys demanding that either the GLA or Veolia cover the banner’s cost, Veolia has agreed to pay £27,216.Ben Stewart, a co-founder of Led By Donkeys, said: “The Parliament Square banner was in collaboration with one of the world’s leading genocide scholars, but still the authorities threw process out the window and simply seized and destroyed our property. Pursuing compensation was never about the money, it was about defending space to protest Israel’s war crimes.“Palestine protests are treated differently in Britain to all other forms of activism.Direct action is regarded as terrorismandwords on a placard are rendered illegal. Over the years we’ve delivered banners, put up billboards and done guerilla projections across the country, but the only time our equipment has been seized and destroyed was when it related to Palestine.”The banner was videoed from the air and a film created that was posted on social media featuring a voiceover from the renowned Israeli scholar Prof Amos Goldberg, a historian of the Holocaust, who said: “This is exactly what a genocide looks like.”In September last year, the UN independent international commission of inquiryconcluded that Israel was committing genocidein Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts.Last month, the commission of inquiry saidIsrael continued to commit genocideby deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza. Israel has persistently denied allegations of genocide. Its foreign ministry called last year’s report by the commission “distorted and false” and Israel’s mission in Geneva rejected last month’s findings as a “libellous sham”.A significant body of research by legal and rights experts has concluded that Israel is committing what is considered the most serious international crime, including analyses by UN investigators, rights bodies such asAmnesty InternationalandHuman Rights Watch, andgenocide scholarsworldwide.In February, the European Legal Support Center, along with the research group Forensic Architecture,launched the “index of repression”, which records instances of Palestinian solidarity being “silenced, criminalised and sanctioned” in Britain. They said more than 900 instances had occurred in the last six years.A spokesperson for the GLA said: “A banner seized by GLA heritage wardens following an unauthorised protest in December was unfortunately damaged during storage and subsequently disposed of by our contractors.”A Veolia spokesperson said: “We were asked by our client to collect the banner and store it temporarily at one of our local depots. Regrettably, after around 12 weeks, the banner’s condition deteriorated and became a health and safety hazard for our operations and the depot had to dispose of it. We have reimbursed Led By Donkeys for the full cost of the banner, due to the unintentional damage caused.”Explore more on these topicsLed By DonkeysProtestLondonLocal governmentGazaIsraelIsrael-Gaza warnewsShareReuse this content

title: Black people’s risk factors for stroke ‘rising faster than for white people’ | Stroke | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: King’s College London analysis finds diabetes and hypertension are more common in Black African and Caribbean people
Author: Tobi Thomas
Headline: Exclusive: King’s College London analysis finds diabetes and hypertension are more common in Black African and Caribbean people
Content: People from Black African backgrounds were also twice as likely to have a stroke without a prior risk factor diagnosis than white people, the study found.Photograph: Blend Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenPeople from Black African backgrounds were also twice as likely to have a stroke without a prior risk factor diagnosis than white people, the study found.Photograph: Blend Images/AlamyStrokeBlack people’s risk factors for stroke ‘rising faster than for white people’Exclusive: King’s College London analysis finds diabetes and hypertension are more common in Black African and Caribbean peopleTobi ThomasHealth and inequalities correspondentTue 28 Jul 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStroke risk factors including high blood pressure and diabetes are rising faster among people from Black African and Caribbean backgrounds compared with their white counterparts, according to analysis.Researchers at King’s College London analysed data from more than 8,500 adults over a 30-year period from the South London Stroke Register, one of the longest-running population-based stroke registers in the world.The study found that while the prevalence of stroke risk factors, including diabetes and hypertension, were increasing faster among Black people, those from Black African backgrounds were also twice as likely to experience stroke without a prior risk factor diagnosis than white people, at a rate of 12% compared with 6%. About one in six people across the UK will have a stroke in their lifetime.Diabetes was about twice as common in Black Caribbean and Black Africans on the stroke register compared with white participants, and high blood pressure was 29% more prevalent in Black Caribbean and 47% more prevalent in Black African people. Although diabetes rates increased for all ethnic groups over the 30-year study period, they increased most rapidly among Black African participants, rising from 21% between 1995 and 2004 to 41% between 2015 and 2024.Dr Eva Emmett, a research fellow at King’s College London and the lead author of the study, said: “Our study shows that the prevalence of pre-stroke hypertension and diabetes is higher and increasing faster in ethnic minority and lower socioeconomic groups. Together with Black people’s younger age at stroke and higher likelihood of having a stroke without a prior risk factor diagnosis, these findings call for targeted and earlier primary prevention efforts.“NHS health checks, which screen for hypertension and diabetes, begin at the age of 40. However, this may be too late for higher-risk groups who often experience stroke at a younger age.”She called for “universal improvements in cardiovascular risk detection” as well as more targeted prevention strategies, such as younger screening age for those most at risk.The data also revealed socioeconomic disparities among the study’s participants. The prevalence of diabetes was 23% higher in participants with manual occupations, such as bus drivers, security guards and plumbers, compared with those in non-manual employment such as teachers and nurses. Diabetes prevalence was also 21% higher in those with lower education levels.While diabetes diagnoses increased in all socioeconomic groups over time, the greatest increases were seen in those with routine and manual jobs and with lower education levels. Similarly, high blood pressure rates increased the most in those with lower socioeconomic status.Dr Maëva May,the director of policy at the Stroke Association, said the findings were a stark reminder that “the benefits of prevention are not being felt equally”.“Too many people from Black African and Black Caribbean communities, and those living in more deprived circumstances, are developing stroke risk factors earlier and are experiencing stroke before those risks have even been identified,” May said.“Stroke is not inevitable. Many strokes can be prevented by finding and treating conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes early, but that only works if people can access the right care at the right time. Preventing stroke means preventing inequalities in who gets the opportunity to stay well.”Explore more on these topicsStrokeDiabetesHigh blood pressureHealthNHSInequalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Gavin Newsom aide shares fresh details of affair | Gavin Newsom | The Guardian
description: Ruby Rippey writes in Vanity Fair of relationship with then San Francisco mayor and appears to contradict his account
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Ruby Rippey writes in Vanity Fair of relationship with then San Francisco mayor and appears to contradict his account
Content: Ruby Rippey and Gavin Newsom in this composite image. Newsom, who was single at the time, acknowledged the relationship in 2007.Composite: AP and Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRuby Rippey and Gavin Newsom in this composite image. Newsom, who was single at the time, acknowledged the relationship in 2007.Composite: AP and Getty ImagesGavin NewsomFormer Gavin Newsom aide shares fresh details of affairRuby Rippey writes in Vanity Fair of relationship with then San Francisco mayor and appears to contradict his accountDani AnguianoTue 28 Jul 2026 17.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 17.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former aide to Gavin Newsom has publicly shared for the first time her fullaccount of their affair, which took place more than two decades ago when Newsom was mayor ofSan Francisco.In a new essay published inVanity Fairon Tuesday, Ruby Rippey writes about her struggles with alcoholism, substance abuse and her relationship with Newsom while she worked as his appointments secretary and was married to his deputy chief of staff and later the manager of the mayor’s re-election campaign.The essay provides the most detailed look yet at Rippey’s relationship with Newsom, now in the final year of his second term as governor ofCalifornia– and is likely to rekindle interest in the scandal ahead of his widely expected run for the White House in 2028. In the essay, Rippey does not refer to Newsom by name, but as her “boss” and the “mayor”.“For my former boss, it is a footnote in a longer arc of ascent,” Rippey writes in the Vanity Fair essay, titled How I Blew Up – Then Rebuilt – My Life. “For me, it is the fracture that split my life into before and after.”Newsom, who was single at the time, publicly admitted to the relationship in 2007, memorably telling reporters at a city hall press conference: “Everything you’ve heard and read is true.” In his new memoir, Newsom describes their relationship as “the briefest of affairs”. But Rippey’s telling complicates his account of their story.Newsom writes in his new book that he “came clean” to her husband and his top aide Alex Tourk – a version Rippey says gives Newsom “credit for something I had already done”.“Technically defensible, perhaps, but one that leaves the unmistakable impression that he, not I, was the one who told Alex the truth,” she writes.In the essay, Rippey describes the early days of the newly elected mayor’s administration, her marriage, pregnancy, struggles with alcohol and her ensuing relationship with Newsom as it veered into an extramarital affair.She eventually went to rehab and left her job with the mayor’s office.After the story became public, Rippey was inundated with calls from journalists and was the subject of frenzied media coverage about the affair.Jennifer Siebel Newsom, the first partner of California who started dating Newsom shortly afterward,told journalistsin 2007 that Rippey was the “culprit”– remarks she later apologized for.The office of the governor and a spokesperson for Siebel Newsom did not immediately respond to a request for comment.In the aftermath of the incident, Kamala Harris, then the district attorney, contacted Rippey, she writes. Rippey was being urged to speak publicly about the incident, she told Harris, who advised her to pause and that taking time would give her “better perspective”.“It turns out to be the best advice I receive. I am newly sober and still inside the wreckage – unable to make sense of anything, let alone speak clearly about it,” Rippey writes.Rippey and her husband eventually divorced.For years, Rippey said little publicly about her relationship with Newsom. During the MeToo movement, she observed a new narrative about their relationship emerge in which Rippey saw herself cast as a “powerless subordinate”, she writes.At the time, Rippey said she was doubtful it applied to her situation. Although she was Newsom’s “subordinate”, shesaid in 2018,she was also “a free-thinking, 33-year-old, adult married woman and mother. Also happened to have an unfortunate inclination toward drinking-to-excess and self-destruction.”Taking responsibility felt like the last form of agency, Rippey writes in the essay. But since the reckoning, she has re-evaluated the role power can play in a relationship between a subordinate and their boss.“Both things are true,” she writes. “I am responsible for what I did. Power does not distribute consequences evenly.”Rippey is now 20 years sober, she writes, and has remarried and rebuilt her relationship with her ex-husband.Explore more on these topicsGavin NewsomSan FranciscoCaliforniaDemocratsUS politicsWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Florida becomes first state in nearly a decade to execute two people on same day | Florida | The Guardian
description: State kills Dominick Occhicone, 80, and James Duckett, 68, as Ron DeSantis pushes executions before term ends
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: State kills Dominick Occhicone, 80, and James Duckett, 68, as Ron DeSantis pushes executions before term ends
Content: Florida state prison in Raiford in Union county.Photograph: Douglas R Clifford/Tampa Bay Times/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFlorida state prison in Raiford in Union county.Photograph: Douglas R Clifford/Tampa Bay Times/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockFloridaFlorida becomes first state in nearly a decade to execute two people on same dayState kills Dominick Occhicone, 80, and James Duckett, 68, as Ron DeSantis pushes executions before term endsAssociated PressTue 28 Jul 2026 19.16 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlorida on Tuesday became the first state in nearly a decade to carry out two executions in a single day, putting to death an 80-year-old man who was the second-oldest inmate known to receive a lethal injection in modern US history.Hours earlier, the state executed a former police officer convicted of the killing of a young girl.Alarm as Florida rushes to carry out ‘incredibly rare’ double executionRead moreRon DeSantis, Florida’s Republican governor, has made the state’s death chamber the nation’s busiest at the end of his final term, saying too many families have waited too long to see justice.The lethal injections just hours apart were the first nearly back-to-back executions since Arkansas put two men to death three hours apart in 2017.DeSantis, who has the authority under Florida law to set execution dates, decided earlier this month to carry out both executions on the same day.Nationwide, the use of the death penalty had been declining for two decades, but that number has ticked up behind the increased pace in Florida. Since 2025 began, Florida has carried out nearly half the state executions across the country.Dominick Anthony Occhicone, the octogenarian, was pronounced dead at 6.13pm at Florida state prison near Starke following a three-drug injection. His execution came nearly five hours after the ex-police officer, James Aren Duckett, 68, received a lethal dose in the same death chamber.The curtain to the chamber went up for the last time on Tuesday at Occhicone’s 6pm scheduled execution hour. Occhicone was strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm and a spiritual adviser near his feet.Asked if he wished to make a statement, Occhicone said he thanked all of his Christian brothers for visiting him over the years. He also apologized to the family of the victims and to his own family for what he had put them through.“I know it don’t mean much, but I’m sorry,” Occhicone said. “I never meant to do what I did.”The injection began at 6.02pm followed by several minutes of deep breathing. When Occhicone’s breathing slowed, a warden shook him and yelled his name but there was no response.Occhicone, who was convicted of killing his ex-girlfriend’s parents in 1986, is the oldest prisoner executed in Florida’s history since modern record-keeping began a century ago.An older inmate, 83-year-old Walter Moody Jr, received a lethal injection in Alabama in 2018 for a wave of mail bombs in 1989 that killed a federal judge and wounded a Black civil rights attorney.Duckett was pronounced dead early on Tuesday afternoon following a three-drug injection. Duckett was convicted of raping and drowning 11-year-old Teresa McAbee while he was working as a police officer in central Florida in 1987.Duckett declined to make a final statement, responding: “No, sir” when asked. About four minutes after the execution began, the prison’s warden shook Duckett and shouted his name, but there was no response.Afterward, the girl’s family members said they had suffered for decades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I waited nearly 40 years to have him dead,” Dorthy Tula, the victim’s mother, said before breaking down. “This man took advantage of his badge,” said Tracy Mcfall-Buskirk, the girl’s cousin.Until Tuesday, a total of 17 executions had been carried out in the US so far this year, with Florida carrying out more than all other states combined.Both men saw last-ditch appeals to the US supreme court denied onTuesday after the Florida supreme court declined to intervene last week.Duckett’s attorneys had unsuccessfully claimed his innocence and argued against the state’s handling of DNA evidence.Occhicone’s attorneys said several age-related ailments, including kidney and prostate problems, could make his execution especially painful, constituting cruel and unusual punishment.DeSantis has not said why he scheduled two executions six hours apart. All Florida executions are by injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the department of corrections.DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw a record 19 executions last year, more in a single year than any other Florida governor since the reinstatement of the death penalty in the US in 1976.Florida now has executed 30 people since the beginning of 2025 while the rest of the US states combined have carried out 35 executions over the same time frame.Another execution in Florida is set for August.Explore more on these topicsFloridaCapital punishmentRon DeSantisUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Joe Biden appears to discuss sensitive information on tape with ghostwriter | Joe Biden | The Guardian
description: In recordings made in 2016 and 2017 former president also appears to describe possessing classified information
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: In recordings made in 2016 and 2017 former president also appears to describe possessing classified information
Content: President Joe Biden speaks at the International African American Museum in Charleston, South Carolina, on 19 January 2025.Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/APView image in fullscreenPresident Joe Biden speaks at the International African American Museum in Charleston, South Carolina, on 19 January 2025.Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/APJoe BidenJoe Biden appears to discuss sensitive information on tape with ghostwriterIn recordings made in 2016 and 2017 former president also appears to describe possessing classified informationAnna BettsTue 28 Jul 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer US presidentJoe Bidenappeared to discuss sensitive information and describe possessing classified documents in audio recordings released on Monday by the Oversight Project, a conservative activist group.The heavily redacted transcripts and recordings were made in 2016 and 2017, while Biden was working with a ghostwriter on his 2017 memoir,Promise Me, Dad: A Year of Hope, Hardship, and Purpose.No classified material was ever alleged to have appeared in the book.Biden, at times, seems to struggle to remember certain details or dates regarding events and topics in the transcripts and recordings, prompting the Oversight Project – as well as some conservative media outlets – to allege that he was “already demonstrating significant cognitive decline”in the years before he ran for president.In arecording dated October 2016, near the end of Biden’s second term as vice- president under former president Barack Obama, Biden can be heard discussing notes he says he kept from his time in office.“There was a lot of stuff going on at the same time in foreign policy,” Bidensaid. “You didn’t want to go into it, but I have extensive notes … over this period of time.”“Oh, that’s in – oh, you actually have those here,” the writer responds. To which Biden says, “yeah, now, there’s a lot of other notes too”, and goes on to say: “These – this is my – they didn’t even know I had this.“Some of this stuff, I’m not, you know, going to – um so I go back, you know what I mean?” Biden continues. “I have stuff on, you know, five – here we go, I mean, it’s like … I have stuff on all the way up to 5/19.”A representative for Biden did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on Tuesday about the recordings. But a spokesperson for Biden toldCBS News: “President Biden’s conversations for a book a decade ago that discussed his late son are private, and were provided to the Department of Justice on the express condition they stay that way.“Reversing course and making them public is just the latest example of this Administration weaponizing the DoJ for political retribution,” they added. “It’s wrong, and while President Biden disagrees with today’s decision, he also respects the courts and the vital role an independent judiciary plays in a healthy democracy.”Classified materialswere also foundat President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club after he left office following his first term. In 2024, a federal judgedismissedthe case, ruling that the special counsel who brought the prosecution had been improperly appointed.The tapes of Biden appear to align with the findings in former special counsel Robert Hur’s2024 reporton his handling of classified documents. That reportconcludedthat Biden had “willfully” kept and shared classified information “after his vice presidency when he was a private citizen” including “classified documents about military and foreign policy in Afghanistan” and handwritten notes about national security and foreign policy “implicating sensitive intelligence sources and methods”.The report also stated that Biden, during his eight years as vice-president, “regularly wrote notes by hand in notebooks” and that some of those notes “related to classified subjects” and that “some of the notes are themselves classified”.It also said that Biden “shared information, including some classified information, from those notebooks with his ghostwriter”.Hur described Biden as a “sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory”,prompting a furious responsefrom the then president and his officials, and claimed that Biden’s “memory was significantly limited, both during his recorded interviews with the ghostwriter in 2017, and in his interview with our office in 2023”.But Hur ultimately determined that no criminal charges were warranted, in part because he said it would be hard to convince a jury that “a former president well into his 80s” was guilty of a felony that “requires a mental state of willfulness”.The Oversight Project, a branch of the Heritage Foundation, sued for the tapes, which had been handed over to the justice department during its investigation into Biden’s handling of the records. House judiciary committee Republicans also sought the tapes. Biden hadfoughtthe release, but recentlywithdrew his legal challengeafter a federal appeals courtrejectedhis effort.In another recording dated 3November 2016, Biden tells the writer: “And, and then – and then the next thing I have here is – this is classified. It’s all – it goes through the 17th.” The context of this clip is not clear.In a separate recording dated16 February 2017,about a month after Biden left office, Biden tells the ghostwriter: “After that diary entry, the next one, between that and the 7th of July” was a “was a long meeting on the security council on – and part of it’s classified”.Later in that recording, Biden says: “So this was – I, early on, in ’09 – I just found all of the classified stuff downstairs. I wrote the President a handwritten 40-page memorandum arguing against deploying additional troops to Iraq – I mean, to Afghanistan – on the grounds that it wouldn’t matter, that the day we left would be like the day before we arrived.”In astatement on Monday,the Oversight Project said that since 2024, it and the Heritage Foundation “fought tooth and nail to bring these tapes to light”.Explore more on these topicsJoe BidenUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ebay and ex-executives to pay $55.7m to couple sent cockroaches in harassment campaign | eBay | The Guardian
description: Bloggers David and Ina Steiner were stalked by eBay executives over their critical coverage of the company
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bloggers David and Ina Steiner were stalked by eBay executives over their critical coverage of the company
Content: David and Ina Steiner arrive at a federal courthouse for the sentencing hearings for former eBay executives, in Boston, Massachusetts, on 29 September 2022.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid and Ina Steiner arrive at a federal courthouse for the sentencing hearings for former eBay executives, in Boston, Massachusetts, on 29 September 2022.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReuterseBayEbay and ex-executives to pay $55.7m to couple sent cockroaches in harassment campaignBloggers David and Ina Steiner were stalked by eBay executives over their critical coverage of the companyReutersTue 28 Jul 2026 14.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEbay and three former top executives have agreed to pay $55.7m to resolve a lawsuit by a Massachusetts couple who fell victim ⁠to a bizarre stalking and ⁠harassment campaign carried out ​by several of its employees in retaliation for their coverage of the e-commerce company in a newsletter they publish.David and Ina Steiner announced the settlement late on Monday, bringing an end to a ⁠case they filed in 2021 in Boston federal court after several formereBayemployees were prosecuted for targeting them in a cyberstalking campaign that involved sending the couple cockroaches, fly larvae and a bloody Halloween pig mask.As part of ⁠the settlement, eBay agreed to pay $46.15m to the couple; fund $6m in charitable contributions to non-profit organizations; and issue a “strongly-worded” statement about the conduct ​of three of its top former executives.“We believe this resolution ‌sends a clear message that corporations and ‌their executives cannot engage in this type of misconduct without facing significant consequences,” Christopher Murphy, the Steiners’ attorney, said in a statement.Ebay said ‌in a statement that what happened to the Steiners was “wrong, reprehensible and should never have happened”.“We continue to extend our deepest apologies to the Steiners,” the company said. “This agreement is consistent with our commitment to fairly compensate the Steiners and fulfills our efforts to make things right.”Seven former eBay workers pleaded guilty and received sentences of as high as 57 months in prison for participating in the scheme, which also involved several of them traveling from California to Natick, Massachusetts, to surveil the Steiners and try to install a GPS tracking ‌device on their car.Prosecutors have said that the aim was to silence them after senior executives deemed their newsletter, EcommerceBytes, critical of the company. The campaign began after the then CEO, Devin Wenig, in August 2019 texted Steve Wymer, then ​its chief communications officer, that it was time to “take her down”, referring to Ina Steiner, according to prosecutors and the Steiners. Ebay itself was criminally charged and agreed in 2024 to pay a $3m fine.Wenig, a former Thomson Reuters executive who stepped down as eBay’s CEO in September 2019, was never charged. His lawyers have argued he had no knowledge or involvement in the harassment campaign and that his messages had been advocating for a ⁠public relations strategy to address Ina Steiner’s reporting.As part of the settlement, the Steiners’ attorneys said Wenig will ​pay them $2m and make a $1m ​donation to a charity focused on protecting first amendment ​rights in the name of Ina Steiner.“No one should ever have been subjected to what the Steiners endured in ​2019, and I’m saddened by ‌it, especially because it occurred ​during my time as CEO ​of eBay,” Wenig said in a statement on Tuesday. “This behavior is antithetical to everything I stand for and believe in.“Wendy Jones, who previously served as senior vice-president of global operations, and Wymer will pay the couple $500,000 and $50,000, respectively, the plaintiffs say. Their lawyers did not respond to requests for comment.The Steiners’ lawyers said additional settlements were reached with all other eBay employees named in their lawsuit.Explore more on these topicseBayE-commercenewsShareReuse this content

title: Qantas plane flies for more than 24 hours in record-breaking flight  | Qantas | The Guardian
description: The A350 landed in Toulouse 24 hours and 24 minutes after leaving Melbourne as airline plans direct London service
Author: Martin Farrer
Headline: The A350 landed in Toulouse 24 hours and 24 minutes after leaving Melbourne as airline plans direct London service
Content: The Qantas Airbus A350-1000ULR lands in Toulouse on Tuesday to complete its record-breaking flight.Photograph: Manuel Blondeau/AOP Press/SIPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Qantas Airbus A350-1000ULR lands in Toulouse on Tuesday to complete its record-breaking flight.Photograph: Manuel Blondeau/AOP Press/SIPA/ShutterstockQantasQantas plane flies for more than 24 hours in record-breaking flightThe A350 landed in Toulouse 24 hours and 24 minutes after leaving Melbourne as airline plans direct London serviceFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMartin Farrerand agenciesTue 28 Jul 2026 10.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQantas completed what is believed to be the longest-ever commercial flight when its Airbus jet landed in Toulouse on Tuesday after a flight from Melbourne lasting 24 hours and 24 minutes.The flight, which triggered a surge in online tracking, is part of the airline’s Project Sunrise in which it plans to use a new A350 jet to fly nonstop from Australia to London.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe specially adapted A350-1000ULR airliner ⁠is due to debut with the Australian carrier’s nonstop Sydney-London route from 2027. ​Airbus has been conducting ‌a two-month test campaign ‌on the aircraft since June.Airbus said the aircraft, which boasts a ‌extra fuel tank, remained in the air for 24 hours and 24 minutes, covering 23,075km (14,338 miles) in a route over the Pacific and Atlantic oceans without stopping, before landing at the plane’s factory in Toulouse in south-west France.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onplatform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueTuesday’s flight is thought to be the longest ever by a commercial plane, beating theprevious recordof 22 hours and 42 minutes set by a Boeing 777–200LR in 2005 between Hong Kong and London via the Pacific in 2005.In a test last week, the plane flew from Toulouse to Melbourne via the Indian Ocean injust over 19 hours.Flight-tracking provider Flightradar24 said the trip was thesecond-most-tracked flight everon its channels – behind a 2022 flight ‌carrying Queen Elizabeth II’s coffin – with more than 3.6 million people following its progress northwards via Canada.Qantas has ordered 12 modified A350-1000ULR aircraft, designed to connect Australia’s east coast with London and New York in ⁠about 20 hours.The services aim to turn what was ​once a five-day ​journey on the “Kangaroo Route” to ​London into a single flight lasting 19 to 21 ​hours, depending on ‌routing and winds.The ​first aircraft, ​which carries 20,000 additional litres of fuel and can seat 238 passengers, is due for delivery in April 2027.Qantas expects to operate daily nonstop flights between Sydney and London from October 2027.This article was amended on 29 July 2026 because the new aircraft will carry 20,000 litres of additional fuel, not 20,000 litres in total as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsQantasAir transportAirline industryBusinessEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: GSK to cut jobs amid £1.9bn cost-cutting plan and bid for faster drug development | Pharmaceuticals industry | The Guardian
description: Pharmaceuticals company is investing £400m in UK life sciences and moving scientists to new Cambridge R&D site
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Pharmaceuticals company is investing £400m in UK life sciences and moving scientists to new Cambridge R&D site
Content: GSK is to move more than 1,000 of its scientists to its new Cambridge research and development centre.Illustration: GSKView image in fullscreenGSK is to move more than 1,000 of its scientists to its new Cambridge research and development centre.Illustration: GSKPharmaceuticals industryGSK to cut jobs amid £1.9bn cost-cutting plan and bid for faster drug developmentPharmaceuticals company is investing £400m in UK life sciences and moving scientists to new Cambridge R&D siteBusiness live – latest updatesJoanna PartridgeTue 28 Jul 2026 09.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British drugmakerGSKis to announce sweeping job cuts as part of a £1.9bn cost-cutting programme to pay for a £400m investment in UK life sciences over the next three years, including in a new research and development centre in Cambridge, as it looks to develop drugs more quickly under its new chief executive.The pharmaceuticals company announced on Tuesday it will move more than 1,000 of its scientists to its new site on the Cambridge biomedical campus. It will close its R&D site in Stevenage inHertfordshireby 2029, while upgrading its R&D laboratories at nearby Ware and moving some employees there.Luke Miels, theGSKchief executive, said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products. It integrates GSK further into one of the world’s leading centres of knowledge and demonstrates the attractiveness of the UK’s life sciences ecosystem.”AstraZeneca boss urges western drugmakers to move at ‘Chinese speed’Read moreGSK’s new 300,000-sq ft (28,000 sq metre)Cambridgesite, which is being developed by the warehouse builder Prologis, is on one of the largest biomedical campuses in Europe. More than 22,000 people working in life sciences and more than 470 biopharma, biotech and AI companies are based there, and more than a million patients treated there each year.View image in fullscreenThe Cambridge site ‘will help us deliver new, competitive products’, said GSK’s chief executive, Luke Miels.Illustration: GSKThe company said the site would feature state of the art, tech-enabled labs to support its focus on research in areas including oncology, respiratory, hepatology, vaccines and HIV.The move will bring more scientists to the UK’s “golden triangle” – Cambridge, Oxford and London – where GSK said its teams would have access to a “world-class ecosystem of biomedical research, patient care and academia”.The company’s investment was welcomed by Andy Burnham, who described it as a “vote of confidence in British business”.The prime minister said it was “a boost for homegrown innovation and expertise. And a step towards more people getting access to new medicines and cutting-edge treatments that will change lives for the better.”GSK’s investment announcement comes just months after its rivalAstraZeneca, Britain’s biggest drugmaker, made a surprise U-turn andannounced a £300m investment in the UK, including a £200m expansion in Cambridge. It had previously paused large-scale projects in its home country in 2025, after becoming disillusioned with the business environment, including with the availability of new medicines on the NHS and drug pricing.Miels, who was previously GSK’s chief commercial officer, began a review of the FTSE 100 company’s drug pipeline when he took over fromEmma Walmsleyat the start of the year in a bid to develop competitive new medicines more quickly.View image in fullscreenA scientist prepares stem cells for research at the GSK research centre in Stevenage, Hertfordshire. This site will be closed by 2029.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersGSK now intends to launch 20 phase 3 trials, large-scale research studies designed to test how well a new treatment works compared with standard treatments or placebos – double the number announced earlier this year.The company, which is headquartered in London, declined to share the number of redundancies it would make globally as it announced a three-year cost savings programme targeting £1.9bn in annual savings by 2029.However, Miels told journalists that about 45% of planned savings would come from cutting support services, working on better procurement and simplifying processes, while a further 40% of targeted savings would come from moving resources away from established treatments in order to focus on new drugs.GSK’s move to close its Stevenage sitecomes just five yearsafter it announced plans to spend £400m in extending its campus, in a bid to build a cluster for new life sciences businesses.Shares in GSK rose by 6% after its announcement, one of the biggest risers on the London stock market on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsPharmaceuticals industryGSKBiotechnology industryCambridgeCambridgeshireHertfordshireStevenagenewsShareReuse this content

title: ICE-linked security firm reports UK revenue slump after asylum contract ends | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: MTC provided security at heavily criticised Manston centre in Kent – and could now make £500m managing arrivals at site
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: MTC provided security at heavily criticised Manston centre in Kent – and could now make £500m managing arrivals at site
Content: The Manston centre in Kent. MTC UK’s contract for providing security there ended in September 2025.Photograph: Stuart Brock/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Manston centre in Kent. MTC UK’s contract for providing security there ended in September 2025.Photograph: Stuart Brock/EPAImmigration and asylumICE-linked security firm reports UK revenue slump after asylum contract endsMTC provided security at heavily criticised Manston centre in Kent – and could now make £500m managing arrivals at siteJasper JollyandRob DaviesTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA private security companylinked to Donald Trump’s immigration crackdownreported a slump in UK revenues after an asylum centre contract ended but could make £500m managing the same facility until 2036.Management & Training Corporation (MTC) said sales fell from £28.4m to £17.6m in 2025 after its contract to provide “security and care” at theheavily criticised Manston sitein Kent ended in September.A public inquiry described Manston as “overcrowded, squalid and insanitary” between June and November 2022, when MTC took over provision of services for the Home Office. MTC said: “Decisions relating to the operation of the site sat outside of MTC’s contractual remit.”Company handling Australia’s immigration detention playing key role in Trump’s ICE migrant crackdownRead moreThe cessation of the contract last September pushed MTC UK to a £1.6m loss, Companies House filings show, compared with a profit of £1.3m in 2024.But MTC Definitive, a joint venture that MTC UK majority owns, won a contract in May for processing people who arrive on small boats “from disembarkation through to dispersal”.The Irregular Migration Management Services contract will run for six years, with the possibility of a further four-year extension. It covers two asylum processing centres, Manston and the Western Jet Foil site in Dover. MTC said: “We are committed to delivering a safe and secure environment at these centres, to enable UK Border Force officials to register and process individuals arriving into the UK by sea with dignity and respect.”Despite the loss, MTC UK’s highest-paid director received £211,000 in remuneration during 2025, an increase of 5%.View image in fullscreenThe contract will cover work across the Manston site and ‘associated disembarkation points’ for people arriving in boats along the Kent coast.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAEllie Reeves, the Labour MP appointed last week as attorney general, previouslycriticised high salaries for executivesat companies such as MTC.The company is owned by an American parent based in Utah, which runs prisons and job training centres in the US. Its facilities include five detention centres used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the department that has received a significant funding increase and been criticised for its brutality during Trump’s presidency.MTC said: “Our work in immigration detention spans multiple presidential administrations and predates the current administration. MTC’s responsibility is to provide safe and humane care to the men and women placed in its facilities by the federal government.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe new UK small boats contract is worth an initial £462m but could be worth as much as £539m if it is extended to last 10 years. The contract will cover the joint venture’s work across the Manston site and “associated disembarkation points” for people arriving in boats along theKentcoast.The award of the contract is being challenged in court by Mitie, another outsourcing company.According to the BBC, Mitie claimed in the high court that the Home Office failed to “prevent, identify and remedy conflicts of interest” because the MTC head of development, Dave Butler, was previously the deputy director of Manston.The Home Office said the claim was baseless and without merit, and there was no conflict of interest, the BBC reported.Before it received the Manston contract, MTC had beencriticised for dangerous conditionsat the Rainsbrook secure training centre, a youth jail in Warwickshire. Ofsted, the education regulator for England, said children were locked up for more than 23 hours a day with “no justifiable rationale” during the coronavirus pandemic, and later inspections found physical assaults, children carrying weapons and warnings from staff that someone was likely to die at the centre.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumManston asylum centreOutsourcingMitieDonald TrumpKentICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’ve always been wary of working together’: Val McDermid and Jo Sharp on writing a novel as a couple | Books | The Guardian
description: The bestselling crime writer and Scotland’s first female Geographer Royal had long kept their work separate, until a chance discovery about a doomed 17th-century expedition forced them to collaborate
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: The bestselling crime writer and Scotland’s first female Geographer Royal had long kept their work separate, until a chance discovery about a doomed 17th-century expedition forced them to collaborate
Content: ‘My mother always said I don’t play well with others’ … Val McDermid (right) and Jo Sharp.Photograph: Ryan RutherfordView image in fullscreen‘My mother always said I don’t play well with others’ … Val McDermid (right) and Jo Sharp.Photograph: Ryan RutherfordBooksInterview‘We’ve always been wary of working together’: Val McDermid and Jo Sharp on writing a novel as a coupleRobyn VinterThe bestselling crime writer and Scotland’s first female Geographer Royal had long kept their work separate, until a chance discovery about a doomed 17th-century expedition forced them to collaborateTue 28 Jul 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe airy, modern house on the outskirts of Edinburgh shared byVal McDermidand Jo Sharp is surrounded by greenery and feels as though it was designed to provide enough space for two minds to think.Both women are high achievers in their fields,a Scottish power couplemade up of theQueen of Crimeand the Scottish Geographer Royal. Happily for them, there is normally no overlap in their work.“We’d always been very wary of working together because we’d quite like to stay together,” says Sharp wryly. She looks at her partner of 13 years. “You don’t generally like to work with others.”McDermid responds: “No, my mother always used to say I don’t play well with others. She wasn’t far wrong.”McDermid’s mother would have to admit that This Door of the Seas – the couple’s jointly written novella, published next week – is an exception. The book is a fictionalised account of the 1698 Darien venture, in which more than 2,000 Scots, mostly fleeing famine, embarked on an ill-fated expedition to modern-day Panama, hoping to establish a trading colony and provide an overland route between the Atlantic and Pacific.It is no spoiler to reveal that the attempt bankrupted a struggling Scottish economy, hampered already by its overbearing neighbour, England. It propelled the country into signing the union agreement only seven years later, taking away Scotland’s parliament, its trading company and much of its pride.From then on, Scotland became an intrinsic part of the union, including the later evils of transatlantic slavery, a role that can sometimes go unacknowledged north of the border.Sharp says: “One of the things that we talked about a lot is that we didn’t want to be part of what is, I think, a bit of a whitewashing of Scotland’s history, to make us seem somehow not as culpable in terms of empire and around issues of race and racism.”View image in fullscreen‘I found it fascinating. It was a bit of history I had not heard about’ … Jo Sharp (right) says.Photograph: Val McDermid/Jo SharpSharp is a human geographer, with a background in geopolitics and international development. She is a professor of geography at the University of St Andrews, a member of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, and became Scotland’s first female Geographer Royal in 2022.Her civil partner, McDermid, has written 51 books, which have been translated into more than 40 languages, sold more than 20m copies and won a wealth of awards.At 71, nearly four decades after her debut,Report for Murder, followed by immensely popular crime series including the Tony Hill and Carol Jordan books, and the Karen Pirie novels, she continues to run rings around her readers, laying breadcrumbs and pulling rugs.The story came about through research Sharp was doing for a book festival talk. She was asked to speak about geography in Scotland, which she thought could be “quite dull”, and instead began researching the first Geographer Royal, who turned out to be “a really interesting character”.“I discovered that shortly after he was appointed, Scotland had this endeavour to set up a trading colony in Panama, and although he didn’t go himself, he sent someone to be his eyes and ears on the ground. I just found this fascinating, because it was a bit of history I had not heard about.”“I was telling Val all the things I’d found out about it and I said, ‘It would make a brilliant story, I just wish I could write it’,” says Sharp. “And Val then said, ‘maybe we should write it together,’ and before she got to the end of the sentence I had said yes.”McDermid says: “My experience of writing books that have elements of historical significance in them is that what you want is something that’s got enough information to hang a story on but enough gaps to colour in.”The aim is for the book to be “charmingly plausible”, a compliment once given to one of her historical novels. “That has been my watchword ever since. Make it charmingly plausible. Get the historical facts right and then colour in the bits around it.”The story is told by Dr James Wallace, a scientist, in letters to his wife, Eliza, and his sponsor, Sir Robert Sibbald, the first Geographer Royal of Scotland, founder of the Edinburgh botanic gardens and physician to the king.Sharp and McDermid worked on the structure during a rainy car journey back to Edinburgh. McDermid recalls: “You said, ‘how do we do this?’ and I said, ‘we’ll make it an epistolary novel’, and I had to explain what that was.” (“That’s not true!” interjects Sharp.)“I was convinced someone might have had this idea already because the more excited I got about it the more I thought, surely someone’s thought about this,” says Sharp. The book felt like a good addition to the publisherBirlinn’s Darkland Talesseries – reimaginings of Scottish historical and folk tales by different authors – for which McDermid had already contributed the Shakespeare retelling Queen Macbeth.“Now the slight complication with all of this,” says Sharp, “is that about two months later, Val went in for open-heart surgery –”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“– Which I hadn’t entirely anticipated,” McDermid adds. She needed an aortic valve replacement and two coronary bypasses to fix a condition spotted initially by her partner, who noticed her heart was skipping a beat.Sharp continues: “But the advantage of that was that I’d taken time off work to look after Val in her recovery, and there was only so much time I could wander around in my nurse’s uniform.”Sharp did the vast majority of the research – hunting down documents including letters and ship manifests at the National Library of Scotland – while McDermid was recovering, but the pair worked together on the writing, taking turns to write and then edit each other’s work.Slowly they began to unpick many of the myths about the Darien venture being a bumbling attempt from Scotland to stand on its own two feet, many of which Sharp realised had come not from factual accounts at the time but from political pamphlets.View image in fullscreen‘Get the historical facts right and then colour in the bits around it’ … Val McDermid (left) and Jo Sharp in their home.Photograph: Ryan RutherfordThe truth was the landscape was considerably harder to navigate than they had been led to believe – the colony unexpectedly came under relentless attack from the Spanish settlers who occupied territory nearby, and more than 80% of the Scots who had travelled over died within a year, mostly from tropical diseases or famine.“People also don’t understand that nations all around Europe were setting up colonies – nine out of 10 failed,” says McDermid. “So this wasn’t that only the Scots failed, everybody failed and everybody failed a lot.”Sharp adds: “It feeds into that story that Scotland just isn’t good enough to go alone, that we need that support of a bigger neighbour and all that kind of stuff.”View image in fullscreenThis Door of the Seas.The couple have worked together once before, editing an anthology,Imagine a Country, in which Scottish writers lay out their vision for a better future. With contributors including Alan Cumming, Ali Smith, Carol Ann Duffy, Ian Rankin and Alexander McCall Smith, the collection came six years after the Scottish independence referendum, in a nation still struggling to heal from some of the divisiveness of the campaign. It was not a political book, but the pair are strong supporters of Scottish independence, believing Scotland should be given a chance to succeed on its own merits.This Door of the Seas is more explicitly political: as the creeping sensation of betrayal by the English and Scottish landed gentry takes over, Wallace’s outrage seems to come freely to the book’s modern writers. It is a multi-generational bruise that lingers for many Scottish people more than 300 years later.Readers will undoubtedly find similarities between those fleeing Scottish famine in the 1600s and modern refugees, many of whom do not fully comprehend the danger of the journey or the hostile environment they will be arriving in. The couple recognise the parallel.“When the country that you’re living in offers you no hope,” says McDermid, “then the slenderest strands of hope you grasp, even if it’s not rooted in a reality.”This Door of the Seas is published on 6 August. McDermid and Sharp will be speaking atEdinburgh international book festivalon 17 August.Explore more on these topicsBooksFictionVal McDermidCrime fictionGeographyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Portrait of a City review – master photographers capture the US cityscape in all its grime, grit and glory | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Era-defining photographs from the likes of Alfred Stieglitz, Saul Leiter and Dorothea Lange showcase the urban landscape, from midnight crime scenes to gloomy corridors
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: Era-defining photographs from the likes of Alfred Stieglitz, Saul Leiter and Dorothea Lange showcase the urban landscape, from midnight crime scenes to gloomy corridors
Content: An immense city … Louis Faurer’s 1949 Looking at the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center.Photograph: Louis Faurer/Howard Greenberg Gallery, New YorkView image in fullscreenAn immense city … Louis Faurer’s 1949 Looking at the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center.Photograph: Louis Faurer/Howard Greenberg Gallery, New YorkArt and designReviewPortrait of a City review – master photographers capture the US cityscape in all its grime, grit and gloryDulwich Picture Gallery, LondonEra-defining photographs from the likes of Alfred Stieglitz, Saul Leiter and Dorothea Lange showcase the urban landscape, from midnight crime scenes to gloomy corridorsCharlotte JansenTue 28 Jul 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 11.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis – only the second photography exhibition in Dulwich Picture Gallery’s history – is a quietly contemplative but gripping show that traces two intersecting developments: the construction of the modern urban environment and the language of photography.Focusing exclusively on works from era-defining photographers of the 20th century made in cities across the US, it’s a concise overview that begins with the pictorialist pioneers of New York, Alfred Stieglitz and Edward Steichen, and keeps moving through masterpieces, starting with early examples of social documentary photography – Dorothea Lange’s Migrant Mother and White Angel Breadline, and Lewis Hine’s emblematic portrait of the high-steel ironworker Victor “Frenchy” Gosselin working on the construction of the Empire State Building.All the greats are here: Ilse Bing, Mary Ellen Mark, Diane Arbus, Saul Leiter, Richard Avedon, among others. This is partly because this show is a bit of an unusual beast: it exclusively presents works belonging to the DNB Savings Bank Foundation collection. That means the curatorial choices are limited.View image in fullscreenAll the greats are here … Mary Ellen Mark’s 1987 The Damm Family in Their Car.Photograph: Mary Ellen Mark/Mary Ellen Mark FoundationA series of short film pieces offer other interpretations. A 44-second clip of footage of the White Angel soup kitchen in San Francisco in 1931, where Lange’s indelible Great Depression image was made, gives an entirely different impression of the place from the grim loneliness depicted in the photograph. Set to an upbeat swing soundtrack, we see a lively community presided over by a jovial matron who distributes food and repairs clothing with a smile.Many of the photographers in the first part of the show trained as painters, and it shows in the glorious attentiveness to composition and light. Aaron Siskind’s Harlem Document reflects the influence of his friendships with Rothko and Kline, searching in Harlem’s torn posters and peeling paint for his own kind of abstract expression that also created a new photographic language for social protest.View image in fullscreenMoments only a city can yield … Arthur Leipzig’s 1948 Divers, East River.Photograph: Arthur Leipzig/Howard Greenberg Gallery, New YorkFrom the Great Depression to the New Deal, urban construction, regeneration and optimism soon slide into something more sinister. Images of solitary figures against the immensity of the city recur – Louis Faurer’s 1949 Looking at the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center says it all – an anonymous figure in a fedora looks towards the building, so mighty it fills the whole frame.At night, a city’s tensions rise to the surface, and all the weirdos come out. The highlights are the images that revel in this, like Weegee’s ominous, sensationalist snapshots of New York after dark, depicting murders, awful accidents and the odd moments only a city can yield – a person’s face, eyes closed, juts out from a column in an urban passageway; a large clock in the background pulls your eye into the inky shadows.There is a work of achingly simple genius by Roy DeCarava. Hallway is a photograph of an empty corridor in a tenement building in Harlem, much like the one the artist grew up in. It’s lit dimly by a single lightbulb, almost entirely swallowed by shadows, as the lines of the walls draw your eye in and down the space. DeCarava’s claustrophobic image makes you feel what it is to stand in that space. He finds the richness and expressivity in the colour black, as complex, volumetric and varied as any other hue.The exhibition as a whole retells the American narrative of the city – almost all of the photographers here are first- or second-generation European immigrants. It also shows how photography became a way for artists to deal with the overwhelming nature of the city, to try to take hold of it, to make it their own – or try, like Garry Winogrand, to disappear into it completely, to come closer to “not existing” as the photographer described his process, a quote emphasised on the exhibition wall. Portrait of a City is about the multiplicity of quiet-but-dazzling instants that happen every day – like Peter Hujar’s Richie, standing to reflect for a second in the rain on a street in New York at night, raindrops glimmering on a car windscreen.View image in fullscreenQuiet but dazzling … Peter Hujar’s 1985 Richie.Photograph: Peter Hujar/Peter Hujar Archive/Artists Rights Society, New York/DACS LondonWe move through the 60s and 70s, where the hair gets hipper and politics get more intense, and end up on the subway, engulfed by 1980s Leica shots that Bruce Davidson made on New York’s graffiti-covered trains. Here we’re in motion again, in the place where city life collides across culture, age, race and class. People go to celebrations, to work, fall asleep, fall in love, fight. The crimson light of sunset skies bathes the carriages in a beautiful, sensuous glow. The train keeps moving. And the unstoppable city remains in maddening, merciless motion.Portrait of a City: A Century of American Photographyis at Dulwich Picture Gallery, London, until 4 OctoberExplore more on these topicsArt and designExhibitionsPhotographyDulwich Picture GalleryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Just when you thought it was safe … the shark movie is back for more | Thrillers | The Guardian
description: Shark Week arrives in an overstuffed period for the film genre even if nothing will ever rival the greatest of them all
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Shark Week arrives in an overstuffed period for the film genre even if nothing will ever rival the greatest of them all
Content: The Devil's Mouth poster.Photograph: AmazonView image in fullscreenThe Devil's Mouth poster.Photograph: AmazonThrillersJust when you thought it was safe … the shark movie is back for moreShark Week arrives in an overstuffed period for the film genre even if nothing will ever rival the greatest of them allJesse HassengerTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 05.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTracy Jordan, Tracy Morgan’s character on 30 Rock, once advised a friend to live every week like it’s Shark Week. In 2026, Hollywood has finally taken these sage words to heart.‘It put the fear of God in the audience’: the incredible story of how Jaws changed HollywoodRead moreThough Discovery Channel is only observing its annual Shark Week of shark-themed programming for the customary seven days, shark movies have been enjoying a yearlong renaissance – in terms of volume, if not necessarily quality. Two shark thrillers – The Devil’s Mouth on Prime Video and Above & Below as a paid VOD rental – are releasing this week, presumably to complement nonfictional Shark Week programming, but they’re far from the only fish in the sea.
