Earlier this month, Clint Eastwood’s daughter starred in The Bay, another VOD title. In June, there was Chum, starring Alice Eve; in May,Deep Water, Renny Harlin’s return to the subgenre following his classic Deep Blue Sea. Before that,Thrashwas a Netflix hit. That’s half a dozen shark movies so far this year. It’s a wonder no one has arranged a 10th-anniversary re-release ofThe Shallows.Obviously there’s a baseline, sellable level of interest in shark thrillers, which are often positioned as something akin to an all-natural slasher: horror movies that expand just slightly beyond the bounds of the world we know (the beach, the ocean, observing nature) and into heightened but not completely outlandish territory. They’re the water equivalent of the masked killer stalking around the woods, only we’ve all seen footage of sharks – thanks to Discovery and the like – so we can all agree that they are definitely out there, and can be deadly to humans – even if the reality is far less gruesome, frequent or vengeful than their movie equivalents.What makes the pursuit of new shark movies more quixotic than some other horror/thriller subgenres is the existence of a single agreed-upon masterpiece that’s near-impossible to match. While it’s unlikely that any given new landlubber slasher will represent a pantheon-level genre-definer, at least there are a variety of near-perfect classics to emulate: the proto-slasher creepiness of Psycho, the unnerving rural underbelly of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, the suburban menace of Halloween, the phantasmagorical dreamscape of A Nightmare on Elm Street. With shark movies, it’sJaws, and then everything else. (Some of those slashers have good and/or interesting sequels with further inventions; not so Jaws, which just has three increasingly ludicrous and cheap brand extensions.) Working from maybe the beachiest beach read of all time with a notoriously finicky fake shark, Steven Spielberg crafted a movie that’s simultaneously a male-bonding character study, an indictment of keep-the-beaches-open American capitalism, and an expertly tuned thrill machine complete with unforgettable theme music. By sheer force of quality, it reinvented the barely there shark movie, and the whole of summer movies along with it.Eventually, a few particularly strong iterations did figure out how to operate within the shadow of Jaws, though they had to wait out those lousy follow-ups, which reached a nadir in 1987 with the all-time stinker Jaws: The Revenge. Deep Blue Sea, Harlin’s amped-up summer movie from 1999, feels like a Jaws sequel done right: it goes the bigger/faster/crazier route, with genetically modified sharks and noticeably dumber humans. Its thematic is the same old monster-movie scientists-playing-god cautionary tale, but as a creature feature it’s juicy, well-cast (Samuel L Jackson!), and a lot of fun. Another highlight goes in the opposite direction. The aforementioned The Shallows, from summer 2016, strips down the three-men-on-a-boat climax of Jaws even further; most of the movie is just Blake Lively stranded on a rock, attempting to outwit a particularly persistent shark as she grieves the loss of her mother. Director Jaume Collet-Serra has multiple movies that play with Hitchcock-style location limitations; The Shallows is one of his most limited and also one of his best.View image in fullscreenBlake Lively in The Shallows.Photograph: Courtesy/Rex/ShutterstockThe Shallows – along with the more bummed-out survival-thriller indies Open Water and47 Meters Down– has managed to help redefine the parameters of the shark thriller. Over the past decade, they tend to either follow the Shallows/47 Meters route of a handful of characters, usually women, exorcising some form of trauma or interpersonal conflict through a trial-by-teeth encounter with sharks; or attempt to be sort of a thinking man’s version of Sharknado, the tediously “knowing” D-movie franchise from cable’s SyFy, where sharks are flown into unlikely places or situations. (Think of the recent Netflix hit Under Paris, which contrived irresistible but ultimately schlocky ways for CG sharks to turn up in the Seine circa the 2024 Olympics.) If nothing else, both styles set up more achievable goals than evoking a truly great movie like Jaws.So how do this year’s crop stack up in that context? Of the two Shark Week releases, The Devil’s Mouth follows the Shallows path, while Above & Below has more of a Sharknado style, though it also borrows heavily from 47 Meters Down. The Devil’s Mouth focuses on friends, led by two besties (Kathryn Newton and Lana Condor), vacationing in Thailand, where they embark on a swimming tour of an off-ocean cave system. The movie, seems, if anything, overly self-conscious about the motivations that are supposed to fuel characters in survival thrillers, which means the two leads both have dead parents, while also engaging in a semi-toxic dynamic that the movie never quite fully defines. As a result, it ultimately feels like it’s a movie about the perils of having a best friend who’s just generally kind of annoying.View image in fullscreenA still from 47 Meters Down.Photograph: Studios/Kobal/Rex/ShutterstockBut its location shooting with built-in atmosphere, and the sparing use of shark effects this allows, goes a long way toward making it watchable Shallows knockoff. If director Jeff Wadlow doesn’t have the B-movie mastery of Collet-Serra, he at least has some B-minus-movie energy and watchable stars, especially scream queen Newton. Above & Below should really be the kickier B-movie affair, following another group of five young people on vacation, whose shark-observing cage-dive boat turns out to be affiliated with a group of criminals. Like 47 Meters Down, much of it involves the logistics of conserving oxygen while trapped underwater, to which DTV veteran Jesse V Johnson adds some criminal bickering and shootouts above sea level; not quite Sharknado bombast, but a similar sense of cross-breeding. Antonio Banderas is entertaining as the courteous but merciless head criminal, but the fusion of literal and metaphorical sharks is disappointingly rote. It’s two chintzy DTV movies in one, a 90-minute time-saver but little else.The thing is, as many inventive ideas as shark-movie-makers can brainstorm, the creatures themselves are fairly inflexible; neither middling CG nor real footage nor mechanical models tend to feel particularly convincing on their own. These real animals are also major visual effects challenges that have largely been shunted downstream to smaller productions that can’t always handle it. Even the odd big-budget attempt, like Jason Statham’s Meg movies, are pretty crummy-looking. Just look at Harlin’s revisitation of his old feeding grounds with Deep Water. It’s not a sequel to Deep Blue Sea, but would-be companion piece that combines a plane-crash survival narrative with a bunch of sharks. Guess which component is more suspenseful and believable on screen? Unlike their Deep Blue Sea counterparts, the sharks wind up feeling like afterthoughts.Maybe that’s why some of the best recent shark-style movies don’t feature sharks at all. 2019’sCrawlfollows the Shallows template of a young woman with family issues thrust into a dangerous solo mission, here rescuing her hurricane-stranded father rather than saving herself, only she’s bedeviled by alligators rather than sharks. It’s so effective that this year’s Netflix shark flagship Thrash more or less ripped it back off, subbing sharks swimming around submerged homes back in for the gators. Or consider the surprise hit Fall, which features two young women with an intense history, stranded at great height, no creatures required.That movie is also just a plain old survival thriller, of course, but it’s also illustrative of how little the sharks themselves often bring to these scenarios, especially when movies can’t afford the effects needed to make them look realistically scary. Shark movies may be flashier offshoots of Shark Week that can run all year (or at least all summer), but apart from their inability to top Jaws, it’s hard for them to compete with the eerie majesty of the real thing. Spielberg incorporated that elusiveness into his work, defined as much by what we can’t see from land as what we might glimpse within the water. That’s not even necessarily an argument for hiding the shark so much as giving both the creature and the human motivations some space. Most contemporary shark pictures are just looking for other movies to chew on.Explore more on these topicsThrillersSharksJawsHorror filmsAction and adventure filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lesvia review – the rise and fall of an amazing lesbian community on Sappho’s actual island home | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Tzeli Hadjidimitriou grew up on Lesbos, and her elegant debut feature explores how the Greek poet’s birthplace became a hub for lesbians
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Director Tzeli Hadjidimitriou grew up on Lesbos, and her elegant debut feature explores how the Greek poet’s birthplace became a hub for lesbians
Content: LesviaPhotograph: Tzeli HadjidimitriouView image in fullscreenLesviaPhotograph: Tzeli HadjidimitriouMoviesReviewLesvia review – the rise and fall of an amazing lesbian community on Sappho’s actual island homeDirector Tzeli Hadjidimitriou grew up on Lesbos, and her elegant debut feature explores how the Greek poet’s birthplace became a hub for lesbiansLeslie FelperinTue 28 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfine-boned, elegantly crafted documentary, this first feature from Greek director Tzeli Hadjidimitriou tells a story at once personal and public: about the lesbian scene that grew up around the town of Eressos on the island of Lesbos (also called Lesvos). Hadjidimitriou is from the island, but not Eressos itself, which was once the home of the seventh century BC poetSappho, whose love poetry threads through the film. Given that pedigree, lesbians, including the director herself, have flocked to Eressos for years to pay homage. By the 1970s, the growing number of queer visitors started to form not just a scene but a community, at first one centred on the nudist beach where many women camped out.Hadjidimitriou’s still photographs are also spliced in throughout, capturing the glorious sensuality of these often naked women, most looking chuffed to bits to have found a little corner of heaven where they can be themselves. But relations with the local people were not always easy, and unsurprisingly the tourists had to contend with homophobia of varying degrees of vocalness, as well as aggressive invasion of their women-only spaces. Luckily, as one woman recalls, there were usually a few butches around to help hustle the intruders off. Over time, tolerance grew, greased by the money the visitors brought to the island, and eventually female-run bars and hotels sprang up.If it all ended there it would be a utopian tale of paradise found. But things go wrong, perhaps related toGreece’s economic crisis that started in 2009,and which exposed the nation’s financial instability. Within a few years, most of the lesbian bars and women-run hotels closed down, and now the community seems much more marginalised.Hadjidimitriou builds her oral history through interviews with some of the many women from all over the world who knew Eressos in its golden years, making for a touching film, and for all the place’s faded glory, it goes on still with younger generations continuing to visit. The sound design, almost constantly incorporating the sea, adds an evocative layer.Lesvia is on digital platforms from 3 August.This article was amended on 28 July to correct the film’s star rating.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsLGBTQ+ rightsGreeceSapphoEuropePoetryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Holly Willoughby Together review – a marginally less agonising With Love, Meghan  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The former This Morning host has done a Meghan, rebranding herself as a cookery guru with a YouTube show that veers from agonisingly dull courgette slicing to sweary banter. Somehow, in spite of it all, I am rooting for her
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The former This Morning host has done a Meghan, rebranding herself as a cookery guru with a YouTube show that veers from agonisingly dull courgette slicing to sweary banter. Somehow, in spite of it all, I am rooting for her
Content: ‘An aggressive audition for whether Holly Willoughby is allowed to be famous again’ … Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy).Photograph: Hungry Bear MediaView image in fullscreen‘An aggressive audition for whether Holly Willoughby is allowed to be famous again’ … Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy).Photograph: Hungry Bear MediaTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewHolly Willoughby Together review – a marginally less agonising With Love, MeghanThe former This Morning host has done a Meghan, rebranding herself as a cookery guru with a YouTube show that veers from agonisingly dull courgette slicing to sweary banter. Somehow, in spite of it all, I am rooting for herStuart HeritageTue 28 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHolly Willoughby is a woman in search of a fresh start. Her stint on This Morning ended messily, with her response to the Phillip Schofield scandal – the infamous “Are you OK? I hope so” monologue – making her a figure of public mockery. Subsequent attempts to relaunch her career, like her short-lived time hosting a Bear Grylls reality show, stalled. So now it has come to this:Holly WilloughbyTogether (With Voy).Your response to it will vary based on how generous you’re feeling. The kindest offering would be to say that Willoughby has pivoted to YouTube, having cannily observed that television is dead and this is where all the eyeballs are these days. It is a cookery and lifestyle show that allows her to be unapologetically herself without the meddling influence of executives who have spent years trying to enforce a persona upon her.Then there is the less kind option, which is to say that Willoughby has done a Meghan.This, unfortunately, is kind of true. Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy, don’t forget) is extremelyWith Love, Meghanin tone and presentation. It is a heavily manicured cookery show, presented by a woman who seems as if she needs quite a lot of help in the kitchen, that exists more as a referendum on the host than a traditional show. However, let’s be clear that this is far better than that, because Willoughby lacks the sweatily desperate control freakery that made With Love, Meghan such an uncomfortable watch. Perhaps it would be better to call this a Saturday Kitchen rip-off and be done with it.From what I can tell, every episode of Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy) will see Willoughby – and, by association, the health company Voy – cook a dish in her monochromatically pastel kitchen with a guest. Episode one’s guest is Stanley Tucci, who is about as safe a pair of hands as you could hope for. He’s chatty. He can cook. He and Willoughby are old friends, since she apparently made him a bottle of toffee vodka in her dishwasher once. He makes some courgette pasta, and is as charmingly snobby as ever.View image in fullscreen‘Absolutely none of this is even slightly about him’ … Stanley Tucci is the guest in the first episode.Photograph: Hungry Bear MediaWhich is great, because absolutely none of this is even slightly about him. That much is evident by the show’s format, which sees him reading his own interview questions off some spoons (“Milk or bag first?” “What’s your favourite type of potato?”), even though typically that role would be filled by the host. Instead, the whole thing comes off as an aggressive audition for whether Willoughby is allowed to be famous again.The weakest elements of the show are the ones where this is most overt. Before Tucci joins her in the kitchen, we see her engaging in some toe-curlingly “candid” banter with the crew, in which she swears a bit and talks about wine. The messaging seems to suggest that this is therealWilloughby, not like that fake automaton who tricked enough people to like her that she qualified as the highest-paid woman on British television between the years 2018 and 2021.Once this burns out, though, we’re left with therealreal Willoughby, who is more or less the same woman who presented This Morning. The best moments come when she stops trying to violently rebrand herself and just allows herself to be quick, funny and endearingly nervous about her new venture. The bits where she seems most like her true self, like when she teasingly provokes Tucci’s culinary sensibilities with microwavable Rustlers, have energy and charm in equal amounts. If that can be sustained over the coming episodes, audiences will naturally find her.The plan seems to be to keep Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy) going as long as possible, in which case it will almost certainly start to become the thing it wants to be as episodes progress. Let’s cross our fingers that it wants to be 15 minutes shorter than it currently is, because plenty could be trimmed from its 45-minute duration. For instance, there is an interminable section near the start where Willoughby painstakingly slices four courgettes with all the concentration of someone trying to defuse a nuclear bomb. It is not essential viewing.But you can’t help but root for the show. Yes, the format might be a little safe and stale, but given the alternatives – a reality show, a wellness podcast, a cynicalAs Ever-style lifestyle store – there’s still some pleasure to be had from watching a person get on with doing something they’re naturally very good at (with or without Voy).Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy) is on YouTube nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionHolly WilloughbyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wham! 10 Days in China review – pop meets politics in George and Andrew’s great leap east | Movies | The Guardian
description: The duo’s groundbreaking 1985 tour reveals a strange collision of pop stardom and communism, a re-edit of Lindsay Anderson’s efforts that got him fired
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The duo’s groundbreaking 1985 tour reveals a strange collision of pop stardom and communism, a re-edit of Lindsay Anderson’s efforts that got him fired
Content: A brilliant coup … George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley in Beijing in 1985.Photograph: Martyn Goddard/Overseas Ltd/Robobuild Ltd/George Michael Ent/Andrew Ridgeley/Big GeoffView image in fullscreenA brilliant coup … George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley in Beijing in 1985.Photograph: Martyn Goddard/Overseas Ltd/Robobuild Ltd/George Michael Ent/Andrew Ridgeley/Big GeoffMoviesReviewWham! 10 Days in China review – pop meets politics in George and Andrew’s great leap eastThe duo’s groundbreaking 1985 tour reveals a strange collision of pop stardom and communism, a re-edit of Lindsay Anderson’s efforts that got him firedPeter BradshawTue 28 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a documentary that has a very important story to tell, maybe more important than it feels comfortable admitting. It’s about two separate subjects – or maybe three: Wham!, China and film-makerLindsay Anderson. A superpower nervously edging towards western-style openness, a pop band nervously doing what needed to be done to make it big in the US, and a great film director, needing the money, taking on a project he didn’t really believe in.In 1985, Wham!’s beetle-browed manager Simon Napier-Bell had a cunning plan for howGeorge Michaeland Andrew Ridgeley could break the US: Wham! would be the first ever western pop band to perform in mainland China. They would play where the Beatles, the Stones and Elvis had never played, and the resulting global publicity would launch them into the US. (He was right – it did.) In our modern age, the movie and music businesses routinely consider China as the key element of the all-important Asian market, but in 1985, Michael and Ridgeley were the Kirk and Spock of the charts, going where no pop act had gone before.After months of patient negotiation with Communist party officials, Napier-Bell pulled off this brilliant coup; he got his boys two sensational, historic gigs in Beijing and then in Guangzhou, with photo-opportunities at the Great Wall. This would be a tough 10-day tour in which, like a royal or presidential visit, they had to tolerate the press in the embedded presence of the hated British red-top tabloids whose coverage they needed. For the same reasons, they also accepted film producer Martin Lewis’s proposal for a fly-on-the-wall documentary, and also his idea for a classy, prestigious director: Lindsay Anderson. But Anderson kept on pushing for a challenging culture-clash theme to the film and the music people just wanted a glorified promo reel, so Anderson was summarily fired after the tour, having been grumpy and disillusioned the entire time, and making no secret of his dislike for Wham!’s music. (Perhaps Anderson thought he could do something like Antonioni’s 1972 immersive TV documentary about China,Chung Kuo: Cina.)A bland PR film was shown a year later, but now the amazing footage has been re-edited, with new talking-head interviews with surviving participants, most prominently Ridgeley – though it brings the film no closer to what Anderson wanted. We see how unbearably tense he and Michael were, and yet how courageous. They were in their early 20s, yet they were expected to make official speeches that might daunt professional diplomats, and had to handle hostile press questioning about the Chinese police cracking down on people dancing at their Beijing concert. (The authorities were, it was suggested, particularly annoyed by the song Freedom, although how much they understood of the English lyrics is an open question.) In Beijing, the audience was glacial, for whom Wham! were creatures from another planet, while in Guangzhou, having had access to Hong Kong pop, the crowd were more enthusiastic.View image in fullscreenTaste of liberty … Wham! 10 Days in China.Photograph: Martyn Goddard/Overseas Ltd/Robobuild Ltd/George Michael Ent/Andrew Ridgeley/Big GeoffBut the point was that Wham! triggered something that could not be untriggered: they gave the Chinese a taste of liberty. Four years later was the Tiananmen Square massacre. Was the Wham! Chinese tour therefore a world-historical event, the butterfly wingbeat that caused an earthquake? Maybe. But it’s not a possibility explored here. It would be nice to conclude that George and Andrew, having been essentially uninterested in China other than as a stepping stone to US glory, were overcome by a great love for that country. (There is incidentally also the question of their views on communism and the left, having played a benefit for striking miners the year before. Did that help get them the gig?)Well … they never returned, although Ridgeley is shown in the present day thoughtfully looking out from the wall. 1985 was their annus mirabilis, the year of the giant US breakthrough and George appearing on stage with Elton John at Live Aid. Maybe the Chinese achievement only fully dawned on them much later. It’s a strange and riveting moment in pop and political history.Wham! 10 Days in China is in cinemas from 28 July.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsGeorge MichaelMusic documentaryLindsay AndersonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ian McDonald obituary | Books | The Guardian
description: Trinidad-born author and poet whose novel The Humming-Bird Tree is a classic of Caribbean literature
Author: Peter Mason
Headline: Trinidad-born author and poet whose novel The Humming-Bird Tree is a classic of Caribbean literature
Content: Ian McDonald in 2013 at the Bocas Lit Festival in TrinidadPhotograph: Courtesy the Bocas Lit FestView image in fullscreenIan McDonald in 2013 at the Bocas Lit Festival in TrinidadPhotograph: Courtesy the Bocas Lit FestBooksObituaryIan McDonald obituaryTrinidad-born author and poet whose novel The Humming-Bird Tree is a classic of Caribbean literaturePeter MasonTue 28 Jul 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIan McDonald, who has died aged 93, wrote only one novel, but it is considered a classic of Caribbean literature. The Humming-Bird Tree (1969), set in Trinidad in the late 1940s, tells the story of Alan, a young white boy, as he falls into friendship with his family’s yard-boy, Kaiser, who is of Indian extraction, and in love with Kaiser’s younger sister, Jaillin, who is also employed by Alan’s wealthy parents.While Alan and Jaillin skirt around each other, trying to come to terms with the confusing feelings of their mutual attraction and the disapproval of Alan’s mother and father, wider emotional turmoil is at play in Trinidad, where the masses are beginning to throw off the yoke of British rule.Alan’s affection for Jaillin is mirrored in unapproved visits to her village, which he finds a vibrant though occasionally distasteful contrast to the stiff atmosphere of his home life. Eventually, when he and Jaillin are found together on an innocent moonlit tryst, their relationship is brought to a forceful end.It is a gently heartbreaking tale about racial boundaries, and a haunting evocation of postwar Trinidad in all its beauty and ugliness, emerging into a new era with the prospect of independence on the horizon.View image in fullscreenThe Humming-Bird Tree is a gently heartbreaking evocation of postwar TrinidadThe book’s sensitive descriptions of time and place also point to the fact that McDonald was more a poet than an author, featured in numerous anthologies and with eight collections to his name.In both prose and poetry, he displayed an ability to celebrate the sensuous joy of Caribbean life in all its complexity, acknowledging the wonder of its dazzling natural world and colourful human relations without skirting over the darker, more brutal side of both.Above all he never failed to show compassion for those he was observing, revealing what the Jamaican poet Ann-Margaret Lim identified as his “caring heart”, something he shared with Caribbean contemporaries such as Mervyn Morris, Eddie Baugh andDerek Walcott. Baugh described McDonald’s poetry as “irradiated by his celebration of life, his gratitude for happy days and for earth’s bounty of joy”.The eldest of six children, McDonald was born in St Augustine in Trinidad, where his father, John, worked as an agricultural director for a local export business and his mother, Thelma (nee Seheult), was a housewife. At Queen’s Royal college in Port of Spain he shone academically and as an outstanding tennis player. Travelling in 1951 to the UK to study history at Cambridge University, he competed for several years running at the Wimbledon singles championships, captained the university tennis team and played for West Indies in their first ever Davis Cup match in 1953.After leaving Cambridge in 1955 he returned to the Caribbean to take up an administrative post in British Guiana (now Guyana) with the Booker group, owner of a series of huge sugar estates. By that time the company was becoming more enlightened and was trying to make itself into a business with an unusual commitment to looking after its workers – something that chimed with McDonald’s humane, liberal approach.Although he continued for a while with his tennis – his last appearance at Wimbledon was in 1959, and he played for the West Indies Davis Cup team into the 1960s – he shifted his focus towards work and immersed himself in Guyana’s culture. He eventually came to consider himself “Trinidadian by birth, Guyanese by adoption”.A parallel writing career began with the publication in 1955 of a first poem, Jaffo the Calypsonian, followed by others, such as The Stick-Fighters, The Cane-Cutter and The Seine-Pullers, that celebrated the artful strength of ordinary folk and appeared in Caribbean literary magazines such as Bim, Poui and Kyk-Over-Al.There were also short stories and a one-act play, The Tramping Man, that addressed the struggles of postcolonial life and was first performed by the Theatre Guild of Guyana in 1969. In the same year The Humming-Bird Tree won the Royal Society of Literature’s Ondaatje prize (then known as the Winifred Holtby memorial prize) and became a set text in schools across the Caribbean.View image in fullscreenThe Humming-Bird Tree was made into a film in 1992 starring Sunil Y Ramjitsingh as Kaiser, Tom Beasley as Alan Holmes and Desha Penco as Jaillin.Photograph: John Jefford/BBCThe novel’s success created greater interest in McDonald’s poetry, and his first collection appeared in Guyana. In 1975 Faber & Faber included 11 of his poems in the third edition of itsPoetryIntroduction series, and collections of his work followed at regular intervals, including Essequibo (poems about wayfarers he met in the hinterland of the Essequibo river) in 1992 and Jaffo the Calypsonian in 1994.In 1992 The Humming-Bird Tree was made into a quietly captivating film directed by Noella Smith, featuring Tom Beasley as Alan and Desha Penco as Jaillin, and broadcast as part of the BBC Screen One series.There were more poetry collections – including Mercy Ward (1998, about his visits to dying patients in a Guyanese hospital), Between Silence and Silence (2003) and The Comfort of All Things (2012). McDonald also edited or co-edited publications including the Heinemann Book of Caribbean Poetry in English (1992) and two anthologies of West Indian writing, They Came in Ships (1998) and This Bowling Was Superfine (2009). In 2014 a selection of his prose from a weekly newspaper column in the Stabroek News was published as A Love of Poetry, followed five years later by essays on sport, An Abounding Joy.McDonald’s career in the sugar industry survived Guyana’s many social and political upheavals: when Bookers was taken over by GuySuCo under a nationalisation programme in 1976, he continued as an administrative director, rising to be director of marketing and administration. He left to become chief executive of the Sugar Association of the Caribbean from 1999 until retirement in 2007. Afterwards he was a member of a panel set up by the West Indies Cricket Board to make recommendations on the governance of regional cricket.New and Collected Poems (2018) included new verse, written in his 80s. Rather more serene than his earlier material, these newer poems continued to explore his interest in the ephemeral nature of life, though perhaps with greater urgency than before. In the opening poem to Mercy Ward, he had reflected that death comes “sudden/quick as light/skin shine/then bone white”.McDonald is survived by his second wife, Mary (nee Callender), whom he married in 1983, their two children, Jamie and Darren, and a son, Keith, from his first marriage to Myrna Foster, which ended in divorce.Ian Archie McDonald, poet and author, born 18 April 1933; died 24 July 2026Explore more on these topicsBooksFictionPoetryTrinidad and TobagoobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Upland by Ed Douglas review – a glorious survey of Britain’s high places | History books | The Guardian
description: The writer and climber brings colour and carnival to his account of a country and people shaped by its mountains
Author: Kathryn Hughes
Headline: The writer and climber brings colour and carnival to his account of a country and people shaped by its mountains
Content: Ben Nevis in the Scottish Highlands.Photograph: John Finney Photography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBen Nevis in the Scottish Highlands.Photograph: John Finney Photography/Getty ImagesBook of the dayHistory booksReviewUpland by Ed Douglas review – a glorious survey of Britain’s high placesThe writer and climber brings colour and carnival to his account of a country and people shaped by its mountainsKathryn HughesTue 28 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 03.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt comes as a shock to learn that Britain’s uplands were not always rocky, covered with coarse grass and suitable only for sheep. About 54,000 years ago – a mere blink in geological time – this island’s high places were teeming with nature. Lushly forested peaks, crags and gorges were home to megafauna including mammoth, woolly rhinoceros and giant elk. The one sour note in this elevated Garden of Eden was the carnivorous cave lions and sabre-tooth cats who prowled the browse looking for a meaty dinner.Ed Douglas’s achievement in this excellent book is to return a proper sense of colour and even carnival to Britain’s high places. His first job, though, is to define his terms. In 1936, the celebrated US geographer Roderick Peattie declared that what made a mountain was not its elevation so much as its capacity to “enter into the imagination of the people who lived in [its] shadows”. But by the 1990s, the United Nations, newly tasked with protecting the world’s high places from environmental and economic decline, insisted on getting out its tape measure and statistical charts and coming up with some universal criteria.Consequently, the current definition of a “mountainous” region is one where the altitude varies by at least 300 metres over a radius of 7km. That means that Douglas’s home on Totley Moor, which sits on the millstone grit uplands of the eastern Peak District, just about qualifies; a matter of obvious satisfaction to this one-time editor of the Alpine Journal. Romping comfortably across the line are whole swathes of Scotland, Wales and northern England, not forgetting the twin domes of Exmoor and Dartmoor.Less pleasing to Douglas, though, is the way in which Britain’s uplands have historically been imagined as places apart, spectacular yet oddly detached from life at lower levels. He reminds us that the country’s high places provide more than 60% of the nation’s water needs. What’s more, the plants that make up much of our diet originate in that same hardy environment: potatoes, barley, maize, apples, tomatoes. Those of us who live at sea level or below would do well to reformulate our ideas about the uplands as a place where nothing much grows beyond the occasional sprig of lucky heather.Equally misguided, suggests Douglas, is a tendency to view Britain’s uplands as existing outside history, politics, culture and even time itself. The truth is that mountains have shaped much of our island story. When the Romans arrived from mainland Europe in the first century AD, they found that low-lying southern England, with its fertile soil and gentle hillocks, quickly rolled over and signed up to the new order. The craggy north, meanwhile, stood aloof – and you can still see evidence of this bifurcated response in the landscape today. Go to a Roman ruin in the south or east of the country, and chances are that it is the remnants of a country estate or, at the very least, a handsome villa. Head to the high north and you will find yourself scrambling over the remains of a garrison or high brick wall aimed at keeping uplanders away from the good stuff.And yet … it frequently turns out that it was precisely in those cold, difficult and, above all, lofty places that actual treasure lay. The Romans eventually overcame their fear of heights to start mining lead in Wanlockhead, which at more than 400 metres remains Scotland’s highest village. A thousand years later and the Norman invaders, who had initially given the rocky spine of England a wide berth, set up shop in the Peak District and insisted on taking a cut of the handsome profits that arose from local lead mining.Douglas suggests that the best way to think of this ceaseless push and pull between the central lowlands and the marginal uplands is as a kind of internal colonialism. For millennia, Britain’s high places have been ransacked for their raw materials. Perhaps the most poignant example in this book is the story of the Elan valley, a beautiful stretch of land in the mountains of rural mid-Wales. In the early 19th century the poet Percy Shelley had roamed over his uncle’s Radnorshire estate, entranced to have found his own version of Wordsworth and Coleridge’s Lake District.But in 1896, the valley was dammed and flooded in order to create a vast reservoir from which Birmingham might draw an everlasting supply of cheap and clean drinking water. It was part of the MP Joseph Chamberlain’s radical programme to clear England’s second city of cholera and dysentery by building a 73-mile aqueduct from the Welsh mountains to the Midlands plateau. This necessitated the village of Nantgwyllt, complete with church and surrounding farms, disappearing permanently under water.double quotation markOne delight of Douglas' capacious, looping narrative is the room it leaves for delightful cameos by remarkable individualsThe compulsory purchase of the Elan valley carries echoes of the earlier Highland clearances, during which tenant farmers in Sutherland, Argyll and Inverness-shire were ordered off the land to make way for the infinitely more profitable sheep. Many of these evicted crofters, just like the Radnorshire farmers 150 years later, were obliged to emigrate as far as the US to find a place to build a stable home.Yet it would be doomy and defeatist to suggest that the uplands have exclusively been places of passive trauma. Douglas does a good job at identifying those times throughout history when Britain’s high places demonstrated a culture of determined resistance. There are the Jacobite rebellions of 1715 and 1745 when Highlanders loyal to the Stuart cause swept down from their mountain fastness in an attempt to overthrow the newly installed Hanoverians. This tartan army got as far as Derby, only 110 miles from London, before being forced to turn back.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDouglas has not, in truth, found out anything new about the ancient uplands, but he has knitted his sources into a deft survey, going all the way from the tectonic plates of prehistory to today, when the chief concern is southern second-homers driving up the prices for young locals. One delight of his capacious, looping narrative is the room it leaves for delightful cameos by remarkable individuals, including several women.There is Janet Lapworth, the daughter of a Galashiels schoolteacher, who in the 1870s sewed her geologist husband a special waistcoat incorporating rows of pockets on the front into which he could sort his specimens on the fly. Or Hannah Mitchell, who grew up on a hard-scrabble tenant farm with a view of Kinder Scout, the highest point in the Peak District, and developed a love of rambling to offset the constricted conditions of her own impoverished life. Mitchell’s determination to walk off her troubles led to her becoming a suffragette, a JP and a campaigner for social justice.My favourite uplander, though, remains Queen Victoria. As a young girl she gorged on the highly confected Highland novels of Walter Scott. Now that Jacobitism was safely defeated, it was delightful to imagine a Highlands full of craggily handsome men in kilts ready to come a lady’s rescue, even if that lady happened to be a Protestant Hanoverian princess. When she bought Balmoral in 1852, the queen was not initially much interested in venturing far. But with the death of Albert she was persuaded to undertake the occasional excursion up famous peaks including Lochnagar and Ben Macdui. Here was the beginning of what the 20th-century novelist George Scott-Moncrieff memorably called “Balmorality”. It was a view of the uplands, spruced up and watered down, best seen on a biscuit tin.Upland: The Strange History and Vital Future of Britain’s Mountains by Ed Douglas is published by Bodley Head (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Underdogs by Louise Powell review – a powerful debut with plenty of northern soul | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A bereaved father and son bond over greyhound racing in an east Durham town in terminal decline
Author: Benjamin Myers
Headline: A bereaved father and son bond over greyhound racing in an east Durham town in terminal decline
Content: Going to the dogs … ‘Powell is strongest when describing the details of track life.’Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGoing to the dogs … ‘Powell is strongest when describing the details of track life.’Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesFictionReviewUnderdogs by Louise Powell review – a powerful debut with plenty of northern soulA bereaved father and son bond over greyhound racing in an east Durham town in terminal declineBenjamin MyersTue 28 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe adjoining villagesof Easington and Easington Colliery in the coalfields of east Durham make the perfect case study of the shift from England’s industrial boomtime to terminal decline. Twenty miles from a major town or city, they’ve been left to languish ever since Thatcher went to war with the industry that made them. If you want to understand why the white working class feel abandoned today, go to Easington Colliery and its surrounding villages.It’s this community that Middlesbrough-born writer Louise Powell brings to life in a powerful debut set in the world of greyhound racing, or “flapping”. Underdogs is an utterly authentic depiction of an England that’s overlooked, but still very much alive. Pigeon lofts and flat caps, meat raffles and social clubs – all still exist, just very rarely in 21st-century novels.Ten-year-old George Wheatley and his broken father Reg, both grieving the loss of George’s mother, who died two years earlier, are drawn into the dog-track culture by charismatic ex-miner Bertie, who despite the “half-pint of black phlegm he hawked up off his lungs every mornin’” decides not to pursue an incapacity benefit claim as he can make better money rinsing out the various illegal bookmakers by racing his dogs. When the bookies refuse to take Bertie’s bets he ropes in those down on their luck to race his dogs for him, and hands over his bitch Goldie, “twenny-nine kilo of muscles coiled like springs … a Ferrari of an engine in her fawn chest and a nose that could been made by Concorde”. Scores of those on the breadline have benefited from Bertie’s hustle.double quotation markIt' s a hard-scratch existence based around family alliances and power struggles in the dying days of an analogue worldThe love that George feels for Goldie is matched only by his need to survive in an uncompromising adult world where the greatest threat comes from aggrieved bookmaker Baz, who has designs on their prized canine charge. Powell is strongest when describing the details of track life, a seemingly simple pursuit given a dark edge by the high-stakes money changing hands and further complicated by the treatment of these graceful creatures who are bred and discarded for human amusement and profit.That the novel is set in 1998 is significant; all of County Durham’s pits had finally closed, but major regeneration investment was on its way from local boy Tony Blair, with his talk of “regional task forces” and “enterprise zones”. Old slag piles were soon to became nature reserves and pithead monuments. A bright new future was promised, though it’s barely glimpsed here; today Easington has one of the whitest demographics in the country (currently 98.4%), and was the place worst hit by 2025 disability allowance cuts.Here, then, is a hard-scratch existence based around family alliances and power struggles in the dying days of an analogue world, where scars received from police truncheons at Orgreave are shown and shared, and where premature death stalks the terraced streets. George and Reg emerge as tender and quietly heroic; the father’s grief for his lost wife is almost overwhelming at times, as are the reminders of George’s malnutrition. This is real first-world poverty, as it still exists today. During the second world war British-based fascist William Joyce, better known as Lord Haw-Haw, remarked that “the people of Easington will be eating greyhounds, not raising them”; he sorely underestimated just how much the English love their dogs, and it’s no coincidence that Powell’s descriptions of the greyhound’s meals are more mouthwatering than anything father and son eat.North-east writers of literary fiction have always had plenty to sing about, but not much in the way of support from the publishing industry; “too bleak” and “too northern” are words familiar to many of us from the region. Given the rich cultural tradition of storytelling and folk song, always told in distinctively melodic vernacular voices, this still feels like an oversight. With recent novels from Eliza Clark, Glen James Brown, Jessica Andrews and Lucy Rose all finding critical favour, it’s clear that there are infinite Englands in existence. And as Underdogs movingly demonstrates, it’s these untold stories that need to be on the page – now more than ever.Benjamin Myers’s most recent novel is Jesus Christ Kinski (Bloomsbury).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The great PlayStation blackout – will kids actually have to leave their bedrooms this summer? | Games | The Guardian
description: Gamers are angry that Sony will be deleting TV shows and films from their libraries as well as getting rid of physical games. Will a boycott make a difference?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Gamers are angry that Sony will be deleting TV shows and films from their libraries as well as getting rid of physical games. Will a boycott make a difference?
Content: Physical attraction … Gamers want discs to continue.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyView image in fullscreenPhysical attraction … Gamers want discs to continue.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyPass notesGamesThe great PlayStation blackout – will kids actually have to leave their bedrooms this summer?Gamers are angry that Sony will be deleting TV shows and films from their libraries as well as getting rid of physical games. Will a boycott make a difference?Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:PlayStationblackout.Age:Forthcoming.Appearance:Thousands of gamers, blinking nervously in the sunlight.This sounds serious.It’s as serious as things could possibly get. Gamers are going to boycott PlayStation next month.Why?For the most serious reason of all: to protest againstSony’s decision to stop producing physical copiesof PlayStation games in 2028.Wait, you can still buy physical copies of PlayStation games?Yes, you can, online and in toy shops and quite often near the sock multipacks at the back of some Sports Direct branches.Well, who knew?Admittedly, fewer and fewer people. Most gamers buy their games digitally, to the extent that only seven PS5 games have sold more than 100,000 physical copies in the US this year.So nobody cares.Not so fast. Lots of people care very deeply about this. If you buy a disc of the game, it belongs to you. You can sell it, lend it to your friends, or display the box as a memento.Whereas if you download it?Then the game is locked to your account, andSonycontrols the pricing, and can even withdraw it completely if it likes.Even though you bought it?Yes. In September, for example, Sony will be deleting 551 movies and TV shows from the UK PlayStation store – including the John Wick franchise, Paddington and Terminator 2 – because its content licensing agreement with StudioCanal has expired. If you bought any of these titles, they will simply vanish from your library.So nobody owns anything?This is the fear. And this is why people are finally doing something about it.The boycott.That’s right. It has been proposed that nobody should use their PlayStation during the last week of August. No playing, no buying, no logging in.Wait, August? They want us to do this during the summer holidays?Yes! This is all about hitting them where it hurts.What am I going to do with my kids if they can’t play games? Will I actually have to parent them?Stay strong, comrade. This is for the greater good.Which is what again?Being able to physically hold a copy of John Carpenter’s Toxic Commando in our hands, like the old days.I’m not sure this will catch on.But it must! Being a console owner in 2026 is like being repeatedly mugged by a large multinational corporation. We need to do something to show that we still matter and stop them taking us for granted.Do say:“I’m mad as hell and I’m not going to take it any more!”Don’t say:“Unless Sony puts Farming Simulator on a CD for me.”Explore more on these topicsGamesPass notesSonyPlayStationPlayStation 5featuresShareReuse this content

title: The Mermaid Mask review – the funniest underwater murder mystery you can play | Games | The Guardian
description: Detective Grimoire is at it again in the long-awaited new entry to this stylish series of comedy whodunnits
Author: Jordan Erica Webber
Headline: Detective Grimoire is at it again in the long-awaited new entry to this stylish series of comedy whodunnits
Content: A submarine full of secrets … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesView image in fullscreenA submarine full of secrets … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesGamesReviewThe Mermaid Mask review – the funniest underwater murder mystery you can playPC, Nintendo Switch/Switch 2, PS5; SFB GamesDetective Grimoire is at it again in the long-awaited new entry to this stylish series of comedy whodunnitsJordan Erica WebberTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a boom time for mystery games, the Detective Grimoire series stands out for its style and sense of humour. The Mermaid Mask continues to build upon the formula laid down in Secret of the Swamp and polished in Tangle Tower, and while there is still room for further improvements this sequel is worth the seven years’ wait.This time, the casually competent Grimoire and his smart if sarcastic sidekick Sally have been summoned to a submarine to solve the locked-room murder of its captain, Magnus Mortuga. You click around the cluttered rooms of the vessel to hear the detectives’ comedic commentary and look for clues and – closer up – click and drag to move objects around for further examination or to solve a puzzle. (For those playing onNintendo Switch 2, the mouse controls are actually useful here, if not comfortable in the long run.)View image in fullscreenNever too taxing … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesPuzzles are never so taxing as to disrupt the flow: variations on “arrange these objects to satisfy some more-or-less apparent rules of logic” with stylistic wrapping. Your reward is generally an opened door and a new object to examine, which – importantly – you can then present to the various suspects.And here is the chewy centre of these games: the fully voice-acted conversations with a cast of colourful characters. I immediately lowered the volume of the music (which sadly doesn’t compare to Tangle Tower’s characterful soundtrack) to better hear the well-performed dialogue. Some of the suspects are more memorable than others, but the somewhat supernatural backdrop (and these games are all set in very much the same world) allows for archetypes not found elsewhere.View image in fullscreenColourful characters … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesMadam Tadpole is buff, green-skinned, and appears to have gills. Mariana Moon is an older woman with an unnaturally keen sense of smell whose voice acting is cleverly muffled when she’s chewing on her pipe. Godric Gripp is a compass repairman with an anthropomorphised stick called Cornelius Cane, whose introduction involves an unavoidable shopfront interface the developers must have coded purely for this one laugh.These stylish moments are one of the more noticeable additions since Tangle Tower, with, for example, new 3D animations to illustrate the suspects’ recollections. But when it comes to solving the mysteries, they haven’t fixed what isn’t broken: as in Tangle Tower, and other deduction games such as the Golden Idol series and The Séance of Blake Manor, you form hypotheses by filling sentence blanks from a selection of nouns and verbs.The overall process is soothingly methodical: your inventory shows blank slots for objects you’ve yet to find, each topic addressed with a suspect gets a satisfying tick, and Grimoire and Sally inform you when you’ve uncovered enough to tackle each suspect’s individual mystery (in one instance I did experience a bug where this unlocked prematurely, but the developers are already fixing bugs raised by early players).Some players may find this completion percentage approach too formulaic, especially if they exhaust their current inventory and resort to pixel hunting to locate the rest. And the pacing does falter in the final chapter, where the game presents you with a more literal checklist to work through before you get to tie up each character’s loose ends and make your final accusation. But while the conclusion of The Mermaid Mask feels far more satisfying than that of Tangle Tower, these games are far more about the twisty journey and the laughs you have along the way.The Mermaid Mask is out now; £17.75Explore more on these topicsGamesPCNintendo SwitchNintendo Switch 2PlayStation 5NintendoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: LPO/Gardner review – squirrels, shepherdesses and a tumultuous storm | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: From Kristine Tjøgersen’s tranquil woodland reverie to Strauss’s thunderous mountainscape, the London Philharmonic – with Louise Alder – conjured colours and brought drama to this vivid programme
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: From Kristine Tjøgersen’s tranquil woodland reverie to Strauss’s thunderous mountainscape, the London Philharmonic – with Louise Alder – conjured colours and brought drama to this vivid programme
Content: Not stinting the big moments… Edward Gardner conducts the London Philharmonic Orchestra at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenNot stinting the big moments… Edward Gardner conducts the London Philharmonic Orchestra at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewLPO/Gardner review – squirrels, shepherdesses and a tumultuous stormRoyal Albert Hall, LondonFrom Kristine Tjøgersen’s tranquil woodland reverie to Canteloube’s Auvergne and  Strauss’s thunderous mountainscape, the London Philharmonic – with Louise Alder – conjured colours and brought drama to this vivid programmeClive PagetTue 28 Jul 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat do you get if you blow into a tuba full of water? With a little imagination it’s the sound of a squirrel eating, the opening salvo of Between Trees by Kristine Tjøgersen. The Norwegian composer’s ingenious nature poem drew on extended techniques and novel effects, such as prepared harp and strings, as it led us beneath the forest floor to explore the mysterious fungal threads that connect the roots of trees and plants like some vast natural internet.Leaving the Scandinavian forests behind, the London Philharmonic’s whistlestop travelogue paused for breath in sun-drenched central France to savour a selection of Canteloube’s Songs of the Auvergne. Louise Alder was the soloist, the languid radiance of her creamy soprano complementing the composer’s rose-tinted orchestrations.Edward Gardnerkept the orchestra on a low light while pointing up the music’s more pungent elements. For her part, Alder brought colour and the gift of storytelling to these tales of lovelorn shepherdesses, opportunistic country lads and conceited quails.View image in fullscreenThe gift of storytelling: Louise Alder with Edward Gardner and the LPO at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouOur final destination was the Bavarian Alps and Richard Strauss’s grandiose tone poem An Alpine Symphony. Opening with the sound of the mountain itself on four trombones and two tubas, the composer throws everything at the orchestrations bar the kitchen sink as he attempts to depict nature in all its glory over the course of a day. Gardner proved a musical Baedeker here, leading his merry band up hill and down dale with big-boned phrasing and a warm romantic sweep. The LPO in turn conjured shady woods, cascading waterfalls and a field of cows you could almost smell.Along the way, Gardner found fleeting oases of calm, drawing out delicate chamber textures despite the humungous forces on the stage in front of him. He didn’t stint the big moments though, like the organ-boosted vision on the summit. The tumultuous storm that soaked the hikers as they scrambled back down featured a deafening cacophony of drums supplemented by wind machine and thunder sheet. All that remained was to usher in the epilogue and a portentous return of the opening motif. Mankind may pass, Strauss seemed to say, yet the mountain will endure.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicLondon Philharmonic OrchestraEdward GardnerreviewsShareReuse this content

title: PalesTEENian review – engaging story of mixed identity is a bit of a muddle | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Joe Haddad’s solo show tilts between family comedy and football fandom as well as the horrors of the Gaza war but never quite finds its focus
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Joe Haddad’s solo show tilts between family comedy and football fandom as well as the horrors of the Gaza war but never quite finds its focus
Content: Effervescent … Joe Haddad in PalesTEENian at Riverside Studios, LondonView image in fullscreenEffervescent … Joe Haddad in PalesTEENian at Riverside Studios, LondonTheatreReviewPalesTEENian review – engaging story of mixed identity is a bit of a muddleRiverside Studios, LondonJoe Haddad’s solo show tilts between family comedy and football fandom as well as the horrors of the Gaza war but never quite finds its focusArifa AkbarTue 28 Jul 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe Haddad’s solo show is a kind of self-referential standup set which tells us about his journey into comedy. It encompasses the negotiation of his dual identity as a Palestinian south Londoner and becomes a coming-of-age story.Born in Croydon, with Arab Christian parents from Jerusalem, he faced prejudice at his Catholic school, including taunts of “Jew-boy” because there was so little understanding of Palestine and its history of occupation. It follows him to adulthood, and an assumed, Anglicised, stage name of Joe Adams, for fear of being cancelled (even his mother tells him not to mention Palestine during gigs).But this show, he makes clear, is not all gloom and doom. There is no need for anyone to blanch at the mention of the P-word. Neither will he use the I-word (indeed, he succeeds in circumventing the naming of Israel even once). He leads with heartiness and humour and exuberantly drawn extended family members on his visits to Jerusalem, and nods to his love of Chelsea FC.There are some good lines – “TonightI’moccupying the stage,” he says, and he has an effervescent presence but none of it quite hangs together or builds its dramatic trajectory far enough. Haddad flags up the hodge-podge nature of the show himself: if it feels jumbled up, that is because his life is too, he tells us at the off.It is not exactly a jumble, but it hops too much in tone, from comic to dramatic, not quite nailing either. He waxes lyrical about zatar, tells us about Arab hospitality and gives us affectionately cartoonish takes on his imperious Palestinian mother. He speaks of the cultural expectation to become a doctor, lawyer or engineer, and his departure from that with an entry into comedy. The show is cute in its humour but soft and over-familiar. Football jerseys hang around him but this set seems like a red herring – football is only ever mentioned in cosmetic ways.He also speaks of 7 October 2023, from hearing about Hamas’s attacks to the horrific images of death coming out of Gaza. But this part comes in short, impressionistic sentences, not grappled with fully enough once it is mentioned. Too many topics are touched on in 80 minutes as a whole and ironically the show feels slight and unfocused as a result – a précis that does not manage to unpack the immense potential of its subject matter.At Riverside Studios, London,until 2 AugustExplore more on these topicsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Laurie Kilmartin review – Oscars gag-writer unleashes a fierce and filthy talent | Comedy | The Guardian
description: She has penned jokes for Jimmy Kimmel, Conan O’Brien and the Academy. Now she’s seizing the limelight with scattergun routines about everything from penises to free-bleeding
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: She has penned jokes for Jimmy Kimmel, Conan O’Brien and the Academy. Now she’s seizing the limelight with scattergun routines about everything from penises to free-bleeding
Content: Clean brutality … Laurie KilmartinPhotograph: PRView image in fullscreenClean brutality … Laurie KilmartinPhotograph: PRComedyReviewLaurie Kilmartin review – Oscars gag-writer unleashes a fierce and filthy talentSoho theatre, LondonShe has penned jokes for Jimmy Kimmel, Conan O’Brien and the Academy. Now she’s seizing the limelight with scattergun routines about everything from penises to free-bleedingKate WyverTue 28 Jul 2026 06.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 06.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLaurie Kilmartin is not afraid of vulgarity. The Peabody award-winner flits between penis jokes, free-bleeding chaos and a taste for vengeance in this scattergun hour that marks her London debut. Having made her career as a staff writer for Jimmy Kimmel and Conan O’Brien, Kilmartin’s own voice is crude, acute and pretty mean, delivering each dark joke with a furrowed-brow intensity, followed by a flash of a wide, are-you-gonna-take-it smile.Jumping through the decades, the US comedian cycles through school bullies, the need for better assassins, and the limited dating pool of men over 50. There’s a pitch-black quality to some of these tales, with a particular knife-edge to her story of an abusive swim coach. Other anecdotes feel drier, like they’ve just had the dust blown off them; she settles too long on lockdowns, which I thought we’d all agreed we were done talking about long ago. Even a moment on Charlie Kirk feels like it missed the moment, though other elements of her US political commentary are easy winners.Kilmartin wrote on the last two years of the Oscars ceremonies, and she’s most confident in the swing of finely tuned bits, delivered with a blazing bullishness. But since the show’s structure is loose and fragmented, she flounders for a few seconds every time she moves from one often-unrelated set piece to the next. She’s less commanding in the moments of audience participation, with one callback to a story of language failure in Japan provided by an audience member instead of the comedian.It’s clear from the amount of haphazard reference checks and mid-story math conversions that she’s not used to UK crowds. At times this gives the show the feel of a work-in-progress, and there’s an oddly distracting focus on the difference between her (American, single mum) and her audience (tonight: neither of those), which we wouldn’t mind at all if she didn’t keep mentioning it. Over the course of the hour, the tone of Kilmartin’s performance is somewhat standoffish, and she repeatedly dismisses us as light clappers. But the more she leans into this, the funnier we find it. Matching the clean brutality of her best anecdotes, severity suits her.At Soho theatre, London, until 28 JulyExplore more on these topicsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People named their kids after us!’ Lost’s Penny and Desmond on being one of TV’s best ever romances | Television | The Guardian
description: Sonya Walger and Henry Ian Cusick created a love so magical that they’re responsible for what’s widely regarded as the greatest TV episode of all time – not to mention inspiring a fan to get a full leg tattoo of their faces
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Sonya Walger and Henry Ian Cusick created a love so magical that they’re responsible for what’s widely regarded as the greatest TV episode of all time – not to mention inspiring a fan to get a full leg tattoo of their faces
Content: ‘The love was true and pure’ … Penny (Sonya Walger) and Desmond (Henry Ian Cusick) in the finale of season four.Photograph: Mario Perez/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The love was true and pure’ … Penny (Sonya Walger) and Desmond (Henry Ian Cusick) in the finale of season four.Photograph: Mario Perez/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesMaking loveTelevision‘People named their kids after us!’ Lost’s Penny and Desmond on being one of TV’s best ever romancesSonya Walger and Henry Ian Cusick created a love so magical that they’re responsible for what’s widely regarded as the greatest TV episode of all time – not to mention inspiring a fan to get a full leg tattoo of their facesMore from our series Making Love:‘We met and two minutes later we were kissing’ – how Gavin and Stacey became Britain’s most bang tidy TV coupleHollie RichardsonTue 28 Jul 2026 05.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLost is one of television’s most romantic dramas. Forget smoke monsters, time travel and that infamous ending – this was a show fuelled by swoony stories. Sun and Jin; Rose and Bernard; Sawyer/Jack/Kate/Juliet; Charlie and Claire; Sayid and Nadia (notShannon). Love was the reason behind so many of the islanders’ need to survive, or to sacrifice themselves.But it was Penny’s and Desmond’s relationship that defined the series.Penelope Widmore (Sonya Walger), a billionaire’s daughter, met Desmond Hume (Henry Ian Cusick), an ordinary Scot, when she went to pick up wine from a monastery, where Des had just quit being a monk. It was love at first sight and they drove off together with the booze. But the relationship was doomed due to Penny’s disapproving (and evil) father, Des’s need to prove himself in a sailing competition and his arrival at a freaky island. Like the Odyssey character after whom she was named, Penny spent a lot of time waiting and wondering. However, as she once forewarned: “With enough money and determination, you can find anyone.” And she did. In fact, without Penny, the survivors of Oceanic flight 815 might never have made it home.Of course, it wasn’t easy. There was a breakup, Charlie’s devastating death and the sob-fest episode The Constant – widely consideredthe best TV episode of all time– in which, after eight years apart, Penny kept her promise to answer Des’s phone call on Christmas Eve. As Penny put it: “All you really need to survive is someone who loves you. And you have her.”How did Walger and Cusick make such a love story for the ages? On the day I put this to them, it is exactly 21 years since the Lost pilot. “It’s the day the plane went down … and I’m flying to LA in two hours!” says Cusick from his home in Hawaii, the filming location of Lost, where he moved his family 20 years ago. “Are you really?” gasps Walger from Santa Monica, California. “It will make the news,” he laughs.The friends quickly exchange life updates: Cusick is filming an indie vampire western; Walger is navigating a new normal after losing her family home in theLos Angeles fires. Then, it’s time to talk about becoming Penny and Desmond …Do you remember meeting for the first time?HC:The writers had an idea for something, but they didn’t know what. When I shot the photo [of Penny and Des, which Des keeps with him on the island], another actor played that – and she was a local extra. Then we did it again with Sonya.SW:Let’s be clear: there was no time for a chemistry read. There was no time for anything, ever. I mean, they were writing these scripts and shooting them 15 minutes later. People were being cast and put on a plane that afternoon.HC:It was night-time! [Their first scene together is at night in a stadium.]View image in fullscreenGrandstand event … Penny and Desmond meet.Photograph: ABCSW:I’d been there on my own, jumping up and down around the stadium and feeling quite adrift – I didn’t know anyone. I was really sticky and thought: I need to meet this guy I don’t know anything about. We immediately discovered that Ian is half Scottish and half Peruvian and I’m half English and half Argentine. And those are strangely exotic and yet neighboured identities. That was something very lovely, very rare.HC:I have a big memory of meeting Sonya and thinking: oh, a proper, proper actress. But then she would pop in and out all the time.SW:I’d be gone for months. Funnily enough, Ian was my constant. I didn’t know anyone else in the show and I really wasn’t getting the intervening scripts. So we’d sit down and I’d be like: “All right, what’s happened?”What do Penny and Des love about each other?SW:When you’ve got a father as domineering as Charles Widmore [Alan Dale], the quiet, gentle devotion of Desmond is the antithesis of that.HC:The love was true and pure – and it was a good love. But it was more about: how will they get back together?What were your favourite romantic moments?HC:Inthe scene with the letter[from Penny, which Desmond finds for the first time on the island], I wasn’t a regular character at that point and I think that helped. There was another scene, where they were shouting out all these crazy directions: “Do it sad! Do it angry!” I was trying to show them my whole colour palette. And then Terry Quinn [who played Locke] said to me: “That was your audition.”View image in fullscreenRead it and weep … Des finds Penny’s letter.Photograph: ABCThe irony of The Constant is that we weren’t even together. I ended up doing it with the assistant director on my side. When Sonya turned up, she did it and I was on the sofa behind. That moment, that phone call – with not a lot of dialogue – was one of those things that worked a bit of magic. What was really hard was when we had to meet [in season four, when Penny finds Des] and I was thinking: how are we going to beat that?Is there anything you wish Penny and Des had done differently?SW:The greedy actor in me would say I’d love to have done more with us.HC:Me too! I think there was more life in us.SW:Spin-off, for fuck’s sake – where was the spin-off?HC:Now I would push that. You, me and Charlie on a boat.SW:I say that partly jokingly. Because what gives this couple its place in the world’s heart is that it wasn’t oversaturated. You only had a handful of episodes to hold. You didn’t get bored of us, that’s for sure.HC:It left people wanting more.SW:We did great and left them on a high note.When did you realise this was a love story for the ages?SW:In this show that had so many contradictions and loose ends and tears in the space time continuum that bent your mind, here was one really classic trope you could hold on to.HC:It was a simple story of two people who couldn’t be together – because of her father, or time, or so many things in their way – who desperately wanted to be together.View image in fullscreen‘You didn’t get bored of us, that’s for sure.’Photograph: ABCSW:I felt very honoured when I got the call asking me to fly in for the finale – if nothing else, it was acknowledgment from the creators of the value of our little duo. But it’s only as the years have crept on, appearing on “the best couple of all time” lists and things. It never ceases to surprise and truly gratify me that we did some work that has endured like this. It’s amazing.HC:I always thought we had a cool storyline. But we didn’t know the legacy it would have. It’s been 20 years and there’s been so much great TV since – and we’re still talking about that relationship.How romantic are you in real life?SW:Romantic is a weird word in your 50s! I’m devoted. I know what devotion is – to my family, to my husband, to the life we have. And it’s something I felt at the time even without them. I felt a strong sense of devotion to the life I had created for myself in LA, so much so that I wasn’t willing to let it go by moving to Hawaii. [Walger was in the running to play the main character Kate Austen, but pulled out.]HC:I think as I’m getting older I’m getting more romantic and softer. I get more emotional about the past, like thinking about my kids as babies.SW:I’m going to push back and say he’s always had that.HC:Really? I’ve never thought of myself like that. I’m a “tough” guy!SW:No he’s not! He’s a deeply, deeply feeling man.What has been the most intense fan reaction to Penny and Des?SW:A full leg tattoo of our faces! I get “Not Penny’s boat” held up to me at airports a lot. It’s like a fan’s secret way of saying: “I see you, but I will respect you.” I really mean it when I say it’s just really humbling to have done anything at all that leaves such a mark.HC:People have named their children after us – that’s odd.SW:Yes! I have 100% had some Pennys.What was your relationship like off camera?SW:It just felt so easy and effortless from day one. It was a pleasure to see Ian. I think he was grateful just to have someone visiting from the mainland who was also from England; there was some sort of familiarity.HC:When I arrived [on the Lost set], the cast was already very integrated. I worked separately, which I really enjoyed, actually. Even on the days I did work with the whole cast, I didn’t really enjoy them, because there are so many actors and you have to wait for your turn. I liked working with two or three people – I love it. It was very easy with Sonya and it was always going to be a good scene when we met up.View image in fullscreen‘All you really need to survive is someone who loves you’ … Penny in the celebrated season four episode The Constant.Photograph: ABCSW:Years later, I came to Hawaii with my family and we met up with Ian. For old time sakes, we went to the church where we unloaded boxes of wine and took photos there. We stay in touch.HC:We did a short film together, too.SW:That’s right – I had just had my baby, I think.HC:No, she was eight months pregnant!SW:Oh yeah! Ian, if you’ve got a day off when you’re in LA and you want a cup of tea, will you come and find me?HC:Yes! I’ll try.Did you keep anything from the set that reminds you of Penny and Des?SW:I lost everything in the house. I don’t even have my children’s baby photos. It’s really shocking and it makes me very, very intentional about what I put back.HC:I had the blue shirt – I stole it and they asked for it back. They were pretty stingy. I auctioned it [for charity] anyway. I’ve seen many reproductions of their photo and I’m asked to sign it.SW:My first novelcame out in February this year,three weeks after the fire. I had to go to a book festival the other day and people handed me Lost photos to sign, and I was like: dude, just buy the book!What can Penny and Des teach us about love?SW:Keep the faith.HC:“Keep the faith” is great – I’ll go with that, too.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionMaking loveLostDramaUS televisionEntertainment TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Giving birth in the shadow of Haiti’s gang violence – photo essay | Global development | The Guardian
description: As fighting intensifies in Port-au-Prince, only a fraction of its maternity services remain, and they are under constant threat
Author: Jelle Krings
Headline: As fighting intensifies in Port-au-Prince, only a fraction of its maternity services remain, and they are under constant threat
Content: Mothers at a clinic in Cité Soleil, a gang-controlled area of Port-au-Prince cut off from basic services, which has now been forced to close. All photographs: Jelle KringsAs fighting intensifies in Port-au-Prince, only a fraction of its maternity services remain, and they are under constant threatByJelle KringsSupported byAbout this contentTue 28 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEight months pregnant, Françoise, 45, arrives early in the morning at a deserted school in Bel Air. The hillside neighbourhood in Port-au-Prince has been controlled by gangs since a violent takeover in 2019. Schools have closed, electricity has been cut off and food is scarce. Gunfights can erupt at any time.View image in fullscreenFrançoise having a Doppler ultrasound in a clinic set up for a few hours inside a deserted school in Bel AirWhat was a school in safer times in Haiti’s capital has been turned into a temporary pop-up health clinic. The only light comes through the cracks in the boarded-up windows and over the sandbags stacked to stop stray bullets. A room lined with wooden benches is packed with newborns and their mothers and pregnant women seeking maternity services provided by the aid organisation Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF).According to Human Rights Watch, the Trump administration’s suspension of USAID funding in 2025deprived about 750,000 women and girlsin Haiti of access to healthcare. On the rare occasion it is still available, women line up and wait for hours.View image in fullscreenThe clinic in the abandoned school in Bel Air is operated by Médecins Sans FrontièresTen days before Françoise’s visit to the clinic, the area was the scene of a violent clash between rival gangs. Dozens ofpeople were killed, including 10 children, a local human rights group told Associated Press.In the final trimester of her pregnancy, Françoise feels she has no choice but to travel to the clinic, despite the risk. She has been diagnosed with a condition that significantly increases the risk of eclampsia, which can cause seizures during pregnancy and in the postpartum period. Left untreated, it can lead to coma, brain injury and, in some cases, death. If the clinic was not there, Françoise says, “only God knows” where she would go.View image in fullscreenThe government controlled Port-au-Prince district of Pétion-VilleView image in fullscreenA month-old baby girl, Luguiona, in the arms of Ruth, a friend of the child’s mother, Adeline, at the Bel Air clinicView image in fullscreenResidents in Pétion-Ville. About 1.4 million Haitians have become internally displaced and more than 6 million people are in need of urgent humanitarian assistanceAfter the assassination of president Jovenel Moïse in 2021,Haiti spiralled deeper into chaos. About1.4 million Haitians have become internally displaced. More than half of the population now faces high levels of food insecurity, andmore than 6 million peopleare in need of urgent humanitarian assistance.The consequences for maternal health have been grim. According to MSF, between February 2022 and April 2025, the proportion of maternal deaths in hospitalsrose from 250 to 350 per 100,000 live births.Only a fraction of health facilities in Port-au-Prince are still operational and accessible for women living in the poorest neighbourhoods, such as Bel Air and Tabarre.
