A clinic in Cité Soleil was forced to close in May due to gang violence. An estimated60% of birthstake place in the city without medical care – at home, in camps or on the streets. Complications such as haemorrhage, infections and hypertension go untreated, making them the leading causes of maternal mortality.View image in fullscreenPrenatal examinations at the Bel Air clinic take place behind a screen by the light of battery-powered lamps because there is no electricity in the gang-controlled area.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: A female patient is treated for a gunshot wound in her upper leg in Tabarre; women seeking healthcare in Cité Soleil; a baby girl, Gamalla, in the arms of her mother, Fabienne, seven days after being delivered at home; expectant mothers hold urine sample cups at the Bel Air clinicThe midwife treating Françoise says her baby will probably need to be delivered by caesarean section. Without it, she or the baby could die. She already has three girls, two of whom were delivered by caesarean section. If this is another girl, Françoise plans to name her Lovinska.After several hours in the clinic, gunshots are reported outside. The medical staff start packing up their equipment, and the women at the clinic disperse. Françoise starts her long walk home through the unpredictable streets of Bel Air to the home where she lives with her husband and children in a camp for the displaced.View image in fullscreenRollens, 5, and his mother, Eliphète, at a hospital run by MSF in Tabarre. Rollens suffered burns on his arms and legs when his foot got caught in the exhaust pipe of a motorcycleThe situation in Port-au-Prince is rapidly deteriorating. Weeks after Françoise attended the clinic in Bel Air, heavy fighting erupted. Seven volunteers working with MSF were trapped inside a building for hours before they were able to evacuate. A former volunteer was wounded and died in front of the building’s gate. Once again, maternal health services were put on hold.Explore more on these topicsHaitiMaternal healthGlobal healthMaternal mortalityAmericasCaribbeanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Black motorcycle clubs come alive in the summer: ‘The best way to build community is on two wheels’ | Black US culture | The Guardian
description: Building on decades-long traditions, Black bikers host rides, picnics and other gatherings nearly every summer weekend to celebrate community and freedom
Author: Morgan Jerkins
Headline: Building on decades-long traditions, Black bikers host rides, picnics and other gatherings nearly every summer weekend to celebrate community and freedom
Content: Dutch with Flaming Knight Members in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.View image in fullscreenDutch with Flaming Knight Members in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Black US cultureBlack motorcycle clubs come alive in the summer: ‘The best way to build community is on two wheels’Building on decades-long traditions, Black bikers host rides, picnics and other gatherings nearly every summer weekend to celebrate community and freedomMorgan Jerkinswith photographs by  Elijah Chukwuka MogoliTue 28 Jul 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe trip was only supposed to be a Memorial Day weekend girls’ getaway to Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, for Patrice “Foxy” Johnson. But once Johnson and her crew arrived, they inadvertently found themselves in the middle of an annual bike week where several thousand riders had convened. Johnson watched the “backpacks”, or the women who rode on the backs of male motorcyclists’ bikes, and realized she too wanted to be part of the community. She didn’t want to accompany the male riders, though. She wanted to ride herself.In that moment about 30 years ago, Johnson decided that next time she would be attending bike week and coming with her own set of wheels. Once she returned to her home town of Raleigh, North Carolina, she enrolled in a foundational bike riding class at Johnston community college to learn more about motorcycles. Since then, she’s become such a staple in the Black motorcycle community nationwide that she holds multiple leadership positions across organizations.View image in fullscreenA female biker at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Just about every weekend, particularly in the summer, a Black motorcycle club in some US city is having their annual ride, picnic or other social gathering amid food and music. A place for bike enthusiasts to convene among like-minded community members, some biker clubs date as far back as the 1940s, starting after the second world war. Today’s rides are part of the culture of freedom of movement that started as a response to exclusion from white motorcycle clubs and labor discrimination due to Jim Crow.History on wheelsOne of the clubs where Johnson invests her time is Black Girls Ride (BGR), which has supported women of color in motorsports since its inception in 2011. The group has meetups several times a year in cities such as Houston, Daytona Beach and Los Angeles, it publishes a digital magazine and a podcast, sells its own gear, and has annual traditions such as participating in the Essence festival, a music festival for Black women, every July in New Orleans. About 250 to 300 BGR members typically make the trip to Louisiana. “The police officers will clear the street for us to walk down Bourbon Street with a second line band,” Johnson, the Carolinas ambassador for BGR, which has five national ambassadors and a rider leader, said. “We’re chanting: ‘Black Girls Ride! Black Girls Ride!’ We’re dancing in the street.” Once, as a part of their civic engagement goals, BGR “adopted” the Boys and Girls Club of New Orleans and raised more than $30,000. Such traditions among Black motorsports enthusiasts help engender leisurely fun and community building.View image in fullscreenBikers playing cards at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Part of that community building is providing members with education on Black history. The Buffalo Soldiers Motorcycle Club, one of the largest motorcycle clubs in the country with roughly 5,000 members, for instance carries the name of the all-Black military units of the ninth and 10th US cavalry regiments established by Congress in 1866. One of its current club members, the air force veteran Randy Hayward, also known as Detroit Randy, recalled a memorial ride called The Buffalo Thunder from Washington DC to Detroit: “We rode through communities and everybody had their flag out … Black soldiers may not have been celebrated when they came home.”Annually, the Buffalo Soldiers Motorcycle Club holds a July convention in select cities such as Tampa, Florida; Concord, North Carolina; and Mobile, Alabama, where safety training sessions, rides, cookouts and community outreach are a part of regular programming. “The best way to fellowship is on two wheels,” Hayward said, before listing some of the history-driven rides that his organization has taken to historic sites like Black Wall Street and the Wilberforce, Ohio, home of Col Charles Young, the first Black US army colonel.Steel Horses bike club members and Brown Sugar and friends of Unapologetic Kweenz at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in -Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn on 19 July 2026.Steel Horses bike club members and Brown Sugar and friends of Unapologetic Kweenz at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in -Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn on 19 July 2026.Black motorcycle culture is inextricably linked to Black military service. When Black soldiers returned home from the second world war in the 1940s,many were still seeking community with a sense of adventure. Tuskegee Airmen couldn’t get jobs as pilotsdue to persistent racism, and motorcycling gave them the opportunity to attain a similar thrill – if they could get their hands on a bike.During the war,military motorcycles were vital in scoping out enemy positions and delivering weapons, messages and orders. Once the war ended, the military turned to Jeeps and armored vehicles and therefore military motorcycles flooded the market. Unfortunately, despite these bikes being surplus and cheap, many dealers would not sell motorcycles to Black people.A former US marine decided to build his own motorcycles.Cliff Vaughsfrom Los Angeles, California, introduced motorcycle riding as a form of organizing via his work with the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) between 1963 and 1964. While visiting working-class Black sharecroppers in Alabama, Vaughs said to the author Paul d’Orléans for his book The Chopper: The Real Story: “I wanted to be a visible example to them; a free Black man on my motorcycle.”View image in fullscreenCash, a young biker, at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.By the late 1960s, bike clubs such as the State Burners of Atlantic City, the East Bay Dragons of Oakland, the Chosen Few of Los Angeles and the Iron Horse Motorcycle Club of Miami, were thriving. The Miami-based organization was founded by Bessie Stringfield, also known as “The Motorcycle Queen of Miami”, who served in the second world war as the only woman in her unit of civilian courier motorcycle dispatchers. She was also the first African American woman to rideacross the US solo.On her rides, Stringfield relied on The Negro Motorist Green Book,a travel and survival guide for Black drivers, so that she could remain safe throughout her journeys.‘An investment in experiences and freedom’Today, owning a bike is just the starting point for entry into an organization. “Every club has its own set of rules,” said Anthony “Zeke” Settle, the national president of the Black Stallions Motorcycle Club, which was founded in Los Angeles. For Settle’s organization, members have to be 21 years old, own a motorcycle bigger than 600 cubic centimeters – which means a mid-sized engine with a great capacity for speed – complete a three-month probationary period involving mandatory rides, cross four state lines and attend events where prospects can acquaint themselves with official members.Membership comes at a financial cost as well. Settle explained: “A basic, say 600 sports bike motorcycle – that’s at least [$10,000]. That’s a good used one. The top-of-the-line sports bike – Kawasaki has one that’s $30,000.”Female and male bikers at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Female and male bikers at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Alvin C Jacobs Jr, a photographer, rider and the author of Chrome, a coffee table bookwhich showcases Black motorcycle culture, spent over $50,000 on his most recent bike. He acknowledges that associated costs have posed challenges in recruiting younger riders: “It’s an expensive hobby and the average millennial is broke,” said Jacobs.Biking runs through the Jacobs family. Alvin C Jacobs Jr’s father, Alvin Jacobs Sr, co-founded The Brothers Club in Rockford, Illinois, in 1976, where Alvin Jr grew up, “near the Kegels Harley-Davidson [store]”, he said. And Alvin Jr’s son, Hassan Jacobs, is a millennial rider who served in the military for eight years. He’s not a part of a motorcycle club and therefore is not subjected to the financial obligations of an organization, but he is proud to be a younger rider: “I feel like when I’m on the open road, particularly on a bike, I am able to move freely at speeds that don’t constrain me,” Hassan said. “When I’m walking, running or even driving, I feel like I’m held back by the arbitrary limits of my body. And even in a car I don’t get that mind-to-body connection that I get on a bike. It’s almost like having a new body to glide through the road with. Freedom.”There are some club-affiliated millennials, however, who face the financial hurdles head-on. Shanika “Tru” Beatty, the founder and president of Caramel Curves, an all-Black women motorcycle club, says: “Some of our members finance their bikes, some buy used and others save until they’re ready. One thing that makes Caramel Curves special is that we support each other. We share maintenance tips, and help new riders navigate the process. We want riding to be accessible, not intimidating. At the end of the day, motorcycling isn’t just an expense to us. It’s an investment in experiences, friendships, personal growth and freedom.”View image in fullscreenDutch with Flaming Knight Members in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Since its inception in 2005, Caramel Curves has expanded to 31 members across two chapters in New Orleans and Atlanta. During the summer, its most active season, Caramel Curves organizes group rides, attends other bike events, and hosts sessions where members get to know one another on and off their bikes. “We organize group rides, attend bike events and create spaces for our members to connect both on and off the bike,” Beatty said. “It’s also a time when we welcome new riders who are just getting started and want to be part of something supportive and empowering.”A supportive community is what also inspired Phillip “Dutch” Boyd to join a motorcycle group, after discovering his love for riding during the pandemic: “My friends rode back in the day and they would always crash! I didn’t think bikes were safe until I did some research during the Covid lockdown.” The first day that Boyd learned how to ride a bike from his brother-in-law changed his life. After solo riding for a year, he had the opportunity to squire, or prospect, at The Flaming Knights, a predominantly Black motorcycle club founded in 1968. He earned his patches, which delineate club affiliation, and became a member.A few weeks ago, the Flaming Knights attended the annual Bike Week in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, a convening of bikers from all over the country. About 200 bikers showed up, mingled with others and shopped the local street vendors. R&B and rap music blasted from nearby speakers, and a few kids played on their mini bikes as the adults relaxed with their coolers or ventured around the corner to the clubhouse of Imperial Bikers, the motorcycle club that hosted the event.Regardless of how Black bikers discovered their love for the sport, biking is less of a hobby and more of a lifestyle. “One of the biggest misconceptions is that Black motorcycle culture is only about clubs, leather and looking tough,” said Beatty of Caramel Curves. “In reality, it’s about community, family, freedom and giving back.”Explore more on these topicsBlack US cultureMotorcyclingMotor sportRaceNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I had my first alcoholic drink at 16. By 26, I was given six months to live | Alcohol | The Guardian
description: Holly Dyson’s addiction led to extreme pain, hospital trips and thousands of pounds’ worth of debt. Here is how she recovered
Author: Emma Russell
Headline: Holly Dyson’s addiction led to extreme pain, hospital trips and thousands of pounds’ worth of debt. Here is how she recovered
Content: ‘I had loads of people looking out for me’: Holly Dyson today.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I had loads of people looking out for me’: Holly Dyson today.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianHow we surviveAlcoholI had my first alcoholic drink at 16. By 26, I was given six months to liveHolly Dyson’s addiction led to extreme pain, hospital trips and thousands of pounds’ worth of debt. Here is how she recoveredEmma RussellTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHolly Dyson’s last alcoholic drink was a can of cider to manage her withdrawal symptoms, which she had in her dad’s car on the way to rehab on 2 May 2023. She’d barely eaten in two weeks. Instead, she spent her last few days at home in the north-west of England vomiting blood into the toilet bowl and lying in bed twitching, feeling unbearably nauseous. Her hand hovered over the numbers 999 on her phone, ready to call an ambulance. At 26 years old, Dyson’s body was shutting down.About a week earlier, a doctor had given her six months to live. For the past few years, her drinking had spiralled out of control. Her liver was “deranged”, the doctor said. To Dyson, it felt like “a bowling ball” – weighing her down so much that she would have to use “two hands to lift my body up out of bed because my liver felt so heavy and swollen.” Her face was also swollen and she was unrecognisable from the sporty young woman she had once been.But Dyson was “past the point of caring,” she says. “I just couldn’t do this any more.”Dyson’s childhood in Tarleton, a rural village between Preston and Southport, in England, was blissful. “I lived in this little bubble where nothing bad ever happened and everything was so lovely.” She was the only child of happily married parents: “This perfect little blond, happy, everyone-loved-us-family,” she says.View image in fullscreenHolly (left) during one of her lowest points; and (right) alcohol-free.Photograph: Courtesy of Holly DysonThat all changed when she turned 12 and her mum moved out. “I absolutely did not see it coming,” she says of her parents’ divorce.Some research has foundthat alcohol dependency can be linked to early childhood trauma, such as divorce, which disrupts emotional development and can cause chronic stress. Now in therapy, Dyson attributes her parents’ separation to her developing “an intense fear” of abandonment.Dyson had her first alcoholic drink at 16 years old – a fruity cider in the park with her friends – but she didn’t get drunk until she went to university in Leeds in 2015. “Everywhere I looked there were people doing cocaine, there were people doing pills, there were people doing MDMA.” But drugs never held the same appeal for Dyson as drink.As a student, she quickly made friends at her halls of residence and fell for a “tall, dark, handsome southerner”, who became her on and off lover. He accompanied Dyson to her mum’s wedding to a new partner in 2016 and became her best friend. But he could also be abusive, particularly on a night out, when he would call her derogatory names and grab her wrists aggressively, she says. When Dyson found out he had been cheating on her with two of her closest friends, she couldn’t cope with the deceit and pain, and she dropped out of university.It was on a sunny day in 2017 that she poured herself the drink that would derail her: a gin and tonic, which she drank before heading to her job as a personal trainer. That one “lit up my brain”, she says.Dyson had moved in with her mum and it wasn’t long before herstash of gin was gone. She refilled the bottles with water so her mum wouldn’t know that Dyson had drunk them alone, then started hiding the evidence in her bedroom and car. It became a full-time obsession. “Your every thought is: ‘Where’s my next drink coming from? Can we afford the next drink? What are we going to get to drink? Where are we going to hide it?’ That’s just on repeat.”For the first couple of years, she was good at hiding her dependency. Dyson began living with her boyfriend of a few years, who was very laid-back and never confronted her about her drinking, but friends started to notice. “I looked dreadful,” she says. “You couldn’t look at me and not know something was wrong.” She doesn’t ever remember blacking out but she would sometimes wake up covered in mysterious bruises.View image in fullscreen‘No physical pain will ever compare to the emotional pain I went through’ … Holly with Luna.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianHer best friend Alice was particularly concerned; on Dyson’s birthday at her house, she bought her non-alcoholic prosecco to celebrate with. “I was deeply offended,” says Dyson, who left the celebrations as quickly as she could because she didn’t see the point in a social event without alcohol. At this point she was drinking several bottles of wine a night.In 2020, Dyson started getting horrendous liver pains and took herself to Southport hospital’s A&E, where she met the hospital alcohol liaison team for the first time. A scan found that she had severe liver disease, but “it meant nothing to me. I wasn’t at the point where I’d hit rock bottom yet,” she says. “I wasn’t at the point where I wanted to stop drinking.”Over the next few years, Dyson was in and out of hospital. She switched from gin to cider, which she sipped first thing in the morning to stop the withdrawal symptoms: shaking, vomiting, irritability and a loss of appetite. She would pour wine into a Lucozade bottle, top it up with Lipton’s peach ice tea, and drink it throughout the day while working as an administrator. When she finished at 2pm, Dyson would buy more wine on her way home.View image in fullscreenDyson with her dogs Luna (left) and Lola.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianBy 8pm, she would be very drunk, she says, but would crack open a few more bottles of cider and line them up by the bed, so as not to wake up her partner when she opened them, drinking them “like water” throughout the night. “I had to do everything I could to be able to drink alcohol 24/7.”It was an expensive habit. As soon as she was paid, Dyson would spend £300-400 on alcohol, thinking it would last her for the month. But it would barely last the week. When she ran out of money, she would ask her mum, then her dad, for petrol money, and use it to buy more booze. And when that still didn’t cover her costs, she took out loan after loan.“When five grand drops in your bank account, you go absolutely wild and get the most expensive gins and all the flavours,” she says, “It was detrimental to my future because when I came out of addiction I had 10 grand’s worth of debt, I couldn’t keep up with the repayments, so now I’ve got a debt management plan, which means, for the next six years, I can’t get a mortgage, and I can’t get a credit card because my credit score is ridiculously low.”During her stints in hospital, Dyson was given Librium, the brand name for chlordiazepoxide, to help her manage her acute alcohol withdrawal symptoms. For alcoholics, withdrawal can be deadly, causing confusion, seizures and hallucinations. However, when she returned home, she would self-medicate with cans of cider. She wouldn’t be able to walk properly or keep food down. But “once I got through that” with a mixture of patience and more alcohol, she would think: “I’m fixed now, I can drink again.”Dyson’s maternal grandmother had died from alcoholism when she was 52, three months after Dyson was born. “My mum thought all the worrying about me might give her a heart attack,” says Dyson. But her dad didn’t understand the severity of the issue until she visited the doctor – and he told her father how long he believed she had left to live. He swiftly moved Dyson back into his house and “there were two or three nights where I was so ill, withdrawing, being sick” that he stayed awake with her through the night. He got rid of any alcohol in the house, took away her bank cards. Previously, Dyson had only seen her dad cry once – the day he told her that her mum had left them. “But those final few days before I went to rehab, I saw him cry quite a lot.”View image in fullscreen‘Those final few days before I went to rehab, I saw my dad cry a lot.’Photograph: Courtesy of Holly DysonHer dad knew there was nothing more he could do for her when she came home with alcohol and downed the lot in her room. Neither of them have any idea how she paid for it. That day, he drove her to a private rehab facility called Ocean Recovery in Blackpool and took out a loan to pay for her care. “If he hadn’t got me into rehab when he did, I wouldn’t be here,” says Dyson.It is estimated that 15% of women in England drink in a way that damages their health, according toAlcohol Change. From 2019 to 2023, there was a39% increase in female alcohol-specific mortality rates. Yet women are significantly less likely to seek out traditional treatment programmes, such as Alcoholics Anonymous. Research has found that women and men often drink for different reasons: women tonumb, hide or alleviate feelings of shamerelated to their own victimisation, whereas men more oftendrink to relaxand to distinguish rest time from work. Stigma around addiction can also reinforce women’s sense of shame, meaning they are more inclined to be in denial about their dependence on alcohol, and keep it hidden.Dyson is the first to admit that she had a set idea of what an alcoholic looks like, and it wasn’t her. “I had everything going for me: I was a young girl, I was fit, I was active, I had a wonderful family, I had a home, I was safe, I was loved, but that didn’t stop it,” she says. “It does not stigmatise.” On the first morning of her rehabilitation, “I put my head round the door at breakfast and I remember going: ‘Shit, everyone is normal.’”Dyson stayed at the facility for 28 days. “I was the youngest by a good 20 years,” she says. “I was the baby. I had loads of people looking out for me.” She went on a lot of walks, did group therapy, meditation and yoga. She would paint in the evening, and spent a long time chatting with her peers.But, she said, the hard work really started when she was discharged, and had to return to life without consistent monitoring and support. In rehab, Dyson was surrounded by people who had shared the same experience as her, who she could talk with at length about her struggles. Dyson says her new job as a support worker for the drug and alcohol service Change Grow Live has also helped her to stay sober – talking openly about the pain of addiction is a daily reminder of the difficulties she went through. She still enjoys painting and exercises regularly; she ran a London Landmarks half marathon in April and is training for a full marathon next. “No physical pain, such as running a marathon, will ever compare to the emotional pain that I went through during addiction.”Now, Dyson notices alcohol everywhere and disapproves of the culture of heavy drinking which is prevalent in the UK. She doesn’t like the way alcohol is marketed in supermarkets, where there are “‘buy two crates for a tenner’ signs everywhere.” She thinks alcohol should be hidden like cigarettes and sweets. “People forget that alcohol is a drug and that there are millions of people with alcohol problems. If you have a really rough day, you walk into a supermarket and before you’ve even picked up your basket you’re seeing all these offers on alcohol in the doorway – that’s going to be detrimental to someone’s health”As part of her role at Change Grow Live, she is keen to share the “raw, unfiltered truth of addiction” in the hope that someone experiencing what she did can find the strength to reach out for help. “Let’s show what alcohol addiction is really like: it’s vomiting blood, it’s not being able to get off the bed, it’s lying to get money. It’s awful,” she says. “Admitting you’re struggling is the bravest and most important thing that you can do to save yourself.”Recently, Dyson had a scan of her liver, which showed she now has no scarring or fatty liver. “It’s more or less completely rejuvenated and has fixed itself.” Her blood results also show that her liver function is in the normal range. “That does make me emotional,” she says.“People say recovery is hard and I get it because you’ve got to work on it every day – once you’re complacent relapses happen,” says Dyson. “But I will say addiction is harder than recovery, 100%. Addiction is a full-time 24/7 job.”In the UK,Taking Action on Addictionprovides links to different support services. In the US, call or textSAMHSA’s National Helpline at 988. In Australia, theNational Alcohol and Other Drug Hotlineis at 1800 250 015; families and friends can seek help atFamily Drug Support Australiaat 1300 368 186Explore more on these topicsAlcoholHow we surviveWomenHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How I Shop with Rosie Jones: ‘Screw it, I deserve it!’ | Rosie Jones | The Guardian
description: Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food, and the basic they scrimp on? The writer and comedian talks grownup crockery, posh hand soap and Abba Voyage with the Filter
Author: Lily Smith
Headline: Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food, and the basic they scrimp on? The writer and comedian talks grownup crockery, posh hand soap and Abba Voyage with the Filter
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignHow I shopRosie JonesInterviewHow I Shop with Rosie Jones: ‘Screw it, I deserve it!’As told toLily SmithAlways wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food, and the basic they scrimp on? The writer and comedian talks grownup crockery, posh hand soap and Abba Voyage with the FilterTue 28 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Rosie Jones is an actor, writer and award-winning standup comedian, and a familiar face on UK television – she’s fronted her own Comedy Central series Out of Order, starred in Channel 4’s hard-hitting documentaryAm I a R*tard?, and led two travel series,Mission: Accessibleand the Bafta-nominatedTrip Hazard.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.She is the creator and star of the Channel 4 comedy-dramaPushers, a six-part series nominated for a Bafta in 2026. Her acting credits span primetime dramas such as Silent Witness, Casualty and Call the Midwife, and she has also appeared as herself on Taskmaster, Live at the Apollo, QI, 8 Out of 10 Cats, the Last Leg and many more. She set up the Rosie Jones Foundation in 2025, which focuses on mental health support for individuals living with cerebral palsy and peer support through events and workshops. She brings her standup showI Can’t Tell What She’s Sayingto the Edinburgh fringe from 5 to 30 August.What’s the last treat you bought for yourself?I bought some “grownup” pasta bowls fromDenby. They were expensive, but I thought “screw it, I deserve it”, so I bought four. Not even a week in, I broke one, and it made me so sad.View image in fullscreenDenby dark grey speckle pasta bowls, set of four£96 at John LewisWhere do you buy your food from?Every week I think I’llgo to Asda and do a big shop for the week. Do I? Never. I am an Uber Eats lady. I order from the Co-op and get all I need for the day, but I mainly shop there for its salt and vinegar crisps. They’re so vinegary, they hurt the roof of your mouth – it’s incredible.View image in fullscreenCo-op sea salt and chardonnay wine vinegar crisps£1.70 at Co-opWhat’s the best present you’ve given?The Dom Pérignon champagne that I got my mum for her 60th, which she opened immediately. I just thought that was the best thing ever because when you get champagne you think “ooh no, I’ll save it for a celebration”, but what’s a better celebration than your 60th birthday?View image in fullscreenDom Pérignon brut vintage champagne£202 at Majestic£219 at Fortnum & MasonYou also can’t beat Abba Voyage. If you’re looking for a present for someone, and you’re like “how do I give them the best night of their lives?”, it’s gotta be Abba Voyage.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Johan Persson/Abba Voyage/PABook Abba Voyage… and the best presentyou’ve received?A bright red, three-wheeled bike when I was a child, that we called “Pickle”. I can’t ride a two-wheeled bike because of my disability, so it was my first taste of freedom and being able to do things that everybody else could do. Then, when I was about 14 or 15, my mum and dad bought me the adult version so I could join them on bike rides. So I’m being greedy and saying two: little pickle and big pickle.View image in fullscreenPashley Pickle child’s tricycle£167.10 at eBayWhat’s your favourite online store?Sugarhill Brighton boutique: it’s my taste all over. It’s bright colours, fancy patterns, jumpsuits, co-ords – it’s just really lovely, fun clothing. Whenever I wear something from there, people go “oh my god, where’s that from?”Shop SugarhillWhat’s your favourite bricks-and-mortar shop?I’m a bougie bitch, and I love Aesop. I can be in central London, running about, and I just go in its shop on Lexington Street and go “ahhhh” and relax. I think everyone knows Aesop for its soap, but I get my perfume from there. I have a spicy, almost unisex scent called Gloam.View image in fullscreenAesop Gloam eau de parfum, 50ml£120 at Liberty London£150 at SpaceNKWhat’s the gadget you use most often?I call it my sex toy because it looks like a swing, but it’s actually a cup carrier. Because of my disability, I can’t carry liquid: this means I can carry my cup without it spilling, so I can drink my coffees wherever, whenever. It’s made my life so much better.View image in fullscreenAnti-spill cup carrier£8.79 at AmazonWhat’s the purchase you regret the most?I’m a Yorkshire girl so I think about things before I spend my money. The thing that comes to mind is when I buy a book and then it turns out the author of that book is a bad man or a bad transphobe. Which makes me think“why did I give them money!?”What’s the thing(s) you get delivered?Toilet roll. It’s amazing that I used to spend life going “oh my god, I’ve only got four rolls left”, and then I’d forget to get more and end up wiping my bum with a bit of paper or a receipt. So now every three months I get a load of lovely toilet roll delivered – it’s a dream come true.View image in fullscreenWho Gives a Crap toilet roll subscriptionFrom £28 a month at Who Gives a CrapWhere do you buy your underwear?I really like Uniqlo for simple, everyday knickers. I’m a large-booby lady, so I buy my bras and bikini tops from Bravissimo, and I like a matching set, so you best be sure I’m getting the matching bottoms. I also want to shout out Curvy Kate. You can just tell that its underwear is made and designed by people who know what it’s like to have a big bosom.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShop women’s underwear at UniqloShop bras at BravissimoShop bras at Curvy KateWhat would you buy with £20 – and £200?£20: Four tins of Perelló olives. My nana is Spanish, so I’ve got Mediterranean olive oil running throughout my body. Perelló green olives are the best I’ve ever tasted.View image in fullscreenPerelló olives, 150g tin£5.10 at Ocado£8.99 for two at Amazon£200: I’m not assed about jewellery or designer clothes or handbags, but I love experiences and shows and going to places. Recently me and my girlfriend went to an amazing restaurant in Mayfair called Rosi at the Beaumont hotel, and they just treated us so well. We had wine, champagne, and for dessert you can make your own sundae. If you gave me £200, I wouldn’t want anything that I could hold or touch, I’d want to make a memory with a loved one.View image in fullscreenDining room at Rosi at the Beaumont hotel.Photograph: John CareyVisit Rosi at the Beaumont hotelWhat’s your ‘saved search’ on eBay/Vinted?I am probably the only person in the country who doesn’t use eBay or Vinted. Maybe I’m lazy, but all of that thinking “ooh, I want that jacket, but someone else wants it too” stresses me out. If I want an item of clothing, I just want to go online, buy it and be done.What item do you buy on repeat?Yorkshire Tea. When I’m down to my last five bags, I start panickingand haveto stock up.View image in fullscreenYorkshire Tea, 160 tea bags£4.75 at Waitrose£7 at MorrisonsHow do you make your coffee at home?In a Nespresso coffee machine. I have a Grind subscription, and I get the lovely little pods delivered. I am not functional in the morning without the little pod with a bit of regular milk – job’s a good ‘un.View image in fullscreenNespresso CitiZ coffee pod machine£179 at John Lewis£189.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenGrind coffee pod subscription£27.95 a month at GrindWhat’s your biggest splurge?Diptyque hand soap. It’s in a glass container, and one of them lasts me an entire year. It makes me so happy whenever I go to the toilet and get to use a little bit of Diptyque. It smells so good.View image in fullscreenDiptyque softening hand wash£59 at John Lewis£59 at SelfridgesAnd what everyday item do you scrimp on?Socks! I don’t care what’s on my feet. I never see them. Just put something between my foot and my shoe, and I’ll be happy.And what’s your greatest vintage find?I went to Sandringham’s Christmas market, and I bought a camera that’s been turned into a lamp. I love it because I know no one else has a lamp like it. I also love it because when friends come into my living room, they go “are you filming us?”, and I’m like “no! It’s a lamp.”For more, read How I shop withAngela HartnettandDavid GandyView image in fullscreenDon’t buy anything until you’ve read the Filter, the Guardian’s home for truly independent product reviews and recommendations. Whether you’re after rigorous tests or shopping inspiration, affordable gifts or advice on how to make your belongings last longer, we’re here to help you make smarter, more sustainable choices.The Filter is packed with trustworthy buying advice on everything from coffee machines to hiking boots, mascara to secateurs. So visit us today and start buying better and smarter, and wasting less.Explore the FilterExplore more on these topicsRosie JonesHow I shopHomesCelebrityComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A self-emptying, frictionless marvel: Shark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro review | Homes | The Guardian
description: Shark’s cordless vacuum is a whiz at cleaning hard floors and pet hair, but a disarmingly short battery life caught our reviewer off guard
Author: Andy Shaw
Headline: Shark’s cordless vacuum is a whiz at cleaning hard floors and pet hair, but a disarmingly short battery life caught our reviewer off guard
Content: Power player … Shark’s self-emptying cordless vacuum cleans brilliantly, but battery life falls short in larger homes.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPower player … Shark’s self-emptying cordless vacuum cleans brilliantly, but battery life falls short in larger homes.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianThe FilterHomesReviewA self-emptying, frictionless marvel: Shark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro reviewShark’s cordless vacuum is a whiz at cleaning hard floors and pet hair, but a disarmingly short battery life caught our reviewer off guardThe best cordless vacuum cleaners – testedAndy ShawTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Vacuuming rarely starts with vacuuming. First you have to clear the floor of stray socks and abandoned toys left behind by children, pets or messy partners. Then there’s the irritation of finding the vacuum’s dustbin still full of dirt, or the battery flat because someone forgot to charge it.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The (take a deep breath – long name coming up) Shark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro cordless vacuum Ultramarine IA3241UKT certainly won’t pick up the scattered toys for you, but it has been designed to make the job of vacuuming as frictionless as possible.Most of that is down to the self-emptying and charging station. Shark claims this will hold 45 days’ worth of dirt before needing to be emptied. Once you’ve finished vacuuming, you put the cleaner back on the stand, and a secondary vacuum in the base pulls the dirt out of the cleaner’s 0.47l collection bin and into a 2l chamber below. If you live with people who are prone to absent-mindedly leaving a vacuum stuffed to the brim after using it, it makes a real difference. The base station also charges the cleaner, so the next time you reach for it, it’s not only empty of dirt but ready to go.View at SharkNinjaView at AOHow I testedView image in fullscreenOn the surface … writer Andy testing on a living room rug.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianWith acordless vacuum cleanersuch as this one, I start with a battery test. The device is fully charged, switched to full suction power, and left to run on a piece of short-pile carpet with the primary floor head attached until the battery runs out. I then recharge the battery and repeat the process on the lowest suction setting, which might not clean the floor as well, but is useful if you want to cover the largest area.View image in fullscreenDog days … the motorised pet tool was put to the test on cocker spaniel hair embedded in mats, sofas and cosy chairs.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianNext I test the suction using a vacuum meter. Powerful suction doesn’t guarantee a great vacuum cleaner, but a weak result here is often accompanied by disappointing cleaning.Lastly, I run through a series of cleaning tests. I measure precise amounts of pet hair, cat litter and flour, depositing them on carpet and hard floor. I weigh the collection bin before and after vacuuming each type of mess, giving the device one chance to pick up whatever it can with a single forward and backward pass.I’ve performed these tests with all thevacuum cleanersI’ve reviewed for the Filter, so I can easily compare the performance with every model I’ve tested.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenAmong the Shark cleaner’s Detect functions is the ability to sense ‘when it’s being pushed up against a wall, skirting or kick-board’.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianView at SharkNinjaView at AOShark sent me the top-end model (theIA3241UKT, RRP £499.99), which comes with the emptying station and a motorised hand tool designed for stairs and pet hair on upholstery. Ditch the self-emptying station and the motorised pet tool and the RRP drops to £429.99 (model numberIA1241UKT); this comes with a non-motorised brush and funnel hand tool instead. If you only want the combination crevice tool and dusting brush that comes with all models, there’s also a version of the cleaner for an RRP of £399.99 (theIA1241UK).The vacuum itself is crammed with Shark’s detection technologies. The floor head knows whether it’s on carpet or hard flooring, and adjusts the suction power and the speed of the roller accordingly. It also senses when it’s being pushed up against a wall, skirting or kick-board, and cranks up the suction to better draw in dirt from the edges.There’s a dirt detection system, too, which increases the power when it thinks it might have hit a particularly grubby patch. Lastly, when it’s on hard flooring, a blue light switches on to make spotting dust and dirt much easier.View image in fullscreenThe Shark can be folded away when not in use because of the 180-degree hinge in its extension wand.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianMost of Shark’s usual cordless stick-vacuum features are included. There’s a 180-degree hinge in the extension wand, for example, which can be used to flatten the device for cleaning under low furniture. It can fold all the way over, which allows the device to stand upright without support, but also means you can store it in a low cupboard if you’d rather put it away than keep it on the base station.The one thing that’s missing from Shark’s usual repertoire is the dual-roller floor head. While the majority of Shark’s most effective cleaners feature a regular brush bar and a fluffy roller in the floor head, this model has ditched the fluffy one. I have to admit this set alarm bells ringing. Dual-roller floor heads have proved effective in my tests, and my favouritecordlessandcorded vacuum cleanershave them. I couldn’t help but wonder if, as withDyson’s Piston Animal, Shark had taken a step too far in reinventing its floor head.SpecificationsWeight (measured):3.2kg (vacuum with extension wand and floor head attached)Max suction power (quoted):150 air wattsMax suction power (measured):24.5kPaBattery life (quoted):1hr (Eco mode without motorised tool)Battery life (tested):49mins 55secs (Eco mode with motorised floor head attached)Charge time (quoted):5hrsDust capacity:0.47l (handheld); 2l (base station)Additional filters supplied?NoDimensions:26 x 37.5 x 114cm (WDH, including base station)What we loveView image in fullscreenMessing about: before (left) and after (right) the Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty got to work on the flour, pet hair and cat litter.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianDuring testing, I quickly realised that I had little cause for concern. The IA3241UKTperformed exceptionally well across all my cleaning tests. On carpet, its floor head cleared 99% of the cat litter and 96% of the flour. You can see the two pieces of cat litter that escaped in my before and after pictures above, and while the flour appears to have left a bit of a streak, that was after a single push and pull motion. When I further tackled it from a few more angles, the vacuum lifted the last remnants.This is slightly better on carpet than my favourite cordless, theIP3251UKT. It also dealt with cat litter better than thecorded LA791UKT, but wasn’t as good as this model when picking up flour.Interestingly, itperformed even better on hard floors, where I was expecting the absence of a fluffy roller to leave it lacking. It gathered every last piece of cat litter, while the flour test results rose to 97%. A vacuum with a fluffy roller may take things a little further and, matching expectations, the IP3251UKT managed to lift more flour in this test. However, I remained hugely impressed with this model’s performance on hard floors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI also tested the vacuum withpet hair– where again it excelled. The trimmed dog hair I placed on carpet and hard flooring was all sucked up, leaving no trace behind. It proved effective on the mats where my cocker spaniel hangs out, and lifted traces of his fur off sofas and cosy chairs with the motorised pet tool.All the tests were run in the vacuum’sDetect mode, which regulates the suction and roller speed based on whether it’s on carpet or a hard floor. This worked well in terms of cleaning: it audibly changed the power depending on the surface, when it detected an increase in dirt, and when it was being pushed along a wall. If you prefer, you can opt to run it in Eco mode for improved battery life, or Boost mode to temporarily max out the power.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenThere was an issue when debris that went into the self-emptying bin blocked the neck of it.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianThe first time I attempted a whole-house clean, the hairball that was coughed out from the vacuum into the self-emptying binblocked the neckof the station. It vacated the cleaner but got stuck at the top of the self-empty station, rather than dropping down into the bin below. So while the vacuum coped with everything I threw at it, the base did not. On subsequent empties I was unable to replicate the problem, although I was wary of overfilling it before popping it on to the base to empty it.I was also caught out by the battery. While some vacuums provide clear guidance on how much charge is left, either as a percentage or in minutes and seconds, the Shark uses a bar with a gradient. Istruggled to notice the battery droppingfrom what the manual defines as half charge to low charge, and as a result, I was never prepared for it to cut out completely. If a battery is about to quit, I’d rather have a much clearer warning, so I can at least prioritise what I want to clean, or make an informed decision to reduce the power to eke out more cleaning time.Having said that, it didn’t help that thebattery life isdisappointing. In my tests, which measure how long the battery lasts when the vacuum is left running on the same piece of carpet, the IA3241UKT outperformed my current favourite cordless, the IP3251UKT. However, in practice the IP3251UKT showed no sign of failing to make it around my house on a single charge, while this model left me short of power. That makes theIP3251UKTa better option in a larger house.Warranty, repairability and sustainabilityView image in fullscreenThere’s a five-year warranty on the IA3241UKT but note that this doesn’t include its battery.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianShark offers a generous five-year warranty that kicks in as long as you register your product within 28 days of purchase. It covers parts and labour, and Shark will repair or replace your product if it breaks down. It doesn’t include the rechargeable battery, although this has its own two-year warranty. It also doesn’t cover normal wear and tear or accidental damage, and it becomes void if you’ve replaced any parts with accessories or consumables that aren’t manufactured by Shark. If bits of your vacuum break or wear out, there is an extensive supply of spare parts available via Shark’s website.If you want to rescue a Shark, the company offers refurbished models on itseBay store. You’re less likely to find the latest models, but it’s good to know that returns are checked, refurbished and offered for resale at a discount.In terms of recycling, Shark complies with the usual WEEE legislation in the UK, which requires that it contributes information and financial support to the recycling of electrical waste via council-run waste collection sites.Shark PowerDetect IA3241UKT: should I buy it?View image in fullscreenClean sweep: ‘It’s easy to use and extremely capable at cleaning up mess.’Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianWhen it comes to cleaning, the vacuum itself is a marvel. It’s easy to use and extremely capable at cleaning up mess. It coped well with all the dirt I threw at it, on carpet and hard floors.Its biggest drawback is its inability to make it around larger spaces. I found the battery life couldn’t quite get around my detached family home, so it’s better suited to a smaller property. The smaller-than-average collection bin is also a limitation, although you can regularly empty it into the larger base station. The imprecise battery power gauge is frustrating, but will be less of a problem in a small house or flat.For longer-lasting battery power without losing the self-emptying base station, I’d recommend theShark PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKT. Or, if you don’t mind a cable and plugging into a wall socket, the cordedShark Detect XL Car + Pet LA791UKTis also superb. That will never run out of power, and its 2.5l collection bin is even larger than the secondary collection bin in the base station of Shark’s self-emptying models.View at SharkNinjaView at AOFor more:Dyson Pencilvac Fluffycones reviewThe best cordless vacuum cleaners, testedThe best vacuum cleaners for hard floors and carpetsThe best robot vacuums to keep your home clean and dust freeAndy Shaw is a consumer journalist and technology addict. Having reviewed tech products professionally for more than 30 years, his favoured working environment is a small desk surrounded by big boxes. His greatest weakness is that he never, ever remembers how things came out of their packaging, so they rarely fit back in again when it’s time to return themExplore more on these topicsHomesThe FilterInteriorsFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Scoop of the year! We taste-test 99 of 2026’s most unusual ice creams, from the unbeatable to the unlickable | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: From olive oil to matcha, soy sauce to sage and onion stuffing, there’s a frozen designer dessert out there to tickle even the most jaded palate. Here’s the best – and worst – of what’s on offer in Britain this summer
Author: Lucy Knight
Headline: From olive oil to matcha, soy sauce to sage and onion stuffing, there’s a frozen designer dessert out there to tickle even the most jaded palate. Here’s the best – and worst – of what’s on offer in Britain this summer
Content: Lucy Knight on her mammoth taste test.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLucy Knight on her mammoth taste test.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianTaste testIce-cream and sorbetScoop of the year! We taste-test 99 of 2026’s most unusual ice creams, from the unbeatable to the unlickableFrom olive oil to matcha, soy sauce to sage and onion stuffing, there’s a frozen designer dessert out there to tickle even the most jaded palate. Here’s the best – and worst – of what’s on offer in Britain this summerLucy KnightTue 28 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s with all the weird ice-cream flavours this year? It feels as if supermarkets and independent companies are vying to make the most novel alternatives to a good old scoop of vanilla. But which are actually worth having? I tried 99 varieties of ice-cream tubs and ranked them from sickeningly sweet to dinner party-worthy.99.Paxo sage and onion stuffing,Anya Hindmarch(One scoop £4.50 or 500ml tub £16, The Ice Cream Project, London)Anya Hindmarch’s Ice Cream Project has become a yearly summer fixture, in which the fashion designer collaborates with well-known brands to create nostalgic novelty flavours (at designer prices) for which customers queue round the block. This year the flavours skew toward roast dinners, and include Oxo (which I couldn’t try, being vegetarian) and Paxo. It tastes exactly like the stuffing … which isn’t really what I want from an ice-cream.Taste 1/10, Value 1/10, Originality 7/10View image in fullscreen‘It tastes exactly like the stuffing’.Photograph: PR98.Highproteinchocolatebrownie, Oppo(240ml, £3.50, Ocado)A disgraceful, claggy, protein bar-flavoured excuse for an ice-cream.Taste 1/10, Value 5/10, Originality 4/1097.Crunchie, Cadbury(425ml, £4.02, Asda)Sickly sweet; very, very orange in colour, with a weird, foamy, almost mousse-like texture.Taste 3/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1096.Hobnobs, McVitie’s(500ml, £4, Iceland)Grainy and overly sweet. Hobnob fans should stay away and avoid disappointment.Taste 3/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1095.Caramelised biscuit swirl, Oppo(475ml, £5.40, Ocado)This sickly-sweet ice-cream demonstrates exactly why “low-calorie” ice-cream shouldn’t be a thing.Taste 3/10, Value 5/10, Originality 3/1094.Jacob’s Mini Cheddars,Anya Hindmarch(One scoop £4.50 or 500ml tub £16, The Ice Cream Project, London)Cheese ice-cream apparently has a long history in the UK, but this version doesn’t do that history any justice. Slightly coarse texture and familiar Mini Cheddars flavour.Taste 3/10, Value 1/10, Originality 7/1093.Amarena cherry cheesecake, Hackney Gelato(460ml, £5.75, Waitrose)I wanted more cheesiness from this one, too, and a less synthetic cherry flavour.Taste 3/10, Value 5/10, Originality 3/1092.Cherryand mascarpone gelato, Crosta & Mollica(450ml, £4.60, Waitrose)Soft-serve style, prettily swirled in its recyclable box, underdelivers on flavour.Taste 4/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1091.Cornish sea salted caramel brittle, No 1 Waitrose(480ml, £4.50, Waitrose)Unlike most salted caramel treats, this was actually well salted, and the brittle was nice and crunchy – even if salted caramel ice-cream feels a bit old hat these days.Taste 4/10, Value 6/10, Originality 1/1090.Strawberry cheesecake,Häagen-Dazs(460ml, £5.75, Tesco)Overly sweet and artificial-tasting.Taste 4/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1089.Milk chocolate digestives, McVitie’s(500ml, £4, Iceland)If you’re going to put biscuit pieces in an ice-cream, you need to find a way to stop them going soft. Nobody wants soggy biscuits!Taste 4/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1088.Peanut butter and milk chocolate, Reese’s(460ml, £5.50, Iceland)I love Reese’s peanut butter cups, so I had high hopes. But though it had a satisfying crackly chocolate swirl, it was slightly cloying and gritty overall.Taste 5/10, Value 4/10, Originality 2/10View image in fullscreen‘Slightly cloying and gritty’ … Peanut butter and milk chocolate.Photograph: Lucy Knight/The Guardian87.Proteinspeculoos, Jude’s(460ml, £5, Ocado)This vegan, high-protein ice-cream is another soggy biscuit offender, and leaves an almost yeasty aftertaste. Avoid.Taste 2/10, Value 5/10, Originality 4/1086.Colombian coffee, M&S collection(500ml, £4.50, Ocado)The crushed-up coffee beans create a sandy texture which I didn’t love.Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 1/1085.Green Giant sweetcorn,Anya Hindmarch(One scoop £4.50 or 500ml tub £16, The Ice Cream Project, London)It’s a bold move to put chunks of sweetcorn in an ice-cream, and I’m not sure it pays off.Taste 4/10, Value 1/10, Originality 7/1084.Walker’s shortbread,Anya Hindmarch(One scoop £4.50, 500ml tub £16, The Ice Cream Project, London)The texture was a bit too hard. The sweet-salty flavour was perfectly nice, though.Taste 4/10, Value 1/10, Originality 7/1083.Oreo(425ml, £3.50, Iceland)Spongey texture; slightly nothing-y flavour.Taste 4/10, Value 6/10, Originality 2/1082.Tunnock’s caramel wafers,Anya Hindmarch(One scoop £4.50, 500ml tub £16, The Ice Cream Project, London)Way too sweet!Taste 4/10, Value 1/10, Originality 7/1081.Macadamia nut brittle, Häagen-Dazs(460ml, £5.75, Ocado)Another one that is far too sickly sweet. There was a slight saltiness for balance, but not enough.Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1080.Nutella(470ml, £5.50, Iceland)It’s fun that this one looks exactly like a jar of Nutella, and you have to break through a layer of Nutella spread to get to the ice-cream. Fans of the spread will love it; it was a bit too intense for me.Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1079.Soy Joy cookie dough, M&S(320ml, £4, Ocado)This soy ice-cream did not, sadly, bring me joy. It’s cloying and artificial-tasting – there are far better vegan ice-creams out there.Taste 3/10, Value 5/10, Originality 4/10View image in fullscreenLucy Knight prepares to try some of the more offbeat flavours of ice-cream.Photograph: Lucy Knight/The Guardian77-73.Capri-Sun orange / Müller Corner strawberry / McVitie’sgingernuts / Yazoo chocolate milk /Illy coffee,Anya Hindmarch(one scoop £4.50 or 500ml tub £16, The Ice Cream Project, London)These all tasted exactly like the products they’re based on.Taste 5/10, Value 1/10, Originality 7/1072.Piñacolada, Soleya(500ml, £9.50, selected UK stores)There is no alcohol in this rather insipid vegan ice-cream, which is more of a sorbet.Taste 3/10, Value 4/10, Originality 6/1071-70.Chocolate salted caramel / Caramel pecan praline, Booja Booja(465ml, £5.65, Booja Booja)Both of these vegan chocolate ice-creams have an intense chocolatey flavour.Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 3/1069.Biscoff, Lotus(425ml, £2.50, Iceland)Anyone who has enjoyed spooning Biscoff spread directly into their mouth will be in heaven.Taste 6/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1068.Blueberry and lemon curd, Yeo Valley(480ml, £4.75, Ocado)Very strong lemon curd flavour, with chunks of fresh blueberry. This isn’t a flavour combination I love, but I can appreciate that it’s a very good ice-cream.Taste 6/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/10View image in fullscreen‘A very good ice-cream’ … Blueberry and lemon curd.Photograph: Yeo Valley67.Kikkoman soy sauce,Anya Hindmarch(one scoop £4.50 or 500ml tub £16, The Ice Cream Project, London)I loved the salty first spoonful of this – but any more than that becomes overwhelming.Taste 5/10, Value 1/10, Originality 7/1066.Rhubarbandcustard, Waitrose(480ml, £3.50, Waitrose)Pure nostalgia!Taste 3/10, Value 7/10, Originality 4/1065.Lurpak salted butter,Anya Hindmarch(one scoop £4.50 or 500ml tub £16, The Ice Cream Project, London)Lovely and creamy, but could have been saltier.Taste 6/10, Value 1/10, Originality 7/1064.Vanilla andblackcardamom, Moonji(100ml, £3.49, selected UK stores and online)I wanted more cardamom from this plant-based ice-cream.Taste 5/10, Value 3/10, Originality 6/1063.Millionaires shortbread with cornish clotted cream, Kelly’s(425ml, £4, Iceland)Crunchy chunks of chocolate and biscuit, a very rich caramel sauce – delicious.Taste 7/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1062.Honeycomb andchocolate, Jude’s(460ml, £5.75, Ocado)This is a much nicer version of the flavours in the Crunchie ice-cream.Taste 6/10, Value 5/10, Originality 3/10View image in fullscreen“Much nicer version’ … Honeycomb & chocolate.Photograph: Jude’s61.Roasted strawberries, Brickell’s(475ml, £7.50, selected UK stores and online)Delicious real strawberry flavour – but the grainiest tub I tried.Taste 5/10, Value 4/10, Originality 5/1060.Trifle Twirl, M&S(500ml, £4.50, Ocado)A fun, Ben & Jerry’s-style loaded ice-cream (I haven’t included any Ben & Jerry’s tubs in this list because their flavours are all now mainstream). The sponge chunks are a bit too chewy.Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 4/1059.Heather honey, M&S(500ml, £5, Ocado)A really yummy, subtle, honey-flavoured ice-cream.Taste 7/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1058.Aunt Bessie’s yorkshire pudding,Anya Hindmarch(one scoop £4.50 or 500ml tub £16, The Ice Cream Project, London)This tastes more like pancakes with syrup than yorkshire puddings – but not in a bad way.Taste 7/10, Value 1/10, Originality 7/1057.Lemon curd, Norfolk County Dairy(500ml, £8.15, selected UK stores)A very subtle lemon flavour; I wasn’t getting curd specifically.Taste 5/10, Value 4/10, Originality 6/10View image in fullscreen‘Phish food on steroids’ … Jefferson’s Rockiest road.Photograph: Jefferson’s56.Rockiest road, Jefferson’s(370ml, £8.50, selected UK stores)Ben & Jerry’s phish food on steroids.Taste 7/10, Value 3/10, Originality 5/1055.Baileys vanilla, Carte D’Or(825ml, £4.50, Ocado)Baileys lovers will enjoy – does exactly what it says on the tub.Taste 4/10, Value 8/10, Originality 3/1054.Cornish honeycomb crunch, Kelly’s(950ml, £4, Iceland)There were nice crunchy bits of honeycomb on top, but it needed more throughout.Taste 5/10, Value 9/10, Originality 1/1053.Raspberry cheesecake withCornish clotted cream, Kelly’s(425ml, £4, Iceland)Way more delicious than I was expecting – the raspberry sauce is genuinely great.Taste 8/10, Value 5/10, Originality 2/1052.Golden syrup, Lyle’s(500ml, £4.75, Iceland)Incredibly sweet – but how could it not be?Taste 6/10, Value 5/10, Originality 4/10View image in fullscreen‘A bit underwhelming’ … Mango sticky rice.Photograph: James Moyle/Araw51.Mango sticky rice, Araw(475ml, £8, available for UK delivery)I wanted to love this vegan ice-cream, but the rice was still hard and the whole thing a bit underwhelming.Taste 3/10, Value 3/10, Originality 9/1050.Sicilian lemon and limoncello, Tesco(480ml, £3.50, Tesco)Inoffensive, but not tart enough.Taste 4/10, Value 5/10, Originality 6/1049-45.Ottolenghistrawberriesand cream with sumac/roasted pistachioand sour cherry/salted malted chocolate/coffee andcardamom/Madagascan vanillaand miso caramel,Waitrose(480ml tub, £6, Waitrose)I wanted more from all of these! More sumac, more sourness, more malt flavour …Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 6/1044.Dubai chocolate, Mister Twist(120ml, £5.50, selected UK stores)A fun, crunchy take on a trendy flavour.Taste 7/10, Value 2/10, Originality 7/10View image in fullscreen‘Fun and crunchy’ …  Dubai chocolate.Photograph: Siwan Jackson/Mister Twist43-40.Stem ginger and marmalade/Mini egg/Gingerbread/Cinnamon, SimplyIceCream(500ml, £6.50, available for UK delivery)All of these flavours from independent ice-cream maker Simply Ice Cream were lovely – but none of them blew my socks off.Taste 6/10, Value 5/10, Originality 5/1039.Matcha, Häagen-Dazs(460ml, £6, Waitrose)It’s easy to write off matcha as a zeitgeisty flavour, but in an ice-cream it’s undeniably refreshing.Taste 6/10, Value 5/10, Originality 6/1038.Irish coffee, SimplyIceCream(500ml, £6.50, available for UK delivery)I don’t love Irish coffees – but I was impressed by how much this tasted like one.Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 7/1037.Cinnamon bun, Waitrose(480ml, £3.50, Waitrose)Way too few chunks of bun – this felt like a missed opportunity! Artificial-tasting.Taste 4/10, Value 7/10, Originality 6/1036.Peach melba, Waitrose(480ml, £3.50, Waitrose)This nails the flavour of tinned peaches with sugary raspberry sauce.Taste 5/10, Value 7/10, Originality 5/1035-33.Basque cheesecake/Earl grey malted crumble/Ube halaya, Araw(475ml, £8, available for UK delivery)These felt like underwhelming representations of the unusual flavours they promised.Taste 5/10, Value 3/10, Originality 9/1032. Caramelised biscuit,Asda(425ml, £2.75, Asda)Layered with biscuit sauce, this might be even tastier than the official Lotus one.Taste 6/10, Value 7/10, Originality 4/1031.Flatwhite, M&S(500ml, £4.50, Ocado)More like an instant coffee than an espresso-based drink.Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 7/1030.Raspberry pavlova,Asda(900ml, £2.67 Asda)If you’re going to sell something as pavlova-flavoured, I think there should be more meringue chunks, but it’s cheap and relatively tasty.Taste 3/10, Value 9/10, Originality 5/1029.Tiramisu, Häagen-Dazs(420ml, £5.75, Tesco)It is my firm belief that no tiramisu-flavoured thing (and there are an increasing number of them) will ever be as good as actual tiramisu. This didn’t prove me wrong.Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 7/1028.Sicilian lemon meringue,Asda(500ml, £3.27, Asda)There were chunks of meringue throughout, and a lemon curd ripple – not bad.Taste 5/10, Value 6/10, Originality 6/10View image in fullscreenOn a quest to taste the best … Knight tries out a cornet with a twist.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian27.Mangolassi, Moonji(100ml, £3.49, selected UK stores and online)I was impressed that this vegan sorbet actually tasted like lassi, rather than just mango.Taste 7/10, Value 3/10, Originality 8/1026.Stem ginger, Salcombe Dairy(500ml, £6, Ocado)A creamy, gingery delight.Taste 9/10, Value 5/10, Originality 4/10View image in fullscreen“Creamy delight’ … Stem ginger.Photograph: Salcombe Dairy25.Matcha green tea, Jude’s(460ml, £5.75, Sainsbury’s)Slightly milder, and better, in my opinion, than Häagen-Dazs’s version.Taste 7/10, Value 5/10, Originality 6/1024.Fig leaf and currant jam, Milktooth Gelato(500ml, £9.50, selected UK stores)Earthy, interesting flavour – but some of the bits of currant were hard and gritty.Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 8/1023.Coconut kefir frozen yogurt, Waitrose(480ml, £3.50, Waitrose)There’s a lot going on here! Fresh, acidic, a bit sun-creamy – it wasn’t as luxurious as I wanted it to be.Taste 5/10, Value 7/10, Originality 6/1022.Tofu apricot ponzu, Clingy Wrap(350ml, £8, selected UK stores)This vegan ice-cream had a slightly strange texture but a lovely apricot flavour.Taste 4/10, Value 4/10, Originality 10/1021.Toscano olive oil, M&S(500ml, £4.50, Ocado)I loved the idea of this, but the flavour reminded me too much of margarine.Taste 5/10, Value 5/10, Originality 8/1020.Lemon meringue gelato,Aldi(480ml, £2.49, Aldi)Layered, lemony soft serve.Taste 6/10, Value 6/10, Originality 6/1019.Marmite on toast, Big Kid(300ml, £8, selected UK stores and online)Bizarre, but somehow actually not terrible.Taste 5/10, Value 4/10, Originality 10/10View image in fullscreen‘Somehow actually not terrible’ … Marmite on toast.Photograph: Big Kid18.Blueberry lavender jam, meringue swirl, Bears(450ml, £11.50, selected UK stores)I don’t love lavender so this wasn’t for me – but I could appreciate its creamy delicateness.Taste 6/10, Value 4/10, Originality 9/1017.Strawberry kefir frozen yoghurt, M&S(500ml, £3.75, Ocado)Refreshingly tangy!Taste 6/10, Value 6/10, Originality 7/1016.Tiramisu gelato,Aldi(480ml, £2.49, Aldi)This layered soft-serve is closer to a real tiramisu (I’d still rather have the dessert).6/10, Value 6/10, Originality 7/1015-12.Chinese jasmine tea/Hongkongues milk tea/Shizuoka matcha/Blacksesame, La Barceloneta(162ml, £4.50, selected UK stores)These east Asian-inspired tubs are absolutely stunning. Well-balanced, exciting and delicious.Taste 9/10, Value 3/10, Originality 8/1011.Icedcoffee, Sainsbury’s(480ml, £3.50, Sainsbury’s)This actually tastes like drinking an iced latte – and it’s great value for money.Taste 7/10, Value 6/10, Originality 7/1010.Not fried chicken, Life Raft(71g, £4, Iceland)OK, I know this doesn’t exactly count as an ice-cream tub, but I couldn’t ignore this ice-cream shaped to look like a chicken drumstick – complete with a chocolate pretzel “bone” inside. And it’s not all about looks – the waffle-flavoured ice-cream and crushed cornflakes coating make for a genuinely delicious treat.Taste 9/10, Value 1/10, Originality 10/109.Flat white coffee, Jude’s(460ml, £5.75, Ocado)Properly strong espresso flavour!Taste 8/10, Value 5/10, Originality 7/10View image in fullscreen‘Delicious and rich’ … Chocolate Guinness cake.Photograph: Lucy Knight/The Guardian8.Chocolate Guinness cake, Jude’s(460ml, £5.85, Waitrose)Delicious, rich – just on the edge of being overwhelming.Taste 7/10, Value 5/10, Originality 8/107-5.Toasted rice/Pineapple jam mezcal/ Peachmascarpone, Clingy Wrap(350ml, £8, selected UK stores)I loved this small independent company’s fun, exciting ice-creams: the toasted rice one has an almost cereal milk flavour, the mezcal one is surprising but not overpowering, and the flavours of real fruit shine through.Taste 7/10, Value 4/10, Originality 9/104.Kalamansi gochujang sorbet, Araw(475ml, £8, available for UK delivery)Zingy and fresh!Taste 7/10, Value 3/10, Originality 10/103.Brown bread, SimplyIceCream(500ml, £6.50, available for UK delivery)For me, this was a great balance of unusual flavour and well-balanced, creamy ice-cream.Taste 8/10, Value 5/10, Originality 8/102.Misobananabutterscotch /Cinnamon sponge, Bramley apple jazz, cream cheese frosting, Bears(450ml, £11.50, selected UK stores)I’ve only just discovered the Kent-based Bears ice-cream and I’m going to be putting everyone I know on to it – both of these flavours were fruity, creamy and delicious. The banana one reminded me of my grandma’s banana bread recipe.Taste 9/10, Value 4/10, Originality 9/10View image in fullscreen‘Perfect balance’ … Brown butter popcorn.Photograph: PR1.Brown butter popcorn, Bears(450ml, £11.50, selected UK stores)Right on the edge of being too salty, this ice-cream is a perfect balance of savoury, sweet, rich and creamy. I’ll be traversing corner shops and delis to track it down again.10/10, Value 4/10, Originality 9/10Explore more on these topicsIce-cream and sorbetTaste testFoodDessertfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cottage pie and glass of red, anyone? Britons shun salad despite heat in ‘reverse comfort eating’ | Food | The Guardian
description: Nostalgic foods like toad-in-the-hole also in demand at Waitrose as people pivot towards familiarity amid climatic and political upheaval
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Nostalgic foods like toad-in-the-hole also in demand at Waitrose as people pivot towards familiarity amid climatic and political upheaval
Content: Cottage pie sales have soared 110% at Waitrose in the last month.Photograph: Tim Hill/AlamyView image in fullscreenCottage pie sales have soared 110% at Waitrose in the last month.Photograph: Tim Hill/AlamyFoodCottage pie and glass of red, anyone? Britons shun salad despite heat in ‘reverse comfort eating’Nostalgic foods like toad-in-the-hole also in demand at Waitrose as people pivot towards familiarity amid climatic and political upheavalCaroline DaviesTue 28 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForget a crisp salad and glass of chilled rosé. Enervated Britons are seemingly more likely to crave a rich cottage pie and a robust red in heatwaves.In a trend termed “reverse comfort eating”, Waitrose’s cottage pie sales have soared 110% in the last month and South African red wine is up 68% compared with the same period last year. The surprise spike in demand for winter comfort foods also includes retro chicken, bacon and leek pie (up 41%), chicken korma (up 67%) and chicken and ham gratin (68%).Meanwhile, home cooks are happy standing over the stove despite the sweltering heat, with searches for traditional food classics on the supermarket chain’s recipe site up 67% for toad-in-the-hole, 91% for spaghetti bolognese and 57% for rarebit mac and cheese.Another 1950s staple, along with cottage pie and toad-in-the-hole, trifle is also high on shopping lists, with the supermarket seeing a 100% year-on-year increase in sales of its strawberry version.View image in fullscreenToad-in-the-hole.Photograph: Dan Matthews/The GuardianThe food historian and authorSeren Charrington-Hollisrecently catered for a VIP event at the Llangollen Eisteddfod music festival, where her cottage pies and lamb hotpots were in huge demand – to her surprise, “as it was unbearably hot”, she said. “But they all wanted these home-cooked meals,” she said, adding that the guests were fed up of salads.The cost of living crisis, global wars and conflicts and political change at home all contributed to uncertainty, while the unusual heat added to the feelings of discomfort, said Charrington-Hollis, whose forthcoming book is on nostalgic food from childhood.If it all seemed very “school dinners,” she said, “I think it’s very much a psychological switch, of people wanting to really indulge in home-cooked food and traditional food.“I mean, not just politically, economically, but also the weather is not quite right. I think we’re completely out of sync. We’re not used to all this warm weather. And what better way to connect with ourselves and almost get back to our roots than through food. And I think that’s what’s going on.“Just simplifying things, because I think we just need to be able to cope and reset. It’s almost like a reset button, that’s what I’m feeling.”View image in fullscreenAnother 1950s staple, trifle, is also high on heatwave menus.Photograph: Shaun A Daley/AlamyThe chef Simon Wood believes the cost of living crisis is a factor. Such dishes have long been pub classics. But with cutbacks on eating out, “I think they’re trying to get that hint of going out to the pubs but maybe doing it at home,” said the 2015 MasterChef winner.As for choosing hot and hearty ready meals in the heat, Wood said time constraints and lack of skills in the kitchen were drivers. Also, people are “sick of salad”, and for those supermarket shopping just once a week “salad may not last”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenIt’s not all 1950s trad wife stuff – chicken korma sales were up 67%.Photograph: Old Visuals/AlamyIn the sense of comfort eating, said Prof Rebecca Earle, food historian the University of Warwick, “trying to use food as a way of assuaging some kind of unhappiness or distress, then I think this is what people have done for a very long time”.That the popular dishes also included chicken korma showed it was “not all 1950s, trad wife stuff”, she said. “Amid all of those, let’s say, postwar kind of white British dishes, we have a little glimmer of a multicultural Britain coming through.”Stephen Parkins-Knight, Waitrose’s senior innovation chef, has his own theories on why people are craving the nostalgic staples. “Forget the thermostat – when a heatwave goes on, raw salads and chilled plates can often lose their cool fast,” he said.“What we’re seeing is a trend in ‘reverse comfort eating’ – after spending all day drained by the heat, people crave rich, grounding staples to recharge, pivoting back toward comfort and familiarity.”Explore more on these topicsFoodFood & drink industrySupermarketsWaitroseSocial trendsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tears at dinner time: the science to rolling out fresh pasta | Chefs | The Guardian
description: Tearing is a common problem with pasta dough say our experts. Culprits include the wrong type of flour, cold dough – or it could even boil down to the size of your egg
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Tearing is a common problem with pasta dough say our experts. Culprits include the wrong type of flour, cold dough – or it could even boil down to the size of your egg
Content: When using a pasta machine, it is vital to practise the art of patience.Photograph: Yasin Caglayan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhen using a pasta machine, it is vital to practise the art of patience.Photograph: Yasin Caglayan/Getty ImagesKitchen aideChefsTears at dinner time: the science to rolling out fresh pastaTearing is a common problem with pasta dough say our experts. Culprits include the wrong type of flour, cold dough – or it could even boil down to the size of your eggAnna BerrillTue 28 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen making fresh pasta, why does the dough sometimes tear when rolling, and other times not?Thomas, by email“I’m sorry to hear your pasta is rippy,” sympathisesJacob Kenedy, chef-patron ofBocca di Lupoin London, who is teaming up with fellow chef Merlin Labron-Johnson to celebrate the Italian midsummer holidayferragostowith two feasts in Somerset next month. Assuming Thomas is rolling an egg pasta dough in a pasta machine, there are a number of possible explanations. First, Kenedy says, he might be using the wrong type of flour (“use 00 flour”), the dough might be too cold (“use it at room temperature”) or too dry (“it should be supple, like Play-Doh”). Naz Hassan, head chef ofOrnellaandLupa, both in London, adds that the latter might be down to the size of the egg(s) Thomas is using: “One egg to 100g of 00 flour is the basic pasta dough recipe, but that will vary depending on the size of your egg,” he says. Of course, some people prefer to use just the yolk, and if that applies to Thomas, Hassan suggests thinking about maybe adding the egg white, too: “It has the structure that allows pasta to have the stretchiness it deserves.”But, in true Goldilocks style, a dough that is too wet might also spell trouble, Kenedy says: “I like my pasta dough wet enough to roll by hand – it gives a more elastic mouthfeel – which means, if I roll it in a machine, it sticks slightly to the roller and may rip.” The fix? Laminate the dough thoroughly and perhaps use “the finest dusting” of flour until the dough passes smoothly through the pasta machine. “Then make sure to roll that flour in, so the outside of the pasta isn’t dusty,” Kenedy adds.As in life, time out is also important. “Like bread and any byproduct of flour, you need to rest the dough to allow the gluten structure to relax and bind together,” says Hassan, who does this overnight, while Kenedy prefers to rest his dough, covered and at room temperature, for half an hour to an hour after kneading.
