In fact, Kenedy reckons that poor gluten development is the most likely suspect of Thomas’s pasta plight: “Laminate the pasta many, many times at the thickest setting,” he says. “Roll, fold in half, roll again, fold in three, roll again – at least 12 times – until the pasta is extremely silky-smooth, before rolling it any thinner.”The rolling is also where Thomas really needs to practise the art of patience, so get some music on and avoid any big jumps in thickness (AKA clicks of the pasta machine wheel). Hassan says: “If you try to force the dough through the machine or skip one of the steps – going straight from setting number three to setting one, say – that will create ridges on the sides of the dough.” And that, in turn, can cause those rips. “Obviously, it’s hard to know which of these reasons it might be without standing next to Thomas in the kitchen,” Hassan adds, but then, having a proper chef alongside would most likely just add to Thomas’s pasta pressure.Got a culinary dilemma? Emailfeast@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsChefsKitchen aideFoodPastaItalian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: We booked a Travelodge but were forced to move hotel after 1am | Money | The Guardian
description: We told it of our 11pm arrival time but when we got there our room was no longer available as it had ‘overbooked’
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: We told it of our 11pm arrival time but when we got there our room was no longer available as it had ‘overbooked’
Content: A couple booked the hotel in King’s Cross, London, because they were due to catch a Eurostar early the next morning.Photograph: Peter DazeleyView image in fullscreenA couple booked the hotel in King’s Cross, London, because they were due to catch a Eurostar early the next morning.Photograph: Peter DazeleyConsumer championsMoneyWe booked a Travelodge but were forced to move hotel after 1amWe told it of our 11pm arrival time but when we got there our room was no longer available as it had ‘overbooked’Anna TimsTue 28 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI booked and paid for a room in the Travelodge London King’s Cross Royal Scot hotel six weeks in advance. It was for myself and my husband, who has heart disease and dementia.I had called the hotel on the day of arrival to advise that we would be checking in at 11pm and was told that was fine.When we arrived, we were told that the hotel had overbooked owing to a football match and our room was no longer available. Two other parties were in the same situation.We had to wait in a lobby full of noisy football fans. We were eventually moved to the Travelodge in Shoreditch after 1am. By this time my husband was distraught and I was exhausted.We had booked the King’s Cross hotel because we were due to catch a Eurostar early the next morning.We have not been offered an apology or a refund, although the Shoreditch hotel is cheaper, and Travelodge has not acknowledged my two complaint letters.MJ,HytheI was not surprised when Travelodge insisted it was a problem with the room rather than an overbooking policy that resulted in your room not being available – that’s what it has said on previous occasions when I have flagged up the ordeal of booked guests turned away in the dead of night.It was an “unexpected maintenance issue”, said the press office. “We are very sorry that they were not informed of this before their arrival at the hotel,” a spokesperson said. “Due to an internal error, MJ’s complaints did not reach the right team, which is unacceptable.”It has now refunded you the £179 cost of the booking and added £200 in compensation – but only because you went to the press.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsMoneyConsumer championsConsumer affairsConsumer rightsHotelsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A family tour de France: cycling and camping in Normandy with two toddlers | Normandy holidays | The Guardian
description: Ebikes with child seats – plus idyllic campsites and pit stops en route – turn a five-day ride on the car-free Véloscénic into a wonderful family holiday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ebikes with child seats – plus idyllic campsites and pit stops en route – turn a five-day ride on the car-free Véloscénic into a wonderful family holiday
Content: Ellie Fazan cycled through the verdant former province of Perche.Photograph: Ellie FazanView image in fullscreenEllie Fazan cycled through the verdant former province of Perche.Photograph: Ellie FazanNormandy holidaysA family tour de France: cycling and camping in Normandy with two toddlersEbikes with child seats – plus idyllic campsites and pit stops en route – turn a five-day ride on the car-free Véloscénic into a wonderful family holidayEllie FazanTue 28 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.“Are you mad?” says a fellow guest over dinner at our campsite. “I heard you’re here on a long-distance cycle ride with your toddlers.”The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.I am in Orne, a region in Normandy, with my sister Issy and our three-year-old sons, Sid and Ralph. The landscape folds around us in green-over-green – hedgerow, oak, mossy manor wall – then opens into meadows where Percheron horses graze, knee-deep in wildflowers. Deer leap from the bocage.Cidreandpoiréhave been pressed here since the middle ages. The villages are sandy stone, blue- and green-shuttered; roses against theboulangerie.Map of towns mentioned in NormandyAnd yes, we are biking through it with the boys in child seats on the back, camping along the way in places found through theFrance Vélo Tourismewebsite. Over five days, we’re travelling 130km (80 miles) from Rémalard-en-Perche to Domfront, mostly along theVéloscénic– a 450kmvoie verte(a “greenway” car-free route) that runs from Mont-Saint-Michel to Paris – but looping off it to explore the fairytale chateaux and villages of the Perche, a historic former province. Issy is intrepid and a serious cyclist (the Lycra kind) but the best I can say is I cycle Sid to nursery, and I haven’t slept under canvas since, well, Glastonbury. So two or three hours’ cycling a day is probably enough …Slightly rumpled from the overnight ferry to Caen from Portsmouth, we pull intoForest View, a campsite three miles south of Rémalard. Jean-Louis from the local bike hire shop is waiting with our ebikes. He’d insisted. I’d resisted: they can’t carry both a child seat and panniers so we’ll rely on Jean-Louis and a patchwork of kindly hosts to move our bags between stops. We test our bike legs onLa Route Royale, an intermediate-level 25km circular route, and within an hour of leaving the campsite, climbing the hill to the pretty church of Moutiers-au-Perche for lunch, I realise Jean-Louis was right. The ebikes are the difference between a holiday and a heart attack.View image in fullscreenThere were plenty of stops so the kids could stretch their legs.Photograph: Ellie FazanThe route is flat, but to really see the Perche you have to venture off it, and once you do, the land begins to roll and hills come without warning. The boys, strapped in behind us, are not light. But they are also loving it: pointing, laughing, bursting into Old MacDonald every time they see a horse, cow, tractor or sheep. It’s going so well that Issy and I are debating another few hours cycling or even a cider tasting on the way home, when a pause in the singing alerts us to the fact that both children have been lulled to sleep, heads wobbling from side to side, and so we take them back to the campsite to rest.Graham Allen bought Forest View three years ago and built wooden camping pods especially for cyclists after watching them arrive “laden like donkeys”. Inside there’s a cosy bed and a skylight that we watch the stars through. Across the field there are hot showers. And in the informal restaurant, more like a kitchen/living room, home-cooked food at a shared table. Along France’s greenways, the number of Accueil Vélo accredited stops (accommodation for cyclists that offer breakfast, basic repair kits and help with luggage, among other things) has tripled since 2019.After some seriously good sleep, eggs on toast and frantic sorting of stuff, we spend the next day on theDîtes-le Avec des Fleursloop: through the oak forest of Réno-Valdieu and past the Manoir de la Moussetière, one of the fortified manor houses typical of the Perche. Even on the open roads, there are just a handful of cars, and some steep climbs reward us with wonderful views. The freewheel back down leaves the boys shrieking with delight. At La Chapelle-Montligeon, a church rises out of the fields, and here we picnic on the bank of a lake.double quotation markThe landscape folds around us in green-over-green, then opens into meadows where Percheron horses graze, knee-deep in wildflowersDenis Hurtaud was also cycling this route when he took a detour from the greenway and stumbled onCafé de la Placein the sleepy village of Courgeon. “The terrace was full of yellow flowers and there were old-fashioned oilcloths on the tables. Dappled sunlight fell across the courtyard,” he says. Over lunch, he overheard the owner say he was planning to retire and, by the end of the meal, he had decided to buy it. Today it is a bistro, village shop, bike repair station, art gallery, music venue and a lifeline to locals.It’s Accueil Vélo-accredited too. No shower yet, but we pitch our tent in the garden and Denis has saved us some dinner. We sit at a long table in the last of the light, doves cooing in the church tower, eating chicken cooked in cider, a Perche speciality. Locals drift in and out. A neighbour’s child arrives with a plate of warm crepes for us.The next day, we ride 8km up the greenway to Mortagne-au-Perche for the market. The queue for the season’s first strawberries goes around the block. A man turns dripping chickens on a spit. The radishes are obscenely pink, the asparagus oh so plump. At the Bar du Marché, locals drink coffee and scratch scratchcards in the sunshine. We join them. Our boys are knackered; both have absolute meltdowns and it’s hard work getting them back on the bikes, so we head directly to Carrouges, where we are to camp at theParc Naturel Régional Normandie-Maine, in an orchard behind the moated, red-brickChâteau de Carrouges.View image in fullscreenPretty Moutiers-au-Perche was an early lunch stop.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyThe Parc is Accueil Vélo too, but the woman at the office says only five or six tents pitch up a year and we have the orchard to ourselves. Just us, a roast chicken and some baguettes, with the kids playing dinosaurs in long grass. Once Sid is snoring I pour myself acidre– from local apples – and write. It is so quiet you can hear the flapping of birds’ wings. Then the storm comes. I’m a tent pole down (Glastonbury?) and the rain hits canvas like gravel. I lie clinging to Sid as the thunder tears the sky open above us, questioning every life choice that has led me to a walled orchard in Normandy with a small child and half a tent.double quotation markJean-Louis says it’s the most beautiful place in the world and I don’t disagreeBy morning, the rain has stopped. The orchard glistens. Issy emerges from the next-door tent having not slept either. We push on through the spa town of Bagnoles-de-l’Orne to Domfront, a town on a rocky outcrop dominated by a medieval keep. The sun bursts out again and the kids race up the ruined stones. Our home for the night is theCabane des Deux Chênes, a handbuilt cabin on stilts between two old oaks. A secret room for the children in the rafters. A Nordic bath on the terrace, a hug after the rain.On our last morning, we stop at theFerme de l’Yonnière, Jérôme Forget’s farm just down the road, where he makes AOP Poiré Domfront. Pear trees take decades to mature, Jerome tells us, which is why most people stopped planting them, and whypoiréwent out of fashion. But he has planted a thousand. Next spring, he’ll start taking cyclists, too.Back at the cabane, Jean-Louis comes to pick us up in his van and drives us, talking in French the whole way: about the pear trees and horses and the lanes we have just cycled. The most beautiful place in the world, he says, and I don’t disagree. Against the odds, it’s been a brilliant family holiday and Issy and I are already planning to come back next summer and do the whole thing. Perhaps we are mad after all.The trip wasprovided byOrne Tourism, with travelto France byBrittany Ferries. Bike hirewithLes Vélos Perchéscosts €35(£30) a day. AtForest Viewa pod sleeping two costs from £38 per night;campsite pitches start at £25per night.Cabane des Deux Chênessleeps 2-4 and costs from£138per a night.Explore more on these topicsNormandy holidaysFrance holidaysCycling holidaysCamping holidaysFamily holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Houseplant hacks: do plant care kits actually work? | Houseplants | The Guardian
description: Skincare-inspired regimes feel unnecessary – but giving your plants more attention is always a good thing
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: Skincare-inspired regimes feel unnecessary – but giving your plants more attention is always a good thing
Content: A damp cloth can do the same job as a cleanser.Photograph: Dima Berlin/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenA damp cloth can do the same job as a cleanser.Photograph: Dima Berlin/Getty Images/iStockphotoHouseplant hacksHouseplantsHouseplant hacks: do plant care kits actually work?Skincare-inspired regimes feel unnecessary – but giving your plants more attention is always a good thingGynelle LeonTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 05.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.TheproblemPlant care has had a glow-up. There is now an entire regime that’s been lifted straight from the bathroom cabinet: cleanse, hydrate, serum, tone. These beautifully boxed kits promise lush plants, make lovely gifts and look wonderful on a shelf, but the question is: does yourmonsteraactually need a four-step routine?The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.ThehackThe promise is that plants, like skin, thrive on a structured routine, and that investing in a multi-product care kit will reward you with glowing foliage.ThemethodWork through the routine. Depending on the kit, this might mean cleansing the leaves, adding feed to the water, then toning and shining the foliage with a spray, serum or oil. Repeat every week.ThetestI worked through each step in turn. The cleanse is genuinely worthwhile, as dust-free leaves absorb light far better, though a damp cloth does the same job. The hydrating and feeding steps were no different from what I already do. The serum was essentially a leaf shine: it left the foliage looking glossy, but products like this can clog the stomata, the tiny pores a plant uses to breathe.The verdictThe useful steps in this routine are the ones you were already doing: cleaning dust off leaves, hydrating consistently, and feeding sensibly. As a gift, these kits are charming. But your plant does not need a skincare regime. A damp cloth, a decent feed and consistent watering will give you a healthy plant without the artificially glossy leaves. That said, if a boxed set of sprays and serums is what tempts you to sit down with your plants each week and pay them proper attention, they will be all the healthier for it.Explore more on these topicsHouseplantsHouseplant hacksGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Spies in the sky: how worried should we be about the arrival of AI-enabled smart lamp-posts? | Surveillance | The Guardian
description: The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?
Content: Hyper-surveillance.SurveillanceSpies in the sky: how worried should we be about the arrival of AI-enabled smart lamp-posts?The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?Zoe WilliamsTue 28 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow would you feel if your neighbourhood lamp-posts could recognise your number plate, and also your face? Maybe you wouldn’t mind, given how long we’ve had automatic number plate recognition and CCTV. What about if that lamp-post could power itself through its own solar panels, and perhaps find another use for any extra power generated – that would be good, right? This is what Conflow Power Group (CPG) inWarwickshireclaims for its iLamps, the first of their kind in the UK.What if lamp-posts had the potential to incorporate new AI capability – gait analysis, suspicious behaviours – that you haven’t even heard of? This is what the organisation Big Brother Watch worries about. And what if the home secretary had explicitly saidshe believed in a “panopticon state”– that is, a state that could watch you at all times (as Shabana Mahmood already has) – and what if she still had a job when the lamp-post eyes got their updates? Or what if the next home secretary was even keener on hyper-surveillance (hard to imagine), and the street apparatus was already in place? What about all the data this would harvest – who would own it?It’s drizzling in Warwickshire, where I’m hoping to answer at least some of these questions in the hospital car park where some of these new “smart” lamp-posts have been installed. But if it wasn’t for me, nobody would probably be talking about them, not least because few have heard anything about them. Not many people know that the iLamp is not just solar-powered but can “double as a revenue-generating distributed AI datacentre”, according to CPG, let alone what that means. And nobody, not even me, knows how much of that potential functionality has been realised in the UK model – only what CPG has announced: that it has signed an agreement with the government of Katsina state, Nigeria, to supply it with 50,000 of these iLamps, which have additional surveillance potential for both vehicles and faces. CPG’s chairman, Edward Fitzpatrick,told the BBC World Service’s Tech Life programmethat the lamp-posts could ultimately track down missing persons or fight crime, with the proviso that this would only be developed in partnership “with the relevant authority”.CPG has been “extensively covered by worldwide media”, according to its own statement, and doesn’t take further questions, directing the media to its online material. As for the Warwickshire lamp-posts, the local authority directs all questions to the hospital, and the hospital doesn’t respond. Fair play – it’s a hospital.View image in fullscreenA London lamp-post well equipped with cameras.Photograph: Shomos Uddin/Getty ImagesA number of local residents have taken refuge from the rain in a bus shelter, most of them waiting for a partner to pick them up, and many are willing to chat. Karl, 52, who has been in a pub nearby, speaks for almost everyone when he says: “The town centre is already full of cameras, and it’s fine. You don’t mind them being there unless you’re up to no good.” No amount of loaded questions (What if you were doing something that was legal today but illegal in a year? What if the surveillance became predictive rather than reactive? What if you didn’t want anyone to know you’d been to the hospital? What if you weren’t supposed to be in a pub? Don’t you think you should at least have been asked whether you wanted it?) can separate anyone I speak to from the view that facial recognition is a tolerable part of life for a right-thinking citizen.Tejal, 41, also waiting at the hospital bus stop, says: “I think we have to move on and accept that things change.” She’s a radiologist, and just seeing AI’s capability in her own sector makes her extremely anxious about AI as a whole. “I have anxieties for my children,” she says. That they won’t find entry-level jobs? “That, and that they’ll lose the ability to celebrate and find joy from the things we used to.” Privacy concerns do seem comparatively minor, compared with that.Policy and technical experts are sceptical about some of the claims made for smart lamp-posts. Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, says: “We see this quite often where local councils or other government agencies are … ‘swindled’ is a strong word, but they’re sold these tools as magic wands when there are limitations to what they can actually do.”Prof Rabih Bashroush, director of the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Data Innovation at the University of East London, is blunt: “AI datacentres? There’s absolutely no chance this will fly: the technology doesn’t work, there’s not enough power, the economics won’t work …” Solar power to run the iLamps off-grid might work in Nigeria, but in Britain the amount generated by the lamp-posts is “negligible”, he says. You might be able to run an app that was “not mission critical, that you didn’t mind shutting down for a few days” – such as recognising whether a parking spot was occupied – but bigger claims for facial recognition are “just hype. Forget it – this has no legs.”If he sounds impatient, it’s because he is: “It’s getting more and more difficult to get an independent opinion on things, because a lot of experts are in the industry now, and their view would have to align with their organisation,” he says. So a company might make a large claim, including a few AI buzzwords, ahead of a funding round; engineers don’t contradict them, local authorities don’t understand them and nobody else is even aware that anything has moved on since CCTV was invented.View image in fullscreenThe Metropolitan Police trialling a facial recognition system in London last May.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersChaggar goes to great lengths to explain the conceptual difference between facial recognition and CCTV: “Facial recognition is not just passively recalling something, unlike CCTV, which you then check after the fact. What facial recognition does is real-time identity check: it’s much more like a fingerprint or DNA. It’s not like a passport – you can’t get another face.”Another problem, Chaggar says, is that, “a lot of these technologies and infrastructures have capacity to add function later. Hammersmith and Fulham [in London] are updating their CCTV and it’s possible to embed facial recognition, monitor suspicious shopping behaviour, add aggression detection. So you can just turn the switch and it’s all there overnight.” A friend who lives in Fulham sent, by chance, a picture of a camera above a parking restrictions sign – it looks like a cross between Darth Vader and a beetle, and it whirrs as you go past, as if to indicate that it’s following your movements.This throws up all the ageless privacy concerns, and it’s interesting how many people will wave away CCTV as a fact of modern life, but spontaneously raise how much they absolutely hate being listened to by their phone. Karl says: “I was talking to my mother the other day about dog nail clippers, and the advert came up on my phone that evening. I had my microphone off. I don’t even have a dog!” His friend Bob, 48, has ended up functionally off-grid, with no computer and a basic brick phone – a policymaker would probably describe him as “excluded” – simply because “some people like to be private”.View image in fullscreenActing suspiciously, or just a bit chilly?Photograph: Posed by model; David Wall/Getty ImagesAnother question about facial recognition software is: exactly how good are algorithms at detecting aggression and suspicious behaviour? “A lot of the software is pseudo-scientific,” Chaggar says. “So a company might try to sell emotion-detection, [claiming that] if people are walking through a train station, you can see if they’re angry or they’re about to be aggressive. There’s very little evidence to suggest that it’s accurate. If you’re a disabled person who moves differently, you might be flagged and have an intervention.” But the real question local authorities and any agents of the state should ask themselves, Chaggar says, is: “Are you happy to have your political enemies having these capabilities? Because you’re building an infrastructure that is here to stay.”You can see that writ large in policing – the Home Office signed off on the use of facial recognition more than a decade ago, and the police have been “essentially using the public as guinea pigs for the past 10 years,” Chaggar says. What happens when the home secretary tells BBC 5 Live,as she did earlier this year, that “you can’t enjoy any of your liberties in any country if you’re not safe”? This sledgehammer logic, in which all liberties are secondary to the state’s rights as your protector, is chilling from a supposedly leftwing government. But the greater worry is that this doesn’t feel like the right time in politics to roll the dice on surveillance technology, basing our acceptance of it on the assumption that all future governments will be pro-social and democratic.View image in fullscreen‘If you haven’t got anything to hide, I don’t see how it would be a problem.’Photograph: Justin Paget/Getty ImagesWherever there’s potential to collect data, it throws up the question of who owns it: Bashroush used to work with the Internet of Things, the European Commission’s attempt to “connect the physical world to a digital environment”. “This was way back, before exiting Europe,” he remembers. “One of the challenges we saw was with a supplier [who was] basically collecting garbage from homes in the Netherlands, then optimising truck journeys and planning, based on your habits. The council that ran the programme was very happy with it, and tried to open the bidding a year later to get a more competitive price. The company said, ‘Sure, but the data is ours.’” That never got resolved: the contracts had been poorly constructed and the local authority lost the data.If you want to see facial recognition go wrong without even any authoritarian intent or tech chicanery, you just have to look at the retail sector, where it’s already widely in use to prevent shoplifting. “We’ve seen misidentification by the police,” Chaggar says, “but in retail, when people are misidentified, it’s Kafkaesque. You’re justblacklisted from the store.”And again, how much do people care, really? If you’re not allowed in a shop and you don’t know why; if a private company has a contract with your NHS trust, vaunting tech that isn’t operational yet and might never work, but nobody told, let alone asked, you; if the home secretary thinks it’s fine for the eyes of the state to be on you at all times – are these the building blocks of a dystopia, or do they just remind us how we used to describe dystopia, back before these surveillance capabilities existed?The New Yorker essayist Ted Chiangwrote some time agoabout the habit of projecting on to AI negatives that were actually not about tech but about economic systems, concluding: “Capitalism is the machine that will do whatever it takes to prevent us from turning it off.” Am I projecting on to AI and surveillance tech anxieties that are really about authoritarian politics?“Well, if you haven’t got anything to hide,” says Sarah, 55, “I can’t see how it would be a problem. I’m presuming they’re actually lamps as well?”Explore more on these topicsSurveillanceWarwickshireFacial recognitionAI (artificial intelligence)Data protectionDatacentresfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Americans feel pinch of continued Iran war: ‘It’s screwed everything up’ | US news | The Guardian
description: Whether in favor of or against the US-Israel war on Iran, people across the country are left holding the bill and wondering on its purpose
Author: George Chidi
Headline: Whether in favor of or against the US-Israel war on Iran, people across the country are left holding the bill and wondering on its purpose
Content: Left: Demonstrators carry signs and chant slogans during a protest against US military action in Iran near the White House in Washington DC in April. Right: The bridge linking Bandar Abbas and Kehuristan, rendered unusable in a US strike, is seen in Iran's Hormozgan province.Composite: AFP, Anadolu, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLeft: Demonstrators carry signs and chant slogans during a protest against US military action in Iran near the White House in Washington DC in April. Right: The bridge linking Bandar Abbas and Kehuristan, rendered unusable in a US strike, is seen in Iran's Hormozgan province.Composite: AFP, Anadolu, Getty ImagesUS newsAmericans feel pinch of continued Iran war: ‘It’s screwed everything up’Whether in favor of or against the US-Israel war on Iran, people across the country are left holding the bill and wondering on its purposeGeorge Chidiin Marietta, Georgia,Shrai Popatin North York, Maine,Rachel Leingangin Superior, Wisconsin, andJoseph Gedeonin Washington. Graphics byAndrew WitherspoonTue 28 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive months after the United States and Israel started a historically unpopular war against Iran that was going to supposedly last weeks, the fighting has refused to resolve in victory, defeat or peace. Iran’s supreme leader had been killed in the opening strikes, ceasefires broke down, and the strait of Hormuz has been closed and reopened.For voters interviewed across the country, while the damage may be distant, the residual effects have shown up at the pump, on the grocery bill and in a phone call telling a spouse they have a day to report for deployment. And for a country still absorbing the aftermath of Israel’s war on Gaza – funded to the tune of billions of dollars by the United States – the war in Iran lands on top of an already raw argument about what American power is for.In North York,Maine, Lydia Stone, 31, works in the logging industry and is raising an 18-month-old daughter. She describes an industry being squeezed from both directions: fuel costs rising while the price customers pay for wood stays flat. “It’s been a huge jump in prices, and makes life a lot harder,” she said.Trump administration’s revision of Iran war casualties ‘huge disrespect’, say veteransRead moreThat squeeze shows up in the data, with the average price of gasoline pushing above $4 a gallon for the first time in years,according to AAA. Analysts have also noted the pain is not evenly shared: lower- and middle-income householdsspend a larger shareof their budgets on fuel, meaning the same price spike lands harder on them than on wealthier consumers.Stone’s frustration isn’t only economic. “A huge part of what has been so frustrating ... is like the fact my tax dollars are going to fund murdering people, at the same time that it’s cutting social services, it’s cutting Snap benefits for my neighbors,” she said, referring to nutrition benefits for low-income Americans.She said the line at her local food pantry had grown noticeably longer and her best friend’s husband, she said, was deployed on little notice.US economic indicators during the war in Iran chartedThat sense of a war without justification reverberated among voters who described themselves as independent or progressive. Terrence Dahmen, 73, a retired, independent-leaning voter from Cable,Wisconsin, who said he usually ends up voting Democrat, called American involvement “a huge mistake”. “We weren’t provoked into that fight, and we weren’t attacked,” he said. “I saw no reason to go there other than possibly controlling oil somehow.”He argued the country should be investing in solar, wind and geothermal power instead, and said he wished the US had taken a different path on climate policy years ago.Robert Edelstein, 62, who runs a window-tinting business in Douglas county, Wisconsin, was more blunt. “In the general election, I would automatically vote for anybody that was against the war,” he said. “I think it’s the stupidest thing that could ever possibly have happened.” Comparing the decision to strike Iran unfavorably with the Iraq war launched under George W Bush, he added: “It’s screwed everything up, as we all know ... it’s absolutely stupid.”In Georgia, Jimmy Carter – a retired teacher not related to the former president – watched Donald Trump’s motorcade arrive near his old school last week with similar disbelief. “It’s a dumbass idea,” he said. “I don’t know who fed him that idea.” He noted that even his own brother, a Trump voter, agreed.Voters with personal connections to the military comprised a wide range of views.Nick Marine, a retired sailor at a Trump rally in Marietta, offered full-throated endorsement of the Trump administration’s approach. “I think what President Trump is doing is good,” he said. “I think it took a long time for us to get to this point ... I’m glad it’s finally being resolved.”He argued for gradualism over overwhelming force – “you don’t want to behead your neighbor, because in a month or so, you’re going to be doing commerce with them” – while voicing concern for Iranian civilians cut off from water, sanitation and electricity by the fighting.Richard Bradley, a retired army major and combat engineer from Mabelton,Georgia, whose son and daughter currently serve, supports the broader rationale for confronting Iran but wants a clear exit. “I’d rather fight bad guys in their land instead of mine,” he said.View image in fullscreenRichard Bradley, a retired army major, supported the Iran war.Photograph: George Chidi/The GuardianStill, he said: “I kind of take a little bit of an issue with where we’re at now ... we need to be figuring out how to finish it up, so it doesn’t turn into another ... enduring war.” His own father fought in the Gulf war, he noted, and he didn’t “want my kids to fight unfinished business that my generation left.”Not all of the war’s critics oppose the war itself. Salman Majidi, an Iranian immigrant and software developer from Atlanta, stood among anti-Trump protesters holding a “Free Iran” sign – but for the opposite reason. A supporter of Iran’s exiled former crown prince, Reza Pahlavi, Majidi argued the American campaign was a rescue rather than a war of choice.“Tens of thousands of Iranian civilians have been murdered by the Islamic regime in just two days,” he said, arguing the toll predates and outweighs the American strikes. “We deserve a better life in Iran.”But given the proximity and relationship of the conflicts, the Iran war has not displaced the argument over Gaza so much as compounded it, blurring into a single grievance about where American money and moral authority are being spent.Clay Harvison, a mixed martial artist from Marietta who voted for the president, said the conflict should have ended months ago. “He should have left it when he had already bombed them,” Harvison said, blaming pressure from Israeli leaders for dragging the US deeper in. He said the war threatens the legacy Trump seems to prize most: “being remembered as being great ... he’s messing with that really bad right now.”Younger voters in particular, he said, were asking why a president who campaigned against foreign wars is now presiding over one, arguing that “the military-industrial complex is laundering our tax dollars instead of going into fixing our streets”.Whether a ceasefire holds, and whether Tehran and Washington ever sit down for something more than a pause, is still an open question.What is not in doubt, from Wisconsin lake towns to the Georgia suburbs, is that voters of nearly every political persuasion are doing the same math: adding up gas receipts, deployment orders and casualty counts, and asking what, precisely, the war is for.Explore more on these topicsUS newsUS-Israel war on IranTrump administrationDonald TrumpGeorgiaMaineWisconsinnewsShareReuse this content

title: US airman accused of ‘spree’ of rapes on sleeping women avoided UK courts | US military | The Guardian
description: Suffolk police ceded investigation into James Loubeau to the US military, leading to court martial acquittal
Author: Rob Evans
Headline: Suffolk police ceded investigation into James Loubeau to the US military, leading to court martial acquittal
Content: Loubeau allegedly attacked women in UK over a four-month period in what US prosecutors called a ‘frightening’ pattern.Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenLoubeau allegedly attacked women in UK over a four-month period in what US prosecutors called a ‘frightening’ pattern.Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyBase justiceUS militaryUS airman accused of ‘spree’ of rapes on sleeping women avoided UK courtsSuffolk police ceded investigation into James Loubeau to the US military, leading to court martial acquittalRob Evans,Harry DaviesandEmine SinmazTue 28 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAUS airman accused of a “spree” of rapes and sexual assaults in England, drugging some women and breaking into the homes of others, was able to avoid British justice after local police handed over part of the case to the American military.Two British women went toSuffolkpolice in August 2019 to allege that James Loubeau and another US airman had drugged and raped them after they met in a nightclub in Bury St Edmunds, a local market town.Less than two weeks later, Suffolk police allowed the US air force to take responsibility for investigating the two alleged rapes.It has since emerged that Loubeau, 38, allegedly attacked a total of six women in East Anglia over a four-month period in 2019, in what US prosecutors described as a “frightening and dangerous” pattern of assaults.In July last year, a court in Miami, Florida, convicted Loubeau of sexual assaulting one of the women on a military base in England. Prosecutors in the case said the airman had believed he could attack women with “impunity”. Hereceived a five-year prison sentenceand will be monitored for two decades after his release because of the risk he poses to the public.The fact Loubeau was eventually brought to justice in a court more than 4,000 miles from his alleged crimes will add pressure on Suffolk police to explain its decision to cede jurisdiction in the case. It is declining to do so.‘In and out of consciousness’How the US bypasses British courts to try its military over crimes in the UKRead moreThree of Loubeau’s alleged victims were female military personnel stationed alongside him at RAF Mildenhall, an American military base in Suffolk. Under the terms of a 1951 agreement between the US and UK, the American military can claim responsibility for investigating alleged crimes when the victim is another member of the US armed forces. They also have jurisdiction over alleged crimes that occur when a member of their military is on duty.In almost all other instances, the local British police force have primary responsibility for investigating crimes on UK soil.Three of Loubeau’s alleged victims were British and accused him of attacking them while he was off-duty. They include the two women who first met him and his friend, another US airman, in a nightclub in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk.Court papers suggest the American airmen offered to drive the women home but instead drove to the Mildenhall base, where they went to Loubeau’s bedroom. One of the women said they were given wine and Disaronno liqueur in plastic cups.The next thing they remembered was waking about 6.30am, naked and confused, according to the documents. Neither woman knew how or why they had passed out, and both believed they had been raped, the documents said.View image in fullscreenLoubeau is alleged to have driven two women he met at a nightclub to RAF Mildenhall base, along with another US airman.Photograph: Jason Bye/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockThe women reported Loubeau and the second US airman to Suffolk police on 3 August 2019, prompting the force to open an investigation. Just 11 days later, on 14 August, the force transferred responsibility for investigating the men toUS militarypolice.The military’s investigation appears to have included not just the two British women but as many as three other women who say they were attacked during Loubeau’s alleged “spree” between April and July 2019.The case culminated in a military trial, or court martial, for Loubeau, who held the rank of airman first class. It centred on allegations by one of his six alleged victims, an American servicewoman who said he had sexually assaulted her in June 2019 after breaking into her bedroom on the base. She alleged she had been woken up by Loubeau, who had sex with her while she was “in and out of consciousness”.James LoubeauPhotograph: Police handoutA lack of transparency around the US military justice system means there is no public record of what happened at the court martial, but such tribunals often involve a jury panel of other American service personnel. It took place on the base in 2020 and resulted in Loubeau’s acquittal.While the military tribunal did not find him guilty, Loubeau, who had been an apprentice in the 100th Logistics Readiness vehicle maintenance squadron at Mildenhall, was dismissed from the US air force in 2020 after three years’ service.He was discharged “under honourable conditions” for a series of what were called “minor infractions”. These included making sexual advances to women who were drunk, using derogatory language towards women and stealing jewellery from a store at RAF Lakenheath, another US airbase. He returned to the US in 2021 and lived with relatives in Miami.It was not until 2025, after an investigation by the FBI, that Loubeau was convicted over allegations from another of the six women, a 19-year-old American who had been serving with him at Mildenhall.DNA breakthroughIt is unclear what prompted the FBI to open its investigation, but the federal agency secured a breakthrough when it connected Loubeau to DNA found on his victim, whom he had met at a bar on the base in May 2019.Later that night, after the 19-year-old had returned to her bedroom, which was locked, Loubeau entered by surreptitiously slipping his hand through her open window and unlatching her door, which was inches away. She was woken at 2.30am by a hooded Loubeau on top of her. According to the court documents, his victim “thought she had been raped”.Prosecutors secured his conviction for sexual assault under an American law that can be used to prosecute American armed forces and its contractors for crimes committed outside the US.They argued that Loubeau was likely to attack women again when he was released from jail. The judge ordered that after completing his prison sentence, he be supervised for two decades to prevent him carrying out further sexual attacks.View image in fullscreenA US aircraft at RAF Mildenhall.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAIn documents submitted to the court, prosecutors cited the allegations of other attacks in England to argue that Loubeau had preyed on sleeping or drunk women in a “disturbing, frightening and dangerous” pattern.In the documents, the prosecutors said he had carried out an “assaultive spree” in Suffolk in 2019, adding that his “brazen conduct reflects his belief that he can act with impunity”.Among the cases US prosecutors referenced was that of the third British woman Loubeau was accused of attacking.Less is known about her case, although the documents suggest she alleged Loubeau had assaulted her in her Cambridgeshire home in April 2019. She reported the alleged attack to Cambridgeshire police a year later, identifying Loubeau.Get in touchContact Rob Evans about this storyIf you have something to share about  this story, you can contact Rob using one of the following methods.Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.To send a message to Rob Evans please choose the investigations team.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can email:rob.evans@theguardian.comSecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreCambridgeshire police said they had decided there was not enough evidence to bring a charge, adding that the victim had not supported a prosecution. While the force said they had not transferred responsibility for investigating the allegation to the US military police, a spokesperson added police had “worked with the United States air force as part of the investigation and assistance was provided”.The Guardian contacted the US air force military police with questions about the Loubeau case and why the US had claimed jurisdiction over alleged rapes for which an English force should have had primary responsibility.The USAF police said that, as an investigative agency, it could not respond to questions about “decisions around jurisdiction, charges, and legal proceedings”. “Questions regarding these issues should be directed to the proper authorities. In this case, the Suffolk police should be better equipped” to respond, it said.A British woman was strangled in the UK – why did the US military try her case? – podcastRead moreSuffolk police declined to answer detailed questions about the case, or to explain their decision to relinquish jurisdiction less than two weeks after the two British women said Loubeau had raped them. In a statement, the force said: “We are in the process of reviewing the decision-making surrounding the transfer of primacy to the US air force and around case transfer practices more generally.”That review is understood to have been initiated as a result of the Guardian’s continuing investigation into crimes committed by US personnel on British soil.In recent weeks the Guardian has reported on the cases of Jacob Wulfson, a US fighter pilotwho strangled a British womanin his apartment in Cambridge; Tyrion Davis, an American airmanwho sexually assaulted a British womanin Brandon, Suffolk; and Hannes Marschalek, a US airman whoallegedly exposed himself to a 16-year-old girland four young women in Littleport, Cambridgeshire, in 2022.In all the cases, US airmen avoided the British justice system after the local police force chose to cede control of the investigation to American military police.Loubeau’s lawyer, who represented him at the Miami hearing, declined to comment.Additional reporting: Sophie SullivanExplore more on these topicsUS militaryBase justicePoliceSuffolkCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Canadians spent $3.3bn less on travel to US in 2025 after Trump’s return to office | Canada | The Guardian
description: Data shows Canadians have replaced US vacations with other international trips in apparent rebuke to Trump
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: Data shows Canadians have replaced US vacations with other international trips in apparent rebuke to Trump
Content: The Blue Water Bridge connecting Canada and Michigan on 12 March 2021.Photograph: Bryce Airgood/Times Herald/USA Today Network/Reuters ConnectView image in fullscreenThe Blue Water Bridge connecting Canada and Michigan on 12 March 2021.Photograph: Bryce Airgood/Times Herald/USA Today Network/Reuters ConnectCanadaCanadians spent $3.3bn less on travel to US in 2025 after Trump’s return to officeData shows Canadians have replaced US vacations with other international trips in apparent rebuke to TrumpOlivia Bowdenin TorontoTue 28 Jul 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanadians spent $3.3bn less on travel to the US in 2025 than in the previous year, as Donald Trump’s hostile policies towards his northern neighbour continue to incur an economic cost, new government data shows.The research also indicates that Canadians are not bucking travel overall and instead have replaced US vacations with other international destinations, in a rebuke to Trump’s tariff regime and the president’s continued musings on annexingCanada.“Following the change in the US administration in early 2025 and the implementation of America First policies, Canadian travel sentiment shifted abruptly,” said authors of the report published by Statistics Canada, the country’s national statistics agency.Total US travel spending in 2025 amounted to $18.8bn, down from $22.1bn in 2024.In contrast, Canadian spending on travel abroad, excluding the US, grew by $3.6bn in 2025, to a total of $22.8bn.Canadian visits to Europe increased by nearly 14% compared with 2024, while visits to Asia increased by almost 17%.‘Canadians don’t want to come here any more’: anger over Trump squeezes US border businessesRead moreThose increases offered a stark contrast to the dwindling US visits. Overall in 2025, return trips toCanadafrom the US by vehicle and by plane dropped by about one quarter compared to 2024. The highest travel declines were recorded in July 2025, when border crossings fell by about one-third from the previous year.Those plummeting border crossings through nearly the entire year were “the deepest and most sustained on record”, the agency said. Since digital record-keeping began in 1972, declines of more than 30% have only ever been seen in September 2001, after the 9/11 World Trade Center attacks.Looking at 2026 data so far, Statistics Canada said the drop in leisure travel to the US was continuing. Return trips to Canada from the US this year are at similar levels seen at the end of 2025, which saw a 27% decline between October and December, it reported.The data signals “a persistent shift away from the United States by Canadian residents in their travel preferences”.Explore more on these topicsCanadaAmericasDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Past fires suggest effects of Europe and North America wildfires may linger for years | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Three years after Maui wildfires many still struggle with ‘biological, emotional and social consequences’, study says
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Three years after Maui wildfires many still struggle with ‘biological, emotional and social consequences’, study says
Content: A hazy Toronto skyline caused by forest fires in northern Ontario, Canada, on 15 July 2026.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA hazy Toronto skyline caused by forest fires in northern Ontario, Canada, on 15 July 2026.Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty ImagesWildfiresPast fires suggest effects of Europe and North America wildfires may linger for yearsThree years after Maui wildfires many still struggle with ‘biological, emotional and social consequences’, study saysOliver MilmanTue 28 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA spate of ferocious wildfires across North America andEurope, worsened by the climate crisis, has incinerated homes and forests and forced thousands of people to flee. Previous fires suggest the effects of these blazes may linger for years to come.The current fires and their plumes of smoke can appear to be a temporary, if immediate, crisis. Nearly 1,000 fires have sprung into life in the boreal forests of Canada, causing the evacuation of towns and toxic smoke to waft into major Canadian and US cities, prompting threats of retribution from Donald Trump, whobizarrely accusedCanada of “poisoning” his country’s air.Smoke is billowing from wildfires in the US too, amid the third major heatwave of the past month which has furthered dried out parched vegetation. Vast, lightning-sparked fires across Washington, eastern Oregon and Idaho have caused a plume of smoke so large that itcould reachFlorida.In Europe, meanwhile, huge fires have gripped parts of theUK,FranceandSpain, causing the evacuation of more than 250,000 people.View image in fullscreenA house damaged by wildfires in Blagon, south-western France, on Monday.Photograph: Laurent Perpigna/EPAThe climate crisis, caused by the burning of fossil fuels, isknownto becreating more fire-prone conditionsaround the world by drying out soils and plants. “The entire Iberian peninsula is suffering the effects of the climate emergency in a very specific way,”saidPedro Sánchez, Spain’s prime minister.Scientists have also long been aware of the unhealthy consequences of wildfire smoke, which can trigger severerespiratoryandcardiacproblems in affected people. A recentstudyfound that exposure to tiny particles carried in wildfire smoke will raise the risk of hospitalization for older people hundreds of miles away from fires.“The cardiovascular toll of wildfire smoke reaches well beyond the fire lines and well beyond the day the sky turns orange,” said Kai Chen, associate professor of epidemiology at the Yale School of Public Health and study co-author.But identifying the ongoing effects of wildfires long after they have been extinguished has been a more recent understanding. There are continuing challenges in Maui, the second largest of Hawaii’s islands, three years after wildfires there caused more than 100 deaths and razed several thousand buildings, a new report highlights.While living and economic conditions have generally improved since the fires, many people in Maui are still struggling with health concerns such as poorer lung functions, higher blood pressure and mental health challenges, according to theMaui Wildfire Exposure Study, led by researchers at the University of Hawaii and released on Monday.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of vegetation regrowth amid areas destroyed or damaged by the Lahaina wildfire, including the iconic banyan tree, on 4 August 2024 in Lahaina, Hawaii.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images“The progress is real, and it should be recognized,” said Alika Maunakea, co-director of the study and a school of medicine professor at the University of Hawaii. “But the biological, emotional and social consequences of a disaster do not disappear on the same timeline as debris removal or reconstruction.”Nearly half of all adults in the Maui study continued to report depressive symptoms, with nearly one in five experiencing post-traumatic stress. The study, which conducted screenings of more than 2,500 participants, also found severe depressive symptoms and post-traumatic stress increased among children and adolescents, as did blood pressure readings and obesity levels.“Children may appear resilient while still carrying significant emotional and physical effects beneath the surface,” said Christopher Knightsbridge, a mental health therapist based in Lahaina, a coastal town that was largely destroyed by the fires.“Supporting children means supporting the entire family, including their housing, food security, daily routines and access to trusted care,” he added.The researchers stressed that long-term monitoring and intervention is required following a major wildfire event due to impacts that can last for years afterwards. While the skies over North America and Europe will eventually clear of smoke after a tinderbox summer of fire, this climate change-driven era of wildfire is set to exact a lengthy toll.As well as better support for those directly affected by fires, experts say that authorities in smoke-affected areas could respond to the threat of repeated smoke exposure by creating “clean air centers” that people can flee to in order to escape smoke and other air pollutants.Aresearch paper from last year, which found a 7% increase in mortality among a cohort of older people living in southern California over a three-year period due to wildfire smoke exposure, recommended that “activation of public health measures such as clean air centers should not only depend on intensity of smoke, as the long-term effects can be harmful, even at low levels.”Lara Schwarz, an environmental health scientist at UC Berkley who led the research, said: “As wildfires become more frequent and severe in the context of climate change, with California being at high risk, understanding how these harmful wildfires will affect us in the long term is critical to informing better public health action and response.”Explore more on these topicsWildfiresFranceCanadaAmericasEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Javier Milei accuses US Democrats of financing ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ at World Cup | Argentina | The Guardian
description: President also blames Brazil and Mexico and says online critics ‘do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed’
Author: Facundo Iglesia
Headline: President also blames Brazil and Mexico and says online critics ‘do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed’
Content: Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, also claimed his political rivals may have ‘validated the woke movement that is now accusing us of being racist’.Photograph: Juan Ignacio Roncoroni/EPAView image in fullscreenArgentina’s president, Javier Milei, also claimed his political rivals may have ‘validated the woke movement that is now accusing us of being racist’.Photograph: Juan Ignacio Roncoroni/EPAArgentinaJavier Milei accuses US Democrats of financing ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ at World CupPresident also blames Brazil and Mexico and says online critics ‘do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed’Facundo Iglesiain Buenos Aires andTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroTue 28 Jul 2026 06.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than a week has passed since Ferran Torres scored the extra-time goal that gave Spain its second World Cup, but – at least for Argentina’s president – the tournament is not over.Javier Milei has claimed that a coordinated “anti-Argentina campaign” was behind criticism of the country’s team,accusations of racismamong its fans and conspiracy theories alleging that Lionel Messi’s side was secretly being favoured by Fifa.Now, the far-right president has taken the narrative a step further, alleging that the supposed campaign was financed by the US Democratic party and the governments ofBraziland Mexico.“It was the work of progressive minds who do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed,” claimed the self-styled libertarian in aninterviewwith a local radio station on Sunday.View image in fullscreenArgentina fans burn a Spain shirt after their team lost in the World Cup final.Photograph: Matias Baglietto/ReutersHe went on to claim that the “government of Brazil”, led by the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, had allegedly provided the largest share of the funding.Analysts in Argentina said Milei had embraced the narrative as adistractionfrom hisplummeting popularity, while others argued that the “real anti-Argentina campaign” was the one thepresident was waging“with hischainsaw” austerity plan.Yet the narrative has gained traction, even reaching people who do not support Milei. Pablo Torres, a 52-year-old bookseller from Buenos Aires who “never voted for him and never would”, said there had been a social media “bombardment” against the country that left him feeling “outrage” and “disgust”.He said some of the accusations of racism had come from “great colonial powers that enslaved people, trafficked enslaved people and decimated populations”, adding: “They denied the existence of theblack populationin Argentina, and ignored our idiosyncrasies and our history … We are a welcoming home for all nations.”View image in fullscreenThe Argentina team, including Lionel Messi (right), had to make do with silver runners-up medals after the final.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPADuring the tournament,incidentsinvolving racist behaviour by some Argentine supporters drew widespread attention. Hours before the final, the US actor Samuel L Jackson posted an Instagram story that said: “Dear black people, please do not cheer or root for Argentina to win the Fifa World Cup. Argentina has historically been one of, if not the most, racist countries in the world.”The post prompted reactions even from human rights organisations such as Amnesty International Argentina, which acknowledged racism in the country butcriticised“reducing the country to a stereotype”.Milei, meanwhile, posted that the criticism could be attributed to Argentina’s opposition, which had “validated the woke movement that is now accusing us of being racist”. Over the weekend, he also decided to blame Brazil – while on Brazilian soil.On Saturday, the Argentinian presidentattendedthe launch of the presidential campaign of the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro and Lula’s main challenger in October’s presidential election.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro, right, joins Javier Milei on stage at a Liberal party convention in São Paulo, Brazil on Saturday.Photograph: Ettore Chiereguini/APIn his speech, as well as calling Lula a“thief” and a “prisoner”– prompting a strongreactionfrom the Brazilian government – Milei said: “If you examine the data from the recent anti-Argentina campaign, the place from which the most attacks came was Brazil.” He reinforced the claim on Sunday, this time adding Mexico and the US Democratic party.The digital anthropologist Mercedes Máspero analysed more than 2m posts on social media andwrotethat she had found “some undeniable patterns” of orchestration such as the repeated use of variations of “disgusting human beings” in different languages. Even so, it was “a tough call” to describe it as a coordinated campaign “because the narrative is incredibly widespread”, she wrote.Natalia Aruguete, a researcher at Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council who specialises in social media and political agendas, said she had seen “no evidence of a large-scale coordinated operation”, despite the existence of “a hostile, widespread and transnational conversation centred on Argentina”.“Brazil had a significant presence [in those messages],” she added, “particularly in the conversation about racism, but … Milei’s accusation of alleged Brazilian involvement was not backed up by any public evidence.”‘Rifts began to appear’: Why many Latin Americans want Spain to beat Argentina in the World Cup finalRead moreSome criticssaidthat the last time the idea of such a campaign was propagated by the state was during thebrutal 1976–83 dictatorship, whose crimes Milei hasrepeatedly downplayed. During the 1978 World Cup, hosted by Argentina, the military junta claimed that criticism of the regime’s human rights violations was part of an “anti-Argentina campaign”.Aruguete said Milei had turned a “diverse online conversation” into a political conflict that fits his narrative of a “culture war” against the left, at a time when his administration is facing “internal deterioration”: inflation appears to be under control, but rising unemployment andcorruption scandalshave driven the president’s popularity to itslowest pointsince taking office.The narrative that suggests Argentinians are all victims of a supposedly orchestrated campaign by leftwing foreign governments “allows Milei to shift the focus of the debate away from his own governance issues and on to an external adversary”, said Aruguete.Explore more on these topicsArgentinaAmericasJavier MileiJair BolsonaroBrazilAmnesty InternationalSamuel L JacksonnewsShareReuse this content

title: FCC bans humanoid robots from China, citing ‘unacceptable risks’ | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Move comes as the Trump administration has increasingly sought to keep Chinese technology out of the US
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Move comes as the Trump administration has increasingly sought to keep Chinese technology out of the US
Content: EngineAI T800 humanoid robots after rolling off the production line at a facility in Zhengzhou, Henan province, China, on 24 July 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEngineAI T800 humanoid robots after rolling off the production line at a facility in Zhengzhou, Henan province, China, on 24 July 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesTrump administrationFCC bans humanoid robots from China, citing ‘unacceptable risks’Move comes as the Trump administration has increasingly sought to keep Chinese technology out of the USDara Kerrand agenciesTue 28 Jul 2026 19.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on humanoid robots from China on Tuesday, saying that the technology poses “unacceptable risks” to the country’s national security. The move comes as theTrump administrationhas increasingly sought to keep Chinese technology out of the US.The FCC defines the banned robots as “advanced robotic devices”, which include humanoids and animal-like quadrupeds.“Advanced robotic devices collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots,” FCC officials wrote in theirdeterminationof the threat posed by robots.In addition to the humanoid robots, the FCC also barred connected power inverters, which enable renewable energy sources and batteries to connect to grids and datacenter equipment.The restrictions point to theTrump administration’s goal of elevating technology made in the US, along with driving firms to shift manufacturing to be done locally.“The President has made clear that the United States must have independent and secure supply chains for critical and emerging technologies like robotic devices and power inverters,” an ⁠administration official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.“Economic security is national security, and theTrump administrationcontinues to implement a nuanced and multi-faceted policy agenda to reindustrialize America,” he added.The restrictions apply only to robot and inverter models that have not yet been released. However, the FCC has the authority to ‌revoke authorizations for sales of models that have already been authorized for purchase in the US.Humanoid robots, topped with ‌AI-enabled “brains”, are forecast by some analysts for broad adoption in ‌consumer and industrial arenas, while explosive datacenter construction in the US will depend on reliable sources of inverters.China is the world’s largest maker of inverters, led by Sungrow Power Supply and Huawei, which are already heavily sanctioned by the US.The Chinese ​embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationRobotsChinaUS politicsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Japan earthquake injures at least 100 and kills two inside shopping mall | Japan | The Guardian
description: Kumamoto shaken by 6.8-magnitude quake, knocking out power and damaging buildings, as people remain trapped inside shopping centre
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Kumamoto shaken by 6.8-magnitude quake, knocking out power and damaging buildings, as people remain trapped inside shopping centre
Content: Aerial footage shows collapsed buildings after 6.8 magnitude Japan earthquake – videoJapanJapan earthquake injures at least 100 and kills two inside shopping mallKumamoto shaken by 6.8-magnitude quake, knocking out power and damaging buildings, as people remain trapped inside shopping centreRachel HallTue 28 Jul 2026 18.14 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 6.8-magnitude earthquake has shaken southJapan, killing at least two people and leaving at least 100 people injured. Some are trapped and presumed dead inside a shopping mall.The earthquake hit Kumamoto prefecture on the southern Kyushu island late on Tuesday afternoon, knocking out power to thousands of homes and damaging roads, bridges and buildings.The prefectural government said rescuers working at the scene overnight had taken eight people out of the Aeon Mall Kumamoto shopping centre.Of those eight, two women in their 20s were confirmed dead, while one other person was reported to be in cardiopulmonary arrest. The ⁠five others were injured but officials said their condition was not life-threatening.Firefighters said earlier that an explosion had occurred in the mall shortly after the earthquake, with a government official telling reporters that a gas leak had been reported but the cause was not known.Footage showed one side of the mall, the prefecture’s largest with roughly 200 shops, was torn away, exposing steel beams ‌and leaving debris strewn across the neighbouring car park. Several ambulances and fire engines were parked outside as rescue teams searched for survivors.A map of Japan showing the epicentre in Kumamoto prefectureThe quake’s magnitude was initially assessed as 7.1 but later revised down to 6.8Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, told reporters authorities were still assessing the extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by another deadly quake a decade ago.“We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings,” Takaichi said. “I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.”View image in fullscreenA house on fire in Yatsushiro, Japan, on Tuesday after the quake hit.Photograph: Kyodo/ReutersAbout 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said. The areas with the biggest tremors will remain at risk of further strong quakes and landslides for about a week since the shallow earthquake is triggering seismic activity in the area, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA).So far there have been more than 60 aftershocks ranging in magnitude from 1 to 4, the agency said. A tsunami warning was issued immediately after the quake, ​but was lifted within two hours.One person was killed in south-west Japan when a house collapsed during the earthquake, Kyodo News reported.Two hospitals reported ​more than 50 injuries each, including 10 in a serious condition, the public broadcaster NHK said.“People are coming in with burns and fractures from being trapped under objects due to the earthquake, and ambulances are constantly bringing in injured people,” NHK quoted one hospital employee as saying.“Inside the hospital, there are water leaks and electrical system failures.”Several people on a high-speed ‌train at the time of the quake were also ‌injured and more were missing after a chimney collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, according to local media reports.View image in fullscreenJapan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, speaks to the media at her official residence in Tokyo on Tuesday.Photograph: Kyodo/ReutersTakaichi pledged late yesterday that emergency responders would work “tirelessly” through the night “starting with the rescue and lifesaving of those affected”.Footage from NHK showed several other buildings on fire or partly collapsed, along with large fissures on ‌major roads, including an elevated highway. TSMC, the world’s largest contract chip maker, Sony and Fujifilm evacuated workers from their factories in the area.View image in fullscreenA smokestack at Nippon Paper Industries’ Yatsushiro mill collapsed in the 6.8m-magnitude earthquake.Photograph: Kyodo News/APChiharu Hara, a 35-year-old recruitment agent who was in Kumamoto, told AFP that she was “terrified” when the quake struck.“The office swayed violently side to side. I was afraid it would collapse. Everyone panicked,” Hara said.The quake’s epicentre was about 12 miles (20km) south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island’s largest city, with a population of about 700,000. The US Geological Survey initially said the earthquake had a magnitude of 7.1, but revised it later to 6.8. The tremor at 4.27 pm local time had a magnitude of 7.1, the JMA said, but reached the highest level of 7 on Japan’s shindo scale. A subsequent aftershock with a magnitude of 6.1 was registered at 5.08pm.Japan, which is located along the “ring of fire” of volcanoes and oceanic trenches in the Pacific basin, is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes. The country accounts for about 20% of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6 or more.The massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739. It damaged thousands of buildings including the city’s castle, a popular tourist site. Some of the castle’s stone walls were damaged in the most recent quake.View image in fullscreenKumamoto castle’s stone walls were damaged by the earthquake.Photograph: Kyodo/ReutersKyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had ​lost power, while ​the railway company JR Kyushu suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains. Kumamoto airport also shut its runway as airlines diverted and ​cancelled flights.The telecoms operators KDDI and NTT Docomo ‌said there was disruption to their ​mobile phone services owing to power shortages ​and transmission-line failures. There were no irregularities reported at the nuclear power stations in the area, Japan’s nuclear regulation authority said.The Japanese military has mobilised 3,600 personnel for disaster relief operations and sent 20 aircraft to assess the damage from the air, the defence minister said.Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that left around 18,500 people dead or missing and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.Explore more on these topicsJapanEarthquakesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We have lost everything’: extreme rainfall across Asia brings flash floods and typhoons | Flooding | The Guardian
description: From Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdown
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: From Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdown
Content: Bangladesh is one of several countries in the region to experience heavy rains and flash floods. Photograph: Rayhan Ahmed/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockFrom Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdownByNatasha MayandJonathan WattsTue 28 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 00.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It rained for 10 days and 10 nights, non-stop – I’d never seen anything like it,” says Anar Gul, a construction worker who lives in the remote district of Dur Baba in easternAfghanistan.The houses in his village are built from stone and mud, which makes them extremely vulnerable to heavy rains. After days of rain, Gul’s kitchen collapsed and his neighbour, Sayed Afsar Sadat, saw a large part of his house completely destroyed. “Rains like this are coming heavier and earlier each year,” says Sadat. “They are destroying the roads and washing away our crops. It’s impacting us directly.”View image in fullscreenAnar Gul, who lives in a remote mountain village in the Dur Baba district of eastern Afghanistan, says he has never seen rain like it.Photograph: IFRC/Mark South.Last week, torrential rains and flash floods wiped out villages and towns in Afghanistan,leaving at least31 people dead and hundreds missing. It’s been a similar picture in neighbouring countries, with the monsoon rains sparking chaos across the region. India, Bangladesh and Pakistan have all seen erratic, sudden heavy dumps of water.Jesmin Akter lived in the city of Chattogram, on the south-eastern coast of Bangladesh, which received a record412.3mm of rainfall in 24 hoursin early July, leading to the flash flood that swept through the Banshkhali district where they live. She says her children “understand that we are in a very bad situation”.Overnight the rains took the little they had; their poultry died, their paddy field flooded, their house collapsed and all their belongings in it – children’s books, school bags, toys, clothes, kitchen items – ruined.Akter carried her six children through chest-deep water to her mother’s house. There they stayed in the crowded conditions for over a week until the water receded.View image in fullscreenResidents and rescue workers inspect buildings damaged by heavy flooding in the eastern province of Nuristan, Afghanistan.Photograph: Wahidullah Kakar/AP“We have lost everything,” Akter said. Their house beside the canal was not in a good condition, but a few months ago the family had repaired it. “Now the flood has destroyed it again. We have no money. We are surviving on the food assistance we receive from different organisations.” They have gone back to the ruins of their home, but her children sleep on plastic sheets laid on the wet floor and she worries for their safety, especially that the unsanitary conditions will lead to disease. Her daughter has developed a fever.Aswildfires rageacross Europe and North America, the unprecedented rains continue elsewhere. While South Korea swings between heatwave and downpour, inJapanand Vietnamtorrential rain has led to landslides. China, meanwhile, has seen bouts of extreme rainfall since the flood season began in April, according to thewater resources ministryin mid-July, marking the start of a month-long peak flood control window. More than 600 rivers have since risen above warning levels – a 35% jump from the average for the same period over the past five years.View image in fullscreenSayed Afsar Sadat in Dur Baba says rains are destroying the roads and washing away crops.Photograph: IFRC/Meer Abdullah Rasikh.In the south-western city of Chongqing, a huge landslide after torrential rain killed at least 11 people and left 50 missing, with rescue efforts still ongoing. Separately, a flash flood at a scenic camping spot in the north-central province of Gansu left 10 people dead and injured 23 others.The flood season across the region has been exacerbated by successive storms. Typhoon Noul, the strongest to make landfall in China so far this year, prompted the evacuation of more than890,000people in Guangdong as of Sunday evening, according to provincial authorities. In early July, Typhoon Maysak inundated parts of Guangxi and swept through commercialsnake farms, allowing hundreds of snakes to escape.Forecasters have warned that more wet weather is on the way.
