Much of northern China, including Beijing, is expected to receive 20% to 50% more rain than usual, while four to six typhoons are forecast to make landfall in or affect the country this summer, above the average of 4.2, according to theChina Meteorological Administration.Taiwan, an island that lies in the path of typhoons in the north-west Pacific, has also seen a rise in extreme rainfall. In June, repeated downpours caused more than NT$330m (about US$10.2m) in agricultural losses across Taiwan, according to theagriculture ministry, while the capital Taipeirecordedits highest monthly rainfall in more than a century.View image in fullscreenTorrential rain flooded the streets of Dhaka in Bangladesh.Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/ReutersThe extreme weather across the region can clearly be linked to climate change. Climate scientists have long predicted that large areas of Asia will disproportionately suffer from more intense heat, humidity and drought as a result of climate disruption caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal. Themost recent reportby the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change said rising temperatures raise the threat of “floods in monsoon regions in south, south-east and east Asia, and glacier melting in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd World Weather Attribution scientistshave warnedthat extreme rainfall from cyclones is being “supercharged” in south-east Asia, with a clear pattern of increasingly heavy rain over recent decades.View image in fullscreenIn early July, Typhoon Maysak inundated parts of Guangxi in south China.Photograph: Cao Yiming/Xinhua/APThe year 2025 saw devastating storms and rainfall across the region. It also sawocean temperaturesrise to record heights. So far, this year has broughtrecord-breaking heatwaves. Extreme rainfall is more common and more intense because of human-caused climate breakdown across most of the world,particularly in Europe, most of Asia, central and eastern North America, and parts of South America, Africa and Australia. This is because warmer air can hold more water vapour and flooding has most likely become more frequent and severe in these locations as a result.“More intense rainfall is an expected consequence of us heating the planet by burning fossil fuels and building up more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. A warmer atmosphere can carry more water, so when it rains, it rains harder. Also hotter conditions cause air to rise faster and drive more intense thunderstorms,” said Richard Betts, head of the climate impacts strategic area at the Met Office Hadley Centre.The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) in providing aid helped the Guardian obtain interviews with those affected.View image in fullscreenTyphoon Noul (pictured in Hong Kong) prompted the evacuation of more than 890,000 people in Guangdong.Photograph: Venron Yuen/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockDr Hosam Faysal, the head of IFRC’s country delegation in Afghanistan, said “these are the very real, humanitarian effects of a changing climate … becoming increasingly volatile”.Faysal urged governments to ensure there was more investment in locally-led preparedness and mitigation in order to reduce the loss of life and suffering before climate-related disasters happened.“The coming forecast El Niño is a clear example – waiting to respond to the extreme needs we can see coming only once they arrive will cost lives.”Research by Yu-chen LiExplore more on these topicsFloodingAsia PacificClimate crisisChinaAfghanistanSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Guardian Essential poll: Angus Taylor’s approval rating crashes and One Nation support plateaus | Essential poll | The Guardian
description: Survey also shows Australians rounding on the government over its handling of inflation and the cost-of-living crisis
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Survey also shows Australians rounding on the government over its handling of inflation and the cost-of-living crisis
Content: The latest Guardian Essential poll shows support for the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has crashed.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe latest Guardian Essential poll shows support for the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has crashed.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesThe Guardian Essential reportEssential pollGuardian Essential poll: Angus Taylor’s approval rating crashes and One Nation support plateausSurvey also shows Australians rounding on the government over its handling of inflation and the cost-of-living crisisFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerTue 28 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 18.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne Nation’s primary vote has plateaued and Angus Taylor’s approval rating has crashed, according to the latest GuardianEssential poll.But it is not all smooth sailing for Labor, with Australians rubbishing the government’s handling of the inflation and cost-of-living crisis.Australians have also shown their reluctance to embrace new AI datacentres, with less than a third saying they’d be happy to have a facility in their local area and sharing concerns about energy demands, water supply, environmental impacts and noise.The (spin) doctor is in: the Albanese government is in good health, but that could all vanish in an instant | Peter LewisRead moreThe Guardian Essential poll, of 1,060 voters last week, found One Nation’s popularity was continuing to level off, attracting a 25% primary vote,down one point from June’s poll. Meanwhile while Labor’s indicative primary vote ticked up one point to 31%, the Coalition’s vote dropped further, down another point to 22%.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAll those movements are within the poll’s margin of error, but it is the second consecutive Essential poll where One Nation’s primary vote has dropped since reaching ahigh of 28% in May. The populist rightwing party has dipped back to where it was in April. It comes after weeks of scrutiny overPauline Hanson’s European trip, herinterview with Tommy Robinson, andcomments about domestic violenceandimmigration policy.Struggling for political oxygen and attention amid One Nation’s rise, the opposition leader has seen his own approval ratings plummet in the last month. In June, 36% of people approved of Taylor’s job performance and 37% disapproved, for a net approval of minus one; but this month’s poll has seen his approvals drop three points and his disapprovals increase by seven points, for a new net approval of minus 12.Taylor’s approval rating has crashed 16 points among men and four points among women, as well as by 20 points among people aged 35 to 54 and 13 points among those aged 18 to 34.Anthony Albanese’s approval rating ticked up one point to minus 14, with 38% approving and 52% disapproving of his performance as prime minister. It’s the fourth straight month in which more than half of voters have disapproved of his performance.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuardian Essential report: have Pauline’s policies plateaued her support? - podcastRead moreRespondents to the poll also rejected Labor’s handling of the inflation and cost-of-living crisis, with a decisive 64% rating the government’s performance as poor; while just 16% of Australians rated it as good.Nearly 80% of voters said cost of living and inflation was one of the most important issues to them, far and away the most-cited issue among respondents. Next most cited was Medicare and health (50%), crime (42%) and immigration (35%).But only 39% of voters rated the Labor government’s performance on Medicare and health as good, with 30% saying poor. On crime, 22% rated Labor as good and 50% as poor, while 24% rated Labor as good on immigration and another 50% as poor.“Cost of living remains the standout issue for voters and the government’s handling of inflation is being rated down,” the executive director of Essential Media, Peter Lewis, said.On managing technology and AI, the subject ofa major speech by Albanese earlier this month, 29% rated Labor’s performance as good and 30% as poor.The Essential report found only 28% of voters would support a new datacentre being built in their area, with 37% against. Men (34% support and 34% oppose) were far more supportive of new datacentres than women (22% support and 39% oppose).Asked about their reservations about datacentre development, 61% raised concerns about impact on energy demand and power prices, and another 44% were worried about water supply.Environmental impacts and noise were raised by 41% of voters, while 39% had general concerns about the growth of AI generally.Albanese this month announced plansto more strongly regulate datacentres and AI, particularly setting rules for power and water use, and building social license for the construction of facilities.Explore more on these topicsEssential pollThe Guardian Essential reportAustralian politicsOne NationLabor partyCoalitionAngus TaylorCost-of-living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Almost 4,000 people evacuated from tourist sites near Bordeaux as wildfires rage in France and Spain | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Return of winds and extreme heat threaten firefighters’ attempts to bring blazes under control
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Return of winds and extreme heat threaten firefighters’ attempts to bring blazes under control
Content: Firefighters work to put out a wildfire at Le Grand Crohot, near the Cap Ferret peninsula, in France’s Gironde department on Tuesday.Photograph: Florion Goga/ReutersView image in fullscreenFirefighters work to put out a wildfire at Le Grand Crohot, near the Cap Ferret peninsula, in France’s Gironde department on Tuesday.Photograph: Florion Goga/ReutersWildfiresAlmost 4,000 people evacuated from tourist sites near Bordeaux as wildfires rage in France and SpainReturn of winds and extreme heat threaten firefighters’ attempts to bring blazes under controlAngela GiuffridaandAjit NiranjanTue 28 Jul 2026 12.42 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly 4,000 people have been evacuated from tourist sites on France’s Atlantic coast as the return of winds and extreme heat jeopardises firefighters’ battles to contain wildfires raging inFranceand Spain.The precautionary evacuation order in France, which covers campsites, holiday villages and other tourist accommodation around the resort of Lacanau to the west of Bordeaux, exacerbated a wildfire emergency described by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, as the “toughest” situation the country had dealt with since the second world war.On a visit to a crisis centre in Bordeaux on Tuesday, Macron warned that “the coming weeks will be tough and we have to hold out”.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron with firefighters on a visit to the fire and rescue operational centre in Bordeaux on Monday.Photograph: Kenzo Tribouillard/EPAIn Spain, meanwhile, a woman who had been injured ina wildfirein the southern province of Almería this month died in hospital, bringing the death toll from that blaze to 14.The woman, who was not named, died at Seville’s Virgen del Rocío university hospital where she had been treated since suffering severe injuries in the wildfire, a hospital spokeswoman told AFP, without giving further details.In France,Rémi Lassoureille, a fire commander in the Gironde department, was quoted by Le Monde as saying that the blaze there, which has destroyed 42,000 hectares (104,000 acres) of forest, was “relatively under control”, although firefighters feared a “potential flare-up of the fire on its north-west flank towards Lacanau”.“That is why we decided to evacuate the campsites,” he said.Map showing burnt areas near French coast west of BordeauxOther large fires have been contained in the nearby Landes, where thousands of evacuees were allowed to return home, and the Écrins massif in the French Alps, although one in the Gros Bessillon massif in the Var area of south-east France has not yet been fully brought under control.Wildfires in France, Spain and Italy have forced the evacuation of about 330,000 people over the past week, with Spain entering Europe’s fourth intense heatwave of the summer attempting to contain some of the worst forest fires in the country’s history.‘Ash fell from the sky’: Tourists describe fleeing ‘apocalyptic’ wildfires in FranceRead moreThe Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said the country faced “difficult hours, complex hours” before the new heatwave, which is forecast to begin on Wednesday and warned about the urgency of responding to the climate emergency.He later said authorities were beginning to “see light at the end of the tunnel in the fight against wildfires”. Spain’s interior ministry announced the end of evacuation orders for 15 municipalities on Tuesday afternoon in rare good news.A fire in the hilly terrain of Ávila, west of Madrid, has become Spain’s largest on record, burning 50,000 hectares.Map showing burnt areas near Ávila, west of MadridA firefighter, Javier García, told Associated Press he had never faced anything like it in his two decades protecting woodlands and rural communities.“This doesn’t have a precedent,” he said, adding that the ferocity of the wildfire was forcing firefighters to fundamentally change their tactics by prioritising evacuations and property protection because of the danger from fast-moving walls of flames and blazes too powerful to attack directly.“The evolution is alarming,” García said.View image in fullscreenFirefighters use controlled burning to halt a wildfire near Cebreros in Spain’s Ávila province on Tuesday.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APAn EU spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said a number of firefighting planes and helicopters from member countries had been deployed to France and Spain.She said it was “important to clarify that no country can maintain alone all the resources that are needed to tackle every possible natural or other disaster and crisis”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year of burnt land area.Wildfire weather across the bloc has been more severe this year than ever before, according to data up to 22 July from the European Forest Fire Information System. In France, which had broken its full-year record for burnt area by then, and in Spain, the cumulative numbers of fires in 2026 have also set new records.Graph showing total burnt area in France so far in 2026, compared with the average and the minimum-maximum range for 2006-25Graph showing total burnt area in Spain so far in 2026, compared with the average and the minimum-maximum range for 2006-25European wildfires have struck at the same time as ferocious North American ones, with hundreds of blazes continuing to devastate the western US and swathes of Canada. Meanwhile,torrential rainshave flooded countries across Asia.“The climate alarm is blaring, from every direction,” Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of UN Climate Change, said on Tuesday. With Europe now facing another heatwave, he said the human and economic costs of the climate crisis were reaching “national emergency” levels.“These spiralling disasters are now the lived reality for billions in a world getting rapidly hotter, as humanity moves too slowly from fossil fuels to clean energy and to protect forests,” he said.Western Europe had a wet winter and also, in some parts, a wet spring, which encouraged heavy plant growth. It has been followed by a dangerously hot and dry summer, with back-to-back heatwaves forcing moisture from plants and leaving behind a surplus of fuel that has fed the flames.The climatic drivers have been made worse by the long-running abandonment of farmland that used to fragment the landscape, preventing small fires from growing into blazing infernos.“If the issue of fuel load isn’t addressed, I think we’re going to have to get used to [fires too strong to put out],” said Dr Jesús Notario del Pino, a soil scientist at the University of La Laguna in Tenerife. “As many forestry specialists and engineers often say: what we don’t manage, the fire will.”Dr Thomas Smith, a wildfire scientist at the London School of Economics, said: “If I was holidaying on the coast of Spain or the south of France, I would make sure I have any fire alerts or fire weather apps installed on my phone and familiarise myself with the evacuation plans for the hotel or residence. It’s very important to understand that timely evacuation saves lives.”Map showing fire danger levels across SpainThe June heatwave would have been “virtually impossible” without the added heat from more than a century of carbon pollution,a rapid analysis found last month, while the level of soil dryness in western Europe was made five times more likely by climate breakdown,according to a separate studyfrom the same international research network last week.Estimates of the death toll from the heatwaves, from national public health agencies and independent scientists, suggest they have claimed at least 10,000 lives.Stiell said: “The science on the cause is unequivocal: global heating, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making protracted heatwaves, severe floods and violent mega-storms more frequent, more intense and more costly.“What needs to be done is equally clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables, and protect people where the impacts are already hitting hardest.”Explore more on these topicsWildfiresFranceSpainClimate crisisExtreme weatherEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ​France and Spain race to control wildfires as fresh heatwave hits, as UN warns ‘the climate alarm is blaring’ – as it happened | France | The Guardian
description: Spanish prime minister also says the fires serve as a reminder to plan for the ‘worsening’ climate emergency
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Spanish prime minister also says the fires serve as a reminder to plan for the ‘worsening’ climate emergency
Content: 06.44 EDT'The climate alarm is blaring, from every direction,' UN climate chief warnsDamian CarringtonEnvironment editorThe costs of the climate crisis are now reaching national emergency levels, the UN’s climate chief Simon Stiell said on Tuesday.“The climate alarm is blaring, from every direction.Around the world, climate-driven disasters are reaching nightmare proportions, as the costs of humanity’s addiction to burning coal, oil and gas keep spiraling upwards.These record-breaking wildfires tearing through France, Spain and other parts of Europe, forcing mass evacuations and hammering regional and national economies, follow brutal heatwaves that have dried out landscapes.With the mercury set to soar again this week, the awful costs of this climate crisis – both human and economic – are nowreaching national emergency levels.”Executive Secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change Simon Stiell delivers a keynote address during a press conference in New Delhi, India.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAStiell saidthe whole globe is suffering the impacts of global heating.“In North Africa, temperatures are approaching 49°C, putting lives and livelihoods in grave jeopardy. In Chile, deadly storms have destroyed homes and lives. While in Japan, records are tumbling as temperatures soar. These spiraling disasters are now the lived reality for billions in a world getting rapidly hotter.The science on the cause is unequivocal: global heating is making protracted heatwaves, severe floods and violent mega-storms more frequent, more intense and more costly.What needs to be done is equally clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables, and protect people where the impacts are already hitting hardest.”Share

title: Dawn raid targets ‘umbrella cheaters’ reserving beach spots in Naples | Italy | The Guardian
description: Umbrellas, deck chairs and loungers seized in Torre del Greco authorities’ crackdown on people reserving spots overnight
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Umbrellas, deck chairs and loungers seized in Torre del Greco authorities’ crackdown on people reserving spots overnight
Content: A beach in Torre del Greco, near Naples.Photograph: Kirill Nikitin/AlamyView image in fullscreenA beach in Torre del Greco, near Naples.Photograph: Kirill Nikitin/AlamyItalyDawn raid targets ‘umbrella cheaters’ reserving beach spots in NaplesUmbrellas, deck chairs and loungers seized in Torre del Greco authorities’ crackdown on people reserving spots overnightAngela Giuffridain RomeTue 28 Jul 2026 07.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAuthorities in a coastal suburb of Naples seized umbrellas, loungers and deck chairs during a dawn sweep of a beach aimed at cracking down on the growing trend of people attempting to reserve prime spots overnight.Torre del Greco’s port authority said coastguard staff and local police had together collected 40 items as part of a national beach and lake safety operation that targets people labelled by the Italian press asfurbetti dell’ombrellone,or umbrella cheaters.The port authority said the sweep at Laghetto, a popular, free-access beach unlike the private concessions that dominate much of Italy’s coastline during the summer, was carried out after numerous complaints about equipment being left unattended for days on end.The operation discovered “unattended chairs, umbrellas and small tables that were continuously occupying the beach, effectively reserving a spot for the owners’ return”.“It is a practice that recurs each summer, but it is expressly prohibited,” the port authority said, adding that “occupying the beach in this manner violates the regulations governing the management of maritime public domain areas”.Those leaving behind their beach equipment after sunset risk fines of up to €500 (£425) while reclaiming the confiscated personal belongings involves a bureaucratic ordeal.There was a similar blitz on a beach in Puglia earlier this month as well as on others in Liguria and in Sardinia.Italian beachgoersare battling to reclaim “free beaches”from private concessions, which, especially in Liguria, Emilia-Romagna and Puglia, are common.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne such battle was recently won in Bacoli, near Naples, with the town saying the municipality aimed to make more than 80% of the local coastline free or equipped for public use.Explore more on these topicsItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: France and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave begins | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Coming days are ‘absolutely critical’ for firefighters before temperatures rise again this week, officials say
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Coming days are ‘absolutely critical’ for firefighters before temperatures rise again this week, officials say
Content: A wildfire burns near Cestas in Gironde province in south-west France.Photograph: Julien Soulard/EPAView image in fullscreenA wildfire burns near Cestas in Gironde province in south-west France.Photograph: Julien Soulard/EPAWildfiresFrance and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave beginsComing days are ‘absolutely critical’ for firefighters before temperatures rise again this week, officials sayAngelique Chrisafisin Bordeaux,Angela Giuffridain Rome andJennifer Rankinin BrusselsMon 27 Jul 2026 22.37 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirefighters inFranceand Spain are racing to bring huge wildfires under control before another heatwave this week that will complicate efforts to tame the flames.Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said Monday and Tuesday were “absolutely crucial days” before temperatures rise again from Wednesday, prompting prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to warn: “We face difficult hours, complex hours” ahead.EU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year for the area of land burned.11:13Race against time to contain wildfires in France and Spain - The LatestA fire in the hilly terrain of Ávila, west of Madrid, has become Spain’s largest on record, burning 50,000 hectares (125,000 acres). Authorities are battling two separate fires north-west of Madrid, taking the total area of scorched land near the capital to 70,000 hectares.Spain’s state meteorological agency, Aemet, said the heatwave would last until “at least” Sunday, “making firefighting efforts more difficult due to high temperatures [and] locally gusty southerly winds”.France was also in “a race against time” to control wildfires before another heatwave this week, said Eric Brocardi, a fire service spokesperson. Weather forecasters have said temperatures could reach 40C (104F) is some parts of the country from Tuesday.View image in fullscreenCharred cars in the Spanish village of Chapinería on Monday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersThis would complicate efforts to control the wildfire in Gironde in south-west France, which the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as “extremely intense and unpredictable … generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area”.The mayor of Bordeaux, Thomas Cazenave, told the BBC he is bracing for “all eventualities”, as the fire advanced to within 15km (nine miles) from the city. “We are preparing to accommodate a large number of people should further evacuations be ordered,” he said.On a visit to Bordeaux, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said: “The coming weeks will be tough and we have to hold out.”But he said a smaller fire in the adjoining Landes – which forced the evacuation of more than 30,000 people – was “contained” but remained “virulent”. “We must be extremely cautious over the next few hours and the coming days,” he said.The Gironde fire has so far burned 42,000 hectares, making it one of the biggest devastations of land in France since the second world war.In the Cestas commune, about 10 miles from the city of Bordeaux, firefighters used mechanical diggers to uproot trees in an attempt to create a firebreak.WildfiresThe vast fire, which has triggered the evacuation of 220,000 people, had not progressed during the early hours of Monday but was “not contained” and remained “very complicated to control”, Nuñez said.Speaking after an emergency meeting of the French government on Monday, he described this year’s wildfires as “completely exceptional”. More than 116,000 hectares of forest and vegetation have been burned since January, far exceeding the 70,000 hectares reported for the whole of 2025.chartSpain’s government said the 172,000 hectares of forested land burned this year was six times greater than the equivalent figure for 2025.Sánchez told a climate conference the wildfires were not isolated incidents.“It is the most painful manifestation of a climate emergency that is making … wildfires more voracious and heatwaves more frequent, and as a result our land more vulnerable,” he said. “It is no longer an exception. It is the rule.”The European Commission’s lead official on the green transition, Teresa Ribera, said Europe was not prepared for the consequences of the climate crisis. Inan interview with El Paísshe said the commission would propose an adaptation strategy in October that would be much more comprehensive than policies implemented so far.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez visits a firefighters’ control centre in La Vall d’Uixo.Photograph: Manuel Bruque/EPAA series of heatwaves, including record-breaking temperatures in June, that scientists saywould have been impossible without the climate crisis, has left parched soils and tinder-dry vegetation that have fuelled this summer’s fires.A European Commission official said the wildfire season had begun in April and could last until early November. Officials also stressed the rising risks for fighting wildfires from the middle of the week in France, Spain and Greece.The EU executive has coordinated the dispatch of seven planes and four helicopters to France, as well as six planes and three forest firefighting teams to Spain, after the countries triggered the bloc’s emergency assistance mechanism. EU officials have also been sent to the Bordeaux region to assist local authorities.View image in fullscreenA fire engine drives through smoke near Marcheprime outside Bordeaux.Photograph: Emma Da Silva/APOfficials stressed the unprecedented nature of recent fires, which have spread rapidly over large areas. A commission official said thata recent fire in southern Spain that killed 13 peoplehad reached speeds of 4 mph, while firefighters are able to react only to fires moving 300 metres an hour or less.The scale of Europe’s wildfires has raised questions about the continent’s ability to respond. Italy is among about 10 European countries that have sent firefighting equipment or teams to France and Spain while grappling with its own blazes.Several fires broke out in northern and central Portugal, officials said, with over 1,000 firefighters and other professionals battling the flames.Firefighters fought to extinguish a major wildfire in Italy’s southern region of Puglia on Monday. More than 400 people, many of them tourists staying in campsites set among pine forests, were evacuated by sea from the Gargano peninsula on Sunday as the blaze, fanned by strong winds, encroached on beaches.A further 58 people were evacuated from their homes in Maratea as a wildfire swept through neighbouring Basilicata.Italy is bracing for its fourth heatwave this year as temperatures edge up towards highs of 38C to 40C from Wednesday.High temperatures in western EuropeSmoke from the fires in France is continuing to cause a “marked deterioration” in air quality across a swathe of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region and beyond, with health authorities warning about the danger.Elderly people, pregnant women and those with respiratory issues and chronic conditions were advised to take precautions. Local health authorities said people should close windows, wear an FFP2 mask outside and avoid strenuous activity.The prime minister’s office said more than 1.5 million FFP2 masks had been sent to the region.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresFranceSpainExtreme weatherExtreme heatClimate crisisEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Prisoners at Iran’s largest jail sew lips shut in hunger strike as executions soar | Iran | The Guardian
description: At least 1,500 protest after six men on drug-related charges put in solitary confinement before possible execution
Author: Deepa Parent
Headline: At least 1,500 protest after six men on drug-related charges put in solitary confinement before possible execution
Content: Screengrab from a video shared by human rights groups showing Iranian prisoners on hunger strike at Ghezel Hesar.Photograph: InstagramView image in fullscreenScreengrab from a video shared by human rights groups showing Iranian prisoners on hunger strike at Ghezel Hesar.Photograph: InstagramIranPrisoners at Iran’s largest jail sew lips shut in hunger strike as executions soarAt least 1,500 protest after six men on drug-related charges put in solitary confinement before possible executionDeepa ParentTue 28 Jul 2026 06.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 16.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrisoners at Iran’s largest jail have sewn their lips shut as hundreds of them joined a mass hunger strike amid a surge in executions over drug offences and charges linked to anti-government protests.The hunger strike, involving at least 1,500 death row prisoners at Ghezel Hesar prison near Tehran, began two weeks ago after six men convicted on drug-related charges were transferred to solitary confinement before their possible execution, according to Iranian rights groups.In a series of videos shared by rights groups in exile, prisoners are seen sitting in a prison hallway, holding placards reading “No to Executions” and chanting “Be our voice”.In one graphic video, a prisoner addresses the camera to say he is sewing his lips shut because, six days into the hunger strike, no prison official has responded to the protest.The footage then shows another prisoner off camera using a needle and thread to stitch the man’s lips together. In another video, a prisoner calls for urgent medical help for those whose conditions he says are deteriorating. “The guards will not open the door so we can take them to the prison infirmary,” he says.The protest is the latest act of defiance in the prisoner-led campaign against executions, which began in January 2024 and has spread across prisons in Iran amid a sharp rise in the use of the death penalty.There has been a huge spike in executions this year amid the war with the US, and families of those on death row and rights groups have raised the alarm over the worsening human rights crisis in the country.At the weekend, Donald Trump abruptly called ​off a two-week bombing campaign, but has threatened to restart strikes unless negotiations with Tehran make progress.One source in Tehran said: “Whenever the shadow of war over the regime lifts even slightly, the regime becomes more savage. They noted that a prisoner was executed on 6 April – the date that the US and Iran agreed to a ceasefire. “The intensity of executions has actually increased since the war supposedly ended.”According to the Oslo-based non-profit Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), at least 424 executions have been carried out this year, with hundreds more on death row. Most executions were handed down in drug-related cases, IHRNGO said.On Tuesday, officials hanged two men who were convicted of “waging war on God” over the deaths of two police officers during the anti-government protests. Twenty-six people linked to the January protests have been hanged this year.Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, the director of IHRNGO, said people sentenced to death for drug offences were among the most marginalised and voiceless prisoners on death row.“Last year alone, at least 795 people were hanged on drug-related charges, with almost no international reaction and hardly any domestic or social media campaigns to save them. By staging this protest, the prisoners in Ghezel Hesar are taking an extraordinary risk. They know that the authorities can execute them at any moment, yet they have chosen to raise their voices in the hope that the international community will finally hear them and increase the political cost of these executions,” he said.According toAmnesty International, revolutionary courts, which have jurisdiction over national security and drug-related offences, lack independence and routinely impose harsh sentences, including death sentences, after grossly unfair trials.In a message relayed to the Guardian, one death-row protester said: “We are prisoners who turned to such mistakes simply to afford the basic necessities of life, and deeply regret our actions. Where else in the world is a human life taken for a first mistake?”A similar protest was held at the prison in October 2025, when more than 1,500 prisoners went on a six-day hunger strike, leading to a rare visit by authorities. But activists say conditions have not improved since. Moein Khazaeli, a human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists, said executions continue following unfair trials over drug-related offences.View image in fullscreenIranians executed this year include (clockwise from top left) Amirhossein Hatami, Babak Alipour, Pouya Ghobadi and Amirali Mirjafari.Photograph: Supplied“In many cases, defendants do not have access to lawyers or a meaningful right to defend themselves. There are also cases in which charges are fabricated against people from ethnic minority or poor backgrounds,” Khazaeli said. “Death sentences issued by the revolutionary courts are a violation of human rights and even Iran’s own laws.”Trump warns of return to ‘strong military action’ if Iran diplomacy failsRead moreExecutions have also surged among political prisoners and protesters arrested after the nationwide protests in January. Many of the death sentences were issued on the basis of confessions extracted under torture, Amiry-Moghaddam said.“The Islamic Republic has no legitimate justification for using the death penalty for drug offences. It is not required by Islam, and the authorities themselves have repeatedly acknowledged that executions have failed to deter drug trafficking or drug use. On the contrary, both drug trafficking and addiction have continued to rise over the years. Those sentenced to death are rarely major traffickers; they are typically the lowest-ranking couriers, recruited because of poverty for a small payment. Many are convicted solely on the basis of confessions extracted under torture,” he added.Families of those on death row in Ghezel Hesar have staged protests outside the prison in support of those inside, but sources said authorities violently cracked down on their gathering.Additional reporting by Patrick WintourExplore more on these topicsIranMiddle East and north AfricaHuman rightsProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: A dog saved Houssein Hamze from a bomb. When war returned, he stayed to care for Lebanon’s animals | Lebanon | The Guardian
description: In normal times the Mashala shelter founder takes in strays, but in wartime, he is the only lifeline for animals in the area
Author: William Christou
Headline: In normal times the Mashala shelter founder takes in strays, but in wartime, he is the only lifeline for animals in the area
Content: Houssein Hamze stayed to take care of animals during the 2026 Israel-Hezbollah war, despite the constant risk of death from Israeli drone and airstrikes.In normal times the Mashala shelter founder takes in strays, but in wartime, he is the only lifeline for animals in the areaByWilliam Christouin Zefta; photographs by Oliver MarsdenTue 28 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 00.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring Israel’s 2006 war against Hezbollah, Houssein Hamze woke up one night to the sound of barking. Alarmed, he got up to check on the dog – his first rescue pet. Moments later, a bomb dropped next to his home and a piece of shrapnel landed right where he had been sleeping.“I swear to God, he really saved me from death.Animalsalways possess a sixth sense we don’t have,” Hamze said.Twenty years and two wars later, the 57-year-old is still repaying his debt to the dog that saved his life.Soon after his near-death experience, Hamze founded theMashalashelter in the village of Zefta, south Lebanon, to take care of animals in the area. In normal times he takes in strays, and in wartime he is the only lifeline for animals in the area.View image in fullscreenWorkers with the rescued dogs at the Mashala shelter near the village of Zefta, on the outskirts of Nabatieh in south Lebanon.On a recent morning, Hamze strolled through his small farm where the shelter is located, checking on fig trees as a line of dogs followed behind him, ears perking up with his every move. He opened an enclosure where two camels – rescued from the Bekaa valley last year – stood among chickens and geese.“This is Jamoola and her son, Jamool. She is so sweet. When I don’t visit for more than two days, she starts to cry. And when I come back, she wraps her neck around me as if she’s hugging me,” Hamze said, as the camel placed her head in his lap, nuzzling him as he scratched behind her ears. Jamool, a calf who was still nursing, hid his face behind his mother.View image in fullscreenHoussein Hamze, 57, hugs Jamoola, one of two camels rescued from the Bekaa valley last year.The donation-supported farm hosts an eclectic collection of rescues. About 200 dogs – some of them missing ears or tails – gnawed on donated chicken feet, while horses whinnied at guests by the entrance. Chickens ran between the camels’ legs while geese patrolled the perimeter of their enclosure. A small conspiracy of ravens flew rings around the forested valley of the farm, never straying too far from the shade in the intense summer heat.Hamze was one of about 20 people who stayed behind in his village during the last Hezbollah-Israel war that started on 2 March 2026 and forced approximately a quarter of Lebanon’s population to flee their homes. He stayed to take care of the animals, despite the constant risk of death from Israeli drone and airstrikes.View image in fullscreenHamze has stayed to take care of the animals despite war returning Lebanon this year.“Many people fled and left their animals behind during their displacement – some of them left their animals tied up. We would go out, untie them and leave them water,” said Hamze. He pointed to one dog he rescued, Lulu, who lost a chunk of her tail in an airstrike and for whom he has been caring ever since. About 50 dogs came to the shelter during the war by themselves, seeking out food.During the conflict, Hamze would make daily rounds in his beaten-up truck, distributing dry food to the abandoned dogs and livestock in the villages of south Lebanon. It was not easy work: food was hard to secure, and he would often have to carry jerrycans of water long distances to dogs in more remote areas. On several occasions, airstrikes hit a building next to where he was working. Once during his feeding rounds, Hamze stumbled on the corpse of a man recently struck by a drone strike.“By the end, all the dogs knew me. I would beep and they would come running,” he said.Hamze would travel between the villages despite a Israeli drone that hovered overhead, watching his every move. He stuck the “Mashala” animal shelter sign on the roof of the car so the drone could identify him – but still it was no sure bet. Drones would regularly strike people in the area, ranging from Hezbollah fighters to medics to a man and his friend who went back to collect clothes from their home.“I wasn’t afraid for myself. I was only afraid for the animals. I kept thinking: if I die, who will look after them? They would be lost,” Hamze said.View image in fullscreenHamze points out the gravestone of his donkey Blanka at the Mashala shelter.Despite his bravado, Hamze quietly made arrangements in case he was killed. He sent eight donkeys to a shelter in Beirut, fearful that unlike the dogs, they would not be able to survive on their own if he died. He would have sent the camels and horses too, but he could not fit them in a pickup truck.Since a ceasefire in June ended most of fighting in Lebanon, life has gone back to almost normal for Hamze and the animals in his shelter. The thud of artillery is more distant now; it no longer sets off a row of furious barking. Hamze is now occupied with more mundane tasks: repairing irrigation tubing chewed on by dogs, and chasing animals with a syringe to give them their tick treatments.View image in fullscreenLife has gone back to almost normal for Hamze and the animals at his shelter since the ceasefire in June.His work during the war made him a minor celebrity in Lebanon. Videos of him braving drones to feed dogs went viral, prompting an outpouring of donations. With the war no longer in the headlines, donations are slowly drying up.Hamze is still famous in the village, though. His farm is hard to find but everyone in the area knows him. “Keep going all the way down the road and take a left. And tell Houssein I say hi,” said a shepherd on the road.View image in fullscreenDisplaced people returning to their homes have begun calling Hamze to assist with animal rescues.And there is more work than ever, Hamze said, as displaced people return to their homes and have begun calling him to assist with animal rescues. Scrolling through his WhatsApp, he estimated he received about 500 messages and calls a day reporting animals that needed help.“The assistance is really not enough. But thank God, we made it through the most dangerous period. I was on my own, there wasn’t a single day when you could stop working and rest. I felt completely drained,” he said.Hamze said he hoped that one day the shelter would not be necessary, that people would value animals as much as they do humans. Maybe, with a proper respect for the sanctity of life, people would stop fighting, he mused.“The conclusion is this: if you don’t have compassion for animals, you won’t have compassion for human beings. Believe me,” Hamze said, before planting a kiss on Jamoola’s outstretched head.Explore more on these topicsLebanonMiddle East and north AfricaAnimal welfareAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pakistan accused of fatally shooting 30 unarmed protesters in Kashmir | Kashmir | The Guardian
description: Local civil rights group alleges authorities removed evidence of killings amid communications blackout
Author: Shah Meer Baloch
Headline: Local civil rights group alleges authorities removed evidence of killings amid communications blackout
Content: Pakistani security personnel stand guard on Monday outside a polling station during the first phase of general elections in Mirpur.Photograph: Amiruddin Mughal/EPAView image in fullscreenPakistani security personnel stand guard on Monday outside a polling station during the first phase of general elections in Mirpur.Photograph: Amiruddin Mughal/EPAKashmirPakistan accused of fatally shooting 30 unarmed protesters in KashmirLocal civil rights group alleges authorities removed evidence of killings amid communications blackoutShah Meer Balochin IslamabadTue 28 Jul 2026 12.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 16.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 30 people are alleged to have been killed in Pakistan-administered Kashmir in the past two days as part of what has been claimed is a brutal state crackdown that has engulfed the disputed region for weeks.According to a local civil society group, Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), the Pakistani security services fired on tens of thousands of peaceful protesters, killing 25 people on Monday and five more on Tuesday.A wave of protests and violence in PakistaniKashmirstarted in June. The state has imposed a severe communication shutdown in response, including an internet blackout that cut the region off from the rest of Pakistan, and began carrying out mass arrests.Amnesty International on Tuesday called for Pakistani authorities to lift the communications blackout.JAAC and their supporters had taken to the streets to call for electoral reform in the heavily militarised region. Monday marked the first phase of an election disputed by local groups who say a system of reserved seats for refugees from Indian-administered Kashmir now living across Pakistan gives outsiders too much control over the region.SA Khan, a spokesperson for JAAC, accused Pakistan’s security agencies of firing on unarmed protesters in Mirpur on Tuesday and then removing the evidence.“Security forces have taken away the dead bodies and locked away the hospital in Mirpur,” he said. “We have the photos and video evidence of dead bodies lying on streets in a pool of blood. The security forces abducted the dead bodies to erase the evidence.”A local resident in Mirpur, requesting anonymity for fear of retribution by the authorities, said the violence had erupted early on Tuesday afternoon when people gathered to protest against killings the previous day. “The bodies were shifted to hospital and then they went missing. Now, all shops nearby have been closed after the violence,” they said.The Guardian could not independently verify the death toll as media were prevented from accessing the area and the internet blackout remained in place, making it hard to reach local communities. Pakistani media have largely ignored the protests and alleged killings.Pakistani authorities have rejected the accusation of state involvement in the killing of civilian protesters. In a press conference over the weekend, the information minister, Atta Tarar, alleged that the protests in Pakistani-administered Kashmir were receiving “funds and instructions” from India.JAAC spokesperson Khan rejected the accusations that the unrest was sponsored by India. “It is nothing new: people asking for political or economic rights are termed India-sponsored or anti-state in Pakistan, same goes in India,” he said.The protests, led by JAAC, have been ongoing for a year, demanding political and economic rights for local people, as well as electoral reforms.Pakistan-administered Kashmir has been rocked by bouts of deadly violence in recent years. The protests that began in June, calling for the abolition of 12 reserved seats for refugees from Indian-administered Kashmir, have prompted the deadliest crackdown in years. Locals say the reserved seats are used by the central government to retain control over the region and destabilise regional politics.About 40 people were alleged to have been killed when violence erupted in June and the government accused protesters of killing police. The local government responded by proscribing JAAC as a terrorist organisation, arresting and detaining its political workers en masse and responding to protests with force.It prompted the UN rights chief, Volker Türk, to call for an investigation into the deadly violence.Isabelle Lassée, Amnesty International’s action regional director for south Asia, said: “The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities’ long history of unlawful violence against protesters in Jammu and Kashmir. A prompt, independent, and transparent investigation must be ordered into the security forces’ use of force against protesters.“So long as an internet and mobile services blackout remains in place, it will severely impede the independent verification of the full extent of the situation on the ground. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area.”Explore more on these topicsKashmirPakistanAmnesty InternationalSouth and central AsiaProtestHuman rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s Cockroach movement threatens to restart protests after mass student arrests | India | The Guardian
description: Cockroach Janta party says government has broken promise, with detentions in Delhi, Assam, West Bengal and Bihar
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Cockroach Janta party says government has broken promise, with detentions in Delhi, Assam, West Bengal and Bihar
Content: Protesters at a gathering organised by supporters of the Cockroach Janta party in Mumbai, India, on Sunday.Photograph: Indranil Aditya/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenProtesters at a gathering organised by supporters of the Cockroach Janta party in Mumbai, India, on Sunday.Photograph: Indranil Aditya/NurPhoto/ShutterstockIndiaIndia’s Cockroach movement threatens to restart protests after mass student arrestsCockroach Janta party says government has broken promise, with detentions in Delhi, Assam, West Bengal and BiharHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiTue 28 Jul 2026 03.23 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 20.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia’s youth-led “Cockroach” movement, whose nationwide protests forced theresignation of the education minister, has accused the government of backtracking on its promise not to act against student protesters and has threatened to restart demonstrations.TheCockroach Janta party(CJP), which organised mass protests over exam paper leaks and other irregularities, said it had received reports of hundreds of students being detained or “harassed” by police.Police cases were filed against students in Delhi, Assam, West Bengal and Bihar, all states ruled by Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).The CJP had agreed to call off the demonstrations on Saturday after the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, resigned and senior BJP ministers assured the group no punitive action would be taken against protesters. But on Monday, the CJP accused the Modi government of reneging on the agreement.“If the government does not honour the agreement and release everyone detained or arrested, we will be compelled to resume the protest,” a CJP spokesperson, Ashutosh Ranka, told reporters.At least 100 people have been arrested, many on stringent, non-bailable charges, according to the CJP.‘I will die for this cause’: how India’s cockroach meme became the biggest challenge to Modi’s grip on powerRead moreOn Monday, Neha Bora, the head of the AllIndiaStudents Association, who became an important figurehead of the CJP movement, travelled to Bihar to put pressure on the authorities to withdraw cases against all protesters in the state.A police officer was suspended in Bihar for using an assault rifle to disperse student protesters on Saturday.In West Bengal, where the BJP recently took power, the hardline chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, inferred that all the protesters last week were Muslims. Cases have been filed against many participants under a draconian new state law.The CJP has set up a legal fund to help cover the expenses of protesters implicated in criminal cases by the police, said Saurav Das, another spokesperson for the group.The youth-led movement has won millions of followers on social media since it waslaunched in Mayby a 30-year-old public relations graduate, Abhijeet Dipke. Hundreds of thousands of protesters, mainly students, rallied last week in New Delhi and other cities, demanding Pradhan’s resignation and broader reforms of the examination system.View image in fullscreenSaurav Das, a spokesperson for the Cockroach movement, addresses a press conference in New Delhi on Monday as his co-spokesperson, Ashutosh Ranka, and Kapil Sibal, an Indian lawmaker, look on.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersDemonstrations in the Indian capital turned violent on 20 July when huge crowds attempted to march to parliament from the Jantar Mantar protest site. Police fired teargas and used batons to disperse them, causing clashes and a wave of detentions.The protests were an unprecedented show of dissent against the Modi government, which has cracked down on critics and opposition over its 12 years in power. Pradhan’s resignation was the first time a senior minister in the Modi government had been forced out by public pressure.The chief justice of India called for an independent investigation after a petition was filed in the supreme court alleging police brutality at the Delhi protest, stating that the “right to peaceful, lawful protest is absolutely guaranteed” under the Indian constitution.The issue also reverberated in parliament on Monday, as opposition lawmakers demanded a response from the government over last week’s police crackdown.The government has promised to act on the issues that sparked the protests, and announced a panel to oversee an overhaul of India’s examination system. On Monday, it introduced a measure in parliament seeking tougher penalties for exam paper leaks.Explore more on these topicsIndiaNarendra ModiProtestSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: UK faces ‘very difficult trade-offs’ in budget because of Iran war, say analysts | Business | The Guardian
description: Leading thinktank says higher oil prices and inflation will give Andy Burnham a ‘challenging inheritance’
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Leading thinktank says higher oil prices and inflation will give Andy Burnham a ‘challenging inheritance’
Content: Ships anchored in the strait of Hormuz off Iran on Monday. The on-off closure of the waterway has pushed up oil prices, putting pressure on inflation.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/APView image in fullscreenShips anchored in the strait of Hormuz off Iran on Monday. The on-off closure of the waterway has pushed up oil prices, putting pressure on inflation.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/APBusinessUK faces ‘very difficult trade-offs’ in budget because of Iran war, say analystsLeading thinktank says higher oil prices and inflation will give Andy Burnham a ‘challenging inheritance’Phillip InmanTue 28 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has been warned by a leading thinktank of “very difficult trade-offs in the next autumn budget” if the Iran war keeps oil prices and inflation high.The National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) said the new prime minister faced a “challenging inheritance” and his plans to revamp public services would meet severe pressure from persistently higher prices.With oil prices having briefly gone back above $100 a barrel, and the strait of Hormuz all but closed since March, the thinktank said it expected inflation to rise to 3.8% over the next seven months, forcing the chancellor,John Healey, to find an extra £24bn by the end of the decade to maintain services and real-terms welfare payments.How the Bab al-Mandab blockade threat helped push oil back above $100Read moreThe thinktank said it had cut its forecast for the chancellor’s spending headroom in the budget from just over £7bn to nearer £3bn. TheOffice for Budget Responsibility, the government’s independent forecaster, estimated in March that the Treasury had about £22bn of spare capacity above existing spending commitments.Underscoring the cost of the Middle East conflict to the UK, the NIESR said the economy would grow at a slower pace this year and in 2027 as a result of higher energy prices and the spillover effects from uncertainty created by the on-off war.It said a downgrade of growth to 1.1% this year and the same slow pace next year meant the UK would suffer £28bn in lost growth over two years compared with forecasts in January.David Aikman, the institute’s director, said Burnham faced “a challenging inheritance” with spending “eroded by inflation”, coupled with the highest borrowing costs in the G7, new spending demands and cost-of-living pressures.He said there would be a temptation to ease the strain on the public finances and pay for new initiatives by raising the level of borrowing.Aikman said this would be a mistake and only cause further strife in later years, especially when another health or economic shock happened.He added: “New commitments on defence or household support should be funded through taxation or savings elsewhere, not through further borrowing. Rebuilding the capacity to absorb future shocks will require a determined attempt to bring debt down.”Burnham has made several announcements since becoming PM last week, including a pledge toimprove adult social care, with an estimated £18.5bn bill for providing an NHS-style system free at the point of use by 2035.He has also singled out for support the 1 million young people classified as not in education, employment or training (Neets), with more extensive mental health services and a revamp of the education system.The NIESR said the government’s total debt, which has reached almost £3tn, or 95% of annual national income, was likely to rise again if the chancellor used borrowing to boost public spending.The institute has proved to be one of the gloomier forecasters, predicting significant economic shocks that proved more muted.Rising oil prices could force up UK interest rates, say economistsRead moreStephen Millard, the head of the thinktank’s macroeconomic forecasting, said the UK economy had proved to be “surprisingly resilient” in the first half of this year “but a slowdown is still to come”.He added: “Even if peace is restored relatively quickly in the Middle East, inflation will still rise and the new chancellor will need to make some difficult decisions with respect to how to fund the latest policy announcements, from cuts to VAT on electricity and business rates for pubs, to the £2 bus fare cap.”Millard said tax changes should be given priority over increases in existing taxes.He said he supported the introduction of a land value tax to replace council tax and stamp duty on home sales. He said the government should also phase out the many exemptions and discounts that affect VAT, including those on energy and children’s clothes.There was further scope to tackle tax avoidance by wealthy individuals and companies, he added.Millard said the latest quarterly economic outlook showed the chancellor would need to cope with a 4% real spending squeeze by the end of the decade – equating to about £24bn in 2023 prices.He said higher and more persistent inflation would create “very difficult trade-offs in the next autumn budget”.The NIESR expects inflation to average 3.1% in 2026, peaking at 3.8% in February 2027 after energy price cap adjustments.It said it would take until early 2029 to fall back to the Bank of England’s 2% target, rather than 2028 as previously forecast.Bank of England officials meet on Thursday. Financial markets expect them to hold interest rates steady before raising them to 4% later in the year.Explore more on these topicsBusinessInflationOilEconomicsIranUS-Israel war on IranAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to seek cross-party consensus over urgent reforms to social care | Social care | The Guardian
description: Prime minister invites Badenoch and Davey – but not Farage – to discuss how to fix one of most intractable issues he faces
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Prime minister invites Badenoch and Davey – but not Farage – to discuss how to fix one of most intractable issues he faces
Content: Andy Burnham is expected to speed up publication of Louise Casey’s review of social care.Photograph: Jeff Overs/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham is expected to speed up publication of Louise Casey’s review of social care.Photograph: Jeff Overs/ReutersSocial careBurnham to seek cross-party consensus over urgent reforms to social carePrime minister invites Badenoch and Davey – but not Farage – to discuss how to fix decades-old funding crisisPippa CrerarandAletha AduTue 28 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has promised “problem-solving, not point-scoring” before a speech on social care in which he will set out his strategy for resolving one of the most intractable problems in British politics.The prime minister has invited Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, and Ed Davey, the Liberal Democrat leader, to discuss how to enact urgent reform on social care, as he attempts to find common ground across party lines. Davey confirmed he would attend via video call while the Conservatives said they would send the shadow health secretary, Stuart Andrew, in Badenoch’s place as she was having pre-planned minor surgery.However, the suggestion that the main Westminster parties could finally reach consensus to fix the crisis that has eluded a generation of political leaders in England already appeared optimistic after the Tories imposed their own red lines and amid negative headlines about inheritance tax.SeveralLabourMPs also expressed concern over how to manage the financial burden of a reformed care sector.Andy Burnham seeks cross-party agreement on future of social careRead moreBefore his speech on Wednesday, Burnham said: “We need a different kind of politics: problem-solving, not point-scoring. Nowhere is that more urgent than social care. For decades, governments have kicked this issue down the road because they’ve seen it as too risky, too difficult and too complicated.“Politicians might have different views but I’m serious about fixing this issue, and to do that we have to find common ground and listen to others to find a way forward. It’s time to draw a line under people playing politics when the human cost of that means carers struggling, families paying the price and our NHS buckling under the strain.”The prime minister is expected to stop short of presenting proposals for a new social care system in this speech, instead confirming plans,previously revealed by the Guardian, to speed up the independent review led by Louise Casey that has been considering possible options.Lady Casey, who will launch the Big Conversation on Care on Wednesday to give the public their chance to share their views on the future of adult social care in England via an online platform, has warned that money alone won’t fix the problem.However, Burnham’s push for a solution is set against a tightening economic backdrop. The economic thinktank NIESR has warned of “very difficult trade-offs” in the autumn budget if the Iran war keeps oil prices and inflation high.He is understood to be committed to exploring a new system that would be free at the point of use, the same principle as the NHS. He is understood to regard other options, such as a care costs cap, as less attractive, though they would be significantly cheaper for the taxpayer.A middle-ground option would be a model similar to Scotland’s, where personal care costs are paid by the state but other costs, such as accommodation and food in care homes, are borne by individuals and their families.My generation shouldn’t be scared of a care tax – we’re paying one already | Gaby HinsliffRead moreWhicheveroption the government pursuesis likely to involve significant extra investment over the long term, most likely through increases in taxation.When Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care as health secretary under Gordon Brown, he suggested replacing inheritance tax with a 10% levy on all estates. At the weekend he did not to rule out this option, which could raise as much as £18bn.Before visiting a care home on Wednesday, Burnham said:“This comes down to a choice. We can carry on passing the problem to the next generation, or we can face it head on and work together to build a care system that gives people dignity, security and the support they deserve.“This is about bringing back hope that we can finally fix the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long, and making Britain believe again. That’s why I’m making this choice and I’m prepared to put everything I’ve got behind it.”An average of 13,600 people a day were stuck in hospital beds last month despite being medically fit to leave, including some delayed because of the availability of adult social care, underlining the pressure on the NHS.While Labour MPs have broadly welcomed the prospect of reform, several cautioned that there would have to be serious consideration of how to protect people from losing their homes to care costs or penalising those who had already saved for retirement and care with new taxes.One minister said the prime minister “must exercise a lot of care” in managing the sensitive trade-offs between the quality of care versus the cost and who pays for it.“There are no easy answers, and I don’t think we can just dive straight into saying ‘This is the solution and this is what’s going to happen,’ because we have a prime minister and in many ways a government … with no specific mandate on a specific measure.”A centrist Labour MP said: “It’s vital that the UK at least tries to do something because we will never be able to contain the rising costs of the NHS. Our ability to genuinely improve the quality of health care will be stymied if we don’t have a quality social care service that relieves pressure.”The Guardian view on social care reform: Andy Burnham is right – this issue must be gripped | EditorialRead moreOthers on the party’s left urged the government to consider adopting a full NHS-style system that would rely on some taxation, but would also highlight that Burnham’s premiership is ready to not just “talk the talk but also walk the walk”.“If we’re talking big and bold we shouldn’t shy away from this option. It took from 1945 to 1948 to get the NHS up and running. We’ve still got years to start the process but we have to really try to shake this broken system,” one said.“Andy doesn’t have the goodwill from the electorate that Keir did in 2024 because we messed it up over the last two years so people feel betrayed and ignored,” another added. “This is a moment where we now have to prove ourselves.”A Tory source said: “If Burnham was serious about working cross-party he would have given us more than 18 hours’ notice for a 30-minute meeting during recess and the invitation wouldn’t have been immediately press released. It’s almost like it’s only being done for show.”Davey posted on X: “I’m with my family in France and as people know I have a disabled son who needs 24/7 care so I can’t be back in Westminster tomorrow but I look forward to meeting Andy Burnham over Zoom. I’m hopeful this call may prove to be the first step towards fixing our broken care service.Nigel Farage, who has not been invited to attend as he is not currently a sitting MP and Reform has just seven seats, accused Burnham of “conspiring behind closed doors with the failed political establishment”.Tell us: what has your experience of adult social care in England been like?Read moreThe Reform leader and candidate for Clacton added: “If Andy Burnham is serious about putting politics aside to solve Britain’s biggest problems, it’s remarkable that he’s chosen to ignore the party that led over 300 national opinion polls and represents thousands of councillors and millions of Britons across the country.”Explore more on these topicsSocial careAndy BurnhamLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: South Korean stock market at three-month low as AI sell-off intensifies | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: Samsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competition
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Samsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competition
Content: Analysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending.Photograph: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAnalysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending.Photograph: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/ShutterstockStock marketsSouth Korean stock market at three-month low as AI sell-off intensifiesSamsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competitionBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaandGraeme WeardenTue 28 Jul 2026 13.43 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sell-off in AI stocks has intensified, driving South Korea’s stock market down to its lowest level in three months.Investors continued to ditch chip stocks on Tuesday, amid rising concerns about the huge amount of borrowing among AI companies to fund their datacentre expansion plans.The South Korean semiconductor companies SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell by more than 10%, dragging the country’s Kospi share index down by 11.5% to its lowest point since mid-April.US chip stocks extended their recent losses when Wall Street opened on Tuesday, with Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital Corp and Seagate Technology all down by more than 4%.The Nasdaq 100 index of leading tech stocks fell by as much as 1.8% at one point, briefly taken into market correction territory with stocks more than 10% below their early June record high. They later rebounded to settle roughly flat on the day.Apple becomes second ever $5tn company as investors flee AI stocksRead moreApple bucked the trend, rising to briefly become the second ever company to pass the $5tn (£3.76tn) valuation mark as investors losing confidence in AI stocks sought a safe haven.Analysts attributed the tech sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending, and competition from cheaper Chinese companies, aftera report by The Informationthat China had begun mass production of homegrown deep ultraviolet (DUV) chip-making tools.“We believe the market was likely spooked by the progress of China’s chip-making equipment capabilities, and was worried that this progress would threaten the competitive position of global chip making and chip equipment leaders,” said Jing Jie Yu, an equity analyst at Morningstar, adding that the sell-off was “largely a kneejerk reaction and overdone”.On Monday, shares in the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT rose by 466% when it floated on the Shanghai stock exchange, underlining China’s drive to create its own AI supply chain.Investors may also be growing jittery aboutthe “circular funding”at the heart of the AI industry, through which artificial intelligence firms finance one another.On Monday, the Wall Street Journal reported thatNvidiawas in discussions with OpenAI about providing $250bn (£188bn) for a massive datacentre project in Ohio. Backing from Nvidia, which has an investment grade credit rating, could make it less expensive to raise funding for the project.News of the talks knocked Nvidia’s shares on Monday; they closed 5% lower, while the cost of insuring the chip company’s debt against default using a credit default swap (CDS) rose.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The market reaction to the Nvidia news was swift. Nvidia fell 5% and closed the session below the $200-per-share mark. More importantly, Nvidia’s five-year CDS spiked, suggesting that it may not yet be the right time to buy the dip,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote.Some analysts have suggested that Beijing, trying to win a tech war with the US, is providing US companies with cheap AI systems, undercutting attempts by Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft and Google to dominate the spread of AI tools.Danni Hewson, the head of financial analysis at the stockbroker AJ Bell, said investors were braced for more AI companies to warn about their outlook, further undermining confidence in the sector.“Nerves about the huge amount of cash being splashed have been building for months. Investors will be keen to hear how those massive sums of cash have been utilised by mega caps like Microsoft and Meta and, crucially, what returns are being made on those investments,” she said.“Chip stocks have once again led declines as the market flexes, some companies like Amazon are upping their own chip capabilities, and China’s CXMT stock market debut has cemented fears about a lost market for US companies constrained by trading restrictions.”London and European exchanges bucked the trend on Tuesday. The FTSE 100 index of leading UK companies rose 89 points to 10,871 while the Paris CAC 40 edged 52 points higher to 8,458.Explore more on these topicsStock marketsAI (artificial intelligence)NvidiaSouth KoreanewsShareReuse this content

title: GSK heads to Cambridge with long-awaited positive vibes  | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Pharmaceutical company’s move to new £400m research centre accompanied by encouraging news for shareholders
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Pharmaceutical company’s move to new £400m research centre accompanied by encouraging news for shareholders
Content: GSK is to move more than 1,000 of its scientists to its new Cambridge research and development centre.Illustration: GSKView image in fullscreenGSK is to move more than 1,000 of its scientists to its new Cambridge research and development centre.Illustration: GSKNils Pratley on financePharmaceuticals industryGSK heads to Cambridge with long-awaited positive vibesNils PratleyPharmaceutical company’s move to new £400m research centre accompanied by encouraging news for shareholdersTue 28 Jul 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.43 EDTShare“A vote of confidence in British business,” trumpeted Andy Burnham, seizing the political gift of GSK splashing out £400m on a shinynew research and development centre in Cambridge.For positive vibes, it definitely beats the early pharma news his predecessor as prime minister received. That was the painful tale of how AstraZeneca, frustrated by indecision in the Treasury,cancelled its intended £450m expansionof a vaccine plant in Speke in Liverpool.In reality, GSK’s investment in Britain is a specific one inCambridge. The group’s historic Stevenage facility will close and most of the scientists (or as many as want to go) will move to the Fens.One shouldn’t be surprised. Around the world, life sciences companies increasingly gather in clusters. Cambridge – thanks to its university, Addenbrooke’shospital, various science institutes and a healthy biotech and biopharma start-up scene – is a genuine world-class rival to Boston and Basel. The Cambridge biomedical campus is the natural place forGSKto be in the UK in the interests of “acceleration” of research and development. Only a cynic would suggest literal proximity to AstraZeneca’s facilities could come in handy for a future merger.The switch of UK research location is the most eye-catching big decision by Luke Miels, the chief executive since the start of the year, but Tuesday’s first-half numbers contained three sources of encouragement for shareholders.First, GSK thinks it can put at least 20 potential medicines into late-stage trials this year, an increase from 10 at the last count. Part of the boost flows fromthe near-£8bn acquisitionof the US-based cancer specialist Nuvalent last month. But the rest probably owes something to Miels’s focus on which drug programmes should be backed harder and which cut. If the 20-plus target indicates more ruthlessness in prioritisation, investors will applaud. It is easy to talk, as Miels has done, about displaying “scientific courage”, but you still need candidates to come through the drug pipeline to make it happen.Second, Miels surprised the market with a plan to cut £1.9bn of annual costs by 2029.
