Even for a company the size of GSK, that’s a big number to find from the general wash of procurement, frontline sales forces, AI efficiencies and a leaner manufacturing presence amid the shift from general medicines to specialist drugs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLuke Miels, the GSK chief executive since the start of the year, surprised the market with plan to cut £1.9bn annual costs by 2029.Photograph: GSK/ReutersThird, the dark cloud hanging over GSK – the expiry during 2028-30 of patents on the HIV medicine dolutegravir, which accounts for about a fifth of group sales – looks less threatening if the group’s latest forecasting proves correct.A critical line in the results was the prediction that operating profits margins will be “stable to improving” even during the patent crunch. Thanks to the intended cost savings, that is a notably clearer statement than the group has offered before now. Meanwhile, the grand target of hitting £40bn-plus of revenue in 2031 is “on track” with “accelerating growth” thereafter.Longstanding GSK shareholders know from experience never to underestimate the scope for disappointment. The past 20 years have witnessed many false dawns; improvements under Miels’s predecessor, Emma Walmsley, ran into bad luck in the form of US litigationover a heartburn drug from the 1990s.But the tone has definitely improved. It’s still too soon to speak about GSK replicating AstraZeneca’s remarkable 15-year blueprint for growth under Pascal Soriot (which also started with expansion in Cambridge). But the big-picture pieces are falling into place. The 2031 revenue target gets more credible with every telling; the pipeline is fuller; the patent cliff is less daunting; the share price is perkier. Put the merger talk on hold.Explore more on these topicsPharmaceuticals industryNils Pratley on financeGSKCambridgeCambridgeshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: White House teleprompter operator accused over Trump bets no longer in job, official says | US politics | The Guardian
description: Official declines to say whether Gabriel Perez, who allegedly bet on prediction market Kalshi, resigned or was fired
Author: Roque Planas
Headline: Official declines to say whether Gabriel Perez, who allegedly bet on prediction market Kalshi, resigned or was fired
Content: Gabriel Perez checks the teleprompter on election night in Palm Beach, Florida, in November 2024.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenGabriel Perez checks the teleprompter on election night in Palm Beach, Florida, in November 2024.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersUS politicsWhite House teleprompter operator accused over Trump bets no longer in job, official saysOfficial declines to say whether Gabriel Perez, who allegedly bet on prediction market Kalshi, resigned or was firedRoque Planasand agenciesTue 28 Jul 2026 19.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 21.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA White House teleprompter operator who reportedly used inside knowledge to make bets about Donald Trump’s speeches on the online prediction market Kalshi is no longer in his post, according to a White House official.The official, who was not authorized to comment publicly about the personnel matter and spoke on condition of anonymity, said on Tuesday that Gabriel Perez “no longer works in the federal government”.The official would not say whether Perez resigned or was fired.The White House confirmed earlier this month that Perez had been placed on unpaid leave afterABC News reportedhe had used his inside knowledge to win more than $100,000 betting on what the president would say in big speeches, including his State of the Union address earlier this year.That figure is more than half the $175,000 salary he earned for his teleprompter work, according toWhite House personnel records.White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt had described the reports of the insider trading as “deeply unfortunate and, frankly, a disgrace”.Robert Denault, Kalshi’s lawyer and head of enforcement, said on X following the ABC News report that the “Kalshi surveillance team promptly flagged, investigated and referred these trades” to the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the body that has regulatory authority over such matters.His statement did not name Perez, who has operated Trump’steleprompter since 2016.The ABC report described suspicious activity on Kalshi’s “Mentions” market, in which users can place bets on phrases and specific words that might be used in public speeches. Kalshi recently began requiring users to disclose their place of employment, and the platform’s policy prohibits betting based on information that users gain because of their job.Prediction markets, which allow users to place speculative bets on a seemingly endless list of public events and trends, have exploded recently. Trading volume on Kalshi, one of the two largest prediction market trading platforms, soared from $100m last year to $3bn today, according to anestimate cited by CNBC.Kalshi recently said it would allow users tobet on drug trial results.The rise in prediction markets has created a major new incentive for insider trading. In April, federal prosecutorsindicted Gannon Ken Van Dykefor allegedly betting on the whether former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro would be deposed. Prosecutors say Van Dyke, a US soldier who worked on the operation to remove and extradite Maduro, walked away with $400,000 in earnings.That same month, Kalshi said it hadfined three political candidateswho placed bets on their own races. In one case, Mark Moran placed a small bet on whether he would run for office before announcing his bid for a US Senate seat in Virginia as an independent.The industry’s proponents describe prediction markets as a form of derivatives, a type of contract that allows parties to make bets on the future value of an asset or commodity.Critics, however, have raised concerns from state authorities who view the industry as little more than unregulated gambling. Minnesota became the first state to ban prediction markets entirely in May, but afederal judge temporarily blockedthe law before it went into effect.Trump hasdefended the prediction markets industry, saying that states should avoid regulating them, leaving the job instead to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsTrump administrationDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Senate confirms Trump ally Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: At confirmation hearing, Clayton sidestepped questions about 2020 election and declined to say Trump lost
Author: Sam Levine
Headline: At confirmation hearing, Clayton sidestepped questions about 2020 election and declined to say Trump lost
Content: Jay Clayton at his confirmation hearing.Photograph: Nathan Posner/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJay Clayton at his confirmation hearing.Photograph: Nathan Posner/ShutterstockTrump administrationSenate confirms Trump ally Jay Clayton as director of national intelligenceAt confirmation hearing, Clayton sidestepped questions about 2020 election and declined to say Trump lostSign up for the Breaking News US newsletter emailSam LevineTue 28 Jul 2026 19.34 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Senate voted to confirm Jay Clayton as the director of national intelligence on Tuesday, giving Trump another key ally directing the nation’s intelligence apparatus.The tally, 51-47, fell along party lines, with all Republicans supporting his nomination and all Democrats opposing it.Clayton, currently the US attorney for the southern district of New York, will replaceBill Pulte, a staunch Trump loyalist who had been temporarily serving in the role since June. Trump’s first director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard,resigned earlier this year. Clayton served as the chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) during Trump’s first term.During hisconfirmation hearingon 15 July, Clayton sidestepped several questions about the 2020 election and declined to say that Trump lost it.During aninterview on CNBCin June, Clayton also suggested there was something amiss about the long period California takes to count ballots. “We had a problem, a deep problem with voting in America,” he said on the network. “On the integrity side, we’re doing an absolutely terrible job, and the American people are right to question it.” Clayton also would not say during his confirmation hearing whether voter fraud was a problem in American elections, even though several studies have shown it isexceedingly rare.His office also issued widely criticized subpoenas to New York Times journalists over their reporting on security concerns around Trump’s Air Force One airplane that was a gift from Qatar. The governmentabruptly withdrewthose subpoenas during a court hearing in which a federal judge pressed an attorney from Clayton’s office about errors and irregularities in the subpoenas.While Democrats saw Clayton as a more preferable pick than Pulte, who has assisted in executing some of Trump’s sloppy and ugly acts of political retribution,including the criminal prosecution of Letitia Jamesand a ham-handed effort to remove Lisa Cook from the Federal Reserve board of governors, Pulte was also leading the office of the director of national intelligence earlier this month when Trump declassified andreleased intelligencein support of false claims about the 2020 election. Pulte oversaw several rounds of layoffs at the agency.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut Clayton’s contentious hearing earlier this month cost him bipartisan backing. Before the vote, the senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, spoke in opposition to the nomination, warning that Clayton was unqualified and would act as the president’s “election conspiracy win”.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ex-FCC officials warn agency sending ‘chilling message’ with ABC license review | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Ex-officials ask FCC to reject petitions to deny renewal of broadcast licenses for eight stations owned by ABC
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Ex-officials ask FCC to reject petitions to deny renewal of broadcast licenses for eight stations owned by ABC
Content: The FCC chairman, Brendan Carr.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe FCC chairman, Brendan Carr.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersTrump administrationEx-FCC officials warn agency sending ‘chilling message’ with ABC license reviewEx-officials ask FCC to reject petitions to deny renewal of broadcast licenses for eight stations owned by ABCJeremy BarrTue 28 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA group of prominent former Federal Communications Commission (FCC) officials, including key staffers and commissioners appointed by both Democratic and Republican presidents, issued a filing on Tuesday that warns the agency is trying to send a “chilling message” to broadcasters after it received petitions to deny ABC license renewals for eight of its local television stations.The network’s licenses are up for early renewal afteran extremely unusual orderfrom the Brendan Carr-led FCC in late April, following criticism of ABC by Donald Trump and Melania Trump.The group behind the filing includes Mark S Fowler, who served as FCC chair during Ronald Reagan’s presidency; Alfred C Sikes, who served as FCC chair during George HW Bush’s presidency; Thomas E Wheeler, who served as FCC chair during Barack Obama’s presidency; and several high-ranking lawyers and advisers to past commissioners.“This early license renewal proceeding is unprecedented in the history of the Federal Communications Commission and a grave violation of both the Communications Act and the Constitution,” the coalition wrote in the filing. “Through this proceeding, the FCC seeks to censor Disney’s and ABC’s speech and send a chilling message to all broadcasters: carry speech we don’t like at your peril.”Seeking to put the ABC license challenge into context, the group called the order “the latest attack in a sustained campaign by Chairman Carr and theTrump administrationof threatening legal sanctions against licensees whose speech President Trump dislikes”.The filing is a response topetitions to deny ABC’s license renewalssubmitted by conservative media watchdog the Media Research Center (MRC) and the Center for American Rights (CAR), a conservative legal organization that is closely aligned with Carr and has initiated several complaints against television networks premised on accusations of liberal bias. CAR’s petition to deny ABC’s license renewal accused the network of “[ignoring] long-standing Commission precedents and principles protecting the integrity of the news” and “[engaging] in explicit racial and gender discrimination”.The coalition said in its Tuesday filing that the petitions should be denied because they ask the FCC to wade into “content and viewpoint regulation” and accusations of bias by punishing a network for their editorial decision-making – “a stunning – and plainly unconstitutional – expansion of the Commission’s role”.“As former Chairs, Commissioners, Chiefs of Staff, General Counsels and Bureau Chiefs, we call on the Commission to respect the constitutional and congressional prohibitions on its ‘power of censorship’ and terminate this proceeding,” the group wrote.Interested parties have until 5 August to reply to petitions to deny ABC’s licenses. After that time, the FCC could either grant the extension requests, a prospect that seems unlikely, or schedule hearings on the matter. The process has no clear timetable, leaving ABC and its eight local television stations mired in a cloud of uncertainty about their ability to continue broadcasting long-term.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationTV newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple becomes second $5tn company as investors flee AI stocks | Apple | The Guardian
description: Share price rally driven by strong product demand as well as decision to sit out AI spending race, amid wider tech sell-off
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Share price rally driven by strong product demand as well as decision to sit out AI spending race, amid wider tech sell-off
Content: Apple’s shares hit a session high ⁠of $342.89 on Tuesday.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APView image in fullscreenApple’s shares hit a session high ⁠of $342.89 on Tuesday.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APAppleApple becomes second $5tn company as investors flee AI stocksShare price rally driven by strong product demand as well as decision to sit out AI spending race, amid wider tech sell-offGraeme Weardenand agencyTue 28 Jul 2026 16.33 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple has become only the second company to pass the $5tn valuation mark, as it benefited from investors fleeing AI and semiconductor stocks amid a wider tech sell-off.The iPhone maker’s shares hit a session high ⁠of $342.89 on Tuesday, giving it a market ⁠capitalisation of $5.04tn (£3.78tn), then eased back down to $340.08 – around the $5tn mark.Applebecame the world’s most valuable companyearlier this month, overtaking the chip giant Nvidia, which had been ⁠at the top since June 2025 and becamethe first company to breach the $5tn thresholdlast October.The US consumer electronics company’s rally has been driven ⁠as much by strong demand for its products as its decision to sit out the ​AI spending race that is sapping cash ‌flows at big tech ‌rivals.Its fresh high valuation came amid an intensifyingsell-off of AI stocks around the worlddriven by rising concerns about AI companies’ borrowing to fund datacentre expansion.US chip stocks extended their recent losses when Wall Street opened on Tuesday, with Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital and Seagate Technology all down by more than 4%.The Nasdaq 100 index of leading tech stocks fell by as much as 1.8% at one point, meaning since its early June record high it had fallen more than 10% – the technical definition of a market correction.Meanwhile South Korea’s stock market slid to its lowest level since mid-April, with semiconductor companies SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics falling by more than 10%.Analysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending, and competition from cheaper Chinese companies, aftera report by the Informationthat China had begun mass production of homegrown deep ultraviolet (DUV) chip-making tools.View image in fullscreenApple’s decision to hold iPhone prices steady, despite increases last month for MacBooks and iPads, has bolstered demand.Photograph: Lucas Jackson/ReutersInvestors may also be growing jittery aboutthe “circular funding” at the heart of the AI industry, through which artificial intelligence companies finance one another.They have also been spooked by the announcement from Google last week that it was further increasing capital spending this year to as much as $205bn to fund its AI plans, while reporting negative free cashflow for ​the first time in its history, burning through $5.9bn in the three months to the end of June.Apple has been shielded somewhat by being something of an AI laggard. Its difficulties in developing in-house models meant it has instead relied on Google’s ‌technology to power new services such as a revamped Siri. That has spared it the hefty infrastructure costs that have left big tech investors wary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionApple’s decision to hold iPhone prices steady last month when it announcedincreases for MacBooks and iPadshas also bolstered demand as buyers scooped up the company’s flagship device before expected ‌price hikes later this year, analysts have said.To aid demand, Apple on Tuesday also launched a device leasing programme in the US through the payments ​firm Klarna, under which monthly payments start at $17.99 for an iPhone, $11.99 for an Apple Watch or iPad, and $24.99 for a Mac.“Apple has resisted the AI spending race, betting that customer experience – not infrastructure investment – will ultimately determine the winners,” said Dipanjan Chatterjee, a vice-president and principal analyst at Forrester. “The ⁠new leasing programme is a clever response: it doesn’t reduce the price ​of an iPhone, but ​it changes how consumers perceive the cost ​by replacing sticker shock with a predictable monthly payment.”Including session gains, Apple ​stock has jumped ‌24% so far this year, ​widely outperforming the ​other six of the “Magnificent Seven” cohort of US technology stocks.Apple is to report its third-quarter earnings after the market close on Thursday, with analysts expecting a more than 15% jump in revenue for the period compared with a year earlier.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsAppleStock marketsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: South Korean stock market at three-month low as AI sell-off intensifies | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: Samsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competition
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Samsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competition
Content: Analysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending.Photograph: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAnalysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending.Photograph: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/ShutterstockStock marketsSouth Korean stock market at three-month low as AI sell-off intensifiesSamsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competitionBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaandGraeme WeardenTue 28 Jul 2026 13.43 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sell-off in AI stocks has intensified, driving South Korea’s stock market down to its lowest level in three months.Investors continued to ditch chip stocks on Tuesday, amid rising concerns about the huge amount of borrowing among AI companies to fund their datacentre expansion plans.The South Korean semiconductor companies SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell by more than 10%, dragging the country’s Kospi share index down by 11.5% to its lowest point since mid-April.US chip stocks extended their recent losses when Wall Street opened on Tuesday, with Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital Corp and Seagate Technology all down by more than 4%.The Nasdaq 100 index of leading tech stocks fell by as much as 1.8% at one point, briefly taken into market correction territory with stocks more than 10% below their early June record high. They later rebounded to settle roughly flat on the day.Apple becomes second ever $5tn company as investors flee AI stocksRead moreApple bucked the trend, rising to briefly become the second ever company to pass the $5tn (£3.76tn) valuation mark as investors losing confidence in AI stocks sought a safe haven.Analysts attributed the tech sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending, and competition from cheaper Chinese companies, aftera report by The Informationthat China had begun mass production of homegrown deep ultraviolet (DUV) chip-making tools.“We believe the market was likely spooked by the progress of China’s chip-making equipment capabilities, and was worried that this progress would threaten the competitive position of global chip making and chip equipment leaders,” said Jing Jie Yu, an equity analyst at Morningstar, adding that the sell-off was “largely a kneejerk reaction and overdone”.On Monday, shares in the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT rose by 466% when it floated on the Shanghai stock exchange, underlining China’s drive to create its own AI supply chain.Investors may also be growing jittery aboutthe “circular funding”at the heart of the AI industry, through which artificial intelligence firms finance one another.On Monday, the Wall Street Journal reported thatNvidiawas in discussions with OpenAI about providing $250bn (£188bn) for a massive datacentre project in Ohio. Backing from Nvidia, which has an investment grade credit rating, could make it less expensive to raise funding for the project.News of the talks knocked Nvidia’s shares on Monday; they closed 5% lower, while the cost of insuring the chip company’s debt against default using a credit default swap (CDS) rose.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The market reaction to the Nvidia news was swift. Nvidia fell 5% and closed the session below the $200-per-share mark. More importantly, Nvidia’s five-year CDS spiked, suggesting that it may not yet be the right time to buy the dip,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote.Some analysts have suggested that Beijing, trying to win a tech war with the US, is providing US companies with cheap AI systems, undercutting attempts by Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft and Google to dominate the spread of AI tools.Danni Hewson, the head of financial analysis at the stockbroker AJ Bell, said investors were braced for more AI companies to warn about their outlook, further undermining confidence in the sector.“Nerves about the huge amount of cash being splashed have been building for months. Investors will be keen to hear how those massive sums of cash have been utilised by mega caps like Microsoft and Meta and, crucially, what returns are being made on those investments,” she said.“Chip stocks have once again led declines as the market flexes, some companies like Amazon are upping their own chip capabilities, and China’s CXMT stock market debut has cemented fears about a lost market for US companies constrained by trading restrictions.”London and European exchanges bucked the trend on Tuesday. The FTSE 100 index of leading UK companies rose 89 points to 10,871 while the Paris CAC 40 edged 52 points higher to 8,458.Explore more on these topicsStock marketsAI (artificial intelligence)NvidiaSouth KoreanewsShareReuse this content

title: Johnson & Johnson to pay $5.5bn settlement in talc cancer lawsuit | Johnson & Johnson | The Guardian
description: Landmark deal covers about 76,000 claims and could end contentious, decade-long legal battle
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Landmark deal covers about 76,000 claims and could end contentious, decade-long legal battle
Content: Plaintiffs’ law firms said the deal was a good resolution after a ⁠long court battle. The agreement must be accepted by 95% of the ovarian cancer claimants before it becomes final.Photograph: Lucas Jackson/ReutersView image in fullscreenPlaintiffs’ law firms said the deal was a good resolution after a ⁠long court battle. The agreement must be accepted by 95% of the ovarian cancer claimants before it becomes final.Photograph: Lucas Jackson/ReutersJohnson & JohnsonJohnson & Johnson to pay $5.5bn settlement in talc cancer lawsuitLandmark deal covers about 76,000 claims and could end contentious, decade-long legal battleReutersTue 28 Jul 2026 01.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohnson & Johnson said it would pay an estimated $5.5bn to resolve tens of thousands of lawsuits alleging its baby ⁠powder and other talc productscaused ⁠ovarian cancer, in a landmark ​deal that could end a contentious, decade-long legal battle.Johnson & Johnson on Monday said the settlement covers about 76,000 claims, including ones consolidated in a federal court in New Jersey, and related cases in state court, ⁠representing nearly all of the remaining talc claims against the company.The US multinational hadpreviously settled most of the casesalleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma.‘When I was a child, everyone used it’: woman blames Johnson & Johnson talc for her cancerRead morePlaintiffs’ law firms confirmed the deal on Monday, saying it was a good resolution after a ⁠10-year court battle. The deal must be accepted by 95% of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.Johnson & Johnson’s vice-president ​of litigation, Erik Haas, said the claims were “meritless” and that the company ‌was willing to settle in order to get ‌closure.“While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, ‌this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save lives,” Haas said.Johnson & Johnson expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028. But the deal could be worth more, depending on how many people participate in the settlement.Chris Seeger, a lawyer who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, saidJohnson & Johnsoncould ultimately pay $7bn or more.The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap Johnson & Johnson’s total payout, Seeger said. “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”Johnson & Johnson reached the settlement after a series of wins in court, including victories in individual trials, successful efforts to disqualify ​plaintiffs’ lawyers from the litigation, and court rulings against experts that plaintiffs had used to prove their cases in court.The company, headquartered in New Jersey, won a significant court victory in the long-running legal battle last week, when a federal judge cast doubt on individual plaintiffs’ ability to prove that talc specifically caused their ovarian cancer.Johnson & Johnson has long denied that its talc products caused cancer, saying that talc was safe and did not contain asbestos.The company stopped selling talc-based baby powder in the US in 2020, switching to ⁠a cornstarch product. But litigation resumed in March 2025, after being put on hold for more than three years while Johnson & Johnson unsuccessfully pursued a strategy known as the “Texas two step”, ​filing three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ​effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal.The multi-million pound baby powder caseRead moreBefore the bankruptcy attempts, Johnson & Johnson had a mixed record in talc trials, ​with a multibillion dollar verdict in ‌favour of 22 women who said ​baby powder caused their ovarian ​cancer. The company won some trials outright and had other verdicts reduced on appeal.Unlike the proposed bankruptcy settlements, Monday’s agreement applies only to existing claims and does not address future lawsuits.The exclusion of future claims made more money available to current plaintiffs than the bankruptcy proposal did, and it also accelerates the payments so that all claims will be paid within 18 months instead of being spread out over more than a decade, Seeger said.Explore more on these topicsJohnson & JohnsonHealthcare industryHealthPharmaceuticals industryShareReuse this content

title: ICE-linked security firm reports UK revenue slump after asylum contract ends | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: MTC provided security at heavily criticised Manston centre in Kent – and could now make £500m managing arrivals at site
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: MTC provided security at heavily criticised Manston centre in Kent – and could now make £500m managing arrivals at site
Content: The Manston centre in Kent. MTC UK’s contract for providing security there ended in September 2025.Photograph: Stuart Brock/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Manston centre in Kent. MTC UK’s contract for providing security there ended in September 2025.Photograph: Stuart Brock/EPAImmigration and asylumICE-linked security firm reports UK revenue slump after asylum contract endsMTC provided security at heavily criticised Manston centre in Kent – and could now make £500m managing arrivals at siteJasper JollyandRob DaviesTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA private security companylinked to Donald Trump’s immigration crackdownreported a slump in UK revenues after an asylum centre contract ended but could make £500m managing the same facility until 2036.Management & Training Corporation (MTC) said sales fell from £28.4m to £17.6m in 2025 after its contract to provide “security and care” at theheavily criticised Manston sitein Kent ended in September.A public inquiry described Manston as “overcrowded, squalid and insanitary” between June and November 2022, when MTC took over provision of services for the Home Office. MTC said: “Decisions relating to the operation of the site sat outside of MTC’s contractual remit.”Company handling Australia’s immigration detention playing key role in Trump’s ICE migrant crackdownRead moreThe cessation of the contract last September pushed MTC UK to a £1.6m loss, Companies House filings show, compared with a profit of £1.3m in 2024.But MTC Definitive, a joint venture that MTC UK majority owns, won a contract in May for processing people who arrive on small boats “from disembarkation through to dispersal”.The Irregular Migration Management Services contract will run for six years, with the possibility of a further four-year extension. It covers two asylum processing centres, Manston and the Western Jet Foil site in Dover. MTC said: “We are committed to delivering a safe and secure environment at these centres, to enable UK Border Force officials to register and process individuals arriving into the UK by sea with dignity and respect.”Despite the loss, MTC UK’s highest-paid director received £211,000 in remuneration during 2025, an increase of 5%.View image in fullscreenThe contract will cover work across the Manston site and ‘associated disembarkation points’ for people arriving in boats along the Kent coast.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAEllie Reeves, the Labour MP appointed last week as attorney general, previouslycriticised high salaries for executivesat companies such as MTC.The company is owned by an American parent based in Utah, which runs prisons and job training centres in the US. Its facilities include five detention centres used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the department that has received a significant funding increase and been criticised for its brutality during Trump’s presidency.MTC said: “Our work in immigration detention spans multiple presidential administrations and predates the current administration. MTC’s responsibility is to provide safe and humane care to the men and women placed in its facilities by the federal government.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe new UK small boats contract is worth an initial £462m but could be worth as much as £539m if it is extended to last 10 years. The contract will cover the joint venture’s work across the Manston site and “associated disembarkation points” for people arriving in boats along theKentcoast.The award of the contract is being challenged in court by Mitie, another outsourcing company.According to the BBC, Mitie claimed in the high court that the Home Office failed to “prevent, identify and remedy conflicts of interest” because the MTC head of development, Dave Butler, was previously the deputy director of Manston.The Home Office said the claim was baseless and without merit, and there was no conflict of interest, the BBC reported.Before it received the Manston contract, MTC had beencriticised for dangerous conditionsat the Rainsbrook secure training centre, a youth jail in Warwickshire. Ofsted, the education regulator for England, said children were locked up for more than 23 hours a day with “no justifiable rationale” during the coronavirus pandemic, and later inspections found physical assaults, children carrying weapons and warnings from staff that someone was likely to die at the centre.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumManston asylum centreOutsourcingMitieDonald TrumpKentICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)newsShareReuse this content

title: Americans feel pinch of continued Iran war: ‘It’s screwed everything up’ | US news | The Guardian
description: Whether in favor of or against the US-Israel war on Iran, people across the country are left holding the bill and wondering on its purpose
Author: George Chidi
Headline: Whether in favor of or against the US-Israel war on Iran, people across the country are left holding the bill and wondering on its purpose
Content: Left: Demonstrators carry signs and chant slogans during a protest against US military action in Iran near the White House in Washington DC in April. Right: The bridge linking Bandar Abbas and Kehuristan, rendered unusable in a US strike, is seen in Iran's Hormozgan province.Composite: AFP, Anadolu, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLeft: Demonstrators carry signs and chant slogans during a protest against US military action in Iran near the White House in Washington DC in April. Right: The bridge linking Bandar Abbas and Kehuristan, rendered unusable in a US strike, is seen in Iran's Hormozgan province.Composite: AFP, Anadolu, Getty ImagesUS newsAmericans feel pinch of continued Iran war: ‘It’s screwed everything up’Whether in favor of or against the US-Israel war on Iran, people across the country are left holding the bill and wondering on its purposeGeorge Chidiin Marietta, Georgia,Shrai Popatin North York, Maine,Rachel Leingangin Superior, Wisconsin, andJoseph Gedeonin Washington. Graphics byAndrew WitherspoonTue 28 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive months after the United States and Israel started a historically unpopular war against Iran that was going to supposedly last weeks, the fighting has refused to resolve in victory, defeat or peace. Iran’s supreme leader had been killed in the opening strikes, ceasefires broke down, and the strait of Hormuz has been closed and reopened.For voters interviewed across the country, while the damage may be distant, the residual effects have shown up at the pump, on the grocery bill and in a phone call telling a spouse they have a day to report for deployment. And for a country still absorbing the aftermath of Israel’s war on Gaza – funded to the tune of billions of dollars by the United States – the war in Iran lands on top of an already raw argument about what American power is for.In North York,Maine, Lydia Stone, 31, works in the logging industry and is raising an 18-month-old daughter. She describes an industry being squeezed from both directions: fuel costs rising while the price customers pay for wood stays flat. “It’s been a huge jump in prices, and makes life a lot harder,” she said.Trump administration’s revision of Iran war casualties ‘huge disrespect’, say veteransRead moreThat squeeze shows up in the data, with the average price of gasoline pushing above $4 a gallon for the first time in years,according to AAA. Analysts have also noted the pain is not evenly shared: lower- and middle-income householdsspend a larger shareof their budgets on fuel, meaning the same price spike lands harder on them than on wealthier consumers.Stone’s frustration isn’t only economic. “A huge part of what has been so frustrating ... is like the fact my tax dollars are going to fund murdering people, at the same time that it’s cutting social services, it’s cutting Snap benefits for my neighbors,” she said, referring to nutrition benefits for low-income Americans.She said the line at her local food pantry had grown noticeably longer and her best friend’s husband, she said, was deployed on little notice.US economic indicators during the war in Iran chartedThat sense of a war without justification reverberated among voters who described themselves as independent or progressive. Terrence Dahmen, 73, a retired, independent-leaning voter from Cable,Wisconsin, who said he usually ends up voting Democrat, called American involvement “a huge mistake”. “We weren’t provoked into that fight, and we weren’t attacked,” he said. “I saw no reason to go there other than possibly controlling oil somehow.”He argued the country should be investing in solar, wind and geothermal power instead, and said he wished the US had taken a different path on climate policy years ago.Robert Edelstein, 62, who runs a window-tinting business in Douglas county, Wisconsin, was more blunt. “In the general election, I would automatically vote for anybody that was against the war,” he said. “I think it’s the stupidest thing that could ever possibly have happened.” Comparing the decision to strike Iran unfavorably with the Iraq war launched under George W Bush, he added: “It’s screwed everything up, as we all know ... it’s absolutely stupid.”In Georgia, Jimmy Carter – a retired teacher not related to the former president – watched Donald Trump’s motorcade arrive near his old school last week with similar disbelief. “It’s a dumbass idea,” he said. “I don’t know who fed him that idea.” He noted that even his own brother, a Trump voter, agreed.Voters with personal connections to the military comprised a wide range of views.Nick Marine, a retired sailor at a Trump rally in Marietta, offered full-throated endorsement of the Trump administration’s approach. “I think what President Trump is doing is good,” he said. “I think it took a long time for us to get to this point ... I’m glad it’s finally being resolved.”He argued for gradualism over overwhelming force – “you don’t want to behead your neighbor, because in a month or so, you’re going to be doing commerce with them” – while voicing concern for Iranian civilians cut off from water, sanitation and electricity by the fighting.Richard Bradley, a retired army major and combat engineer from Mabelton,Georgia, whose son and daughter currently serve, supports the broader rationale for confronting Iran but wants a clear exit. “I’d rather fight bad guys in their land instead of mine,” he said.View image in fullscreenRichard Bradley, a retired army major, supported the Iran war.Photograph: George Chidi/The GuardianStill, he said: “I kind of take a little bit of an issue with where we’re at now ... we need to be figuring out how to finish it up, so it doesn’t turn into another ... enduring war.” His own father fought in the Gulf war, he noted, and he didn’t “want my kids to fight unfinished business that my generation left.”Not all of the war’s critics oppose the war itself. Salman Majidi, an Iranian immigrant and software developer from Atlanta, stood among anti-Trump protesters holding a “Free Iran” sign – but for the opposite reason. A supporter of Iran’s exiled former crown prince, Reza Pahlavi, Majidi argued the American campaign was a rescue rather than a war of choice.“Tens of thousands of Iranian civilians have been murdered by the Islamic regime in just two days,” he said, arguing the toll predates and outweighs the American strikes. “We deserve a better life in Iran.”But given the proximity and relationship of the conflicts, the Iran war has not displaced the argument over Gaza so much as compounded it, blurring into a single grievance about where American money and moral authority are being spent.Clay Harvison, a mixed martial artist from Marietta who voted for the president, said the conflict should have ended months ago. “He should have left it when he had already bombed them,” Harvison said, blaming pressure from Israeli leaders for dragging the US deeper in. He said the war threatens the legacy Trump seems to prize most: “being remembered as being great ... he’s messing with that really bad right now.”Younger voters in particular, he said, were asking why a president who campaigned against foreign wars is now presiding over one, arguing that “the military-industrial complex is laundering our tax dollars instead of going into fixing our streets”.Whether a ceasefire holds, and whether Tehran and Washington ever sit down for something more than a pause, is still an open question.What is not in doubt, from Wisconsin lake towns to the Georgia suburbs, is that voters of nearly every political persuasion are doing the same math: adding up gas receipts, deployment orders and casualty counts, and asking what, precisely, the war is for.Explore more on these topicsUS newsUS-Israel war on IranTrump administrationDonald TrumpGeorgiaMaineWisconsinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Marmite and Dove owner Unilever warns of price rises due to growing costs | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: Consumer goods group reports strong sales growth, owing in part to World Cup marketing campaigns
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Consumer goods group reports strong sales growth, owing in part to World Cup marketing campaigns
Content: Consumers are said to have continued buying Unilever’s branded products, which include Marmite, Dove and Hellmann’s, rather than switching to cheaper alternatives.Photograph: Sebastian Kahnert/DPA/PA ImagesView image in fullscreenConsumers are said to have continued buying Unilever’s branded products, which include Marmite, Dove and Hellmann’s, rather than switching to cheaper alternatives.Photograph: Sebastian Kahnert/DPA/PA ImagesFood & drink industryMarmite and Dove owner Unilever warns of price rises due to growing costsConsumer goods group reports strong sales growth, owing in part to World Cup marketing campaignsBusiness live – latest updatesKalyeena MakortoffTue 28 Jul 2026 08.12 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnilever has warned it will push through further price rises over the coming months, as the Marmite, Dove and Hellmann’s owner tries to recoup its own growing costs.The Anglo-Dutch company said that while the pace of price rises slowed in the second quarter, owing in part to World Cup-related discounts and efforts to stay competitive in Brazil, these were “temporary factors” and would not shield consumers for long.“We expect underlying price growth to accelerate in the second half as commodity-driven pricing continues to land in market,” the company told shareholders on Tuesday.Cottage pie and glass of red, anyone? Britons shun salad despite heat in ‘reverse comfort eating’Read moreThat could end up translating to higher profits for Unilever, depending on whether consumers keep buying its products, despite the price rises. Unilever said in its release that its underlying sales were up 5.8% in the second quarter, pushing turnover up 3.8% to €13bn (£11.1bn).“Consumers continued to demand Unilever’s branded products, rather than switching to unbranded cheaper alternatives, despite cost of living pressures, proving the strength of Unilever products’ brand loyalty,” said Victoria Scholar, the head of investment at Interactive Investor.Companies such as Unilever have been grappling with a rise in costs for ingredients and services, owing to higher oil prices since March, when the US-Israeli war on Iran effectively stopped tanker traffic through the strait of Hormuz.Although oil prices have been oscillating amid temporary ceasefires, that has yet to lead to a sustained drop in prices for manufacturers, which are hoping to pass higher costs on to customers.UK inflation dropped by more than expected in June to 2.6%, but City economists are warning that the Bank of England could be forcedto tear up its economic forecastsand raise interest rates later this year if oil prices return to above $100 a barrel.Mohamed El-Erian, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania and a former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, suggested a sustained increase in oil prices to $90 a barrel could be enough to rewrite UK policymakers’ forecasts.“Should oil prices remain above $90 a barrel, an important ‘if’, then headline inflation would face significant upward pressure. This, in turn, would heighten concerns over immediate indirect effects, including rising food prices driven by diesel transportation costs, and broader second-round effects over time,” he said.That could put further pressure on customers of London-listed Unilever, which has factories across the country making Pot Noodle in Crumlin, Wales, and Hellmann’s, Marmite and Colman’s products in Burton-on-Trent.View image in fullscreenUnilever’s personal care products, including Dove, Vaseline and Sunsilk, were driving much of the group’s sales growth, said one analyst.Photograph: Andrew Kelly/ReutersUnilever indicated that its investment in marketing had paid off, after sales growth beat expectations. “The days of underinvesting in our businesses are over,” the chief financial officer, Srinivas Phatak, told investors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDiana Radu, an equity analyst at the investment research firm Morningstar, agreed that Unilever’s turnaround strategy was working. “Strong volume growth, market share gains and an upgraded outlook suggest that increased investment behind its brands is translating into stronger consumer demand,” she said.Unilever also raised its outlook for 2026. It now expects underlying sales growth of between 4% and 5% in the second half of the year, which will be “led by pricing” – another indication that it is planning price rises.Unilever’s shares climbed by more than 8% on Tuesday.Chris Beckett, a consumer staples analyst at the wealth managers Quilter Cheviot, said markets had reacted positively to Unilever’s latest results.“The company comfortably exceeded sales growth expectations, with volumes increasing 5.5%, roughly double what had been anticipated,” he said. “While earnings only came in modestly ahead of forecasts, most of the focus will rest on the strength of its sales performance. Pricing remained relatively subdued during the quarter, with a greater contribution expected in the second half of the year.“Personal care was the standout performer, with beauty and wellbeing brands such as Dove, Vaseline and Sunsilk driving much of the growth.”Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryUnileverInflationEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Is the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens next | World Cup | The Guardian
description: Gianni Infantino is under fire from Uefa over plans to sell off commercial rights for the tournament but he says they are ‘about the democratisation of football worldwide’
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Gianni Infantino is under fire from Uefa over plans to sell off commercial rights for the tournament but he says they are ‘about the democratisation of football worldwide’
Content: Gianni Infantino is poised to win an unprecedented fourth term as Fifa president next year.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino is poised to win an unprecedented fourth term as Fifa president next year.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAWorld CupExplainerIs the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens nextGianni Infantino is under fire from Uefa over plans to sell off commercial rights for the tournament but he says they are ‘about the democratisation of football worldwide’Paul MacInnesTue 28 Jul 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 16.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhatis Fifa up to now?A week after the World Cup finished, Fifa has yet to announce whether Argentina will be punished for the violence seen on the pitch at the end of the final. What it has been able to do, however, is devise an entirely new way of running international football, which – in the words of its president,Gianni Infantino– “is about the democratisation of football worldwide”. It is also an idea to allow private investors to take a stake in Fifa’s competitions and potentially make money from the World Cup.Fifa accused of ‘selling the soul of football’ over $20bn World Cup commercial rights sale planRead moreSo how will this idea work?After reporting in the Times and the Financial Times broke the news on Tuesday afternoon,Fifapublished a lengthy statement extolling the new venture. To be known as Fifa Forward Enterprise, or FFE, the new body would sell all of Fifa’s commercial rights – across broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing – and also take charge of “operational delivery” of Fifa tournaments. It would focus all Fifa’s money-making endeavours in one place and the governing body would “retain sole control of FFE”, but it would also “invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments”. These investors “would be selected against clear long-term, governance, and strategic criteria”.So Fifa is taking the people’s game and selling it off?Well, only a small “non‑controlling” bit of it. But whose game is it anyway? And yes, Fifa confirmed to the Times that the proposed lead investor to take a stake in FFE would be Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared, but why should that matter? As Infantino pointed out onhis 15-slide Instagram poston Monday, Fifa has been “on the front lines organising, working hard, and delivering the best show in the world”. Maybe give Fifa a break?View image in fullscreenFifa confirmed that the proposed lead investor to take a stake in FFE would be Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersWhat about Fifa’s member associations? Surely they won’t be happy to see money going out of the game?Sources have told the Guardian that the FFE plans would not allow investors to take dividends from the scheme (though the investors could later sell their stake). The governing body’s messaging, meanwhile, is very much focused on the financial benefits the scheme would bring to its member associations. Fifa has promised that any external investment would deliver an “optional” $20m in extra funding to any nation that wants it. It has also promised an increase in annual disbursements and predicted a total of $10bn in extra funding would eventually be shared around. Fifa has said that a majority of its 211 members must express an interest in taking the extra funding if the external investment is to be allowed. Many nations are already dependent on Fifa in order to run their operations, however, and this year Infantino said that without the governing body “there would be no football in 150 countries in the world”. So he would seem likely to receive the necessary expressions of interest.Who dares ridicule Gianni Infantino as the World Cup boss creates global peace? Not me: is it you? | Marina HydeRead moreInfantino has previous in this regard, does he not?Yes, he announced a deal with the Japanese investment management firm Softbank to fund the development of the Club World Cup in 2018 until a backlash brought it down. Reports in the Times suggested that that Infantino could become chief executive of the FFE once he leaves Fifa –he is poised to win an unprecedented fourth termnext year which would extend his stay until 2031. Fifa also insists that joint ventures are par for the course – Uefa has one such with the group known as European Football Clubs to sell the commercial rights to its competitions. Fifa said: “Many major sporting organisations have restructured their commercial operations in similar ways in recent years in pursuit of the same long‑term goal – sustainable growth that can be reinvested in the sport itself.”So what happens now?The Guardian reported on Tuesdaythat the launch of the FFE – which has been planned since well before the World Cup – has caught the rest of football by surprise. Members of the key decision‑making body, the Fifa council, were unaware of the scheme and not included in its development. Uefa, meanwhile, has released its second statement in a month warning of a Rubicon being crossed. There will probably be further expressions of discontent and questions will be asked as to the process that led to these events. But whether any football stakeholder will actually do anything to stop the plans is uncertain.Explore more on these topicsWorld CupGianni InfantinoFifaWorld Cup 2026Football politicsexplainersShareReuse this content

title: F1 summer report card: from top of the class to the team that must do better | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: As the paddock disperses for its traditional mid-season three-week break, the race is on to catch Kimi Antonelli
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: As the paddock disperses for its traditional mid-season three-week break, the race is on to catch Kimi Antonelli
Content: George Russell (left) has struggled and Kimi Antonelli (centre) has prospered at Mercedes, while Lewis Hamilton is rolling back the years.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorge Russell (left) has struggled and Kimi Antonelli (centre) has prospered at Mercedes, while Lewis Hamilton is rolling back the years.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesFormula One 2026F1 summer report card: from top of the class to the team that must do betterAs the paddock disperses for its traditional mid-season three-week break, the race is on to catch Kimi AntonelliGiles RichardsTue 28 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 06.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTop of the classMercedes came into the season as favourites and have lived up to the billing. Their car has been dominant with eight wins from 11 meetings, a strike rate greater perhaps even than the team had expected. Despite the rather skewed conclusions of the Aduo engine assessment, which declared the Red Bull the cream of the crop (on the basis of internal combustion output rather than overall capacity) the Mercedes power unit as a whole, including the hybrid electrical element that is now so vital, is without doubt the class of the field.They have been challenged, not least byFerrari, and pushed hard on occasion by Red Bull and McLaren, but have repeatedly shown that when given a run in clean air, out of a fight, and allowed to use their electrical deployment at its maximum efficiency, the car is fearsomely hard to catch. Moreover, they have now demonstrated that superiority over most types of circuit. They are leading the constructors’ championship from Ferrari by 72 points, and reliability problems have been their only difficulty. Another title appears to be within their grasp.New head boyThe car’s potential has been exploited brilliantly by Kimi Antonelli, with the Italian teenager coming good on his innate talent with an alacrity and composure after only one season in the formula that has been extraordinary to witness. The 19-year-old has stepped up to the new regulations and to competing at the front with striking skill and an assurance that belies his age. Five successive wins andthen another in Spaproved not only that he can close out but is fearless. He has been overeager and impetuous on occasion but anything else from one so young might be disappointing. As the team principal, Toto Wolff, said, he would rather rein in a charger than take a stick to a donkey. Even at the times he has not been leading, his precocious talent has helped him challenge at every opportunity. Antonelli is the real deal and, leading by 50 points from Lewis Hamilton, is on course to take the world championship. On this form it may well be the first of many.Ready for a summer breakIn stark contrast, Antonelli’s teammate George Russell has been buffeted from pillar to post and a chance to refocus over the summer will doubtless be welcome. Russell openedwith a win in Australiabut it was a false dawn. Antonelli endured energy deployment problems in Melbourne and since then Russell has endured the same difficulty, among many others. He has repeatedly suffered bad luck, not least the anti-stall kicking in at the Hungaroring, but also knows he has often not been quick enough on race day compared with the Italian. Worse still, there appears to be no quick fix. He was ready to take on board that his driving style was at issue but since Belgium that appears not to be the case. Nonetheless, Russell remains optimistic, and onwards and upwards was the attitude according to a post on social media after Spa – by the sounds of which over the summer he might be forgiven for enjoying a whisky drink. A vodka drink, a lager drink and a cider drink. “Knocked down, we get back up. No matter how many times,” he wrote. “So many tough moments this year but I will not stop fighting.”View image in fullscreenGeorge Russell has struggled since winning the first race of the season.Photograph: Florent Gooden/DPPI/ShutterstockMost improvedIt would have taken a heart of stone not to enjoy watching Lewis Hamilton return to a level of performance much closer to his best. After the worst season of his career in 2025, when an underperforming Ferrari left him jaded and disconsolate, Hamilton has returned with a new lease of life. This year’s cars – lighter, more nimble and without the ground-effect aero – are far more suited to his driving style and he has embraced them. He has developed his relationship with his new team and the Scuderia have brought a competitive car.Hamilton’s win in Barcelona, his first since 2024, showed he had lost none of his competitive edge, a salutary reminder that at 41 he remains a force to be reckoned with. Ferrari have another engine upgrade to come which may yet move them even closer to Mercedes, an enthralling prospect. There is work to be done, as the strategy calls in Hungary demonstrated.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton celebrates with the Ferrari team after winning the Spanish Grand Prix.Photograph: Bruna Casas/ReutersMust do betterAfter enormous investment in personnel and infrastructure there has been no shortage of ambition atAston Martinbut the team have endured a savage comedown, having anticipated the genius designer Adrian Newey would be the final piece in their jigsaw. From the first race in Australia, when Newey admitted the car was suffering with vibrations from the Honda engines that were in danger of causing permanent nerve damage to the drivers, Aston have been beset on all sides. Apart from the vibrations – largely solved – the engine remains woefully underpowered, the car was overweight and Newey’s bold aerodynamic approach has produced unexpected problems.They have 10 retirements, with a highest finish of 10thearning them their solitary point. In Belgium they were almost six seconds off Mercedes’s pole time and two seconds off the team in front of them, Cadillac, who are F1 debutants. Honda’s expected engine upgrade did not come before the summer break and the team opted not to develop the car in favour of a complete overhaul, which made its debut in Hungary.“Hopefully, we can get at least to a point of respectability now, that is the immediate goal,” Newey said in Budapest, and the B-spec car was a step forward, with Fernando Alonso making it into Q2 for the first time this season. The car looks to have made up about two seconds in pace but a long slog lies ahead.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportMercedes GPKimi AntonelliGeorge RussellLewis HamiltonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Geneva lands world chess title match as Gukesh and Sindarov set to make history | World Chess Championship 2026 | The Guardian
description: Geneva will host the world chess championship from 25 November, where Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov will contest the youngest title match ever
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Geneva will host the world chess championship from 25 November, where Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov will contest the youngest title match ever
Content: Javokhir Sindarov (left) and Gukesh Dommaraju face off in May during the Grand Chess Tour super rapid and blitz tournament in Warsaw, Poland.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJavokhir Sindarov (left) and Gukesh Dommaraju face off in May during the Grand Chess Tour super rapid and blitz tournament in Warsaw, Poland.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesWorld Chess Championship 2026Geneva lands world chess title match as Gukesh and Sindarov set to make historyGeneva chosen over US, India and CyprusSwitzerland to host for first time since 2004Gukesh and Sindarov both 20 at first moveBryan Armen GrahamTue 28 Jul 2026 13.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeneva has been chosen to host this year’s world chess championship match, with Fide announcing on Tuesday that reigning championGukesh Dommarajuwill defend his title against challenger Javokhir Sindarov in the Swiss city from 25 November to 15 December.Both Gukesh, of India, and Sindarov, of Uzbekistan, will be 20 when the best-of-14-games match begins, making it the youngest world championship encountersince the title was first contested in 1886.Fide said several countries, including India, the United States and Cyprus, had expressed interest in hosting the match before the governing body opted for Geneva.From Bobby Fischer to Magnus Carlsen: 22 of the most famous world chess championship gamesRead more“After carefully considering all the proposals, Fide has decided to stage the match on neutral soil and bring it to Geneva, a city with a historic tradition of bringing nations and cultures together,” Fide interim president Viswanathan Anand said in a statement.“We look forward to welcoming the global chess community to Switzerland. The local chess fans will have the opportunity to experience world-class chess in person, while millions of fans around the globe can follow the battle online as the duel for the highest title in chess unfolds.”The SwissChessFederation hailed the decision, calling it a landmark moment for the game in the country. Switzerland last hosted a world championship match in 2004, when Vladimir Kramnik defeated Peter Leko in Brissago.Sindarov earned the right to challenge for the crownby winning this year’s Candidates tournamentin Cyprus with a round to spare. The Uzbek grandmaster finished unbeaten with six wins and seven draws from 13 games, sealing first place after a 58-move draw with Anish Giri and underlining the accelerating shift toward a younger generation at the top of the game.The eight-man tournament had been billed as a potential last stand for the established elite, but AmericansFabiano Caruanaand Hikaru Nakamura never mounted a sustained challenge as Sindarov produced one of the most commanding Candidates performances in recent memory.View image in fullscreenGukesh has dropped to No 26 in the Fide classical rankings since winning the world championship.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyGukeshbecame the youngest world champion in historywhen he defeated China’s Ding Liren in Singapore in December 2024 at the age of 18, breaking the previous record held by Garry Kasparov. Their showdown had marked the first time in the 138-year history of world championship matchplay that two men from Asia competed for the sport’s most prestigious title. Now it will happen for a second world title match in a row.Chess: Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, breaks world age record from 38 years agoRead moreDespite having abdicated the title in 2023, Magnus Carlsen remains the world’s highest-rated player. The 35-year-old Norwegian has held the No 1 ranking for more than 16 years but declined to defend his world championship followinghis fourth successful defense, saying he no longer had the motivation for the months-long slog of preparation required for title matches. Dingwon the crown vacated by Carlsenbefore losing it to Gukesh the following year.While Sindarov arrives after a breakthrough year, Gukesh enters the match searching for form. The 20-year-old has endured a prolonged slump in classical chess, finishing near the bottom of the standings at the Tata Steel Masters and Prague International Chess Festival before placing last at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters.The Indian grandmaster failed to win a single game in Chennai, drawing four and losing three, extending a run of disappointing results that has seen him drop to No 26 in the world and raised doubts over his chances of retaining the title despite becoming the youngest world champion in history less than two years ago.The world championship match will consist of 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion. Fide said further details on the schedule, prize fund, ticketing and exact venue will be announced at a later date.Explore more on these topicsWorld Chess Championship 2026ChessGukesh DommarajuFabiano CaruanaGarry KasparovShareReuse this content

title: Conor McGregor calls for ‘Last Dance’ rematch with Max Holloway in 2027 | Conor McGregor | The Guardian
description: In their welterweight fight at UFC 329 earlier this month, Holloway won by technical knockout in just 69 seconds after McGregor hurt his knee
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In their welterweight fight at UFC 329 earlier this month, Holloway won by technical knockout in just 69 seconds after McGregor hurt his knee
Content: Conor McGregor lost to Max Holloway in their UFC 329 fight in Las Vegas earlier this month.Photograph: Chris Unger/Zuffa LLCView image in fullscreenConor McGregor lost to Max Holloway in their UFC 329 fight in Las Vegas earlier this month.Photograph: Chris Unger/Zuffa LLCConor McGregorConor McGregor calls for ‘Last Dance’ rematch with Max Holloway in 2027Irishman’s UFC return v Holloway ended after 69 secondsMcGregor tore ACL in fight and is out for lengthy spellAgenciesTue 28 Jul 2026 10.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConor McGregor is seeking a rematch ⁠of his recent loss to Max Holloway in what would be the final bout of ⁠his UFC deal.In ⁠an ​Instagram post Monday that references the UFC’s International Fight Week next July, McGregor wrote, “What was ⁠to be a generational beating is now to be reset. IFW 2027. The Last Dance.”Should McGregor ⁠fight Holloway again, it would be the pair’s third ​matchup.Conor McGregor plans to fight again in UFC despite return lasting just 69 secondsRead moreIn a welterweight fight ‌at UFC 329 ‌in Las Vegas on 11 July, Holloway (28-9) won by technical ‌knockout injust 69 secondsafter McGregor (22-7) hurt his right knee on an early kick.The two fighters also squared off in August 2013, when McGregor won by unanimous decision.McGregor, a 38-year-old Irishman, is due to have his ‌torn anterior cruciate ligament surgically repaired, which likely explains the long wait for the rematch.Even though McGregor ​recently posted an Instagram video showing him going through leg exercises, UFC president Dana White said Sunday of McGregor, “Conor McGregor’s out for a year.“The 11 July fight was McGregor’s ⁠first action in the octagon in five years, since breaking his left leg in a 2021 defeat to Dustin Poirier ​at UFC 264 in Las Vegas. McGregor ​has lost each of ‌his past ​three bouts ​and four of the past five.McGregor had been the UFC’s most marketable star before that injury, in 2016 becoming the first to hold two titles simultaneously at dif­ferent weights. He reportedly earned more than $100m after losing a ­boxing ­superfight against Floyd Mayweather Jr in 2017.McGregor was alsoembroiled in multiple lawsuitsduring his time away from the octagon, and became aligned with hard-right figures­during an aborted runfor the Irish ­presidency.Holloway, a 34-year-old Honolulu native, dropped a unanimous decision to Charles Oliveira at UFC 326 in March in Las Vegas before bouncing back to defeat McGregor.Explore more on these topicsConor McGregorUFCMMAUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wrexham face Liverpool with Premier League still in their sights despite setback | Wrexham | The Guardian
description: Ryan Reynolds says Wrexham playing Liverpool in a pre-season friendly at Yankee Stadium is a “punch me moment”
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Ryan Reynolds says Wrexham playing Liverpool in a pre-season friendly at Yankee Stadium is a “punch me moment”
Content: Ryan Reynolds has seen Wrexham climb from the National League to the Championship in five years since he and Rob McElhenney bought the club.Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PAView image in fullscreenRyan Reynolds has seen Wrexham climb from the National League to the Championship in five years since he and Rob McElhenney bought the club.Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PAWrexhamWrexham face Liverpool with Premier League still in their sights despite setbackClub have been promoted three times in four yearsPhil Parkinson’s side missed out on playoffs in 2026Andy Hunterin New YorkTue 28 Jul 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Wrexham co-owner Ryan Reynolds called it a “punch-me moment” – his club playingLiverpoolin a pre-season friendly at Yankee Stadium just five years after he and Rob McElhenney (now simply Rob Mac) completed their takeover of a club languishing in the National League. The knockout blow would be playing Liverpool at Anfield in the Premier League in 2027-28 and the manager, Phil Parkinson, accepts there is expectation on Wrexham to complete their remarkable rise through the divisions next season.Parkinson’s team face Liverpool with confidence in the Bronx on Wednesday having defeated Manchester United and Leeds in pre-season so far and moved on from the anguish of missing out on the Championship playoffs on the final day of last season. The near-miss was undoubtedly a setback to an ambitious club’s grand vision but finishing seventh in the Championship at the first time of asking, Parkinson insists, was an accomplishment that should not be dismissed lightly.Milos Kerkez: ‘I’m delighted – Andoni Iraola is the perfect fit for Liverpool’Read moreTheWrexhammanager said: “If we’re honest, to say five years down the line we’d have finished seventh in the Championship we would have said that was going to take some going. To get three promotions back-to-back-to-back is unheralded. Even though there’s always been ambition within the club and we’ve had resources, to take the club from the National League to seventh in the Championship is a lot of big steps and particularly the one last year. League One to the Championship is a huge step.“Of course we would have loved to have got in the playoffs but I think the staff and the players should be really very proud of their achievements because that was a tough ask, especially with making so many changes.”Wrexham are among the favourites for promotion next season but are the only Championship club not to make a signing – though a deal for Crystal Palace full-back Danny Imray is close – and will not be the only well-funded team with that aim, given the parachute payments availableto relegated West Ham, Burnley and Wolves.“I think the division is going to be stronger this season with the teams coming down,” Parkinson says. “We’ve got work to do within the squad to make us competitive again. We’re close to one signing but we need several more before the window closes. We have to be patient and we will be, but the squad’s not where we want it to be, to be competitive to meet the demands of a Championship season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It is going to be a tough second season, we know that, but we feel there is more to come from the existing group. It was difficult last season with a lot of players coming in later and having to relocate to the area and settle as the season started, but they were great for us and I feel there is more to come this season.”Explore more on these topicsWrexhamLiverpoolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Motorbikes and mountains: photographing the 2026 Tour de France – photo essay | Tour de France 2026 | The Guardian
description: Pete Goding has been photographing the Tour de France for 20 years – here he gives an insight into what it’s been like to document this year’s race
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pete Goding has been photographing the Tour de France for 20 years – here he gives an insight into what it’s been like to document this year’s race
Content: An excited fan runs along side a rider from NSN Cycling Team as the peloton passes through a town during Stage 18 from Voiron to Orcieres-Merlette. All photographs: Pete GodingPete Godinghas been photographing the Tour de France for 20 years – here he gives an insight into what it’s been like to document this year’s raceByPete GodingTue 28 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwenty Tours de France. It seems faintly ridiculous when I write it down. My first was the year Lance Armstrong’s carefully constructed empire was beginning to wobble. I photographed him circling the Champs-Élysées with a film SLR, blissfully unaware that neither film cameras nor Armstrong’s reputation would age particularly well.Today I’m back where it all began, sitting outside a cafe a stone’s throw from the Place de la Concorde nursing acafé crèmewhile Paris carries on entirely oblivious. A couple laugh over breakfast. Someone walks an exceptionally pampered poodle. A waiter in a waistcoat unsuccessfully attempts to persuade two tourists that vodka is an acceptable accompaniment to a croissant. In a few hoursthe world’s biggest bike race will thunder through these streets. Right now, it’s just another Sunday morning.Untouchable and a world apart: cycling world reacts to Pogacar’s fifth Tour winRead moreThat’s one of the peculiar things about the Tour. It arrives like a travelling circus, creates absolute chaos for a few hours, then quietly disappears.First stage of the Tourand I’m on the moto. Those days have become something of a luxury. Before Covid, there were 18 accredited in-race photography motos weaving through the Tour. Now there are just nine, with smaller agencies pooling their allocations and sharing pictures to retain access. I work with a small Belgian-Italian collective, so when it’s your turn, you make the most of it.This year, my draw included the opening team time trial, a handful of sprint stages, and the mountain finish in Orcières-Merlette. It wasn’t Alpe d’Huez, but nobody turns down a day on the back of a Tour moto.The opening stage offered little drama from the bike itself, so I let Barcelona do the storytelling instead. The Sagrada Família became my backdrop. As my characteristically cheerful moto driver disappeared into the distance, I realised every one of my water bottles had disappeared with him. Good job it wasn’t the middle of a Spanish heatwave. This could be a long day.View image in fullscreenThe UAE Emirates XRG team, lead by Tadej Pogacar, power around the streets of Barcelona.A 400mm lens picked riders out from the cathedral’s shadows before I switched to a 24mm as they swept past, trying to cram Gaudí’s masterpiece into the frame – crane and all. By the time the final teams rolled through, I’d become surprisingly adept at juggling cameras while panning at speed.Between runs an older guy leaning over the barriers, brandishing a couple of professional cameras, entertained me, saying that, having started as a Navy photographer, he’d photographed everyone from Reagan to Obama. I quietly Googled him afterwards, half expecting to discover he was a bit of a lune. A quick search revealed that he wasn’t making it up. He’d had the sort of career most photographers could only dream about.Perhaps sensing I was slowly dehydrating on the baking tarmac, a group of Danish fans adopted me for the afternoon, keeping me supplied with ice-cold water until the final team rolled through.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTeam Visma - Lease a Bike pass the Sagrada Família in Barcelona city centre before winning the stage, and then celebrate on the podium.Returning to the motofor stage 18couldn’t have contrasted more with Barcelona.
