The narrow Alpine roads left barely enough room for riders, support cars and the occasional motorcycle. We spent most of the afternoon leapfrogging between the breakaway and the chasing peloton, stopping occasionally for sweeping mountain views before racing back into position.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenSpectators take pictures as the riders pass through their town; the breakaway with Mads Pedersen at the front ride through the Alpes during stage 18 from Voiron to Orcières Merlette.Then, with three kilometres remaining, Richard Carapaz attacked. Unfortunately for us, he chose our side of the road. One moment he was behind us, the next he was almost alongside. My driver instinctively grabbed another handful of throttle just as I swung the camera round. For a few entertaining seconds I was photographing one-handed while hanging on to the back of the bike for dear life. Unsurprisingly, the sharpest thing about some of those pictures was the memory.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenRichard Carapaz makes a break in front of Valentin Paret Peintre in the final kilometers of the stage and then celebrates as he crosses the line to win stage 18.Stage 19 belonged to Tadej Pogacar. On the Alpe d’Huez, he eclipsed Marco Pantani’s longstanding climbing record, and my role that day was to wait at the finish rather than out on the mountain. Recent Tours have tightened access around the winner, replacing the old scrum of photographers with a far more controlled finish, so positioning becomes everything. At this point, it’s about second-guessing how the riders will react after the stage.As it’s uphill and the podium wasn’t far from the finish, you can be certain he won’t be going too far – so I positioned myself on the back line of grey-bibbed photographers, getting ready with my wide-angle lens for close encounters. To avoid missing the finish line, I shot the celebrations over the line and kept a close eye on where Pogacar would end up. Ducking and weaving to find my position, I made sure not to block my fellow photographers and camera operators while commanding my space and ensuring I could find the right angle.The shots worked out, and I can rest easy knowing that my colleagues and I have what we need for the evening news. Records have a habit of sounding abstract until you’re standing 20 metres away when they fall.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreendouble quotation markIt’s very cool to win up here. It was a crazy atmosphere on the whole climb. It’s thanks to all the team that I could pull it off. I was riding for my teammates today. I’m super happy to take the winTadej PogacarView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar celebrates his Stage 19 victory after crossing the finish line and on the podium.On the final Alpine stage, stationed on the Galibier, I’d found the composition and set up the camera on a tripod with a cable release, but needed someone to trigger the remote camera while I worked elsewhere. Ryan, a cycling journalist and travel companion with absolutely no photography experience, suddenly found himself responsible for my third camera. I walked him through the task at hand. See man on bike: press button! A few nervous nods. Then I walked away, hoping for the best. He nailed it!Chapeau, Ryan.View image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar descends the Galibier.On the final day, I wander down the now-barriered Champs-Élysées as the publicity caravan dances its way towards the finish. I’ve left plenty of time to walk the two-kilometre stretch, passing burlygendarmeswho wave me through with practised indifference. Dressed in dark blue uniforms, bulletproof vests, heavy black boots and sunglasses, with pistols resting neatly on their hips, they’re an imposing sight. I smile and offer a quietbonjouras I pass each one, just to see whether I can coax the faintest smile in return.Tadej Pogacar’s ability to win unopposed stands champion out among Tour legends | William FotheringhamRead moreThe Champs feels different these days. Security is tighter than ever, with officers stationed every few metres behind the barriers. They don’t tolerate mistakes. Years ago an American photographer tried to take a shortcut into the race by hopping a barrier and spent the afternoon in the back of a police van. It’s a useful reminder that, however relaxed the Tour may appear, it never really is.By the time I reach my position, a dozen photographers are already lined up. After a few laps I head back to collect some extra kit before making my way across to the central reservation. Normally it’s second nature: step over the low plastic barrier, land neatly, carry on. I’ve climbed volcanoes, scrambled across mountain passes and waded through mangrove swamps without incident. Yet a two-foot plastic barrier on the Champs-Élysées proves my undoing.The camera breaks most of my fall. Unfortunately, I still need it for the rest of the race.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenYellow jersey holder Tadej Pogacar accelerates up the climb of Montmartre to catch Fred Wright; the peloton race round the streets of Paris; Remco Evenpoel clearly enjoying the final stage as he races past the Arc de Triomphe; Mathieu van der Poel collapsed after his all out effort to win the final stage on the Champs-Élysées.An organiser runs over to check I’m all right while another photographer helps me to my feet. Apart from a few grazes, I’m fine. My pride, however, has taken almost as much damage as the camera. Looking up, I catch the sympathetic grin of another photographer and a TV camera operator trying very hard not to laugh. Right. I need another camera.I call Jim, my travelling companion, who’s somewhere in the crowd shooting his own pictures. A few minutes later he appears clutching a spare camera body. Disaster averted.Twenty Tours later, I’ve realised the race isn’t really about yellow jerseys or mountain stages. It’s about the people you meet, the mishaps you survive and the friends who quietly rescue you when everything goes wrong. That’s what keeps me coming back.Explore more on these topicsTour de France 2026Tour de FranceCyclingPhotographynewsShareReuse this content

title: Football transfer rumours: Manchester United to sign Juve’s Francisco Conceição? | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Bruno Guimarães and Vinícius Júnior to Arsenal? | Ruben Vargas to Aston Villa? | James Trafford to Leeds?
Author: Luke McLaughlin
Headline: Bruno Guimarães and Vinícius Júnior to Arsenal? | Ruben Vargas to Aston Villa? | James Trafford to Leeds?
Content: Francisco Conceição in action for Portugal.Photograph: Michaela Stache/ReutersView image in fullscreenFrancisco Conceição in action for Portugal.Photograph: Michaela Stache/ReutersRumour millTransfer windowFootball transfer rumours: Manchester United to sign Juve’s Francisco Conceição?Today’s rumours are napping on the beachLuke McLaughlinTue 28 Jul 2026 04.33 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 06.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs sports fans everywhere eagerly await the resumption of cricket’sCounty Championship season, what better way to while away a few minutes than to contemplate the latest football transfer rumours?Manchester Unitedand Michael Carrick want to sign the 23-year-old Portugal wingerFrancisco Conceiçãofrom Juventus. The tricky former Porto player, who recently returned from theWorld Cup, is valued at about £43m (€50m). United are also said to be ahead of Chelsea in the race to snap upAlex Scottfrom Bournemouth.Men’s transfer window summer 2026: all deals from Europe’s top five leaguesRead moreReal Madrid, meanwhile, have increased their offer to RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande – whom Leipzig had hoped to replace with Conceição–to about £98m. Reports in Germany say further talks are in order to get the deal for the 19-year-old Côte d’Ivoire international over the line.Liverpoolhave emerged as favourites to sign the France internationalBradley Barcolafrom Paris Saint-Germain, having reportedly held preliminary talks with the 23-year-old over alucrative transfer.Bruno Guimarãescontinues to be the subject of strong interest from the Premier League champions,Arsenal. Newcastle, naturally, have insisted the Brazilian is not for sale, but personal terms have reportedly been agreed between the Gunners and Guimarães’s people,so a bid is surely imminent.Arsenal are also being linked withVinícius Júnior, with Mikel Arteta apparently determined to sign the Madrid and Brazil forward. Speculation reached fever pitch on Tuesday when it was reported Vinícius would not train this week, further increasing uncertainty over his future. José Mourinho is keen to keep the winger.Paris Saint-Germainhave distanced themselves from a move the forall-conquering Manchester City midfielderRodri, but the Premier League clubexpect an offer from Real Madrid.Seemingly having fought offChelsea’s pursuit of Granit Xhaka, Sunderland are ready to boost their defensive options by signing the full-backDayann MethaliefromToulouse.Over in Spain, it has been reported thatSevillaare ready to sellRuben Vargasfor about £17m and Aston Villa, Newcastle and Brighton are among potential suitors in His Majesty’s Premier League.Leedsare poised to confirm a £40m deal forJames Trafford, who re-signed for Manchester City after a couple of seasons at Burnley, while Manchester United are keen to sendJoshua Zirkzeeon a season-long loan toJuventus, with an option for theBianconerito buy the 25-year-old.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChelseahave held talks with the Brighton forwardDanny Welbeck(35) and are alsokeen to signJordan Henderson(36). Welbeck knocked in 13 Premier League goals for the Seagulls last season and was fancied as a possible option for England at the World Cup, while Henderson made the cut, only to suffer a freak wrist injury. Chelsea are presumably drawing up eight-year contracts for both veterans.In Germany,Borussia Dortmundhave agreed to sign the midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas from Racing Genk in Belgium, for a fee that could rise to £32m.AndJohn Stones,a free agent after leaving Manchester City, has moved closer to completing his move to Interas reported in these pages: a deal has been verbally agreed.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowRumour millfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fifa accused of ‘selling the soul of football’ over $20bn World Cup commercial rights sale plan | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Fifa has announced plans to sell a share of its commercial operations to private investors, a deal that would include the media and sponsorship rights of the World Cup
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Fifa has announced plans to sell a share of its commercial operations to private investors, a deal that would include the media and sponsorship rights of the World Cup
Content: Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump clutch the World Cup at last month’s final between Spain and Argentina and at the end of a hugely lucractive tournament.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino and Donald Trump clutch the World Cup at last month’s final between Spain and Argentina and at the end of a hugely lucractive tournament.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoFifaFifa accused of ‘selling the soul of football’ over $20bn World Cup commercial rights sale planWorld governing body set to raise millions from ventureUefa hits out at proposal and could take legal actionExplainer: what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens nextMatt HughesandPaul MacInnesTue 28 Jul 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa has announced plans to sell the commercial rights to its tournaments, including theWorld Cup, to private investors in a controversial move that triggered an immediate backlash from Uefa, leading European clubs and politicians.Uefa released a strongly worded statement accusing Fifa of “attempting to sell the soul of football” and is believed to be considering its legal position, while sources at numerous elite clubs were highly critical of the proposal in private. Andy Burnham, the UK’s new prime minister, condemned the move.Is the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens next | Paul MacInnesRead moreFifa has confirmed it is working with the US bank JP Morgan on setting up a new entity – to be calledFifaForward Enterprise (FFE) – that would raise hundreds of millions of dollars by selling a significant stake in the commercial rights of the men’s and women’s World Cups, and the Club World Cup to investors, with promises of an increase in distribution of “over $10bn” (£7.5bn) then being redistributed back to Fifa’s 211 member associations.Thrive Capital, an investment company founded by Joshua Kushner – the brother of Donald Trump’s son‑in-law Jared Kushner – is leading the search for investors.Gianni Infantino, the Fifa president, said the plan would see “the commercial side of the game [operating] as a focused, dedicated business, with its value shared more and better all around the world”. The plans are subject to approval by a “majority” of member associations, but Fifa declined to comment when asked when a vote will take place.Numerous sources with knowledge of Fifa’s proposals said it is valuing the new commercial venture at about $20bn, with Infantino looking to cash in on football’s growing global popularity after this summer’s World Cup in the US, Canada and Mexico.The Guardian revealed this monththat Fifa’s revenues for the tournament would exceed $15bn, a significant increase onthe projected figure of $13bn, with such growth appearing to embolden Infantino to seek further riches.The revelation of the plans provoked an immediate backlash from Uefa, with the European governing body accusing Fifa of attempting to sell the soul of football. Relations between the two most powerful organisations in the sport are at an all-time low, with Uefa claiming Fifa undermined the integrity of the World Cup this month when it intervened to overturn the USA striker Falorin Balogun’s red card after Trumpcalled and asked Infantino to do so.“This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross,” Uefa said of the FFE plan.“Uefa takes it extremely seriously. So should every national football association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game. The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade – especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not Fifa’s to sell.”View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino is looking to cash in on football’s growing global popularity following this summer’s World Cup.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersBurnham, an Everton fan, posted on social media: “Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine. The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone’s to sell. Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInfantino had succeeded in keeping Fifa’s plans under wraps until reports of the proposal first emerged in the Times and Financial Times. Fifa council members are understood to have been surprised by the announcement, having been sidelined from the decision‑making process.It is the second occasion that Infantino has attempted to attract private capital to fund Fifa. In 2018, he agreed a deal in principle with the Japanese bank SoftBank to provide $25bn in funding for an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League, but failed to get sufficient support, largely due to opposition from Europe. Uefa and the clubs are again united against Fifa’s plans, but Infantino may have enough backing from elsewhere to be able to disregard them.In its statement, Fifa said the new enterprise would enable it to increase the funding provided to each of the associations from $8m to $20m each year, a huge sum for the majority of their 211 members.Fifa insisted it would retain responsibility for football’s governance and the international match calendar, but in reality inviting private investment in its commercial rights would subject the decision makers to significant external pressures. Investors could ultimately be given significant influence over decisions that affect the entire sport, leading to fears they would seek to stage the World Cup more regularly and permit it to be hosted in only the most lucrative markets, such as the US. Fifa said it would “carefully select long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests in FFE – all net benefits of FFE will be reinvested back into football worldwide”.Infantino is expected to be re‑elected unopposed as president next year despite the huge controversy he attracts, but under Fifa statutes must stand down in 2031 after serving three full terms. The Times reported, however, that Infantino has aspirations to serve as chair of the new commercial company, which could earn him tens of millions of dollars.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoUefaWorld Cup 2026World CupFootball politicsFinancesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Abusive chanting against immigrants in English football on rise, new data reveals | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Kick It Out data said reported incidents of all discrimination had reached a new high, while abuse in grassroots football rose for a fifth consecutive year
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Kick It Out data said reported incidents of all discrimination had reached a new high, while abuse in grassroots football rose for a fifth consecutive year
Content: The growth in anti-immigrant rhetoric was consistent with a broader rise in reports of discrimination, both at matches and online.Photograph: Kick It OutView image in fullscreenThe growth in anti-immigrant rhetoric was consistent with a broader rise in reports of discrimination, both at matches and online.Photograph: Kick It OutSoccerAbusive chanting against immigrants in English football on rise, new data revealsReported incidents of all discrimination reach new highReports of abuse in grassroots football rose for fifth yearPaul MacInnesTue 28 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbusive chanting against immigrants has become a feature of football matches in England, according to new data fromKick It Out.Last season 39 reports of anti-immigrant chanting were made to the anti-discrimination charity, more than the previous two seasons combined. Phrases such as “stop the boats” and “send them back” were reported as being heard “at all levels of the game”, as part of a growing trend of discriminatory “mass chanting” at matches, Kick It Out said.Increase in racism during World Cup reflects ‘growing pattern of abuse’Read moreThe growth in anti-immigrant rhetoric was consistent with a broader rise in reports of discrimination, at matches and online. Kick It Out received 1,744 reports of discriminatory behaviour in total during the 2025-26 season, a record and a 25% increase on the previous campaign.The number of reported incidents increased across every type of discrimination to new highs. Reports of racism remained the most common, rising 19% year-on-year, the 792 reports making up 45% of the total. Complaints of sexist behaviour rose 12% to 216, homophobia rose 46% to 203, antisemitism rose 43% to 93, ableism rose 20% to 89, and Islamophobia rose 88% to 60. Kick it Out said all six areas had seen their biggest totals in five years.Reports of abuse in grassroots football rose for a fifth consecutive year, up by 33% in 2025-26 to a record 248 reports. Equally, the 98 reports of abuse against match officials was the same as the past three seasons combined.Samuel Okafor, chief executive at Kick It Out, said such behaviour at matches and in online spaces was matched by a rise in hateful rhetoric elsewhere in British society, but he praised the willingness of supporters – and players – to speak out.“These figures show that discrimination remains deeply embedded across the game at a time when we’re also seeing rises in hate crime and divisive political rhetoric in Britain,” he said. “But they also show that people are more willing to stand up to abuse when they see it, and it’s encouraging to see professional players set that example last season.”For example, in March, a 60-year-old man was given a suspended sentence forsending offensive messagesto the England Women defender Jess Carter, who went public over the attacks during the European Championship last year. In the men’s game, Antoine Semenyo drew attention to the racist abuse he had received over the course of the season, with a charge ofracially aggravated behaviouragainst one man scheduled to go to trial in September.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKick It Out’s findings concur with those reported by the UK Football Policing Unit last week. The police said that some of the increase could be explained by improved reporting mechanisms, with misogynist abuse only introduced as a separate category of discrimination at the start of last season. Both police and Kick It Out have called on online platforms to do more to stop abuse.Okafor said: “We will continue to work with football authorities, clubs, leagues, regulators and government to ensure we match the courage shown to report abuse with clear and consistent action so that football is welcoming to everyone.”Explore more on these topicsFootballKick It OutRacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Retaining Rodri is key to Manchester City success under Enzo Maresca | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: New manager’s No 1 priority must be to persuade World Cup-winning captain to stay as Real Madrid circle
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: New manager’s No 1 priority must be to persuade World Cup-winning captain to stay as Real Madrid circle
Content: Rodri helped Manchester City win two trophies last season.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenRodri helped Manchester City win two trophies last season.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAManchester CityRetaining Rodri is key to Manchester City success under Enzo MarescaNew manager’s No 1 priority must be to persuade World Cup-winning captain to stay as Real Madrid circleJamie JacksonTue 28 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Welcome home,” was Khaldoon al-Mubarak’s warm greeting to Enzo Maresca onhis appointment last monthas Manchester City manager. Now, after two previous spells at the club, the Italian’s task is to keep the chair content, and ensure a three-year contract does not end early. To achieve that, Maresca’s tenure must continue Pep Guardiola’s glittering legacy of 20 trophies across a decade of excellence.The key to the 46-year-old, who was Guardiola’s assistant during the 2022-23 treble season and City’s elite development squad leader two years before that, being successful can be summed up in two words: “Keep Rodri”. Yet with Real Madrid almost certain to launch a bid for the peerless No 6, and him seemingly wanting to play for the Spanish giants, a move away from City may become inevitable.Manchester City hope Rodri will sign new deal as Real Madrid weigh up offerRead moreMaresca’s best hope of avoiding “doing a David Moyes” – who succeeded Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United in May 2013 and lasted a mere 34 Premier League games – and thriving as the man who followsthe manis to retain Rodri, whohas just captained Spain to World Cup glory, winning the Golden Ball as best player in the process. The 30-year-old is contracted until June. City’s stance is that they have no wish to sell and remain intent on persuading him to sign the new terms that have been on offer for a while.Saying City will definitely be contenders for the biggest prizes next season if they retain Rodri may sound simplistic until you examine his CV and are reminded of the pivotal role he has played for the club. Rodri was key to City’s treble glory, includingscoring the winner in the Champions League final against Inter. Then there was the 74-game unbeaten sequence with him in the colours that ran from February 2023 to May 2024. “He’s unbelievable, irreplaceable,” said Guardiola. “The best midfielder in the world by far.”The World Cup triumph also came after Rodri had been part of Spain’s Euro 2024 glory and City’s 2023 Club World Cup success, again winning the player of the tournament in each. In the two seasons before the World Cup, injury plagued him, however. The result: no Premier League titles in either year for City, halting a record four-in-a-row run for Guardiola’s garlanded team.Rodri’s ability to mould and control contests wasreiterated by his World Cup displays. Exhibit A: the chokehold imposed on France in the semi-finals. At domestic and international level, this is a priceless quality. So if Maresca can field Rodri, City will be feared in the league and on the continent. The back injury for which Rodri underwent surgery on Monday is minor, but the desire to broaden his club horizons – primarily in Spain – remains, meaning there is no certainty he will stay put. Particularly so given the initial resistance of Real Madrid’s president, Florentino Pérez, to acquiring Rodri has shifted, due, surely, to his resurgence at the World Cup and maybe José Mourinho, returning as head coach, expressing a need for the player’s calm and elan.View image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca worked under Pep Guardiola as Manchester City won the treble in 2023.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPACity haveinvested £116m on Elliot Andersonthis summer, an England first-choice midfielder who may be joined by another midfielder inLille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi, the 18-year-old who also impressed at the World Cup for Morocco, and would cost around £85m. However, neither of them or Tijjani Reijnders, Mateo Kovacic nor Nico González can claim to be in the class of Rodri, who may well be in line to claim a second Ballon d’Or following his World Cup exploits.Maresca won the Championship with Leicester in 2024 and the following season led Chelsea to fourth in the Premier League and to a Conference League triumph, following that up with glory at the expanded Club World Cup, which featured the3-0 demolition of Paris Saint-Germainin the final. All of this convinced al-Mubarak and his chief executive, Ferran Soriano, that Maresca is the one who can thrive after the era-defining Guardiola.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideGvardiol says 'great things' will happen under MarescaShowJoško Gvardiol has signed a new five-year contract with Manchester City, the defender stating that “great things” can be achieved with Enzo Maresca, the new manager.While the terms include an option of a further 12-months, the Croatian is confident that the Italian’s first season will be successful. “I remember when he was at Chelsea [2024-26] it was difficult to play against them – especially away. We struggled. He’s here and I think we can achieve some great things together,” Gvardiol said.The 24-year-old has made 122 appearances and claimed six trophies with City since joining from RB Leipzig in 2023 for £77m and was voted the club’s 2024-5 player of the season.Gvardiol said: “I remember my first season when I arrived – back then I was kind of still young. In these three years I’ve learned a lot of things from all my team-mates, my friends in the dressing room and on the pitch in the last three years."I still think there are a lot of things to improve and learn but I’m only 24, I have enough time.”Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.However, as Maresca made clear with his “after Sir Alex [Ferguson]” referencein his unveiling on Friday, directly following greatness can be treacherous. The comparison between him and Moyes is hardly precise, though. Moyes arrived at United trophyless and with no experience of the pressures of an elite club. Maresca’s résumé shows a season and a half in the Chelsea hothouse and, with his prior experience of City, he is versed in the organisation where he now plays a crucial role.City have five weeks of the market remaining to try to persuade Rodri his future is at the club. Guardiola’s stance was never to stop any player exiting who wished to do so. The logic is understandable: what is the point in retaining an unhappy employee? In this case it would also be one who wants to return to his native city. “Having played for Atlético [Madrid] before would not prevent me from playing for Real Madrid,” Rodri said in March. “There are other players who have done that before. Maybe not direct transfers, but eventually. You can’t turn down one of the world’s best clubs.”EvenReal Madrid boycotting Rodri’s Ballon d’Or-crowning ceremonyin November 2024 in protest at Vinícius Júnior’s failure to win the vote has clearly not dissuaded the midfielder that the Bernabéucan be the home al-Mubarak characterises City as for Maresca.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityEnzo MarescaPep GuardiolafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Xabi Alonso plays down Welbeck and Henderson moves after Chelsea win | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: The manager said: ‘There will be a lot of links, a lot of rumours,’ after João Pedro scored a hat-trick in Chelsea’s 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The manager said: ‘There will be a lot of links, a lot of rumours,’ after João Pedro scored a hat-trick in Chelsea’s 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers
Content: Xabi Alonso talks tactics with Cole Palmer during Chelsea’s pre-season victory in Sydney.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PAView image in fullscreenXabi Alonso talks tactics with Cole Palmer during Chelsea’s pre-season victory in Sydney.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PAChelseaXabi Alonso plays down Welbeck and Henderson moves after Chelsea win‘There will be a lot of transfer links, a lot of rumours’Chelsea hit back to beat Western Sydney Wanderers 6-4Adam Hancock at Accor StadiumTue 28 Jul 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleXabi Alonso refused to confirm Chelsea are interested in signing theveterans Danny Welbeck and Jordan Hendersonafter his first game in charge of the team, a 6-4 pre-season victory against Western Sydney Wanderers on Tuesday, but said he was looking to build a squad that had “proper balance”.Chelsea are understood to be in talks over a surprise move to sign the 35-year-old Welbeck from Brighton, with the club also reportedly interested in signing the 36-year-old Henderson from Brentford. The links to two Premier League stalwarts reflects a revised transfer strategy under Alonso, withChelseaseeking to recruit more experienced players into their squad as opposed to focused solely on signing young players, often tying them to lengthy contracts.Chelsea explore surprise moves for Danny Welbeck and Jordan HendersonRead more“I’m sure that from today to the last day of the transfer [window] there will be a lot of links, a lot of rumours, so to be commenting on all of them, it’s going to be a hard task,” Alonso said. “But for sure, we need proper balance in terms of qualities, in terms of positions, in terms of balance. We want to have a complete squad and we want to make a good team.”The new Chelsea manager fielded a youthful side at the Accor Stadium at Sydney Olympic Park in Homebush, with Liam Delap and Tosin Adarabioyo the most experienced members of the starting lineup. Alonso waited until the 63rd minute to bring on a host of star names, including Cole Palmer and João Pedro. The Brazilian forward, who missed out on a place in Carlo Ancelotti’s World Cup squad, made a significant impact off the bench, scoring a hat-trick in just nine minutes as Chelsea took control of the game against their A-League opponents.João Pedro scored 20 goals during an excellent debut season for Chelsea, havingarrived from Brighton for £60m 12 months ago, and asked about the player’s mood before the upcoming campaign, Alonso said: “Very hungry. João is really, really determined to have a great season. He wants to, after a great last year, when he scored many goals. He wants to keep scoring more and more.”A number of Chelsea’s youngsters showed plenty of promise, with the 17-year-old Dastan Satpayev opening the scoring after six minutes. The Kazakh forward is yet to sign officially for the club and is playing in pre-season as a triallist. His opening goal came from a defence-splitting pass from another teenager, Ryan Kavuma-McQueen, with Satpayev smashing the ball home at the near post.Chelsea’s back four struggled in the first half against a lively Wanderers frontline and their reported new set-piece coach, Aston Villa’s Austin MacPhee, will have plenty to work on judging by the ease with which Brandon Borrello and Anthony Pantazopoulos won headers from a corner as the latter scored at the back post for the hosts.View image in fullscreenJoão Pedro scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming on as a second-half substitute.Photograph: Mark Evans/EPAThe Wanderers took the lead through Aydan Hammond before a lovely finish from the Portuguese midfielder Dário Essugo made it 2-2 at the break. The goals kept coming in the second half when the left-back Landon Emenalo, who impressed going forward, saw his clearance deflected into the path of Dylan Scicluna, who put the Sydney side 3-2 ahead. Alonso then turned to his bench and his substitutions made an immediate impact. João Pedro held off a number of challenges on the edge of the box before pulling the ball back to Jamie Gittens, who fired home from close range.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut this topsy-turvy game, which felt like England’s third-place playoff against France at the World Cup andfinished with the same scoreline, provided more entertainment as the Australian side went ahead for a third time after Estêvão Willian lost possession on the edge of his own area. Awan Lual was on hand to slide the ball through Robert Sánchez’s legs to put his side 4-3 ahead.The Wanderers, who are also in pre-season, again failed to hold on to a lead as Chelsea overpowered a team that finished bottom of their domestic league last season. João Pedro looked sharp as he showed great composure to score twice in five minutes, before scrambling home an effort from a corner to wrap up his match-winning exploits.João Pedro’s performance was in stark contrast to that of Delap, who has been repeatedly linked with a move away from west London. The 23-year-old endured another frustrating evening for Chelsea, going close on two occasions but failing to find the back of the net. Assessing Delap’s attitude since returning from the summer break, Alonso said: “I see him in a good mood, in a good desire to get proper fitness, proper football, feeling good and he’s doing great.”Explore more on these topicsChelseaXabi AlonsoWestern Sydney WanderersA-League MenAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Milos Kerkez: ‘I’m delighted – Andoni Iraola is the perfect fit for Liverpool’ | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: The full-back tells Andy Hunter about being reunited with his former manager, the shock of Arne Slot’s sacking and being mistaken for a bridegroom
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: The full-back tells Andy Hunter about being reunited with his former manager, the shock of Arne Slot’s sacking and being mistaken for a bridegroom
Content: Milos Kerkez is looking forward to once again playing with ‘intensity’ under Andoni Iraola in what will be the Hungary international’s second season at Liverpool.Photograph: Nick Taylor/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMilos Kerkez is looking forward to once again playing with ‘intensity’ under Andoni Iraola in what will be the Hungary international’s second season at Liverpool.Photograph: Nick Taylor/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesLiverpoolInterviewMilos Kerkez: ‘I’m delighted – Andoni Iraola is the perfect fit for Liverpool’Andy Hunterin New YorkFull-back on being reunited with former manager, the shock of Arne Slot’s sacking and being mistaken for a bridegroomTue 28 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been quite the summer for Milos Kerkez. There was time at home in Serbia, holidays in Montenegro and Spain, a frantic knock on his bedroom door one day to tell him that Arne Slot had been sacked, an unexpected reunion with Andoni Iraola shortly afterwards, and thousands of well‑wishes sent his way after being photographed escorting a bride into church in his hometown of Vrbas. Congratulations on the wedding are also extended at the start of our interview on a rooftop terrace at Liverpool’s team hotel.Chiesa wants ‘new chapter’ with Iraola after frustrating time under Slot at LiverpoolRead more“No! This is wrong, everyone gets this wrong!” the full-back exclaims. “It was my oldest brother. In Serbia it is normal for the younger brothers to take the bride to the church. That’s what I did and now everyone thinks I got married. It was Rade, not me. There are three of us – Rade is the oldest, I’m the youngest and Marko is the middle one. I keep having to explain to people that I never got married. I was going around the club when we started back and people were congratulating me. I’m like: ‘No, I’m not ready for this yet!’”Well, that’s one way of breaking the ice with an interviewee. Marriage is categorically not on the agenda for Kerkez, a humorous and engaging force of energy, but he is ready to embrace other responsibilities: notably stepping out of Andy Robertson’s shadow and stepping up at Liverpool. Early days, of course, but it has been noted during Liverpool’s pre‑season training camp at Chicago Fire’s performance centre how the 22-year-old and his fellow Hungary international Dominik Szoboszlai have taken a leading role among a relatively young squad.Kerkez – who was eligible to play for Hungary through his paternal grandparents – is in an advantageous position as the Iraola era begins with gruelling double training sessions and a pre-seasonfriendly win over Sunderlandin Nashville on Saturday. He knows the new boss better than any other Liverpool player, having matured into a £40m left-back during two seasons with Iraola at Bournemouth. He knows he doesn’t have to win over the new head coach as Iraola rates him highly. And he knows that, to convince Liverpool fans after a difficult debut season at Anfield, he is now working for a coach who can bring the best out of him.View image in fullscreenMilos Kerkez tussles with Newcastle’s Anthony Elanga during a difficult debut season at Anfield.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA“I was delighted, honestly,” Kerkez says on discovering Liverpool’s choice to replace Slot. “He helped me and improved me a lot in the two years I spent with him. I was really happy, obviously for myself but also for the team. Everyone knows what type of football he plays so I think he is the perfect fit for us.“It’s the intensity. He’s not scared to play one-on-one all over the pitch, to press high and to be on the front foot always. If you see footage of how we all are after training, all lying down, then you can see what he is preparing us for. You definitely need legs and good condition for what he wants us to do, but we will be all right. When we play games with three or four teams he calls it ‘consequences’ and the losing team and the team that finishes second has to run. How much you have to run depends on what he decides in that moment, but there is always running for the team that loses.“He’s intense and he likes details. He’s very professional. He likes to talk sometimes but not a lot. I think maybe he doesn’t want to get too close to some players and wants to show that everyone is the same in the team, so he doesn’t want to get too close to anyone in particular. He keeps it professional, with a lot of hard work.”There were times last season when Kerkez appeared inhibited by Slot’s insistence on building from the back and full-backs coming inside. It was his pace and energy up and down the flank with Bournemouth that had attracted Liverpool and earned him a place in the Professional Footballers’ Association’s team of the year in 2024-25. He should be able to play to his strengths more often next season.As he explains: “The gaffer likes to play more with the full-backs down the line, underlapping, overlapping. It worked well for me at Bournemouth, so I think it will also work well for me here. He always told me that defending is really important, for him that is first of all, and because you are a full-back you need to defend really hard. Everything you can do in front of you is like a bonus. So I was always focused first on defending and then running forward to help the wingers. He showed me that when you do your job then you are free to do what you want, so I felt really free with him. He lets you be more free to do your stuff.”Not that Kerkez blames Slot for last season’s turbulence, far from it. The pair remain in contact. “I was surprised,” he says of the Dutchman’s sacking, 12 months after delivering the Premier League title. “I really didn’t know. I was back in Serbia, I was sleeping and my brother woke me up. He knocks on my door and it was a big surprise. Nobody knew. I couldn’t believe it, I was like: ‘Wow.’ I have been in touch with him since, we have exchanged a few messages.”View image in fullscreenMilos Kerkez celebrates scoring at a time he was playing brilliantly well for Andoni Iraola at Bournemouth.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersKerkez admits last season was “tough for everyone” at Liverpool as every time the team seemed to have solved one problem, another would appear. As part of the expensive recruitment drive of last summer that failed to bear fruit – though Kerkez achieved far more than others – the scrutiny on the left-back and his fellow new signings was particularly intense. He insists he did not feel it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Honestly, I don’t care about pressure,” says the full-back, who will face Wrexham in the second game of Liverpool’s US tour in New York on Wednesday. “I don’t like ‘pressure’ and that stuff. I grew up a bit different in Serbia. We grew up different. You could say maybe we are built a bit different. For example, I started to drive a truck when I was 10 years old.” Sorry? “It was with my dad,” Kerkez says. “I climbed in and then I took the wheel. He was doing the pedals, I was only quite small so I couldn’t reach them.”Kerkez’s father, Sebastijan, still drives his son to Liverpool’s training centre on occasions. He and Kerkez’s mother, Tijana, moved to England to help their second son settle into life as a Premier League player. “They are very important,” says the defender. “My brothers have their own lives now but my parents are with me and I am much happier they are with me. My dad is here to smack me sometimes on the top of the head and to remind me. Sometimes you play a few good games and maybe you start to get a bit carried away. But my dad is here to smack me. I come straight back down and I switch straight back on.”‘Don’t become the protagonist’: Andoni Iraola on the secret of Spain’s success and his role at LiverpoolRead moreAnother important influence on Kerkez has been Robertson, the man – and the Liverpool legend – he was bought to replace. The Scotland captain and now Tottenham left-back regularly took Kerkez aside last season to pass on his experience. But there was no big parting message when the time came for Robertson to say goodbye to Anfield in May.“I didn’t want to get a lot on to him,” says Kerkez, who became close friends with Mohamed Salah last season. “He was a bit emotional as everything was coming to an end. I didn’t want to get on to him too much, but throughout the year he helped me. We had a few conversations about crosses and about the big lungs we need to have so we can run until tomorrow. He did a lot of seasons, I should also have the same. We had conversations like that. Also, where to put the last ball, to focus, to put your head up and sometimes put better crosses in.“We all know what Andy did for the club. I’m not running away from that. I want to make my own way. I’m going to work hard. I know what it means to play for Liverpool. I showed it a bit last year and I am going to show it more this year. Before we left the Axa [Liverpool’s training ground, to come to Chicago] I saw on TV a show about how many goals and assists Mo had, it was something like 380. I just walked out! ‘What is this?’ I was thinking. Time flies. A new generation comes and hopefully everything will be good.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He’s back’: Zinedine Zidane named France head coach in long-awaited homecoming | France | The Guardian
description: Zinedine Zidane is France’s new head coach, replacing Didier Deschamps at the helm of the team he led to glory as arguably their greatest ever player
Author: Raphaël Jucobin
Headline: Zinedine Zidane is France’s new head coach, replacing Didier Deschamps at the helm of the team he led to glory as arguably their greatest ever player
Content: Zinedine Zidane described becoming France’s new head coach as the “only thing I wanted”.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/EPAView image in fullscreenZinedine Zidane described becoming France’s new head coach as the “only thing I wanted”.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/EPAFrance‘He’s back’: Zinedine Zidane named France head coach in long-awaited homecomingFour-year deal agreed with successor to Deschamps‘I have so many emotions, I am ready for the challenge’Raphaël Jucobinin ParisTue 28 Jul 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor Tuesday’s front page, L’Équipe simply went with “Il revient” – “He’s back” – echoing the newspaper’s 2005 headline whenZinedine Zidanecame out of international retirement. At the time, the midfielder’s upcoming return was seen as a major boost toLes Bleus’ ailing World Cup qualifying campaign. There was a similar sense of anticipation now as the roads around the French Football Federation headquarters in Paris were closed off for Zidane’s unveiling as head coach. A crowd of France fans had gathered outside by the overground Métro tracks with flags, flares and drums, as more than a hundred journalists and TV cameras were ushered into the building.The fact that Zidane would be next in line to leadFranceafter Didier Deschamps had been an open secret for several years and by the end of the World Cup his arrival was all but confirmed. The new head coach entered the press conference room on Tuesday morning only minutes after his appointment was confirmed by the FFF’s executive committee, but the feeling in France was that the occasion was a couple of decades in the making.“It’s a new cycle,” the FFF president, Philippe Diallo, said after a preamble in which he paid tribute to Deschamps’ 14-year tenure. Talks with the 1998 World Cup hero, Diallo said, began in February 2025, the month after Deschamps announced he would step down this summer. “Zinedine Zidane is one of the legends of French football and he had made it known that it was one of his dreams to manage the French national team,” Diallo said. “We wanted someone with the aura, the ability, and the hearts of our fans and the French people to manage what is one of the best national teams in the world.”View image in fullscreenFrance supporters gather in Paris to celebrate the confirmation of one of the greatest players inLes Bleus’history as their new head coach.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/EPAFor Zidane, this announcement was the culmination of nearly half a decade of waiting in the wings. “I had several offers from clubs in the last four to five years, but I turned them all down for France,” the former Real Madrid manager said. “The national team is the only thing I wanted. I’ve been with the French teams since I was a kid, all the way up to the senior team. I’m a bit emotional. You might not be able to tell, but I am incredibly excited.”Zidane declared it was the greatest day of his managerial career. “It’s an immense joy. I am ready for the challenge.”The five years that have passed since the end of Zidane’s second spell in Madrid will have been spent preparing to take overLes Bleus. “I’ve been watching France as a supporter, but also as a future manager. I don’t think there are any traps. It’s new to me, but I’m not scared. This is what I wanted.” The 54-year-old’s first public appearance as head coach was light on the details of his plans for the national team. He notably sidestepped a question about whether Kylian Mbappé would retain the armband, insisting that he would have to meet the team and its “extraordinary players” first of all. “We need to keep this team winning,” he said, adding that he was impressed with what he had seenduring the World Cup.“I was a No 10 in my playing days,” he said when asked about the style of play he would look to implement. Whether his answer implies a continuation of Deschamps’ attacking shift remains to be seen, but his answers did hint at some kind of change of direction. “Laurent [Blanc] was Laurent, Didier was Didier, and Zizou is Zizou,” he said playfully.One of Zidane’s long-term objectives will be to compete with the reigning world champions, who have now beaten France in three consecutive tournament semi‑finals. “I spent 25 years in Spain and you know what that means,” he said, before pointing out that the task ahead went beyond beatingLa Roja. “I know Spanish football very well, but they won’t be the only opponents. You have to beat all of the teams.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenZinedine Zidane was sent off by Horazio Elizondo for butting Italy’s Marco Materazzi in the chest in the 2006 World Cup final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianZidane’s four-year contract will begin next month, with his extended staff to be unveiled a few weeks before the first internationals of the new season. “We’ll see each other again in September to talk about it. It’s a good thing that we’ll have three weeks with the players.” The focus for now, Zidane said, is on his first match in charge, which will be in Turkey on 25 September.His homecoming, meanwhile, will be against Italy, just over 20 years after hisdramatic exit from the international stage. If the raucous reception as he stepped out of the FFF headquarters is anything to go by, it will be one of the more memorable evenings in the Stade de France’s history.Explore more on these topicsFranceZinedine ZidanenewsShareReuse this content

title: Roberto Mancini returns as Italy head coach with Claudio Ranieri named technical director | Italy | The Guardian
description: Roberto Mancini has agreed to coach Italy again, three years after stepping down, in the wake of Andrea Pirlo being rejected
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Roberto Mancini has agreed to coach Italy again, three years after stepping down, in the wake of Andrea Pirlo being rejected
Content: Roberto Mancini during a charity match in L’Aquila this month.Photograph: Augusto Casasoli/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoberto Mancini during a charity match in L’Aquila this month.Photograph: Augusto Casasoli/ReutersItalyRoberto Mancini returns as Italy head coach with Claudio Ranieri named technical directorMancini replaces Gattuso for second spell in chargeRanieri takes over from Paolo Maldini in overseeing roleReutersTue 28 Jul 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoberto Mancini has agreed to be Italy head coach for a second time, the president of the Italian Football ​Federation (FIGC), Giovanni Malagò, said on Tuesday, also confirming Claudio Ranieri would take over as technical director.Mancini replaces Gennaro Gattuso, who ⁠left the post in April after Italy failed to qualify for a third World Cup in succession, and returns to a job he held between 2018 and 2023. He led the national team toEuropean Championship glory in 2021with a penalty shootout victory over England at Wembley but then failed to reach the 2022 World Cup and a slow start to Euro 2024 qualifying. In total, Mancini managed Italy for 58 matches during his first spell and at club level has managed Inter, Fiorentina and Manchester City, where he spent three years and guided them to theirfirst Premier League title in 2011-12.“Mancini is the coach,” Malago ‌said on Tuesday. “I believed that the best person to become head coach was ‌Roberto Mancini.”The former FIGC technical director ‌Paolo Maldini and his adviser, Leonardo, resigned from their roles on Monday after Andrea Pirlo’sappointment as head coach was blockedbecause of the former midfielder’s ties to a Russian betting firm. Pep Guardiola was the association’s first choice but turned down the job last month.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRanieri replaces ⁠Maldini. The 74-year-old, wholed Leicester City to the Premier League title in ​2016, will oversee technical operations and ​elite football development across Italy’s national team structures. “I needed someone with ​whom I could share ‌the decision on ​the coach, because ​without that shared view my reasoning would have carried little weight,” Malago said. “So consequently, we have a new coach and a new technical director for Italy.”Explore more on these topicsItalyRoberto MancininewsShareReuse this content

title: Sunderland close in on Dayann Methalie signing after Newcastle back off | Sunderland | The Guardian
description: Sunderland are poised to sign the long-time Newcastle target Dayann Methalie, Toulouse’s 20-year-old France Under-21s defender
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Sunderland are poised to sign the long-time Newcastle target Dayann Methalie, Toulouse’s 20-year-old France Under-21s defender
Content: Dayann Methalie made 27 Ligue 1 appearances for Toulouse last season.Photograph: Nathan Barange/DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDayann Methalie made 27 Ligue 1 appearances for Toulouse last season.Photograph: Nathan Barange/DPPI/ShutterstockSunderlandSunderland close in on Dayann Methalie signing after Newcastle back offToulouse defender expected to cost about £26mNewcastle still looking for defensive reinforcementsLouise TaylorTue 28 Jul 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 08.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSunderland are poised to sign the long-time Newcastle target Dayann Methalie from Toulouse. The France Under-21s defender, who can play left-back or wingback and also operate in the centre, has attracted widespread interest this summer but Régis Le Bris now appears close to acquiring him for about £26m.Newcastle had extensively scouted Methalie, who made 27 Ligue 1 appearances for Toulouse last season, and reportedly tried to sign him in January. The club have now indicated they opted against the idea of recruiting the 20-year-old and have not submitted a bid this summer. Nonetheless, Methalie appeared an ideal fit for Newcastle’s new transfer policy of recruiting young players in the £20m-£40m price bracket.Football transfer rumours: Manchester United to sign Juve’s Francisco Conceição?Read moreSunderland can offer the 6ft 2in defender Europa League football and he is understood to have verbally agreed a five-year deal at the Stadium of Light, where he would not merely be coached by a compatriot in Le Bris but be part of a sizeable contingent of French-speaking players including Enzo Le Fée, Nordi Mukiele and Habib Diarra. Methalie will be Le Bris’s second summer signing after the arrival of the Belgium right-back Thomas Meunier, who arrived on a free transfer after leaving Lille.While Methalie is likely to face considerable competition from Reinildo to establish himself as Sunderland’s first-choice left-back, his amalgam of impressive recovery pace, robust physicality and assured left foot have seen him shine as a left-sided central defender in a back three and a back four.Newcastle, meanwhile, remain in the market for cover at left-back and right-back, with the latter position one Eddie Howe is particularly anxious to reinforce after Kieran Trippier’s departure at the end of last season.Howe’s hopes of keeping Bruno Guimarães appear to still rest on Arsenal’s willingness or otherwise to pay a fee in the region of £80m for the 28-year-old captain, who has been on a post-World Cup holiday in Brazil and is due to return to Newcastle on Friday, before travelling to a training camp at La Manga with the rest of the first-team squad.Joe Willock’s future at St James’ Park also remains uncertain. Although Newcastle have rejected an offer in the region of £10m from Besiktas for the former Arsenal midfielder, they appear open to selling him, albeit for a fee closer to £20m.Explore more on these topicsSunderlandNewcastle UnitedTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Kyle Chalmers casts doubt on Olympics after losing 100m freestyle crown: ‘I have to be a realist’ | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: The freestyle king missed out on becoming Australia’s most decorated male Commonwealth Games swimmer, finishing third in the 100m final
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The freestyle king missed out on becoming Australia’s most decorated male Commonwealth Games swimmer, finishing third in the 100m final
Content: Kyle Chalmers won bronze in the men’s 100m freestyle final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreenKyle Chalmers won bronze in the men’s 100m freestyle final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPCommonwealth Games 2026Kyle Chalmers casts doubt on Olympics after losing 100m freestyle crown: ‘I have to be a realist’Flynn Southam wins gold medal ahead of Chalmers in thirdGymnasts Breanna Scott and Jesse Moore add to gold medal tallyAustralian Associated PressTue 28 Jul 2026 19.32 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKyle Chalmers has been dethroned as theCommonwealth Games100m freestyle king in Glasgow after being reeled in by young friend and rival Flynn Southam in a landmark changing-of-the-guard moment.With a potential record-breaking 10th Commonwealth gold in his sights, Chalmers had his proud run of never being beaten by an Australian in major international competition dismantled by 21-year-old Southam in the Tollcross pool.Silver bullet: Lachie Kennedy breaks national record to end Australia’s 64-year wait for 100m medalRead moreSoutham’s glory, fuelled by indignation at being dismissed as just a relay workhorse, set the tone for yet another magisterial five-gold night for the Dolphins as they equalled their record tally of titles at any Games with 28 – with still one more day left to blitz the Gold Coast tally.“It’s pretty incredible,” Southam said. “I had a lot of people doubting me and saying my success only comes from relays, and that’s really pissed me off and motivated me to be the best in the world.”Jenna Forrester sealed a golden treble in her remarkable breakthrough meet, adding a 200m medley win to her surprise 200m backstroke and 400m IM titles, while 400m and 1500m queen Lani Pallister completed her freestyle distance hat-trick with the 800m title in a Games record 8 minutes 11.12 seconds.The session was book-ended by Queenslander Kirralee Hayes opening up with a para 50m freestyle S13 final win, with teammate Jenna Jones taking bronze, and the quartet of Iona Anderson, Sam Williamson, Matt Temple and Meg Harris ending with mixed 4x100 medley relay gold.But Southam was the standout, the young Fremantle-born, NSW-raised prospect finally fulfilling his potential as the most likely successor to Chalmers, clocking a searing 47.13 seconds to the bronze medallist’s 47.74. The pair were split by Welshman Matt Richards (47.64).View image in fullscreenFlynn Southam after winning the men’s 100m freestyle final.Photograph: Mickael Chavet/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockAnd while the gracious Chalmers was left pondering if he’d go on to the Los Angeles Games, Southam made it clear he was the future, even if he hopes their rivalry flourishes.“It’s my time to shine, and I know that,” said Southam. “I’ve been due for this, and this is my breakout meet. Four years ago, I came here as a little boy – but now I’m a man, and I belong here.“Kyle’s had a pretty tough year, it’s the first year of being a dad, I know that’s pretty impressive that he’s even here competing. But I want to see Kyle back at his biggest and his baddest and his bestest – I’d love to see that rivalry continue!”Chalmers, cheered on by his wife, Norwegian international swimmer Ingeborg Loyning with baby daughter Astrid, couldn’t land the 10th gold and 12th medal that would have taken him past the great Ian Thorpe as Australia’s most successful men’s swimmer ever at the Games.The 28-year-old still has a chance, though, in the 50m butterfly final, for which he’s qualified fastest, on the final day of competition. It shapes as his farewell to the Games.Admitting he knew the passing-of-the-baton moment was coming, Chalmers, the first to congratulate the young gun, shrugged: “I’m completely fine with it. In the medal presentation, I really said, ‘you know, this is your moment. I’m so proud of you, enjoy your moment, enjoy singing the anthem’. I truly am so proud of him.“I would love to get to that point [in 2028], but I’m also a realist and know that what is important to me now is my wife and daughter. And I really feel that I’ve won in life by having them, that if I don’t get to that point, I’m not going to be disappointed.“I have to be a realist at this point in my career, too. I’m not an 18-year-old kid that’s coming on, that’s got no other things going on in life.“I don’t want to be a selfish parent. I want to be there for her and work out what is the best possible thing. And I don’t mean that in any other way. I desperately want to be in LA, but you have to work that out being a parent.”Away from the pool, gymnasts Breanna Scott and Jesse Moore added to Australia’s gold medal bonanza, taking out individual apparatus titles in Glasgow.View image in fullscreenBreanna Scott on her way to gold in the women’s balance beam final.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockJust minutes after Scott nailed a flashy balance beam routine to take out the title on her speciality apparatus, Moore hit every mark on parallel bars to win another gold for Australia at Glasgow International Arena. Scott scored 13.933 points for her routine, beating Singapore’s Amanda Yap (13.233) and Lia-Monica Fontaine (13.00) of Canada.Scott finishes her campaign in Glasgow by winning her second gold medal of the Games, having earlier contributed to Australia’s dominant team all-around victory. It is Scott’s first individual gold medal, having also claimed silver in the women’s individual all-around.“[Balance beam] is definitely my favourite when it’s going well,” Scott said. “It’s kind of crazy, to be honest. It definitely hasn’t sunk in yet. The last three days have just been absolutely wild. The team gold was such a special medal for all of us, and that was really the main goal coming into this. All of us in finals, now getting these extra little medals is just topping it off.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026GymnasticsAustralia sportCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My fingers were underwater’: Amy Hunt settles for 100m silver in torrid conditions | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: New Zealand’s Zoe Hobbs won the women’s 100m in a personal best of 10.93sec, while Emmanuel Eseme surged to the men’s 100m title in 9.83
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: New Zealand’s Zoe Hobbs won the women’s 100m in a personal best of 10.93sec, while Emmanuel Eseme surged to the men’s 100m title in 9.83
Content: Zoe Hobbs (left) holds off England’s Amy Hunt to win Commonwealth Games gold in the women’s 100m.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenZoe Hobbs (left) holds off England’s Amy Hunt to win Commonwealth Games gold in the women’s 100m.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesCommonwealth Games 2026‘My fingers were underwater’: Amy Hunt settles for 100m silver in torrid conditionsNew Zealand’s Zoe Hobbs wins with 10.93secEmmanuel Eseme surges to men’s 100m victorySean Ingleat Scotstoun StadiumTue 28 Jul 2026 17.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a filthy summer’s night in Glasgow, Amy Hunt defied almost everything the elements dared to throw at her. The track was so wet that her fingernails were submerged underwater as she lined up. Her start was so horrendous it could have carried an X-certificate. And she spent most of the women’s 100m final sloshing through puddles. It was nearly enough.But while she hit top speed late in the race, it was too late to catch the New Zealander Zoe Hobbs, who ran the race of her life to takeCommonwealth Gamesgold in a personal best of 10.93sec.Commonwealth Games 2026: Hobbs and Eseme win 100m finals as Nowacki earns swimming gold for Jersey – liveRead moreFor Hunt there was at least a silver lining in coming second in 10.98, with Australia’s Torrie Lewis claiming bronze, after so much went wrong.“I had a really, really terrible first 60m,” Hunt explained. “I am a legitimate starter. But today I got it really badly wrong. I was able to dig myself out of the horrendous ditch that I dug in the first half of the race, but I think gold was definitely there for the taking.”Hunt made no excuses about the cold and the rain, but said: “It was pretty gross on the start line. My fingers were underwater, which is a bit novel. But you have to roll with the punches at champs, and bringing away a medal is the most important thing, no matter what happens.”Indeed it was so wet that several of her fake fingernails had come off – afterwards she pointed to them and her silver rings. “I need to start wearing some gold jewellery,” she joked, after adding another silver medal to the one she won over 200m at last year’sworld championships in Tokyo.And while nine Team England athletes have pulled out of these championships in the past week, Hunt also made an eloquent case for why it was important to show up.“I think it’s really important as a track athlete,” she said. “We don’t get much representation in terms of media. We’re not NBA players. We’re not on TV three times a week and everyone’s seeing our faces.“And it’s really important in terms of my journey and my legacy as an athlete,” she said. “I don’t want to go on my Wikipedia page in 30 years’ time and just see one or two medals. I want to see lists and lists of medals.”Earlier on a night where conditions could hardly have been more spiteful, Cameroon’s Emmanuel Eseme defied Australia’s Lachlan Kennedy in the final strides to take gold in the men’s 100m.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Eseme is all smiles after winning the men’s 100m final in a Commonwealth Games record.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersFor 95 metres, Kennedy ran a stormer. But moments before the line he stuttered slightly, as Eseme charged from third to first to come through in a Commonwealth Games record of 9.83sec. For Kennedy there was a compensation of a silver medal and an Australian record of 9.85.But this night will linger longest in memory for the rainageddon that settled over Glasgow and never stopped.As it hammered down, some high jumpers sported umbrellas in between jumps. Others winter coats. The Indian Pooja Singh, the 19-year-old Asian champion, took even fewer chances. She wore a thick coat, a woolly hat and gloves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionConditions had eased slightly by the time that the women’s high jump resumed at 9.08pm after a 90-minute delay. However conditions were far from ideal and England’s Morgan Lake went out early having failed three attempts at 1.82m, her opening height.Long after almost everyone had gone home it was finally won by Australia’s Eleanor Patterson, who jumped 1.96m, ahead of her compatriot Nicola Olyslagers.Other field events on the night were affected too. The first thrower in the hammer competition, Scotland’s Angela McAuslan-Kelly, found the protective net. So did Australia’s Stephanie Ratcliffe, who went second. No wonder there were ironic cheers when the third competitor to throw, England’s Charlotte Payne, found the field.But it turned out to be a great evening for Australia as Ky Robinson sprinted clear to win 10,000m gold in 27mins 48.93sec, ahead of India’s Gulveer Singh. Not far behind was the Isle of Man’s David Mullarkey, who won bronze – and his island’s first-ever track and field medal at a Commonwealth Games.Meanwhile, although Hunt left the track wanting more, she was eventually able to find perspective.“I might have a little glass of champagne,” she said. “Because I think you have to celebrate the moments. Otherwise, you kind of get 70 years old and think, have I even enjoyed my life?”And with that she broke into a broad smile.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026AthleticsCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jersey boy Filip Nowacki comes of age with showstopping gold | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jersey teenager Filip Nowacki led from start to finish to claim gold in the men’s 200m breaststroke, adding to the silver he got in the 100m version
Author: Yara El-Shaboury
Headline: Jersey teenager Filip Nowacki led from start to finish to claim gold in the men’s 200m breaststroke, adding to the silver he got in the 100m version
Content: Filip Nowacki enjoys the taste of success after winning the men's 200m breaststroke final at Tollcross Swimming Centre.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFilip Nowacki enjoys the taste of success after winning the men's 200m breaststroke final at Tollcross Swimming Centre.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Jersey boy Filip Nowacki comes of age with showstopping goldTeenager dominates men’s 200m breaststroke finalWin makes him island’s most successful Games athleteYara El-Shabouryat Tollcross Swimming CentreTue 28 Jul 2026 17.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilip Nowacki secured his status as Jersey’s most successfulCommonwealth Gamesathlete by storming to a historic gold medal in the men’s 200m breaststroke.The 18-year-old led from start to finish in a commanding display, touching the wall in 2min 07.87sec before erupting in celebration as he climbed on to the lane dividers and slapped the water in delight while soaking up the enthusiastic applause as Jersey flags waved. Canada’s Oliver Dawson won silver, with Australia’s Olympic champion, Zac Stubblety-Cook, taking bronze.It’s ‘Chico’ time: Glasgow curry restaurateur ready to face ‘creme de la creme’ of lawn bowlsRead more“It’s completely surreal,” said Nowacki. “Coming from an island like Jersey and competing against athletes from Australia, Canada, England and the other home nations is very special. To get my hand on the wall first in such a great time, and to back up the 59.7 I swam last year, is really special.”Having captured silver in the 100m breaststroke earlier in the Games, Nowacki arrived as the favourite and delivered under the weight of expectation. The teenager took control from the opening 50m, remained in front at halfway and produced a superb pull-out after the turn to extend his advantage.By the 150m mark, Nowacki had opened up a lead of more than seven-tenths of a second and never looked in danger of surrendering it, powering home to claim Jersey’s first Commonwealth swimming gold.It was Jersey’s first Commonwealth gold medal in any sport since Colin Mallett won the individual fullbore shooting title in Auckland in 1990 before teaming up with his father, Cliff, to take bronze in the pairs.Nowacki’s triumph marks another milestone in the remarkable rise of the world junior and British senior champion, who is widely viewed as the heir to the British breaststroke great Adam Ramsay-Peaty, having already finished ahead of the Olympic champion in the 100m breaststroke final in Glasgow. He has made it no secret that he is aiming for a place at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games with Team GB.“I’ve said before that the water doesn’t care who I am now, if I can’t do it again next year,” he said. “It’s all about continuing to track my progress over the next couple of weeks, then having a good summer break and consolidating everything I’ve been doing. After that, it’s about improving again next year and the year after.”View image in fullscreenAmalie Smith on her way to bronze in the 200m individual medley, adding to the silver she secured in the 400m individual medley.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianScotland produced a dramatic late comeback to claim bronze in the mixed 4x100m medley relay with Duncan Scott delivering a stunning anchor leg in front of a jubilant home crowd. Scott dived into the pool in sixth place but powered through the field with a blistering 48.03sec freestyle split to haul Scotland on to the podium, overtaking Canada in the closing stages.Australia claimed gold in a record time of 3min 40.46sec. The quartet of Iona Anderson, Sam Williamson, Matthew Temple and Meg Harris secured victory to match Australia’s Commonwealth Games record haul of 28 swimming gold medals.South Africa took silver after Pieter Coetze laid the foundations with a Games record backstroke leg to give his team an early advantage, although they were unable to hold off Australia over the remaining legs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScotland’s relay featured Katie Ward on backstroke, Kara Hanlon Evans on breaststroke, and Keanna Macinnes on butterfly before Scott’s remarkable freestyle anchor sealed bronze. England, featuring Ramsay-Peaty, finished sixth despite hopes of challenging for gold.England’s teenage sensation Amalie Smith claimed her second medal of the Games with bronze in the women’s 200m individual medley. The 16-year-old, who won silver in the 400m individual medley on her Games debut on Monday, again impressed against an experienced international field, finishing third behind Australia’s Jenna Forrester and South Africa’s Aimee Canny.“It’s quite hard to believe I’m here at 16,” Smith said. “If you’d said to me last year I’d come away from the Commonwealth Games with two medals around my neck, I wouldn’t have believed it. I still can’t quite believe it to be honest.”Smith qualified third fastest for the final, with Forrester the quickest and the favourite for gold. Scotland’s Katie Shanahan delighted the home crowd by leading at the halfway stage after 100m, while Smith remained firmly in contention throughout. The English teenager briefly hit the front during the closing stages before Forrester surged clear to win in 2:09.24, with Canny securing silver.Smith held on for bronze, adding another podium finish to an outstanding first Commonwealth Games campaign. Shanahan narrowly missed out on a medal in fourth after her fast start, while Wood was unable to challenge for the podium.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026SwimmingCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Moore stays ice cool on Scandinavia to lift Goodwood Cup after loose horse drama | Glorious Goodwood | The Guardian
description: A riderless horse led the field for much of the way and veered across the leaders with three furlongs to run in a dramatic Goodwood Cup
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: A riderless horse led the field for much of the way and veered across the leaders with three furlongs to run in a dramatic Goodwood Cup
Content: Ryan Moore rides Scandinavia to victory in the Goodwood Cup, finishing behind the loose horse.Photograph: Matt Alexander Media Assignments/PAView image in fullscreenRyan Moore rides Scandinavia to victory in the Goodwood Cup, finishing behind the loose horse.Photograph: Matt Alexander Media Assignments/PAGlorious GoodwoodMoore stays ice cool on Scandinavia to lift Goodwood Cup after loose horse dramaJockey fell off Amiloc as horse was leaving stallsTrawlerman lost all momentum after interferenceGreg Woodat GoodwoodTue 28 Jul 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScandinavia confirmed the form of his Ascot Gold Cup defeat of Trawlerman with a wide-margin win in the Group One Goodwood Cup on Tuesday, but the bare result does not tell the full story of a race in which a riderless horse led the field for much of the way and veered across the leaders with three furlongs to run.The drama began at the start, when Hector Crouch was unshipped from Amiloc, the jockey catching his foot on the stalls as the horse jinked to the right. The gelding then worked his way to the head of the field with nearly 12 furlongs still to run and, having veered wide on the home turn, drifted sharply across both Scandinavia and Trawlerman soon afterwards.Jockey Club staff cull leaves Derby feeling flat with Ascot and Goodwood riding highRead moreScandinavia, the favourite, was half a length behind Trawlerman at the time andRyan Moore, his rider, did not stop riding but William Buick, on Trawlerman, lost all momentum.
