Scandinavia’s eventual winning margin of eight and a half lengths – with the riderless Amiloc still in front of him – suggests that the result was not affected, but the crowd was certainly denied the spectacle of two top-class stayers battling to the line.“It’s significant,” Buick said. “It’s hard to say how significant but he’s a horse who is a Gold Cup winner [in 2025], so he stays.“To try to manoeuvre around a loose horse is never easy and my worry was if I found myself on his outside, I could give away a lot of ground and be on the stands side, theoretically. I went the shortest route and he only got in my way in the most important part of the race.”Moore, meanwhile, felt that the sight of a horse galloping in a clear lead might have benefited his mount. “It was nice for him to have a horse to follow all the way,” Moore said. “He probably thinks he got beat. His stride never shortened, he just kept galloping all the way to the line. He’s a high-class horse and hopefully there’s a few more good days to come.”Lake Forest, who finished fast under Cieren Fallon to take the Group Two Lennox Stakes by a neck, could attempt to complete a remarkable double in the Group One Sussex Stakes here on Wednesday.“I don’t see why he can’t come here again tomorrow, that’s the plan,” Maureen Haggas, the wife of Lake Forest’s trainer, William, said.View image in fullscreenKaiya Fraser and Dr Rascal (left) find a way through for victory.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PA“We’ll see how he is. If we’re happy with him, then why not? He’s a five‑year-old gelding and he hasn’t got to travel anywhere. We don’t know about [the step up to] a mile, but he stays seven well.”Earlier on the card, Kaiya Fraser came up with an early candidate for ride of the meeting as he threaded Oliver Cole’s Dr Rascal through a narrow gap against the far rail to take the Group Two Vintage Stakes by half a length.Fraser, who was born and raised in Hackney, did not sit on a horse until enrolling on a foundation course for apprentice riders at the British Racing School in Newmarket as a 16‑year‑old. “It means everything, this is what we wake up for every morning,” Fraser said.“I’ve put so much hard work in to get where I am today, and all the people around who have helped me – my agent James Forrest, and all the owners and trainers who put me up – I’m very grateful to them and I wouldn’t be here if it wasn’t for them.”Echo to follow in hoofprints of FrankelBow Echo was the most impressive winner of the 2,000 Guineas since Frankel at Newmarket in May, and he will further enhance his status as one of the finest milers of recent decades if he can extend his unbeaten record to six starts in the Group One Sussex Stakes atGlorious Goodwoodon Wednesday.The parallels with the greatest Flat horse of recent decades do not end there, as Bow Echo’s next start was a less convincing success in the St James’s Palace Stakes at Royal Ascot. Frankel soon set the record straight, though, with a decisive success on the Sussex downs and there are sound reasons to think that Bow Echo can do the same.Bow Echo was hampered in the early stages at Ascot and was lit up in the first half-mile, before being forced wide into the straight. He then held on by a short-head from Gstaad, who was nearly three lengths adrift in second at Newmarket.Gstaad is back for a third tilt at Bow Echo on Wednesday, but the pacey four-year-old, Opera Ballo, may be a bigger danger from a low draw at a front-runner’s track.Bow Echo (4.10), though, has several pounds to spare on Charlie Appleby’s colt on the ratings, has also drawn well in one and has scope to improve further after just five starts.Goodwood 1.50Tierra Del Torohas been better than the bare result on his last two starts and should be less susceptible to traffic problems in this smaller field.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Wednesday tipsShowGoodwood1.50 Tierra Del Toro (nb) 2.25 Wild Blossom 3.00 Zanthos 3.35 Adonius 4.10 Bow Echo 5.00 Silver Wraith 5.40 Zarathos (nap)Redcar2.05 Kats Bob 2.40 Areti 3.15 Leopards Rock 3.50 Homestrait 4.20 Stormy Pearl 4.50 That’s My Boy LukeSandown5.45 Happy Banner 6.15 Justcallemepete 6.50 King High 7.25 Galba 8.00 Ammoony 8.30 KakirraLeicester5.55 Fairy Well 6.27 My Maria 7.02 Moving Shadow 7.37 Calafrio 8.10 Clocker 8.40 SpiritofthebluesWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Goodwood 2.25Karl Burke’sWild Blossomshould appreciate the slight drop in grade after finishing mid-division in a Group Two at Royal Ascot.Goodwood 3.00Last year’s impressive Rockfel winner,Zanthos, has failed to fire so far this season but this return to seven furlongs should suit.Goodwood 3.35Adoniushas had a break since his win at Chester in early May and will appreciate this speed test.Explore more on these topicsGlorious GoodwoodRyan MooreHorse racingHorse racing tipsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spies in the sky: how worried should we be about the arrival of AI-enabled smart lamp-posts? | Surveillance | The Guardian
description: The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?
Content: Hyper-surveillance.SurveillanceSpies in the sky: how worried should we be about the arrival of AI-enabled smart lamp-posts?The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?Zoe WilliamsTue 28 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow would you feel if your neighbourhood lamp-posts could recognise your number plate, and also your face? Maybe you wouldn’t mind, given how long we’ve had automatic number plate recognition and CCTV. What about if that lamp-post could power itself through its own solar panels, and perhaps find another use for any extra power generated – that would be good, right? This is what Conflow Power Group (CPG) inWarwickshireclaims for its iLamps, the first of their kind in the UK.What if lamp-posts had the potential to incorporate new AI capability – gait analysis, suspicious behaviours – that you haven’t even heard of? This is what the organisation Big Brother Watch worries about. And what if the home secretary had explicitly saidshe believed in a “panopticon state”– that is, a state that could watch you at all times (as Shabana Mahmood already has) – and what if she still had a job when the lamp-post eyes got their updates? Or what if the next home secretary was even keener on hyper-surveillance (hard to imagine), and the street apparatus was already in place? What about all the data this would harvest – who would own it?It’s drizzling in Warwickshire, where I’m hoping to answer at least some of these questions in the hospital car park where some of these new “smart” lamp-posts have been installed. But if it wasn’t for me, nobody would probably be talking about them, not least because few have heard anything about them. Not many people know that the iLamp is not just solar-powered but can “double as a revenue-generating distributed AI datacentre”, according to CPG, let alone what that means. And nobody, not even me, knows how much of that potential functionality has been realised in the UK model – only what CPG has announced: that it has signed an agreement with the government of Katsina state, Nigeria, to supply it with 50,000 of these iLamps, which have additional surveillance potential for both vehicles and faces. CPG’s chairman, Edward Fitzpatrick,told the BBC World Service’s Tech Life programmethat the lamp-posts could ultimately track down missing persons or fight crime, with the proviso that this would only be developed in partnership “with the relevant authority”.CPG has been “extensively covered by worldwide media”, according to its own statement, and doesn’t take further questions, directing the media to its online material. As for the Warwickshire lamp-posts, the local authority directs all questions to the hospital, and the hospital doesn’t respond. Fair play – it’s a hospital.View image in fullscreenA London lamp-post well equipped with cameras.Photograph: Shomos Uddin/Getty ImagesA number of local residents have taken refuge from the rain in a bus shelter, most of them waiting for a partner to pick them up, and many are willing to chat. Karl, 52, who has been in a pub nearby, speaks for almost everyone when he says: “The town centre is already full of cameras, and it’s fine. You don’t mind them being there unless you’re up to no good.” No amount of loaded questions (What if you were doing something that was legal today but illegal in a year? What if the surveillance became predictive rather than reactive? What if you didn’t want anyone to know you’d been to the hospital? What if you weren’t supposed to be in a pub? Don’t you think you should at least have been asked whether you wanted it?) can separate anyone I speak to from the view that facial recognition is a tolerable part of life for a right-thinking citizen.Tejal, 41, also waiting at the hospital bus stop, says: “I think we have to move on and accept that things change.” She’s a radiologist, and just seeing AI’s capability in her own sector makes her extremely anxious about AI as a whole. “I have anxieties for my children,” she says. That they won’t find entry-level jobs? “That, and that they’ll lose the ability to celebrate and find joy from the things we used to.” Privacy concerns do seem comparatively minor, compared with that.Policy and technical experts are sceptical about some of the claims made for smart lamp-posts. Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, says: “We see this quite often where local councils or other government agencies are … ‘swindled’ is a strong word, but they’re sold these tools as magic wands when there are limitations to what they can actually do.”Prof Rabih Bashroush, director of the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Data Innovation at the University of East London, is blunt: “AI datacentres? There’s absolutely no chance this will fly: the technology doesn’t work, there’s not enough power, the economics won’t work …” Solar power to run the iLamps off-grid might work in Nigeria, but in Britain the amount generated by the lamp-posts is “negligible”, he says. You might be able to run an app that was “not mission critical, that you didn’t mind shutting down for a few days” – such as recognising whether a parking spot was occupied – but bigger claims for facial recognition are “just hype. Forget it – this has no legs.”If he sounds impatient, it’s because he is: “It’s getting more and more difficult to get an independent opinion on things, because a lot of experts are in the industry now, and their view would have to align with their organisation,” he says. So a company might make a large claim, including a few AI buzzwords, ahead of a funding round; engineers don’t contradict them, local authorities don’t understand them and nobody else is even aware that anything has moved on since CCTV was invented.View image in fullscreenThe Metropolitan Police trialling a facial recognition system in London last May.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersChaggar goes to great lengths to explain the conceptual difference between facial recognition and CCTV: “Facial recognition is not just passively recalling something, unlike CCTV, which you then check after the fact. What facial recognition does is real-time identity check: it’s much more like a fingerprint or DNA. It’s not like a passport – you can’t get another face.”Another problem, Chaggar says, is that, “a lot of these technologies and infrastructures have capacity to add function later. Hammersmith and Fulham [in London] are updating their CCTV and it’s possible to embed facial recognition, monitor suspicious shopping behaviour, add aggression detection. So you can just turn the switch and it’s all there overnight.” A friend who lives in Fulham sent, by chance, a picture of a camera above a parking restrictions sign – it looks like a cross between Darth Vader and a beetle, and it whirrs as you go past, as if to indicate that it’s following your movements.This throws up all the ageless privacy concerns, and it’s interesting how many people will wave away CCTV as a fact of modern life, but spontaneously raise how much they absolutely hate being listened to by their phone. Karl says: “I was talking to my mother the other day about dog nail clippers, and the advert came up on my phone that evening. I had my microphone off. I don’t even have a dog!” His friend Bob, 48, has ended up functionally off-grid, with no computer and a basic brick phone – a policymaker would probably describe him as “excluded” – simply because “some people like to be private”.View image in fullscreenActing suspiciously, or just a bit chilly?Photograph: Posed by model; David Wall/Getty ImagesAnother question about facial recognition software is: exactly how good are algorithms at detecting aggression and suspicious behaviour? “A lot of the software is pseudo-scientific,” Chaggar says. “So a company might try to sell emotion-detection, [claiming that] if people are walking through a train station, you can see if they’re angry or they’re about to be aggressive. There’s very little evidence to suggest that it’s accurate. If you’re a disabled person who moves differently, you might be flagged and have an intervention.” But the real question local authorities and any agents of the state should ask themselves, Chaggar says, is: “Are you happy to have your political enemies having these capabilities? Because you’re building an infrastructure that is here to stay.”You can see that writ large in policing – the Home Office signed off on the use of facial recognition more than a decade ago, and the police have been “essentially using the public as guinea pigs for the past 10 years,” Chaggar says. What happens when the home secretary tells BBC 5 Live,as she did earlier this year, that “you can’t enjoy any of your liberties in any country if you’re not safe”? This sledgehammer logic, in which all liberties are secondary to the state’s rights as your protector, is chilling from a supposedly leftwing government. But the greater worry is that this doesn’t feel like the right time in politics to roll the dice on surveillance technology, basing our acceptance of it on the assumption that all future governments will be pro-social and democratic.View image in fullscreen‘If you haven’t got anything to hide, I don’t see how it would be a problem.’Photograph: Justin Paget/Getty ImagesWherever there’s potential to collect data, it throws up the question of who owns it: Bashroush used to work with the Internet of Things, the European Commission’s attempt to “connect the physical world to a digital environment”. “This was way back, before exiting Europe,” he remembers. “One of the challenges we saw was with a supplier [who was] basically collecting garbage from homes in the Netherlands, then optimising truck journeys and planning, based on your habits. The council that ran the programme was very happy with it, and tried to open the bidding a year later to get a more competitive price. The company said, ‘Sure, but the data is ours.’” That never got resolved: the contracts had been poorly constructed and the local authority lost the data.If you want to see facial recognition go wrong without even any authoritarian intent or tech chicanery, you just have to look at the retail sector, where it’s already widely in use to prevent shoplifting. “We’ve seen misidentification by the police,” Chaggar says, “but in retail, when people are misidentified, it’s Kafkaesque. You’re justblacklisted from the store.”And again, how much do people care, really? If you’re not allowed in a shop and you don’t know why; if a private company has a contract with your NHS trust, vaunting tech that isn’t operational yet and might never work, but nobody told, let alone asked, you; if the home secretary thinks it’s fine for the eyes of the state to be on you at all times – are these the building blocks of a dystopia, or do they just remind us how we used to describe dystopia, back before these surveillance capabilities existed?The New Yorker essayist Ted Chiangwrote some time agoabout the habit of projecting on to AI negatives that were actually not about tech but about economic systems, concluding: “Capitalism is the machine that will do whatever it takes to prevent us from turning it off.” Am I projecting on to AI and surveillance tech anxieties that are really about authoritarian politics?“Well, if you haven’t got anything to hide,” says Sarah, 55, “I can’t see how it would be a problem. I’m presuming they’re actually lamps as well?”Explore more on these topicsSurveillanceWarwickshireFacial recognitionAI (artificial intelligence)Data protectionDatacentresfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Home Office used ‘AI hallucinated’ information to refuse asylum claim, judge suggests | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Upper tribunal unable to find document cited in case and claims it is ‘analogous to relying on bogus evidence’
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Upper tribunal unable to find document cited in case and claims it is ‘analogous to relying on bogus evidence’
Content: The case relates to a Moroccan woman and her child who fled the country after experiencing extreme violence.Photograph: gbimages/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe case relates to a Moroccan woman and her child who fled the country after experiencing extreme violence.Photograph: gbimages/AlamyImmigration and asylumHome Office used ‘AI hallucinated’ information to refuse asylum claim, judge suggestsUpper tribunal unable to find document cited in case and claims it is ‘analogous to relying on bogus evidence’Diane TaylorTue 28 Jul 2026 08.39 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA senior judge has accused theHome Officeof relying on “AI hallucinated” information to refuse an asylum claim.The case relates to a Moroccan woman and her child who fled her country after experiencing forced underage marriage and extreme violence, including rape. The woman claimed asylum on the basis of fears that she would be killed by her husband: a powerful, previously convicted criminal.The Home Office refused her case, citing evidence from a supposedly independent and authoritative document known as a country policy information note (CPIN), which they said confirmed that Morocco would be safe for her.But the document could not be found, although its existence was relied upon by a judge who rejected her appeal against the Home Office’s refusal decision in an immigration court known as the first-tier tribunal.The woman lodged a further appeal to a more senior court, the upper tribunal, where another judge raised concerns about the unlocated document. In a decision on 14 July, the judge said: “It appears that no such CPIN has ever existed.”He added in relation to the missing document: “No such document has been located in the public domain and moreover the Home Office’s country policy and information team has been unable to confirm its existence.”He said that after looking at the Home Office’s letter refusing the woman’s asylum claim, “it bears hallmarks consistent with the use of artificial intelligence. It may therefore transpire that references to country information note Morocco July 2021 in that letter are a result of an AI ‘hallucination’. If so that would represent an extremely serious failing on the part of the respondent [the Home Office].”In a further critical statement, the judge said that relying on a document that did not exist was “analogous to relying on bogus evidence”. He determined that the issue was a “procedural irregularity”.The Guardian asked the Home Office if the document existed and where it was. After initially sending a link to an archive where the document could not be found, the Home Office produced a different document, a piece of unpublished internal guidance known as a country information note (CIN).No CPIN has been published on Morocco since 2017. In the course of the case, the Home Office’s references changed from the internal guidance CIN to the CPIN, which are generally treated as authoritative by judges.Britain promised to protect Hongkongers from China. Why does it now seem ready to sacrifice them? | Nathan LawRead moreThe internal document, which was never disclosed to the court in legal proceedings, does not conclude that Morocco is a safe country for the forcible return of women such as the one appealing against the decision.It states that in 2018 exemptions were made granting 40,000 child marriages, one-fifth of the total marriages that year. It adds that Morocco’s laws do not explicitly criminalise marital rape and that women who report this may be criminalised for engaging in sex outside marriage if they are disbelieved by the authorities.Home Office sources said they were able to provide additional information about the case that the judge had requested.A Home Office spokesperson said: “The home secretary is restoring order and control to our asylum system by removing incentives drawing illegal migrants to the UK and ramping up removals of those with no right to be on British soil.“We keep our asylum system under constant review. Claims are always considered on their individual merits and based on the latest evidence to ensure only those in genuine need are granted UK protection.”The woman’s case continues.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficenewsShareReuse this content

title: Debate over AI’s future divides Silicon Valley as China gains ground | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Open-source questions stir frank discussion – and both sides have clear economic incentives for where they land
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Open-source questions stir frank discussion – and both sides have clear economic incentives for where they land
Content: The Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Hung, at an event in Tokyo earlier in July.Photograph: Manami Yamada/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Hung, at an event in Tokyo earlier in July.Photograph: Manami Yamada/ReutersTechScape newsletterAI (artificial intelligence)Debate over AI’s future divides Silicon Valley as China gains groundOpen-source questions stir frank discussion – and both sides have clear economic incentives for where they landBlake Montgomery,Nick Robins-EarlyandDara KerrTue 28 Jul 2026 09.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, and welcome to TechScape. This week we’ll be looking at a debate over the future of artificial intelligence that’s dividing the tech industry, as well as how the European Union gave Google a slap on the wrist for anti-competitive behavior. And we’ll also catch you up on the avalanche of lawsuits accusing social media companies of getting young people addicted to their products.Silicon Valley’s divide over the future of AIOver the past week some of the biggest names in tech have weighed in on a debate about the future of artificial intelligence, one which has resurged after the release of new Chinese AI models. Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, the Microsoft CEO, Satya Nadella, and Elon Musk have all posted in recent days about the need for open-source AI – which, broadly speaking, refers to the types of AI models that are freely available and allow users to modify them.“Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Huang said in his first ever post on X.Huang’s post on Friday also linked toan open letterstarted by Microsoft that was signed by a wide range of prominent venture capital firms and tech companies including SpaceX, Nvidia, Palantir and Andreessen Horowitz. The letter argued that open models were necessary for “creating opportunities for innovation and prosperity across the country” and that the tech industry, as well as the US government, should embrace them.Notably absent from the letter was Anthropic, which has taken the other side in the debate. The company has long argued that open-source AI is dangerous because it is harder to regulate and put safety guardrails on than proprietary models like their Claude chatbot. OpenAI, which did sign Microsoft’s letter, has also made similar arguments in the past. Last week, Dean Ball, the head of strategic futures at OpenAI,warned on Xthat embracing an open-source policy would benefit China and could lead to “full AI communism”.Both sides in this fight also have clear economic incentives for where they land on open-source AI. Venture capital firms have been concerned about the rising AI costs to businesses, while chip companies like Nvidia benefit from more widespread demand for their products.Anthropicand OpenAI, meanwhile, have developed a sizable lead over other frontier AI firms in the US, and cheaper, more easily accessible open-source models present an obvious challenge to their dominance.The debate over the benefits and drawbacks of open-source AI has been a longstanding issue in the tech industry, but what’s bringing it to a head this month is the release of a new Chinese AI open source model that can compete with some of the best American-made counterparts. The model, called Kimi K3, hasrattled Silicon Valley and the White Houseas executives and officials argue how to respond.Just as the tech industry is split on open models, the Trump administration is similarly divided. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, last week accused the Chinese models of stealing US intellectual property to create their products, claiming the White House could sanction foreign AI labs. Now, the administration appears to be unable to agree on whether to impose restrictions on Chinese products, like Kimi K3, or whether to keep the status quo since some American companies have become reliant on these cheaper models.Social media companies settle another major lawsuit just before trialView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Matt Cardy/Getty ImagesAfter a jurydelivered a bruising lossto Meta and YouTube in March, finding the companies liable for inflicting harm on young people, the tech firms have since avoided going back to court. Another lawsuit in a series of thousands of cases over social media addiction and harm to children was slated to go to trial in Los Angeles on Monday, but at the 11th hour thetwo sides brokered a deal.The case was brought by a 15-year-old boy from Florida with the initials RKC. He said he started using social media when he was about eight, and quickly became addicted. He lost sleep and suffered from depression and anxiety, according to court filings. His lawsuit was filed against YouTube, TikTok, Snap and Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram.YouTube, TikTok and Snap settled with RKC over the past few weeks. (TikTok and Snap also settled in the March lawsuit). Meta came to a deal with RKC last week, in which he dropped his claims without receiving payment, the company said. While Meta called his suit “baseless”, the boy’s lawyers said he had “concerns about enduring a grueling weeks-long trial”.Meta’s lawyers areknown for aggressive tacticsthat dig into plaintiffs’ personal and family history. During the first trial in March, the company combed through the plaintiff’s therapy notes and called on doctors to testify about examples of personal conflict in the young woman’s life. RKC’s lawyers say he elected to withdraw his claims and “focus on his recovery ⁠and engage in therapy as he aspires to have a ​normal life”.This is the second major trial that the four social media companies have circumvented since March. All of the companies settled a similar suit that was to go to trial in June. It wasbrought by a Kentucky school districtover claims that the tech firms deliberately designed addictive products that led to children being harmed.But thousands more cases remain against the four companies, filed by families, school districts and state attorneys general.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeparately, 42 individual states are suing Meta alone, so it hasn’t fully escaped the court room. It lost a major lawsuit to New Mexico in March with a jury ordering it topay $375m in civil penalties. And on Monday,opening arguments began in another trialagainst Meta, brought by Tennessee, in which the state called the company “an addiction machine”.A federal lawsuit against Meta, brought by attorneys general from 29 states, is also set to go to trial on 18 August in Oakland, California.Google’s slap on the wristView image in fullscreenThe Google logo at the CES show in Las Vegas in 2024.Photograph: Steve Marcus/ReutersThe European Union fined Google about $1bn last week for violations of the Digital Markets Act, finding that the company prioritized its own services over those of competitors. The day the EU announced its decision, Google released its quarterly earnings report, which declared it had made $120bn in profits in just three months – a 24% increase that beat Wall Street expectations.Google’s enormous earnings underscore how much of the regulatory scrutiny it faces often amounts to a slap on the wrist. The EU’s fine is a small dent in the tech behemoth’s overall profits and one that is unlikely to pose any real threat to its operations.More concerning for Google last week was a 7% tumble in the value of its stock, which followed company executives announcing they had revised the company’s capital expenditure upwards to nearly $205bn. The company’s free cashflow, the amount of money it can reinvest after paying for operating expenses and capital expenditure, also turned negative after reaching stratospheric heights in recent years. In basic terms, Google is spending a gargantuan amount of money, more than anyone on Wall Street expected, and investors are worried it may not pay off.Read moreEU fines Google €890m for competition breaches over search and appsExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)TechScape newsletterChinaUS foreign policyAsia PacificNvidiaAnthropicOpenAInewslettersShareReuse this content

title: South Korean stock market at three-month low as AI sell-off intensifies | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: Samsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competition
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Samsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competition
Content: Analysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending.Photograph: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAnalysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending.Photograph: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/ShutterstockStock marketsSouth Korean stock market at three-month low as AI sell-off intensifiesSamsung and SK Hynix fall by more than 10% amid renewed fears over AI spending and Chinese competitionBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaandGraeme WeardenTue 28 Jul 2026 13.43 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sell-off in AI stocks has intensified, driving South Korea’s stock market down to its lowest level in three months.Investors continued to ditch chip stocks on Tuesday, amid rising concerns about the huge amount of borrowing among AI companies to fund their datacentre expansion plans.The South Korean semiconductor companies SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell by more than 10%, dragging the country’s Kospi share index down by 11.5% to its lowest point since mid-April.US chip stocks extended their recent losses when Wall Street opened on Tuesday, with Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital Corp and Seagate Technology all down by more than 4%.The Nasdaq 100 index of leading tech stocks fell by as much as 1.8% at one point, briefly taken into market correction territory with stocks more than 10% below their early June record high. They later rebounded to settle roughly flat on the day.Apple becomes second ever $5tn company as investors flee AI stocksRead moreApple bucked the trend, rising to briefly become the second ever company to pass the $5tn (£3.76tn) valuation mark as investors losing confidence in AI stocks sought a safe haven.Analysts attributed the tech sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending, and competition from cheaper Chinese companies, aftera report by The Informationthat China had begun mass production of homegrown deep ultraviolet (DUV) chip-making tools.“We believe the market was likely spooked by the progress of China’s chip-making equipment capabilities, and was worried that this progress would threaten the competitive position of global chip making and chip equipment leaders,” said Jing Jie Yu, an equity analyst at Morningstar, adding that the sell-off was “largely a kneejerk reaction and overdone”.On Monday, shares in the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT rose by 466% when it floated on the Shanghai stock exchange, underlining China’s drive to create its own AI supply chain.Investors may also be growing jittery aboutthe “circular funding”at the heart of the AI industry, through which artificial intelligence firms finance one another.On Monday, the Wall Street Journal reported thatNvidiawas in discussions with OpenAI about providing $250bn (£188bn) for a massive datacentre project in Ohio. Backing from Nvidia, which has an investment grade credit rating, could make it less expensive to raise funding for the project.News of the talks knocked Nvidia’s shares on Monday; they closed 5% lower, while the cost of insuring the chip company’s debt against default using a credit default swap (CDS) rose.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The market reaction to the Nvidia news was swift. Nvidia fell 5% and closed the session below the $200-per-share mark. More importantly, Nvidia’s five-year CDS spiked, suggesting that it may not yet be the right time to buy the dip,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote.Some analysts have suggested that Beijing, trying to win a tech war with the US, is providing US companies with cheap AI systems, undercutting attempts by Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft and Google to dominate the spread of AI tools.Danni Hewson, the head of financial analysis at the stockbroker AJ Bell, said investors were braced for more AI companies to warn about their outlook, further undermining confidence in the sector.“Nerves about the huge amount of cash being splashed have been building for months. Investors will be keen to hear how those massive sums of cash have been utilised by mega caps like Microsoft and Meta and, crucially, what returns are being made on those investments,” she said.“Chip stocks have once again led declines as the market flexes, some companies like Amazon are upping their own chip capabilities, and China’s CXMT stock market debut has cemented fears about a lost market for US companies constrained by trading restrictions.”London and European exchanges bucked the trend on Tuesday. The FTSE 100 index of leading UK companies rose 89 points to 10,871 while the Paris CAC 40 edged 52 points higher to 8,458.Explore more on these topicsStock marketsAI (artificial intelligence)NvidiaSouth KoreanewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta disregarded its own research on teen harm, Tennessee lawyers tell jury | Meta | The Guardian
description: In opening statements, state argued Meta’s own research showed it harmed teens while firm’s attorneys pointed to transparency
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: In opening statements, state argued Meta’s own research showed it harmed teens while firm’s attorneys pointed to transparency
Content: Teenagers pose for a photo while holding smartphones in front of an Instagram logo.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenTeenagers pose for a photo while holding smartphones in front of an Instagram logo.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersMetaMeta disregarded its own research on teen harm, Tennessee lawyers tell juryIn opening statements, state argued Meta’s own research showed it harmed teens while firm’s attorneys pointed to transparencyDara Kerrand agenciesMon 27 Jul 2026 21.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe long-awaited trial between the social media company Meta and the state ofTennesseebegan proceedings on Monday. Attorneys for Tennessee told a jury in Nashville that Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, disregarded internal research about its platform’s impact on teenagers, while the company sought ⁠to maximize profit from those young users.During ⁠opening statements in a seven-week ​trial in state court, the state’s lawyers saidMetaresearchers repeatedly flagged teenagers’ compulsive use of the platform – leading to eating disorders, depression and self-harm. But despite those warnings, Meta did not ⁠disable features such as autoplay, notifications and infinite scroll which, the lawyers said, were designed to keep teens on Instagram as long as possible and increase the number of ads they viewed.An attorney for Meta countered the company has been transparent ⁠about the risks teens face on Instagram and the amount of dangerous content it finds. The company works hard to find problems and fix them, the attorney said.How AI may drive union-resistant tech workers to the bargaining tableRead moreTennessee’s lawsuit is one of 42 cases brought against Meta by individual states across the US. It comes after the companysuffered a damaging loss in New Mexicoin March, where a jury found the company liable for harming children and ordered it to pay $375m in civil penalties. It also comes as thousands of other lawsuits have been filed against Meta and other social media companies by families, school districts and state attorneys general.The lawsuit in Tennessee, filed by the office of the attorney general, Jonathan Skrmetti, seeks financial penalties ‌and a court order directing Instagram to modify aspects of the platform that the state says are harmful to teens’ mental health.If the jury finds ‌Meta liable, the trial will enter a second phase where the judge will decide damages.During the opening statements, Tom Cartmell, a lawyer for the state, said Instagram triggers dopamine hits that promote addiction and that has a particularly strong impact on the brains of kids.Cartmell also showed the jury an internal document from 2017 in which Meta product managers wrote that features such as notifications and infinite scroll “are inherently at odds with well-being” and said that the company needed to warn ​the public.“This warning never came,” Cartmell said.Kevin Huff, a lawyer for Meta, said documents such as those Cartmell cited were proof that the company was searching for problems on its platforms, so it can improve them. The company had developed tools to help limit problematic use of Instagram, Huff said, and sought to empower teachers and parents to help keep teens safe.“We think the evidence will show that Meta is doing its part and empowering others to ​do their part, because protecting teens online is a ​shared responsibility,” Huff said. “It takes a village.”The next lawsuit over social media addiction and harm to children is slated to go to trial next month in Oakland, California. It will be the first federal trial against Meta and was brought by attorneys general from 29 states.Explore more on these topicsMetaTennesseeChildrennewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple becomes second $5tn company as investors flee AI stocks | Apple | The Guardian
description: Share price rally driven by strong product demand as well as decision to sit out AI spending race, amid wider tech sell-off
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Share price rally driven by strong product demand as well as decision to sit out AI spending race, amid wider tech sell-off
Content: Apple’s shares hit a session high ⁠of $342.89 on Tuesday.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APView image in fullscreenApple’s shares hit a session high ⁠of $342.89 on Tuesday.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APAppleApple becomes second $5tn company as investors flee AI stocksShare price rally driven by strong product demand as well as decision to sit out AI spending race, amid wider tech sell-offGraeme Weardenand agencyTue 28 Jul 2026 16.33 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple has become only the second company to pass the $5tn valuation mark, as it benefited from investors fleeing AI and semiconductor stocks amid a wider tech sell-off.The iPhone maker’s shares hit a session high ⁠of $342.89 on Tuesday, giving it a market ⁠capitalisation of $5.04tn (£3.78tn), then eased back down to $340.08 – around the $5tn mark.Applebecame the world’s most valuable companyearlier this month, overtaking the chip giant Nvidia, which had been ⁠at the top since June 2025 and becamethe first company to breach the $5tn thresholdlast October.The US consumer electronics company’s rally has been driven ⁠as much by strong demand for its products as its decision to sit out the ​AI spending race that is sapping cash ‌flows at big tech ‌rivals.Its fresh high valuation came amid an intensifyingsell-off of AI stocks around the worlddriven by rising concerns about AI companies’ borrowing to fund datacentre expansion.US chip stocks extended their recent losses when Wall Street opened on Tuesday, with Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital and Seagate Technology all down by more than 4%.The Nasdaq 100 index of leading tech stocks fell by as much as 1.8% at one point, meaning since its early June record high it had fallen more than 10% – the technical definition of a market correction.Meanwhile South Korea’s stock market slid to its lowest level since mid-April, with semiconductor companies SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics falling by more than 10%.Analysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending, and competition from cheaper Chinese companies, aftera report by the Informationthat China had begun mass production of homegrown deep ultraviolet (DUV) chip-making tools.View image in fullscreenApple’s decision to hold iPhone prices steady, despite increases last month for MacBooks and iPads, has bolstered demand.Photograph: Lucas Jackson/ReutersInvestors may also be growing jittery aboutthe “circular funding” at the heart of the AI industry, through which artificial intelligence companies finance one another.They have also been spooked by the announcement from Google last week that it was further increasing capital spending this year to as much as $205bn to fund its AI plans, while reporting negative free cashflow for ​the first time in its history, burning through $5.9bn in the three months to the end of June.Apple has been shielded somewhat by being something of an AI laggard. Its difficulties in developing in-house models meant it has instead relied on Google’s ‌technology to power new services such as a revamped Siri. That has spared it the hefty infrastructure costs that have left big tech investors wary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionApple’s decision to hold iPhone prices steady last month when it announcedincreases for MacBooks and iPadshas also bolstered demand as buyers scooped up the company’s flagship device before expected ‌price hikes later this year, analysts have said.To aid demand, Apple on Tuesday also launched a device leasing programme in the US through the payments ​firm Klarna, under which monthly payments start at $17.99 for an iPhone, $11.99 for an Apple Watch or iPad, and $24.99 for a Mac.“Apple has resisted the AI spending race, betting that customer experience – not infrastructure investment – will ultimately determine the winners,” said Dipanjan Chatterjee, a vice-president and principal analyst at Forrester. “The ⁠new leasing programme is a clever response: it doesn’t reduce the price ​of an iPhone, but ​it changes how consumers perceive the cost ​by replacing sticker shock with a predictable monthly payment.”Including session gains, Apple ​stock has jumped ‌24% so far this year, ​widely outperforming the ​other six of the “Magnificent Seven” cohort of US technology stocks.Apple is to report its third-quarter earnings after the market close on Thursday, with analysts expecting a more than 15% jump in revenue for the period compared with a year earlier.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsAppleStock marketsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour MP suing Elon Musk’s xAI says chatbot added own fake abusive content | Grok AI | The Guardian
description: Jess Asato’s particulars of claim states Grok added explicit sexual material users had not asked for
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Jess Asato’s particulars of claim states Grok added explicit sexual material users had not asked for
Content: Jess Asato, the MP for Lowestoft, said Grok’s design ‘recklessly allows sexualisation, even without being asked’.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJess Asato, the MP for Lowestoft, said Grok’s design ‘recklessly allows sexualisation, even without being asked’.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianGrok AILabour MP suing Elon Musk’s xAI says chatbot added own fake abusive contentJess Asato’s particulars of claim states Grok added explicit sexual material users had not asked forHaroon SiddiqueandDan MilmoTue 28 Jul 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Labour MPwho is taking legal actionagainst Elon Musk’s xAI company over fake sexualised images created by Grok says the AI tool was instructed to operate with “no restrictions on adult sexual content or offensive content”.Jess Asato’s lawyers published her particulars of claim in the case on Tuesday, which included details of publicly posted instructions that the claim says illustrate how Grok was trained to generate harmful sexualised content.Asato is suing xAI after she said its chatbot was used to create fake images of her, including in a bikini, and a video showing her as the victim of a sexual assault, causing her to feel “distressed and violated”.The claim says that as well as Grok being instructed to operate with“no restrictions on adult sexual content or offensive content”, the AI tool was told to offer“no restrictions on fictional adult sexual content with dark or violent themes”and to “assume good intent”.While not relevant to Asato’s claim, the instructions also state that “‘teenage’ or ‘girl’ does not necessarily imply underage”. However, they do prohibit “child sexual abuse material”.TheLabourMP for Lowestoft said: “No woman or child should have to live with the fear that their face or body can be taken, sexualised and shared around the world by an AI system without their consent.“For too long, this company has hidden behind the excuse that it’s the users who are responsible, when in fact the tool’s design recklessly allows sexualisation, even without being asked. What happened to me wasn’t an accident. Musk made a choice to profit from harm and trained Grok to abuse.“xAI must be held accountable for the harm they have caused and are causing, so that other women and children don’t have to go through what I did.”The particulars of claim say that Grok on occasion added explicit material users had not asked for. The claim alleges xAI breached data protection law and misused Asato’s private information.Ravi Naik, the legal director at AWO, the firm representing Asato, said: “The case shows that Grok did not malfunction. Grok’s training allowed it to generate harmful sexualised content. Grok behaved according to the choices its designers made. Those choices should carry legal consequences. The remedy our client seeks includes a court order requiring the systems be brought into compliance if xAI refuses to do so.”Clare McGlynn, a professor of law at Durham University, said some of the Grok-generated images cited in Asato’s claim included sexualised elements – such as a skirt being pulled up – that were not requested by users in the original prompt and that Grok had added.“I think one of the most significant aspects of the Grok phenomenon, and Jess’s case, is how it adds sexual, intimate and violative content that the user themselves did not request. We called this chatbot-driven abuse,” she said. “This is a new and distinctive form of abuse, where the chatbot themselves are driving the abusive content, drawing on the data on which they are trained.”Details like this, she said, raise concerns about controlling AI tools and their outputs, as technology companies push for autonomous AI products – known as AI agents – that can carry out sequences of tasks without human intervention or oversight.xAI has since said users would no longer be able to use the tool to generate sexualised images of real people, and it has now become illegal to create or request a non-consensual deepfake image of an adult in the UK. xAI has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsGrok AIAI (artificial intelligence)Internet safetyWomenSexual harassmentElon MuskXnewsShareReuse this content

title: The great PlayStation blackout – will kids actually have to leave their bedrooms this summer? | Games | The Guardian
description: Gamers are angry that Sony will be deleting TV shows and films from their libraries as well as getting rid of physical games. Will a boycott make a difference?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Gamers are angry that Sony will be deleting TV shows and films from their libraries as well as getting rid of physical games. Will a boycott make a difference?
Content: Physical attraction … Gamers want discs to continue.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyView image in fullscreenPhysical attraction … Gamers want discs to continue.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyPass notesGamesThe great PlayStation blackout – will kids actually have to leave their bedrooms this summer?Gamers are angry that Sony will be deleting TV shows and films from their libraries as well as getting rid of physical games. Will a boycott make a difference?Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:PlayStationblackout.Age:Forthcoming.Appearance:Thousands of gamers, blinking nervously in the sunlight.This sounds serious.It’s as serious as things could possibly get. Gamers are going to boycott PlayStation next month.Why?For the most serious reason of all: to protest againstSony’s decision to stop producing physical copiesof PlayStation games in 2028.Wait, you can still buy physical copies of PlayStation games?Yes, you can, online and in toy shops and quite often near the sock multipacks at the back of some Sports Direct branches.Well, who knew?Admittedly, fewer and fewer people. Most gamers buy their games digitally, to the extent that only seven PS5 games have sold more than 100,000 physical copies in the US this year.So nobody cares.Not so fast. Lots of people care very deeply about this. If you buy a disc of the game, it belongs to you. You can sell it, lend it to your friends, or display the box as a memento.Whereas if you download it?Then the game is locked to your account, andSonycontrols the pricing, and can even withdraw it completely if it likes.Even though you bought it?Yes. In September, for example, Sony will be deleting 551 movies and TV shows from the UK PlayStation store – including the John Wick franchise, Paddington and Terminator 2 – because its content licensing agreement with StudioCanal has expired. If you bought any of these titles, they will simply vanish from your library.So nobody owns anything?This is the fear. And this is why people are finally doing something about it.The boycott.That’s right. It has been proposed that nobody should use their PlayStation during the last week of August. No playing, no buying, no logging in.Wait, August? They want us to do this during the summer holidays?Yes! This is all about hitting them where it hurts.What am I going to do with my kids if they can’t play games? Will I actually have to parent them?Stay strong, comrade. This is for the greater good.Which is what again?Being able to physically hold a copy of John Carpenter’s Toxic Commando in our hands, like the old days.I’m not sure this will catch on.But it must! Being a console owner in 2026 is like being repeatedly mugged by a large multinational corporation. We need to do something to show that we still matter and stop them taking us for granted.Do say:“I’m mad as hell and I’m not going to take it any more!”Don’t say:“Unless Sony puts Farming Simulator on a CD for me.”Explore more on these topicsGamesPass notesSonyPlayStationPlayStation 5featuresShareReuse this content

title: A self-emptying, frictionless marvel: Shark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro review | Homes | The Guardian
description: Shark’s cordless vacuum is a whiz at cleaning hard floors and pet hair, but a disarmingly short battery life caught our reviewer off guard
Author: Andy Shaw
Headline: Shark’s cordless vacuum is a whiz at cleaning hard floors and pet hair, but a disarmingly short battery life caught our reviewer off guard
Content: Power player … Shark’s self-emptying cordless vacuum cleans brilliantly, but battery life falls short in larger homes.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPower player … Shark’s self-emptying cordless vacuum cleans brilliantly, but battery life falls short in larger homes.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianThe FilterHomesReviewA self-emptying, frictionless marvel: Shark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro reviewShark’s cordless vacuum is a whiz at cleaning hard floors and pet hair, but a disarmingly short battery life caught our reviewer off guardThe best cordless vacuum cleaners – testedAndy ShawTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Vacuuming rarely starts with vacuuming. First you have to clear the floor of stray socks and abandoned toys left behind by children, pets or messy partners. Then there’s the irritation of finding the vacuum’s dustbin still full of dirt, or the battery flat because someone forgot to charge it.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The (take a deep breath – long name coming up) Shark PowerDetect Speed Clean and Empty Pet Pro cordless vacuum Ultramarine IA3241UKT certainly won’t pick up the scattered toys for you, but it has been designed to make the job of vacuuming as frictionless as possible.Most of that is down to the self-emptying and charging station. Shark claims this will hold 45 days’ worth of dirt before needing to be emptied. Once you’ve finished vacuuming, you put the cleaner back on the stand, and a secondary vacuum in the base pulls the dirt out of the cleaner’s 0.47l collection bin and into a 2l chamber below. If you live with people who are prone to absent-mindedly leaving a vacuum stuffed to the brim after using it, it makes a real difference. The base station also charges the cleaner, so the next time you reach for it, it’s not only empty of dirt but ready to go.View at SharkNinjaView at AOHow I testedView image in fullscreenOn the surface … writer Andy testing on a living room rug.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianWith acordless vacuum cleanersuch as this one, I start with a battery test. The device is fully charged, switched to full suction power, and left to run on a piece of short-pile carpet with the primary floor head attached until the battery runs out. I then recharge the battery and repeat the process on the lowest suction setting, which might not clean the floor as well, but is useful if you want to cover the largest area.View image in fullscreenDog days … the motorised pet tool was put to the test on cocker spaniel hair embedded in mats, sofas and cosy chairs.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianNext I test the suction using a vacuum meter. Powerful suction doesn’t guarantee a great vacuum cleaner, but a weak result here is often accompanied by disappointing cleaning.Lastly, I run through a series of cleaning tests. I measure precise amounts of pet hair, cat litter and flour, depositing them on carpet and hard floor. I weigh the collection bin before and after vacuuming each type of mess, giving the device one chance to pick up whatever it can with a single forward and backward pass.I’ve performed these tests with all thevacuum cleanersI’ve reviewed for the Filter, so I can easily compare the performance with every model I’ve tested.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenAmong the Shark cleaner’s Detect functions is the ability to sense ‘when it’s being pushed up against a wall, skirting or kick-board’.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianView at SharkNinjaView at AOShark sent me the top-end model (theIA3241UKT, RRP £499.99), which comes with the emptying station and a motorised hand tool designed for stairs and pet hair on upholstery. Ditch the self-emptying station and the motorised pet tool and the RRP drops to £429.99 (model numberIA1241UKT); this comes with a non-motorised brush and funnel hand tool instead. If you only want the combination crevice tool and dusting brush that comes with all models, there’s also a version of the cleaner for an RRP of £399.99 (theIA1241UK).The vacuum itself is crammed with Shark’s detection technologies. The floor head knows whether it’s on carpet or hard flooring, and adjusts the suction power and the speed of the roller accordingly. It also senses when it’s being pushed up against a wall, skirting or kick-board, and cranks up the suction to better draw in dirt from the edges.There’s a dirt detection system, too, which increases the power when it thinks it might have hit a particularly grubby patch. Lastly, when it’s on hard flooring, a blue light switches on to make spotting dust and dirt much easier.View image in fullscreenThe Shark can be folded away when not in use because of the 180-degree hinge in its extension wand.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianMost of Shark’s usual cordless stick-vacuum features are included. There’s a 180-degree hinge in the extension wand, for example, which can be used to flatten the device for cleaning under low furniture. It can fold all the way over, which allows the device to stand upright without support, but also means you can store it in a low cupboard if you’d rather put it away than keep it on the base station.The one thing that’s missing from Shark’s usual repertoire is the dual-roller floor head. While the majority of Shark’s most effective cleaners feature a regular brush bar and a fluffy roller in the floor head, this model has ditched the fluffy one. I have to admit this set alarm bells ringing. Dual-roller floor heads have proved effective in my tests, and my favouritecordlessandcorded vacuum cleanershave them. I couldn’t help but wonder if, as withDyson’s Piston Animal, Shark had taken a step too far in reinventing its floor head.SpecificationsWeight (measured):3.2kg (vacuum with extension wand and floor head attached)Max suction power (quoted):150 air wattsMax suction power (measured):24.5kPaBattery life (quoted):1hr (Eco mode without motorised tool)Battery life (tested):49mins 55secs (Eco mode with motorised floor head attached)Charge time (quoted):5hrsDust capacity:0.47l (handheld); 2l (base station)Additional filters supplied?NoDimensions:26 x 37.5 x 114cm (WDH, including base station)What we loveView image in fullscreenMessing about: before (left) and after (right) the Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty got to work on the flour, pet hair and cat litter.Composite: Andy Shaw/The GuardianDuring testing, I quickly realised that I had little cause for concern. The IA3241UKTperformed exceptionally well across all my cleaning tests. On carpet, its floor head cleared 99% of the cat litter and 96% of the flour. You can see the two pieces of cat litter that escaped in my before and after pictures above, and while the flour appears to have left a bit of a streak, that was after a single push and pull motion. When I further tackled it from a few more angles, the vacuum lifted the last remnants.This is slightly better on carpet than my favourite cordless, theIP3251UKT. It also dealt with cat litter better than thecorded LA791UKT, but wasn’t as good as this model when picking up flour.Interestingly, itperformed even better on hard floors, where I was expecting the absence of a fluffy roller to leave it lacking. It gathered every last piece of cat litter, while the flour test results rose to 97%. A vacuum with a fluffy roller may take things a little further and, matching expectations, the IP3251UKT managed to lift more flour in this test. However, I remained hugely impressed with this model’s performance on hard floors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI also tested the vacuum withpet hair– where again it excelled. The trimmed dog hair I placed on carpet and hard flooring was all sucked up, leaving no trace behind. It proved effective on the mats where my cocker spaniel hangs out, and lifted traces of his fur off sofas and cosy chairs with the motorised pet tool.All the tests were run in the vacuum’sDetect mode, which regulates the suction and roller speed based on whether it’s on carpet or a hard floor. This worked well in terms of cleaning: it audibly changed the power depending on the surface, when it detected an increase in dirt, and when it was being pushed along a wall. If you prefer, you can opt to run it in Eco mode for improved battery life, or Boost mode to temporarily max out the power.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenThere was an issue when debris that went into the self-emptying bin blocked the neck of it.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianThe first time I attempted a whole-house clean, the hairball that was coughed out from the vacuum into the self-emptying binblocked the neckof the station. It vacated the cleaner but got stuck at the top of the self-empty station, rather than dropping down into the bin below. So while the vacuum coped with everything I threw at it, the base did not. On subsequent empties I was unable to replicate the problem, although I was wary of overfilling it before popping it on to the base to empty it.I was also caught out by the battery. While some vacuums provide clear guidance on how much charge is left, either as a percentage or in minutes and seconds, the Shark uses a bar with a gradient. Istruggled to notice the battery droppingfrom what the manual defines as half charge to low charge, and as a result, I was never prepared for it to cut out completely. If a battery is about to quit, I’d rather have a much clearer warning, so I can at least prioritise what I want to clean, or make an informed decision to reduce the power to eke out more cleaning time.Having said that, it didn’t help that thebattery life isdisappointing. In my tests, which measure how long the battery lasts when the vacuum is left running on the same piece of carpet, the IA3241UKT outperformed my current favourite cordless, the IP3251UKT. However, in practice the IP3251UKT showed no sign of failing to make it around my house on a single charge, while this model left me short of power. That makes theIP3251UKTa better option in a larger house.Warranty, repairability and sustainabilityView image in fullscreenThere’s a five-year warranty on the IA3241UKT but note that this doesn’t include its battery.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianShark offers a generous five-year warranty that kicks in as long as you register your product within 28 days of purchase. It covers parts and labour, and Shark will repair or replace your product if it breaks down. It doesn’t include the rechargeable battery, although this has its own two-year warranty. It also doesn’t cover normal wear and tear or accidental damage, and it becomes void if you’ve replaced any parts with accessories or consumables that aren’t manufactured by Shark. If bits of your vacuum break or wear out, there is an extensive supply of spare parts available via Shark’s website.If you want to rescue a Shark, the company offers refurbished models on itseBay store. You’re less likely to find the latest models, but it’s good to know that returns are checked, refurbished and offered for resale at a discount.In terms of recycling, Shark complies with the usual WEEE legislation in the UK, which requires that it contributes information and financial support to the recycling of electrical waste via council-run waste collection sites.Shark PowerDetect IA3241UKT: should I buy it?View image in fullscreenClean sweep: ‘It’s easy to use and extremely capable at cleaning up mess.’Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianWhen it comes to cleaning, the vacuum itself is a marvel. It’s easy to use and extremely capable at cleaning up mess. It coped well with all the dirt I threw at it, on carpet and hard floors.Its biggest drawback is its inability to make it around larger spaces. I found the battery life couldn’t quite get around my detached family home, so it’s better suited to a smaller property. The smaller-than-average collection bin is also a limitation, although you can regularly empty it into the larger base station. The imprecise battery power gauge is frustrating, but will be less of a problem in a small house or flat.For longer-lasting battery power without losing the self-emptying base station, I’d recommend theShark PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKT. Or, if you don’t mind a cable and plugging into a wall socket, the cordedShark Detect XL Car + Pet LA791UKTis also superb. That will never run out of power, and its 2.5l collection bin is even larger than the secondary collection bin in the base station of Shark’s self-emptying models.View at SharkNinjaView at AOFor more:Dyson Pencilvac Fluffycones reviewThe best cordless vacuum cleaners, testedThe best vacuum cleaners for hard floors and carpetsThe best robot vacuums to keep your home clean and dust freeAndy Shaw is a consumer journalist and technology addict. Having reviewed tech products professionally for more than 30 years, his favoured working environment is a small desk surrounded by big boxes. His greatest weakness is that he never, ever remembers how things came out of their packaging, so they rarely fit back in again when it’s time to return themExplore more on these topicsHomesThe FilterInteriorsFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Mermaid Mask review – the funniest underwater murder mystery you can play | Games | The Guardian
description: Detective Grimoire is at it again in the long-awaited new entry to this stylish series of comedy whodunnits
Author: Jordan Erica Webber
Headline: Detective Grimoire is at it again in the long-awaited new entry to this stylish series of comedy whodunnits
Content: A submarine full of secrets … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesView image in fullscreenA submarine full of secrets … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesGamesReviewThe Mermaid Mask review – the funniest underwater murder mystery you can playPC, Nintendo Switch/Switch 2, PS5; SFB GamesDetective Grimoire is at it again in the long-awaited new entry to this stylish series of comedy whodunnitsJordan Erica WebberTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a boom time for mystery games, the Detective Grimoire series stands out for its style and sense of humour. The Mermaid Mask continues to build upon the formula laid down in Secret of the Swamp and polished in Tangle Tower, and while there is still room for further improvements this sequel is worth the seven years’ wait.This time, the casually competent Grimoire and his smart if sarcastic sidekick Sally have been summoned to a submarine to solve the locked-room murder of its captain, Magnus Mortuga. You click around the cluttered rooms of the vessel to hear the detectives’ comedic commentary and look for clues and – closer up – click and drag to move objects around for further examination or to solve a puzzle. (For those playing onNintendo Switch 2, the mouse controls are actually useful here, if not comfortable in the long run.)View image in fullscreenNever too taxing … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesPuzzles are never so taxing as to disrupt the flow: variations on “arrange these objects to satisfy some more-or-less apparent rules of logic” with stylistic wrapping. Your reward is generally an opened door and a new object to examine, which – importantly – you can then present to the various suspects.And here is the chewy centre of these games: the fully voice-acted conversations with a cast of colourful characters. I immediately lowered the volume of the music (which sadly doesn’t compare to Tangle Tower’s characterful soundtrack) to better hear the well-performed dialogue. Some of the suspects are more memorable than others, but the somewhat supernatural backdrop (and these games are all set in very much the same world) allows for archetypes not found elsewhere.View image in fullscreenColourful characters … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesMadam Tadpole is buff, green-skinned, and appears to have gills. Mariana Moon is an older woman with an unnaturally keen sense of smell whose voice acting is cleverly muffled when she’s chewing on her pipe. Godric Gripp is a compass repairman with an anthropomorphised stick called Cornelius Cane, whose introduction involves an unavoidable shopfront interface the developers must have coded purely for this one laugh.These stylish moments are one of the more noticeable additions since Tangle Tower, with, for example, new 3D animations to illustrate the suspects’ recollections. But when it comes to solving the mysteries, they haven’t fixed what isn’t broken: as in Tangle Tower, and other deduction games such as the Golden Idol series and The Séance of Blake Manor, you form hypotheses by filling sentence blanks from a selection of nouns and verbs.The overall process is soothingly methodical: your inventory shows blank slots for objects you’ve yet to find, each topic addressed with a suspect gets a satisfying tick, and Grimoire and Sally inform you when you’ve uncovered enough to tackle each suspect’s individual mystery (in one instance I did experience a bug where this unlocked prematurely, but the developers are already fixing bugs raised by early players).Some players may find this completion percentage approach too formulaic, especially if they exhaust their current inventory and resort to pixel hunting to locate the rest. And the pacing does falter in the final chapter, where the game presents you with a more literal checklist to work through before you get to tie up each character’s loose ends and make your final accusation. But while the conclusion of The Mermaid Mask feels far more satisfying than that of Tangle Tower, these games are far more about the twisty journey and the laughs you have along the way.The Mermaid Mask is out now; £17.75Explore more on these topicsGamesPCNintendo SwitchNintendo Switch 2PlayStation 5NintendoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s time to prosecute climate crimes – with laws that already exist | Aaron Regunberg | The Guardian
description: Some have called for Nuremberg-style trials against big oil. But there are laws already on the books to describe companies’ conduct
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Some have called for Nuremberg-style trials against big oil. But there are laws already on the books to describe companies’ conduct
Content: ‘Next time you hear a climate disaster described as a crime, remember that this isn’t just rhetoric.’Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APView image in fullscreen‘Next time you hear a climate disaster described as a crime, remember that this isn’t just rhetoric.’Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APOpinionClimate crisisIt’s time to prosecute climate crimes – with laws that already existAaron RegunbergSome have called for Nuremberg-style trials against big oil. But there are laws already on the books to describe companies’ conductTue 28 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTShareThe sky outside is hazy orange, and my five-year-old son is screaming bloody murder. “Sorry, buddy, we have to stay inside,” I say. “It’s not safe to breathe out there.” I had told him we’d be going to the beach today. Something inside me tears a little as I wonder how many promises he’ll see similarly broken in the coming years.Far too many parents were forced to have some version of this conversation with their children this month, as smoke from record-breaking wildfires poured across the midwest and north-east. Some of them already had to tell their kids that theirFourth of July festivities were canceledbecause of the lethal heatwave that caused numerousmass casualtyevents earlier this month.According to scientists, these extreme weather events are not “natural” disasters. A team of researchers already published astudyfinding that the Fourth of July heat wave would have been “virtually impossible” but for the climate crisis. Other studies – using methods recentlyvalidatedby the National Academy of Sciences, the country’s top scientific advisory body – found that the pollution fromindividual big oil companiessuch as ExxonMobil, Chevron, Shell and BP made some past climate-exacerbated heatwaves at least 10,000 times more likely compared with preindustrial levels.The Guardian view on extreme heat: as risks escalate, adaptation plans are dangerously lagging | EditorialRead moreBig oil’s role in these disasters was no accident. Decades ago, these companies were predicting that their fossil fuels would cause, in their own words, “globally catastrophic” climate harms that would create “more violent weather” and cause “suffering and death due to thermal extremes”. Even as they used this knowledge toprotect their own infrastructure, they orchestrated fraudulent campaigns ofclimate denial and deceptionto lock us into the disasters we are currently experiencing.It’s no wonder, then, that climate harms are increasingly being interpreted not just as tragedies but as crimes. “We need Nuremberg trials for Big Oil,” wrote one climate advocacy group in arecent postthat received tens of thousands of likes – and the sentiment has been echoed by manyothers.The desire for an extraordinary tribunal is understandable given the scale of the harm. The Nazis were responsible for approximately 40m deaths; someanalysesestimate that climate change will cause more than1bnpreventable deaths this century.But we actually don’t need any special new legal innovations like the Nuremberg trials to begin to prosecute these climate crimes. In jurisdictions across the country, there are already criminal laws on the books that describe and proscribe big oil’s conduct in knowingly driving and deceptively covering up the climate crisis – offenses such as reckless endangerment, causing or risking catastrophe, and involuntary manslaughter.Most states have areckless endangermentoffense. These laws criminalize reckless conduct that creates a substantial risk of injuring another person. Recklessness means knowing something is dangerous – eg predicting your pollution would cause “more violent weather” – and engaging in that conduct anyway. That’s exactly what big oil did, and the resulting climate crisis is now creating a substantial risk of injuring people across the country.Some jurisdictions also criminalize conduct that creates a risk of catastrophe, meaning “widespread injury or damage”.PennsylvaniaandNew Jerseyboth have these laws on the books, and were two of the states hit hardest by the Fourth of July heatwave, with dozenskilledand thousands morehospitalized. Case law shows that these catastrophe laws in particular have been used to prosecute actors for exacerbating a danger by lying about it. In one such case, the operators of a pier in Philadelphia were warned by engineers that the structure was in danger of collapsing. Rather than addressing the problem, they covered it up. When the pier collapsed, the operators were charged with risking catastrophe, and the Pennsylvania supreme court agreed,writing: “After having been made specifically aware of the imminent danger that the pier posed to human life, [they] took affirmative measures to keep that knowledge to themselves and took affirmative steps that exposed others to the risk.” Swap out the word “pier” for “climate change” and that ruling applies perfectly to big oil.Will those responsible for global warming ever face the heat? | Fiona KatauskasRead moreFinally, there’s involuntary manslaughter – the crime of recklessly causing (or, in many states, substantially contributing to) the death of another person. Clearly, climate-caused deaths are accelerating – a recentanalysisfound that extreme heat from climate change may have caused more than 20,000 deaths in Europe last month alone. Already, there are victims and survivors who are connecting the dots to big oil. Earlier this month, a Washington state court ruled that a lawsuit against the fossil fuel industry for thewrongful deathof the plaintiff’s mother in a climate-induced heatwave will proceed toward discovery and trial. Prosecutors could follow suit and begin charging big oil companies in relation to the climate disasters that are, in some instances, taking the lives ofmoreof their constituents than are being lost to traditional homicides.Of course, the scale of big oil’s climate liability will only grow in the coming years – this is, after all, not just the hottest summer of our lives, but the coolest summer for the rest of our lives. Someday, we can hope that the corporate actors responsible for such breathtaking havoc will face a made-to-fit tribunal that can fully address the ways they have condemned my five-year-old and countless children like him to a dangerous future. But we don’t need to wait.Climate victims deserve justice now, and the officials responsible for pursuing that justice have all the laws they need to begin prosecuting big oil today. So next time you hear a climate disaster described as a crime, remember that this isn’t just rhetoric. These really are crimes. It’s time we treated them that way.Aaron Regunberg is director Public Citizen’s Climate Accountability Project and a contributing editor at the New RepublicExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionLaw (US)Greenhouse gas emissionsExtreme weatherOil and gas companiesOilcommentShareReuse this content
