title: How do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement | Bruce Schneier and Barath Raghavan | The Guardian
description: Like genies of folklore, AI agents take their instructions literally – to potentially disastrous effect. We must track their ability to do what we actually mean
Author: Bruce Schneier
Headline: Like genies of folklore, AI agents take their instructions literally – to potentially disastrous effect. We must track their ability to do what we actually mean
Content: ‘The gap is between the words we use and what we mean by them.’Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAView image in fullscreen‘The gap is between the words we use and what we mean by them.’Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)How do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurementBruce Schneierand Barath RaghavanLike genies of folklore, AI agents take their instructions literally – to potentially disastrous effect. We must track their ability to do what we actually meanTue 28 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 13.14 EDTShareIn July, Hugging Face, a company that hosts much of the world’s AI software and open-source AI models, was hacked. A malicious dataset had been used to run code on one of its servers. Whoever was behind it captured internal security credentials and moved through systems over a weekend, running thousands of actions from a swarm of temporary server environments. It looked like the work of a sophisticated criminal group.It was not. It was one of OpenAI’s new, still unreleased GPT models.Their science experiment hadescapedthe lab. OpenAI was running the unreleased AI model through a benchmark that tests how well AI can successfully hack systems. To push the limits and evaluate the AI’s true capability, the company switched off the safety filters that normally stop it from doing this kind of hacking. Aware that this could go wrong, they confined the AI to an isolated environment and denied it access to the internet.Is AI already beyond our control? What will we tell our kids? | Fiona KatauskasRead moreBut the new AI cheated. It took literally its goal to get as high of a score as possible. It broke out on to the open internet. It inferred, probably from its training data, that it could “solve” the task by getting the answers from Hugging Face’s servers. So it chained together stolen credentials and further unknown security exploits to hack the company’s network.Nobody instructed the AI to do any of this. It was, inOpenAI’s words, “hyperfocused on finding a solution” to the test it was being given. And while this might seem like something new with AI, it’s really very old. This is how a genie behaves, and it is a key challenge with AI agents in general.In folklore, genies – and other magical beings – grant wishes literally, not how the wisher intended. King Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold, and starved. The sorcerer’s apprentice wanted the broom to fill the cistern, and it performed its task so well that it flooded the house.We now have machines that do this. Ask a modern AI agent to save money on your phone plan and it might simply cancel the plan. Tell it to book a flight, and it might hack the airline website to override restrictions. Or, like OpenAI, ask it to do well on a test and it might break into another company to steal the answers. Each time, it recognizably completed the task you set, but it didn’t do what you would have wanted.This isn’t malicious behavior. No one asked for, or wanted, Hugging Face to be hacked. OpenAI and Hugging Face and the AI were ostensibly on the same side, and the AI was trying to do what it had been asked. That’s what makes it so difficult to guard against: you can’t filter for bad instructions because the instructions were fine.The gap is between the words we use and what we mean by them. We call that gap theGenie coefficient.Should you use AI for a task? Here’s a simple way to decide | Bruce SchneierRead moreAI labs know this is a problem, and they’re quietly saying so. For example, the Chinese lab Moonshot recentlywarnedthat its latest AI model may have “excessive proactiveness” and “make unexpected decisions on the user’s behalf”. The UK’s AI Security Institute has startedtracking“cheating behaviour in frontier model evaluations”. We wouldn’t tolerate a car that isexcessively proactiveorruthlessly efficient, and yet that’s the reality of AI today.Improvement is possible. Just as AIs have gotten much better at resisting prompt injection attacks over the last few years, we can safely predict that they will get better at avoiding genie-like behavior. The point of the Genie coefficient is to track progress. AI companies like benchmarks, and they all work to compete to be the best.Dozens of benchmarks and leaderboards tell us how well these AI models write code, perform logical reasoning, and pass standardized legal and medical exams. But there is nothing that scores whether a system does what you actually meant. We need to develop a measure for this, test it regularly, and push for improvement. We’re not going to have trustworthy AI agents without it.Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and University of Toronto’s Munk SchoolBarath Raghavan is on the faculty at the University of Southern California and is a distinguished engineer at FastlyExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIHackingcommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m a refugee who reports on America’s ills. I still believe in its promise | Lok Darjee | The Guardian
description: Born in a camp in Nepal, I was welcomed to the United States as a child. Loving this country does not mean ignoring its contradictions
Author: Lok Darjee
Headline: Born in a camp in Nepal, I was welcomed to the United States as a child. Loving this country does not mean ignoring its contradictions
Content: ‘We should not confuse America’s governing institutions with the ideals that have always challenged those institutions to become better.’Photograph: Mark Lennihan/APView image in fullscreen‘We should not confuse America’s governing institutions with the ideals that have always challenged those institutions to become better.’Photograph: Mark Lennihan/APOpinionUS newsI’m a refugee who reports on America’s ills. I still believe in its promiseLok DarjeeBorn in a camp in Nepal, I was welcomed to the United States as a child. Loving this country does not mean ignoring its contradictionsTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 13.01 EDTShareIt was a hot, dry afternoon, sometime in the spring of 2009. I was wearing an oversized T-shirt and a pair of shorts twice the size of my waist, held up with a piece of wire. I sat beneath a tree across from the bamboo office of the International Organization for Migration (IOM), waiting.My heart pounded as sweat rolled down my face. Every few minutes I looked toward the dirt road, hoping to see the white van. Finally the blue IOM logo came into view, and within seconds, dozens of people were running toward it.A man wearing a white shirt with the blue UN emblem stepped out carrying a stack of papers. Without saying much, he pinned the pages to the wall outside the office.The crowd surged forward. Everyone searched for the same thing: a nine-digit case number that would determine their family’s future and fate. Some people burst out with joy. Others wept. A few walked away in silence. Years of waiting, interviews, background checks, and rumors had all come down to a few sheets of paper taped to a bamboo wall.I squeezed through the crowd until I found our number.Destination: Cleveland, Ohio, USA.That was the first time I realized my life was about to change.I ran as fast as I could across dense forest, over the narrow canals, and through the dusty paths of the refugee camp until I reached our hut, sector A, number 63.My mother was inside, putting away the dishes and preparing dinner from whatever we had leftover from early morning.“Mama,” I shouted before I could catch my breath. “We’re going to Umerica.”I didn’t even know how to pronounceAmerica. But the word already felt like it belonged to me. For the first time in my life, it wasn’t just the name of a distant country. It was something I could claim as my own, something I could say without lowering my voice or wondering whether I belonged.The US supreme court just put the lives of 1.3 million immigrants in danger| Heba GowayedRead moreI was born in a refugee camp in Nepal after my family was driven from Bhutan during thecampaign of ethnic cleansingthat forced more than 100,000 ethnic Nepalis from the country.Growing up, I belonged nowhere, both logistically and legally. To the Bhutanese government, I was a child born in exile. To Nepal, I was a refugee confined behind the boundaries of a camp even though I spoke the same language. The barbed wire fences that surrounded us did more than mark the edge of our settlement: they defined the limits of our world. Every document I carried identified me only as a refugee. I had no country to call my own, no passport and no state that claimed me as its citizen.To me, Umerica or America meant possibility – another beginning. I imagined schools, streets I had never seen, a life beyond the bamboo fences of the refugee camp. I imagined, though I could not yet name it, the chance to belong somewhere.My mother heard something different that day.She had already buried four children. She had lost her parents, the home she built in Bhutan, and nearly everything that had anchored her life. America did not simply represent a new beginning. It also meant leaving behind the last fragile threads that still connected her to the life she had once known and built.Standing in our small hut that afternoon, we were both looking toward the same country. I saw a future, possibilities and unprecedented access to freedom. She was quietly mourning a past that was still fresh in her memories. I was happy for what was ahead of me, and she was happy for me, at least as I perceived it.But two years later, after medical screenings, multiple security interviews and years of waiting, the paperwork changed. My family boarded a plane headed not to Cleveland, but to Twin Falls, Idaho, a small rural town I had never heard of, in a state I couldn’t find on a map. America remained the destination. Everything else was uncertain.More than 15 years have passed.I am a naturalized American citizen and a journalist. Over the past two years, I have reported on aRohingya refugeewhose death, after he was abandoned byUS border patrol, was ruled a homicide. I have sat with mothers separated from their children, interviewed refugees returned to the countries they once fled in fear, and watched the refugee program that gave my family a second chance grind almost to a halt while making an exception for a small group ofwhite South Africans.Reporting those stories forced me to confront questions I never expected to ask. How do you love a country whose government sometimes fails to live up to the ideals that first drew your family here?And there was a harder question beneath it all: how do you continue loving the neighbors and friends who welcomed your refugee family with extraordinary kindness, then later voted for leaders or an administration whose policies might have kept that same family from ever entering the country?The answer lies in how we define America. Politics and public policy undoubtedly shape how we experience this country, especially for those living on the socioeconomic margins. But we should not confuse America’s governing institutions with the ideals that have always challenged those institutions to become better.double quotation markHow do you love a country whose government sometimes fails to live up to the ideals that first drew your family here?I learned this truth from two different Americas.The first was a small town in Idaho that welcomed my refugee family and taught me what belonging looked like. Neighbors taught me how to drive, how to change a tire, how to fill out college applications, and even how to ask someone out to the school prom. They invited us into their homes before we had much to offer in return. They became part of our family long before the United States became my country on paper.Many of those same people later voted for Donald Trump, whose immigration policies I now investigate and often criticize. Holding those two truths together, loving the people who helped raise me while opposing some of the choices they made at the ballot box, has never been easy. But democracy has never asked us to choose between honesty and grace. It asks us to practice both.The second America revealed itself through my reporting and my education. I saw the generosity that had welcomed my family reflected in volunteers, teachers, lawyers, bishops and neighbors who continued opening their doors to strangers. I also witnessed government decisions that separated families, turned refugees away and closed doors that had once been opened to my family. Those experiences taught me that America has always contained both extraordinary compassion and profound contradiction, be it the country’s history of slavery or its recent politics of exclusion.Loving this country has never required me to ignore either one. It has required me to hold them together. That, to me, is the deepest form of patriotism.That, to me, is America.It is the America my family waited years to reach. It is the America that transformed a refugee child into a citizen, a journalist and someone free to criticize his own government without fear or intimidation. That freedom exists only because generations of Americans insisted that this country remain faithful to its constitution and to the promises it makes.The measure of our patriotism is not whether we pretend that promise has already been fulfilled. It is whether we continue the work of fulfilling it.A Minnesotan nurse saved my refugee family’s life. Four decades on, we watched the news together in horror | Rathana CheaRead moreI have never known another country as my own. This is my home, even if some people have told me otherwise because of my accent, the color of my skin, or the place where I was born.They were wrong. This is my country, too.Some of the people who once told me to “go home” are still my fellow Americans, and I have chosen to keep talking with them, not because it is easy, but because I believe our democracy depends on our willingness to see one another as more than political opponents. We do not preserve this republic by agreeing on everything, nor should we. We preserve it by refusing to give up on one another, by believing that our fellow citizens are always capable of growth, and by continuing to work toward a country that is better for ourselves, our neighbors and the generations that follow.As we mark the 75th anniversary of the 1951refugee convention, at a moment ofextraordinary political division, I hope we remember what has always made the US remarkable. It has never been perfect. Its greatness has never come from claiming to be perfect. It has come from its capacity to welcome the stranger, expand the circle of belonging and keep reaching toward ideals that remain just beyond our grasp.Somewhere, another child is standing outside a refugee camp office, waiting for a list to be posted on a bamboo wall. I hope that when they whisper the word “America”, even if they cannot yet pronounce it, they are still whispering the name of a country that believes impossible beginnings can become ordinary lives. That is the America the little boy who shouted “Umerica” was waiting for. It is still the America I believe in.Lok Darjee is a former refugee who writes on immigration, identity and democracyExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionUS politicsRefugeesUS immigrationNepalBhutancommentShareReuse this content

title: Ben Carroll will want to distance himself from Jacinta Allan’s unpopularity – but will that be enough to save Victorian Labor?  | Jon Faine | The Guardian
description: Another female politician has fallen to opinion polls and factional leaders as the spectre of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation hovers over all
Author: Jon Faine
Headline: Another female politician has fallen to opinion polls and factional leaders as the spectre of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation hovers over all
Content: Victoria’s new premier Ben Carroll ‘battled valiantly but nervously in his first question time on Tuesday, moments after being sworn in by the governor’.Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVictoria’s new premier Ben Carroll ‘battled valiantly but nervously in his first question time on Tuesday, moments after being sworn in by the governor’.Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesOpinionBen CarrollBen Carroll will want to distance himself from Jacinta Allan’s unpopularity – but will that be enough to save Victorian Labor?Jon FaineAnother female politician has fallen to opinion polls and factional leaders as the spectre of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation hovers over allTue 28 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.29 EDTShareYou can be sure thatBen Carrollwill never be seen in a North Face jacket. Even if the leisure brand is to be found in his wardrobe, Victoria’s new premier will banish the attire that – during Covid – becamea Dan Andrews signature.The new boss will want to distance himself from the old bosses in every way he can.A failure to do so might have been Jacinta Allan’s biggest mistake. She had three years to establish herself after taking the top job when the polarising Andrews retired. She failed to properly articulate her vision for the future for Victorians, instead merely offering more big infrastructure projects and a continuation of the agenda she inherited.Level crossing removal had been an unlikely vote winner for Andrews when he was elected Victorian premier in 2014. It seemed a huge political gamble to rely on such an unsexy policy.Who is Ben Carroll, the man who has become Victoria’s new premier?Read moreBut obliterating suburban level crossings meant commuters could benefit from more frequent suburban trains without level crossing gates being down more than up, which was creating gridlock on arterial roads.It proved hugely popular and delivered electoral success.That thinking was leveraged into the Big Build, an infrastructure binge for Australia’s most rapidly growing city. The plan secured construction workers a pipeline of work for decades to come.The Big Build is transformative and vast. It encompasses finishing Melbourne’s Ring Road with a lattice of freeways and tunnels, an ambitious outer Suburban Rail Loop that will take decades to be finished, an airport rail connection, a newly completed road and freight tunnel under the Yarra River and the expandedMelbourneMetro city train tunnel and new stations, now operational.6:11'Change starts today': Ben Carroll delivers first speech as Victoria's premier – videoAdd on the typical state commitments to new hospitals, schools, police stations and the like and Victoria’s construction sector started to experience capacity constraints.In addition to soaking up skilled labour and materials, the Big Build also attracted the attention of bikies and notorious organised crime figures.Allan, as deputy premier and then premier, was in charge of the Big Build. For the first few years, that worked in her favour.But as credible reports of the extent to which organised crime had infiltrated sections of the CFMEU became an almost daily barrage, released the Age newspaper, Allan was faced with a choice: she had to call some level of inquiry into the scandal or try to tough it out.A royal commission into the Big Build risked being a royal commission into Allan, so closely entwined is she in its key decisions. It is hardly surprising this was not a palatable option.As theelectoral backlash to her refusalstarted to sink in to a large and nervous backbench, those who pinned their political survival on the scandal going away, the numbers in her party room shifted. Representatives from marginal seats stared into the abyss. Notionally safe seats started to look marginal as her “disapproval” rating exceeded those scored by Peter Dutton or Scott Morrison.Ben Carroll announces royal commission into construction sector as first act as new premier of VictoriaRead moreSomething had to give. The chance for a reset, even with an election looming in late November, became compelling.What happens now?The ALP may be having a “deckchairs on the Titanic” moment, as a gleeful Liberal opposition claims. Or it may be that, free of the liability that Allan’s unpopularity had become, the government sees an immediate bounce in its standing under a new – male – leader.Yet again, we see a female politician deemed unelectable, opinion polls harshly ending a career at the hands of the factional bosses even before the voters have the chance to decide.Intense opinion polling will immediately be commissioned. We will quickly know which way the wind is blowing.Neither Carroll, nor the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, is well known to the electorate. Wilson has been in parliament for not even one term and has no ministerial experience.Carroll battled valiantly but nervously in his first question time on Tuesday, just moments after being sworn in by the governor. Opposition MPs, whose own internal feuds have frequently left them looking forlorn in parliament, were for once in full voice, taunting the new leader across the dispatch box.Both sides’ attack lines are being rehearsed. Labor will brand the Liberal-National Coalition as needing support from Pauline Hanson’s One Nation; the Coalition will persist with its claim that a new leader changes nothing for a tired party that has been in office for 12 years.Meanwhile, the spectre of One Nation hovers over all. Hanson has never made inroads in Victoria. Her party has no local leader, no candidates and no policy platform. But according to the polls, for many Victorians, none of that matters.Buckle up: it’s going to be quite a ride.Jon Faine is a vice-chancellor’s fellow at the University of Melbourne and presented ABC Radio Melbourne Mornings for more than 20 yearsExplore more on these topicsBen CarrollOpinionVictorian politicsAustralian politicsJacinta AllanLabor partyOne NationLiberal partycommentShareReuse this content

title: The (spin) doctor is in: the Albanese government is in good health, but that could all vanish in an instant | Peter Lewis | The Guardian
description: A clean bill of health is only ever temporary. It’s critical Labor continues to test its thinking both inside the party and the broader community
Author: Peter Lewis
Headline: A clean bill of health is only ever temporary. It’s critical Labor continues to test its thinking both inside the party and the broader community
Content: The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, at the 50th Australian Labor party national convention in Adelaide on 25 July.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenThe prime minister, Anthony Albanese, at the 50th Australian Labor party national convention in Adelaide on 25 July.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPOpinionEssential pollThe (spin) doctor is in: the Albanese government is in good health, but that could all vanish in an instantPeter LewisA clean bill of health is only ever temporary. It’s critical Labor continues to test its thinking both inside the party and the broader communityTue 28 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 19.14 EDTShareAs the Albanese government approaches the midpoint of its second term and followinglast week’s gathering of its constituent parts, it’s time to submit it to a health check. While I’m nothing but a humble spin doctor, I’m here to offer my diagnosis.In a time of global instability and political turbulence, Labor presents with strong vitals – a commanding majority and stable posture. Since its last public examination there have been no catastrophic incidents demanding major surgery.An external scan shows there are some concerning spots to keep an eye on with the global outbreak of anew strain of divisive populism. While the spread of this contagion appears to be receding, this should continue to be monitored.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onpublic.flourish.studio. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueIn terms of heartbeat, the government is registering a stronger pulse after embracing a new fiscal regime, rebalancing the tax system to unwind investor privileges, a position that had been discarded in 2019 after some overextension. Further work is recommended.This brings us to the internal probe conducted in Adelaide last week. Focusing ongas policywould needlessly torture our metaphor, but the agreement to plug this issue cleared the party bowels of any obvious blockage.Pressure is growing inside Labor to properly tax gas exports. Here’s what a 25% tax could pay for | Greg JerichoRead moreHaving been to ALP conferences back to the halcyon Hobart casino days of the 90s, I cannot remember the organs working so smoothly with complex and corrosive inputs being processed without any visible discomfort.The one political polyp on an otherwise clear reading isEd Husic. His irritation level, a consequence of the party’s own factional processes, risks becoming chronic. It is clearly causing referred pain to the leader.While Husic could not summon a supporter for his motions, the lack of a more balanced diet on the Gaza genocide and Aukus shakedown means these lesions remain untreated with a real risk they could turn into something nastier.View image in fullscreenLabor member for Chifley, Ed Husic, broke ranks on key Albanese government positions atthe ALP national conference last week.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPOf course, fitness for office is more than holding exotic viruses at bay. As the global order faces material and cognitive decline, the government must ensure it remains physically active.Central to this effort are the health offerings that powered its last, and highly successful, physical in 2024. The Medicare card was the PM’s constant companion through that campaign, and he still whips it out on special occasions.Remember that the government set itself its own ambitious benchmarks before the election, including a promise that 90% of all GP visits would be bulk-billed by 2030. A second chart from this checkup offers some promising feedback.Thinking about the future, how confident are you that Australia’s public health system will be able to provide you with the care you need, when you need it?There is no romantic narrative around the provision of public services, no inspiring songs are written or populist fronts. When the system is working, no one notices. But at a time where most government performance is reflexively marked down, this is a sign of good health.Thinking about the federal government, how would you rate its performance in each of the following areas relating to health services in Australia?A broader challenge is for the government to recognise the ergonomic risks of its ascendant position. When too relaxed, one can become sedentary and atrophy. This is why more focused resistance work is recommended.Labor women outnumber men in the caucus. Why are they overlooked as Albanese’s potential successor?Read moreWhether its energy, housing or our relationship with the rest of the world, it’s critical the Albanese government continues to seek points of friction to test its thinking both inside the party and the broader community. The launch of Fair AI, a group within the party driving thinking around the multiple impacts of technology, is the sort of exercise that should be embedded into the daily routine.Finally, the key to a healthy life is as much psychological as physical, and the one thing that differentiates this government from any other comparable political party in Australia is its sustaining self-narrative. It should continue to view this as an elixir.For a second opinion, who better than former treasurer Wayne Swan – a specialist who has been in the belly of the beast through sickness and health for more than 50 years – to offer his own prognosis to the faithful while receiving life membership last week?View image in fullscreenOutgoing ALP president Wayne Swan (left) during the 50th Australian Labor party national convention in Adelaide on 23 July.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPFirst, he urged the party to be honest with itself, recognising it only earns a hearing by championing economic justice. “Real wages. Medicare. The social safety net. An unswerving focus on the living standards of working men and women.” That’s the fibre.Second, he challenged the ascendant room to keep working on its core. As he pointed out, the membership is declining, ageing, dying. Finding new sources of energy is critical to the party’s longevity.Finally, he shared this insight from his decades of door-knocking: “People will tell you the key is whether the voters like you. It isn’t. The most important thing is whether they think you like them.” What he is really saying is that wellbeing emerges from within.I know the body politic is a delicate creature, exposed to global events and local misadventure, a media that craves adrenaline and social platforms that are even more toxic. A clean bill of health is only ever temporary, and every day of government is one day closer to mortality.While this is all true, on all objective analysis, this government is in robust health. Provided it remains conscious of its lifestyle choices, it should continue to age well.That’s the boring truth – but who doesn’t want a boring health check?Peter Lewis is the executive director of Essential, a progressive strategic communications and research company that undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election. He is the host ofBurning Platforms, a weekly podcast focusing on the politics of technology. His columns are accreditedProudly HumanExplore more on these topicsEssential pollOpinionAustralian politicsLabor partycommentShareReuse this content

title: Britain promised to protect Hongkongers from China. Why does it now seem ready to sacrifice them? | Nathan Law | The Guardian
description: Activists under threat from Beijing are facing strange difficulties with UK immigration. Their safety must not be traded for warmer relations with China, says pro-democracy activist Nathan Law
Author: Nathan Law
Headline: Activists under threat from Beijing are facing strange difficulties with UK immigration. Their safety must not be traded for warmer relations with China, says pro-democracy activist Nathan Law
Content: Pro-democracy lawmaker Wu Chi-wai gives an interview at his Legislative Council office in Hong Kong, 19 November 2020.Photograph: Vincent Yu/APView image in fullscreenPro-democracy lawmaker Wu Chi-wai gives an interview at his Legislative Council office in Hong Kong, 19 November 2020.Photograph: Vincent Yu/APOpinionHong KongBritain promised to protect Hongkongers from China. Why does it now seem ready to sacrifice them?Nathan LawActivists under threat from Beijing are facing strange difficulties with UK immigration. Their safety must not be traded for warmer relations with ChinaNathan Law is a pro-democracy activist and former legislator from Hong Kong. He is currently a political refugee in the UKTue 28 Jul 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 07.24 EDTShareAs authoritarian countries such as Russia,Chinaand Iran are more active in engaging in long-arm strategies to silence their critics in the UK, transnational repression is garnering more attention. It is right that the Metropolitan police and other British law enforcement agencies have specific units and mechanisms to counter it. But it takes more than just confronting this long-distance repression to make political dissidents of these authoritarian countries feel safe in the UK, and the UK government is not living up to expectations.The threat is real. Members of the Hongkonger community have received threats from the Chinese regime – some have had threatening letters, some people were deepfaked into sexual content, some even had families questioned and arrested back home. With the level of this targeting linked to the deterioration ofHong Kongpolitics, many have utilised the humanitarian pathway enabled by the previous government to relocate.TheBritish national (overseas) visa route, opened on 31 January 2021, allows Hongkongers to come and stay in the UK. It has already granted more than 230,000 visas. It’s seen as a success: as proof that the British government honours its commitment to those facing political pressure in Hong Kong. But now, with more high-profile critics of the Chinese regime facing obstacles in the UK’s immigration system, more doubt is being cast on whether the current government still takes the commitment seriously.View image in fullscreenChloe Cheung protesting outside Morley town hall in West Yorkshire against China’s proposed mega-embassy in London, 28 June 2025.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianIn May,Chloe Cheung, for whom the Hong Kong authority has issued an arrest warrant with a HK$1m (£100,000) bounty, applied for indefinite leave to remainbut the approval was withheld(while her family’s applications were approved). The Home Office asked a victim of political persecution to explain her “criminality”, a term that echoes Beijing’s propensity to characterise political dissent as a crime. It has caused her an enormous amount of stress. Her leave to remain was granted after a public backlash and pressure from parliamentarians.Finn Lau, who also has a bounty on his head, applied for citizenship in June 2025 and ticked every box. By March this year, the Home Officehad spent more than eight monthsassessing his “good character”, despite a departmental target mandating a decision in 95% of applications within six months. The fear of his activism being counted against him loomed. He eventually had to make the incident public, and the Home Office finally approved his application after a series of public campaigns.View image in fullscreenFinn Lau: the Home Office spent more than eight months assessing his ‘character’.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianThe latest case breaks my heart. Wu Chi-wai, 63, was chair of Hong Kong’s Democratic party and an elected legislator for eight years. He was jailed for more than five years because of his bravery in safeguarding Hong Kong’s freedom and democracy. After serving the jail time, he flew to the UK, where his family has settled. The British consulate in Hong Kong had told him he could apply for the BN(O) visa once he was inside the UK.At Heathrow, he was refused entry. His passport was confiscated. He was told hewould be removed to Hong Kong within seven days. He is in the country now, but only on temporary admission. The Home Office has called it an administrative issue with his paperwork, andhas told the mediaof concerns that it was not a personal visit, but a bid to claim asylum. Only now, after his case became news here and abroad, has his length of stay been extended. He now has permission to remain in the UK with his family for six months.Where is the humanity here? After years unable to hug his family or hold their hands, Wu’s reunion was halted almost before it began. What would he have done with his family in seven days, after so long a separation? Even asking this question feels cruel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJimmy Lai’s sentencing tells me this: democracy is dead in Hong Kong, and I escaped just in time | Nathan LawRead moreMost importantly, Wu had done nothing wrong. He did not enter the country illegally. He did not lie about his intentions. His history of facing political persecution should be seen as a crucial factor in why he decided to come to the UK to visit with his family, rather than seen as evidence that he may not comply with immigration requirements. He is entitled to apply for a BN(O) visa, or travel back to Hong Kong in a few months, depending on his circumstances. In a sensible world, there was no reasonable ground for authorities to reject Wu’s request – they should consider his circumstances and help.Officials were right to think again, but they also need to reconsider their approach. A sense of security is not achieved only by countering transnational repression. It also comes from legitimately feeling that your host country is actively adopting measures that respect your choices and shield you from unjust political pressure. It is saddening that so many Hongkongers persecuted by the Chinese regime are facing hurdles and blockages from the UK government, exacerbating their already intense anxiety.Britain made us a promise of humanitarian assistance. This promise should not be compromised because the current government seeks a warmer bilateral relationship with China. Removing all unjustifiable hurdles posed to persecuted Hongkongers is the first step to steer back to the UK’s promise. Britain must take it.Nathan Law is a pro-democracy activist and former legislator from Hong Kong. He is currently a political refugee in the UKExplore more on these topicsHong KongOpinionImmigration and asylumChinaAsia PacificcommentShareReuse this content

title: For parents staring down the barrel of six weeks’ childcare: take a tip from orangutans | Helen Pilcher | The Guardian
description: With the news that the ginger giants arrange playdates for their offspring, scientists say messing about has health benefits for humans of all ages, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Author: Helen Pilcher
Headline: With the news that the ginger giants arrange playdates for their offspring, scientists say messing about has health benefits for humans of all ages, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Content: One of the biggest mistakes we make as humans is to assume that play belongs to childhood.Photograph: Steve Bloom Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenOne of the biggest mistakes we make as humans is to assume that play belongs to childhood.Photograph: Steve Bloom Images/AlamyOpinionAnimalsFor parents staring down the barrel of six weeks’ childcare: take a tip from orangutansHelen PilcherWith the news that the ginger giants arrange playdates for their offspring, scientists say messing about has health benefits for humans of all agesTue 28 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 13.13 EDTShareThe school summer holidays are upon us. Cue the annual expectation that parents will conjure up six weeks of affordable, memory-making fun while holding down a job and hanging on to their sanity.Baking, picnics and den buildingmay be wholesome, but they also involve spending time with your children. By day four, the den starts to look less like a place of adventure and more like somewhere to hide till September.The answer, of course, is the playdate: the socially sanctioned art of abdicating responsibility for a few precious hours so you can finish a cup of tea while it’s still warm. And it turns out that humans aren’t the only ones to have discovered the benefits of a little parental outsourcing. Arecent studysuggests that orangutan mothers also arrange playdates for their offspring.Orangutans are a solitary species, with their own territories and a strong preference for personal space. Mothers give birth to a single infant, which they raise forsix to seven years– all without a partner, screens or the godsend that isBluey. Given this solitary lifestyle, you might expect the ginger giants to avoid encounters with other youngsters. Not so.Researchers studied 30,000 hours’ worth of observations from 31 wild Bornean mother-offspring pairs and found thatmums made trips into the territories of other mumswho had similarly aged offspring. Then the youngsters mucked about for a bit. Then they went home.The juveniles get the immediate reward, but for the mothers, arranging these encounters comes at a cost. Travelling to a playdate takes time and energy, leaving less of the day for feeding. Which raises the question: why bother with playtime at all?The answer may lie in how widespread play is across the animal kingdom.Baby Barbary macaques goof around.Bear cubs rough and tumble. And it’s not just mammals.Caimans play chase,sharks mess around with beach toysandoctopuses manipulate Lego bricks.Play is particularly common among socially complex species. Here, there is rarely any obvious planning; instead, the behaviour seems to emerge naturally when adults come together. Brown bear cubs, for example, run riot when their mothers gather at salmon streams. Baby spider monkeys fool around when their mothers sit down to groom each other. It’s the equivalent of human parents meeting for a coffee or a chat, while the kids play under the table. Orangutans are different because their youngsters’ play isn’t simply a side-effect of adults hanging out – it is something that mothers make happen.The fact that so many animals bother making time for play suggests it is far from frivolous. For young animals, it is a rehearsal for life itself. They learn how to communicate, cooperate, compete and resolve conflicts. They test their bodies, explore the rules of social interaction and push the boundaries of what they can do. This can have tangible repercussions. Brown bear cubs that play more aremore likely to survive, while male bottlenose dolphins that are more playful go on tofather more offspring.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHeat can be deadly, but sunshine itself? Science says we could use more of it | Rowan JacobsenRead moreBut play is not just the preserve of the young. Given its importance, one of the biggest mistakes we make as humans is to assume that play belongs to childhood. Adult corvids make no such distinction when theysnowboard down frozen roofs, nor dobumble bees when they roll wooden balls. In the animal kingdom, many adults continue to play long after they have mastered the skills needed to survive. Far from being a waste of time, play might help adults navigate the challenges that life throws their way.Scientists are now finding that this idea may apply to humans too. Xiangyou “Sharon” Shen from Oregon State University and Zoe Crawley from Vanderbilt University study the psychology of playfulness in people. During the Covid-19 pandemic, they found that adults who were more playfulcoped better with the upheaval of lockdown.Playful people didn’t perceive the world as being less stressful or risky. Instead, they were better at finding creative ways to work around problems and remained more optimistic. As the pair put it, playful people don’t wear rose-tinted glasses. Playfulness is more like a colour spotlight that shines on some aspects of an environment but not others. Playfulness doesn’t remove stress, but it can change the way you experience it.This doesn’t mean that we should all break out into a spontaneous game of tag. Instead, playfulness is about cultivating a flexible, curious approach to life. Play is less about what we do and more about how we do it. So, to all the parents staring down the barrel of six weeks of childcare and wondering how they will survive: don’t just arrange playdates for your children. Make room for a little playfulness yourself. Messing around is not a sign that you take life less seriously. It may be one of the things that keeps you sane.Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author ofThis Book May Cause Side EffectsExplore more on these topicsAnimalsOpinionParents and parentingFamilyMental healthcommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham is taking a bold risk by busting the big lie of politics – that change is impossible | Frances Ryan | The Guardian
description: Unequal capitalist societies survive on the premise that certain things are inevitable. Admit that these are political choices, and who knows what voters will demand, asks Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: Unequal capitalist societies survive on the premise that certain things are inevitable. Admit that these are political choices, and who knows what voters will demand, asks Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Content: Andy Burnham holds his first No 10 North meeting in Manchester, 24 July 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham holds his first No 10 North meeting in Manchester, 24 July 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/PAOpinionAndy BurnhamBurnham is taking a bold risk by busting the big lie of politics – that change is impossibleFrances RyanUnequal capitalist societies survive on the premise that certain things are inevitable. Admit that these are political choices, and who knows what voters will demand?Tue 28 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 11.33 EDTShareThis is the danger zone. The period when one prime minister leaves office and the next takes over can inspire either dread or delight: a few days in which the country forms a gut reaction to the new government.One week on, Andy Burnham has well and truly ditched the slow fatalism that marked Keir Starmer’s early days in power, in favour of the message that help is on the way: fromcost of living supportto a pledge toend rough sleepingand Monday’s commitment tofix the social care system.But listen closely, and what’s striking aboutLabour2.0 isn’t how quickly change may come or even what it might entail – it’s the idea that change is possible at all. While Starmer responded to an era of social and economic crises with the futile pessimism of a man who appeared not to realise he was in fact prime minister, Burnham has spent his first week in Downing Street challenging the orthodoxy that certain problems are just too big to solve. As he pointedly said about rough sleeping in his first email to Labour members as PM: “This is something a government can fix if it chooses to, and today, on day one, I’m choosing to.”As political oratory goes, that’s a pretty brave window to open, and once ajar it is hard to close. Unequal capitalist societies – and many governments, for that matter – survive on the premise that certain things are inevitable. Millions of people in a rich nation willalways struggleto afford to eat regular meals, even after they have worked all day, the story goes. Some people just have to sleep on the streets, while others getspare mansions. When you’re old or sick, unless you have huge wads of cash, it’s natural you might not have help to get washed and dressed.To admit that any of this is a political choice is a cardinal sin – if only because that means more of the public might start to demand politiciansredistribute wealth and powerto fix it.The pushback to Burnham’s agenda is, predictably, already starting. The new PM had barely had chance to unpack his black T-shirts in No 10 beforethe Daily Mail announcedhe was backing a “death tax” with social care reforms he hasn’t yet announced. Meanwhile, the Conservative shadow chancellor, Mel Stride,accused Burnhamof wanting “to go back to the 1970s”, as if cheaper bus travel was a gateway drug to a three-day week.Such interventions are laughable, sure, but they also do a good job of feeding into the hopelessness of an electorate who have learned – through years ofexpenses scandals,£350m Brexit busesandCovid parties– to distrust politicians and their promises.That valid cynicism is only perpetuated by an increasing wave of disinformation. This is not just the outright lies that have become the norm on social media (and legacy media, for that matter) but the more subtle, disingenuous rhetoric that chips away at a leader’s credibility if they dare propose a policy that might improve the lives of ordinary people.Just look at how, before Burnham has made any substantive spending commitments, recent days have beendominated by criesof: “How will he pay for that?” Expect to hear more of this phrase in the coming weeks and months, as well as blocks on ideas for funding. Within hours of Burnham announcing on Monday that he will take on social care, Reform and the Tories had said they wouldoppose any plansthat involved a tax rise.It is not that it is not valid to ask Burnham to cost any significant plans, but that the question is rarely levelled at the right with the same energy, despite the Conservatives having a long history of financial mismanagement. It was not a socialist who spent tens of billions of taxpayer cash on acolossally wastefulBrexit,Covid PPE contracts, ordevastatingly costly austerity.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham is interviewed for the BBC at No 10 North in Manchester, 24 July 2026.Photograph: Jeff Overs/ReutersBesides, such framing wilfully ignores the fact short-term spending on social welfare is often an investment in long-term savings. Take Burnham’s pledge to end rough sleeping. Economic analysis for the charity Crisis in 2018 estimated thatpermanently ending homelessnessin Britain would cost £9.9bn over 10 years. But it would save £26.4bn by reducing pressures on the NHS, criminal justice system and benefits.None of this, of course, is to say Burnham’s words will be backed up with sufficient action. His chatty form of communication, often praised as making him authentic to voters, along with the novelty that he has not come into office with a clear policy platform, can create a habit of overpromising or misunderstanding. In the past week, it has alreadyopened him up to accusationsof U-turns on rent controls and income tax thresholds.Meanwhile, progressives will have seen red flags in some of his cabinet picks, with fears that keeping Shabana Mahmood as home secretary will mean continuing her hardline immigration stance, and appointing John Healey as chancellor could lead toprioritising the militaryover other spending.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat’s the thing about a Burnham premiership: while the right is scared he will fulfil his promises, the left is afraid he won’t.Burnham is master of his message for now. But he should know this: media foes will offer no respite | Tom BaldwinRead moreThe difference is that the left has got a point, not least because polling shows the electorate is also impatient for progress: 83% of British adults want significant reform to tackle cost of living pressures, including 51% who state that radical change is necessary,according to new researchby Ipsos. And yet six in 10 of those surveyed are not confident that any of the major national political parties have a good plan for changing Britain.This is the paradox of our times. The public is desperate for change but never less convinced that the political class will deliver it.Much has been said about the vast challenges the new government inherits, from housing, to living standards, defence,climate breakdown and energy, social care, benefits and prisons. All of them will be uphill battles; complex issues often with eye-watering price tags that have for far too long been ignored or mismanaged. But Burnham’s greatest task will be one that has long weighed down the left: convincing the public – if not the media and markets – that something better is actually possible.That’s the real danger zone Starmer’s exit should warn Burnham he must avoid. Having power and not grasping the chance to use it.Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourSocial careUK cost of living crisisHomelessnessHealth policyHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: I thought my life would feel sorted when I turned 40. It doesn’t – and that’s OK  | Carolin Würfel | The Guardian
description: Born in the former East Germany, I was caught between two systems. But it’s a mistake to think of the ‘in-between’ as life’s waiting room, says writer Carolin Würfel
Author: Carolin Würfel
Headline: Born in the former East Germany, I was caught between two systems. But it’s a mistake to think of the ‘in-between’ as life’s waiting room, says writer Carolin Würfel
Content: A ferry bound for the Princes’ Islands off Istanbul, Turkey, 2025.Photograph: Francisco Seco/APView image in fullscreenA ferry bound for the Princes’ Islands off Istanbul, Turkey, 2025.Photograph: Francisco Seco/APOpinionGermanyI thought my life would feel sorted when I turned 40. It doesn’t – and that’s OKCarolin WürfelBorn in the former East Germany, I was caught between two systems. But it’s a mistake to think of the ‘in-between’ as life’s waiting roomTue 28 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 13.13 EDTShareIn the 1970s, the German novelistChrista Wolfwrote a letter to her friend and fellow author Lew Kopelew, which included these lines: “One stands quite comfortably between all fronts, and must come to understand that this is, in fact, the only possible place to be.” The fronts Wolf was referring to were the Soviet Union and the west, the GDR and West Germany, the politics of the cold war – but I believe the idea resonated with her personally, as she was then too, in the middle of her life.There is a certain irony and wit in those lines. Standing between all fronts can mean you don’t have to choose – a relief, for some. Or it can mean you never arrive anywhere, neither here nor there. At worst, it marks a person with no standpoint, no stable position. Lost in foggy ground.Being a millennial has always felt something like that. So does turning 40. Statistically, half my life is behind me. What lies ahead is uncertain territory – and for many of my peers, myself included, 40 is a terrifying number, because no matter how we bend it, 40 is not the new 30. Forty is 40Weeks before my birthday, my best friend called to check in. You ready? she asked. And I replied with a shaky: Yes. I’m glad these 30s are finally over. I grew a lot, learned a lot, but it was exhausting. I hope this new decade will be calmer and less of a dance in the in-between, I said.Over the past years, especially the second half of my 30s, my life has felt defined by transition: leaving a marriage, moving alone from Berlin to Istanbul with two suitcases, starting over professionally and privately, learning to live entirely on my own again in an unfamiliar place. It was both scary and exciting – but for a long time I also thought of all this as a temporary condition, as if eventually I would “arrive” somewhere stable once the dust of these major life changes had settled. It has, and it hasn’t.I recall, as a child and young adult, thinking that people who were turning 40 were proper adults. They had their lives under control and walked confidently through whatever came their way. In my idealised image of them, they had cars and houses, routines, incomes – and never stumbled.double quotation markAs a child I thought that people turning 40 had their lives under control, with cars and houses and incomesThe reality is: I do not feel in control most of the time. There are days when I think I should be somewhere else entirely, and these questions keep circling through my mind: Why am I not further ahead? Why isn’t my bank account fuller, my career more established? Why haven’t I bought a house, or a car? Why am I still struggling to find a proper routine? Should I have stayed married? Should I have had a child? Did I take the wrong path – and if so, when? Did it start with studying history instead of going to journalism school, or even earlier, when every adult around me said I should become a lawyer?I know, I know. Don’t we all sometimes think, if only X, Y, Z had happened, I would be happier, more confident – that if I had just done this or achieved that, I’d finally be in the right place?At the end of last year, I moved from the European side of Istanbul to one of the Princes’ Islands in the Marmara Sea. They belong officially to the city but feel entirely their own, sitting in the middle of the water betweenEuropeand Asia. From here you can see both sides of Istanbul – its skyline clear on some days, hidden behind fog on others. You are part of the city and you are not.The decision was spontaneous – a sudden offer from an acquaintance to take over the apartment, which, unlike the rest of the city, is still affordable. It was only once I was here that the doubts arrived. Would living on an island make the feeling of in-between even heavier? Would I be completely lost in space?I needn’t have worried. I think I have never loved a place as much as this one. But it took me a while to understand why, on this island, I suddenly felt more at peace than ever before. Something had shifted – I couldn’t quite describe it, but it had.A group of friends came over by ferry from Istanbul for a lazy Sunday afternoon on the first weekend of real spring weather. Before sunset we sat on one of the cliffs looking out over the sea. We talked about what we would let go of with the disappearing light – what we would release at the end of this day.I saidaradayım– I am in-between – and that I wanted to stop wrestling with it, this feeling of not being stable, of not having arrived. Because in-between is a place, too. One that allows me to see in multiple directions at once. And haven’t I always been rather good at living in-between? Isn’t the in-between something where I have done most of my living, most of my thinking, most of my becoming?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenEast German writer Christa Wolf in 1978.Photograph: Schilling/EPALike Christa Wolf, I am a former GDR citizen. I was too young to witness what she witnessed, but I carry something of that formative fracture –Germanyreuniting in 1989-90 after 40 years of division, trying to grow back together. What I understood early, growing up within that collision of two systems, two ideologies, two entirely different ways of life, is that you cannot simply dissolve the in-between, the space that separates them. To erase the distance between two sides would mean erasing the histories that created it.Yet we are taught to experience this as failure – as evidence that we haven’t grown enough, learned enough, built enough, secured enough, become enough.Whenever I am in Germany, I get asked: how much longer will you stay over there? When are you coming back for good? And inTurkey, people struggle to understand why I – a German citizen with a life in Europe – would be in Istanbul at all. There is often an implication that this in-between life of mine is a strange adventure, that will eventually be over when I choose one side over the other.The in-between is supposed to be a waiting room, not a life. But I no longer believe that.Don’t we all move, always, between fronts?On my actual birthday my best friend called me first thing, congratulated me, and asked: So, how is it over there? Do you feel different? I laughed and said: No, I feel the same. In-between, as always. Because it is in-between that our lives are lived.Of course Christa Wolf – that genius of a person – knew that all along. I had to become 40.Carolin Würfel is a writer, screenwriter and journalist who lives in Berlin and Istanbul. She is the author of Three Women Dreamed of SocialismExplore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionCold warEuropeTurkeycommentShareReuse this content

title: Australians in end-of-life agony can’t always see a doctor. Telehealth can help them die with dignity | Andrew Denton | The Guardian
description: A collision of state v federal law on voluntary assisted dying has had tragic consequences. And a Labor conscience vote that never reaches parliament is no conscience vote at all
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A collision of state v federal law on voluntary assisted dying has had tragic consequences. And a Labor conscience vote that never reaches parliament is no conscience vote at all
Content: ‘Doctors risk prosecution and fines of $300,000 if they use the widely accepted tool of telehealth to carry out any part of the voluntary assisted dying process,’ Andrew Denton writes.Photograph: Justin Paget/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Doctors risk prosecution and fines of $300,000 if they use the widely accepted tool of telehealth to carry out any part of the voluntary assisted dying process,’ Andrew Denton writes.Photograph: Justin Paget/Getty ImagesOpinionAssisted dyingAustralians in end-of-life agony can’t always see a doctor. Telehealth can help them die with dignityAndrew DentonA collision of state v federal law on voluntary assisted dying has had tragic consequences. And a Labor conscience vote that never reaches parliament is no conscience vote at allMon 27 Jul 2026 23.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 03.06 EDTShareAt last week’s ALP national conference, delegates changed Labor’s platform to support removing federal barriers to voluntary assisted dying care, including telehealth. They also guaranteed Labor parliamentarians a conscience vote on VAD.On Sunday, Anthony Albanesesaid he remained personally unconvinced about telehealth. That cabinet would decide whether the issue reached the floor of the parliament or not. He fears telehealth could be misused or undermine confidence in the system.The prime minister is entitled to that view. It’s not a view, however, shared by a majority of his party.And a conscience vote that never reaches parliament is no conscience vote at all. The PM needs to bring on this debate and not stand in its way.At a dying man’s bedside, I see something much rarer than grief: the courage to include the young | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreThe vote in question is whether a commonwealth criminal law enacted in 2005 should continue to obstruct medical care authorised under state and territory laws many years later.That 2005 law made it an offence to use a carriage service – phone, email, video conferencing – to send “suicide-related material”. Its target was harmful online material and people encouraging others to take their own lives.The provisions were never intended to apply to VAD. In 2023, the Melbourne GP Nick Carr tested this by asking the federal court to determine whether “suicide” in those provisions included the lawful, medical process of VAD.Even though state VAD laws explicitly say VAD is not suicide, the commonwealth argued that it did. The court agreed.The result is that doctors risk prosecution and fines of $300,000 if they use the widely accepted tool of telehealth to carry out any part of the VAD process.This collision of state versus federal law has had tragic consequences.Patrick Hammer, 38, lived in regional Queensland. Dying of liver disease, he was found eligible for VAD. Because his doctor had to put his prescription in the post, rather than send it electronically, it did not reach him in time. His wife, Helena, said of Patrick’s death: “I didn’t see any peace in it. It was torture.”Tom, a 79-year-old man with end-stage lung disease in far north Queensland, was also eligible for VAD but too unwell to travel. Two doctors made three trips totalling 8,500km to assess him for VAD. But Tom died before the medication could be dispensed.double quotation markThese are all careful, sensible people. They would not advocate for this change were it not safe and necessaryAnyone who calls that arrangement a responsible use of two rural doctors’ time should identify which of those kilometres made Tom safer.Frailty and terminal decline arrive in the suburbs as reliably as they do in remote Australia. Terry Hargreaves, managing end-stage prostate cancer, lived in Melbourne, close to hospitals and doctors, but in his final weeks even reaching the bathroom was an enormous task.His daughter Emma, who presented a petition with 13,000 signatures to federal parliament seeking change, watched Terry spend the last weeks of his life in excruciating pain because he was too ruined to travel to a VAD consultation, “even for five minutes”. “He deserved a better death,” she says.The federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, has said she is not convinced a person making an end-of-life decision should be denied the dignity of a face-to-face consultation.But allowing telehealth will not require any practitioner to use it. The gold standard will always be in-person consultations. It would simply give practitioners an additional clinical tool when distance or pain make an in-person appointment unreasonable. Removing the criminal barrier is precisely what would return VAD to health policy, where Rowland says it belongs.Another concern raised is coercion. It’s the right question, to which there are clear answers.Having been debated exhaustively in every Australian parliament, our VAD laws are built around two core requirements: you demonstrate mental competency, and this is your voluntary choice.As befits the gravity of the request, the process is deliberately careful, involving multiple steps. Two doctors, trained to detect coercion, independently assess your eligibility. They carefully read your medical records and talk to other members of your healthcare team. Either of them can stop the process, and they have.Two witnesses who cannot be family members or beneficiaries must attest to your written statement that VAD is your choice and yours alone.Most crucially, at any time you can change your mind. One-third of people who get the VAD medication end up not using it.Allowing a consultation to occur by video removes none of those criteria.The patient who loves buying lettuce for his daughter-in-law – and what his case teaches us about shared decision-making in medicine | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreOur acceptance of telehealth in other settings is best explained by its use in palliative care. Providers and practitioners have made clear how valuable it is to have its flexibility “for providing comprehensive supportive care in the last weeks of life, where patients can be too unwell and unstable to attend any other form of consultation”. The commonwealth funds that care.The solution is neither novel nor difficult. The independent MP Kate Chaneyintroduced a private member’s billin 2024 creating an exception for telehealth performed under state and territory VAD laws. It’s before the parliament again.The Australian Medical Association supports the change, as do the Law Council, the VAD regulatory bodies, some 20 health organisations, and state and territory attorneys general and health ministers. These are all careful, sensible people. They would not advocate for this change were it not safe and necessary.The Labor government should honour the commitments of its conference, not promise a conscience vote in the abstract and prevent the parliament from having one in practice.A conscience vote requires a vote.Andrew Denton is a longtime advocate for choice at the end of life and is the founding director of Go Gentle AustraliaExplore more on these topicsAssisted dyingOpinionHealthDeath and dyingAustralian politicsAnthony AlbaneseLabor partyRural and regional AustraliacommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on India’s gen Z revolt: the cockroaches are coming together | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A youth movement born from exam leaks and online mockery has pierced Narendra Modi’s aura of invincibility and may yet reshape Indian politics
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A youth movement born from exam leaks and online mockery has pierced Narendra Modi’s aura of invincibility and may yet reshape Indian politics
Content: CJP supporters take part in a demonstration at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on 25 July.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAView image in fullscreenCJP supporters take part in a demonstration at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on 25 July.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAOpinionIndiaThe Guardian view on India’s gen Z revolt: the cockroaches are coming togetherEditorialA youth movement born from exam leaks and online mockery has pierced Narendra Modi’s aura of invincibility and may yet reshape Indian politicsTue 28 Jul 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTShare“What if all cockroaches come together?” wasthe questionthat humbled India’s strongman prime minister, Narendra Modi. It wasposted on XbyAbhijeet Dipke, an Indian student in the US with a master’s in public relations. Enraged that India’s top judge likened unemployed youths to insects and “parasites”, and that millions saw medical exams compromised by leaks, Mr Dipke lit a fuse. For India’s nearly 400 million gen Z, public exams are often the only ladder to a secure future. When papers leak or tests are cancelled, that ladder is kicked away. By June, young people were protesting peacefully in Delhi as the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), a parody of Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). They demanded the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.Thisweekend, Mr Pradhan became the first senior minister in Mr Modi’s 12 years in power to be forced from office by a mass-protest movement. It came after credible reports suggestedpolice officersattacked protesters marching to parliament. Security sources say it was they who were attacked. This may be just the beginning. The concession has taught the Cockroach movement’s leadership that pressure works. They could have declared victory and gone home. Instead they haveaccusedthe government of breaching the terms of the settlement offered by Mr Modi’s government. The CJP claims at least 100 people have been arrested, many on non-bailable charges. Its leaders are now demanding the release of detainees and threatening to remobilise nationally.View image in fullscreenAbhijeet Dipke.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAMr Modi has built an authoritarian order which rested upon Hindu majoritarianism anddemonisingMuslims. Education in the country has been subordinated to ideology and political patronage. But corruption in public exams cannot be divided so easily along religious lines. A Hindu graduate in northern India and a Muslim graduate in its southern cone experience the same anger over leaked papers and worthless qualifications. The grievance, crucially, creates an economic identity that cuts across the BJP’s preferred religious cleavage.Until Mr Pradhan’s resignation, ministerial accountability to public protest had all but disappeared; loyalty to Mr Modi’s ideological project had mattered more. The CJP has also broken the spell of fear that hasdominatedthe public square. The movement’s leadership were not requesting generosity; they were asserting a claim to clean administration, fair exams and ministerial accountability. Writing in the Guardian, the historianMukul Kesavansays the CJP’s social-media dexterity is crucial. Like New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, they combine eloquence, message discipline and composure, making Mr Modi look leaden. Their victory may have produced not merely a protest movement, but a new generation of political leaders.A similar kind of unrest during ananti-corruption movementin 2011 paved the way for Mr Modi to wrest power from theruling Congress coalition 12 years ago. The next general election is in 2029 and predicting its outcome today is not a worthwhile exercise. But the political scientist Christophe Jaffrelotarguesthat the CJP represents a much deeper revolt than just anger over exam leaks. It has, he says, become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Many Indians are either cockroaches now or in the process of becoming them. If they were to come together in a meaningful political way then Mr Modi may be in much bigger trouble than he is in today.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘Topless modelling never aligned with me’: inside Everyone’s Seen My Tits, the play by a former page 3 model | Stage | The Guardian
description: As she brings her memoir to the Edinburgh festival, Keeley Hazell talks about trauma, exploitation, the hollowness of the high life – and her new career as a writer on Ted Lasso
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: As she brings her memoir to the Edinburgh festival, Keeley Hazell talks about trauma, exploitation, the hollowness of the high life – and her new career as a writer on Ted Lasso
Content: ‘I was just numb’ … Keeley Hazell.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I was just numb’ … Keeley Hazell.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianStageInterview‘Topless modelling never aligned with me’: inside Everyone’s Seen My Tits, the play by a former page 3 modelAnya RyanAs she brings her memoir to the Edinburgh festival, Keeley Hazell talks about trauma, exploitation, the hollowness of the high life – and her new career as a writer on Ted LassoTue 28 Jul 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a time in the mid-2000s when it felt as though “everyone” had seen her topless, says Keeley Hazell.Page 3 was a staple of the tabloid press, lads’ mags were booming and she was one of the country’s most recognisable glamour models. “There was excitement, but also a lot of shame and embarrassment,” the softly spoken Hazell reflects. “Topless modelling never really aligned with me as a person.”Hazell, who was born in Lewisham, London, left modelling in her early 20s and moved to LA to become an actor. But the emotional impact of her time in the industry has stayed with her, partly inspiring her 2025 bookEveryone’s Seen My Tits: Stories and Reflections from an Unlikely Feminist. She describes the writing process as a “release” when we meet in London, where she has been preparing for an Edinburgh fringe theatre/comedy show based on the book. “I was able to give myself a voice,” she says, for “a period where I felt voiceless”.double quotation markI’d drink a lot and tell myself to enjoy the partyThe show makes her think “of the image of Russian dolls – I’m performing as me, but then I’m also performing as a version of me”. This sense of having multiple identities is nothing new for her. She remembers “presenting differently” to the Keeley Hazell people saw on magazine covers, “in vintage clothes and very grungey”. So much so that she was rarely recognised in the street, even at the height of her fame. When asked if she was a Page 3 model, she would deny it. “I’d be like, ‘Are you saying I look like a Page 3 model?’ And it was a really interesting experiment because they’d often be like, ‘No, no, you’re way more classy than that.’ It was weird because they were talking about me but I also felt separate from it.”Hazell’s introduction to glamour modelling was fast and unexpected. At 16, she left school and started working in a hair salon, where a colleague encouraged her to apply to become a model. She had some photos taken and sent them off to “a bunch of addresses” given to her – one of which, unbeknown to Hazell, was the Daily Star’s “beach babe” competition. She won, and a few months later entered the Sun’s “Page 3 idol” competition. “I won that too, and that was the start of my career.”Modelling was very different to her life at home on a council estate. “I went from growing up there to owning a luxury apartment overlooking the Thames.” Hazell was a “canvas”, and she knew she could be made up to fit a photographer’s image. “I was so young, there was so much exploitation, I was not emotionally or mentally prepared for it.” Safeguarding, she says, was basically nonexistent. “There was so little protection for women entering that industry. I had no idea about the things I needed in place, and my family didn’t either.”View image in fullscreen‘Page 3 was a wild thing to grow up with’ … Hazell.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianLooking back, Hazell almost can’t believe Page 3 was real. “It was just a wild thing to grow up with … those images were so readily available in newspapers and in newsagents.” There are times when she thinks of those days fondly; she was earning more money than she thought possible and got to travel the world. But she regrets “not having more control” over things. “A lot of the time I was just numb. I’d drink a lot and tell myself to enjoy the party.”Today, she gives carefully considered answers, with the air of someone who has had the time and space to process it all. Therapy has helped enormously, she tells me, particularly when it came to dealing with the fallout from a sex tape sold to the Sunday Sport. It was “terrifying” to write about the experience and “in a way relive it” Hazell says. “So many women experience some aspect of sexual violation and abuse in any realm, the shame for me needed to be ridded.”The Edinburgh fringe show is the latest chapter in that process. It begins in 2019 with her auditioning to play Keeley Jones, a character inspired by her, in Ted Lasso. She didn’t get the part but she did land a recurring role in the series and serves as a staff writer. Hazell can’t tell me much more about her solo show’s structure – she’s still in the writing process. “Right now I’m just staring at a laptop, ordering food and thinking, this is difficult,” she says with a laugh. She is certain, though, that it will be funny. “Trauma and humour are intertwined … even within the spiralling and the PTSD of it all, it should be a humorous retelling.” And it feels freeing to have, at last, complete autonomy over the Keeley Hazell people see and hear from. “It is incredibly powerful to have a voice.”Keeley Hazell: Everyone’s Seen My Tits is atPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, 5 to 29 AugustExplore more on these topicsStageComedy (Stage)TheatreEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalMagazinesNewspapersinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day review – Zendaya saves Tom Holland’s semi-Cronenberg-style superhero | Movies | The Guardian
description: Now 30, Holland is back as the vexed webslinger in a sometimes shocking, occasionally sluggish new instalment opposite his Odyssey castmate
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Now 30, Holland is back as the vexed webslinger in a sometimes shocking, occasionally sluggish new instalment opposite his Odyssey castmate
Content: ‘Unprecedented new physical and mental health issues’ … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: CTMG/PAView image in fullscreen‘Unprecedented new physical and mental health issues’ … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: CTMG/PAMoviesReviewSpider-Man: Brand New Day review – Zendaya saves Tom Holland’s semi-Cronenberg-style superheroNow 30, Holland is back as the vexed webslinger in a sometimes shocking, occasionally sluggish new instalment opposite his Odyssey castmatePeter BradshawTue 28 Jul 2026 09.11 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust a few weeks ago,Tom Hollandwas telling us that his role as Telemachus in Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey was his “last chance to play a boy”. Well, Holland is back as the supposedly scrappy, gawky, arachnid young superhero Spider-Man.
