Not Spider-Boy admittedly, and these days Holland is actually a chunkier and more stacked Spidey than previously, flexing some pretty serious biceps. He is maturing in the role. But is the role maturing with him?View image in fullscreenPeter Parker (Tom Holland) peers through the web.Photograph: CTMG/PAThe point is that this film is a reset. At the end of the last movieSpider-Man: No Way Home, courtesy of Dr Strange’s colossal psychic powers – which might have come in handy in this episode incidentally, part of the narrative-universe inconsistency that you just have to overlook – Peter Parker was able to erase everyone’s knowledge that he is, in fact, Spider-Man, and that includes his goofy best friend Ned Leeds (Jacob Batalon) and more to the point, the love of his life MJ (Zendaya).So now Peter is simply back where he started, adored by New Yorkers for crime-fighting as Spider-Man, living in a scuzzy single room with all his screens and tech gear, his secret identity a secret once more, but pining for the people he loves. And he’s not getting any younger. How much of a “brand new day” is this?View image in fullscreenGiving proceedings a boost … Zendaya in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyNow Spidey has to tackle a sinister new entity that appears to be possessing the bodies of important people around town – starting with the villainous Scorpion (Michael Mando) – with a view to attacking and infiltrating a key government unit, the department of Damage Control, run by Bill Metzger, played by the excellent Tramell Tillman (from TV’s Severance). It is a disquieting new development that coincides with unprecedented new physical and mental health issues for Parker. He has headaches, and these appear to be taking our hero to what I can only describe as the David Cronenberg zone.To tackle these inner and outer crises, Parker/Spidey has to consult Black Widow (an amusing cameo from Florence Pugh) who talks to him while reclining in a plunge pool in which shy Spidey joins her while wearing his mask and also underpants. He also has to seek advice from ageing academic Dr Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo) AKA the Hulk, a revived acquaintance which ends in chaos. And Spider-Man finds himself in a fractious frenmity-bromance with the highly strung tough guy Frank “Punisher” Castle, whose life he once saved, played by Holland’s Odyssey castmate Jon Bernthal.But most importantly of all, Parker is obsessed with finding ways to cross paths with MJ, effectively stalking her and masochistically witnessing her making out with her new boyfriend. And he has some very big, even slightly shocking scenes withZendaya– the other Odyssey cast-member, in fact. These are encounters which hold out the painful hope that he can somehow rekindle the flame, somehow find happiness while pursuing his lonely vocation.Zendaya saves this film. She rescues it from silliness and the generic deja vu overfamiliarity that is always threatening to sink it. Something in MJ’s civilian status, her non-superhero identity, brings Zendaya’s grownup acting presence to the fore in ways denied to everyone else on screen, including Holland. Her naturally relaxed style and self-possession give the proceedings a boost, especially with the flash of transgressive sexuality that she shows us at one moment. Director Destin Daniel Cretton gets the best out of her.View image in fullscreenHolding a flame … Zendaya and Holland in the film.Photograph: CTMG/PAOtherwise, things are the same in Spideyworld in ways that we will recognise with affectionate exasperation. As ever, Spider-Man can swing through the air across Manhattan without the overhead horizontal plane that his web would surely need to attach to, even in non-built-up areas (although he might be using power lines). And Spider-Man: Brand New Day, like all MCU movies, always gravitates towards apocalyptic but weirdly temporary destruction in the digitally confected big city. It’s an entertaining spectacle, but really without the novelty of movie-iterations like the more experimental Spider-Verse animations. A more radical reboot is needed.Spider-Man: Brand New Day is out on 29 July in the UK, 31 July in the US, and 30 July in Australia.Explore more on these topicsFilmSuperhero moviesTom HollandZendayareviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’ve always been wary of working together’: Val McDermid and Jo Sharp on writing a novel as a couple | Books | The Guardian
description: The bestselling crime writer and Scotland’s first female Geographer Royal had long kept their work separate, until a chance discovery about a doomed 17th-century expedition forced them to collaborate
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: The bestselling crime writer and Scotland’s first female Geographer Royal had long kept their work separate, until a chance discovery about a doomed 17th-century expedition forced them to collaborate
Content: ‘My mother always said I don’t play well with others’ … Val McDermid (right) and Jo Sharp.Photograph: Ryan RutherfordView image in fullscreen‘My mother always said I don’t play well with others’ … Val McDermid (right) and Jo Sharp.Photograph: Ryan RutherfordBooksInterview‘We’ve always been wary of working together’: Val McDermid and Jo Sharp on writing a novel as a coupleRobyn VinterThe bestselling crime writer and Scotland’s first female Geographer Royal had long kept their work separate, until a chance discovery about a doomed 17th-century expedition forced them to collaborateTue 28 Jul 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe airy, modern house on the outskirts of Edinburgh shared byVal McDermidand Jo Sharp is surrounded by greenery and feels as though it was designed to provide enough space for two minds to think.Both women are high achievers in their fields,a Scottish power couplemade up of theQueen of Crimeand the Scottish Geographer Royal. Happily for them, there is normally no overlap in their work.“We’d always been very wary of working together because we’d quite like to stay together,” says Sharp wryly. She looks at her partner of 13 years. “You don’t generally like to work with others.”McDermid responds: “No, my mother always used to say I don’t play well with others. She wasn’t far wrong.”McDermid’s mother would have to admit that This Door of the Seas – the couple’s jointly written novella, published next week – is an exception. The book is a fictionalised account of the 1698 Darien venture, in which more than 2,000 Scots, mostly fleeing famine, embarked on an ill-fated expedition to modern-day Panama, hoping to establish a trading colony and provide an overland route between the Atlantic and Pacific.It is no spoiler to reveal that the attempt bankrupted a struggling Scottish economy, hampered already by its overbearing neighbour, England. It propelled the country into signing the union agreement only seven years later, taking away Scotland’s parliament, its trading company and much of its pride.From then on, Scotland became an intrinsic part of the union, including the later evils of transatlantic slavery, a role that can sometimes go unacknowledged north of the border.Sharp says: “One of the things that we talked about a lot is that we didn’t want to be part of what is, I think, a bit of a whitewashing of Scotland’s history, to make us seem somehow not as culpable in terms of empire and around issues of race and racism.”View image in fullscreen‘I found it fascinating. It was a bit of history I had not heard about’ … Jo Sharp (right) says.Photograph: Val McDermid/Jo SharpSharp is a human geographer, with a background in geopolitics and international development. She is a professor of geography at the University of St Andrews, a member of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, and became Scotland’s first female Geographer Royal in 2022.Her civil partner, McDermid, has written 51 books, which have been translated into more than 40 languages, sold more than 20m copies and won a wealth of awards.At 71, nearly four decades after her debut,Report for Murder, followed by immensely popular crime series including the Tony Hill and Carol Jordan books, and the Karen Pirie novels, she continues to run rings around her readers, laying breadcrumbs and pulling rugs.The story came about through research Sharp was doing for a book festival talk. She was asked to speak about geography in Scotland, which she thought could be “quite dull”, and instead began researching the first Geographer Royal, who turned out to be “a really interesting character”.“I discovered that shortly after he was appointed, Scotland had this endeavour to set up a trading colony in Panama, and although he didn’t go himself, he sent someone to be his eyes and ears on the ground. I just found this fascinating, because it was a bit of history I had not heard about.”“I was telling Val all the things I’d found out about it and I said, ‘It would make a brilliant story, I just wish I could write it’,” says Sharp. “And Val then said, ‘maybe we should write it together,’ and before she got to the end of the sentence I had said yes.”McDermid says: “My experience of writing books that have elements of historical significance in them is that what you want is something that’s got enough information to hang a story on but enough gaps to colour in.”The aim is for the book to be “charmingly plausible”, a compliment once given to one of her historical novels. “That has been my watchword ever since. Make it charmingly plausible. Get the historical facts right and then colour in the bits around it.”The story is told by Dr James Wallace, a scientist, in letters to his wife, Eliza, and his sponsor, Sir Robert Sibbald, the first Geographer Royal of Scotland, founder of the Edinburgh botanic gardens and physician to the king.Sharp and McDermid worked on the structure during a rainy car journey back to Edinburgh. McDermid recalls: “You said, ‘how do we do this?’ and I said, ‘we’ll make it an epistolary novel’, and I had to explain what that was.” (“That’s not true!” interjects Sharp.)“I was convinced someone might have had this idea already because the more excited I got about it the more I thought, surely someone’s thought about this,” says Sharp. The book felt like a good addition to the publisherBirlinn’s Darkland Talesseries – reimaginings of Scottish historical and folk tales by different authors – for which McDermid had already contributed the Shakespeare retelling Queen Macbeth.“Now the slight complication with all of this,” says Sharp, “is that about two months later, Val went in for open-heart surgery –”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“– Which I hadn’t entirely anticipated,” McDermid adds. She needed an aortic valve replacement and two coronary bypasses to fix a condition spotted initially by her partner, who noticed her heart was skipping a beat.Sharp continues: “But the advantage of that was that I’d taken time off work to look after Val in her recovery, and there was only so much time I could wander around in my nurse’s uniform.”Sharp did the vast majority of the research – hunting down documents including letters and ship manifests at the National Library of Scotland – while McDermid was recovering, but the pair worked together on the writing, taking turns to write and then edit each other’s work.Slowly they began to unpick many of the myths about the Darien venture being a bumbling attempt from Scotland to stand on its own two feet, many of which Sharp realised had come not from factual accounts at the time but from political pamphlets.View image in fullscreen‘Get the historical facts right and then colour in the bits around it’ … Val McDermid (left) and Jo Sharp in their home.Photograph: Ryan RutherfordThe truth was the landscape was considerably harder to navigate than they had been led to believe – the colony unexpectedly came under relentless attack from the Spanish settlers who occupied territory nearby, and more than 80% of the Scots who had travelled over died within a year, mostly from tropical diseases or famine.“People also don’t understand that nations all around Europe were setting up colonies – nine out of 10 failed,” says McDermid. “So this wasn’t that only the Scots failed, everybody failed and everybody failed a lot.”Sharp adds: “It feeds into that story that Scotland just isn’t good enough to go alone, that we need that support of a bigger neighbour and all that kind of stuff.”View image in fullscreenThis Door of the Seas.The couple have worked together once before, editing an anthology,Imagine a Country, in which Scottish writers lay out their vision for a better future. With contributors including Alan Cumming, Ali Smith, Carol Ann Duffy, Ian Rankin and Alexander McCall Smith, the collection came six years after the Scottish independence referendum, in a nation still struggling to heal from some of the divisiveness of the campaign. It was not a political book, but the pair are strong supporters of Scottish independence, believing Scotland should be given a chance to succeed on its own merits.This Door of the Seas is more explicitly political: as the creeping sensation of betrayal by the English and Scottish landed gentry takes over, Wallace’s outrage seems to come freely to the book’s modern writers. It is a multi-generational bruise that lingers for many Scottish people more than 300 years later.Readers will undoubtedly find similarities between those fleeing Scottish famine in the 1600s and modern refugees, many of whom do not fully comprehend the danger of the journey or the hostile environment they will be arriving in. The couple recognise the parallel.“When the country that you’re living in offers you no hope,” says McDermid, “then the slenderest strands of hope you grasp, even if it’s not rooted in a reality.”This Door of the Seas is published on 6 August. McDermid and Sharp will be speaking atEdinburgh international book festivalon 17 August.Explore more on these topicsBooksFictionVal McDermidCrime fictionGeographyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Portrait of a City review – master photographers capture the US cityscape in all its grime, grit and glory | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Era-defining photographs from the likes of Alfred Stieglitz, Saul Leiter and Dorothea Lange showcase the urban landscape, from midnight crime scenes to gloomy corridors
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: Era-defining photographs from the likes of Alfred Stieglitz, Saul Leiter and Dorothea Lange showcase the urban landscape, from midnight crime scenes to gloomy corridors
Content: An immense city … Louis Faurer’s 1949 Looking at the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center.Photograph: Louis Faurer/Howard Greenberg Gallery, New YorkView image in fullscreenAn immense city … Louis Faurer’s 1949 Looking at the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center.Photograph: Louis Faurer/Howard Greenberg Gallery, New YorkArt and designReviewPortrait of a City review – master photographers capture the US cityscape in all its grime, grit and gloryDulwich Picture Gallery, LondonEra-defining photographs from the likes of Alfred Stieglitz, Saul Leiter and Dorothea Lange showcase the urban landscape, from midnight crime scenes to gloomy corridorsCharlotte JansenTue 28 Jul 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 11.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis – only the second photography exhibition in Dulwich Picture Gallery’s history – is a quietly contemplative but gripping show that traces two intersecting developments: the construction of the modern urban environment and the language of photography.Focusing exclusively on works from era-defining photographers of the 20th century made in cities across the US, it’s a concise overview that begins with the pictorialist pioneers of New York, Alfred Stieglitz and Edward Steichen, and keeps moving through masterpieces, starting with early examples of social documentary photography – Dorothea Lange’s Migrant Mother and White Angel Breadline, and Lewis Hine’s emblematic portrait of the high-steel ironworker Victor “Frenchy” Gosselin working on the construction of the Empire State Building.All the greats are here: Ilse Bing, Mary Ellen Mark, Diane Arbus, Saul Leiter, Richard Avedon, among others. This is partly because this show is a bit of an unusual beast: it exclusively presents works belonging to the DNB Savings Bank Foundation collection. That means the curatorial choices are limited.View image in fullscreenAll the greats are here … Mary Ellen Mark’s 1987 The Damm Family in Their Car.Photograph: Mary Ellen Mark/Mary Ellen Mark FoundationA series of short film pieces offer other interpretations. A 44-second clip of footage of the White Angel soup kitchen in San Francisco in 1931, where Lange’s indelible Great Depression image was made, gives an entirely different impression of the place from the grim loneliness depicted in the photograph. Set to an upbeat swing soundtrack, we see a lively community presided over by a jovial matron who distributes food and repairs clothing with a smile.Many of the photographers in the first part of the show trained as painters, and it shows in the glorious attentiveness to composition and light. Aaron Siskind’s Harlem Document reflects the influence of his friendships with Rothko and Kline, searching in Harlem’s torn posters and peeling paint for his own kind of abstract expression that also created a new photographic language for social protest.View image in fullscreenMoments only a city can yield … Arthur Leipzig’s 1948 Divers, East River.Photograph: Arthur Leipzig/Howard Greenberg Gallery, New YorkFrom the Great Depression to the New Deal, urban construction, regeneration and optimism soon slide into something more sinister. Images of solitary figures against the immensity of the city recur – Louis Faurer’s 1949 Looking at the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center says it all – an anonymous figure in a fedora looks towards the building, so mighty it fills the whole frame.At night, a city’s tensions rise to the surface, and all the weirdos come out. The highlights are the images that revel in this, like Weegee’s ominous, sensationalist snapshots of New York after dark, depicting murders, awful accidents and the odd moments only a city can yield – a person’s face, eyes closed, juts out from a column in an urban passageway; a large clock in the background pulls your eye into the inky shadows.There is a work of achingly simple genius by Roy DeCarava. Hallway is a photograph of an empty corridor in a tenement building in Harlem, much like the one the artist grew up in. It’s lit dimly by a single lightbulb, almost entirely swallowed by shadows, as the lines of the walls draw your eye in and down the space. DeCarava’s claustrophobic image makes you feel what it is to stand in that space. He finds the richness and expressivity in the colour black, as complex, volumetric and varied as any other hue.The exhibition as a whole retells the American narrative of the city – almost all of the photographers here are first- or second-generation European immigrants. It also shows how photography became a way for artists to deal with the overwhelming nature of the city, to try to take hold of it, to make it their own – or try, like Garry Winogrand, to disappear into it completely, to come closer to “not existing” as the photographer described his process, a quote emphasised on the exhibition wall. Portrait of a City is about the multiplicity of quiet-but-dazzling instants that happen every day – like Peter Hujar’s Richie, standing to reflect for a second in the rain on a street in New York at night, raindrops glimmering on a car windscreen.View image in fullscreenQuiet but dazzling … Peter Hujar’s 1985 Richie.Photograph: Peter Hujar/Peter Hujar Archive/Artists Rights Society, New York/DACS LondonWe move through the 60s and 70s, where the hair gets hipper and politics get more intense, and end up on the subway, engulfed by 1980s Leica shots that Bruce Davidson made on New York’s graffiti-covered trains. Here we’re in motion again, in the place where city life collides across culture, age, race and class. People go to celebrations, to work, fall asleep, fall in love, fight. The crimson light of sunset skies bathes the carriages in a beautiful, sensuous glow. The train keeps moving. And the unstoppable city remains in maddening, merciless motion.Portrait of a City: A Century of American Photographyis at Dulwich Picture Gallery, London, until 4 OctoberExplore more on these topicsArt and designExhibitionsPhotographyDulwich Picture GalleryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People named their kids after us!’ Lost’s Penny and Desmond on being one of TV’s best ever romances | Television | The Guardian
description: Sonya Walger and Henry Ian Cusick created a love so magical that they’re responsible for what’s widely regarded as the greatest TV episode of all time – not to mention inspiring a fan to get a full leg tattoo of their faces
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Sonya Walger and Henry Ian Cusick created a love so magical that they’re responsible for what’s widely regarded as the greatest TV episode of all time – not to mention inspiring a fan to get a full leg tattoo of their faces
Content: ‘The love was true and pure’ … Penny (Sonya Walger) and Desmond (Henry Ian Cusick) in the finale of season four.Photograph: Mario Perez/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The love was true and pure’ … Penny (Sonya Walger) and Desmond (Henry Ian Cusick) in the finale of season four.Photograph: Mario Perez/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesMaking loveTelevision‘People named their kids after us!’ Lost’s Penny and Desmond on being one of TV’s best ever romancesSonya Walger and Henry Ian Cusick created a love so magical that they’re responsible for what’s widely regarded as the greatest TV episode of all time – not to mention inspiring a fan to get a full leg tattoo of their facesMore from our series Making Love:‘We met and two minutes later we were kissing’ – how Gavin and Stacey became Britain’s most bang tidy TV coupleHollie RichardsonTue 28 Jul 2026 05.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLost is one of television’s most romantic dramas. Forget smoke monsters, time travel and that infamous ending – this was a show fuelled by swoony stories. Sun and Jin; Rose and Bernard; Sawyer/Jack/Kate/Juliet; Charlie and Claire; Sayid and Nadia (notShannon). Love was the reason behind so many of the islanders’ need to survive, or to sacrifice themselves.But it was Penny’s and Desmond’s relationship that defined the series.Penelope Widmore (Sonya Walger), a billionaire’s daughter, met Desmond Hume (Henry Ian Cusick), an ordinary Scot, when she went to pick up wine from a monastery, where Des had just quit being a monk. It was love at first sight and they drove off together with the booze. But the relationship was doomed due to Penny’s disapproving (and evil) father, Des’s need to prove himself in a sailing competition and his arrival at a freaky island. Like the Odyssey character after whom she was named, Penny spent a lot of time waiting and wondering. However, as she once forewarned: “With enough money and determination, you can find anyone.” And she did. In fact, without Penny, the survivors of Oceanic flight 815 might never have made it home.Of course, it wasn’t easy. There was a breakup, Charlie’s devastating death and the sob-fest episode The Constant – widely consideredthe best TV episode of all time– in which, after eight years apart, Penny kept her promise to answer Des’s phone call on Christmas Eve. As Penny put it: “All you really need to survive is someone who loves you. And you have her.”How did Walger and Cusick make such a love story for the ages? On the day I put this to them, it is exactly 21 years since the Lost pilot. “It’s the day the plane went down … and I’m flying to LA in two hours!” says Cusick from his home in Hawaii, the filming location of Lost, where he moved his family 20 years ago. “Are you really?” gasps Walger from Santa Monica, California. “It will make the news,” he laughs.The friends quickly exchange life updates: Cusick is filming an indie vampire western; Walger is navigating a new normal after losing her family home in theLos Angeles fires. Then, it’s time to talk about becoming Penny and Desmond …Do you remember meeting for the first time?HC:The writers had an idea for something, but they didn’t know what. When I shot the photo [of Penny and Des, which Des keeps with him on the island], another actor played that – and she was a local extra. Then we did it again with Sonya.SW:Let’s be clear: there was no time for a chemistry read. There was no time for anything, ever. I mean, they were writing these scripts and shooting them 15 minutes later. People were being cast and put on a plane that afternoon.HC:It was night-time! [Their first scene together is at night in a stadium.]View image in fullscreenGrandstand event … Penny and Desmond meet.Photograph: ABCSW:I’d been there on my own, jumping up and down around the stadium and feeling quite adrift – I didn’t know anyone. I was really sticky and thought: I need to meet this guy I don’t know anything about. We immediately discovered that Ian is half Scottish and half Peruvian and I’m half English and half Argentine. And those are strangely exotic and yet neighboured identities. That was something very lovely, very rare.HC:I have a big memory of meeting Sonya and thinking: oh, a proper, proper actress. But then she would pop in and out all the time.SW:I’d be gone for months. Funnily enough, Ian was my constant. I didn’t know anyone else in the show and I really wasn’t getting the intervening scripts. So we’d sit down and I’d be like: “All right, what’s happened?”What do Penny and Des love about each other?SW:When you’ve got a father as domineering as Charles Widmore [Alan Dale], the quiet, gentle devotion of Desmond is the antithesis of that.HC:The love was true and pure – and it was a good love. But it was more about: how will they get back together?What were your favourite romantic moments?HC:Inthe scene with the letter[from Penny, which Desmond finds for the first time on the island], I wasn’t a regular character at that point and I think that helped. There was another scene, where they were shouting out all these crazy directions: “Do it sad! Do it angry!” I was trying to show them my whole colour palette. And then Terry Quinn [who played Locke] said to me: “That was your audition.”View image in fullscreenRead it and weep … Des finds Penny’s letter.Photograph: ABCThe irony of The Constant is that we weren’t even together. I ended up doing it with the assistant director on my side. When Sonya turned up, she did it and I was on the sofa behind. That moment, that phone call – with not a lot of dialogue – was one of those things that worked a bit of magic. What was really hard was when we had to meet [in season four, when Penny finds Des] and I was thinking: how are we going to beat that?Is there anything you wish Penny and Des had done differently?SW:The greedy actor in me would say I’d love to have done more with us.HC:Me too! I think there was more life in us.SW:Spin-off, for fuck’s sake – where was the spin-off?HC:Now I would push that. You, me and Charlie on a boat.SW:I say that partly jokingly. Because what gives this couple its place in the world’s heart is that it wasn’t oversaturated. You only had a handful of episodes to hold. You didn’t get bored of us, that’s for sure.HC:It left people wanting more.SW:We did great and left them on a high note.When did you realise this was a love story for the ages?SW:In this show that had so many contradictions and loose ends and tears in the space time continuum that bent your mind, here was one really classic trope you could hold on to.HC:It was a simple story of two people who couldn’t be together – because of her father, or time, or so many things in their way – who desperately wanted to be together.View image in fullscreen‘You didn’t get bored of us, that’s for sure.’Photograph: ABCSW:I felt very honoured when I got the call asking me to fly in for the finale – if nothing else, it was acknowledgment from the creators of the value of our little duo. But it’s only as the years have crept on, appearing on “the best couple of all time” lists and things. It never ceases to surprise and truly gratify me that we did some work that has endured like this. It’s amazing.HC:I always thought we had a cool storyline. But we didn’t know the legacy it would have. It’s been 20 years and there’s been so much great TV since – and we’re still talking about that relationship.How romantic are you in real life?SW:Romantic is a weird word in your 50s! I’m devoted. I know what devotion is – to my family, to my husband, to the life we have. And it’s something I felt at the time even without them. I felt a strong sense of devotion to the life I had created for myself in LA, so much so that I wasn’t willing to let it go by moving to Hawaii. [Walger was in the running to play the main character Kate Austen, but pulled out.]HC:I think as I’m getting older I’m getting more romantic and softer. I get more emotional about the past, like thinking about my kids as babies.SW:I’m going to push back and say he’s always had that.HC:Really? I’ve never thought of myself like that. I’m a “tough” guy!SW:No he’s not! He’s a deeply, deeply feeling man.What has been the most intense fan reaction to Penny and Des?SW:A full leg tattoo of our faces! I get “Not Penny’s boat” held up to me at airports a lot. It’s like a fan’s secret way of saying: “I see you, but I will respect you.” I really mean it when I say it’s just really humbling to have done anything at all that leaves such a mark.HC:People have named their children after us – that’s odd.SW:Yes! I have 100% had some Pennys.What was your relationship like off camera?SW:It just felt so easy and effortless from day one. It was a pleasure to see Ian. I think he was grateful just to have someone visiting from the mainland who was also from England; there was some sort of familiarity.HC:When I arrived [on the Lost set], the cast was already very integrated. I worked separately, which I really enjoyed, actually. Even on the days I did work with the whole cast, I didn’t really enjoy them, because there are so many actors and you have to wait for your turn. I liked working with two or three people – I love it. It was very easy with Sonya and it was always going to be a good scene when we met up.View image in fullscreen‘All you really need to survive is someone who loves you’ … Penny in the celebrated season four episode The Constant.Photograph: ABCSW:Years later, I came to Hawaii with my family and we met up with Ian. For old time sakes, we went to the church where we unloaded boxes of wine and took photos there. We stay in touch.HC:We did a short film together, too.SW:That’s right – I had just had my baby, I think.HC:No, she was eight months pregnant!SW:Oh yeah! Ian, if you’ve got a day off when you’re in LA and you want a cup of tea, will you come and find me?HC:Yes! I’ll try.Did you keep anything from the set that reminds you of Penny and Des?SW:I lost everything in the house. I don’t even have my children’s baby photos. It’s really shocking and it makes me very, very intentional about what I put back.HC:I had the blue shirt – I stole it and they asked for it back. They were pretty stingy. I auctioned it [for charity] anyway. I’ve seen many reproductions of their photo and I’m asked to sign it.SW:My first novelcame out in February this year,three weeks after the fire. I had to go to a book festival the other day and people handed me Lost photos to sign, and I was like: dude, just buy the book!What can Penny and Des teach us about love?SW:Keep the faith.HC:“Keep the faith” is great – I’ll go with that, too.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionMaking loveLostDramaUS televisionEntertainment TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: This Booker longlist may have two previous winners, but it’s keen to experiment | Books | The Guardian
description: Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout may be names we know, but there’s a welcome element of absurdism and surrealist thought here
Author: Justine Jordan
Headline: Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout may be names we know, but there’s a welcome element of absurdism and surrealist thought here
Content: A trove of ideas … this year’s Booker prize longlist novels.Photograph: Booker Prize FoundationView image in fullscreenA trove of ideas … this year’s Booker prize longlist novels.Photograph: Booker Prize FoundationBooksThis Booker longlist may have two previous winners, but it’s keen to experimentJustine JordanMarlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout are names we know, but there’s a welcome element of surprise elsewherePrevious winners Douglas Stuart and Marlon James lead Booker prize longlistTue 28 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.59 EDTShareThis year’s Booker longlist is led by two previous winners. Twelve years on from A Brief History of Seven Killings, Marlon James returns to Jamaica inThe Disappearers, out in September: a polyphonic epic of a murderous mob attack on a gay theatre group in 1988 Kingston, and the two-decade aftermath of trauma and revenge that follows. A brutal expose of Jamaica’s homophobia, it’s also an energetic portrait of queer culture and the Caribbean diaspora. Douglas Stuart, whose debut Shuggie Bain won in 2020, is included forJohn of John, in which a young gay man returns to his childhood home on the Hebridean island of Harris, where his devout father is also hiding his sexuality. Both novels open up territory not often trod in literature, with Stuart illuminating faith, repression and the fading traditions of the Scottish Hebrides.It’s no surprise either to see a third nomination for Elizabeth Strout.The Things We Never Sayintroduces new characters to her fictional universe, in the story of a fiftysomething teacher with a secret in his marriage and a sadness in his heart. Strout has always been interested in class and deprivation in American society; the spectre of Trump brings a growing darkness, but as ever her spiky warmth and wisdom carry the reader through. The other big-name American author on the list is Emma Cline;Switzy, out in September, takes us inside the mind of a high flyer whose grip on the world is failing as dementia encroaches. David is taking his last journey, to a euthanasia clinic in Zurich, and on the way will hopefully make his final reckonings with friends and family while he can still recognise them. It’s a technical tour de force of the unreliable narrator, and a hugely moving account of life’s meaning as everything is stripped away.This year’s big omission is also American: Ben Lerner was widely seen as a shoo-in forTranscription, his compact but intricately allusive meditation on family inheritance, technology and the effect of smartphones on the way we see the world. But there will be rejoicing at a nomination at last for British author Gwendoline Riley, who has been writing devastatingly precise indictments of family relationships and emotional narcissism for a quarter of a century.The Palm Housefinds her in a more tender mood, investigating a long friendship against the precarity of London life.It’s fantastic too to see M John Harrison’sThe End of Everything, a fabulously destabilising vision of an England drifting through alien invasion into terminal decline. Harrison, who has been called “the missing evolutionary link between William Burroughs and Virginia Woolf”, began his career in the late 1960s as part of the science fiction New Wave, and has been subverting genre and perspective in steely modernist sentences ever since. This portrait of apocalypse-at-a-remove, with wars in the distance, reality bending, new forms of intelligence on the rise while humans dissociate and muddle confusedly through, perhaps speaks more to our times than realism ever could.Indeed judge Patricia Lockwood, known for her own dazzlingly idiosyncratic prose, claimed in aninterview with the Observer that“in the face of AI and the fractured attention span, I think we’re going to see a new avant garde that insists on the participation of the human … there is a new, weird literature emerging”. She jokingly threatened to choose “the craziest book on﻿ Earth!” And there’s certainly a weird and wild undercurrent in this year’s list, soaked through with absurdism and surrealism.If one theme is the journey from margins to mainstream, it’s been a rapid progression for Missouri Williams, only on her second novel after cult success The Doloriad. Set in a university town overrun by vegetation,The Vivisectorsis a deeply strange parable of culture wars, family dysfunction and civilisational decline, and an even stranger love story. “At the centre of my soul there was a big dead rock that wanted nothing to do with anything else,” says our young antiheroine, and while there are echoes of Ottessa Moshfegh here, Williams has a vision and energy all her own.Rebecca Perry’s debutMay We Feedthe Kingis similarly uncategorisable, contrasting a contemporary narrative about a curator who recreates furnishings and feasts in historic houses with the story of an unwilling medieval ruler. It’s a puzzle box of a novel that toys with the reader but keeps them rapt throughout. American Makenna Goodman’sHelen of Nowhereis more unusual still: organised as a series of dramatic scenes, it is a witty fable of male entitlement based around a university professor whose status is upended by the changing zeitgeist. Like The Vivisectors, it’s interested in nature v civilisation, culture wars and identity politics.“History repeats itself so fast in Turkey, faster than in any other country.” Kenan Orhan’sThe Renovationuses a Kafkaesque absurdity – a bathroom in an Italian flat that suddenly becomes a prison cell in Istanbul – to open up a story about migration, home and political repression, in which the trials of loss and memory extend to the narrator’s father’s dementia. Even Luke Kennard’s comic rompBlackBagis tinged with absurdism. Here a failing actor who has “measured out my life in coffees I cannot technically afford” takes part in a university experiment, hanging around campus dressed only in a black leather bag: his parents appear as stone menhirs, and his best conversations are with a dog. Full of zinging one-liners, this is a very funny take on work, friendship, masculinity and other modern confusions.Irish author Djamel White’s debutAll Them Dogs, a tale of drug deals, bad choices and queer desire in the ganglands of Dublin, has a similarly riotous energy, while the Mexican-British author Chloe Aridjis’sThe Shadow of the Objectis a quieter, almost dreamlike story of a woman drawn into a fascination with magic lanterns and the technology of illusion; the ruminative mood is reminiscent of WG Sebald. The shortlist, released on 22 September, may have a different emphasis, but for the moment this is a longlist that’s eager to experiment.Explore more on these topicsBooksBooker prizeAwards and prizesFictioncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘She wasn’t acting, she wanted to live it’: how a fake pregnancy resulted in the wildest true crime film of the year | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: Netflix documentary A Child of My Own tells the stranger-than-fiction story of a hospital worker who went to extreme lengths in her efforts to become a mother. Its director recounts their meetings in a Mexican prison
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Netflix documentary A Child of My Own tells the stranger-than-fiction story of a hospital worker who went to extreme lengths in her efforts to become a mother. Its director recounts their meetings in a Mexican prison
Content: All the qualities of a Greek tragedy … Ana Celeste as Alejandra in A Child of My Own.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenAll the qualities of a Greek tragedy … Ana Celeste as Alejandra in A Child of My Own.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixDocumentary films‘She wasn’t acting, she wanted to live it’: how a fake pregnancy resulted in the wildest true crime film of the yearNetflix documentary A Child of My Own tells the stranger-than-fiction story of a hospital worker who went to extreme lengths in her efforts to become a mother. Its director recounts their meetings in a Mexican prisonCath ClarkeTue 28 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 00.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe CCTV footage of the hospital corridor is grainy but you can make out a young woman carrying an oversized gift bag. Nothing unusual there. Except that inside the bag is a newborn baby girl, just hours old. And the woman carrying the bag, walking out of the hospital’s main entrance, past two security guards who are idly chatting, is not the baby’s mother.Her name is Eleonor Alejandra Marín Mendoza, known to everyone as Alejandra. When film-makerMaite Alberdimet her in a low-security Mexican prison, Alejandra was in the final year of a 13-year jail sentence for snatching the baby. Alberdi listened rapt as Alejandra told her story: “Everything she was telling me was extraordinary, stranger than fiction.”It was a tale full of drama and intrigue. Alejandra was 17 and already pregnant when she married her husband Arturo in a fairytale wedding. She’d always wanted children and Arturo was desperate for a son. But then she had a miscarriage, and then another. Still only in her 20s, she underwent IVF. After she became pregnant for the third time, she miscarried again – but kept this miscarriage a secret and faked the rest of her pregnancy.View image in fullscreen‘Everybody has an opinion about motherhood’ … director Maite Alberdi.Photograph: John Phillips/Getty Images for BFIAs Alejandra told her story, the twists kept coming. She worked in admin at a hospital, where she met a single mother, Mayra, who was pregnant but did not want to keep her baby. The two women struck a deal: after giving birth, Mayra would hand her baby over to Alejandra. Five months later, Alejandra arrived at the hospital and collected the baby girl. But something went wrong and the police were called. Alejandra was arrested hours later at a nearby hotel and the baby was returned to Mayra.“For two years I only heard Alejandra’s version of what happened,” says Alberdi, who is Chilean and earned an Oscar nomination for her 2020 filmThe Mole Agent. She continued to visit Alejandra in prison in Mexico and applied for transcripts of her criminal trial. The process was slow, but finally she received the court bundle. “When I saw the evidence, I thought: ‘Oh no, I was so wrong.’ I crashed into reality.”Alejandra’s story did not fit the facts. In her witness statements, Mayra said she actually met Alejandra for the first time after she gave birth, when Alejandra walked on to the hospital ward posing as a social worker. There never had been any arrangement between them. Instead, Mayra faced the unimaginable terror of her newborn baby being kidnapped from her hospital cot. The evidence was on her side.Alberdi could not ignore what she was reading. Did she think about ditching the film? “Yes! I wasn’t sure if I could continue. I was really disappointed.” But the thought of doing that must have been difficult, after spending so much time with Alejandra, being so invested in her story? “Si, yes. I trusted her, but my gut feeling was that I believed the evidence. It was hard.”Did she confront Alejandra? “Yes! She denied everything, and she continues saying that until today.”Despite the shock revelation, Alberdi stuck with the film. She says that from the beginning, what she connected to in the story was the pressure that drove Alejandra to the edge – to conceal her miscarriage and pretend that she was still pregnant. “It was not about the case; it was about the situation. I was more interested in why she faked a pregnancy. It was a question of the social pressure of motherhood in Mexico, in Latin America.”View image in fullscreenA Child of My Own tells Alejandra’s version of events in the style of a Mexican telenovela.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixHer Netflix documentaryA Child of My Ownbegins with a dramatic reconstruction starring actor Ana Celeste as Alejandra. The story has all the qualities of a Greek tragedy. But the way Alejandra recounted it was more like a soap opera, over the top and full of melodrama. And that’s how Alberdi has filmed it, depicting Alejandra’s version of what happened in the style of a Mexican telenovela. She guesses it’s about 80% accurate. And it is hilarious in places – farcical and wacky as Alejandra binge eats to gain weight and fakes an ultrasound scan. “When she told me the story, we were laughing.”It’s funny until it isn’t. At her lavish baby shower, surrounded by family and friends, Alejandra looks dazed and alone. “You know, she went to yoga pregnancy classes,” says Alberdi. “She wasn’t just acting for others. She really wanted to live it.”Does Alberdi think Alejandra came to believe her own deception? “Completely. And if you see the archive footage, it’s not a fat woman, it’s a pregnant woman. So it’s like she did have a psychological pregnancy. She wanted to believe, and at some point, she was living that lie.”In the dramatisation, Alberdi reveals the pressure Alejandra felt to have a baby. After each of her miscarriages, she is castigated as a failure. Her mother-in-law blames her: “You should have been more careful.” Her husband Arturo is sympathetic up to a point, but his disappointment adds to her guilt. Alberdi is at pains to point out that she is not trying to justify Alejandra’s crime but to understand the context.Has the situation changed for women since 2009, when Alejandra faked her pregnancy, I ask. Before the sentence is finished, Alberdi cuts in: “In Mexico and in Latin America, no. There is the same pressure to be married and have kids.” At a recent screening in Mexico, a Q&A was derailed as women in the audience stood up to share their stories of struggling with fertility and the pressure to have a baby.As a mother of an eight-year-old, Alberdi says she too is aware of constant judgment: “Everybody has an opinion about how you are living motherhood, all the time.” She has lost count of the number of times that people at film festivals – “mostly men” – will ask her who is looking after her son.Alberdi’s film crashes down to earth, just as she did. In the second part of A Child of My Own, the reconstruction ends and Alberdi interviews Alejandra and her husband Arturo, who was also arrested and spent two years in prison before being acquitted at trial. She speaks to the judge at Alejandra’s trial, and a psychologist. There is also an interview with Mayra, the baby’s mother, whose fury and trauma are still raw. For her, a 50-year prison sentence wouldn’t have been long enough, Alberdi says. “She suffered so much. I understand that she cannot forgive Alejandra.”Alberdi also interviewed Mayda’s baby, who is now a healthy and happy teenager. She joked that her parents are over-protective and won’t let her go to parties in case she’s kidnapped. It was a good interview but in the end Alberdi decided not to include it in her film: “I didn’t want to victimise her when she’s not a victim. Her friends don’t know. In school she would just become the girl who was kidnapped. I didn’t want to create an issue in her adolescence.”View image in fullscreenDesperate for a son … Armando Espitia as Arturo, with CelestePhotograph: Luis Antonio Rojas/NetflixA Child of My Own is not a typical Netfix true-crime documentary, nor is Alberdi the kind of director you’d expect to make one. She has built a reputation for the kind of documentaries that premiere at prestigious film festivals. The Mole Agent followed a spy in a care home for the elderly, revealing the loneliness of residents.The Eternal Memorywas an intimate study of a celebrity couple in Chile coping with Alzheimer’s disease. Alberdi made her fiction debut with the 2024 dramaIn Her Place.I’m curious if she watches true crime. “Yes,” Alberdi replies, not exactly brimming with enthusiasm. She proceeds diplomatically: “I enjoy it as a viewer, but I don’t connect emotionally.”The trouble is, she says, that we live in an age of snap judgments and instant opinion. But she never has an instant opinion. “El matiz…” she frowns, pulling out her phone to translate a word from Spanish “Nuance! True crime is the opposite of nuance. Everything is more complex in reality.”A Child of My Own is on Netflix from 13 AugustExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsCrime filmsPregnancyParents and parentingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mary Beth Barone on provocative jokes, Palestine and manosphere misogyny: ‘It’s hard to stomach that those are my co-workers’ | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: The comedian and actor’s new Netflix special is a gleefully absurd take on politics and potty-mouthed humor
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The comedian and actor’s new Netflix special is a gleefully absurd take on politics and potty-mouthed humor
Content: Mary Beth Barone in her new Netflix special Galaxy Brain.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenMary Beth Barone in her new Netflix special Galaxy Brain.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixTV comedyInterviewMary Beth Barone on provocative jokes, Palestine and manosphere misogyny: ‘It’s hard to stomach that those are my co-workers’Owen MyersThe comedian and actor’s new Netflix special is a gleefully absurd take on politics and potty-mouthed humorTue 28 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 17.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMary Beth Barone knows exactly who will be offended by her newNetflixspecial. “JK Rowling, Republicans, establishment Democrats, the British, the Irish and Zionists,” she tells me, reading a list from her Notes app. Then there’s “Katy Kats – which is whatKaty Perrycalls her fans – and male comedians and one specific girl named Tatiana”. When informed that this encompasses over half of the population of the US, she beams.Barone’scomedyis a delicate balance between sweetness and cynicism. In her standup she’ll adopt a ditzy pose while she tears down morally bankrupt politicians, sends up cis male entitlement or implores her audience to have sex with moderates in the hope of bringing them over to the left. In the past five years, she has edged her way closer to the mainstream with a Comedy Central web-series, a couple of standup spots on Jimmy Fallon’s late-night show, and apodcastco-hosted with her friendBenito Skinnerthat is so popular it has its own merch line. The past 12 months have seen her career go into overdrive: now she is the co-lead of a wildly popular TV show (Overcompensating, created by Skinner), chats to the A-list on the Golden Globes’ red carpet and sits front row at New York fashion week.Acting the fool: why have Hollywood press tours become so gimmicky?Read moreShe says that herNetflixspecial, Galaxy Brain, is one of the most meaningful milestones yet. “So many of the goalposts have changed [for comedians] with the internet, but the one constant is the hour-long special with an esteemed network or streamer,” Barone says, tucking into a plate of scrambled eggs at a Brooklyn cafe. “With the special, it feels like you’ve achieved something pretty rare and they’re betting on you.”Galaxy Brain is a riot, 55 minutes of whip-smart laughs that tackle all the no-nos of polite dinner party conversation – sex and politics, bad men and good girls – with gusto. Barone describes the Israel-Palestine conflict as a “genocide” twice (“just in case you didn’t hear it the first time”), and later invites the audience to cheer if they like doggy style. In the most outrageous tonal shift, she caps off a critique of Maga amorality by conceding that the Trump-aligned draconianProject 2025was at least focused in its aim to take from the poor and give to the rich. “That shit wasairtight,” she says. “That shit was like a pussy in a denim romper.” She then launches into a manic impression of a vagina with its air supply cut off, clawing at fabric and screaming to be let out.“It sounds cheesy to be like, ‘I want to make people think,’” she says. “But I feel that’s one of the core tenets of being a comedian. With the special it was like, ‘How can we look at darker, heavier themes in the dumbest way possible?’ The goal was that it’s so dumb that it comes back around to being smart.”Keith David on his incredible career: ‘I want you to understand Black men as full-scope human beings’Read moreHer approach wasn’t so different when hosting theGolden Globesofficial red carpet live stream this year. Dressed to the nines, Barone teased out a looser side to celebrities with absurd questions that cut through media-trained platitudes. It felt like many A-listers’ realest red carpet interview in memory:The Rockoffered to pick up Barone with one arm,Tessa Thompsongamely played “pork, marry, kill” with fellow nominees – both human and Na’vi – and Hudson Williams ofHeated Rivalrywas forced to ponder whether it was tougher to be a gay male hockey player or a straight male flight attendant.“I wanted to make everyone feel comfortable and feel like they didn’t have to do the hard work,” says Barone, who worked on the jokes with the comedian George Civeris. “I’ve been on the other side of it where I’ve been asked questions and everything I’ve ever known has escaped my brain and I can’t form a sentence … So I did not want to make people feel that way.”Backlash was slight. “We got a couple of people whose publicists were like, ‘We don’t want that out there.’ I don’t want to say who, but if you walk me to my spray tan I’ll tell you off the record.” (Sadly, I can’t make it.)She also made a last-minute edit to a moment in Galaxy Brain to avoid a moment that could be viewed as punching down, in a section where she discusses her personal battle with an eating disorder. “I had this joke where I said my goal weight is 1.5 Ariana Grandes,” Barone says. “And I go on to say that 1.5 Ariana Grandes is one Bella Hadid or two Troye Sivans. That’s really a joke about me and my mental illness. But I didn’t want people to hear it and think I was making a joke about Ariana Grande.”Barone brings a similar thoughtfulness to her role in Overcompensating. As Grace, the uptight older sister to Skinner’s character of Benny, she adds a touching depth to a character that could be a caricature. After becoming a hit with both viewers and critics, it became one of the few recent LGBTQ+-focused shows to be renewed for a second season. How did it feel for her first big acting gig to be so warmly received? “I could get chills just thinking about it,” Barone says, running her hands up and down her bare arms.Barone has been grinding in New York since she dropped out of Boston College and moved to the city in 2011. While working at a startup, she took classes at the local improv-focused group Upright Citizens Brigade and soon after quit her job to focus on comedy full-time. “I’ve been in this industry for 10 years now, so it was a slow start,” she says.Ride, Barone’s podcast with Skinner, shares space in the upper reaches of the comedy podcast chart with right-leaning shows fromJoe Rogan, Theo Von and Andrew Schulz, hosts whose brashness and casual misogyny has led them to be grouped in with themanosphere.“Comedy has become increasingly polarised,” Barone says. “There’s people who want to make a cash grab and there’s nothing they could do that would make their audience turn against them. It’s genius if you think about it. It’s creating a space where you can say anything and do anything and you’ll never be held accountable.”She is particularly horrified by the rise of Schulz, the self-styled everyman doofus whose Flagrant podcast series cultivates a machismo-fueled atmosphere of casual racism and sexist views, and whoinvitedTrump on for a cosy chat ahead of the 2024 election. “I would always see him at [New York’s] Comedy Cellar when I was starting out,” she says. “He was so funny – I literally thought he was hot. I think I slid into his DMs one time,” she recalls with a shudder.“I’ve watched him create this space where I’m like, ‘You just want to perpetuate the bigotry and the systems that have benefited people that look like you for all of time.’ I guess if money is the most important thing to you, that makes sense,” she says tartly. “But I have integrity, so I could never do something like that. It’s just hard to stomach that those are my co-workers, technically.”Audiences on the left do not give their entertainers the same freedom, she thinks, and especially not to women. “I love comedy,” she told the audience in her 2024 YouTube specialThought Provoking. “And being a woman in comedy is so fun because the goal is to get so successful that you become the most hated person on the planet.”View image in fullscreenMary Beth Barone and Benito Skinner at Teen Vogue Fest in Brooklyn, New York, on 25 July 2026.Photograph: Valerie Terranova/Getty Images for 2026 Teen Vogue FestI think ofLena Dunham, who somehow became the most hated woman in America after the success of her hit TV showGirls. “And it goes back as far as Lucille Ball – she was accused of being a communist!” Barone adds, before reeling off a list of female comedians who have faced vicious backlash for minor perceived missteps. “Kathy Griffin, Amy Schumer, Mindy Kaling, Tiffany Haddish … Tina Fey ate cake on SNL andpeople were mad.“Pursuing [comedy] as a career is such a funny choice because I’m sort of setting myself up for that,” she says. “Unfortunately it is a sign that things are going pretty well when people start to turn on you.”Not that it has stopped Barone from sticking her neck out for what she believes in. In early 2025, she DMedZohran Mamdaniand asked if he would guest at her standup show as part of a segment called Politics for Hot People. On stage at Brooklyn’s the Bell House, shegrilledNew York’s future mayor about his policies, saying: “Politicians are liars, so how can we trust these things are achievable?”The end of Heartstopper is a bittersweet loss – it’s never felt scarier to be young and queer | Alim KherajRead moreThat takes guts, I say. “Maybe there’s something in my brain where I don’t even know when things are socially unacceptable,” she replies. “I just asked him questions that I wanted to know the answers to! It’s the same with my jokes. Sometimes I’ll say things on stage and people will be like, ‘I can’t believe you said that.’ And I’m like, ‘But it’s true.’”Comedy isn’t the only way to change people’s minds, but laughter can sure make politics feel like less of a black box. To celebrate the special, Barone is planning a series of fun release-week events including a pool party at a Brooklyn spa and the Galaxy Brain Ball, a party co-hosted with Skinner at a local queer club. “I really wanted to do events with the people I made this special for,” she says.It’s tough to picture Barone’s down-to-earth qualities changing as more eyes turn towards her. “It’s hard to know how much to continue to say,” she says. “But I want to write about what’s going on in my life. And even though that can be really vulnerable and personal, it is what I want to talk about. I just can’t help it.”Mary Beth Barone: Galaxy Brain is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTV comedyComedy (Culture)TelevisionNetflixComedy (Stage)US politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Previous winners Douglas Stuart and Marlon James lead Booker prize longlist | Books | The Guardian
description: Chair of judges Mary Beard said each of the 13 books in contention for the £50,000 award ‘takes the reader to new places’
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Chair of judges Mary Beard said each of the 13 books in contention for the £50,000 award ‘takes the reader to new places’
Content: Range of tastes and openness of mind ... this year’s Booker prize longlist.Photograph: Booker Prize FoundationView image in fullscreenRange of tastes and openness of mind ... this year’s Booker prize longlist.Photograph: Booker Prize FoundationBooksPrevious winners Douglas Stuart and Marlon James lead Booker prize longlistChair of judges Mary Beard said each of the 13 books in contention for the £50,000 award ‘takes the reader to new places’Comment: This Booker longlist may have two previous winners, but it’s keen to experimentEmma LoffhagenTue 28 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDouglas Stuart andMarlon James,two previous winners of the Booker, have been named on this year’s longlist, alongside three-time nomineeElizabeth Strout,in a collection that “rewards risk”.The 13 novels selected for the 2026 prize, announced on Tuesday, feature authors of seven nationalities across three continents, with almost half from the UK. Ten of the writers are appearing on a Booker longlist for the first time, including three debut novelists: Kenan Orhan, Rebecca Perry and Djamel White.Chairing this year’s judging panel is the classicist and broadcasterMary Beard,who is joined on the panel by Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker.Beard said that each book on the longlist “brilliantly musters the power of words on the page to take the reader to new places, to see old places from new angles, to change minds.“I would not be telling the truth if I said that I hadn’t occasionally felt daunted, as a new box of 30 or so gleaming volumes landed on my doorstep,” she added.Quick GuideThe Booker prize 2026 longlistShowThe Shadow of the Objectby Chloe Aridjis (Chatto & Windus)Switzy by Emma Cline (Chatto & Windus)Helen of Nowhereby Makenna Goodman (Fitzcarraldo Editions)The End of Everythingby M John Harrison (Serpent's Tail)The Disappearers by Marlon James (Hamish Hamilton)Black Bagby Luke Kennard (John Murray)The Renovation by Kenan Orhan (Hamish Hamilton)May We Feed the Kingby Rebecca Perry (Granta)The Palm Houseby Gwendoline Riley (Picador)The Things We Never Sayby Elizabeth Strout (Viking)John of Johnby Douglas Stuart (Picador)All Them Dogsby Djamel White (John Murray)The Vivisectorsby Missouri Williams (4th Estate)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.James is longlisted for his fifth novel, The Disappearers, based around a homophobic mob attack in 1980s Jamaica, to be published in September. The judges called it “a reckoning” from “a singular literary talent”.James won the prize in 2015for A Brief History of Seven Killings. Stuart,who won in 2020 with his debut, Shuggie Bain,returns with his third novel,John of John,which the judges praised for its “rich, textural detail”. Should either win again, they would become only the fifth author to take the Booker twice, joining JM Coetzee, Peter Carey, Hilary Mantel and Margaret Atwood.Strout, meanwhile, picks up her third Booker nomination forThe Things We Never Say,her critically acclaimed 11th novel, which reckons with Trump’s America. Strout was longlisted in 2016 for My Name Is Lucy Barton and shortlisted in 2022 for Oh William!Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said the judges’ “range of tastes” and “openness of mind” had produced a list that “shows how capacious an art form the novel is”, adding that it “rewards risk” and contains “genuinely original work”.The list also opens the door to two firsts. Chloe Aridjis, who is Mexican-British and longlisted forThe Shadow of the Object,could become the first winner of Mexican heritage with her “mysterious and free-wheeling novel”. Kenan Orhan, Turkish-American and longlisted for his debut novelThe Renovation,in which a woman discovers that her bathroom has become a prison cell, could become the first of Turkish heritage.At 81, M John Harrison is the oldest on the list, longlisted for the first time forThe End of Everythingafter 12 previous novels and a stint as a Booker judge himself in 2022. Should he go on to win, he would surpass Atwood as the prize’s oldest ever recipient (she was 79 when she jointly won in 2019). At the other end of the list is 28-year-old Djamel White, the only Irish writer on the list, whose debut, All Them Dogs, grew out of a short story and is set in the “criminal badlands” of west Dublin.A total of 163 books were submitted, all written in English and published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.Joining Beard and Cockeron the judging panelare writer Raymond Antrobus, Booker prize-shortlisted novelist, poet and essayist Patricia Lockwood, and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. Cocker follows in the footsteps of others in the entertainment industry who have judged the prize in recent years, including Sarah Jessica Parker, Adjoa Andoh and Robert Webb.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I was aware that I was, shall we say, the least formally qualified person on this jury, but I didn’t really let that bother me,” Cocker said in an interview. “Knowing that the Booker prizes tend to create panels including people who aren’t necessarily part of the literary world – but can read! – helped me, and I thought I was obviously supposed to bring something that others don’t: a different perspective.”The list also includes Emma Cline’s Switzy, out in September, which tells the story of a man’s final journey to a euthanasia clinic in Zurich; Luke Kennard’sBlack Bag,a comedy about a struggling actor; Rebecca Perry’sMay We Feed the King,which has already won the 2026 Waterstones debut fiction prize; Gwendoline Riley’sThe Palm House,a portrait of literary London; and Missouri Williams’s The Vivisectors, billed as an antidote to the “cosy campus novel”.The shortlist will be announced at the Southbank Centre in London on 22 September, with the winner named at a ceremony on 9 November.Last year’s winner was David Szalay’s Flesh. Other recent winners include Samantha Harvey, Paul Lynch, Shehan Karunatilaka and Damon Galgut.To explore all the books on the longlist for the Booker prize 2026 visitguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsBooksBooker prizeMarlon JamesElizabeth StroutAwards and prizesFictionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Naga Munchetty to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years for Radio 5 Live | BBC | The Guardian
description: Move comes after the presenter has faced allegations of bullying, but there is no suggestion it is related
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Move comes after the presenter has faced allegations of bullying, but there is no suggestion it is related
Content: Naga Munchetty will take up her new role in January.Photograph: Gavin Rodgers/AlamyView image in fullscreenNaga Munchetty will take up her new role in January.Photograph: Gavin Rodgers/AlamyBBCNaga Munchetty to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years for Radio 5 LiveMove comes after the presenter has faced allegations of bullying, but there is no suggestion it is relatedJamie GriersonTue 28 Jul 2026 06.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNaga Munchetty is to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years on the television show to become co-presenter of Radio 5 Live’s breakfast show.The current 5 Live Breakfast hosts, Rachel Burden and Rick Edwards, announced on Tuesday’s programme that they would step down in December.Munchetty, who has presented the station’s weekday mid-morning programme since 2021, will move to 5 Live Breakfast alongside a new co-host to be recruited in due course, theBBCsaid.The move comes after reports thatMunchetty had faced allegations of bullying on the breakfast TV show. There has been no suggestion her move and the allegations are connected.The BBC has been contacted for comment, but at the time that the bullying allegations were reported it said: “We do not comment on individual HR matters.”Munchetty said of her move: “I’m thrilled to be joining 5 Live Breakfast in January. Live news, great conversations and connecting with audiences are what I love most about broadcasting, and 5 Live does all of that brilliantly.“It has been a privilege to be part of the BBCBreakfast TVteam for the past 17 years, working alongside an incredibly talented and hard-working group of journalists who are not only outstanding colleagues but also great friends.“Presenting a flagship programme on 5 Live is an opportunity that was simply too good to pass up. It will take a huge amount of work and require 100% of my focus and energy, and I’m really looking forward to throwing myself into the role.“Over the last five years, I’ve been privileged to build a relationship with 5 Live listeners on the mid-morning programme and help shine a light on the issues that matter most to them. I’m excited to build on that in the Breakfast slot and to start each day with our listeners every morning.“Between now and January, I’ll continue presenting the two programmes I love. I’m sure there will be plenty of news to cover, and it will very much be business as usual.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurden will move to present the weekday mid-morning programme, Monday to Wednesday from 11am to 2pm, after 15 years on the station’s breakfast show, while Edwards will continue to front Fighting Talk on Saturday mornings.It was revealed earlier this month that Munchetty earned between £360,000 and £364,999 in the 2025-26 financial year.Explore more on these topicsBBCBBC OneRadio 5 LiveRadio industryTelevision industryBreakfast TVTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Top Gear’s Richard Hammond fined for speeding in Bentley and Porsche | Richard Hammond | The Guardian
description: Former co-presenter of BBC motoring show given penalty after being caught twice in three weeks
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Former co-presenter of BBC motoring show given penalty after being caught twice in three weeks
Content: A photograph by West Mercia police of Richard Hammond speeding in his Porsche on 2 December 2025.Photograph: West Mercia Police/PAView image in fullscreenA photograph by West Mercia police of Richard Hammond speeding in his Porsche on 2 December 2025.Photograph: West Mercia Police/PARichard HammondTop Gear’s Richard Hammond fined for speeding in Bentley and PorscheFormer co-presenter of BBC motoring show given penalty after being caught twice in three weeksJamie GriersonTue 28 Jul 2026 04.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former Top Gear hostRichard Hammondhas been fined £999 by a court after being caught speeding twice in three weeks while driving his luxury cars.The 56-year-old was in a Porsche when he broke the speed limit on 2 December last year, and was caught out again 20 days later while driving a Bentley.West Mercia police brought two prosecutions against Hammond, putting forward the speed camera images of him driving the cars in Herefordshire to prove the offences.The presenter, who hosted Top Gear with Jeremy Clarkson and James May between 2002 and 2015, before the trio launched The Grand Tour on Amazon Prime, pleaded guilty through his lawyers to two charges of speeding.At Telford magistrates court last week he was handed seven penalty points for his licence. The magistrate, Ann Minton, ordered him to pay a total of £1,771, comprising two fines of £333 and £666, £240 in costs and victim surcharges totalling £532.View image in fullscreenA West Mercia police handout from 22 December last year shows Hammond speeding in his Bentley.Photograph: West Mercia police/PAHammond, nicknamed The Hamster by his TV co-stars, nearly died in a 320mph jet car crash in 2006 while filming Top Gear, and he and Clarkson received a three-month driving ban in France in 2013 after they were caught speeding while making an episode of the show.Documents from his court case show Hammond was caught by a police officer with a handheld speed camera just before 1pm on 2 December last year.View image in fullscreenHammond, left, with Jeremy Clarkson, centre and James May posing for a Top Gear studio shot in 2015.Photograph: Zuma Press /AlamyHis Porsche Taycan Cross Turismo was clocked at 68mph in a 50mph limit on the A40 in Pencraig, Herefordshire.At about 11.45am on 22 December, Hammond’s Bentley Continental GT was speeding at 82mph in a 70mph limit on the A50 Rudhall overbridge in Herefordshire.Police sent speeding tickets to a Grade II*-listed Herefordshire castle Hammond bought in 2012 and a £1m farm estate near Hereford, but the letters were returned marked as “addressee gone away”.They tracked him down to his £2m mansion near Abergavenny in Monmouthshire, where it was noted more than 30 vehicles are registered.Police set out in court papers that Hammond had been accused of another driving offence in August last year.Hammond was prosecuted for two offences of speeding and two further allegations that he had ignored the police letters and failed to identify himself as the guilty driver.Explore more on these topicsRichard HammondHertfordshireMotoringTransportEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ariana Grande sues hackers who allegedly sold unreleased music and photos online | Music | The Guardian
description: Pop star aims to use legal process to name ‘wrongdoers who hide in the shadows and wreak technological havoc with impunity’
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Pop star aims to use legal process to name ‘wrongdoers who hide in the shadows and wreak technological havoc with impunity’
Content: Ariana Grande at the Critics Choice awards in Los Angeles in January.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APView image in fullscreenAriana Grande at the Critics Choice awards in Los Angeles in January.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APMusicAriana Grande sues hackers who allegedly sold unreleased music and photos onlinePop star aims to use legal process to name ‘wrongdoers who hide in the shadows and wreak technological havoc with impunity’Ben Beaumont-ThomasTue 28 Jul 2026 05.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAriana Grande has filed a lawsuit against hackers who she alleges have stolen unreleased music, as well as private photos and video footage, and sold them online.Grande filed the lawsuit in a Los Angeles court on Monday. It doesn’t name the hackers, who are referred to with the generic name John Doe. Grande will look to have them identified during the legal process “in order to hold them accountable for their invasive and reprehensible conduct”, the lawsuit reads.As reported by Billboard, the Hollywood Reporter and more, it is alleged that the hackers accessed the online accounts of various people working with Grande, leading to the leaking of 45 songs in 2023 alone. In one instance, Grande alleges a hacker impersonated a photographer to dupe an employee into sending images of Grande to them. Behind-the-scenes photos and footage from recording sessions and music videos are also alleged to have been stolen. The assets are alleged to have been sold on the dark web.“This malicious invasion of Ms Grande’s privacy and disruption of her career have caused her substantial and irreparable harm due to this breach of privacy,” the lawsuit reads. “The unauthorised misappropriation and disclosure of these materials is a violation of Ms Grande’s identity and artistry, and the direct and sacred relationship that exists between her and her fans … Neither Ms Grande nor any other public or private figure should have to suffer such violations caused by these wrongdoers who hide in the shadows and wreak technological havoc with impunity.”After seven albums which have all reached No 1 or No 2 in the US charts, as well as being a 20-time Grammy nominee and three-time winner, Grande remains one of the most successful pop artists in the world. Her single Hate That I Made You Love Me is currently the third most-streamed song globally on Spotify each day, and a chart-topper in the US and UK. It is taken from her new album Petal, released on Friday.She has also successfully branched out into acting in recent years, taking a lead role in Wicked and its sequel Wicked: For Good, and also opposite Robert De Niro and Ben Stiller in the latest instalment of the Meet the Parents franchise, Focker-in-Law, released in November. In 2027, she will appear alongside her Wicked co-star Jonathan Bailey in a stage production of Sondheim musical Sunday in the Park with George, at London’s Barbican.She begins a 10-night run of concerts at London’s O2 Arena on 15 August.Explore more on these topicsMusicAriana GrandePop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Betye Saar, pioneering figure of Black arts movement, dies aged 99 | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Leading assemblage artist was known for reclaiming Jim Crow-era memorabilia as images of Black liberation
Author: Roque Planas
Headline: Leading assemblage artist was known for reclaiming Jim Crow-era memorabilia as images of Black liberation
Content: Betye Saar on her patio at home in Los Angeles in 2016.Photograph: Gina Ferazzi/Los Angeles Times/APView image in fullscreenBetye Saar on her patio at home in Los Angeles in 2016.Photograph: Gina Ferazzi/Los Angeles Times/APArt and designBetye Saar, pioneering figure of Black arts movement, dies aged 99Leading assemblage artist was known for reclaiming Jim Crow-era memorabilia as images of Black liberationRoque PlanasMon 27 Jul 2026 21.33 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 15.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArtist Betye Saar, the pioneering figure of the Black arts movement,died on Sunday morningin her home town of Los Angeles. She was 99.Betye Saar: the brilliant artist who reversed and radicalised racist stereotypesRead moreSaar, a famous practitioner of assemblage, an artistic style that builds sculpture from everyday objects, was best known for reclaiming Jim Crow era memorabilia such as dolls and washboards and recasting them as images of Black liberation. Saar also worked in genres including printmaking and film, exploring themes from family to spirituality.“Her symbolically rich body of work has evolved over time to demonstrate the environmental, cultural, political, racial, technological, economic, and historical context in which it exists,” according to Roberts Projects, theLos Angelesgallery that represents her.Saar began her career in design and shifted to art at the age of 35. She continued to make art into her 90s.
