Saar grew up in Pasadena and was part of a community of Black artists in nearby Altadena; she often cited Simon Rodia’sWatts Towersas an early source of inspiration.Throughout her career, Saar combed flea markets and yard sales for discarded objects showing how consumer culture depicted Black Americans.“My work has to do with recycling,” she told a documentary crew in the 1970s, according to the Los Angeles Times. “Each item I collect has a certain energy from its previous function that carries over into its new use.”She is perhaps best known for her 1972 revolutionary reimagination of Aunt Jemima, the image once used to market a pancake mix and syrup brand founded at the tail-end of the 19th century. Aunt Jemima was based on “mammy” images that depicted enslaved Black women as contented domestic servants. Saar’sLiberation of Aunt Jemimaholds a rifle in her left hand, and a grenade wedged between her right arm and chest.Quaker Oats retired the Aunt Jemima image in 2021.Saar work also used natural materials gathered from travels around the world exploring the African diaspora and spirituality.“Wherever I go, I say, ‘What’s the alternative religion?’ because every country has it,” she said in a2021 interview with the Guardian. “There are lots of other people that believe in magic and they have their own religion, and I was just really interested in what they did and what their ceremonies were, but mostly what the visual images would be.”Saar taught and mentored a generation of Black artists, including the painter Kerry James Marshall. Saar has long been considered a leading figure of the west coast arts landscape.In spring 2026, Saar was inducted to the American Academy of Arts and Letters.Explore more on these topicsArt and designCaliforniaLos AngelesWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Black motorcycle clubs come alive in the summer: ‘The best way to build community is on two wheels’ | Black US culture | The Guardian
description: Building on decades-long traditions, Black bikers host rides, picnics and other gatherings nearly every summer weekend to celebrate community and freedom
Author: Morgan Jerkins
Headline: Building on decades-long traditions, Black bikers host rides, picnics and other gatherings nearly every summer weekend to celebrate community and freedom
Content: Dutch with Flaming Knight Members in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.View image in fullscreenDutch with Flaming Knight Members in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Black US cultureBlack motorcycle clubs come alive in the summer: ‘The best way to build community is on two wheels’Building on decades-long traditions, Black bikers host rides, picnics and other gatherings nearly every summer weekend to celebrate community and freedomMorgan Jerkinswith photographs by  Elijah Chukwuka MogoliTue 28 Jul 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe trip was only supposed to be a Memorial Day weekend girls’ getaway to Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, for Patrice “Foxy” Johnson. But once Johnson and her crew arrived, they inadvertently found themselves in the middle of an annual bike week where several thousand riders had convened. Johnson watched the “backpacks”, or the women who rode on the backs of male motorcyclists’ bikes, and realized she too wanted to be part of the community. She didn’t want to accompany the male riders, though. She wanted to ride herself.In that moment about 30 years ago, Johnson decided that next time she would be attending bike week and coming with her own set of wheels. Once she returned to her home town of Raleigh, North Carolina, she enrolled in a foundational bike riding class at Johnston community college to learn more about motorcycles. Since then, she’s become such a staple in the Black motorcycle community nationwide that she holds multiple leadership positions across organizations.View image in fullscreenA female biker at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Just about every weekend, particularly in the summer, a Black motorcycle club in some US city is having their annual ride, picnic or other social gathering amid food and music. A place for bike enthusiasts to convene among like-minded community members, some biker clubs date as far back as the 1940s, starting after the second world war. Today’s rides are part of the culture of freedom of movement that started as a response to exclusion from white motorcycle clubs and labor discrimination due to Jim Crow.History on wheelsOne of the clubs where Johnson invests her time is Black Girls Ride (BGR), which has supported women of color in motorsports since its inception in 2011. The group has meetups several times a year in cities such as Houston, Daytona Beach and Los Angeles, it publishes a digital magazine and a podcast, sells its own gear, and has annual traditions such as participating in the Essence festival, a music festival for Black women, every July in New Orleans. About 250 to 300 BGR members typically make the trip to Louisiana. “The police officers will clear the street for us to walk down Bourbon Street with a second line band,” Johnson, the Carolinas ambassador for BGR, which has five national ambassadors and a rider leader, said. “We’re chanting: ‘Black Girls Ride! Black Girls Ride!’ We’re dancing in the street.” Once, as a part of their civic engagement goals, BGR “adopted” the Boys and Girls Club of New Orleans and raised more than $30,000. Such traditions among Black motorsports enthusiasts help engender leisurely fun and community building.View image in fullscreenBikers playing cards at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Part of that community building is providing members with education on Black history. The Buffalo Soldiers Motorcycle Club, one of the largest motorcycle clubs in the country with roughly 5,000 members, for instance carries the name of the all-Black military units of the ninth and 10th US cavalry regiments established by Congress in 1866. One of its current club members, the air force veteran Randy Hayward, also known as Detroit Randy, recalled a memorial ride called The Buffalo Thunder from Washington DC to Detroit: “We rode through communities and everybody had their flag out … Black soldiers may not have been celebrated when they came home.”Annually, the Buffalo Soldiers Motorcycle Club holds a July convention in select cities such as Tampa, Florida; Concord, North Carolina; and Mobile, Alabama, where safety training sessions, rides, cookouts and community outreach are a part of regular programming. “The best way to fellowship is on two wheels,” Hayward said, before listing some of the history-driven rides that his organization has taken to historic sites like Black Wall Street and the Wilberforce, Ohio, home of Col Charles Young, the first Black US army colonel.Steel Horses bike club members and Brown Sugar and friends of Unapologetic Kweenz at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in -Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn on 19 July 2026.Steel Horses bike club members and Brown Sugar and friends of Unapologetic Kweenz at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in -Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn on 19 July 2026.Black motorcycle culture is inextricably linked to Black military service. When Black soldiers returned home from the second world war in the 1940s,many were still seeking community with a sense of adventure. Tuskegee Airmen couldn’t get jobs as pilotsdue to persistent racism, and motorcycling gave them the opportunity to attain a similar thrill – if they could get their hands on a bike.During the war,military motorcycles were vital in scoping out enemy positions and delivering weapons, messages and orders. Once the war ended, the military turned to Jeeps and armored vehicles and therefore military motorcycles flooded the market. Unfortunately, despite these bikes being surplus and cheap, many dealers would not sell motorcycles to Black people.A former US marine decided to build his own motorcycles.Cliff Vaughsfrom Los Angeles, California, introduced motorcycle riding as a form of organizing via his work with the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) between 1963 and 1964. While visiting working-class Black sharecroppers in Alabama, Vaughs said to the author Paul d’Orléans for his book The Chopper: The Real Story: “I wanted to be a visible example to them; a free Black man on my motorcycle.”View image in fullscreenCash, a young biker, at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.By the late 1960s, bike clubs such as the State Burners of Atlantic City, the East Bay Dragons of Oakland, the Chosen Few of Los Angeles and the Iron Horse Motorcycle Club of Miami, were thriving. The Miami-based organization was founded by Bessie Stringfield, also known as “The Motorcycle Queen of Miami”, who served in the second world war as the only woman in her unit of civilian courier motorcycle dispatchers. She was also the first African American woman to rideacross the US solo.On her rides, Stringfield relied on The Negro Motorist Green Book,a travel and survival guide for Black drivers, so that she could remain safe throughout her journeys.‘An investment in experiences and freedom’Today, owning a bike is just the starting point for entry into an organization. “Every club has its own set of rules,” said Anthony “Zeke” Settle, the national president of the Black Stallions Motorcycle Club, which was founded in Los Angeles. For Settle’s organization, members have to be 21 years old, own a motorcycle bigger than 600 cubic centimeters – which means a mid-sized engine with a great capacity for speed – complete a three-month probationary period involving mandatory rides, cross four state lines and attend events where prospects can acquaint themselves with official members.Membership comes at a financial cost as well. Settle explained: “A basic, say 600 sports bike motorcycle – that’s at least [$10,000]. That’s a good used one. The top-of-the-line sports bike – Kawasaki has one that’s $30,000.”Female and male bikers at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Female and male bikers at the Imperial Bike Club Annual Bike Blessing in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Alvin C Jacobs Jr, a photographer, rider and the author of Chrome, a coffee table bookwhich showcases Black motorcycle culture, spent over $50,000 on his most recent bike. He acknowledges that associated costs have posed challenges in recruiting younger riders: “It’s an expensive hobby and the average millennial is broke,” said Jacobs.Biking runs through the Jacobs family. Alvin C Jacobs Jr’s father, Alvin Jacobs Sr, co-founded The Brothers Club in Rockford, Illinois, in 1976, where Alvin Jr grew up, “near the Kegels Harley-Davidson [store]”, he said. And Alvin Jr’s son, Hassan Jacobs, is a millennial rider who served in the military for eight years. He’s not a part of a motorcycle club and therefore is not subjected to the financial obligations of an organization, but he is proud to be a younger rider: “I feel like when I’m on the open road, particularly on a bike, I am able to move freely at speeds that don’t constrain me,” Hassan said. “When I’m walking, running or even driving, I feel like I’m held back by the arbitrary limits of my body. And even in a car I don’t get that mind-to-body connection that I get on a bike. It’s almost like having a new body to glide through the road with. Freedom.”There are some club-affiliated millennials, however, who face the financial hurdles head-on. Shanika “Tru” Beatty, the founder and president of Caramel Curves, an all-Black women motorcycle club, says: “Some of our members finance their bikes, some buy used and others save until they’re ready. One thing that makes Caramel Curves special is that we support each other. We share maintenance tips, and help new riders navigate the process. We want riding to be accessible, not intimidating. At the end of the day, motorcycling isn’t just an expense to us. It’s an investment in experiences, friendships, personal growth and freedom.”View image in fullscreenDutch with Flaming Knight Members in Bedford-Stuyvesant,Brooklyn, on 19 July 2026.Since its inception in 2005, Caramel Curves has expanded to 31 members across two chapters in New Orleans and Atlanta. During the summer, its most active season, Caramel Curves organizes group rides, attends other bike events, and hosts sessions where members get to know one another on and off their bikes. “We organize group rides, attend bike events and create spaces for our members to connect both on and off the bike,” Beatty said. “It’s also a time when we welcome new riders who are just getting started and want to be part of something supportive and empowering.”A supportive community is what also inspired Phillip “Dutch” Boyd to join a motorcycle group, after discovering his love for riding during the pandemic: “My friends rode back in the day and they would always crash! I didn’t think bikes were safe until I did some research during the Covid lockdown.” The first day that Boyd learned how to ride a bike from his brother-in-law changed his life. After solo riding for a year, he had the opportunity to squire, or prospect, at The Flaming Knights, a predominantly Black motorcycle club founded in 1968. He earned his patches, which delineate club affiliation, and became a member.A few weeks ago, the Flaming Knights attended the annual Bike Week in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, a convening of bikers from all over the country. About 200 bikers showed up, mingled with others and shopped the local street vendors. R&B and rap music blasted from nearby speakers, and a few kids played on their mini bikes as the adults relaxed with their coolers or ventured around the corner to the clubhouse of Imperial Bikers, the motorcycle club that hosted the event.Regardless of how Black bikers discovered their love for the sport, biking is less of a hobby and more of a lifestyle. “One of the biggest misconceptions is that Black motorcycle culture is only about clubs, leather and looking tough,” said Beatty of Caramel Curves. “In reality, it’s about community, family, freedom and giving back.”Explore more on these topicsBlack US cultureMotorcyclingMotor sportRaceNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Holly Willoughby Together review – a marginally less agonising With Love, Meghan  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The former This Morning host has done a Meghan, rebranding herself as a cookery guru with a YouTube show that veers from agonisingly dull courgette slicing to sweary banter. Somehow, in spite of it all, I am rooting for her
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The former This Morning host has done a Meghan, rebranding herself as a cookery guru with a YouTube show that veers from agonisingly dull courgette slicing to sweary banter. Somehow, in spite of it all, I am rooting for her
Content: ‘An aggressive audition for whether Holly Willoughby is allowed to be famous again’ … Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy).Photograph: Hungry Bear MediaView image in fullscreen‘An aggressive audition for whether Holly Willoughby is allowed to be famous again’ … Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy).Photograph: Hungry Bear MediaTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewHolly Willoughby Together review – a marginally less agonising With Love, MeghanThe former This Morning host has done a Meghan, rebranding herself as a cookery guru with a YouTube show that veers from agonisingly dull courgette slicing to sweary banter. Somehow, in spite of it all, I am rooting for herStuart HeritageTue 28 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHolly Willoughby is a woman in search of a fresh start. Her stint on This Morning ended messily, with her response to the Phillip Schofield scandal – the infamous “Are you OK? I hope so” monologue – making her a figure of public mockery. Subsequent attempts to relaunch her career, like her short-lived time hosting a Bear Grylls reality show, stalled. So now it has come to this:Holly WilloughbyTogether (With Voy).Your response to it will vary based on how generous you’re feeling. The kindest offering would be to say that Willoughby has pivoted to YouTube, having cannily observed that television is dead and this is where all the eyeballs are these days. It is a cookery and lifestyle show that allows her to be unapologetically herself without the meddling influence of executives who have spent years trying to enforce a persona upon her.Then there is the less kind option, which is to say that Willoughby has done a Meghan.This, unfortunately, is kind of true. Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy, don’t forget) is extremelyWith Love, Meghanin tone and presentation. It is a heavily manicured cookery show, presented by a woman who seems as if she needs quite a lot of help in the kitchen, that exists more as a referendum on the host than a traditional show. However, let’s be clear that this is far better than that, because Willoughby lacks the sweatily desperate control freakery that made With Love, Meghan such an uncomfortable watch. Perhaps it would be better to call this a Saturday Kitchen rip-off and be done with it.From what I can tell, every episode of Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy) will see Willoughby – and, by association, the health company Voy – cook a dish in her monochromatically pastel kitchen with a guest. Episode one’s guest is Stanley Tucci, who is about as safe a pair of hands as you could hope for. He’s chatty. He can cook. He and Willoughby are old friends, since she apparently made him a bottle of toffee vodka in her dishwasher once. He makes some courgette pasta, and is as charmingly snobby as ever.View image in fullscreen‘Absolutely none of this is even slightly about him’ … Stanley Tucci is the guest in the first episode.Photograph: Hungry Bear MediaWhich is great, because absolutely none of this is even slightly about him. That much is evident by the show’s format, which sees him reading his own interview questions off some spoons (“Milk or bag first?” “What’s your favourite type of potato?”), even though typically that role would be filled by the host. Instead, the whole thing comes off as an aggressive audition for whether Willoughby is allowed to be famous again.The weakest elements of the show are the ones where this is most overt. Before Tucci joins her in the kitchen, we see her engaging in some toe-curlingly “candid” banter with the crew, in which she swears a bit and talks about wine. The messaging seems to suggest that this is therealWilloughby, not like that fake automaton who tricked enough people to like her that she qualified as the highest-paid woman on British television between the years 2018 and 2021.Once this burns out, though, we’re left with therealreal Willoughby, who is more or less the same woman who presented This Morning. The best moments come when she stops trying to violently rebrand herself and just allows herself to be quick, funny and endearingly nervous about her new venture. The bits where she seems most like her true self, like when she teasingly provokes Tucci’s culinary sensibilities with microwavable Rustlers, have energy and charm in equal amounts. If that can be sustained over the coming episodes, audiences will naturally find her.The plan seems to be to keep Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy) going as long as possible, in which case it will almost certainly start to become the thing it wants to be as episodes progress. Let’s cross our fingers that it wants to be 15 minutes shorter than it currently is, because plenty could be trimmed from its 45-minute duration. For instance, there is an interminable section near the start where Willoughby painstakingly slices four courgettes with all the concentration of someone trying to defuse a nuclear bomb. It is not essential viewing.But you can’t help but root for the show. Yes, the format might be a little safe and stale, but given the alternatives – a reality show, a wellness podcast, a cynicalAs Ever-style lifestyle store – there’s still some pleasure to be had from watching a person get on with doing something they’re naturally very good at (with or without Voy).Holly Willoughby Together (With Voy) is on YouTube nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionHolly WilloughbyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: True Blood meets Eurovision in an outrageous vampire romp  | Television | The Guardian
description: Sam Reid revels in the role as Lestat, a glam rock prince of darkness. Plus: Shabaz ‘King of the Povos’ Ali meets a billionaire. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Sam Reid revels in the role as Lestat, a glam rock prince of darkness. Plus: Shabaz ‘King of the Povos’ Ali meets a billionaire. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Stage fright … Sam Reid as vampire glam rocker Lestat.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 AMC Networks Entertainment LLC.  All Rights Reserved./Sophie GiraudView image in fullscreenStage fright … Sam Reid as vampire glam rocker Lestat.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 AMC Networks Entertainment LLC.  All Rights Reserved./Sophie GiraudTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: True Blood meets Eurovision in an outrageous vampire rompSam Reid revels in the role as Lestat, a glam rock prince of darkness. Plus: Shabaz ‘King of the Povos’ Ali meets a billionaire. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Ali Catterall,Phil Harrison,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellTue 28 Jul 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Vampire Lestat: Interview with the Vampire9pm, BBC TwoTrue Blood meets Eurovision in this ludicrously camp vampire drama. This is the third series of Interview with the Vampire but it takes a new turn, now set in 2025 with the spotlight on blood-sucking glam rocker Lestat – played so erotically by Sam Reid that he can pull off lines such as “MDMA and LSD: the Torvill and Dean of hallucinogens” and “I carry with me an immortal erection”.Hollie RichardsonThe Great British Sewing Bee8pm, BBC OneIt’s reduce, reuse and recycle week: the sewers must transform landfill scraps – everything from potato sacks to curtain rope tassels – into fast fashion and couture. But not before refashioning old T-shirts into three pairs of knickers. Emma: “I’m just going to bask in the glory that Patrick Grant liked my knickers.”Ali CatterallHotel Chocolat Unwrapped8pm, Channel 4This bumper advert for the chocolatier returns for a second series – and it kicks off with the first Hotel Chocolat instore bakery. Elsewhere, the Chocmobile – a van filled with chocolates – hits the summer festivals, while across the Atlantic, a store is set to open in Chicago.HRThe Undeclared War9pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenDr Barbara Napier (Siân Brooke) in The Undeclared War.Photograph: Simon Ridgway/Channel 4The focus is on Siân Brooke’s Dr Barbara Napier as Peter Kosminsky’s portentous cyber thriller continues. There’s some deep background as we flashback to an ill-fated MI6 mission in 2014 and another in 2022. Barbara’s charming but shifty ex, Nicky, is the thread connecting these operations. Surely that can’t be a coincidence?Phil HarrisonShabaz Asks: Are Billionaires Bad?9pm, BBC ThreeThe answer is straightforward, but former Blackburn teacher turned TikTok sensationShabaz “King of the Povvos” Aliis a hoot as he goes on a journey to find out – with the aim of meeting a billionaire. Along the way, he’ll meet economists, Zack Polanski and an ex-Apprentice candidate. Plus, will his 2 million followers be able to help out?HRGomorrah: The Origins9pm, Sky AtlanticHow did a disco-loving Naples gutter rat grow up to be ice-cold kingpin Don Pietro? This 1970s-set prequel to Sky’s brutal Italian gangster drama shades in the backstory. The opening double bill sees pimply teen Pietro glimpse a less glamorous side of Camorra life when hunky local underboss Angelo goes on the warpath.Graeme VirtueFilmThe New Boy (Warwick Thornton, 2023),11.05pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenCate Blanchett and Aswan Reid in The New Boy.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyThe Australian state’s former policy of separating Indigenous children from their parents, to assimilate them into western culture, gets a sideways take in Warwick Thornton’s mystical period drama. Aswan Reid stars as a blond-haired Indigenous boy found in the outback and taken to a Benedictine orphanage run by Cate Blanchett’s unconventional Sister Eileen. It’s an alien world to him, but when he displays miraculous powers, Eileen sees in him a very Christian divinity.Simon WardellLive sportRacing, Glorious Goodwood,1.30pm, ITV1Day one of the meeting, including the Goodwood Cup.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Upland by Ed Douglas review – a glorious survey of Britain’s high places | History books | The Guardian
description: The writer and climber brings colour and carnival to his account of a country and people shaped by its mountains
Author: Kathryn Hughes
Headline: The writer and climber brings colour and carnival to his account of a country and people shaped by its mountains
Content: Ben Nevis in the Scottish Highlands.Photograph: John Finney Photography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBen Nevis in the Scottish Highlands.Photograph: John Finney Photography/Getty ImagesBook of the dayHistory booksReviewUpland by Ed Douglas review – a glorious survey of Britain’s high placesThe writer and climber brings colour and carnival to his account of a country and people shaped by its mountainsKathryn HughesTue 28 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 03.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt comes as a shock to learn that Britain’s uplands were not always rocky, covered with coarse grass and suitable only for sheep. About 54,000 years ago – a mere blink in geological time – this island’s high places were teeming with nature. Lushly forested peaks, crags and gorges were home to megafauna including mammoth, woolly rhinoceros and giant elk. The one sour note in this elevated Garden of Eden was the carnivorous cave lions and sabre-tooth cats who prowled the browse looking for a meaty dinner.Ed Douglas’s achievement in this excellent book is to return a proper sense of colour and even carnival to Britain’s high places. His first job, though, is to define his terms. In 1936, the celebrated US geographer Roderick Peattie declared that what made a mountain was not its elevation so much as its capacity to “enter into the imagination of the people who lived in [its] shadows”. But by the 1990s, the United Nations, newly tasked with protecting the world’s high places from environmental and economic decline, insisted on getting out its tape measure and statistical charts and coming up with some universal criteria.Consequently, the current definition of a “mountainous” region is one where the altitude varies by at least 300 metres over a radius of 7km. That means that Douglas’s home on Totley Moor, which sits on the millstone grit uplands of the eastern Peak District, just about qualifies; a matter of obvious satisfaction to this one-time editor of the Alpine Journal. Romping comfortably across the line are whole swathes of Scotland, Wales and northern England, not forgetting the twin domes of Exmoor and Dartmoor.Less pleasing to Douglas, though, is the way in which Britain’s uplands have historically been imagined as places apart, spectacular yet oddly detached from life at lower levels. He reminds us that the country’s high places provide more than 60% of the nation’s water needs. What’s more, the plants that make up much of our diet originate in that same hardy environment: potatoes, barley, maize, apples, tomatoes. Those of us who live at sea level or below would do well to reformulate our ideas about the uplands as a place where nothing much grows beyond the occasional sprig of lucky heather.Equally misguided, suggests Douglas, is a tendency to view Britain’s uplands as existing outside history, politics, culture and even time itself. The truth is that mountains have shaped much of our island story. When the Romans arrived from mainland Europe in the first century AD, they found that low-lying southern England, with its fertile soil and gentle hillocks, quickly rolled over and signed up to the new order. The craggy north, meanwhile, stood aloof – and you can still see evidence of this bifurcated response in the landscape today. Go to a Roman ruin in the south or east of the country, and chances are that it is the remnants of a country estate or, at the very least, a handsome villa. Head to the high north and you will find yourself scrambling over the remains of a garrison or high brick wall aimed at keeping uplanders away from the good stuff.And yet … it frequently turns out that it was precisely in those cold, difficult and, above all, lofty places that actual treasure lay. The Romans eventually overcame their fear of heights to start mining lead in Wanlockhead, which at more than 400 metres remains Scotland’s highest village. A thousand years later and the Norman invaders, who had initially given the rocky spine of England a wide berth, set up shop in the Peak District and insisted on taking a cut of the handsome profits that arose from local lead mining.Douglas suggests that the best way to think of this ceaseless push and pull between the central lowlands and the marginal uplands is as a kind of internal colonialism. For millennia, Britain’s high places have been ransacked for their raw materials. Perhaps the most poignant example in this book is the story of the Elan valley, a beautiful stretch of land in the mountains of rural mid-Wales. In the early 19th century the poet Percy Shelley had roamed over his uncle’s Radnorshire estate, entranced to have found his own version of Wordsworth and Coleridge’s Lake District.But in 1896, the valley was dammed and flooded in order to create a vast reservoir from which Birmingham might draw an everlasting supply of cheap and clean drinking water. It was part of the MP Joseph Chamberlain’s radical programme to clear England’s second city of cholera and dysentery by building a 73-mile aqueduct from the Welsh mountains to the Midlands plateau. This necessitated the village of Nantgwyllt, complete with church and surrounding farms, disappearing permanently under water.double quotation markOne delight of Douglas' capacious, looping narrative is the room it leaves for delightful cameos by remarkable individualsThe compulsory purchase of the Elan valley carries echoes of the earlier Highland clearances, during which tenant farmers in Sutherland, Argyll and Inverness-shire were ordered off the land to make way for the infinitely more profitable sheep. Many of these evicted crofters, just like the Radnorshire farmers 150 years later, were obliged to emigrate as far as the US to find a place to build a stable home.Yet it would be doomy and defeatist to suggest that the uplands have exclusively been places of passive trauma. Douglas does a good job at identifying those times throughout history when Britain’s high places demonstrated a culture of determined resistance. There are the Jacobite rebellions of 1715 and 1745 when Highlanders loyal to the Stuart cause swept down from their mountain fastness in an attempt to overthrow the newly installed Hanoverians. This tartan army got as far as Derby, only 110 miles from London, before being forced to turn back.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDouglas has not, in truth, found out anything new about the ancient uplands, but he has knitted his sources into a deft survey, going all the way from the tectonic plates of prehistory to today, when the chief concern is southern second-homers driving up the prices for young locals. One delight of his capacious, looping narrative is the room it leaves for delightful cameos by remarkable individuals, including several women.There is Janet Lapworth, the daughter of a Galashiels schoolteacher, who in the 1870s sewed her geologist husband a special waistcoat incorporating rows of pockets on the front into which he could sort his specimens on the fly. Or Hannah Mitchell, who grew up on a hard-scrabble tenant farm with a view of Kinder Scout, the highest point in the Peak District, and developed a love of rambling to offset the constricted conditions of her own impoverished life. Mitchell’s determination to walk off her troubles led to her becoming a suffragette, a JP and a campaigner for social justice.My favourite uplander, though, remains Queen Victoria. As a young girl she gorged on the highly confected Highland novels of Walter Scott. Now that Jacobitism was safely defeated, it was delightful to imagine a Highlands full of craggily handsome men in kilts ready to come a lady’s rescue, even if that lady happened to be a Protestant Hanoverian princess. When she bought Balmoral in 1852, the queen was not initially much interested in venturing far. But with the death of Albert she was persuaded to undertake the occasional excursion up famous peaks including Lochnagar and Ben Macdui. Here was the beginning of what the 20th-century novelist George Scott-Moncrieff memorably called “Balmorality”. It was a view of the uplands, spruced up and watered down, best seen on a biscuit tin.Upland: The Strange History and Vital Future of Britain’s Mountains by Ed Douglas is published by Bodley Head (£25). title: Underdogs by Louise Powell review – a powerful debut with plenty of northern soul | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A bereaved father and son bond over greyhound racing in an east Durham town in terminal decline
Author: Benjamin Myers
Headline: A bereaved father and son bond over greyhound racing in an east Durham town in terminal decline
Content: Going to the dogs … ‘Powell is strongest when describing the details of track life.’Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGoing to the dogs … ‘Powell is strongest when describing the details of track life.’Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesFictionReviewUnderdogs by Louise Powell review – a powerful debut with plenty of northern soulA bereaved father and son bond over greyhound racing in an east Durham town in terminal declineBenjamin MyersTue 28 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe adjoining villagesof Easington and Easington Colliery in the coalfields of east Durham make the perfect case study of the shift from England’s industrial boomtime to terminal decline. Twenty miles from a major town or city, they’ve been left to languish ever since Thatcher went to war with the industry that made them. If you want to understand why the white working class feel abandoned today, go to Easington Colliery and its surrounding villages.It’s this community that Middlesbrough-born writer Louise Powell brings to life in a powerful debut set in the world of greyhound racing, or “flapping”. Underdogs is an utterly authentic depiction of an England that’s overlooked, but still very much alive. Pigeon lofts and flat caps, meat raffles and social clubs – all still exist, just very rarely in 21st-century novels.Ten-year-old George Wheatley and his broken father Reg, both grieving the loss of George’s mother, who died two years earlier, are drawn into the dog-track culture by charismatic ex-miner Bertie, who despite the “half-pint of black phlegm he hawked up off his lungs every mornin’” decides not to pursue an incapacity benefit claim as he can make better money rinsing out the various illegal bookmakers by racing his dogs. When the bookies refuse to take Bertie’s bets he ropes in those down on their luck to race his dogs for him, and hands over his bitch Goldie, “twenny-nine kilo of muscles coiled like springs … a Ferrari of an engine in her fawn chest and a nose that could been made by Concorde”. Scores of those on the breadline have benefited from Bertie’s hustle.double quotation markIt' s a hard-scratch existence based around family alliances and power struggles in the dying days of an analogue worldThe love that George feels for Goldie is matched only by his need to survive in an uncompromising adult world where the greatest threat comes from aggrieved bookmaker Baz, who has designs on their prized canine charge. Powell is strongest when describing the details of track life, a seemingly simple pursuit given a dark edge by the high-stakes money changing hands and further complicated by the treatment of these graceful creatures who are bred and discarded for human amusement and profit.That the novel is set in 1998 is significant; all of County Durham’s pits had finally closed, but major regeneration investment was on its way from local boy Tony Blair, with his talk of “regional task forces” and “enterprise zones”. Old slag piles were soon to became nature reserves and pithead monuments. A bright new future was promised, though it’s barely glimpsed here; today Easington has one of the whitest demographics in the country (currently 98.4%), and was the place worst hit by 2025 disability allowance cuts.Here, then, is a hard-scratch existence based around family alliances and power struggles in the dying days of an analogue world, where scars received from police truncheons at Orgreave are shown and shared, and where premature death stalks the terraced streets. George and Reg emerge as tender and quietly heroic; the father’s grief for his lost wife is almost overwhelming at times, as are the reminders of George’s malnutrition. This is real first-world poverty, as it still exists today. During the second world war British-based fascist William Joyce, better known as Lord Haw-Haw, remarked that “the people of Easington will be eating greyhounds, not raising them”; he sorely underestimated just how much the English love their dogs, and it’s no coincidence that Powell’s descriptions of the greyhound’s meals are more mouthwatering than anything father and son eat.North-east writers of literary fiction have always had plenty to sing about, but not much in the way of support from the publishing industry; “too bleak” and “too northern” are words familiar to many of us from the region. Given the rich cultural tradition of storytelling and folk song, always told in distinctively melodic vernacular voices, this still feels like an oversight. With recent novels from Eliza Clark, Glen James Brown, Jessica Andrews and Lucy Rose all finding critical favour, it’s clear that there are infinite Englands in existence. And as Underdogs movingly demonstrates, it’s these untold stories that need to be on the page – now more than ever.Benjamin Myers’s most recent novel is Jesus Christ Kinski (Bloomsbury).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
