title: Wham! 10 Days in China review – pop meets politics in George and Andrew’s great leap east | Movies | The Guardian
description: The duo’s groundbreaking 1985 tour reveals a strange collision of pop stardom and communism, a re-edit of Lindsay Anderson’s efforts that got him fired
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The duo’s groundbreaking 1985 tour reveals a strange collision of pop stardom and communism, a re-edit of Lindsay Anderson’s efforts that got him fired
Content: A brilliant coup … George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley in Beijing in 1985.Photograph: Martyn Goddard/Overseas Ltd/Robobuild Ltd/George Michael Ent/Andrew Ridgeley/Big GeoffView image in fullscreenA brilliant coup … George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley in Beijing in 1985.Photograph: Martyn Goddard/Overseas Ltd/Robobuild Ltd/George Michael Ent/Andrew Ridgeley/Big GeoffMoviesReviewWham! 10 Days in China review – pop meets politics in George and Andrew’s great leap eastThe duo’s groundbreaking 1985 tour reveals a strange collision of pop stardom and communism, a re-edit of Lindsay Anderson’s efforts that got him firedPeter BradshawTue 28 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a documentary that has a very important story to tell, maybe more important than it feels comfortable admitting. It’s about two separate subjects – or maybe three: Wham!, China and film-makerLindsay Anderson. A superpower nervously edging towards western-style openness, a pop band nervously doing what needed to be done to make it big in the US, and a great film director, needing the money, taking on a project he didn’t really believe in.In 1985, Wham!’s beetle-browed manager Simon Napier-Bell had a cunning plan for howGeorge Michaeland Andrew Ridgeley could break the US: Wham! would be the first ever western pop band to perform in mainland China. They would play where the Beatles, the Stones and Elvis had never played, and the resulting global publicity would launch them into the US. (He was right – it did.) In our modern age, the movie and music businesses routinely consider China as the key element of the all-important Asian market, but in 1985, Michael and Ridgeley were the Kirk and Spock of the charts, going where no pop act had gone before.After months of patient negotiation with Communist party officials, Napier-Bell pulled off this brilliant coup; he got his boys two sensational, historic gigs in Beijing and then in Guangzhou, with photo-opportunities at the Great Wall. This would be a tough 10-day tour in which, like a royal or presidential visit, they had to tolerate the press in the embedded presence of the hated British red-top tabloids whose coverage they needed. For the same reasons, they also accepted film producer Martin Lewis’s proposal for a fly-on-the-wall documentary, and also his idea for a classy, prestigious director: Lindsay Anderson. But Anderson kept on pushing for a challenging culture-clash theme to the film and the music people just wanted a glorified promo reel, so Anderson was summarily fired after the tour, having been grumpy and disillusioned the entire time, and making no secret of his dislike for Wham!’s music. (Perhaps Anderson thought he could do something like Antonioni’s 1972 immersive TV documentary about China,Chung Kuo: Cina.)A bland PR film was shown a year later, but now the amazing footage has been re-edited, with new talking-head interviews with surviving participants, most prominently Ridgeley – though it brings the film no closer to what Anderson wanted. We see how unbearably tense he and Michael were, and yet how courageous. They were in their early 20s, yet they were expected to make official speeches that might daunt professional diplomats, and had to handle hostile press questioning about the Chinese police cracking down on people dancing at their Beijing concert. (The authorities were, it was suggested, particularly annoyed by the song Freedom, although how much they understood of the English lyrics is an open question.) In Beijing, the audience was glacial, for whom Wham! were creatures from another planet, while in Guangzhou, having had access to Hong Kong pop, the crowd were more enthusiastic.View image in fullscreenTaste of liberty … Wham! 10 Days in China.Photograph: Martyn Goddard/Overseas Ltd/Robobuild Ltd/George Michael Ent/Andrew Ridgeley/Big GeoffBut the point was that Wham! triggered something that could not be untriggered: they gave the Chinese a taste of liberty. Four years later was the Tiananmen Square massacre. Was the Wham! Chinese tour therefore a world-historical event, the butterfly wingbeat that caused an earthquake? Maybe. But it’s not a possibility explored here. It would be nice to conclude that George and Andrew, having been essentially uninterested in China other than as a stepping stone to US glory, were overcome by a great love for that country. (There is incidentally also the question of their views on communism and the left, having played a benefit for striking miners the year before. Did that help get them the gig?)Well … they never returned, although Ridgeley is shown in the present day thoughtfully looking out from the wall. 1985 was their annus mirabilis, the year of the giant US breakthrough and George appearing on stage with Elton John at Live Aid. Maybe the Chinese achievement only fully dawned on them much later. It’s a strange and riveting moment in pop and political history.Wham! 10 Days in China is in cinemas from 28 July.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsGeorge MichaelMusic documentaryLindsay AndersonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Just when you thought it was safe … the shark movie is back for more | Thrillers | The Guardian
description: Shark Week arrives in an overstuffed period for the film genre even if nothing will ever rival the greatest of them all
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Shark Week arrives in an overstuffed period for the film genre even if nothing will ever rival the greatest of them all
Content: The Devil's Mouth poster.Photograph: AmazonView image in fullscreenThe Devil's Mouth poster.Photograph: AmazonThrillersJust when you thought it was safe … the shark movie is back for moreShark Week arrives in an overstuffed period for the film genre even if nothing will ever rival the greatest of them allJesse HassengerTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 05.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTracy Jordan, Tracy Morgan’s character on 30 Rock, once advised a friend to live every week like it’s Shark Week. In 2026, Hollywood has finally taken these sage words to heart.‘It put the fear of God in the audience’: the incredible story of how Jaws changed HollywoodRead moreThough Discovery Channel is only observing its annual Shark Week of shark-themed programming for the customary seven days, shark movies have been enjoying a yearlong renaissance – in terms of volume, if not necessarily quality. Two shark thrillers – The Devil’s Mouth on Prime Video and Above & Below as a paid VOD rental – are releasing this week, presumably to complement nonfictional Shark Week programming, but they’re far from the only fish in the sea. Earlier this month, Clint Eastwood’s daughter starred in The Bay, another VOD title. In June, there was Chum, starring Alice Eve; in May,Deep Water, Renny Harlin’s return to the subgenre following his classic Deep Blue Sea. Before that,Thrashwas a Netflix hit. That’s half a dozen shark movies so far this year. It’s a wonder no one has arranged a 10th-anniversary re-release ofThe Shallows.Obviously there’s a baseline, sellable level of interest in shark thrillers, which are often positioned as something akin to an all-natural slasher: horror movies that expand just slightly beyond the bounds of the world we know (the beach, the ocean, observing nature) and into heightened but not completely outlandish territory. They’re the water equivalent of the masked killer stalking around the woods, only we’ve all seen footage of sharks – thanks to Discovery and the like – so we can all agree that they are definitely out there, and can be deadly to humans – even if the reality is far less gruesome, frequent or vengeful than their movie equivalents.What makes the pursuit of new shark movies more quixotic than some other horror/thriller subgenres is the existence of a single agreed-upon masterpiece that’s near-impossible to match. While it’s unlikely that any given new landlubber slasher will represent a pantheon-level genre-definer, at least there are a variety of near-perfect classics to emulate: the proto-slasher creepiness of Psycho, the unnerving rural underbelly of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, the suburban menace of Halloween, the phantasmagorical dreamscape of A Nightmare on Elm Street. With shark movies, it’sJaws, and then everything else. (Some of those slashers have good and/or interesting sequels with further inventions; not so Jaws, which just has three increasingly ludicrous and cheap brand extensions.) Working from maybe the beachiest beach read of all time with a notoriously finicky fake shark, Steven Spielberg crafted a movie that’s simultaneously a male-bonding character study, an indictment of keep-the-beaches-open American capitalism, and an expertly tuned thrill machine complete with unforgettable theme music. By sheer force of quality, it reinvented the barely there shark movie, and the whole of summer movies along with it.Eventually, a few particularly strong iterations did figure out how to operate within the shadow of Jaws, though they had to wait out those lousy follow-ups, which reached a nadir in 1987 with the all-time stinker Jaws: The Revenge. Deep Blue Sea, Harlin’s amped-up summer movie from 1999, feels like a Jaws sequel done right: it goes the bigger/faster/crazier route, with genetically modified sharks and noticeably dumber humans. Its thematic is the same old monster-movie scientists-playing-god cautionary tale, but as a creature feature it’s juicy, well-cast (Samuel L Jackson!), and a lot of fun. Another highlight goes in the opposite direction. The aforementioned The Shallows, from summer 2016, strips down the three-men-on-a-boat climax of Jaws even further; most of the movie is just Blake Lively stranded on a rock, attempting to outwit a particularly persistent shark as she grieves the loss of her mother. Director Jaume Collet-Serra has multiple movies that play with Hitchcock-style location limitations; The Shallows is one of his most limited and also one of his best.View image in fullscreenBlake Lively in The Shallows.Photograph: Courtesy/Rex/ShutterstockThe Shallows – along with the more bummed-out survival-thriller indies Open Water and47 Meters Down– has managed to help redefine the parameters of the shark thriller. Over the past decade, they tend to either follow the Shallows/47 Meters route of a handful of characters, usually women, exorcising some form of trauma or interpersonal conflict through a trial-by-teeth encounter with sharks; or attempt to be sort of a thinking man’s version of Sharknado, the tediously “knowing” D-movie franchise from cable’s SyFy, where sharks are flown into unlikely places or situations. (Think of the recent Netflix hit Under Paris, which contrived irresistible but ultimately schlocky ways for CG sharks to turn up in the Seine circa the 2024 Olympics.) If nothing else, both styles set up more achievable goals than evoking a truly great movie like Jaws.So how do this year’s crop stack up in that context? Of the two Shark Week releases, The Devil’s Mouth follows the Shallows path, while Above & Below has more of a Sharknado style, though it also borrows heavily from 47 Meters Down. The Devil’s Mouth focuses on friends, led by two besties (Kathryn Newton and Lana Condor), vacationing in Thailand, where they embark on a swimming tour of an off-ocean cave system. The movie, seems, if anything, overly self-conscious about the motivations that are supposed to fuel characters in survival thrillers, which means the two leads both have dead parents, while also engaging in a semi-toxic dynamic that the movie never quite fully defines. As a result, it ultimately feels like it’s a movie about the perils of having a best friend who’s just generally kind of annoying.View image in fullscreenA still from 47 Meters Down.Photograph: Studios/Kobal/Rex/ShutterstockBut its location shooting with built-in atmosphere, and the sparing use of shark effects this allows, goes a long way toward making it watchable Shallows knockoff. If director Jeff Wadlow doesn’t have the B-movie mastery of Collet-Serra, he at least has some B-minus-movie energy and watchable stars, especially scream queen Newton. Above & Below should really be the kickier B-movie affair, following another group of five young people on vacation, whose shark-observing cage-dive boat turns out to be affiliated with a group of criminals. Like 47 Meters Down, much of it involves the logistics of conserving oxygen while trapped underwater, to which DTV veteran Jesse V Johnson adds some criminal bickering and shootouts above sea level; not quite Sharknado bombast, but a similar sense of cross-breeding. Antonio Banderas is entertaining as the courteous but merciless head criminal, but the fusion of literal and metaphorical sharks is disappointingly rote. It’s two chintzy DTV movies in one, a 90-minute time-saver but little else.The thing is, as many inventive ideas as shark-movie-makers can brainstorm, the creatures themselves are fairly inflexible; neither middling CG nor real footage nor mechanical models tend to feel particularly convincing on their own. These real animals are also major visual effects challenges that have largely been shunted downstream to smaller productions that can’t always handle it. Even the odd big-budget attempt, like Jason Statham’s Meg movies, are pretty crummy-looking. Just look at Harlin’s revisitation of his old feeding grounds with Deep Water. It’s not a sequel to Deep Blue Sea, but would-be companion piece that combines a plane-crash survival narrative with a bunch of sharks. Guess which component is more suspenseful and believable on screen? Unlike their Deep Blue Sea counterparts, the sharks wind up feeling like afterthoughts.Maybe that’s why some of the best recent shark-style movies don’t feature sharks at all. 2019’sCrawlfollows the Shallows template of a young woman with family issues thrust into a dangerous solo mission, here rescuing her hurricane-stranded father rather than saving herself, only she’s bedeviled by alligators rather than sharks. It’s so effective that this year’s Netflix shark flagship Thrash more or less ripped it back off, subbing sharks swimming around submerged homes back in for the gators. Or consider the surprise hit Fall, which features two young women with an intense history, stranded at great height, no creatures required.That movie is also just a plain old survival thriller, of course, but it’s also illustrative of how little the sharks themselves often bring to these scenarios, especially when movies can’t afford the effects needed to make them look realistically scary. Shark movies may be flashier offshoots of Shark Week that can run all year (or at least all summer), but apart from their inability to top Jaws, it’s hard for them to compete with the eerie majesty of the real thing. Spielberg incorporated that elusiveness into his work, defined as much by what we can’t see from land as what we might glimpse within the water. That’s not even necessarily an argument for hiding the shark so much as giving both the creature and the human motivations some space. Most contemporary shark pictures are just looking for other movies to chew on.Explore more on these topicsThrillersSharksJawsHorror filmsAction and adventure filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lesvia review – the rise and fall of an amazing lesbian community on Sappho’s actual island home | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Tzeli Hadjidimitriou grew up on Lesbos, and her elegant debut feature explores how the Greek poet’s birthplace became a hub for lesbians
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Director Tzeli Hadjidimitriou grew up on Lesbos, and her elegant debut feature explores how the Greek poet’s birthplace became a hub for lesbians
Content: LesviaPhotograph: Tzeli HadjidimitriouView image in fullscreenLesviaPhotograph: Tzeli HadjidimitriouMoviesReviewLesvia review – the rise and fall of an amazing lesbian community on Sappho’s actual island homeDirector Tzeli Hadjidimitriou grew up on Lesbos, and her elegant debut feature explores how the Greek poet’s birthplace became a hub for lesbiansLeslie FelperinTue 28 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfine-boned, elegantly crafted documentary, this first feature from Greek director Tzeli Hadjidimitriou tells a story at once personal and public: about the lesbian scene that grew up around the town of Eressos on the island of Lesbos (also called Lesvos). Hadjidimitriou is from the island, but not Eressos itself, which was once the home of the seventh century BC poetSappho, whose love poetry threads through the film. Given that pedigree, lesbians, including the director herself, have flocked to Eressos for years to pay homage. By the 1970s, the growing number of queer visitors started to form not just a scene but a community, at first one centred on the nudist beach where many women camped out.Hadjidimitriou’s still photographs are also spliced in throughout, capturing the glorious sensuality of these often naked women, most looking chuffed to bits to have found a little corner of heaven where they can be themselves. But relations with the local people were not always easy, and unsurprisingly the tourists had to contend with homophobia of varying degrees of vocalness, as well as aggressive invasion of their women-only spaces. Luckily, as one woman recalls, there were usually a few butches around to help hustle the intruders off. Over time, tolerance grew, greased by the money the visitors brought to the island, and eventually female-run bars and hotels sprang up.If it all ended there it would be a utopian tale of paradise found. But things go wrong, perhaps related toGreece’s economic crisis that started in 2009,and which exposed the nation’s financial instability. Within a few years, most of the lesbian bars and women-run hotels closed down, and now the community seems much more marginalised.Hadjidimitriou builds her oral history through interviews with some of the many women from all over the world who knew Eressos in its golden years, making for a touching film, and for all the place’s faded glory, it goes on still with younger generations continuing to visit. The sound design, almost constantly incorporating the sea, adds an evocative layer.Lesvia is on digital platforms from 3 August.This article was amended on 28 July to correct the film’s star rating.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsLGBTQ+ rightsGreeceSapphoEuropePoetryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The Messi of ballet’: Marianela Núñez, the Buenos Aires bombshell shaking up British dance | Marianela Núñez | The Guardian
description: The superlative Royal Ballet star finally has her own show. She talks about fabulous footwork, her Argentina-inspired leotard – and why she named her cat after a certain footballer
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: The superlative Royal Ballet star finally has her own show. She talks about fabulous footwork, her Argentina-inspired leotard – and why she named her cat after a certain footballer
Content: ‘Just give me my ballet shoes and I’m in love’ … Marianela Núñez.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Just give me my ballet shoes and I’m in love’ … Marianela Núñez.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianMarianela NúñezInterview‘The Messi of ballet’: Marianela Núñez, the Buenos Aires bombshell shaking up British danceLyndsey WinshipThe superlative Royal Ballet star finally has her own show. She talks about fabulous footwork, her Argentina-inspired leotard – and why she named her cat after a certain footballerTue 28 Jul 2026 04.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 05.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarianela Núñez is talking about football. This is before the World Cup final, after England’s game with Argentina. “That was a hard position for me!” she says. Núñez moved to England from Buenos Aires aged 15 and has danced with the Royal Ballet for 28 years. She’s a British citizen, but her loyalties are clear: check out her Argentina-inspired leotard on Instagram or her cat named after Lionel Messi.In Argentina, they call her the Messi of ballet – although when it comes to who has the finest footwork, they should really be calling him the Núñez of football. A principal dancer since the age of 20, Núñez has been at the top of her game for so long you can forget what a remarkable dancer she is. When she faces the ballerina’s equivalent of a penalty kick –Swan Lake’s 32 fouettés,Sleeping Beauty’s Rose Adagio– you never doubt her, but it’s her romantic spirit, the bright beaming energy, her vivacity in Don Quixote, the tragic yearning of her Odette, the way she breathes in ballet like oxygen, that make her special. She is deeply besotted with what she does.double quotation markBallet doesn’t have to be perfect to be beautifulOn this, she feels an affinity with her footballing counterpart. When she hears interviewers tell Messi how great he is: “He says, ‘The thing is, I’m just happy kicking the ball.’ I can totally relate. Just give me my [ballet] shoes and I’m in love.” Núñez decided at five that she wanted to take ballet seriously, and by 14 was dancing leading roles at Buenos Aires’ Teatro Colón. But after such a rocketing start, she didn’t race to advance her career in the way some top principals do, with a frantic schedule of international guest appearances and solo productions. Only now, at 44, is she about to perform herown show, Timeless.The reason it hasn’t happened sooner, she says, is because she doesn’t have an agent. Many top dancers now do have agents, as well as personal PRs to promote their brands and side projects. Núñez doesn’t go in for that – the greatSylvie Guillemnever had an agent, she tells me, so that’s good enough for her. So perhaps it has taken longer, but now she has five days at the Royal Opera House, with the orchestra and her pick of repertoire. “So actually it was the perfect way,” she says. “I’m glad that I had to wait this long.” It’s not the first time I’ve heard Núñez spin something others could see as a downside into a positive, a sign of resilience that must contribute to keeping herself at the top of a tough profession for so long.View image in fullscreenKnown for her sunny temperament … Marianela Núñez and Reece Clarke rehearse Everywhere We Go by Justin Peck.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianNúñez is known for her sunny temperament. The morning we speak she’s under the weather, she started feeling feverish doing yoga last night (she swears by yoga at the start and end of each day), but here she is first thing, laughing and smiling. A consummate ballerina, all the effort is hidden. When it comes to ballet though, for her, it’s not effort, it’s what gives her life, especially doing daily class.“Class, for me, is everything,” she says. “Ballet class is where I can reallyfeelthe body, every little …” she gestures the tiniest atom. “It has that ritual feeling. You have your same spot at the barre that you had when you first joined the company.” She calls it a safety net, and a kind of meditation. What’s it like to have such an intense, lifelong love affair with something? “It’s so strong, and it feels so good,” she says. Even when it’s not good, it’s good. “You know, today I don’t feel great, and I know I’m not going to have a great rehearsal, but just being here, I’m sure something will come out of that,” she says. “Ballet doesn’t have to be perfect to be beautiful.”Age has brought Núñez self-acceptance. She used to chastise herself for feeling nervous. Now, it’s: “OK, you’ve done the work. Be nervous.” Accept it and get on with the job. “With all the insecurities too: now I’m like, well, yeah, you feel insecure. What are you gonna do?” What does she feel insecure about? “No, I’m not going to bore you with this,” she says, closing that door.For Timeless, Núñez chose the programme based on who she wanted to dance with –Vadim Muntagirov,Matthew Ball,William Bracewelland the Royal Ballet’s new principalPatricio Revé– partners who have “given me confidence, ways of going out of my comfort zone so I could take risks, have freedom on stage, be vulnerable,” she says. “And with these four guys I would just laugh the whole way though rehearsal. Each of them, maybe without knowing, helped me a lot through really hard times.”View image in fullscreen‘Partners who give me confidence’ … Marianela Núñez (Odette/Odile) and Vadim Muntagirov (Prince Siegfried) in Swan Lake.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianSome of the programme remains a surprise, but she will be dancing Jerome Robbins’ magical In the Night, set to Chopin nocturnes (“It’s so simple yet has so much depth. It’s very classy”), and Frederick Ashton’s Marguerite and Armand, the drama of an ageing courtesan and her young lover, created for Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev. Some retiring dancers choose it as their farewell piece, but Núñez is nowhere near saying farewell. “There’s no expiry date!” she says. Unlike the rumours of retirement swirling round a certain footballer, Núñez looks as strong and as winning as ever.Marianela: Timeless is atRoyal Ballet and Opera, London, 29 July to 2 August.Explore more on these topicsMarianela NúñezBalletRoyal BalletDancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Laurie Kilmartin review – Oscars gag-writer unleashes a fierce and filthy talent | Comedy | The Guardian
description: She has penned jokes for Jimmy Kimmel, Conan O’Brien and the Academy. Now she’s seizing the limelight with scattergun routines about everything from penises to free-bleeding
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: She has penned jokes for Jimmy Kimmel, Conan O’Brien and the Academy. Now she’s seizing the limelight with scattergun routines about everything from penises to free-bleeding
Content: Clean brutality … Laurie KilmartinPhotograph: PRView image in fullscreenClean brutality … Laurie KilmartinPhotograph: PRComedyReviewLaurie Kilmartin review – Oscars gag-writer unleashes a fierce and filthy talentSoho theatre, LondonShe has penned jokes for Jimmy Kimmel, Conan O’Brien and the Academy. Now she’s seizing the limelight with scattergun routines about everything from penises to free-bleedingKate WyverTue 28 Jul 2026 06.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 06.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLaurie Kilmartin is not afraid of vulgarity. The Peabody award-winner flits between penis jokes, free-bleeding chaos and a taste for vengeance in this scattergun hour that marks her London debut. Having made her career as a staff writer for Jimmy Kimmel and Conan O’Brien, Kilmartin’s own voice is crude, acute and pretty mean, delivering each dark joke with a furrowed-brow intensity, followed by a flash of a wide, are-you-gonna-take-it smile.Jumping through the decades, the US comedian cycles through school bullies, the need for better assassins, and the limited dating pool of men over 50. There’s a pitch-black quality to some of these tales, with a particular knife-edge to her story of an abusive swim coach. Other anecdotes feel drier, like they’ve just had the dust blown off them; she settles too long on lockdowns, which I thought we’d all agreed we were done talking about long ago. Even a moment on Charlie Kirk feels like it missed the moment, though other elements of her US political commentary are easy winners.Kilmartin wrote on the last two years of the Oscars ceremonies, and she’s most confident in the swing of finely tuned bits, delivered with a blazing bullishness. But since the show’s structure is loose and fragmented, she flounders for a few seconds every time she moves from one often-unrelated set piece to the next. She’s less commanding in the moments of audience participation, with one callback to a story of language failure in Japan provided by an audience member instead of the comedian.It’s clear from the amount of haphazard reference checks and mid-story math conversions that she’s not used to UK crowds. At times this gives the show the feel of a work-in-progress, and there’s an oddly distracting focus on the difference between her (American, single mum) and her audience (tonight: neither of those), which we wouldn’t mind at all if she didn’t keep mentioning it. Over the course of the hour, the tone of Kilmartin’s performance is somewhat standoffish, and she repeatedly dismisses us as light clappers. But the more she leans into this, the funnier we find it. Matching the clean brutality of her best anecdotes, severity suits her.At Soho theatre, London, until 28 JulyExplore more on these topicsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: PalesTEENian review – engaging story of mixed identity is a bit of a muddle | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Joe Haddad’s solo show tilts between family comedy and football fandom as well as the horrors of the Gaza war but never quite finds its focus
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Joe Haddad’s solo show tilts between family comedy and football fandom as well as the horrors of the Gaza war but never quite finds its focus
Content: Effervescent … Joe Haddad in PalesTEENian at Riverside Studios, LondonView image in fullscreenEffervescent … Joe Haddad in PalesTEENian at Riverside Studios, LondonTheatreReviewPalesTEENian review – engaging story of mixed identity is a bit of a muddleRiverside Studios, LondonJoe Haddad’s solo show tilts between family comedy and football fandom as well as the horrors of the Gaza war but never quite finds its focusArifa AkbarTue 28 Jul 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe Haddad’s solo show is a kind of self-referential standup set which tells us about his journey into comedy. It encompasses the negotiation of his dual identity as a Palestinian south Londoner and becomes a coming-of-age story.Born in Croydon, with Arab Christian parents from Jerusalem, he faced prejudice at his Catholic school, including taunts of “Jew-boy” because there was so little understanding of Palestine and its history of occupation. It follows him to adulthood, and an assumed, Anglicised, stage name of Joe Adams, for fear of being cancelled (even his mother tells him not to mention Palestine during gigs).But this show, he makes clear, is not all gloom and doom. There is no need for anyone to blanch at the mention of the P-word. Neither will he use the I-word (indeed, he succeeds in circumventing the naming of Israel even once). He leads with heartiness and humour and exuberantly drawn extended family members on his visits to Jerusalem, and nods to his love of Chelsea FC.There are some good lines – “TonightI’moccupying the stage,” he says, and he has an effervescent presence but none of it quite hangs together or builds its dramatic trajectory far enough. Haddad flags up the hodge-podge nature of the show himself: if it feels jumbled up, that is because his life is too, he tells us at the off.It is not exactly a jumble, but it hops too much in tone, from comic to dramatic, not quite nailing either. He waxes lyrical about zatar, tells us about Arab hospitality and gives us affectionately cartoonish takes on his imperious Palestinian mother. He speaks of the cultural expectation to become a doctor, lawyer or engineer, and his departure from that with an entry into comedy. The show is cute in its humour but soft and over-familiar. Football jerseys hang around him but this set seems like a red herring – football is only ever mentioned in cosmetic ways.He also speaks of 7 October 2023, from hearing about Hamas’s attacks to the horrific images of death coming out of Gaza. But this part comes in short, impressionistic sentences, not grappled with fully enough once it is mentioned. Too many topics are touched on in 80 minutes as a whole and ironically the show feels slight and unfocused as a result – a précis that does not manage to unpack the immense potential of its subject matter.At Riverside Studios, London,until 2 AugustExplore more on these topicsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Climate anxiety was consuming me. Then I learned to laugh about it | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The daily dread pushed me to enroll in a standup class. Could I channel my despair into something lighter?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The daily dread pushed me to enroll in a standup class. Could I channel my despair into something lighter?
Content: A globe on a stool beside a microphone against red curtains.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA globe on a stool beside a microphone against red curtains.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesComedyClimate anxiety was consuming me. Then I learned to laugh about itThe daily dread pushed me to enroll in a standup class. Could I channel my despair into something lighter?Emily StrasserTue 28 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 11.57 EDTShareIf you had told me six months ago that I would soon be performing standup comedy to dozens of strangers, I would have assumed it was a bad dream.Public speaking ranks about as high as driving in rush hour traffic through downtown Boston on my list of favorite activities. That I would choose to do standup, with its potential for public humiliation, is basically unimaginable.And yet, in late April, there I was, spooling out jokes about AI, the manosphere, gnomes, immigration and my three-year-old nephew.I hadn’t signed up for a comedy class because I’d always dreamed of doing standup; I was there because the daily dread of political and planetary freefall had become untenable.‘How do you laugh about death?’: the comedians tackling climate changeRead moreIn 2019, a convergence of grim climate predictions had catapulted me into despair. I climbed out about six months later after finding a community that shared my grief and helped me move through it. But relief isn’t permanent. And for anyone paying attention, things are not looking good.To my detriment, I have a habit of jumping into the deep end. Last year, I spent monthsinterviewing the scientistswho set the Doomsday Clock, a graphic representation of how close humanity is to self-annihilation. As you might imagine, adding nuclear winter and bioweapons to my paniclistdidn’t help. (Yes, I’m fun at parties.)I don’t want to numb out or come unglued. So when I found a listing for the most unlikely of antidotes, I had to try it.Climate comedy. What?!I signed up.Over a decade ago, Belina Raffy, an improv consultant and comedy coach, grew concerned that dire warnings about climate change were making people shut down in fear and guilt. At the same time, those trying to communicate the crisis were in danger of burning out from overwhelm.She developed a course calledSustainable Stand Upto help people working on social and environmental issues find humorous ways to share serious messages. Since then, she has taught the course, internationally and online, to everyone from Nasa climate scientists to human rights lawyers, Extinction Rebellion activists, humanitarian workers and more.This iteration was for members of the Climate Psychology Alliance, therapists who help people navigate the psychological toll of living through the climate crisis.I’m not a climate-aware therapist, as these professionals call themselves, but I could have used one. In 2019, when I told therapists I was distressed by wildfires and mass extinctions, they asked about my mother or suggested an ADHD screening or thyroid test. None of that helped. What did was finding other people to ask existential questions and cry with, who validated that big feelings might be an appropriate response to scary times.Raffy’s class offered something tantalizingly different: could I learn to find lightness in the dark?double quotation markMight doing comedy help us to show up with more resilience when the difficulties we face are collective, political and planetary?We know that laughter hasphysicalandemotionalbenefits. And though more research needs to be done, there’spromising evidencethat learning to do comedy is good for mental health: it helps people reframe difficult experiences, build social bonds and gain confidence.In the pastfew years, the UK’s National Health Service has even begun to offerstandup classesas a mental health intervention as part of its expanding “social prescribing” program, in which patients are referred by healthcare providers to non-clinical services and activities, such as exercise classes, art classes or social services, to support holistic wellbeing.Might doing comedy help us to show up with more resilience when the difficulties we face are collective, political and planetary?The seven-week online course would culminate in a live online show.And I wanted in.For the first class, in mid-March, we Zoomed in from our homes. The class was limited to six participants due to its intensity.Karen Taylor, a trauma therapist based in Hartford, Connecticut, was drawn to the invitation to combine play, art and creativity with her commitment to climate psychology. Jessica Bleuer, a professor of drama therapy in Montreal, hoped comedy would help her communicate with people across political differences. Jeremy Lehrer, a therapist based in Brooklyn, was intrigued by the opportunity to try to express his values in a comedic form.I was the only non-therapist. I was anxious and edgy, slogging through a Boston winter that refused to end, sapped by teaching, waking every day to worse news. I was relieved when our first exercise wasn’t comedy, but a rant.Raffy asked each of us to pick something that made us grumpy. Not the red hot thing, more like a six out of 10. We needed to ease in before tackling the big stuff, she cautioned.We took turns ranting for a minute each – perimenopause, entitled people. I could have gone on about customer service chatbots for ages.After each rant, Raffy asked us to describe “the beautiful thing” the ranter cared about. The group told me I cared about labor justice, human connection, communication and flexibility. It made me feel like a “very good person”.Still, when Raffy told us to write three jokes for homework, just like that, I was back to grumpy. As I wrote rambling, pointless notes, I wondered: did I even know what a joke was?When Raffy saw An Inconvenient Truth sometime around its release in 2006, she left the theater in a panic. The vision of a harrowing future activated a prepping instinct: “I want to get into a Hummer and go shopping with a big shotgun,” she thought.Unsettled by her visceral response, she reflected that there was a danger in delivering such frightening information with little regard to what emotions it might ignite in viewers.Al Gore, she thought, seemed like kind of an asshole.Around that time, Raffy was beginning to develop improv workshops for businesses and NGOs; in 2014, she built on that work to offer her first standup class in Baltimore.At first, Raffy was primarily concerned with helping people doing good work communicate more effectively. But she discovered that the internal, emotional process of finding the “expansive, joyful aspects” of their work was just as important for participants.Raffy teaches what she calls “loving comedy”, an approach informed by the psychology of humor.double quotation markIn the polycrisis we are living through, people are so activated that they want to jump straight into the fireAs it turns out,not all humor is good for us. Humor that is used to amuse and affirm others, build social bonds, and regulate emotions by finding amusement in difficult circumstances is psychologically beneficial. But humor that is used to mock others, overly disparage the self, or avoid facing difficult feelings, is detrimental.Our aim, Raffy told us, was to come from a place of, “I love myself. I love the audience. ‘The system’ is silly. And share what would be awesome.”That’s all becoming more difficult lately, she admits. In thepolycrisiswe are living through, people are so activated that they want to jump straight into the fire. She’s been trying to offer more structure and bite-size exercises to help participants access their “unique wisdom”. That first week, she planted seeds for our first jokes by having us brainstorm what made us especially wise or quirky as children.I remembered how I used to make “fairy feasts” as a child, filling acorn caps with flower petals. How every day of fourth grade, I wore a long fleece stocking cap, decorated with lizards and frogs. How I sobbed when I learned that the live lobsters I had been playing with on the kitchen floor were bound for our dinner plates.I couldn’t see how any of it would become a joke, particularly about anything that mattered. But I felt a little affection for that insistently weird and empathetic kid who had believed so passionately in the magic of the world.Things started to shift in the following weeks, as I studied the sample sets Raffy sent us and hunted for joke material throughout my day, seeking absurdity in mundane frustrations. Inscrutable bureaucratic speech during one of my faculty meeting was actually a coded message, evidence of a highly covert operation. I hadn’t wasted hours trying to figure out where to responsibly dispose of a lithium battery; I was Frodo on a dangerous quest to Mount Doom to destroy my precious.I kept a running list of ideas in my phone. I told my friends I had to do my “joke homework”.One lesson on joke structure especially stuck with me. First, Raffy explained, you create a “circle of expectation”. Then, in the punchline, you leap outside that circle while still playing by its rules. “What happens,” she asked, “when we map one domain or pattern on to a different one?”I immediately thought about AI.Emily Strasser performs her standup routineI wanted to rant about all of AI’s sins, from labor exploitation to amplifying risks of nuclear war … But Raffy’s advice was to pick a six instead of a 10, so I focused on one fear: that in a world of large language models, the skill of writing will become like knitting – a beloved craft, but an optional hobby – rendering my job as a professor of writing obsolete.If the expectation is AI’s inevitable takeover, what would its opposite look like? What if knitting became a graduation requirement?I imagined a world in which the universities indoctrinate students in the “radical woke ideology” of knitting, transforming women’s work into the latest alpha male status symbol. I envisioned a culture shift where the manosphere bros start livestreaming knitting sessions, eventually “fibermaxxing” by raising their own sheep and spinning their own wool. I built to the requisite penis joke.“Spin that fiber long and thick,” I said, fanning myself. “Hot.”Scientists and comedians join forces to get climate crisis message acrossRead moreThen after a pause: “I’m gay, but even I can’t resist the insulating power of a wool sweater.”It felt good to transform a helpless thought into something silly and playful. It felt good to imagine that my fellow professors and I could be as powerful as those who call us the enemies say we are.The political potency of comedy is ancient and evergreen. From the archetypical trickster to the medieval court jester to Stephen Colbert, fools have always been subverting social order, revealing hypocrisy and challenging authority.But it’s not easy to make light of nightmares, especially for beginners. Raffy wanted our sets to land on some sort of possibility or call to action that was also, somehow, light and playful. That was a hard ask for a Zoom full of people used to holding personal trauma beside planetary pain. We all wanted to say thething, and our sets veered into speeches, rants or laments.Bleuer, the drama therapist in Montreal, beautifully captured our collective despair in an early version of her set. “As a Latina Canadian whose best friend is from Iran, me finding hope looks like,” she paused, looked around the room, searched the ceiling as if to find hope scuttling there like a spider.We began to smile as we saw the joke coming.She tried again, haltingly, “like um, I – I find hope in – the um … OK, so I cry. So I cry.”We released our laughs in recognition.Then she spun into a poignant defense of crying as a healthy response to the world. “There’s a whole world in a tear … I speak the truth in a tear. The world is really sad. Let’s cry together.”double quotation markPart of authoritarianism is shutting down the parts of ourselves that can remain … connected to others through playRebecca WestonWe nodded, solemn, a bit glassy-eyed.“This is a comedy course,” Belina reminded us, as she offered suggestions for finding something funny in a tear.In her final set, Bleuer imagined a movement of crying activists.“Oh fuck! The crying activists are back! They teared us again,” she acted out an irate legislator arriving to his office in sopping clothes.Everyone laughed.Rebecca Weston, co-executive director of Climate Psychology Alliance North America, had taken the class in the winter. It felt like a necessary response to the relentless dread.“Part of authoritarianism,” she said, “is shutting down the parts of ourselves that can remain open, that can remain joyful, that can remain connected to others through play. And when … that gets much more rigid and brittle, I think huge parts of our own capacity suffer.”But while watching the horrors unfold in Minneapolis and doing her own rapid response work in New York, sometimes Weston’s fear and anger felt too big for the class. She considered dropping out.My own too-big anger flared up during a one-on-one coaching session a couple of weeks before our final show. I had built my set by using my teaching, knitting and three-year-old nephew Jack’s love of gnomes to comment on AI, toxic masculinity, environmental concerns and immigration justice (all are welcome, except for “Kristi’s Gnomes”).But I was struggling to find an ending.What if, Raffy suggested, you invite the gnomes and your nephew and the manosphere bros to engage in some beautiful possibility together?Some flaming righteous rage shot through me and I cried right there on Zoom. I didn’t want those hateful, dangerous men anywhere near Jack, a sweet, goofy, energetic kid who stomps through puddles, meows to my cats over FaceTime, and investigates birdhouses at hardware stores in search of their resident gnomes. I want to protect a world in which he can be playful and kind and curious and brave, in which every child can be.I had reached a limit of my playfulness.For a few days after that, I walked around all up in my feelings, wondering if this thing had been one giant mistake. Weston had stuck with the class and ultimately found her way through her anger to a set that felt affirming. I wondered if I could do the same.Underneath the anger, I knew, was that ferocious instinct to protect. What was funny about that?When I finally had an idea, though, I hurried to dismiss it. Absolutely too vulnerable. Surely, I will not let them see the silliest, witchiest most cringy and earnest version of me.I scrambled for other ideas.I have had many dreams of being thrust inexplicably into a situation for which I am completely inadequate. You know the type – didn’t study, wrong clothes, missed the meeting.Some days, it feels like we’re sharing the worst version of that collective bad dream. No one prepared us to face all of this – the climate crisis and fascism and the AI assault of all we hold dear, all at once. We don’t have the skills … We are not the kind of people who …I am not the kind of person who does standup. But here I was, feeling a little faint, searching a grid of unfamiliar faces for the few guests I had invited. And then I did the thing I had not wanted to. I asked a bunch of internet strangers to join me in a big, goofy “spell” of protection, one I had originally made up for my three-year-old nephew on the solstice.“Stop it!” we yelled together, to Kristi’s Gnomes and all the others who are spreading fear and hatred, thrusting our palms forward in the gesture of “halt!”I felt ridiculous and powerful all at once.Jack was there on the screen, in a sun-drenched living room with his mom and dad. He shoved his hand out, too, grinning and yelling.‘It turned out I had a brain tumour …’ Six standup comics on what spurred them to get on stageRead moreDoing amateur standup is a silly, tiny thing. It won’t save the planet and it doesn’t replace any of the vital work of resistance and legislation and new world-building. And believe you me, I’m still angry and scared as hell. But standup helped me reconnect to my young, silly, tender heart, and showed me capacities I didn’t know I had.Stretching to find funny, authentic ways to talk about the things that keep us up at night, the therapists and I had found a way back to ourselves.“These times are meant to make us feel confused and there’s so many competing needs,” said Bleuer, who dubbed herself the niche superhero “the tear fairy” in her set. “Maybe re-tapping into what we know about ourselves prepares us for resistance better.” The comedic process had helped to reaffirm the political importance of her work as a therapist.Maybe we leap outside the circle of our own expectations and find we were already there.And so I geared up part two of the spell: “To all other gnomes, to the immigrants and queer people and trans people, to anyone who wants to care for this earth and each other and knit together, we say ‘welcome.’”And we flapped our hands rapidly at our shoulders, ululating our hearts out.

title: The Mermaid Mask review – the funniest underwater murder mystery you can play | Games | The Guardian
description: Detective Grimoire is at it again in the long-awaited new entry to this stylish series of comedy whodunnits
Author: Jordan Erica Webber
Headline: Detective Grimoire is at it again in the long-awaited new entry to this stylish series of comedy whodunnits
Content: A submarine full of secrets … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesView image in fullscreenA submarine full of secrets … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesGamesReviewThe Mermaid Mask review – the funniest underwater murder mystery you can playPC, Nintendo Switch/Switch 2, PS5; SFB GamesDetective Grimoire is at it again in the long-awaited new entry to this stylish series of comedy whodunnitsJordan Erica WebberTue 28 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a boom time for mystery games, the Detective Grimoire series stands out for its style and sense of humour. The Mermaid Mask continues to build upon the formula laid down in Secret of the Swamp and polished in Tangle Tower, and while there is still room for further improvements this sequel is worth the seven years’ wait.This time, the casually competent Grimoire and his smart if sarcastic sidekick Sally have been summoned to a submarine to solve the locked-room murder of its captain, Magnus Mortuga. You click around the cluttered rooms of the vessel to hear the detectives’ comedic commentary and look for clues and – closer up – click and drag to move objects around for further examination or to solve a puzzle. (For those playing onNintendo Switch 2, the mouse controls are actually useful here, if not comfortable in the long run.)View image in fullscreenNever too taxing … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesPuzzles are never so taxing as to disrupt the flow: variations on “arrange these objects to satisfy some more-or-less apparent rules of logic” with stylistic wrapping. Your reward is generally an opened door and a new object to examine, which – importantly – you can then present to the various suspects.And here is the chewy centre of these games: the fully voice-acted conversations with a cast of colourful characters. I immediately lowered the volume of the music (which sadly doesn’t compare to Tangle Tower’s characterful soundtrack) to better hear the well-performed dialogue. Some of the suspects are more memorable than others, but the somewhat supernatural backdrop (and these games are all set in very much the same world) allows for archetypes not found elsewhere.View image in fullscreenColourful characters … The Mermaid Mask.Photograph: SFB GamesMadam Tadpole is buff, green-skinned, and appears to have gills. Mariana Moon is an older woman with an unnaturally keen sense of smell whose voice acting is cleverly muffled when she’s chewing on her pipe. Godric Gripp is a compass repairman with an anthropomorphised stick called Cornelius Cane, whose introduction involves an unavoidable shopfront interface the developers must have coded purely for this one laugh.These stylish moments are one of the more noticeable additions since Tangle Tower, with, for example, new 3D animations to illustrate the suspects’ recollections. But when it comes to solving the mysteries, they haven’t fixed what isn’t broken: as in Tangle Tower, and other deduction games such as the Golden Idol series and The Séance of Blake Manor, you form hypotheses by filling sentence blanks from a selection of nouns and verbs.The overall process is soothingly methodical: your inventory shows blank slots for objects you’ve yet to find, each topic addressed with a suspect gets a satisfying tick, and Grimoire and Sally inform you when you’ve uncovered enough to tackle each suspect’s individual mystery (in one instance I did experience a bug where this unlocked prematurely, but the developers are already fixing bugs raised by early players).Some players may find this completion percentage approach too formulaic, especially if they exhaust their current inventory and resort to pixel hunting to locate the rest. And the pacing does falter in the final chapter, where the game presents you with a more literal checklist to work through before you get to tie up each character’s loose ends and make your final accusation. But while the conclusion of The Mermaid Mask feels far more satisfying than that of Tangle Tower, these games are far more about the twisty journey and the laughs you have along the way.The Mermaid Mask is out now; £17.75Explore more on these topicsGamesPCNintendo SwitchNintendo Switch 2PlayStation 5NintendoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He made Damien Hirst look like a sideshow’: the bloodsplash horrors of Gunther von Hagens | Culture | The Guardian
description: The German scientist showman turned corpses into gruesome entertainment and scored a global hit – but he sidestepped the moral questions truly great art asks
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The German scientist showman turned corpses into gruesome entertainment and scored a global hit – but he sidestepped the moral questions truly great art asks
Content: ‘The art of horror is a race to the bottom’ … Gunther von Hagens with a preserved human corpse in his Body Worlds show in 2001.Photograph: Jockel Finck/APView image in fullscreen‘The art of horror is a race to the bottom’ … Gunther von Hagens with a preserved human corpse in his Body Worlds show in 2001.Photograph: Jockel Finck/APCulture‘He made Damien Hirst look like a sideshow’: the bloodsplash horrors of Gunther von HagensThe German scientist showman turned corpses into gruesome entertainment and scored a global hit – but he sidestepped the moral questions truly great art asksJonathan JonesTue 28 Jul 2026 04.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 04.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGunther von Hagens, the inventor of “plastination”, will be remembered as the man who killed off 1990s shock art. He certainly plastinated any reputation Damien Hirst had as a disturbing artist of mortality.When this German scientist turned showman made a popular bloodsplash around the world in the latter half of the 90s, Hirst was still pickling sheep, sharks and pigs and displaying them as philosophical specimens. Other artists, too, played with carnality and horror, from endoscopy videos to model landscapes filled with Nazi atrocities. But it was just art. Then along came Von Hagens with his Body Worlds exhibitions, using plastination to perfectly preserve dissected bodies. He did what Hirst and co never dared: he displayed actual human corpses as a kind of grisly but purportedly educational art object.Gunther von Hagens, creator of Body Worlds and plastination, dies aged 81Read moreEdmund Burke, the 18th-century politician and aesthetician, pointed out that if you told a theatre audience watching a tragic drama there was a public hanging outside, everyone would flock to the hanging. To put it another way, the art of horror is a race to the bottom. When Von Hagens offered the public real dead people to gawp at, opened up and preserved in the blood-red flesh, he drew global crowds in the millions, leaving the Hirst generation looking like an elite sideshow. He even staged a live, televised autopsy in London in 2002, reviving the kind of gory spectacle William Hogarth satirised in his print The Reward of Cruelty, which depicts the dissection of a hanged criminal.The difference is that Hogarth sees something monstrous in the cold eyes of the anatomists as they cut up a judicially killed man and even let a dog eat his entrails. That’s the difference between art and plastination. Von Hagens didn’t invite thoughts about mortality. He instead treated human flesh as cheap and meaningless material to be arranged in poses out of old anatomy books. In all honesty I found Body Worlds repellent.Von Hagens, however, had an impeccable pedigree for what he did: he was a professor with a long association with Germany’s prestigious Heidelberg University. And of course the frontier of art and science he exploited has a long and gruesome history. Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo both carried out their own dissections of human bodies. Michelangelo wanted to understand muscles in order to portray nude bodies better: surviving records of his anatomies are quite literally sketchy. Leonardo, however, had true scientific ambition and was years ahead of university doctors in his stunning drawings and notes that dig into every part of the human machine from the brain to the genitals, the foetus to the eye. His infinitely subtle observations make the body’s goriest secrets beautiful.A closer model for Von Hagens is Andrea Vesalius, the first “modern” anatomist whose 1543 book the Fabrica is illustrated with prints thought to have been made by a pupil of Titian. Its combination of sculptural poses and flayed horror has a lot in common with Body Worlds: in the frontispiece an avid (male) audience watch as Vesalius calmly cuts open a (female) corpse.View image in fullscreenProfessor Gunther Von Hagens unveils the man he previously publicly dissected at the Edinburgh festival fringe.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/the GuardianAfter that, the art of anatomy got increasingly “real” and disturbing. In the 18th and 19th centuries Italian art skills produced uncanny replicas of anatomised human bodies in wax, meticulously copying colours and textures, supposedly in the service of science. La Specola, the natural history museum of Florence, lets you visit its vast collection of these hyperreal eviscerated bodies to look at and learn from until you feel sick.Gunther von Hagens brought this tradition into our time but also made it seem too natural, as if death could be rationalised away. At La Specola, the weirdness is explicit – you know this is odd, macabre stuff to be looking at. Body Worlds has a false acceptance that treats death as nothing to get emotional about.This acceptance of mortality also has its artistic precedents, not least in the use of bones to create spectacular ossuaries in many parts of Europe. In the crypt of the church of Santa Maria della Concezione in Rome you can see the bones of thousands of Capuchin friars arranged in an artistic manner that might have made Ed Gein blush – there’s a grotto of skulls, a chamber of thigh bones. The Marquis de Sade was stunned. You leave with a sense of disgust and confusion, wondering why they did it, and why you went.At the opposite pole there is Rembrandt’sAnatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp, in which the body being dissected is seen as an infinite mystery, the pale ghost of us all. Artists, from Leonardo and Rembrandt to the young Hirst, have glimpsed the enigma of life in the relics of death. But Gunther von Hagens was no artist.Explore more on these topicsCultureExhibitionsMuseumsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A family tour de France: cycling and camping in Normandy with two toddlers | Normandy holidays | The Guardian
description: Ebikes with child seats – plus idyllic campsites and pit stops en route – turn a five-day ride on the car-free Véloscénic into a wonderful family holiday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ebikes with child seats – plus idyllic campsites and pit stops en route – turn a five-day ride on the car-free Véloscénic into a wonderful family holiday
Content: Ellie Fazan cycled through the verdant former province of Perche.Photograph: Ellie FazanView image in fullscreenEllie Fazan cycled through the verdant former province of Perche.Photograph: Ellie FazanNormandy holidaysA family tour de France: cycling and camping in Normandy with two toddlersEbikes with child seats – plus idyllic campsites and pit stops en route – turn a five-day ride on the car-free Véloscénic into a wonderful family holidayEllie FazanTue 28 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.“Are you mad?” says a fellow guest over dinner at our campsite. “I heard you’re here on a long-distance cycle ride with your toddlers.”The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.I am in Orne, a region in Normandy, with my sister Issy and our three-year-old sons, Sid and Ralph. The landscape folds around us in green-over-green – hedgerow, oak, mossy manor wall – then opens into meadows where Percheron horses graze, knee-deep in wildflowers. Deer leap from the bocage.Cidreandpoiréhave been pressed here since the middle ages. The villages are sandy stone, blue- and green-shuttered; roses against theboulangerie.Map of towns mentioned in NormandyAnd yes, we are biking through it with the boys in child seats on the back, camping along the way in places found through theFrance Vélo Tourismewebsite. Over five days, we’re travelling 130km (80 miles) from Rémalard-en-Perche to Domfront, mostly along theVéloscénic– a 450kmvoie verte(a “greenway” car-free route) that runs from Mont-Saint-Michel to Paris – but looping off it to explore the fairytale chateaux and villages of the Perche, a historic former province. Issy is intrepid and a serious cyclist (the Lycra kind) but the best I can say is I cycle Sid to nursery, and I haven’t slept under canvas since, well, Glastonbury. So two or three hours’ cycling a day is probably enough …Slightly rumpled from the overnight ferry to Caen from Portsmouth, we pull intoForest View, a campsite three miles south of Rémalard. Jean-Louis from the local bike hire shop is waiting with our ebikes. He’d insisted. I’d resisted: they can’t carry both a child seat and panniers so we’ll rely on Jean-Louis and a patchwork of kindly hosts to move our bags between stops. We test our bike legs onLa Route Royale, an intermediate-level 25km circular route, and within an hour of leaving the campsite, climbing the hill to the pretty church of Moutiers-au-Perche for lunch, I realise Jean-Louis was right. The ebikes are the difference between a holiday and a heart attack.View image in fullscreenThere were plenty of stops so the kids could stretch their legs.Photograph: Ellie FazanThe route is flat, but to really see the Perche you have to venture off it, and once you do, the land begins to roll and hills come without warning. The boys, strapped in behind us, are not light. But they are also loving it: pointing, laughing, bursting into Old MacDonald every time they see a horse, cow, tractor or sheep. It’s going so well that Issy and I are debating another few hours cycling or even a cider tasting on the way home, when a pause in the singing alerts us to the fact that both children have been lulled to sleep, heads wobbling from side to side, and so we take them back to the campsite to rest.Graham Allen bought Forest View three years ago and built wooden camping pods especially for cyclists after watching them arrive “laden like donkeys”. Inside there’s a cosy bed and a skylight that we watch the stars through. Across the field there are hot showers. And in the informal restaurant, more like a kitchen/living room, home-cooked food at a shared table. Along France’s greenways, the number of Accueil Vélo accredited stops (accommodation for cyclists that offer breakfast, basic repair kits and help with luggage, among other things) has tripled since 2019.After some seriously good sleep, eggs on toast and frantic sorting of stuff, we spend the next day on theDîtes-le Avec des Fleursloop: through the oak forest of Réno-Valdieu and past the Manoir de la Moussetière, one of the fortified manor houses typical of the Perche. Even on the open roads, there are just a handful of cars, and some steep climbs reward us with wonderful views. The freewheel back down leaves the boys shrieking with delight. At La Chapelle-Montligeon, a church rises out of the fields, and here we picnic on the bank of a lake.double quotation markThe landscape folds around us in green-over-green, then opens into meadows where Percheron horses graze, knee-deep in wildflowersDenis Hurtaud was also cycling this route when he took a detour from the greenway and stumbled onCafé de la Placein the sleepy village of Courgeon. “The terrace was full of yellow flowers and there were old-fashioned oilcloths on the tables. Dappled sunlight fell across the courtyard,” he says. Over lunch, he overheard the owner say he was planning to retire and, by the end of the meal, he had decided to buy it. Today it is a bistro, village shop, bike repair station, art gallery, music venue and a lifeline to locals.It’s Accueil Vélo-accredited too. No shower yet, but we pitch our tent in the garden and Denis has saved us some dinner. We sit at a long table in the last of the light, doves cooing in the church tower, eating chicken cooked in cider, a Perche speciality. Locals drift in and out. A neighbour’s child arrives with a plate of warm crepes for us.The next day, we ride 8km up the greenway to Mortagne-au-Perche for the market. The queue for the season’s first strawberries goes around the block. A man turns dripping chickens on a spit. The radishes are obscenely pink, the asparagus oh so plump. At the Bar du Marché, locals drink coffee and scratch scratchcards in the sunshine. We join them. Our boys are knackered; both have absolute meltdowns and it’s hard work getting them back on the bikes, so we head directly to Carrouges, where we are to camp at theParc Naturel Régional Normandie-Maine, in an orchard behind the moated, red-brickChâteau de Carrouges.View image in fullscreenPretty Moutiers-au-Perche was an early lunch stop.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyThe Parc is Accueil Vélo too, but the woman at the office says only five or six tents pitch up a year and we have the orchard to ourselves. Just us, a roast chicken and some baguettes, with the kids playing dinosaurs in long grass. Once Sid is snoring I pour myself acidre– from local apples – and write. It is so quiet you can hear the flapping of birds’ wings. Then the storm comes. I’m a tent pole down (Glastonbury?) and the rain hits canvas like gravel. I lie clinging to Sid as the thunder tears the sky open above us, questioning every life choice that has led me to a walled orchard in Normandy with a small child and half a tent.double quotation markJean-Louis says it’s the most beautiful place in the world and I don’t disagreeBy morning, the rain has stopped. The orchard glistens. Issy emerges from the next-door tent having not slept either. We push on through the spa town of Bagnoles-de-l’Orne to Domfront, a town on a rocky outcrop dominated by a medieval keep. The sun bursts out again and the kids race up the ruined stones. Our home for the night is theCabane des Deux Chênes, a handbuilt cabin on stilts between two old oaks. A secret room for the children in the rafters. A Nordic bath on the terrace, a hug after the rain.On our last morning, we stop at theFerme de l’Yonnière, Jérôme Forget’s farm just down the road, where he makes AOP Poiré Domfront. Pear trees take decades to mature, Jerome tells us, which is why most people stopped planting them, and whypoiréwent out of fashion. But he has planted a thousand. Next spring, he’ll start taking cyclists, too.Back at the cabane, Jean-Louis comes to pick us up in his van and drives us, talking in French the whole way: about the pear trees and horses and the lanes we have just cycled. The most beautiful place in the world, he says, and I don’t disagree. Against the odds, it’s been a brilliant family holiday and Issy and I are already planning to come back next summer and do the whole thing. Perhaps we are mad after all.The trip wasprovided byOrne Tourism, with travelto France byBrittany Ferries. Bike hirewithLes Vélos Perchéscosts €35(£30) a day. AtForest Viewa pod sleeping two costs from £38 per night;campsite pitches start at £25per night.Cabane des Deux Chênessleeps 2-4 and costs from£138per a night.Explore more on these topicsNormandy holidaysFrance holidaysCycling holidaysCamping holidaysFamily holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tears at dinner time: the science to rolling out fresh pasta | Chefs | The Guardian
description: Tearing is a common problem with pasta dough say our experts. Culprits include the wrong type of flour, cold dough – or it could even boil down to the size of your egg
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Tearing is a common problem with pasta dough say our experts. Culprits include the wrong type of flour, cold dough – or it could even boil down to the size of your egg
Content: When using a pasta machine, it is vital to practise the art of patience.Photograph: Yasin Caglayan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhen using a pasta machine, it is vital to practise the art of patience.Photograph: Yasin Caglayan/Getty ImagesKitchen aideChefsTears at dinner time: the science to rolling out fresh pastaTearing is a common problem with pasta dough say our experts. Culprits include the wrong type of flour, cold dough – or it could even boil down to the size of your eggAnna BerrillTue 28 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen making fresh pasta, why does the dough sometimes tear when rolling, and other times not?Thomas, by email“I’m sorry to hear your pasta is rippy,” sympathisesJacob Kenedy, chef-patron ofBocca di Lupoin London, who is teaming up with fellow chef Merlin Labron-Johnson to celebrate the Italian midsummer holidayferragostowith two feasts in Somerset next month. Assuming Thomas is rolling an egg pasta dough in a pasta machine, there are a number of possible explanations. First, Kenedy says, he might be using the wrong type of flour (“use 00 flour”), the dough might be too cold (“use it at room temperature”) or too dry (“it should be supple, like Play-Doh”). Naz Hassan, head chef ofOrnellaandLupa, both in London, adds that the latter might be down to the size of the egg(s) Thomas is using: “One egg to 100g of 00 flour is the basic pasta dough recipe, but that will vary depending on the size of your egg,” he says. Of course, some people prefer to use just the yolk, and if that applies to Thomas, Hassan suggests thinking about maybe adding the egg white, too: “It has the structure that allows pasta to have the stretchiness it deserves.”But, in true Goldilocks style, a dough that is too wet might also spell trouble, Kenedy says: “I like my pasta dough wet enough to roll by hand – it gives a more elastic mouthfeel – which means, if I roll it in a machine, it sticks slightly to the roller and may rip.” The fix? Laminate the dough thoroughly and perhaps use “the finest dusting” of flour until the dough passes smoothly through the pasta machine. “Then make sure to roll that flour in, so the outside of the pasta isn’t dusty,” Kenedy adds.As in life, time out is also important. “Like bread and any byproduct of flour, you need to rest the dough to allow the gluten structure to relax and bind together,” says Hassan, who does this overnight, while Kenedy prefers to rest his dough, covered and at room temperature, for half an hour to an hour after kneading. In fact, Kenedy reckons that poor gluten development is the most likely suspect of Thomas’s pasta plight: “Laminate the pasta many, many times at the thickest setting,” he says. “Roll, fold in half, roll again, fold in three, roll again – at least 12 times – until the pasta is extremely silky-smooth, before rolling it any thinner.”The rolling is also where Thomas really needs to practise the art of patience, so get some music on and avoid any big jumps in thickness (AKA clicks of the pasta machine wheel). Hassan says: “If you try to force the dough through the machine or skip one of the steps – going straight from setting number three to setting one, say – that will create ridges on the sides of the dough.” And that, in turn, can cause those rips. “Obviously, it’s hard to know which of these reasons it might be without standing next to Thomas in the kitchen,” Hassan adds, but then, having a proper chef alongside would most likely just add to Thomas’s pasta pressure.Got a culinary dilemma?
